Boehm-Bawerk answered that interest is not theft at all but payment for something else the saver supplies to the production process. What is the saver actually being paid to do?
context: Boehm-Bawerk's answer to Marx: production takes TIME, and someone must release present resources so that future output can exist. That someone is the saver, and interest is the market price paid to persuade him to wait. It is not stolen from the worker; it is compensation for the postponement of consumption. Source: Capitalism Magazine, Ebeling on Boehm-Bawerk (https://capitalismmagazine.com/2016/02/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-refuter-marxism-theorist-economics-capitalism/).

question: In Positive Theory of Capital (1889) Boehm-Bawerk lists three separate reasons a person would value a good in hand today more than the identical good delivered a year from now. He called these his three grounds for what?
context: The three grounds Boehm-Bawerk offers in Volume 2 -- expectation of future prosperity, systematic underestimation of future wants, and the technical superiority of longer production processes -- are his positive theory of INTEREST specifically, the price the market pays for the postponement of consumption. Rent, profit, and wages are separately theorised elsewhere in the Austrian tradition. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: The first volume of Boehm-Bawerk's 1884 treatise -- a critical history of every existing theory -- sorted rival explanations of interest into three main families. One family said interest is what capital pays because capital PRODUCES; a second said interest is STOLEN from labor (Marx); a third said interest is the reward for POSTPONING consumption. The third family had a specific 19th-century name attached to it. Which English economist did Boehm-Bawerk identify with that abstinence account?
context: Nassau William Senior (1790-1864), Oxford's first Drummond Professor of Political Economy, is the name Boehm-Bawerk associates in Volume 1 with the abstinence theory of interest -- the view that interest rewards the saver for the self-denial of postponing consumption. Ricardo and Mill worked mainly within cost-of-production and productivity accounts; Marshall came later. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Boehm-Bawerk's positive account of interest starts from a simple observation about how goods actually get made in a real economy -- a fisherman weaves a net before he catches fish, a farmer builds a plough before he plants grain, a factory tools its assembly line before shipping a car. Which single feature of the production process is he asking his reader to notice?
context: The insight the whole Positive Theory rests on: production is a process across TIME, not an instant. Because the saver must release resources today for output that will only exist next month or next year, and because people prefer present to future goods, someone must be paid a premium to bridge the wait. Interest is the market price of that time gap. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Boehm-Bawerk gives interest three separate grounds in Volume 2. Ground one is that people expect the future to be more prosperous than the present, so a future good is worth less to them now. Ground two is that people are shortsighted and systematically underestimate their future wants. Ground three was the most controversial, because it implies positive interest rates would exist even if grounds one and two failed. What does ground three appeal to?
answer: The technical superiority of longer production processes
choices: The technical superiority of longer production processes
The moral virtue of self-denial by the saver
The bargaining power of capitalists over workers
The state's legal enforcement of debt contracts
context: Ground three -- the technical superiority of longer, more roundabout production methods -- is Boehm-Bawerk's most disputed claim. It says that even without shortsightedness or expected prosperity, more roundabout methods yield more output per unit input, so waiting is intrinsically worth something. The American economist Frank Fetter later argued ground two (time preference) does all the real work and ground three is redundant; John Bates Clark defended a rival pure-productivity account. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: After Boehm-Bawerk's death, an American economist argued that ground two alone -- people's systematic preference for present over future goods -- did all the real work in the positive theory, and that the technical roundaboutness ground was redundant. Which economist pressed that streamlining critique of Boehm-Bawerk?
context: Frank A. Fetter (1863-1949), an American Austrian, argued that time preference (ground two) is the whole explanation of interest and that Boehm-Bawerk's technical-productivity ground three is dispensable. John Bates Clark went the other direction and defended a pure productivity-of-capital theory; Irving Fisher tried to combine productivity and impatience; Knut Wicksell developed the natural-rate concept in a different direction. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Suppose a modern socialist argues that interest income is unearned because the saver contributes no labor -- the money simply sits and grows. Using the reasoning move Boehm-Bawerk pressed against Marx in 1889, how would an Austrian answer directly, without invoking risk or entrepreneurship?
answer: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
choices: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
The saver takes on the risk that the borrower will default, and interest is the premium compensating that risk
The saver exercises entrepreneurial judgment about which projects deserve capital, and interest is the reward for that judgment
The saver enjoys legal protection under contract law, and interest is the state-enforced return on lawful lending
context: The clean Boehm-Bawerkian move: production takes time; someone must release today's resources for tomorrow's output; that release is what the saver contributes; the interest payment is the market price of that contribution. Risk, entrepreneurship, and legal enforcement are separate real phenomena but they answer different questions -- this specific question is about where interest itself comes from, and the answer is time-preference plus waiting. Source: Capitalism Magazine, Ebeling on Boehm-Bawerk (https://capitalismmagazine.com/2016/02/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-refuter-marxism-theorist-economics-capitalism/).

question: Consider a modern central bank that pushes interest rates to zero to stimulate the economy. A Boehm-Bawerkian would say the interest rate is not an arbitrary policy dial but a market signal reflecting something real about how people trade present and future goods. Which specific price does the ABCT tradition, building on Boehm-Bawerk, say the artificial-zero-rate distorts?
answer: The price of time itself -- of releasing present resources for future output
choices: The price of time itself -- of releasing present resources for future output
The nominal exchange rate between the dollar and other currencies
The wage rate paid to workers in the export sector
The retail price of consumer goods purchased with credit
context: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory, developed by Mises and Hayek on the Boehm-Bawerkian foundation, treats the interest rate as the price of time -- the price coordinating how much of today's resources get released for tomorrow's output through more roundabout production. Forcing that price down artificially misleads entrepreneurs into starting more roundabout projects than real savings can complete; when the bust arrives the malinvested projects have to be liquidated. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: In 1962 the University of Chicago Press published Milton Friedman's most influential single volume outside monetary economics. Grown from lectures he had given at Wabash College in 1956, it sold well over half a million copies. What was the book's title?
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
context: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962). Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo25839091.html.

question: Capitalism and Freedom's core argument links two kinds of liberty in a specific one-way conditional relationship. What is the relationship the book argues for?
answer: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
choices: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
Political freedom always suffices for economic freedom
Economic freedom is irrelevant to political freedom
Political freedom is a sufficient condition for economic freedom
context: Friedman's move: once government controls the means of employment, the media, and the currency, dissent cannot be sustained -- the dissenter cannot eat. Economic freedom is necessary though not sufficient for political freedom. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 1.

question: Capitalism and Freedom proposed several policies that seemed eccentric in 1962 and later became mainstream US practice. Which of the following was NOT proposed in the 1962 book?
context: Friedman proposed vouchers, NIT, all-volunteer army, floating exchange rates, and drug decriminalization in the 1962 book. Universal single-payer health insurance is the Canadian model and was not part of Friedman's proposal package. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962).

question: The US ended peacetime military conscription and moved to what Friedman had recommended a decade earlier -- an all-volunteer force. In which year did the last man be drafted?
context: Congress let the induction authority expire in 1973, ending the American peacetime draft. Friedman had proposed abolishing the draft in Capitalism and Freedom (1962). Source: history.army.mil (draft history).

question: In 1980 Milton Friedman and his wife Rose Friedman published a companion book that appeared simultaneously as a ten-episode PBS television series filmed on location in Hong Kong, Chicago, and Washington. What was that book and series called?
choices: There's No Such Thing as a Free Lunch
context: Milton + Rose Friedman, Free to Choose: A Personal Statement (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1980), with companion PBS series in ten episodes. It was the best-selling nonfiction book of 1980 in the United States. Source: pbs.org (Free to Choose archive).

question: The Free to Choose TV series was filmed in ten episodes on location in Hong Kong, Chicago, and Washington. Where did the companion book rank on US book sales for its year of publication?
context: Free to Choose was the best-selling nonfiction book of 1980 in the United States. The PBS series reached millions of viewers and became a curriculum staple. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998), memoir chapter on Free to Choose.

question: Free to Choose was translated into more than a dozen languages and, per Friedman's memoirs, was smuggled into a specific bloc of countries in samizdat translations, where it influenced later economic reformers. Which region was that?
answer: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
choices: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
context: Free to Choose was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in samizdat translations. Vaclav Klaus later credited the book as an intellectual source of Czechoslovakia's post-1989 economic reforms. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The school-voucher proposal now most closely associated with Capitalism and Freedom actually first appeared as a standalone Friedman essay published in 1955, five years earlier. Which essay was that?
answer: The Role of Government in Education
choices: The Role of Government in Education
The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education' (in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest, Rutgers UP 1955). The voucher proposal was collected into Capitalism and Freedom (1962). Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: In August 1971 President Nixon closed the US gold window and let the dollar float, ending the Bretton Woods fixed-exchange-rate system. Friedman had been recommending this move since 1953 in his essay 'The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates.' What did the resulting international monetary regime become?
answer: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
choices: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 closing of the gold window ended dollar-gold convertibility; the international regime shifted to floating major-currency exchange rates by 1973. Friedman had argued the case since 1953. Source: Friedman, 'The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates' (1953, in Essays in Positive Economics).

question: Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom is remembered as much for what it proposed as for how many of those proposals eventually happened. Which one-sentence summary best captures its historical significance?
answer: Many proposals that seemed eccentric in 1962 later became mainstream policy
choices: Many proposals that seemed eccentric in 1962 later became mainstream policy
None of its proposals were ever tried anywhere
It advocated returning to a nineteenth-century gold standard exclusively
It called for immediate abolition of all federal agencies
context: The all-volunteer military (1973), floating exchange rates (1971-73), and state-level voucher programs (1990s-2020s) all trace to Capitalism and Freedom proposals that were dismissed as eccentric at the time. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: A Habsburg-Galicia-born clerk in the press department of the Austrian prime minister's office publishes a book on economics in 1871 whose German title is 'Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre'; the University of Vienna gives him a chair two years later. The book founds what is soon called the Austrian School of economics. Who is he?
context: Carl Menger (1840-1921), the founder of the Austrian School, published 'Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre' (Principles of Economics) in 1871 while still working in the prime minister's press office; the book won him a Vienna chair in 1873. Wieser and Boehm-Bawerk were his students; Mises a generation later still. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger: The Founding of the Austrian School' (https://mises.org/articles-interest/carl-menger-founding-austrian-school).

question: The 1870s saw the same core idea -- that a good's value comes from the subjective usefulness of the LAST unit consumed, not from the labor put in -- worked out independently by three economists in three different countries: Carl Menger in Vienna, William Stanley Jevons in England, and Leon Walras in Lausanne. What is this simultaneous burst usually called?
context: Menger's Principles (1871), Jevons's Theory of Political Economy (1871), and Walras's Elements of Pure Economics (1874) all worked out marginal-utility subjective value theory within a few years of each other, an event later known as the 'marginal revolution.' The Keynesian revolution came in the 1930s; monetarism was Milton Friedman's later counter to it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginal revolution' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_revolution).

question: In 1876 Emperor Franz Joseph asked the newest professor of political economy at Vienna to serve as tutor to his seventeen-year-old only son, the heir to the Habsburg throne. The professor spent the next two years travelling with the boy through Europe and the British Isles, teaching political economy from his own notes. Who was the pupil?
context: Menger tutored Crown Prince Rudolf of Habsburg -- the only son of Emperor Franz Joseph and heir to the throne -- from 1876 to 1878. Franz Ferdinand was Rudolf's cousin and the eventual heir after Rudolf's death; Karl I became emperor in 1916; Otto was a different Habsburg. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger, Crown Prince Rudolf, and the Marginal Revolution That Never Was' (https://mises.org/mises-wire/carl-menger-crown-prince-rudolf-and-marginal-revolution-never-was).

question: Menger's teaching at Vienna trained two second-generation Austrians who between them wrote almost the whole next chapter of the school -- capital theory, the theory of imputation, the refutation of Marx. They were also brothers-in-law, having married two sisters. Who were these two Menger students?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
context: Menger's two most important direct students were Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk (capital theory, Marx refutation) and Friedrich von Wieser (imputation, opportunity cost); the two were brothers-in-law, having married sisters. Mises and Hayek were the third and fourth generation; Kirzner and Rothbard the fifth; Schumpeter and Bauer were students of Boehm-Bawerk not Menger. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Menger did NOT come to economics through a mathematics or engineering degree. His formal training was in law: he studied at Prague and Vienna and took a doctorate in jurisprudence in 1867 at the oldest university in Poland. At which university did he take that law doctorate?
context: Menger took his doctorate in jurisprudence at Jagiellonian University in Krakow in 1867, then joined the Austrian civil service. Charles University in Prague was where he studied earlier; Humboldt in Berlin was the leading German university of the era but not his; Vienna was where he later held his chair. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Menger's civil-service job before he was famous involved digesting daily commodity-market reports for the Austrian prime minister's press office. That routine work produced the founding insight of the Austrian school: the textbook classical account of price -- that a good's price reflects the labor put into it -- did not match what actual traders did. Menger's book replaced the labor account with a different starting point. What did he say determines price?
answer: The subjective usefulness of the last unit to each individual consumer
choices: The subjective usefulness of the last unit to each individual consumer
The average number of labor hours embodied in the good
The long-run natural rate of return on invested capital
The state's ability to enforce a fair-price statute
context: Menger's Principles (1871) replaced the classical labor-cost account of value with marginal utility -- price emerges from individual consumers each valuing the LAST unit of a good by its subjective usefulness to them. Labor-hours-embodied was Marx's version; natural-rate-of-return was Ricardo's cost-of-production account; fair-price statutes were medieval scholastic doctrine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Principles of Economics (Menger book)' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book)).

question: In January 1889 -- eleven years after Menger's tutoring of Crown Prince Rudolf ended -- Rudolf shot his young mistress Baroness Mary Vetsera and then himself at a Habsburg hunting lodge. The incident, known to historians by the lodge's name, destroyed the Habsburg succession plan. At which lodge?
context: Rudolf and Vetsera died at the Mayerling hunting lodge on the night of 29-30 January 1889; the murder-suicide displaced Rudolf's cousin Franz Ferdinand as heir (who was himself assassinated at Sarajevo in 1914, triggering the First World War). Menger, deeply affected by his former pupil's death, withdrew further into scholarship. Schoenbrunn was the imperial summer palace; Ischl the emperor's holiday town; Belvedere Franz Ferdinand's Vienna residence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf%2C_Crown_Prince_of_Austria).

question: Menger's son, born in 1902 to the founder of the Austrian school of economics, became a famous mathematician in his own right -- a member of the Vienna Circle, a contributor to dimension theory, and the man after whom a well-known 3-D fractal is named. What is the fractal called?
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) -- son of the Austrian-school founder -- was a mathematician of the Vienna Circle who defined the Menger sponge, the 3-D fractal you get by iteratively removing the central subcube of every cube. The Sierpinski triangle (Waclaw Sierpinski, 1915) and Cantor dust (Georg Cantor, 1883) are older; the Mandelbrot set (Benoit Mandelbrot, 1980) is later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Karl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Menger).

question: In 1892 Menger published an essay -- second in reputation only to the 1871 Principles -- explaining how money emerges without any government or committee designing it: traders in a barter economy notice that some commodities are more widely accepted than others and converge on the most SALEABLE one as the general medium of exchange. What was the essay's German title?
context: Menger's 1892 essay 'Ueber den Ursprung des Geldes' ('On the Origins of Money') is his second most-cited work and the Austrian foundation for the theory that money emerges spontaneously from barter as traders converge on the most SALEABLE commodity. 'Untersuchungen ueber die Methode' (1883) was his methodological work; 'Der natuerliche Werth' (1889) was Wieser's; 'Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems' (1896) was Boehm-Bawerk's Marx refutation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Menger built one of the largest private economics libraries in 19th-century Europe. After his death in 1921 his family sold the whole collection abroad, where it survives today as the 'Menger Library' at a major university. Which university now houses the collection?
context: Menger's private economics library, one of the largest in Europe, was sold by his heirs to Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo after his 1921 death; the collection is still catalogued there as the 'Menger Library.' Harvard, Cambridge (England), and the University of Chicago all built major economics libraries in the same era but not from Menger's holdings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: In April 1980, after the 1979 Iranian Revolution drove world crude prices from $15 per barrel to over $35, a US president signed a law imposing an excise tax on the difference between the market price of domestic crude oil and a lower government-set base price. Who signed the law?
context: The Crude Oil Windfall Profit Tax Act was signed in Carter's last year in office. Reagan campaigned against the tax in the 1980 election and eventually got it repealed in 1988. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: The 1980 Crude Oil Windfall Profit Tax was pitched to the public as a way to recover unfair 'windfall' profits US oil companies were reaping from a specific 1979 event. Which event?
answer: The Iranian Revolution and the second oil crisis
choices: The Iranian Revolution and the second oil crisis
The collapse of the Bretton Woods system
The Yom Kippur War oil embargo
context: The 1979 revolution overthrew the Shah and disrupted Iranian oil exports; world crude went from about $15/barrel in 1978 to over $35 by 1981. The Carter administration argued domestic producers should not keep the price increase as pure profit. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1979_oil_crisis.

question: A 1990 Congressional Research Service report estimated what the 1980 Carter Windfall Profits Tax actually did to US domestic oil production during the 1980s. What did the report find?
answer: Domestic production fell by roughly 3 to 6 percent and imports rose by similar amounts
choices: Domestic production fell by roughly 3 to 6 percent and imports rose by similar amounts
Domestic production rose by roughly 30 percent
Domestic production was unaffected either way
Domestic production fell by roughly 50 percent
context: The tax raised the effective cost of producing each additional barrel of US oil, so marginal wells were not drilled. The country supposedly worried about energy independence produced less domestic oil as a result. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: A Texas senator in 1985 complains that the Windfall Profits Tax has cut jobs in his state's oil patch. A Bastiatian economist points to a specific reasoning move about the barrels that never came out of the ground. Which move is he pressing?
answer: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue -- the undrilled barrels and unhired workers are the unseen cost
choices: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue -- the undrilled barrels and unhired workers are the unseen cost
The tax is a Keynesian aggregate-demand stimulus that raises drilling investment
The tax is a Coasean bargaining solution that internalizes drilling externalities
The tax is a Pigovian correction that equates marginal social benefit and marginal social cost
context: A tax on the return to production at the margin reduces production at the margin. Applied Bastiat: the seen is oil-company profit recovery for the public; the unseen is domestic supply that never enters the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: The Carter Windfall Profits Tax was formally repealed in 1988, having collected almost nothing in its final years. Which president signed the repeal?
context: By the mid-1980s world oil prices had collapsed to below the tax's base-price threshold, so it was collecting almost nothing. Reagan had campaigned against the tax in 1980 and the repeal completed a signature deregulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: Whenever a modern 'windfall tax' is proposed -- on banks in 2008, on oil companies in 2022, on drug companies in 2020, or the UK's May 2022 Energy Profits Levy under Rishi Sunak -- a specific Bastiatian question resurfaces. Which question?
answer: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
choices: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
What is the highest tax rate the affected industry can bear before bankruptcy?
How does the tax score under the Congressional Budget Office static model?
How much revenue will the tax collect in its first fiscal year?
context: The Bastiat pattern: measure the seen benefit against the unseen response. Any tax on the reward for producing during a shortage removes some of the incentive to produce during the crisis when society most needs it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Windfall_tax.

question: On June 24, 2009 President Obama signed a federal program offering car buyers a $3,500-$4,500 rebate for trading in a working older vehicle, provided the trade-in was destroyed by a specific method. Which method destroyed the engines?
answer: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
choices: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
Draining the fuel tank and towing the car to a landfill for compaction
Removing and melting the catalytic converter, then junking the shell
Shipping the vehicle intact to a licensed scrapyard for parts recovery
context: The mandate that engines be seized with sodium silicate (liquid glass) was written to keep the trade-ins from being resold as running cars; some 690,000 running vehicles were destroyed this way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Allowance_Rebate_System.

question: The 2009 federal trade-in program is best known by its popular nickname; its statutory name was the Car Allowance Rebate System (CARS Act). What is its popular name?
context: Signed June 24 2009, the program ran July-August 2009 and burned through its $3B appropriation faster than expected. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Allowance_Rebate_System.

question: Cash for Clunkers is the textbook 21st-century application of one particular 1850 Bastiat argument, because the program deliberately destroyed usable stock to justify a subsidy for new production. Which Bastiat argument is it the modern worked example of?
choices: The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: Bastiat's broken-window: destruction of a usable good is not creation. Cash for Clunkers spent $3B destroying about 690,000 usable cars to make the subsidized new-car sale look like fresh economic activity. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: Under Cash for Clunkers roughly 690,000 running vehicles were destroyed, falling largely in the price range low-income and student buyers actually shop in ($1,500-$4,500 blue-book). What visible price-effect appeared in the year AFTER the program ended?
context: Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index for 2009-10 showed a roughly 10% jump in used-car prices, pricing out the very households the auto-stimulus was said to help. Source: manheim.com/used-vehicle-value-index (2010 press releases).

question: A 2013 Brookings Institution evaluation of Cash for Clunkers by Ted Gayer and Emily Parker made one specific negative finding about the program's headline sales gain: most of the 'new' sales would have happened within six to nine months anyway. What did the study call this effect?
context: Gayer & Parker (Brookings, October 2013) estimated the program pulled forward about 380,000 vehicles, generated no long-run net jobs, and produced CO2 savings at $91-$301 per ton -- well above the EPA's own social cost of carbon. Source: brookings.edu/articles/cash-for-clunkers-an-evaluation-of-the-car-allowance-rebate-system.

question: Cash for Clunkers was administered under one specific US federal department, which set the eligibility rules and processed the destruction certifications. Which department ran the program?
context: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, inside DOT, administered the CARS Act rebate and destruction certification; final DOT figures put new-vehicle sales under the program at 677,842. Source: nhtsa.gov/cars-allowance-rebate-system.

question: In the Bastiat framing of Cash for Clunkers, the SEEN benefit is the shiny new car in the buyer's driveway. Name the UNSEEN victims Austrian and Chicago critics kept pointing at.
answer: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
choices: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
Auto-parts manufacturers whose supply contracts came under EPA review
Insurance companies whose collision policies subsidized the rebate
Foreign auto brands excluded from the eligibility criteria
context: Destroying 690,000 vehicles in the $1,500-$4,500 range is destroying exactly the price band low-income buyers actually shop; used-car prices rose accordingly. This is Bastiat's UNSEEN victim: the low-income family that no longer finds a cheap running car. Source: cato.org/commentary/cash-clunkers-textbook-example.

question: Cash for Clunkers, argued Austrian and Chicago critics, is the 21st-century worked example of a book-length restatement of Bastiat published in 1946 by an American journalist. Which 1946 book anticipated the whole critique?
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is the seen/unseen method in modern American English; every 21st-century commentator applying it to Cash for Clunkers is applying Hazlitt's chapter on public-works make-work. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: In the Bastiat framing, Cash for Clunkers' single largest UNSEEN cost is not the cars destroyed or the used-car buyers priced out, but a broader resource-allocation loss. What is that loss?
answer: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
choices: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
The additional carbon emissions from the mandated new-car manufacturing
The regulatory-compliance staff the auto dealers had to hire to process claims
The tax revenue foregone on the salvage value of the destroyed trade-ins
context: Every $3B of federal spending had to come from a taxpayer or a lender; that money's alternative use is the Bastiat UNSEEN. The seen is the DOT sales figure; the unseen is the private consumption and investment that never happened. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: In 1977 three men founded a libertarian think tank in San Francisco that later moved to Washington DC and became a major public-choice institutional hub. Which trio founded it?
answer: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
choices: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
William Buckley, Milton Friedman, and Barry Goldwater
James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Douglass North
Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, and Wilhelm Ropke
context: Crane served as founding president, Koch was the principal early funder, and Rothbard was the intellectual leader. The institute relocated to Washington DC in 1981. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute takes its name from a series of 1720-1723 political-philosophy essays whose authors used the pen name of a Roman republican. Who wrote the essays?
choices: John Locke and John Stuart Mill
context: 'Cato's Letters' were published in London and reprinted heavily in the American colonies, where they influenced the founders. Hamilton and Madison wrote The Federalist Papers as Publius, a different pen-name project. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato%27s_Letters.

question: In 1981 the Cato Institute's founding intellectual leader was pushed out after a bitter dispute with the co-founders over strategy and personnel. He responded by founding a rival think tank in 1982 with Lew Rockwell. Who was he, and what did he found?
answer: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
James Buchanan, who founded the Center for Study of Public Choice
Milton Friedman, who founded the Free To Choose Network
Friedrich Hayek, who founded the Mont Pelerin Society
context: The Mises Institute (Auburn, Alabama, 1982) took a more radical Austrian direction than Cato, which pursued a Washington-focused policy engagement. The split defined two wings of the modern American libertarian movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: One economist chaired the Cato Institute from 1985 until his death in 2011, having previously served as a member of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers. Who was he?
context: Niskanen was best known for his 1971 book 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government,' a foundational public-choice analysis of bureaucratic behavior. His long chairmanship shaped Cato's public-choice orientation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: In 2012 the Cato Institute became the subject of a specific legal dispute among its founding funders that briefly threatened its independence. What happened?
answer: Charles and David Koch sued Cato in a fight over board control; the case was settled and Cato remained independent
choices: Charles and David Koch sued Cato in a fight over board control; the case was settled and Cato remained independent
The US Department of Justice charged Cato with tax fraud; the case was dismissed
The Ludwig von Mises Institute sued Cato for trademark infringement over the name 'Cato'
Congress subpoenaed Cato's donor list under the Foreign Agents Registration Act
context: The dispute concerned Cato's board structure. Under the settlement, Ed Crane was succeeded as president by former BB&T CEO John Allison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute is often compared with two earlier libertarian institutions -- the Foundation for Economic Education (1946) and the Mont Pelerin Society (1947). What was Cato's distinctive institutional focus that differentiated it from those two?
answer: Day-to-day policy influence in Washington -- Congressional testimony, staffer events, and studies aimed at real legislation
choices: Day-to-day policy influence in Washington -- Congressional testimony, staffer events, and studies aimed at real legislation
General-public educational outreach through pamphlets and lectures
Private scholarly networks meeting biennially in Swiss mountain resorts
Formal academic training programs granting master's and doctoral degrees
context: The Foundation for Economic Education (Leonard Read, 1946) focused on general educational outreach; the Mont Pelerin Society (Hayek, 1947) organized scholarly networks. Cato uniquely aimed at the real-time DC policy process. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute's flagship academic outlet publishes work by James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, Friedrich Hayek, and other public-choice and Austrian-tradition scholars. What is the journal called?
choices: The Journal of Law and Economics
context: Distinct from Public Choice (the disciplinary flagship founded by Tullock in 1966), the Cato Journal aims to bridge scholarly work with policy-oriented readership. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Romanian communist leader whose 24-year rule ended in December 1989 with a live-television booing followed by execution by firing squad was known by his surname. Who was he?
context: Nicolae Ceausescu ruled Socialist Romania from 1965 as party general secretary. His wife Elena served as effective co-ruler. Both were tried and shot on December 25, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Ceausescu.

question: Ceausescu's signature Bucharest project was the world's second-largest administrative building, cleared by demolishing an old district of the capital including 26 churches in the 1980s. What is the building now called?
context: Built as Casa Poporului (House of the People), 365,000 square meters, using 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. It now houses Romania's Parliament. It remains one of the heaviest and most expensive buildings ever constructed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_the_Parliament.

question: In October 1966 the Ceausescu government issued a decree banning abortion and contraception -- previously legal in Romania since 1957 -- as part of a forced-birth demographic policy. What number is the decree known by?
context: Decree 770, October 2, 1966. Unmarried women and childless couples over 25 paid a special tax; birth rates jumped from 14.3 to 27.4 per 1,000 within a year. The state proved unable to house the resulting babies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_770.

question: The forced-birth policy of Decree 770 produced a crisis Western television publicized in 1990 when foreign reporters entered Romanian state facilities for the first time. What was the nature of that crisis?
answer: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
choices: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
A mass wave of infant mortality on farms
A polio outbreak in three major cities
context: By 1989 roughly 100,000 children were in Romanian state institutions. Western television footage after 1990 showed severe neglect and drove international adoption reform for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_orphans.

question: Ceausescu's signature domestic urban policy in the 1980s demolished thousands of villages and old city neighborhoods to force populations into standardized concrete apartment blocks. What was this policy called?
context: Sistematizare demolished over 40,000 Bucharest buildings alone during the 1980s to make room for the Centrul Civic. Villages across Romania were slated for erasure under the policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematization_(Romania).

question: The Romanian revolution began on December 16, 1989 with protests in a specific Transylvanian city, over the attempted eviction of a Hungarian Reformed pastor. Which city touched off the uprising?
context: Timisoara protests defending Laszlo Tokes on December 16, 1989 spread across the city and were met with lethal force. Within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: On December 21, 1989 Ceausescu tried to address a mandatory rally from a Central Committee balcony in Bucharest and lost control of the crowd on live state television for the first time in 24 years. What did the crowd do?
answer: Booed him live on state television
choices: Booed him live on state television
context: The recording of Ceausescu's stunned face as the crowd's boos rose is preserved. Within four days he had fled by helicopter, been captured, tried, and shot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: Ceausescu and his wife Elena were tried before a military tribunal and shot by firing squad on a specific holiday date. Which date?
context: The Christmas Day execution at Targoviste military barracks makes Ceausescu the only communist leader shot during the 1989 collapse. The military tribunal proceeding lasted about an hour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Nicolae_and_Elena_Ceausescu.

question: Ceausescu's 1980s foreign-debt strategy prioritized full external repayment above all else, exporting food and fuel abroad while Romanians rationed both. What everyday hardship did this decision impose on Romanian households?
context: Ceausescu personally decided to pay off Romania's foreign debt at all cost. The 1980s saw scheduled blackouts, chronic queues for meat, sugar, and cooking oil, and gasoline severely rationed while agricultural goods were exported for hard currency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania.

question: The internal-security apparatus that enforced Ceausescu's rule -- known for a wide informant network in a country of 22 million -- ran to roughly 10,000-15,000 officers. What was it called?
context: Securitate (Departamentul Securitatii Statului) was Romania's secret police 1948-1989. Its file archive was opened after the revolution under a series of transparency laws; the National Council for the Study of the Securitate Archives (CNSAS) still processes access requests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitate.

question: About 35 US states plus DC have a state-law regime that requires healthcare providers to obtain government approval before building new hospitals or buying major imaging equipment. What is the regime called?
context: Certificate of Need (CON) laws vary by state but share the core requirement: state approval before adding capacity. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Certificate_of_need.

question: The stated official rationale for Certificate of Need laws is to prevent one specific supposed problem. What is the rationale usually given?
context: Advocates argue CON prevents duplicative capacity and concentrates patients at higher-volume facilities. The empirical record does not bear out the cost-reduction claim. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Certificate_of_need.

question: Bastiat's method surfaces the practical operation of the CON application process. Who typically shows up to file objections against a competitor's application?
answer: Existing hospitals with a veto interest
choices: Existing hospitals with a veto interest
context: The incumbent-veto mechanism: existing hospitals routinely file objections to competitor CON applications, delaying approvals by years or defeating them entirely. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: A Mercatus Center researcher at George Mason has published multiple studies from 2011-2020 documenting that CON states have fewer hospitals per capita and higher prices. Who is that researcher?
context: Matthew Mitchell's Mercatus Center work is the leading modern empirical case against CON regimes. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: Empirical work on CON states has shown three concrete outcomes at odds with the law's stated goal. What are the three findings?
answer: Fewer hospitals, fewer MRI machines, higher prices
choices: Fewer hospitals, fewer MRI machines, higher prices
More hospitals, more MRI machines, lower prices
Same hospital count, fewer beds, lower emergency-room wait times
More rural clinics, more emergency departments, higher outcomes scores
context: CON states show fewer hospitals per capita, fewer MRI machines per capita, and higher per-service prices -- the opposite of the stated 'lower costs from consolidation' rationale. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: When existing hospitals have effective veto power over their competitors' state-approval applications, a specific 1971 reasoning move by George Stigler explains why this happens. What is the reasoning move called?
context: George Stigler's 1971 'Theory of Economic Regulation' (Bell Journal) is the founding theoretical statement of regulatory capture: regulators come to serve the industries they regulate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Regulatory_capture.

question: The Institute for Justice has litigated a specific 2022 case challenging Kentucky's home-health CON regime as an unconstitutional protection of incumbents. What is that case called?
answer: Bogdanchik v. Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services
choices: Bogdanchik v. Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services
context: IJ's Bogdanchik case argues Kentucky's home-health CON regime violates the 14th Amendment's protection of the right to earn a living. Source: ij.org/case/kentucky-home-health-care.

question: In November 1978 farmers in a small Anhui village secretly signed what they called a 'life-and-death contract' dividing collective land into family plots, knowing they could be executed if discovered. Which village signed the contract?
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed the December 1978 secret pact. The contract is preserved in Beijing's National Museum of Modern Chinese History. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: The name Chinese reformers gave to the post-1978 arrangement that let farming households take charge of specific plots and keep any surplus after delivering a state quota is a specific formal phrase. What is it usually rendered as?
context: Jiating lianchan chengbao zeren zhi (Household Responsibility System) was legalized nationwide by 1983. It restored the family plot and let households keep above-quota production. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: The specific reason the Xiaogang farmers took on such personal risk was that the collective commune system had left them and their families chronically at what condition?
context: Xiaogang villagers had been sending members to beg for food in other counties for decades under the commune system. The famine memory of 1959-61 was still living. The life-and-death contract was a rational response to a chronic shortage economy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: Within a single year of the Xiaogang secret contract, the village's grain output rose dramatically. Roughly by what multiple did output climb?
context: Xiaogang's grain output rose roughly six-fold in one year under the household contract. The neighboring villages watched, imitated, and the practice spread county by county before official legalization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: By 1983 the Household Responsibility System was legalized nationwide under Deng Xiaoping's leadership. Chinese grain output rose about 33 percent between 1978 and 1984 -- and one economist's decomposition attributed roughly half of that gain to the incentive-restoration itself, not to inputs. Who did the decomposition?
context: Lin's 1992 China Economic Review paper 'Rural Reforms and Agricultural Growth in China' decomposed the growth. About half came from the incentive-restoration, not from fertilizer, weather, or better seed. Lin later served as World Bank Chief Economist 2008-12. Source: China Economic Review 1992.

question: The reasoning move at the heart of the Household Responsibility System's success is that farmers who could keep any surplus after paying the state quota worked differently from those who could not. What is the standard analytic name for this incentive?
context: The residual claim -- the right to keep whatever is left after fixed obligations -- gives the actor sharp incentive to increase output and improve technique. This is the load-bearing move behind private property in economic theory. Source: mises.org/library/residual-claim.

question: Deng Xiaoping justified the Household Responsibility System and other Reform-and-Opening moves with a specific animal saying about pragmatism over doctrine. What was the phrase?
answer: It does not matter whether the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
choices: It does not matter whether the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
The eagle sees what the sparrow misses
The camel walks where the horse cannot
The tiger and the lion share the same forest
context: Deng's black-cat-white-cat saying (revived from a 1961 speech) became the shorthand slogan of Reform and Opening. Empirical results trump ideological purity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: The Chinese state's own 1978 admission that market-priced incentives outperformed commune allocation is often called by Austrian analysts a decisive natural experiment. Whose 1920 argument does it most directly vindicate?
answer: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
choices: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
John Maynard Keynes on effective demand
context: Mises's 1920 argument that socialist commonwealths cannot calculate rationally without market prices was empirically confirmed at the largest possible scale by the Chinese state's own reforms. Same land, same farmers, radically more output when prices returned. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The Xiaogang secret contract of 1978 is now preserved and displayed. Where is the physical document kept?
choices: The Ministry of Agriculture in Beijing
context: The original life-and-death contract is displayed in Beijing's National Museum of Modern Chinese History. It marks the practical starting point of Reform and Opening. Source: national museum catalog.

question: The Household Responsibility System's teaching for the calculation debate is that when residual claim is restored, the same land, same farmers, and same seed can produce dramatically more output. What is the standard shorthand for this pattern?
context: 'Incentives matter' is the compressed lesson of the Chinese agricultural reform, taught in every introductory economics course. It captures the incentive-recognition side of the calculation debate. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: In November 1937 the London School of Economics journal Economica published a paper by a 26-year-old Ronald Coase that eventually helped him win the 1991 Nobel. What was the paper's title?
context: Ronald Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (Economica, November 1937). Coase was 26 and had done most of the thinking as a 21-year-old undergraduate on a US scholarship trip in 1931-32. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Coase 1937).

question: As a 21-year-old undergraduate on a Cassel Traveling Scholarship in 1931-32, Coase visited large integrated American firms to try to understand why they existed at all. Which iconic Detroit automaker was one of his visits?
context: Coase's Cassel Scholarship US visit included Ford in Detroit, US Steel, and other integrated firms. Watching those hierarchies is what led him to ask why the firm existed rather than the market coordinating everything through prices. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: Coase's 1937 paper asked a question standard price theory had not addressed. If the market efficiently coordinates production through prices and contracts, why do FIRMS with employees exist at all? What was Coase's answer?
answer: Because using the market itself has transaction costs
choices: Because using the market itself has transaction costs
Because governments require firms to exist
Because workers prefer wages to independent contracting
Because firms enjoy special tax advantages
context: Coase's key move: using markets is costly (finding partners, negotiating, monitoring, enforcing). When those costs exceed the costs of managing inside a firm, hierarchies replace market transactions. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: In Coase's 1937 analysis, the SIZE of a firm is determined by a specific comparative-cost equation. Where does the firm's boundary sit?
answer: Where the cost of in-house organization equals the cost of a market transaction
choices: Where the cost of in-house organization equals the cost of a market transaction
Where the number of employees exceeds one thousand
Where the tax rate on payroll drops below ten percent
Where the regulatory-compliance staff equals production staff
context: Coase's boundary condition: the firm grows until the marginal in-house transaction cost equals the marginal market transaction cost. Cheaper in-house transactions are absorbed; cheaper market transactions are outsourced. Source: Coase, Economica (1937), section III.

question: The 1937 Coase paper founded a whole subfield now named after its central analytical variable. What is the standard modern name for this field?
context: Transaction cost economics (or New Institutional Economics) grew directly out of Coase 1937. Oliver Williamson's 2009 Nobel-winning work on 'markets and hierarchies' extends the framework substantially. Source: Williamson, Markets and Hierarchies (Free Press 1975).

question: The economist whose 2009 Nobel Prize was awarded partly for extending Coase's 1937 framework into a full theory of 'markets and hierarchies' shared the prize with Elinor Ostrom. Who was that co-laureate?
context: Oliver Williamson shared the 2009 Nobel with Elinor Ostrom, cited for his work on the economic governance of the firm. Source: nobelprize.org (2009 Economic Sciences).

question: Applying Coase's 1937 framework to the modern tech industry, what shift has been observed as globalization and information technology have lowered market transaction costs?
answer: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
choices: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
A move from outsourced supply chains toward vertical integration
A move from stock ownership toward partnership structures
A move from public listing toward private ownership
context: Apple in the 1980s made much of its hardware in-house; Apple in the 2000s+ largely designs in-house and manufactures through contract firms like Foxconn. Falling market transaction costs move the firm boundary outward. Source: Baldwin + Clark, Design Rules (MIT 2000).

question: Coase's 1991 Nobel Prize citation named him for two specific papers, one from 1937 and one from 1960. The 1937 paper explained the firm; what did the 1960 paper analyze?
answer: The problem of social cost -- externalities and property rights
choices: The problem of social cost -- externalities and property rights
The efficiency of central-bank monetary policy
The distribution of income across households
The theory of international trade under quotas
context: 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960). The 1991 Nobel citation names both 1937 and 1960 as the key contributions. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: Coase's 1937 paper reframed the economist's task in analyzing an industry. What comparative question does the framework tell the analyst to ask about any given transaction?
answer: Why is this transaction organized inside a firm rather than through the market
choices: Why is this transaction organized inside a firm rather than through the market
How large is the industry's marketing budget
Which continent produces the most output
Which political party currently regulates the industry
context: Coase's move: for every transaction, ask why it is organized the way it is. The answer is always the relative transaction cost of the two arrangements. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: Coase's 1937 paper was written from a specific institutional starting point that shaped his skepticism of centrally-planned alternatives. Where did the young Coase receive his undergraduate degree in commerce?
context: Coase took his BCom at the London School of Economics (1932). His US Cassel Scholarship trip in 1931-32 provided the empirical observations behind Nature of the Firm. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: In October 1960 the University of Chicago Law School's journal published Ronald Coase's most-cited paper -- one of the most-cited in the whole history of economics -- overturning half a century of externality analysis. What was the paper called?
context: Ronald Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960). Its argument reframed the whole economics of externalities. Source: chicagounbound.uchicago.edu (Coase 1960).

question: Coase's 1960 paper directly attacked the standard mid-century treatment of externalities that had been given by a Cambridge welfare economist in his 1920 book The Economics of Welfare. Whose analysis was Coase pushing back against?
context: Arthur Pigou (1877-1959) had argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) that pollution should be corrected by government tax. Coase said the Pigouvian analysis was incomplete because it treated the causation as one-directional. Source: Pigou (1920); Coase (1960).

question: Coase's key insight in 1960 was that externalities are RECIPROCAL rather than one-directional. What does that phrase mean when a factory pollutes a neighbor's air?
answer: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
choices: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
The neighbor is legally required to endure the pollution
The neighbor loses standing to sue in federal court
The factory automatically owes triple damages
context: Coase's move: the economic question is not who is at fault. It is which use of the resource creates more value. Both parties have legitimate uses; a rule imposes costs on whichever party is prevented from its use. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960).

question: Coase's famous rancher-and-farmer illustration in the 1960 paper describes cattle straying onto neighboring crops. In Coase's analysis, if transaction costs are low, which arrangement will emerge regardless of who initially holds the property right?
answer: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
choices: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
The rancher always keeps the cattle
The farmer always keeps the crops
context: The initial rights determine WHO PAYS in the bargain; they do not determine the final resource allocation if transaction costs are low enough for the parties to negotiate. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960), section IV.

question: The result at the heart of Coase's 1960 paper was later named a theorem by another economist, though Coase himself was ambivalent about the honorific. Which Chicago economist coined the name 'the Coase Theorem'?
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase Theorem' in his 1966 textbook Theory of Price. Coase himself argued the textbook version was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: Coase repeatedly complained that his 1960 argument was misread as claiming government intervention is unnecessary. What was his ACTUAL position when transaction costs are HIGH -- for instance, many affected parties and prohibitive negotiation?
answer: Government intervention may be justified, but its own transaction costs must be counted too
choices: Government intervention may be justified, but its own transaction costs must be counted too
Nothing can be done and the parties must live with the outcome
The market always still reaches an efficient outcome by magic
Only judicial rulings, never legislation, are appropriate
context: Coase's actual argument in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: when private bargaining is too costly, government intervention may be superior -- provided the analysis honestly counts the transaction costs of government administration too. Source: Coase, The Firm, the Market, and the Law (Chicago 1988).

question: The 1960 paper's real influence on environmental policy has been to reshape a specific class of instruments used to reduce pollution efficiently at scale. Which pair of Coase-inspired mechanisms became mainstream in the 1990s and 2000s?
answer: Tradeable pollution permits and individual transferable fishing quotas
choices: Tradeable pollution permits and individual transferable fishing quotas
Purely command-and-control emission limits and moral suasion
Federal ownership of all polluting facilities
context: The 1990 US SO2 cap-and-trade Acid Rain Program, EU ETS (2005), and Iceland + New Zealand fisheries individual transferable quotas all trace their intellectual pedigree to Coase 1960. Source: Ellerman + Joskow, Markets for Clean Air (Cambridge 2000).

question: In addition to reshaping environmental policy, Coase's 1960 paper is credited with inspiring another major 20th-century economist's work on how communities self-govern shared resources without state or market takeover. Whose 1990 Cambridge UP book is the standard reference?
choices: Kenneth Arrow's Social Choice and Individual Values
Douglass North's Structure and Change in Economic History
context: Ostrom's Governing the Commons (Cambridge UP 1990) draws directly on Coase's institutional-analysis framework, extending it from two-party bargaining to many-party self-governance of common-pool resources. Source: Ostrom (1990); Coase (1960).

question: Coase's 1960 paper is 44 pages long and, together with his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm, was cited by the Royal Swedish Academy as the basis for his 1991 Nobel Prize. Together, what did the two papers earn him recognition for?
answer: The significance of transaction costs and property rights for institutional structure
choices: The significance of transaction costs and property rights for institutional structure
The mathematical foundations of general equilibrium
The theory of comparative advantage in international trade
The empirical measurement of national income
context: The 1991 Nobel citation named Coase 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Both 1937 and 1960 papers are the pillars. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: Coase's real methodological contribution across 1937 and 1960 was a specific move about how to compare institutional forms honestly. Which sentence best captures the Coase move?
answer: Never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative
choices: Never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative
Always favor markets over any form of state action
Always favor state action over any form of markets
All externalities disappear if you draw the diagram correctly
context: Coase's move: compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms. Firms, markets, private bargains, and government all have their own transaction costs. Honest comparative institutional analysis counts them all. Source: Coase, The Firm, the Market, and the Law (Chicago 1988).

question: Coase's 1960 paper produced a common textbook version of the Coase theorem that Coase himself considered a misreading. Which version does Coase's actual writing endorse?
answer: Transaction costs are high in the real world, so initial rights matter enormously
choices: Transaction costs are high in the real world, so initial rights matter enormously
Externalities disappear in every real market regardless of institutions
Government intervention is never justified for any externality
Property rights should be assigned to whichever party is wealthier
context: Coase in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: the zero-transaction-cost world of the textbook Coase Theorem does not exist. In the real world, transaction costs are high, so initial rights and institutional design matter enormously. Source: Coase (1988).

question: The US Harmonized Tariff Schedule applies rates that vary systematically by product tier: cheap imported sneakers face about 15-20%, while high-end leather dress shoes face only about 5-8%. Which income group therefore bears the higher effective tariff burden?
context: Because low-income households spend a larger share of income on the tariffed low-end goods, they bear a disproportionately higher effective burden. Source: usitc.gov/tariff_affairs/tariff_databases.

question: In 2002 a Progressive Policy Institute analyst (later at the U.S. Trade Representative office) published a landmark paper documenting how the American tariff schedule hits low-income households hardest. What is his name?
context: Ed Gresser's 'Toughest on the Poor: America's Flawed Tariff System' (PPI, 2002) is the definitive empirical treatment of tariff incidence across US household-income quintiles. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: Gresser's headline finding put the effective tariff burden on the bottom household-income quintile at a specific multiple of the burden on the top quintile as a share of income. What is that multiple?
context: Bottom-quintile households pay roughly 3-4x the top-quintile burden as a share of income; the schedule targets specifically the goods the poor buy most. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: Bastiat's method surfaces a striking political characterization of protectionism aimed at helping working-class Americans. Thomas Sowell states the reversal in Basic Economics as which of these?
answer: The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are taxing them the most
choices: The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are taxing them the most
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are helping them the most
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are unrelated to consumer prices
The people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are always wealthy foreigners
context: Sowell's Basic Economics distills the incidence result: protectionism sold as pro-worker functions economically as a regressive consumption tax hitting working-class families most. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: The classical-economics theorem that mutually voluntary trade benefits both parties even when one has an absolute advantage in every good was published by an English classical economist in 1817. Which economist?
context: Ricardo's 1817 Principles of Political Economy and Taxation formulated comparative advantage; every tariff that overrides it necessarily leaves both trading nations poorer. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comparative_advantage.

question: Economically, a tariff functions like which specific kind of tax on the domestic buyer of the imported good?
context: A tariff raises the domestic price of the imported good and is paid, in economic incidence, by the domestic consumer -- like a targeted sales tax. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tariff.

question: The tariff schedule's systematic high-on-cheap-goods pattern arose in a specific way over decades. Which mechanism best describes how the schedule came to look this way?
answer: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
choices: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
The World Trade Organization mandates the pattern
Federal statute requires 20% rates on all consumer goods
Foreign governments retaliated against US textile exports
context: The schedule is not accidental. Producers of low-end goods (footwear, apparel) had the strongest incentive to lobby for protection and the tariff schedule reflects their trade-lobby lawyers' work. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: US states range along a spectrum for concealed-carry permitting. At one extreme, some states require no permit at all to carry a handgun in public. What is this no-permit-required regime called?
context: As of 2024 about 27 US states allow constitutional carry (no permit required); the other extreme was 'may-issue' at official discretion, largely struck down by the Bruen decision. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Concealed_carry_in_the_United_States.

question: A University of Chicago Press book by John Lott, first published in 1998 and now in a 3rd edition, argues from empirical data that shall-issue permitting reduces violent crime. What is the book's title?
context: John Lott's More Guns, Less Crime (Chicago, 1998; 3rd ed. 2010) is the most-cited empirical work on the effects of concealed-carry laws. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: Lott's empirical work documented that jurisdictions with LOWER permit fees and SHALL-ISSUE standards had substantially higher permit uptake among a specific demographic that lives most in high-crime neighborhoods. Which demographic?
context: Lower fees and non-discretionary issuance disproportionately raised permit uptake among lower-income and minority residents, who tend to live in higher-crime neighborhoods and cannot rely on rapid police response. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: On June 23, 2022 the US Supreme Court struck down New York's may-issue concealed-carry law, holding that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry firearms outside the home. What is the case's short name?
context: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022), majority opinion by Justice Clarence Thomas, invalidated may-issue regimes requiring 'proper cause'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: After the 2022 Bruen decision, the most restrictive states responded not by ending restrictions but by shifting them to a different set of tools. Which specific set of tools did they turn to?
answer: Higher fees, extensive training requirements, and sensitive-place restrictions
choices: Higher fees, extensive training requirements, and sensitive-place restrictions
Age limits raised to 30 for all applicants
Federal preemption of local permitting entirely
Direct federal ownership of all firearms in the state
context: Restrictive states shifted from discretionary denial to cost-based and geography-based restriction after Bruen. The Bastiat move: the SEEN policy changed; the UNSEEN restriction on the low-income permit-seeker did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: Bastiat's method surfaces a specific class of person invisible in official statistics on gun policy. Which class does the method make visible?
answer: The victim who could not afford the fee and was disarmed against her attacker
choices: The victim who could not afford the fee and was disarmed against her attacker
The firearm dealer who lost a small-caliber sale
The state licensing office that lost fee revenue
The insurance company that paid a smaller premium
context: The seen: revenue-generating fees and training requirements. The unseen: the woman being stalked who could not afford the $400+20-hours barrier and could not lawfully carry for self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: The 1995 Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology paper 'Armed Resistance to Crime' estimated defensive gun uses in the US at around 2.2 million per year. Which pair of researchers authored that study?
context: Kleck and Gertz's estimate of ~2.2 million annual defensive gun uses in the US is contested but remains a widely-cited figure in the empirical literature on self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Defensive_gun_use.

question: In May 1984 a Chicago-based bank -- the seventh-largest US bank by assets, having grown aggressively in the late 1970s by buying bad energy loans from the failed Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma -- suffered a global run and had to be rescued by federal regulators. Which bank was it?
context: Continental Illinois had about $40 billion in assets at the time of its 1984 crisis -- roughly $120 billion in 2026 dollars. It had bought energy loans from the failed Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma in 1982. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: The Continental Illinois run of May 1984 was different from traditional bank runs at teller windows. It was primarily driven by large uninsured depositors -- institutional holders and foreign banks -- pulling funds by wire. What is this new kind of run called?
context: A wholesale run happens over telecommunications rather than at teller windows. It moves orders of magnitude faster than a classic retail run. Continental Illinois was the first major US bank collapse to be primarily wholesale-driven. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank run' (2026-09-05).

question: On May 17 1984, the FDIC and the Fed announced a historic expansion of the deposit-insurance guarantee. What did they commit to?
answer: Protecting all depositors at Continental Illinois, including those above the standard FDIC insurance limit
choices: Protecting all depositors at Continental Illinois, including those above the standard FDIC insurance limit
Nationalizing Continental Illinois for a period of five years
Merging Continental Illinois with First Chicago at par value
Letting Continental Illinois fail while paying insured depositors only
context: At the time, FDIC insurance covered up to $100,000 per depositor. Extending protection above that cap for a specific bank was a discretionary expansion of the guarantee. It set a precedent that shaped every major US bank rescue since. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: On September 19 1984 the Comptroller of the Currency told Congress that federal regulators would protect a specific group of large US banks against failure. Which group did he name?
choices: The 25 largest banks by branch count
context: Comptroller C.T. Conover's September 19 1984 testimony was the first time a federal regulator used the phrase 'too big to fail' publicly to describe a policy commitment. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: The Comptroller's September 1984 congressional testimony is the origin point for a specific policy phrase that has shaped US banking regulation ever since. What was the memorable phrase?
context: Comptroller Conover's 1984 testimony gave 'too big to fail' its policy meaning. The phrase was later popularized by Congressman Stewart McKinney and became the shorthand for the moral-hazard structure of modern banking regulation. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: In the years after Continental Illinois, US bank consolidation accelerated significantly. What was the change in the market share of the four largest US banks between 1984 and 2020?
answer: From about 10% of deposits to over 45%
choices: From about 10% of deposits to over 45%
From about 30% of deposits to about 40%
From about 20% of deposits to about 22%
From about 50% of deposits to about 55%
context: The four largest US banks held about 10% of deposits in 1984. By 2020 they held over 45%. The Continental Illinois precedent created an incentive for the biggest banks to take larger risks -- upside privatized, downside socialized. Source: Grokipedia 'Concentration in the banking industry' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian and public-choice critique of Continental Illinois centers on the specific incentive change the rescue created. What did large banks learn from the 1984 precedent?
answer: Regulators would protect uninsured depositors and creditors in a crisis, so larger risks were now safer to take
choices: Regulators would protect uninsured depositors and creditors in a crisis, so larger risks were now safer to take
Regulators would strictly enforce capital requirements to prevent future rescues
Regulators would break up any bank that grew above a specific size
Regulators would nationalize any bank that engaged in risky lending
context: This is the moral-hazard structure of every subsequent bailout episode -- LTCM 1998, Bear Stearns 2008, TARP 2008, SVB 2023. All extended the Continental Illinois precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Moral hazard' (2026-09-05).

question: Continental Illinois was itself eventually purchased in 1994 by a major US commercial bank, after the FDIC took majority ownership for a decade. Which bank was the eventual buyer?
context: The FDIC took majority ownership of Continental Illinois in 1984 and gradually reduced its stake. Bank of America completed the acquisition in 1994. The name Continental Illinois disappeared from American banking. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: The Continental Illinois episode teaches a specific recognition move about how emergency exceptions become permanent structural features. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: A discretionary exception granted once becomes a structural precedent that shapes every future risk-taking decision in the sector
choices: A discretionary exception granted once becomes a structural precedent that shapes every future risk-taking decision in the sector
Emergency exceptions are always time-limited and never generalize
Discretionary exceptions can be revoked at any time without political cost
Bank rescues never influence the behavior of banks that were not directly rescued
context: The 1984 above-cap protection was framed as an exception. Every subsequent major rescue extended the pattern until 'too big to fail' was a well-understood implicit guarantee. The 2023 SVB extension of full protection was the direct heir of the 1984 precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: The Continental Illinois episode also produced a specific critique from Austrian economists about the relationship between banking regulation and banking consolidation. Which recognition move do they press?
answer: Regulation that guarantees the biggest banks against failure is itself a subsidy that drives ever-greater concentration in the sector
choices: Regulation that guarantees the biggest banks against failure is itself a subsidy that drives ever-greater concentration in the sector
Regulation always reduces concentration in the banking sector
