Bank consolidation has no relationship to deposit-insurance policy
Deposit insurance protects small banks preferentially over large ones
context: The Austrian point: too-big-to-fail is not just moral hazard for the biggest banks; it is an active subsidy over their smaller competitors. Depositors rationally prefer the guaranteed bank. Consolidation is the mechanical result. Source: Selgin, Bagehot's Legacy (Cato commentary, 2013-2020).

question: Since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act 2017, the US federal statutory tax rate on C-corporation profits sits at a specific level. What is the current federal rate?
context: The 2017 TCJA cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 21%; the tax applies to C-corporation profits and is separate from personal income tax paid on dividends and capital gains. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: In his 1980 PBS television series Free to Choose, Milton Friedman gave a compact statement about who really bears the burden of any tax. What was his line?
answer: Corporations do not pay taxes; only people pay taxes
choices: Corporations do not pay taxes; only people pay taxes
Corporations pay taxes; people never pay taxes
Taxes always fall on the top 1% regardless of design
Taxes always fall on foreign investors regardless of design
context: Friedman's line summarizes the incidence point: a corporation is a legal fiction and every dollar of tax comes from a real human's pocket -- a consumer, a worker, or a shareholder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: Public-finance economics distinguishes two kinds of tax incidence: statutory (who legally remits the tax) and a second kind (who really bears the reduction in income). What is the second kind called?
context: Statutory vs economic incidence: the check-writer is often not the party whose income is reduced. This distinction is the analytic core of tax-policy analysis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tax_incidence.

question: Bastiat's method surfaces a specific class of person who bears a substantial share of the corporate income tax through a specific mechanism. Which of these groups bears the largest share via lower earnings?
choices: Retirees via smaller Social Security checks
Foreign investors via US border tariffs
context: Empirical research (Suarez Serrato and Zidar, AER 2016; CBO 2012 distributional update) shows a large share of the corporate income tax is ultimately borne by workers through lower wages. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: The economic reason workers bear such a large share of the corporate tax comes down to a specific asymmetry between two production factors. Which asymmetry drives the result?
answer: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
choices: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
Labor is more mobile internationally than capital
Capital and labor are equally mobile
Neither capital nor labor moves across borders
context: Mobile capital's after-tax return is set by world markets; when the US taxes capital, mobile capital exits or requires a compensating gross return, and the burden shifts to less-mobile labor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: A 2016 American Economic Review paper 'Who Benefits from State Corporate Tax Cuts?' is the standard modern local-labor-markets analysis of the incidence question. Which pair of authors wrote it?
answer: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
choices: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
context: Suarez Serrato and Zidar, 'Who Benefits from State Corporate Tax Cuts? A Local Labor Markets Approach with Heterogeneous Firms' (AER, 2016), is the workhorse modern study of state corporate-tax incidence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: One frequently-overlooked non-worker group also bears part of the corporate tax whenever the incidence falls partly on capital. Which group holds shares broadly through retirement accounts?
answer: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' retirement savings
choices: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' retirement savings
context: The shareholder class is not only 'the rich' -- large pools of public-employee and private-sector pension fund savings hold corporate equity, so the incidence that falls on capital hits ordinary retirement accounts too. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: On September 7 2021, one country became the first ever to accept Bitcoin as legal tender alongside its national currency (the US dollar). Which country was it, and under which president?
context: Bukele announced the plan at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference in Miami. Same-day September 7 the government launched the Chivo Wallet and issued each adult citizen a $30 Bitcoin allocation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: In April 2022, an African country became the second nation ever to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender. Which one?
context: President Faustin-Archange Touadera signed the law, but the country had scant electricity infrastructure, low smartphone penetration, and IMF opposition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cryptocurrency_in_the_Central_African_Republic.

question: The Central African Republic adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in April 2022 and then repealed the law less than a year later. In which month did the parliament reverse the decision?
context: The reversal made the CAR experiment the shortest sovereign Bitcoin adoption in history. Lack of a reliable electricity grid, low smartphone penetration, and IMF opposition were the cited reasons. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cryptocurrency_in_the_Central_African_Republic.

question: In November 2023 Argentine voters elected as president a self-described anarcho-capitalist economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as a prop representing budget cuts. Who was he?
context: Milei was inaugurated December 10, 2023. He has praised Bitcoin as 'the return of money to the private sector' and legalized Bitcoin-denominated contracts, though he has not made Bitcoin legal tender. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Javier_Milei.

question: The tiny Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan (population roughly 700,000) took an approach to Bitcoin very different from El Salvador's legal-tender declaration or Argentina's Milei-era deregulation. What has Bhutan quietly done since around 2019?
answer: Mined Bitcoin using its hydroelectric power and accumulated one of the world's largest sovereign Bitcoin reserves
choices: Mined Bitcoin using its hydroelectric power and accumulated one of the world's largest sovereign Bitcoin reserves
Banned Bitcoin entirely and criminalized possession
Made Bitcoin its sole legal tender, replacing the ngultrum
Issued a state-backed stablecoin as an alternative to Bitcoin
context: 2024 disclosures revealed Bhutan holds an estimated 13,000+ BTC. The mining is run through Druk Holding & Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund. The scale, on a population of 700,000, is proportionally very large. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Bhutan.

question: Three national approaches to Bitcoin -- El Salvador's legal-tender declaration, Milei-era Argentina's legalization of Bitcoin contracts, and Bhutan's sovereign mining -- all provoked the same institutional opposition. Which body has publicly opposed all three?
context: The IMF cited financial-stability risks and monetary-policy independence concerns in each case. Its consistent stance is a factual pattern the ladder teaches without moralizing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: A high-school student asks which of the three national Bitcoin experiments (El Salvador legal tender, Argentina under Milei, Bhutan sovereign mining) was 'the right way' to engage with Bitcoin. A Hayekian economist declines to pick a single winner. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Recognizing that different tradeoffs (infrastructure needs, deregulation without mandate, energy-into-savings) suit different national circumstances
choices: Recognizing that different tradeoffs (infrastructure needs, deregulation without mandate, energy-into-savings) suit different national circumstances
Insisting that only central-bank digital currency can be legitimate national money
Declaring that any state Bitcoin engagement is always successful regardless of context
Concluding that only the largest economies can adopt any new monetary technology
context: The CAR reversal warns that infrastructure prerequisites matter as much as legal declarations. Milei's legal-friendliness lets adoption grow organically. Bhutan converts stranded hydro energy into a portable savings asset. Different national situations, different fits. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: By 2024, Bhutan's Bitcoin holdings were estimated at roughly 13,000+ BTC accumulated through mining -- a scale that, for a nation of 700,000 people, exceeded the per-capita Bitcoin exposure of El Salvador. Which specific state instrument runs the Bhutanese mining operation?
answer: Druk Holding & Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund
choices: Druk Holding & Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund
The Royal Bhutan Army's engineering corps
A joint venture with the Bank of China
The Bhutan Ministry of Foreign Affairs directly
context: Druk Holding & Investments (DHI) is Bhutan's state investment vehicle. The mining uses hydroelectric power from Bhutan's mountain rivers -- energy that would otherwise be exported or wasted, converted into a portable, hard-cap asset. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Bhutan.

question: In the early weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020, most US states enforced laws making it illegal to sell N95 masks and hand sanitizer above pre-emergency prices. What are these laws commonly called?
context: Anti-price-gouging statutes existed in most US states before 2020 and were activated as emergencies were declared. Enforcement agencies threatened fines and jail terms in March-April 2020. Source: NCSL.org state-by-state summary.

question: The Duke University economist most associated with the 'price gouging is the solution, not the problem' argument uses a memorable Kentucky-to-Florida example. What is his surname?
context: Michael Munger, political-science and economics professor at Duke, has written and podcast repeatedly about the Shepperson-generators case. His EconTalk episodes on price gouging are widely cited. Source: sites.duke.edu/munger.

question: The Munger example concerns a Kentucky entrepreneur named John Shepperson who in September 2004, after Hurricane Frances hit Florida, rented a U-Haul, bought a supply of scarce equipment, and drove them 600 miles to a county without power. What did he transport?
context: Shepperson bought 19 generators in Kentucky and drove them to a Florida county after Hurricane Frances. He planned to sell them at approximately double the retail price. Source: Michael Munger, EconTalk (2007).

question: What happened to Shepperson when he arrived in Florida offering to sell the generators at roughly double what he had paid for them?
answer: He was arrested and the generators were confiscated
choices: He was arrested and the generators were confiscated
He sold out within an hour to grateful buyers
He was given a permit to operate a temporary market
Local authorities helped him distribute them
context: Florida police arrested Shepperson under the state's anti-price-gouging law and confiscated the generators. His family did without power, the Florida county went without generators, and the incentive-signal was clear to any other Kentucky entrepreneur. Source: Michael Munger case discussion.

question: Bastiat's reasoning-move applied to the price-gouging case: SEEN was the low-feeling ceiling. What was UNSEEN?
answer: Every entrepreneur who does not drive supplies to a disaster area because the reward has been criminalized
choices: Every entrepreneur who does not drive supplies to a disaster area because the reward has been criminalized
The producers whose profits rise from the ceiling
The government's tax revenue from the fine imposed
The neighboring state's competing anti-gouging law
context: Bastiat's method: the ceiling looks fair (SEEN); the hidden cost is the surge of supply that the price signal would have called forth (UNSEEN). Criminalizing the reward silences the signal and prolongs the shortage. Source: bastiat.org.

question: In early 2020, some US states did NOT actively enforce their gouging laws on PPE. Those markets restocked measurably faster than states that did enforce. Which state briefly waived enforcement in 2020 as a natural experiment?
context: Tennessee briefly waived enforcement on PPE gouging in 2020. Steven Horwitz and other economists documented that unwaived states saw longer shortages. The natural experiment matched the Bastiatian prediction. Source: mercatus.org COVID studies 2020.

question: Munger frames the reasoning move with a specific memorable slogan about the role of temporary high prices in emergency supply response. What is his slogan?
answer: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
choices: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
Consumers pay whatever the seller demands
Regulation is the answer to shortages
context: Munger's framing: the high price is the market's shout to producers and importers 'HERE, RUSH SUPPLY HERE'; the anti-gouging law silences the shout and prolongs the shortage. Source: EconTalk, Munger episodes on gouging.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics quotes the Shepperson case explicitly. In Sowell's framing, what is the deep reasoning-move error that anti-gouging laws commit?
answer: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
choices: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
They confuse macroeconomic and microeconomic scales
context: Sowell's move: the high price is information about scarcity, not evidence of bad character. The law that criminalizes the messenger destroys the message the market was trying to send. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: The Munger argument specifically frames the anti-gouging law's cost as falling on a hidden group of would-be suppliers -- not on the arrested seller alone. Which group bears the cost the ceiling really imposes?
answer: Future entrepreneurs who now know they will not be rewarded for driving supplies to emergencies
choices: Future entrepreneurs who now know they will not be rewarded for driving supplies to emergencies
The insurance industry paying out claims
context: The reasoning move's most powerful step: the visible arrest teaches every future entrepreneur that the risk of driving supplies to a disaster area will not be rewarded. Supply-response permanently degrades. Source: Munger on price gouging.

question: The reasoning move Munger applies to hurricane generators is the same one applied to COVID PPE and to gasoline after storms. What is the standard analytic name for that reasoning move?
context: Prices signal both scarcity (to buyers, to conserve) and profit opportunity (to sellers, to bring more supply). Ceilings that suppress the signal degrade both responses. This is the operating mechanism behind every emergency-supply anti-gouging analysis. Source: mercatus.org, mises.org.

question: From 2015 onward an Australian computer scientist repeatedly claimed in public interviews and in court to be Satoshi Nakamoto. Which name did he go by while pursuing that claim?
context: Craig Steven Wright, born 1970, is the Australian computer scientist who claimed the Satoshi identity from 2015 until a UK court rejected the claim in 2024. Dan Kaminsky was the security researcher who exposed one of Wright's 'proofs'; Antonopoulos is a Bitcoin educator. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: The one demonstration that could have settled the Satoshi question in a matter of minutes -- and that Craig Wright never performed convincingly during a decade of claiming the title -- involves the private keys Satoshi is known to have used. Which single act would have been decisive?
answer: signing a message with a known Satoshi private key
choices: signing a message with a known Satoshi private key
producing a birth certificate from Japan
moving one Bitcoin from a random address
context: A cryptographic signature made with one of Satoshi's known keys is a five-second, unforgeable proof. A photograph or birth certificate proves nothing about key control; moving Bitcoin from a random address proves nothing about Satoshi's addresses. Wright has never produced a valid signature. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: In 2016 Craig Wright staged a private demonstration for a select group of journalists claiming to prove key ownership. Bitcoin developers -- most prominently one security researcher who investigated the setup -- publicly exposed the demonstration as a technical trick within hours. Which developer led the exposure?
context: Dan Kaminsky (1979-2021), a well-known security researcher, publicly explained within hours that Wright's 'proof' was a copy-pasted old Satoshi signature rather than a fresh sign. Buterin created Ethereum; Antonopoulos is an educator; Satoshi is the missing party being impersonated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Instead of stepping back after his 2016 demonstration was exposed, Craig Wright doubled down. He co-founded a Bitcoin altcoin that broke away from Bitcoin Cash in 2018, whose ticker symbol carried his identity claim in its very name. Which altcoin did he help launch?
context: BSV split from Bitcoin Cash in November 2018 and made 'Satoshi's Vision' part of its name -- an identity claim embedded in the ticker. Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee), Ripple (2012, Chris Larsen and Jed McCaleb), and Ethereum Classic (2016 fork) are unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_SV.

question: On March 14, 2024, a UK High Court judge issued a ruling that decisively answered the Craig Wright question after months of examining his documentary evidence. Which court case delivered the ruling?
context: The Crypto Open Patent Alliance (COPA) brought the London High Court action; Mr Justice Mellor issued the March 14, 2024 ruling. Kleiman v Wright was the earlier Florida case (2018-21) over disputed early Bitcoin holdings; the other cases are hypothetical or minor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright#COPA_v._Wright.

question: The March 14, 2024 COPA v Wright ruling was not merely a finding of insufficient evidence. Mr Justice Mellor's judgment described Craig Wright's own courtroom conduct in specific and unusually strong terms. Which conclusion did the judge draw about the documents Wright had brought to court?
answer: he had forged and backdated them
choices: he had forged and backdated them
he had forgotten crucial details under stress
he had shown a scattered but genuine chain of proof
he had refused to testify about them
context: Mr Justice Mellor found that Wright had forged and backdated his documents; many showed forensic evidence of manipulated fonts and metadata inconsistent with claimed dates. Wright testified extensively; the ruling was not about incomplete or forgotten details but affirmative fabrication. Source: COPA v Wright judgment, 20 March 2024.

question: The COPA case against Craig Wright was brought by an alliance of technology and cryptocurrency companies formed specifically to defend open-source developers from patent lawsuits. The alliance's founding was heavily funded by one particular former Twitter CEO's payments-and-Bitcoin company. Which company?
context: COPA (Crypto Open Patent Alliance, launched 2020) was founded and heavily funded by Jack Dorsey's Square (renamed Block in 2021), which held Bitcoin on its balance sheet and pledged its Bitcoin patents. Tesla briefly held Bitcoin but is not a COPA founder; Palantir and Meta are unrelated. Source: https://open-crypto.com/about.

question: Before the COPA ruling, Craig Wright had already been on the losing end of a large civil verdict. In the 2021 Florida case Kleiman v Wright, the estate of his late business partner argued that partner had co-created Bitcoin with Wright. Roughly what damages did the Florida jury award against Wright?
context: The Kleiman v Wright jury (December 2021) awarded roughly $100 million against Wright's W&K Info Defense Research firm. The verdict declined to affirm Kleiman was Satoshi's partner. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: After the COPA ruling in 2024, the UK court took further action against Craig Wright related to his conduct during the case. What consequence has Wright faced since the ruling?
answer: he was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
choices: he was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
he was awarded costs and legal fees
he was granted permission to continue publishing as Satoshi
he was appointed to a Bitcoin standards committee
context: Following the March 2024 ruling, the court held Wright in contempt for repeated post-judgment claims and referred aspects of his conduct for possible criminal-prosecution consideration (perjury and forgery). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: A Bitcoin educator writing about the Craig Wright decade often presses one specific procedural claim about what the whole saga demonstrates about identity in a cryptographic system. Which reasoning move does that argument make?
answer: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only meaningful identity claim in a system whose entire security model rests on private-key signatures
choices: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only meaningful identity claim in a system whose entire security model rests on private-key signatures
That the courts alone should adjudicate who Satoshi is
That academic credentials and public speaking are the correct grounds for accepting an identity claim
That anonymous founders should be legally required to reveal themselves
context: The Bitcoin argument (Antonopoulos, Song, Kaminsky) is that in a system built on private-key signatures, the only relevant proof of any 'is-Satoshi' claim is a fresh signature -- courts and credentials cannot substitute for the primitive the system is built on. Legal-adjudication, credentialing, and forced-doxxing responses are precisely what the argument rejects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: The Cuban government gave the years 1990-1994 a specific official name after the Soviet Union collapsed and billions of dollars of annual subsidy vanished. What did Havana call the period?
answer: The Special Period in Time of Peace
choices: The Special Period in Time of Peace
context: In Spanish, 'Periodo Especial en Tiempo de Paz.' The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and its subsidy to Cuba (fuel at below-world-market prices, guaranteed sugar purchases at above-world prices) ended essentially overnight. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: Peer-reviewed public-health studies documented what happened to the average Cuban's body weight during the 1990-1993 collapse phase of the Special Period. What was the range of average weight loss?
context: Per-capita daily caloric intake fell from roughly 3,100 kcal in 1989 to roughly 1,900 kcal in 1993. The Special Period is one of the few modern rich-data natural experiments in what a fully price-controlled economy does when hit by a supply shock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: During the worst of the Special Period, meat became so scarce that a specific category of animal population in Havana collapsed, documented by ethnographers and journalists. Which population?
context: Some pets were eaten; many others starved or were abandoned. Zoo animals faced similar pressure. The pet-population collapse became one of the visible human-scale markers of how deep the caloric shock had gone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: During the Special Period, Cuba KEPT its central-planning apparatus (price controls, the libreta rationing system, state distribution). But it ALLOWED a set of specific market openings that began the slow recovery. Which pair of openings?
answer: Small-plot urban agriculture (organoponicos) and legalized self-employment plus 1993 limited dollarization
choices: Small-plot urban agriculture (organoponicos) and legalized self-employment plus 1993 limited dollarization
Full price liberalization and privatization of state enterprises
Withdrawal from the socialist bloc and entry into NAFTA
Return to the pre-1959 pre-revolutionary property regime
context: The recovery lever was NOT more planning; it was permitting Cubans to grow and sell food and hold dollars. Where the market was let in, calories followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: A high-school student asks why the 1990-93 Cuban caloric collapse is more useful to economists than, say, wartime famines. A Mises-influenced analyst points to a specific feature that makes it a rare natural experiment. Which feature?
answer: The Soviet subsidy simply vanished while everything else (planning apparatus, US embargo, weather) stayed constant
choices: The Soviet subsidy simply vanished while everything else (planning apparatus, US embargo, weather) stayed constant
The US Congress passed a new embargo law timed to the Soviet collapse
A drought and locust plague coincided with the Soviet withdrawal
Cuba's rainfall changed dramatically during the period
context: The US embargo had been in place since 1962; weather was normal; the planning apparatus was retained. The subsidy loss isolates central planning's ability (or inability) to adapt to a supply shock. This is Mises's 1920 calculation-debate prediction played out in body-weight units. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cuba%E2%80%93Soviet_Union_relations.

question: In 1993 Fidel Castro himself publicly acknowledged the caloric collapse in a series of speeches. What did he blame for the shortage?
answer: The US trade embargo, not the retained central-planning apparatus
choices: The US trade embargo, not the retained central-planning apparatus
The Soviet Union's decision to end the subsidy
context: The embargo had been in place since 1962; the collapse was specifically timed to the 1991 subsidy loss. The rhetorical move blamed a constant factor for a variable outcome. The 1993 recovery began precisely when Cuba legalized the organoponicos and self-employment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: An American cryptographer often called the father of digital cash invented a technique in 1982 that lets a bank sign a digital coin without knowing what serial number is on the coin -- making the resulting money anonymous by design. Which mathematician was that?
context: David Chaum invented blind signatures in 1982. Diffie co-invented public-key cryptography (1976); Rivest is the R in RSA; Merkle developed hash trees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Chaum.

question: In 1989 David Chaum founded a company in the Netherlands to sell his blind-signature invention as an anonymous digital-cash system. In which European city was the company headquartered?
context: DigiCash was founded in Amsterdam in 1989 and operated from there through the mid-1990s. Zurich, London, and Berlin were homes of other 1990s payment and cryptography ventures but not DigiCash. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: The specific cryptographic technique that let DigiCash issue digital coins anonymously -- the bank could confirm a coin was genuine without knowing which customer received it -- has a distinctive name. What is the technique called?
context: Blind signatures (Chaum 1982) let a signer authenticate a message whose contents are hidden from them. Ring signatures (Rivest, Shamir, Tauman 2001) provide sender-anonymity from a group; Schnorr signatures are a different signing scheme; elliptic-curve is a mathematical family used by many signature schemes including Bitcoin's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_signature.

question: DigiCash was cryptographically excellent -- provably anonymous and unforgeable in the 1990s -- yet by 1998 the company had filed for bankruptcy. Which structural feature of DigiCash's design was the fatal weakness that cypherpunks would spend the next decade trying to remove?
answer: the system required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins
choices: the system required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins
the underlying blind-signature math was later found broken
the anonymity was only partial and revealed users to the bank
the coins could only be used inside the Netherlands
context: DigiCash's anonymity was strong but issuance still required a partnered bank; without one, no coins. That single trusted issuer became the point of failure. The blind-signature math held up; the design achieved bank-facing anonymity; DigiCash worked across borders. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In the mid-1990s the world's largest software company reportedly offered DigiCash a nine-figure sum to integrate its anonymous digital cash into a shipping operating system. Which company made the offer to David Chaum?
context: Bill Gates and Microsoft reportedly offered David Chaum a nine-figure sum -- widely cited as either $100M or $180M -- to license DigiCash for Windows 95 integration. Chaum turned it down. Apple, Sun, and IBM had adjacent ambitions but did not make the specific DigiCash offer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: Beyond the Microsoft approach, at least two other major companies offered DigiCash licensing or acquisition deals in the mid-1990s -- one a browser company, one a payment-card network. Which pair also reportedly made offers Chaum declined?
context: In addition to Microsoft, Netscape (the dominant early web-browser company) and Visa made offers Chaum declined. MasterCard, AOL, Amex, Yahoo, and Diners Club are commonly asked about but were not the specific ones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: David Chaum's DigiCash filed for bankruptcy in November 1998 -- the very same month one cypherpunk posted a decentralized-cash design that specifically eliminated the trusted issuer DigiCash had needed. Which 1998 proposal shared that month?
context: Wei Dai posted b-money on the cypherpunk list in November 1998 -- the same month DigiCash's bankruptcy filing. Hashcash was 1997; Szabo's bit gold was drafted 1998 (posted later); Finney's RPOW came in 2004. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: The lesson the cypherpunk community drew from DigiCash's failure has one specific technical form. Which reasoning move did figures like Wei Dai, Nick Szabo, and later Satoshi Nakamoto press about any anonymous-cash design that depends on a bank?
answer: even brilliantly-designed anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted, or shut down
choices: even brilliantly-designed anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted, or shut down
cryptography is inherently unsuited to money and every attempt at digital cash must always fail regardless of the design of the surrounding system
anonymous digital cash requires explicit government backing to succeed because private customers will never trust a purely mathematical monetary system
cash must be physical to be trusted; every attempt to build purely electronic money fails because ordinary users refuse to accept intangible balances
context: The DigiCash lesson (Dai, Szabo, Nakamoto) was that removing the trusted issuer was the central task -- because whoever ran issuance had a single point of business failure. The other options are the opposite of what the cypherpunks concluded. Source: Nakamoto white paper 2008 sec 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: A close reader of the 2008 Bitcoin white paper argues that Satoshi did not merely improve DigiCash -- he specifically removed the one piece that had killed it. Which architectural piece did Bitcoin design out of the system that DigiCash could not do without?
answer: the trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency
choices: the trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency
the requirement for cryptographic signatures on transactions
the concept of an anonymous unit of value
the concept of a fixed unit denominations
context: Bitcoin retains signatures, anonymous (pseudonymous) value units, and fixed denominations; the piece it removed is the trusted issuer -- issuance is by proof-of-work; validation is by a distributed network. Source: Nakamoto white paper 2008 sec 1-4.

question: An economist looking back at DigiCash's fate presses one specific lesson about what really killed the company -- a claim about the relative importance of technical brilliance and system design in monetary innovation. Which move does the argument press?
answer: the operator of any trusted issuer, no matter how brilliant, can tank the whole project through ordinary business decisions
choices: the operator of any trusted issuer, no matter how brilliant, can tank the whole project through ordinary business decisions
the mathematics of blind signatures was fundamentally too slow for real commerce
the users of digital cash lacked the education to adopt any technology in the 1990s
the internet was too small to support any digital payment system before 2000
context: The DigiCash argument (Ammous, Antonopoulos, and Bitcoin historians) is that Chaum's turning down the Microsoft/Netscape/Visa offers -- an ordinary business choice -- was fatal to the whole system. The other options are widely-refuted alternative theories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: In 1973 Harper & Row published a book by an American economist that has since become the most widely-read English introduction to anarcho-capitalist system design. The author was the son of Milton Friedman. Who was he, and what was the book called?
answer: David D. Friedman; 'The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism'
choices: David D. Friedman; 'The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism'
Milton Friedman Jr.; 'Free to Choose: A Personal Statement'
context: David Friedman was born February 12, 1945, the son of Milton and Rose Director Friedman. He took his PhD in theoretical physics (Chicago, 1971) before crossing into economics and law. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: David Friedman's political-economic position differs from his father Milton Friedman's in a specific and important way. What is the difference?
answer: David is an anarcho-capitalist (no state at all); Milton was a classical liberal (minimal state)
choices: David is an anarcho-capitalist (no state at all); Milton was a classical liberal (minimal state)
David is a democratic socialist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a monarchist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a technocratic centrist; Milton was a classical liberal
context: Milton Friedman defended a minimal state (national defense, courts, some social insurance). David Friedman argues no state is necessary at all, with all such functions in principle providable by competing private firms. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: 'The Machinery of Freedom' walks the reader through specific institutional designs for functions usually provided by the state -- private protection agencies with subscription contracts, arbitration firms providing courts, private money issuance, road firms charging tolls. What is David Friedman's core methodological move?
answer: Describe HOW specific mechanisms would work and let the reader evaluate the design
choices: Describe HOW specific mechanisms would work and let the reader evaluate the design
Argue from natural rights that the state is inherently illegitimate
Prove mathematically that no state can ever be efficient
Chronicle historical cases of state failure without proposing alternatives
context: Friedman insists on institutional specifics rather than doctrinal claims. Chapters like 'How Would Private Law Enforcement Really Work?' walk through the contract-and-arbitration architecture with realistic edge cases. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: David Friedman argues for anarcho-capitalism on a specific philosophical ground that distinguishes his position from Murray Rothbard's argument for the same conclusion. What is the ground?
answer: Consequentialism -- anarcho-capitalism would produce better outcomes for most people most of the time
choices: Consequentialism -- anarcho-capitalism would produce better outcomes for most people most of the time
Natural rights -- the state inherently violates property rights
Divine command -- the state is forbidden by religious scripture
Aesthetic preference -- the state is inelegant as a system
context: Rothbard defended the same conclusion from natural rights (the state as an inherent violator of self-ownership). Friedman's consequentialist framing lets the reader compare outcomes without accepting the underlying rights premise. The distinction matters inside libertarian debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: David Friedman co-authored a 2019 book examining real historical and contemporary legal systems that operated without a monopoly state -- Somali xeer law, Icelandic saga-age law, Jewish rabbinical courts, Amish law, prison-gang law, Roma law, Comanche law. What was the book called and who were his co-authors?
answer: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
choices: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
'Free to Choose,' with Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
'The Constitution of Liberty,' with Friedrich Hayek
'The Sovereign Individual,' with James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg
context: Peter Leeson is a George Mason University economist; David Skarbek is a Brown University political scientist. The book presents these historical cases as natural experiments in the decentralized private legal architecture 'The Machinery of Freedom' described in theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: The Friedman family constitutes a three-generation libertarian intellectual line. Milton and Rose Director produced David; David produced a son who founded a specific 2008 organization dedicated to floating experimental communities in international waters. What was David's son's project?
answer: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
choices: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
Patri Friedman founded the Institute for Justice
Patri Friedman founded the Cato Institute
Patri Friedman founded the American Enterprise Institute
context: The Seasteading Institute proposes floating city-states on the high seas as a physical experiment in the polycentric governance David Friedman describes in theory. The Institute was funded early by Peter Thiel. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Patri_Friedman.

question: The third edition of 'The Machinery of Freedom' (2014) made David Friedman's book available in a distinctive way that the earlier editions had not. What was the specific change?
answer: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
choices: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
It was translated into every major world language simultaneously
It was published exclusively as an audio book
It was released only through university-press subscriptions
context: Consistent with the book's political stance, Friedman made the third edition freely downloadable. Any curious reader with internet access can read the complete text at no cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: A 1931 federal statute requires that construction projects funded by the US federal government pay 'prevailing local wages' as determined by the Department of Labor. What is the statute called?
context: The Davis-Bacon Act 1931 (sponsored by Rep. Robert Bacon R-NY and Sen. James Davis R-PA) has been the AFL-CIO's core piece of federal-project protection for 90 years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: In practice the Department of Labor's prevailing-wage survey process defaults to a specific reference wage in most US metropolitan areas. Which reference wage does the survey default to?
choices: The Bureau of Labor Statistics median
context: The DOL wage-survey process defaults to the union scale in most metropolitan areas, making Davis-Bacon a de-facto union-wage protection on federally-funded projects. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: Empirical estimates from the Beacon Hill Institute and the Congressional Budget Office put a specific cost premium on federal construction under Davis-Bacon rules relative to comparable state or private work. What is the estimated premium range?
context: A 10-15% cost premium on federal construction translates to roughly $100-180 billion on the $1.2 trillion 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act alone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: The 1931 Congressional Record contains explicit statements from Davis-Bacon's supporters framing the bill as excluding a specific group of migrant workers from federal jobsites. Which group did the sponsors' statements target?
context: The 1931 debate shows sponsors explicit that the point was to keep Southern Black workers, who had been migrating north to compete for federal-project work at lower wages, off federal jobsites. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: Representative Robert Bacon's own words during the 1931 House debate spelled out his explicit motive for excluding lower-wage migrant workers. Which line did he speak on the House floor?
answer: Colored labor is being brought in to demoralize wage rates
choices: Colored labor is being brought in to demoralize wage rates
The southern states must build their own hospitals
Union labor is the only safe federal contractor
Immigration must be halted for national security
context: Bacon's 1931 House-floor statement is on the Congressional Record; the racial-exclusion motive was overt, and the Act retains that exclusionary effect even after the framing was dropped. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: Bastiat's method surfaces the two-sided political-economy pattern of Davis-Bacon most cleanly using a specific 1965 book's framework. Which two-sided pattern applies?
answer: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
choices: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
Concentrated benefit to taxpayers, dispersed cost to unions
Uniform benefit and uniform cost across the population
Concentrated benefit to foreign contractors, dispersed cost to domestic firms
context: Mancur Olson's Logic of Collective Action (1965) explains the pattern: organized construction unions capture the concentrated benefit while every federal-project taxpayer bears a small share of the dispersed cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: A Cato Institute economist has been the most persistent modern reformer arguing for Davis-Bacon repeal on cost, efficiency, and equity grounds. Who is he?
context: Chris Edwards at Cato has published Policy Analyses on Davis-Bacon in the 2010s and 2020s calling for repeal. Source: cato.org/blog/davis-bacon-inflates-federal-construction-costs.

question: By the mid-1960s the United States was running deficits to fund two major programs at once, and the dollar was becoming overvalued at the $35-per-ounce Bretton Woods peg. Which pair of American programs was straining the peg?
answer: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
choices: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
the Korean War and the Marshall Plan
the Cold War missile buildup and the Interstate Highway System
the Iraq War and the Bush tax cuts
context: The 1960s fiscal pressures came from Vietnam War spending and Johnson's Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty). Korea/Marshall Plan (1950s), missile buildup/highways (1950s), and Iraq/Bush tax cuts (2000s) are the wrong eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: In February 1965 the President of France used a press conference to denounce what he called the 'exorbitant privilege' that the dollar gave the United States -- and to announce his country would systematically convert its dollar reserves to gold at the $35 peg. Which French leader made the speech?
context: Charles de Gaulle, French President 1959-69, made the February 1965 press conference challenging the dollar peg. Pompidou succeeded him; Giscard was his finance minister at the time; Mitterrand came to the presidency in 1981. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle.

question: The phrase 'exorbitant privilege' -- widely associated with Charles de Gaulle's 1965 speech -- was actually coined by his Finance Minister, who later became President of France himself. Which minister coined the phrase?
context: Giscard d'Estaing coined 'exorbitant privilege' in his role as de Gaulle's finance minister; he later served as President 1974-81. De Gaulle used the phrase publicly but did not originate it. Chirac and Mitterrand were later French presidents unrelated to the coinage. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: The 'exorbitant privilege' that the dollar peg gave the United States captured a specific asymmetry between the US and every other country. Which asymmetry did the phrase describe?
answer: the US could import goods and pay in newly-printed dollars that other countries had to hold
choices: the US could import goods and pay in newly-printed dollars that other countries had to hold
the US could impose tariffs without any WTO review
the US could veto UN Security Council decisions
the US could station troops in foreign countries without permission
context: The asymmetry: the US paid for imports in dollars that were the world's reserve currency, so foreign banks accumulated dollar reserves -- effectively lending the US real goods in exchange for paper claims. Tariffs, Security Council vetoes, and troop stationing are separate political privileges. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: During 1965 alone, in France's opening move against the dollar peg, France converted a specific dollar-reserve amount into physical gold at the $35 peg. Roughly how much did France convert that first year?
context: France converted about $150 million of dollar reserves to gold in 1965. Larger conversions followed over the next several years; other central banks followed France's lead more quietly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: The physical gold France was reclaiming from the United States in the mid-1960s was held in a specific New York vault -- one of the world's largest gold repositories, located in the bedrock of lower Manhattan. Which vault?
answer: the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's gold vault at 33 Liberty Street
choices: the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's gold vault at 33 Liberty Street
the New York Stock Exchange's basement vault
context: Foreign central-bank gold is held in the New York Fed's vault at 33 Liberty Street, dug into Manhattan bedrock. Fort Knox holds US-owned gold; NYSE has no gold vault; West Point Mint stores US bullion but does not warehouse foreign central-bank reserves. Source: https://www.newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/goldvault.html.

question: To hold the $35 peg against rising private gold demand, eight Western central banks pooled their gold reserves in 1961 as a defensive mechanism, selling into any private-market run to keep the price down. What was this pool called?
context: The London Gold Pool (1961-68) coordinated 8 central banks (USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland). The other names are fabrications. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: France withdrew from the London Gold Pool in June 1967, weakening the defense of the $35 peg. When did the remaining Pool members finally give up and dissolve the arrangement?
context: The London Gold Pool was dissolved March 17, 1968 after the remaining members had lost so much gold defending the peg that they gave up; a two-tier market emerged (official $35 for central banks, market price for private buyers). Nixon closed the gold window August 15, 1971; October 24, 1929 was Black Thursday; September 19, 1985 was the Plaza Accord. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: After the March 1968 collapse of the London Gold Pool, gold traded at two different prices at once -- the official $35 peg used for central-bank redemptions and a separate market-determined price for private buyers. What is this arrangement called in monetary history?
context: A two-tier gold market means official ($35 for central banks) and free-market prices coexist. Bimetallism uses both silver and gold; a currency board pegs a national currency to a foreign one; 'fiat peg' is not a standard term. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: A Bastiat-pattern retelling of the 1965-68 gold drain presses one specific reasoning move about what de Gaulle's action actually revealed rather than caused. Which move does the argument make about the peg's condition BEFORE France tested it?
answer: That once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was arithmetically impossible to sustain and would break the moment any large holder tested it
choices: That once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was arithmetically impossible to sustain and would break the moment any large holder tested it
That the peg would have held indefinitely if France had shown more solidarity with the United States and had refrained from redeeming its dollar reserves for gold
That the peg's collapse was purely a matter of speculative attack by private market participants unrelated to the underlying arithmetic of US reserves against issuance
That the Bretton Woods peg was a political fiction that had never really existed in practice and only appeared to work because no country had tried to redeem before France
context: The Bastiat 'seen vs unseen' move: SEEN, a stable peg; UNSEEN, the arithmetic that once dollar issuance had outrun gold reserves, the peg was already dead and only needed testing. De Gaulle was the tester, not the cause. The other options misidentify the mechanism. Source: Rothbard; Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Frederic Bastiat died on a specific holiday eve of 1850, aged 49, in an Italian city where he had traveled hoping the warmer climate would ease his tuberculosis. On which day of the year did he die?
context: Bastiat died December 24, 1850 in Rome, at 49, of tuberculosis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The Italian city where Bastiat spent his final months in September-December 1850, and where he died, was the capital of the Papal States at the time. Which city was it?
context: Bastiat arrived in Rome in September 1850 hoping the warmer air would restore his failing throat and lungs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: During his final months Bastiat continued to work from his Roman sickroom on the page proofs of a book he did not live to finish. What book was he correcting?
context: Harmonies economiques, Bastiat's one attempt at a positive systematic theory, was being corrected and expanded from the sickroom right up to his death. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: After Bastiat's death, a specific friend edited the incomplete Economic Harmonies into an expanded 1851 second edition, adding fragments from Bastiat's papers. Who edited that expanded edition?
context: Prosper Paillottet, a close friend and Bastiat's chosen editor, prepared the expanded 1851 Economic Harmonies from Bastiat's manuscripts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat is buried in a specific Renaissance church in Rome that serves as the French national church there and stands near Piazza Navona. What is the church's name?
context: San Luigi dei Francesi (Saint Louis of the French) is the French national church in Rome. A memorial plaque marks Bastiat's tomb inside. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: San Luigi dei Francesi is also famous for holding three paintings of the life of Saint Matthew, completed 1599-1600, by a specific Italian Baroque master. Which artist painted them?
context: Caravaggio's Contarelli Chapel cycle (The Calling, The Inspiration, and The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew), 1599-1600, in San Luigi dei Francesi, are among the most-visited paintings in Rome. Source: grokipedia.com/page/San_Luigi_dei_Francesi.

question: Bastiat lived exactly 49 years, born in Bayonne on June 30 of a specific year and dying in Rome on December 24, 1850. In what year was he born?
context: Bastiat was born June 30, 1801 in Bayonne, France, and died December 24, 1850 in Rome. His enormous public output was compressed into the last five years of his life. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Between 1800 and today, real per-capita income in Western countries has risen by roughly 3,000 percent. A Chicago-trained economic historian argues that capital, institutions, and geography cannot explain WHEN or WHERE that Great Enrichment happened. Which historian is best known for pressing that argument in a three-book series?
context: Deirdre McCloskey (born September 11, 1942) is a Chicago-trained economic historian who taught at the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois at Chicago. Her Bourgeois Trilogy pressed the culture-of-innovation thesis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: Deirdre McCloskey's three-volume study of the modern world's economic explosion, published by the University of Chicago Press between 2006 and 2016, is collectively known by what name?
context: The Bourgeois Trilogy comprises The Bourgeois Virtues (2006), Bourgeois Dignity (2010), and Bourgeois Equality (2016), all from University of Chicago Press. Source: press.uchicago.edu (author page, Deirdre McCloskey).

question: The middle volume of Deirdre McCloskey's trilogy, published by Chicago in 2010, uses its subtitle to press a bold claim against the standard growth story. What is that subtitle?
answer: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
choices: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
Institutions and the Wealth of Nations
context: Bourgeois Dignity: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World (Chicago 2010). The provocation is that the standard economic inputs (capital, geography, institutions) do not account for the timing and place of the Great Enrichment. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo8474162.html.

question: The third volume of Deirdre McCloskey's Bourgeois Trilogy, published by Chicago in 2016, names the driver of modern wealth right in its subtitle. Which subtitle appears on the cover?
answer: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
choices: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
The Rise of the Middle Class in Northwestern Europe
Merchants, Inventors, and the Industrial Revolution
context: Bourgeois Equality: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World (Chicago 2016). The subtitle is McCloskey's thesis in one sentence -- IDEAS about the merchant and inventor, not stocks of capital or formal rules, produced the modern world. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo22269023.html.

question: Deirdre McCloskey names a specific cultural shift in Northwestern Europe between roughly 1600 and 1800 as the missing ingredient in the standard growth story. In her account, what began to receive new moral respect during that shift?
context: McCloskey argues that before roughly 1600, aristocratic and clerical cultures held merchants and inventors in contempt. After the shift, businesspeople acquired dignity, and millions of ordinary people started trying to invent things. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (2010), introduction.

question: McCloskey names her one-word summary of the missing ingredient in the standard explanation for the modern world's economic takeoff. Which word does the title of her 2010 volume put at the center of that story?
context: Bourgeois Dignity (2010) argues that once innovation and trade were DIGNIFIED in ordinary talk and public rhetoric, ordinary people started innovating in earnest. It is a rhetoric-and-culture story, not a capital-and-institutions story. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: A student objects that McCloskey's cultural story simply throws out property rights and formal institutions. McCloskey's actual position is more careful. Which best describes her stance toward institutional-economics explanations?
answer: The cultural dignity of innovation COMPLEMENTS institutions rather than replacing them
choices: The cultural dignity of innovation COMPLEMENTS institutions rather than replacing them
Institutions are a purely illusory factor with no growth effect
Institutions matter only in societies that never industrialized
Institutional analysis should be abandoned in favor of pure rhetoric studies
context: McCloskey's move is to argue that the SAME capital and institutions that produced Ming stagnation produced British industrial takeoff -- because the CULTURE around the merchant differed. She adds a missing input, she does not remove the others. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Equality (Chicago 2016), preface.

question: Before her later career as an economic historian, Deirdre McCloskey wrote a 1985 book on how economists actually argue and persuade -- their metaphors, stories, and appeals to authority. Which title did that book take?
context: The Rhetoric of Economics (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985) opened the field of rhetorical study of economic writing and argued that economists persuade each other by narrative and metaphor as much as by proofs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: The reasoning move at the heart of the Bourgeois Trilogy compares two societies with similar formal inputs but very different outcomes. Which pair best illustrates the puzzle McCloskey pushes economists to explain?
answer: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
choices: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
Roman North Africa's decline versus medieval Italy's revival
Iberian empires' silver imports versus Dutch banking innovation
Ottoman guild economies versus Persian bazaars
context: McCloskey argues that Ming China had comparable capital, technology, and formal institutions to early-modern Britain -- but the culture around the merchant differed. Same inputs, different cultural legitimation, opposite outcomes. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: In the Bastiat pattern of SEEN and UNSEEN, McCloskey's argument identifies a specific UNSEEN factor that made the SEEN inputs (capital, institutions, geography) actually productive. Which factor does she name as the missing UNSEEN?
answer: The cultural legitimation of the merchant-inventor
choices: The cultural legitimation of the merchant-inventor
The concentration of gold and silver bullion
The centralization of political authority in nation-states
The technical superiority of European engineering guilds
context: McCloskey's reasoning move: the SEEN is capital and institutions and geography; the UNSEEN is the cultural dignity of the merchant and inventor. Without that legitimation, the same seen inputs stagnate. With it, they compound into the Great Enrichment. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Equality (Chicago 2016).

question: A high-school student asks how big the Great Enrichment actually was -- how much real income growth are we talking about, per person, across the roughly two centuries since 1800 in the countries that industrialized first? Which figure does McCloskey use as her headline number?
context: The 3,000-percent figure (roughly 30x) is the standard estimate from Angus Maddison and OECD historical statistics for real per-capita income growth in Western countries since 1800. McCloskey uses it as the puzzle to explain. Source: Maddison Project Database (2020 update); McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: In late 1929 Joseph Stalin gave a speech announcing a policy of erasing an entire class of Soviet peasants -- defined not by anything they had done but by owning a horse or hiring a farmhand. What was the Russian word for the targeted class?
context: 'Kulak' (Russian for 'fist') was Soviet propaganda's label for any peasant slightly more prosperous than his neighbors. Stalin's December 27, 1929 speech to a conference of agrarian Marxists made kulak-status a target category for erasure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: In his December 1929 speech Stalin used a specific chilling phrase for the treatment of the wealthier peasantry -- a phrase that became notorious. What was the phrase?
answer: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
choices: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
context: The phrase 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class' (likvidatsiya kulachestva kak klassa) was delivered at the December 27, 1929 conference and formalized in a Politburo decree of January 30, 1930. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: On January 30, 1930 the Politburo formalized the anti-kulak campaign by sorting targeted families into three categories with different treatments. What was the sorting into three groups meant to do?
context: The Politburo's January 30, 1930 decree sorted kulak families: category one shot, category two deported to the far north / Siberia / Kazakhstan, category three resettled locally on marginal land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: Over 1930-32 the state acted at scale on the anti-kulak order. Roughly how many alleged kulaks were deported to Siberia, Kazakhstan, and the far north in cattle wagons?
context: About 30,000 alleged kulaks were shot; about 2 million were deported to the far north, Siberia, and Kazakhstan; another 4-5 million were dispossessed of property and reassigned. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (Oxford UP, 2007).

question: The mechanism-purpose of dekulakization was not just class-warfare theater. What was the specific tactical purpose the campaign served for the collectivization drive that followed?
answer: It removed the most experienced farmers so collective farms would face no organized resistance
choices: It removed the most experienced farmers so collective farms would face no organized resistance
It freed land for state ecological reserves
It provided cash reserves for industrial imports
It filled quotas for Red Army recruitment
context: The most competent farmers were destroyed because they were the most competent. The villages that remained had lost their most capable people BEFORE the 1932-33 famine hit -- a mechanism the Holodomor then exploited. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: The deportation flow fed the fast-growing Soviet camp system and required a new category of settlements to hold deported peasant families. What agency built and administered those settlements?
choices: The Red Army Corps of Engineers
context: The OGPU (unified state political directorate, renamed NKVD in 1934) built 'special settlements' in Siberia and the Urals to hold deported kulak families. Winter 1931-32 death rates in these settlements ran to hundreds of thousands. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (2007).

question: Contemporary agents and local officials expanded the meaning of the label so elastically that any peasant who resisted joining a collective farm could be reclassified. What did local activists call this reclassification move?
choices: Registering them as a class enemy
context: 'Unmasking' (razoblachenie) redefined kulak-status as anyone who resisted collectivization. The label became a catch-all administrative tool for eliminating opposition. Source: Fitzpatrick, Stalin's Peasants (1994).

question: The standard modern archival monograph on the special-settlement system that held deported kulak families is by an American historian at the University of Toronto and was published by Oxford in 2007. Which historian?
context: Lynne Viola's The Unknown Gulag (Oxford, 2007) uses newly opened OGPU archives to reconstruct the settlement system for deported peasants. Fitzpatrick, Conquest, and Applebaum work on adjacent Soviet-terror topics. Source: global.oup.com.

question: Dekulakization is the mechanism that made a specific 1932-33 catastrophe possible by removing agricultural competence from the villages first. What was that catastrophe?
context: With the most productive farmers gone, forced grain requisitions in 1932-33 stripped Ukrainian villages of their remaining food. The resulting famine killed several million Ukrainians. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: The Bastiat-style seen-versus-unseen reading of dekulakization: the visible move was 'expropriating rich peasants for social justice'. What was the unseen cost the villages bore in the following years?
answer: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
choices: The permanent loss of agricultural competence and the famine that followed
An inflation in the price of textiles
A drop in industrial productivity in Moscow
context: The Bastiat move: the SEEN was 'redistributing kulak property'; the UNSEEN was the collapse of village agricultural knowledge (which farmer knew which fields, which seed variety, which threshing techniques) and the famine that used the resulting vulnerability. Source: mises.org/library/theft-of-a-nation-holodomor.

question: In October 1976 a 77-year-old Austrian economist published a short London pamphlet proposing that governments give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete for consumers. Which economist wrote it?
context: Hayek (1899-1992) had won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics two years earlier, in 1974, sharing it with Gunnar Myrdal. The 1976 pamphlet was the most radical monetary proposal of his career. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 monetary pamphlet was published in London as Hobart Paper Special 70 by a policy institute founded by Antony Fisher on Hayek's own advice. Which institute published it?
context: The IEA, founded 1955, is Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank; Hayek personally counselled Antony Fisher to start it after Fisher read The Road to Serfdom. The Cato Institute (1977) and Adam Smith Institute (1977) did not yet exist. The Mont Pelerin Society is a scholarly society, not a publisher. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet made a single radical monetary proposal. What did he propose that governments do?
answer: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
choices: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
Return to a fixed exchange rate anchored on a single ounce of gold
Adopt a common global reserve currency issued by the International Monetary Fund
Delegate all monetary policy to an independent panel of academic economists
context: Hayek argued money is no different from any other good: competition between private issuers, checked by consumer choice, would supply it better than a state monopoly. The proposal was radical enough that even fellow Austrian economists mostly rejected it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet carried a full title naming the historical practice it studied. Which full title did it carry?
answer: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
choices: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies
The Constitution of Liberty: A Restatement of the Principles of a Free Society
The Fatal Conceit: A Study of the Errors of Socialism from Marx to the Present
Prices and Production: Four Lectures Delivered at the University of London
context: 'Concurrent currencies' referred to the historical episodes, such as pre-Civil-War American free banking or private banknote issuance in nineteenth-century Scotland, in which several currencies circulated together. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's diagnosis in the 1976 pamphlet rested on a claim about the historical track record of every fiat currency ever issued by a sovereign monopoly. What was the pattern he pointed to?
answer: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
choices: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
Every such currency has appreciated against gold across the twentieth century
Every such currency has stabilized once its central bank became independent
Every such currency has held value so long as its government retained a fiscal surplus
context: Hayek's examples ran from the Roman denarius under Diocletian to the Weimar mark of 1923 to modern post-war fiat currencies. His conclusion was that debasement is not a scandal but the predictable equilibrium of a monopoly issuer facing short-run political incentives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet answered the natural objection 'but how would competing private currencies stay honest?' with a specific mechanism. Which discipline did he say would keep them honest?
answer: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
choices: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
Government auditors inspecting each issuer's reserve ratios annually
International treaty obligations enforced through the World Bank
A gold-parity peg required by domestic constitutional law
context: Hayek's mechanism was identical to the market discipline any producer faces. Issuers whose currency lost purchasing power would see it refused in commerce, lose deposits, and fail; issuers who kept it stable would win business. No government auditor, treaty, or peg was needed. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/hayeks-plan-private-money.

question: In 1978 Friedrich Hayek published a revised and enlarged second edition of Denationalisation of Money under a subtitle marking the update. Which subtitle did it carry?
choices: A Sequel to the Road to Serfdom
context: In the second edition Hayek added the speculation that a free monetary market would not sustain an unmanageable number of currencies but would converge on a limited number of stable standards. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1976 proposal for competing private fiat currencies was rejected even by his fellow Austrian economist Murray Rothbard, who insisted on a different requirement for any free-market money. What did Rothbard require?
answer: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
choices: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
That the currency circulate only within a single sovereign jurisdiction
That the currency be issued exclusively by chartered depository institutions
That the currency be redeemable at par into government-issued specie
context: Rothbard remained a strict commodity-money advocate: free banking, yes, but the notes had to be redeemable claims on a real commodity such as gold. On this account Hayek's proposal for competing PAPER currencies with no commodity backing was more radical than Rothbard would go. Source: cameronharwick.com/writing/hayek-vs-rothbard-on-money.

question: A high-school student reads Hayek's 1976 pamphlet and asks 'why single out MONEY for competition? Why not government-supplied bread or telephones?' Which of Hayek's Austrian-tradition reasoning moves gives the answer?
answer: Money is no different in principle; consumer choice supplies bread and telephones better too, so the burden of proof runs the other way
choices: Money is no different in principle; consumer choice supplies bread and telephones better too, so the burden of proof runs the other way
Money is uniquely a natural monopoly because network effects concentrate one currency in any region
Money is a public good in the strict economic sense because no user can be excluded from its price signal
Money's value depends on macroeconomic aggregates that only a central authority can measure
context: The Austrian methodological move: reject the special-pleading claim that money is uniquely unsuited to markets. Hayek argued the same competitive discipline that improves other goods would improve currency; the burden falls on defenders of the state monopoly to say why money is the exception. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Bitcoin advocates such as Saifedean Ammous credit Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet as intellectual grandfather of their project. Which specific engineering move made Bitcoin an implementation Hayek did not have available in 1976?
answer: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
choices: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
A gold-parity peg administered by an international clearinghouse
A one-to-one deposit-insurance guarantee from a sovereign issuer
A statutory reserve requirement enforced by domestic banking regulators
context: Hayek imagined competing private BANKS disciplined by consumer refusal to hold debased notes; Bitcoin, launched thirty-three years later by Satoshi Nakamoto, hard-codes the discipline into the protocol itself with a 21-million-coin cap and a halving schedule no operator can override. Ammous's 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard makes the intellectual-descent argument explicit; the European Central Bank has publicly noted the same theoretical lineage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In December 1978 a Chinese Communist Party plenum turned the country away from Mao-era pure command economics and toward price-signaled markets. The program is called by a two-word Chinese phrase in translation. What is it usually rendered as?
context: Gaige kaifang -- Reform and Opening -- was launched at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee, December 18-22, 1978, under Deng Xiaoping. It ended pure central planning first in agriculture, then in industry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.

question: The Chinese leader whose faction won direction of the party in December 1978 and drove Reform and Opening had already survived being purged twice during the Mao years. Who was he?
context: Deng Xiaoping had been purged in 1966 and again in 1976. He returned to power in 1977 and by December 1978 had consolidated his faction's control. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: The first major reform of Reform and Opening reversed collectivization by restoring private plots to individual farming households, who could sell above-quota production at market prices. What was the system called?
context: The Household Responsibility System (baochan daohu) tested in Anhui in late 1978 (informally in Xiaogang village) then rolled out nationally by 1982-83. Households farmed their own plots and sold surplus at market. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: The Household Responsibility System was piloted informally in December 1978 by peasants of a specific village in Anhui province who secretly signed a contract dividing land plots among their families. Which village made the pact?
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed a secret agreement in December 1978 to divide land plots, pledging to raise each other's children if any were arrested. Local officials tolerated the pact after harvest yields rose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: The result of restoring market prices to Chinese agriculture in the late 1970s was immediate and startling. Roughly what happened to grain output between 1978 and 1984?
context: Chinese grain output rose about 34% from 1978 to 1984 on essentially the same land and labor -- once farmers again had market price signals to guide planting and keep the surplus. The famine memory of 1959-61 (36 million dead) was over within five years. Source: World Bank data.

question: The industrial reforms of the 1980s created foreign-investment zones with market-pricing rules, starting with four coastal locations in 1980. What are these zones called?
context: The first four SEZs were Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, and Xiamen (1980); Hainan Island became a fifth SEZ in 1988. Shenzhen grew from a fishing village of 30,000 to a metropolis of over 17 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China.

question: During the 1980s Chinese industrial reforms operated a hybrid arrangement in which state-planned quotas kept old prices while above-plan output could be sold at market rates. What is this scheme called?
context: Dual-track pricing (shuang gui zhi) let firms sell state quotas at planned prices and any additional output at market prices. This let market signals reach production margins without a shock discontinuation of the plan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual-track_pricing.

question: Deng gave the reform its most famous justification with an animal metaphor about the acceptability of pragmatic methods over ideological purity. What was the essence of his 'cat' saying?
answer: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
choices: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
The best cat sleeps by day and hunts by night
One cat is not enough for a granary of rats
Feed the cat with rice and it will forget the mice
context: Deng's black-cat-white-cat saying, from a 1961 speech he revived in the reform era, meant that empirical results should outweigh ideological purity. It became the shorthand slogan of Reform and Opening. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: Deng also gave the reform a caution about incremental method with a river metaphor -- meaning that policy should proceed by testing what works rather than by grand theoretical design. What is the phrase?
answer: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
choices: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
Climbing a mountain step by step
Planting a forest one seed at a time
Building a wall from small bricks
context: 'Mo zhe shi tou guo he' -- crossing the river by feeling the stones -- became a rule for the whole reform: experiment locally, adopt what works, avoid theoretical grand plans. Xiaogang, then Anhui, then nationally. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.
