question: For a Mises-Hayek reading, Reform and Opening was the largest natural experiment the calculation debate ever received. What is the standard World Bank measure of how many Chinese were lifted out of extreme poverty between 1981 and 2015?
context: World Bank data show roughly 800 million Chinese moved above the extreme-poverty line between 1981 and 2015 as market pricing extended sector by sector. This is the largest sustained poverty reduction ever measured. Source: worldbank.org China country data.

question: Austrian analysts observe that within China's post-1978 growth the fastest sectors were exactly those the state planned LEAST -- household agriculture, township enterprises, and the SEZs. What was slowest?
context: Chinese state-owned banks and SOEs continued to underperform the private and township-enterprise sectors through the 1990s and 2000s. The Austrian reading of Chinese growth attributes it to the market-priced sectors, not to state industrial policy. Source: mises.org/library/china-and-austrian-school.

question: Bitcoin's protocol is designed so that on average a new block is added to the chain every ten minutes. Individual blocks vary -- some come in one minute, some in thirty -- but the long-run average is fixed. Which mechanism keeps that average steady even as the number of miners on the network changes?
context: Every node in the Bitcoin network computes the difficulty target identically from the timestamps of recent blocks. It is Bitcoin's homeostatic clock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment runs on a fixed schedule: every N blocks, every node checks how long those N blocks took and turns the difficulty up or down. What is N?
context: 2,016 blocks equals two weeks at exactly ten minutes per block. The 210,000-block figure is the halving interval (roughly four years), a separate protocol constant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: If the last 2,016 Bitcoin blocks arrived faster than the target two weeks, the network automatically responds at the next retarget. What does it do?
answer: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
choices: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
Rewards existing miners with a one-time bonus in newly minted coin
Reduces the block-reward payout for the next 2,016 blocks
Sends a policy signal to the Federal Reserve to raise rates
context: The target hash gets a smaller numerical value, making valid hashes rarer. Miners then take longer per block on average, restoring the ten-minute cadence. If blocks had been slow, the adjustment goes the other way. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: In May and June 2021 China's central government banned Bitcoin mining, and roughly half the world's hashing power went offline within weeks. Blocks began arriving noticeably slower than every ten minutes. What did Bitcoin do next, without any human decision-maker?
answer: At the July 3 2021 retarget, difficulty dropped by roughly 28 percent -- the largest downward adjustment in Bitcoin's history
choices: At the July 3 2021 retarget, difficulty dropped by roughly 28 percent -- the largest downward adjustment in Bitcoin's history
The remaining miners voted to switch the algorithm to proof-of-stake
The Bitcoin Core developers issued an emergency patch changing the block interval
Coinbase paused all Bitcoin trading until the network recovered
context: Every node computed the adjustment independently and identically. Blocks returned to a ten-minute cadence immediately after the retarget. Chinese miners then physically relocated to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_China.

question: A high-school student asks how the Bitcoin network kept its ten-minute cadence in July 2021 when half the world's miners had just been forced offline. A Hayekian economist points to a specific systems property that no central bank possesses. Which property?
answer: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
choices: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
The discretionary override of a benevolent central authority
The one-off emergency bailout mechanism triggered by a supervisory committee
The centrally-planned reallocation of hashing capacity by a global regulator
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument is exactly this: no central agency could set the correct difficulty target in real time across a global mining industry it did not know intimately. A rule-based system aggregates the dispersed information automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: By March 2022, roughly nine months after the China mining ban and the subsequent difficulty crash, Bitcoin's total network hashing power had done what?
answer: Recovered to a new all-time high
choices: Recovered to a new all-time high
Remained roughly half of pre-ban levels
Fallen further as miners quit permanently
Migrated entirely to a single US state
context: Displaced Chinese miners physically shipped their hardware to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. The rule-based difficulty adjustment absorbed a 50-percent supply shock in weeks and then handled the recovery just as automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: In 301 AD a Roman emperor issued a wide-ranging edict capping the maximum prices for over 1,000 goods and services -- with the death penalty for sellers who charged more. Which emperor?
context: Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) is the earliest documented major price-control experiment. Fragments survive on stone in over 100 places across the eastern empire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: The penalty Diocletian's 301 AD edict prescribed for selling above the ceiling was the harshest imaginable. What was it?
context: The edict's own text prescribed death for sellers exceeding the fixed prices. Enforcement was uneven but the threat was real; the historian Lactantius records that 'much blood was shed for the sake of small and cheap things'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: The context for Diocletian's 301 edict was decades of imperial currency debasement -- the silver denarius had been minted with progressively less silver to pay the armies. In the edict's own preamble, whom did Diocletian blame for the price rises?
answer: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
choices: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
The Sassanid Persians for currency counterfeiting
The African provinces for hoarding grain
The Christian communities for boycotting Roman markets
context: The edict's preamble cursed sellers rather than acknowledging that the emperor's own mint had cheapened the coin. This is the emblematic 'blame the messenger' move in the history of price controls. Source: primary text of the Edict of Diocletian.

question: Within weeks of the edict's proclamation, a specific market phenomenon appeared across the empire. What was the immediate effect on shelves?
answer: Goods disappeared from the open market
choices: Goods disappeared from the open market
context: Sellers withdrew goods rather than sell at a loss. Merchants preferred to hoard, sell only to family, or move goods to black markets in other cities. The visible-shelf empty is the seen-versus-unseen result. Source: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors.

question: A contemporary Christian writer, Lactantius, recorded the edict's failure in his book 'On the Deaths of the Persecutors'. Roughly how long after the edict's proclamation was it quietly abandoned?
context: The edict was allowed to fall into disuse within roughly a decade. Diocletian himself abdicated in 305 AD -- the only Roman emperor to voluntarily step down. Source: Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum c. 315 AD.

question: The Bastiat-style seen-versus-unseen reading of Diocletian's edict: SEEN was the low legal price stamped on the tablet. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who now goes hungry
choices: The seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who now goes hungry
The tax revenue that continued to flow
The Roman legions that continued to be paid
The Byzantine trade that continued to flow
context: Bastiat's method applied 15 centuries earlier: the visible ceiling gives the illusion of low prices; the invisible cost is the goods that disappear because their sale at the ceiling would be at a loss. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Fragments of Diocletian's edict survive today on stone inscriptions across the eastern Mediterranean. Where is the most complete surviving copy?
context: Aphrodisias, in southwestern Turkey, has the fullest surviving copy of the edict inscribed on stone. Archaeologists reconstructed hundreds of specific price lines from the fragments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisias.

question: Modern Austrian economists (Rothbard, Sowell, others) treat Diocletian's edict as the founding case study of a specific recurring reasoning error. What is the error?
answer: Blame merchants for the price rises the government's own currency debasement caused
choices: Blame merchants for the price rises the government's own currency debasement caused
Assume that lowering prices raises supply
Believe that inflation is always transitory
context: The archetypal pattern: currency debasement raises prices; the state blames sellers; a ceiling is imposed; goods disappear; the ceiling is eventually withdrawn. This pattern recurs from 301 AD through modern hyperinflations. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: One long-lasting monument to Diocletian's rule -- built as his retirement palace after his 305 AD abdication -- still stands today, having been continuously inhabited for 17 centuries. Where is it?
context: Diocletian's Palace at Split (modern Croatia) has been continuously inhabited since 305 AD -- housing today's Old Town within its walls. UNESCO World Heritage site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian%27s_Palace.

question: On July 21, 2010, President Barack Obama signed the largest US financial regulatory overhaul since the New Deal, passed in response to the 2008 crisis. Under what name did the act become known?
context: Formally the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Pub. L. 111-203), named for Senate Banking chair Chris Dodd and House Financial Services chair Barney Frank. It ran over 800 pages and delegated hundreds of rulemakings to regulators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Dodd-Frank_Wall_Street_Reform_and_Consumer_Protection_Act.

question: The 2010 Dodd-Frank Act created a new federal agency to police everyday household borrowing products such as mortgages, credit cards, and payday loans. Which agency did it establish?
choices: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board
context: The CFPB was the signature institutional creation of Dodd-Frank, championed by then-Harvard-professor Elizabeth Warren. It absorbed consumer-protection authority previously spread across the Fed, OCC, FDIC and other agencies. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Consumer_Financial_Protection_Bureau.

question: One Dodd-Frank rule, named for a former Federal Reserve chairman, forbids federally insured banks from engaging in proprietary trading (betting the bank's own money on securities for its own profit). What is the rule called?
context: Named for Paul Volcker (Fed chairman 1979-87), who argued that banks with federal deposit insurance should not be running hedge-fund-style trading books. The rule took years to finalize and became a byword for the compliance-cost burden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Volcker_Rule.

question: The number of US commercial banks stood at roughly 7,000 in 2010, the year Dodd-Frank passed. According to FDIC banking-industry data cited by a 2022 Congressional Research Service report, roughly how many US commercial banks were left by 2023?
context: A decline of roughly one third in thirteen years. Consolidation into regional and money-center banks accelerated after 2010; most community banks were acquired rather than closed. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: In the 1990s and 2000s the FDIC approved roughly 130 new (de novo) bank charters every year. From 2010 through 2016, in the aftermath of Dodd-Frank, that annual average collapsed. Roughly what was the new average?
context: The 2022 Congressional Research Service report (R47014) documents the collapse. In 2009 regulators had also raised the de novo review period from three years to seven years and stiffened capital requirements for new-bank applicants. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: A rural senator complains in 2016 that his state has lost half its independent community banks since 2010, and that no one has chartered a new one. A Columbia banking economist points to the fixed cost of complying with hundreds of new Dodd-Frank rules, which a $500M-asset bank cannot absorb the way a $500B bank can. Which reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: That a rule with a fixed compliance cost falls heaviest on the smallest players
choices: That a rule with a fixed compliance cost falls heaviest on the smallest players
That interest rates set by the central bank determine bank formation
That community banks fail because of local economic conditions
That deposit insurance eliminates the need for small banks entirely
context: Charles Calomiris of Columbia Business School and Stephen Haber made this the standard critique in Fragile by Design (Princeton 2014). Compliance-officer and legal staffing is largely a fixed cost per institution, so it consumes a much larger share of a small bank's revenue. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Charles_Calomiris.

question: Clemson economist Bruce Yandle coined a pattern (Regulation magazine, 1983) in which a regulation typically attracts both a moral coalition publicly campaigning for it and a commercial interest quietly benefiting from its anti-competitive effect. Yandle has since cited Dodd-Frank compliance costs as a modern example. What name did he give the pattern?
context: The pattern is named for Prohibition, where evangelical preachers publicly urged alcohol bans while bootleggers quietly welcomed the elimination of legal competition. Yandle argues the same coalition structure recurs whenever a rule concentrates benefits on a well-organized incumbent. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bootleggers_and_Baptists.

question: By 2018 Congress had acknowledged that Dodd-Frank's smallest-bank requirements had been miscalibrated and passed a partial rollback, raising the asset threshold for enhanced prudential standards from $50 billion up to $250 billion. What was the rollback law called?
answer: The Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act
choices: The Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act
context: Signed May 24, 2018 by President Trump, sponsored by Senator Mike Crapo (R-Idaho). The law was a bipartisan concession that fixed compliance costs on small banks had shrunk community banking without protecting the system from another 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Growth,_Regulatory_Relief,_and_Consumer_Protection_Act.

question: The NASDAQ Composite Index rose from 1,000 in April 1995 to a specific peak on March 10 2000, driven by internet-company stocks trading at extreme multiples of revenue. What was that peak?
context: The NASDAQ peaked at 5,048 on March 10 2000 -- a five-fold gain in five years. Many internet companies had no profits at all. Source: Grokipedia 'Dot-com bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: On December 5 1996 the Fed chair used a specific two-word phrase in a speech to warn about high asset prices -- but did not act to restrain the market. What phrase did Alan Greenspan use?
context: Greenspan's December 5 1996 speech to the American Enterprise Institute used 'irrational exuberance' to describe asset markets. The warning was widely quoted; the policy response was minimal. Source: Grokipedia 'Irrational exuberance' (2026-09-05).

question: From March 2000 through October 2002 the NASDAQ Composite fell from its peak by a specific percentage. What was the decline?
context: The NASDAQ fell from 5,048 to 1,114 -- a 78% decline over 31 months. Trillions of dollars of paper wealth vanished and hundreds of dot-com companies failed. Source: Grokipedia 'Dot-com bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed responded to the 2000-02 crash with an aggressive rate-cutting cycle. Between January 2001 and June 2003 it cut the federal funds rate from 6.5% down to a specific low, then held it there for over a year. What was the low?
context: The Fed cut 13 times between January 2001 and June 2003, reaching 1.0% on June 25 2003 -- the lowest US policy rate in 46 years. It held the 1.0% rate through June 2004. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2001-03 rate-cutting cycle had one massive unintended effect that the Fed did not anticipate: fueling a bubble in another asset class. Which asset class did the cheap-money response inflate?
context: The Case-Shiller 20-City Home Price Index rose over 100% from January 2000 to April 2006. Cheap mortgages (subprime adjustable-rate loans at low teaser rates) drove the boom. Source: Grokipedia 'United States housing bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: A specific Austrian-tradition analyst was ridiculed on CNBC and Fox Business through 2005-07 for warning that Greenspan's low rates were creating malinvestment in housing that would collapse. Which analyst was most publicly mocked, later vindicated?
context: Schiff's CNBC and Fox Business appearances 2005-07 were compiled into the viral 'Peter Schiff was right' YouTube video (over 3 million views). His warnings were vindicated by the 2008 crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Peter Schiff' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian business-cycle-theory reading of the 2001-2008 sequence identifies a specific causal chain the Fed's actions produced. Which chain does the theory describe?
answer: The 2001-03 rate cuts (a response to the 2000-02 crash caused by 1990s easy money) were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one
choices: The 2001-03 rate cuts (a response to the 2000-02 crash caused by 1990s easy money) were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one
The 2001-03 rate cuts had no relationship to the housing bubble that followed
The 2001-03 rate cuts prevented all subsequent financial crises
The 2001-03 rate cuts caused a sustained fall in commodity prices
context: The Austrian reading: each bubble is caused by the monetary response to the previous bubble. The 1990s cheap money produced the dot-com bubble; the 2001-03 cheap money produced the housing bubble; the 2008-14 QE produced the 2020-24 everything bubble. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Even Fed researchers themselves later documented the direct link from 2001-04 rate policy to subprime issuance. Two Federal Reserve Bank of Boston economists were the internal source of this in-house acknowledgment. Which two produced the documenting research?
context: Willen and Gerardi, at the Boston Fed, produced research linking the 2001-04 rate cuts directly to subprime mortgage origination. Their finding was implicit acknowledgment from inside the Fed system that the Austrian critique had a real basis. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2000-2008 sequence teaches a specific recognition move about Fed reaction functions and future crises. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The Fed's monetary response to a bust plants the seeds of the next bust; there is no exit from the cycle without accepting the liquidation the theory requires
choices: The Fed's monetary response to a bust plants the seeds of the next bust; there is no exit from the cycle without accepting the liquidation the theory requires
The Fed can smooth out business cycles indefinitely by lowering rates aggressively
Each Fed response fully resolves the underlying imbalances of the prior cycle
Fed rate cuts have no effect on asset prices in later cycles
context: The Austrian point: the boom-bust cycle is not an exogenous shock to a stable economy; it is generated by discretionary monetary policy. Attempting to prevent each bust by easing produces the next bust larger. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: The 1996 'irrational exuberance' speech illustrates a specific failure mode of central-bank crisis prevention. Which recognition move does the ladder press about it?
answer: A central-bank chair who publicly warns about a bubble without acting to restrain it has effectively endorsed continued speculation
choices: A central-bank chair who publicly warns about a bubble without acting to restrain it has effectively endorsed continued speculation
Public warnings by central-bank chairs always successfully deflate asset bubbles
Central banks lack the tools to affect asset prices during a bubble
Verbal intervention is always more effective than actual rate changes
context: Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' warning was famous precisely because the Fed did nothing to follow through. Markets read the non-action as a green light. The speech is now studied as an example of failed verbal intervention. Source: Grokipedia 'Irrational exuberance' (2026-09-05).

question: From 1957 to 1991 East Germany produced a small two-cycle-engine car that became the national symbol of the DDR's shortage economy. The name meant 'little satellite'. What was the car called?
context: The Trabant ('little satellite') was manufactured at the Zwickau plant from 1957 to 1991 -- about 3 million total. Its body was made of Duraplast (resin mixed with cotton fibers) because the DDR lacked steel supply chains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: The East German Trabant's body was not made of steel because the DDR lacked steel supply chains. What material did engineers use instead?
context: Duraplast was a fiberglass-like resin reinforced with waste cotton fibers -- cheap, lightweight, and produced from materials the DDR could source without hard currency. The material also famously would not rust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: The DDR set the Trabant's price below the market-clearing level and used a state-planned waiting list for allocation. Families would sometimes register a child at birth. Roughly how long was the delivery queue for a new Trabant?
context: Delivery queues stretched to 10-15 years. Used Trabants sold at higher prices than new ones (because you could have it today), inverting the usual depreciation curve. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: The Bastiat seen-versus-unseen reading of the Trabant supply system: SEEN was the affordable sticker price. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The 10-15-year queue and the used market that priced above new
choices: The 10-15-year queue and the used market that priced above new
The environmental cost of two-cycle engines
context: The visible low price hid the invisible time-cost (years in queue) and the black secondary market above the state sticker. The waiting list was the real 'price'. Source: mises.org/library/east-germany.

question: The Trabant's fundamental engine design ran essentially unchanged for the entire 34-year production run. Why did the design stagnate?
answer: No competitive pressure to redesign since no rival could enter the market
choices: No competitive pressure to redesign since no rival could enter the market
State engineers were forbidden to sketch alternatives
The Zwickau plant lacked qualified engineers
The Politburo mandated periodic conservative redesigns
context: The last Trabants rolled off the line in 1991 with essentially the same 1957 two-cycle engine. No competitor could enter the DDR market to force redesign. This is the incentive side of the calculation debate applied to industrial design. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: On the night of November 9, 1989 and in the weeks after, thousands of small blue East German cars puffing two-cycle exhaust drove through the checkpoints into West Berlin. Which event triggered this iconic sight?
answer: The fall of the Berlin Wall
choices: The fall of the Berlin Wall
context: November 9, 1989 photographs of Trabants at the checkpoints became one of the visual symbols of the DDR's collapse. Within months of reunification, West-German used cars flooded the market and the Trabant disappeared almost overnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall.

question: The Trabant is often cited as 'the calculation debate on wheels' because its 34-year design freeze illustrates a specific Austrian argument at physical scale. Whose 1920 essay predicted exactly this pattern?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
choices: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
context: Mises's 1920 argument: without market prices reflecting real scarcities and consumer preferences, planners cannot know when a design needs updating -- so they build the same one for decades while the world moves on. The Trabant is the argument made physical. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The DDR produced a slightly larger sedan alongside the Trabant, following the same shortage-economy pattern of long queues and design stagnation. What was that sister car called?
context: The Wartburg (Eisenach plant) was the DDR's larger sedan, with 10-year queues of its own. Like the Trabant, production ended shortly after reunification. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wartburg_(car).

question: The Trabant case study collapses three Austrian reasoning-moves at once. Which pair of moves does the design-freeze most sharply illustrate (alongside the seen-vs-unseen queue)?
answer: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
choices: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
The Cantillon effect plus the Fisher effect
The Kondratiev cycle plus the Kuznets curve
The Phillips curve plus Okun's law
context: The knowledge problem: planners cannot know when a design needs updating. The incentive problem: with no competition, no reason to bear the cost of redesign. Together they produce the 34-year design freeze. Source: mises.org/library/east-germany.

question: In 1920, three years after the Bolshevik Revolution, a 39-year-old Vienna economist published a German-language essay whose title translated as 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' The essay would open a forty-year argument. Who wrote it?
context: Mises (born 1881) was 39 in 1920, working as chief economist for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Hayek was still a 21-year-old student who would later attend Mises's private seminar. Boehm-Bawerk had died in 1914. Schumpeter was a contemporary Austrian but held Keynesian-adjacent views on money. Source: Wikipedia, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: The 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' made a startlingly narrow claim about central planning. Mises did NOT argue that socialism was immoral, or that its workers would be lazy, or that its bureaucrats would be corrupt. What did he argue instead?
answer: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
choices: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
That socialist regimes will always turn to political violence
That socialism destroys the incentive to work hard
That planners will inevitably use their power to enrich themselves
context: Mises deliberately set aside every other objection to isolate a technical one: without market prices for capital goods, a planner has no way to compare the cost of alternatives. It is not that planning is unwise -- it is that no rational plan can be drawn up at all. Source: Wikipedia, Economic calculation problem.

question: Mises's 1920 essay first appeared in a German-language academic journal edited from Heidelberg -- the same journal Max Weber had co-edited before the war. Which journal ran the essay in its volume 47?
context: The essay appeared as 'Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen' in Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, volume 47 (1920), pages 86 to 121. The other three were also real German-language economics journals of the era but did not publish this essay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: Two years after the 1920 essay, Mises expanded its argument into a full-length 1922 book. The book was later translated into English in 1936 under a shorter one-word title. Which book was the expansion?
context: 'Die Gemeinwirtschaft: Untersuchungen ueber den Sozialismus' (1922) was translated by J. Kahane in 1936 as simply 'Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis.' The Road to Serfdom (1944) was Hayek's; Human Action (1949) came later, from Mises himself; Bureaucracy (1944) was another shorter Mises book. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: A Soviet planner in 1925 is deciding whether to build a new rail line using rolled steel or aluminum. Both are available; both would work; each pulls labor and raw material from other uses. Mises's 1920 essay says the planner cannot rationally choose between them. What specifically is missing that would allow a rational choice?
answer: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
choices: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
A larger central-planning bureau with more statisticians
Better labor-hour accounting for each metal
A more accurate five-year forecast of demand
context: Prices arise only when privately-owned goods change hands. Abolish private ownership of the means of production, and iron ore and aluminum ore are no longer exchanged -- they are merely moved from one state enterprise to another. Without money prices, there is nothing to compare. More statisticians, better labor-hour books, and better forecasts all presuppose a common unit of value the planner does not have. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: Friedrich Engels had argued that socialist bookkeeping was easy: 'society can simply calculate how many hours of labour are invested in a steam engine, a quarter of last harvest's wheat, and a 100 yards of linen.' Mises quoted this in 1920 and rejected it. Which reasoning move did Mises press against Engels?
answer: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
choices: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
That workers will always misreport how many hours they worked
That machines age at different rates, so hours-per-output changes
That some labor is skilled and some unskilled
context: Two goods can each embody ten hours of labor, yet the first may swallow scarce iron ore while the second uses abundant clay -- the labor count is identical, the real cost is not. Only exchange-set prices reflect scarcity across all inputs at once. The skilled/unskilled point was actually granted by Marx himself and does not touch the calculation problem. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: In 1935 a London-published volume brought Mises's 1920 essay into English for the first time, alongside contributions from N.G. Pierson, Georg Halm, and Enrico Barone. Who edited that volume and wrote its foreword and afterword?
context: 'Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism' (George Routledge and Sons, London, 1935), edited by Hayek at the LSE, put Mises's argument in front of the English-speaking economics profession for the first time. Robbins was Hayek's LSE colleague; Keynes was Hayek's Cambridge opponent; Schumpeter was writing at Bonn and later Harvard. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: After Mises's 1920 argument reached English readers in 1935, two economists proposed a reply: let the state own the means of production but instruct plant managers to imitate market pricing by adjusting output until surpluses and shortages disappeared. This response, offered in the late 1930s, was named for its two principal authors. Which reply attempted to answer Mises within his own framework?
answer: The Lange-Lerner theorem of market socialism
choices: The Lange-Lerner theorem of market socialism
The Keynes-Hansen doctrine of secular stagnation
The Samuelson-Solow doctrine of the neoclassical synthesis
The Sraffa-Robinson critique of capital theory
context: Oskar Lange and Abba Lerner argued central planners could simulate market prices by trial and error. Mises and Hayek replied that simulation without genuine private ownership still lacks the profit-and-loss discipline that generates real price information. The other three were real 20th-century economic controversies but on different questions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: Hayek reframed Mises's 1920 argument in a landmark 1945 American Economic Review paper. Prices, Hayek said, are not just accounting numbers -- they compress dispersed knowledge held in millions of individual minds into signals no central planner can otherwise assemble. Which title did Hayek give that reformulation?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: Published September 1945 in the American Economic Review, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' is now the most-cited paper in the whole Austrian tradition. 'Economics and Knowledge' was Hayek's 1937 warm-up; 'The Meaning of Competition' was his 1946 follow-up; 'The Pretence of Knowledge' was his 1974 Nobel lecture. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: The Soviet planning apparatus at its height set roughly 22 million prices, 460,000 wage rates, and more than 90 million work quotas -- and still produced chronic shortages of ordinary goods together with warehouses full of things nobody wanted. When the planned economies collapsed in 1989-1991, several formerly hostile Western economists (including Robert Heilbroner) wrote lines to the effect that a Vienna economist had been right all along. Which historical judgment did they concede?
answer: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
choices: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
That Keynesian demand management would have saved the East
That the Soviet failure was due chiefly to a shortage of computers
That the fault lay only with Stalin's personal cruelty, not with planning
context: Heilbroner wrote in 1990: 'Mises was right.' The other three explanations were all offered during the Cold War and all set aside once the archives opened: computing power was irrelevant if the prices being computed did not track real scarcity; the same shortages appeared in every planned economy, not just Stalin's. Source: econlib.org/the-collapse-of-the-soviet-union-and-the-continued-relevance-of-ludwig-von-mises; fee.org/articles/the-soviets-tried-to-run-an-economy-without-market-prices.

question: Bastiat's other writings are mostly destructive of bad arguments; his one attempt at a POSITIVE systematic theory of a free economy was published by Guillaumin in Paris in 1850. What is the book's short title?
context: Harmonies economiques (Guillaumin, 1850) was Bastiat's positive treatise, cut short by his December 1850 death. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The book's central thesis about how human interests fit together in a free society goes directly against Karl Marx's later class-conflict view. Which thesis does Bastiat defend?
answer: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
choices: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
Interests in any society always trend toward violent revolution
Interests are always aligned only under state central planning
Interests are unknowable and unpredictable in every case
context: Bastiat argued that when exchange is voluntary, one party's gain does not require another's loss, so class interests are not fundamentally opposed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In one famous passage Bastiat compares two equally-useful diamonds, one found by chance in a stream and one dug from a mine at great labor. What does he say the two share equally to their buyers?
context: The diamond example: value depends on the service rendered to the user, not on labor spent producing the good. This move anticipated Menger's 1871 subjective-value revolution. Source: bastiat.org/en/harmonies.html.

question: Bastiat's Harmonies argument that market prices form a communication system letting strangers coordinate without a central plan anticipated a famous 1945 essay by which Austrian economist?
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' made the same point about price signals aggregating dispersed information -- ninety-five years after Bastiat. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: The subjective-value revolution that vindicated Bastiat's service-value hint came in 1871 from two economists working independently. One was Carl Menger in Vienna. Who was the parallel English figure?
context: Jevons's Theory of Political Economy (1871) and Menger's Principles of Economics (1871) launched the marginal-utility revolution independently and near-simultaneously. Bastiat's 1850 hint predated both. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_utility.

question: Bastiat finished a specific number of chapters of Economic Harmonies before his death; the rest existed only as drafts and fragments. Roughly how many complete chapters did he leave?
context: Bastiat completed ten chapters and drafted portions of ten more; Prosper Paillottet edited the drafts into an expanded 1851 second edition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: In his 1954 History of Economic Analysis, one Austrian-trained American economist called Bastiat a great pamphleteer but dismissed Economic Harmonies as unfinished and second-rate. Whose 1954 verdict was that?
context: Schumpeter's History of Economic Analysis (Oxford, 1954) is famously dismissive of Bastiat's positive theory; modern Austrian scholarship has reappraised the diamond passage upward. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Schumpeter.

question: Bastiat's satirical essay collection appeared in two series published by Guillaumin in Paris, the First Series in 1845 and the Second in January 1848. What is the collection's short title?
context: Sophismes economiques (Guillaumin, 1845 and 1848) is Bastiat's satirical corpus, comprising 39 short essays across two series. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: Across Economic Sophisms Bastiat uses a recurring French-peasant character who keeps encountering protectionist deputies and demolishing their arguments. What is the character's name?
context: Jacques Bonhomme is Bastiat's literary device; he lets the arguments play out through dialogue rather than lecture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: One famous essay in Economic Sophisms has a mayor forbidding a specific carpentry tool because using it would put unskilled men out of work. Which tool does the mayor ban?
context: Bastiat's 'Two Axes' essay has the mayor forbidding a woodcutter's sharp axe to protect the jobs of dull-axe men -- a reductio of make-work arguments. Source: bastiat.org/en/two_axes.html.

question: The First Series of Economic Sophisms opens with a two-word paired-concept essay arguing the goal of economic activity is more goods at lower prices, not fewer at higher. What is its title?
context: 'Abundance and Scarcity' is the opening essay of the First Series (1845); it clarifies the direction of economic reasoning. Source: bastiat.org/en/es1.html.

question: The most famous individual satire in Economic Sophisms is a mock petition from a domestic industry asking the government for legal protection from unfair foreign competition. Which industry files the petition?
context: The Petition of the Candlemakers demands a law against the sun to protect domestic makers of candles and lamps -- a reductio of protectionism that appears in the First Series (1845). Source: bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: Economic Sophisms aims its arguments in both political directions. Which pair of policy targets does the collection go after most consistently?
answer: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
choices: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
Personal income tax and corporate income tax
context: Bastiat's seen/unseen method is applied to left-flavored make-work schemes and right-flavored protective tariffs alike; that even-handedness makes the collection a METHOD text. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: The standard 19th-century English translation of Economic Sophisms was by a British political-economist in 1873, and stayed the standard English edition for about a century. Who was the translator?
context: Stirling's 1873 English edition, retitled Economic Sophisms, was the standard English text until the FEE editions of the mid-20th century and the Liberty Fund Collected Works of the 2010s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: The current standard scholarly English edition of Economic Sophisms appears in Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat volume 3, published in 2017. Who translated the Liberty Fund edition?
context: Jane Willems's Liberty Fund translation restored many chapters and cleaned up 19th-century Britishisms; it is the current best English-language edition. Source: libertyfund.org/collected-works-bastiat-vol-3.

question: On September 7 2021 a specific Central American country became the first in the world to make Bitcoin legal tender alongside another already-adopted currency. Which country made the move?
context: The Bitcoin Law passed the Salvadoran Legislative Assembly on June 9 2021 and took effect September 7 2021, making Bitcoin legal tender alongside the US dollar, which had been El Salvador's official currency since 2001. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: El Salvador had already replaced its previous national currency with a foreign one in 2001, twenty years before the Bitcoin adoption. Which currency did it use as its official money in 2001?
context: El Salvador dollarized in 2001, abandoning its colon; the dollar remained the official currency after the 2021 Bitcoin adoption -- Bitcoin was added ALONGSIDE the dollar, not as a replacement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_El_Salvador.

question: The Salvadoran president who pushed the 2021 Bitcoin Law through the Legislative Assembly is a young populist elected in 2019. What is his name?
context: Nayib Bukele, elected 2019, announced the Bitcoin plan at the Bitcoin 2021 conference in Miami in June 2021 and pushed the Bitcoin Law through the assembly within days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nayib_Bukele.

question: Bukele announced the El Salvador Bitcoin plan at a specific June 2021 conference held in Miami's Wynwood convention center. What was the conference called?
context: Bitcoin 2021 (Wynwood, Miami, June 4-5 2021) was a live-streamed Bitcoin conference; Bukele's video announcement of the coming legal-tender law hit thousands of attendees in real time. Source: b.tc/conference.

question: Alongside legal-tender status, the El Salvador government launched a national mobile wallet running on the Lightning Network so small merchants could accept Bitcoin without heavy on-chain fees. What is the wallet's name?
context: Chivo (Salvadoran slang for 'cool') was distributed to every adult who signed up, with a $30 Bitcoin signing bonus. It had significant early bugs but did drive initial mass adoption. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivo_(wallet).

question: Every adult Salvadoran who downloaded the Chivo wallet was offered a signing bonus in Bitcoin. What was the amount?
context: The $30 signing bonus (paid at Bitcoin's market rate at the moment of registration) was intended to hard-launch wallet adoption; it drove millions of downloads in the first weeks. Source: reuters.com (September 2021 rollout coverage).

question: The International Monetary Fund publicly opposed El Salvador's Bitcoin adoption and pressed the country to reverse the legal-tender designation, particularly during 2022 loan negotiations. What was the IMF's stated reason for opposition?
answer: That Bitcoin price volatility posed macroeconomic risk
choices: That Bitcoin price volatility posed macroeconomic risk
That Bitcoin adoption violated existing dollar-clearing treaties
That Bitcoin transactions could not meet Basel III capital rules
That Bitcoin ran afoul of anti-money-laundering directives
context: The IMF's stated reasoning was Bitcoin's price volatility and its consequences for macroeconomic stability, fiscal reporting, and financial-sector supervision. El Salvador refused; Bukele mocked the IMF on Twitter and pressed on. Source: imf.org (Article IV consultations with El Salvador, 2021-2024).

question: During 2021-2024 the El Salvador government adopted a specific national-treasury Bitcoin accumulation policy, buying at a fixed daily rate regardless of price. What was the pace?
context: Bukele announced in November 2022 that El Salvador would buy one BTC per day into national reserves; treasury holdings grew accordingly over 2022-2024. Source: bloomberg.com (El Salvador BTC treasury coverage, 2022-24).

question: El Salvador's Bitcoin-adoption experiment made it the first modern sovereign state to legalize as tender a monetary asset whose supply could not be controlled by any government or central bank. What did the act directly defy?
answer: The consensus of international financial institutions like the IMF
choices: The consensus of international financial institutions like the IMF
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision recommendations
The World Trade Organization Financial Services Annex
The Bank for International Settlements clearing protocols
context: The Bastiat/Austrian sound-money reading of the move: any successful sovereign adoption of a non-state monetary asset weakens the influence of the international financial institutions built around fiat currency. The IMF's opposition was rational from that perspective. Source: mises.org/library/el-salvador-bitcoin.

question: Alongside the daily-buy treasury policy, Bukele announced a proposed geothermal-powered city on the flanks of a specific volcano in eastern El Salvador, designed as a tax-free zone for Bitcoin businesses. Which volcano was chosen?
context: 'Bitcoin City' near the Conchagua volcano in La Union department was announced November 2021, to be powered by geothermal energy from the volcano and funded by Bitcoin-denominated bonds. Development has been slow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_City.

question: In 2009 an Indiana University political scientist became the first woman ever to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, honored for her studies of how ordinary users can govern shared resources without either state ownership or privatization. Who was she?
context: Elinor Ostrom (1933-2012) won the 2009 economics Nobel with Oliver Williamson 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.' She was the first woman to win in the field. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom.

question: Elinor Ostrom's most influential book, published by Cambridge University Press in 1990, defended a claim that shocked most policy economists: that user groups could successfully manage shared resources for centuries without state control. What was the book's main title?
context: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (Cambridge University Press, 1990). Its case studies became the empirical spine of her Nobel citation. Source: cambridge.org/core/books/governing-the-commons.

question: In 1968 a widely-cited paper in Science warned that any common-pool resource must eventually be destroyed by its users unless privatized or nationalized. Ostrom's Governing the Commons was written to challenge that verdict as too sweeping. Who was the ecologist who wrote that famous 1968 paper?
context: Garrett Hardin's 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (Science, December 13, 1968) became the standard citation for the pessimistic view. Ostrom argued that Hardin's tragedy was conditional, not inevitable. Source: science.org (Hardin, Science 1968).

question: Ostrom shared the 2009 Nobel with another American institutional economist, whose work on the governance of firms and long-term contracts had been developing on a parallel track. Who split the prize with her?
context: The 2009 Nobel citation honored Ostrom for commons governance and Williamson for the economics of the firm and hierarchies. Both work on how real-world institutions solve coordination problems. Source: nobelprize.org (2009 Economic Sciences).

question: One of Ostrom's most vivid European cases documents a mountain pasture where cattle from a dozen surrounding villages graze the same alpine slopes under rules established in the medieval period and still enforced today. Which country's alpine commons is she describing?
context: Swiss alpine grazing commons (Toerbel and other villages in Valais) have been governed by user-written rules on stocking rates since the 1200s. The rules survived centuries of state changes and remain in force. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge 1990), Chapter 3.

question: Ostrom's American case study describes local lobstermen enforcing informal territorial boundaries at sea, punishing outsiders who set traps in claimed waters -- a self-governed fishery that has held together for generations. In which state's fishery did she document this?
context: The Maine lobster fishery's informal harbor gangs enforce territorial boundaries with cut buoy lines and social pressure. Ostrom's coauthor James Acheson wrote The Lobster Gangs of Maine (1988) alongside her project. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), Chapter 5.

question: Central to Ostrom's book is a chapter listing empirically derived features shared by long-lasting self-governed commons -- clear boundaries, local rule-matching, low-cost dispute resolution, and so on. How many such design principles did she distill from her comparative case studies?
context: Governing the Commons Chapter 3 lists exactly eight design principles for successful long-lived commons. She derived them from case comparison, not from theory. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), Chapter 3.

question: Elinor and Vincent Ostrom built up an institutional home for their research at Indiana University in Bloomington that became known worldwide as their school of political economy. What did they call the institute they founded there in 1973?
answer: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
choices: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
The Center for the Study of Public Choice
The Bureau of Applied Political Economy
context: The Ostroms founded the Workshop at IU Bloomington in 1973. Its research program became known as the 'Bloomington School' of institutional analysis. Source: ostromworkshop.indiana.edu.

question: Ostrom's framework for large multi-user commons rejected the idea that a single central authority is required. Instead, overlapping decision centers at different scales coordinate through voluntary arrangements. What one-word name did the Ostroms give to that arrangement?
context: Vincent Ostrom introduced the term 'polycentricity' in his 1961 paper on metropolitan governance; Elinor made it central to her nested-enterprise principle for large commons. Source: Ostrom + Tiebout + Warren, American Political Science Review (1961).

question: A senator argues that any unmanaged shared resource inevitably collapses, so only nationalization or full privatization can save it. Ostrom's decades of case-study evidence add a third empirical option to that binary. Which option does her work document?
answer: User groups can self-govern the resource with the right institutional design
choices: User groups can self-govern the resource with the right institutional design
The resource inevitably collapses regardless of governance form
Only religious authorities can enforce sustainable use
The resource must be split into individual homesteads
context: Ostrom's central contribution: SEEN is the state-vs-market binary; UNSEEN is the polycentric self-organized alternative that empirically works when the eight design principles are present. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), preface and conclusion.

question: Ostrom insisted throughout her career that her work should not be read as a blanket refutation of Garrett Hardin's tragedy. How did she characterize the relationship between his 1968 warning and her empirical findings?
answer: Hardin's tragedy is a conditional outcome, not an inevitable one
choices: Hardin's tragedy is a conditional outcome, not an inevitable one
Hardin's tragedy applies only to fisheries
Hardin's paper contained a mathematical error
Hardin's tragedy holds only where users lack literacy
context: Ostrom argued Hardin identified a real failure mode that occurs when users cannot communicate, monitor, or enforce rules. Her cases showed that when those conditions are present, tragedy is avoided. She did not deny his mechanism; she conditioned it. Source: Ostrom, 'A General Framework for Analyzing Sustainability of Social-Ecological Systems' (Science, 2009).

question: In the winter of 362 AD a Roman emperor wintering in Antioch tried to solve a grain shortage by imposing a price cap and importing his own imperial grain to sell at the mandated price. Which emperor?
context: The emperor Julian (ruled 361-363 AD) was the last non-Christian Roman emperor. He wintered in Antioch in 362-63 preparing his Persian campaign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor).

question: Julian's grain-price cap in Antioch produced an immediate market response. What happened to grain supply in the city?
answer: Merchants and farmers withdrew their grain rather than sell at a loss
choices: Merchants and farmers withdrew their grain rather than sell at a loss
Grain flooded the market from imperial reserves
Prices fell further than the mandated cap
context: Antioch merchants and surrounding-region farmers withdrew grain from the market. The imperial grain was quickly bought up (often by the same merchants for resale on the black market), and shelves went empty again. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor).

question: Furious at the merchants for the shortage his own price cap had caused, Julian wrote a public pamphlet blaming the Antiochenes and their sellers for greed and godlessness. What is the pamphlet called?
context: Misopogon ('Beard-Hater') survives complete and is one of the very few first-person books written by a Roman emperor. Its title mocks the Antiochenes' derision of Julian's philosopher's beard. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misopogon.

question: Julian's response to the market-clearing failure was NOT to lift the price cap but to blame the sellers publicly. This is what recurring reasoning-error pattern in the history of price controls?
answer: Blame the messenger for the message
choices: Blame the messenger for the message
Rescind the policy at the first sign of failure
context: Julian sees the empty shelves and blames the seller's character rather than his own ceiling. Sowell treats this as the archetype of the recurring blame-the-messenger move that shows up in every price-control failure. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Julian himself died a few months after the Antioch grain episode, in June 363 AD, on the campaign he had been preparing all winter. Which enemy was he fighting when killed?
context: Julian was killed in battle against the Sassanid Persians on June 26, 363 AD. His death ended the last non-Christian Roman ruling dynasty. The Antioch price cap was quietly ended after his death. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor).

question: Thomas Sowell in Basic Economics uses Julian's Antioch episode alongside Diocletian's earlier 301 AD edict to teach one consistent point about price controls across 1,700 years. What is Sowell's core teaching move?
answer: Compared to what? -- name the counterfactual before praising or condemning a policy
choices: Compared to what? -- name the counterfactual before praising or condemning a policy
The state cannot outrun the market
The visible hand is more efficient than the invisible
context: Sowell's 'compared to what?' move: any critique of high grain prices in Antioch must name the counterfactual (higher prices with grain on the shelves vs low prices with empty shelves). Applied to any policy analysis. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Julian is sometimes called by a Christian polemical name assigned after his death by the church he had been trying to demote. What is that later name?
context: 'Julian the Apostate' (Iulianus Apostata) was the Christian polemical label applied after his death. Historians in the bank's neutral history-voice call him 'the emperor Julian' or 'the last non-Christian Roman emperor'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor).

question: The ancient city of Antioch is now the modern Turkish city of what name, sitting near Turkey's southern border with Syria?
context: Antakya (Antioch) is in Hatay Province, southern Turkey, near the Syrian border. The 2023 earthquake heavily damaged the modern city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antakya.

question: Julian's Antioch episode and Diocletian's earlier 301 AD edict are cited together by Austrian economists to argue that price-control reasoning errors are structural, not modern. What is the modern shorthand for the recurring pattern the two cases share?
answer: Ruler sets a low price; goods vanish; ruler blames the seller
choices: Ruler sets a low price; goods vanish; ruler blames the seller
Ruler sets a low price; supply rises; consumers benefit
Ruler sets a high price; demand falls; producers benefit
Ruler sets a high price; foreign supply floods in
context: The three-step recurring pattern -- cap, disappearance, blame -- shows up in Diocletian 301, Julian 362, Nixon 1971, Venezuela 2013, Argentina 2020, and everywhere else. The reasoning-error is not modern. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: For 41 years (November 1944 to April 1985) one man led communist Albania -- the longest tenure of any Warsaw-orbit communist head of party. Who was he?
context: Hoxha (pronounced 'ho-ja') was First Secretary of the Party of Labor of Albania from November 29, 1944 until his death April 11, 1985. He outlasted Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev, and Andropov, and was still in power when Mikhail Gorbachev took charge in Moscow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enver_Hoxha.

question: From the late 1960s through the early 1980s the Albanian state built enough concrete pillbox bunkers that many are still standing in the 21st century as tourist curiosities. Roughly how many were built, in a country of about 2.8 million people?
context: Roughly one bunker for every 16 citizens, or one for every 4 households. The concrete cost has been estimated at 2-3 times the cost of housing Albanians would have preferred to build with the same resources. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Albanian_bunkers.

question: Enver Hoxha's Albania serially ruptured with each of its major communist allies over the decades. By the early 1980s the country stood entirely alone as the sole self-declared 'purely Marxist-Leninist' state. Which sequence of breaks did Hoxha lead?
answer: With Yugoslavia in 1948, with the USSR in 1961, and with China in 1978
choices: With Yugoslavia in 1948, with the USSR in 1961, and with China in 1978
With China in 1949, with Cuba in 1965, and with Yugoslavia in 1978
With North Korea in 1953, with the USSR in 1963, and with Romania in 1980
With Poland in 1956, with East Germany in 1968, and with Bulgaria in 1975
context: Hoxha sided with Stalin against Tito in 1948, with Mao against Khrushchev in 1961, and with orthodoxy against Deng's Reform and Opening in 1978. Each rupture left him more isolated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enver_Hoxha.

question: In 1967 the Albanian state issued a decree closing every mosque, church, and monastery in the country -- repurposing many as warehouses or gymnasiums. The move made Albania a first-of-its-kind polity. What kind?
answer: The first officially atheist state in the world
choices: The first officially atheist state in the world
The first officially neutral state in Europe
The first officially bilingual state in the Warsaw Pact
The first officially nuclear-armed state in the Balkans
context: The 1967 ban followed from Hoxha's ideological commitment to eliminating religious civil-society intermediaries. Source: grokipedia.com/page/People%27s_Socialist_Republic_of_Albania.

question: Albania's secret police under Hoxha ran a surveillance operation of roughly 10,000 officers and up to 40,000 informants in a country of about 3 million people. What was the agency called?
context: Sigurimi (short for Drejtoria e Sigurimit te Shtetit, 'Directorate of State Security') is the Albanian analogue of Romania's Securitate, East Germany's Stasi, and Czechoslovakia's StB. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sigurimi.

question: Records collected since 1990 by the Institute for the Studies of Communist Crimes and Consequences in Tirana document specific totals for Albania's political-repression apparatus. Which set of numbers do the ISKK records support?
answer: About 34,000 prisoners in labor camps and at least 6,000 people executed for political offenses
choices: About 34,000 prisoners in labor camps and at least 6,000 people executed for political offenses
Under a hundred prisoners and no political executions
context: The ISKK is the Tirana-based scholarly institution that opened after 1990 and documented the regime's records. The scale is smaller than the USSR's or China's in absolute terms but very large on a per-capita basis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/People%27s_Socialist_Republic_of_Albania.

question: In December 1990 a wave of student protests brought down the last Stalinist regime in Europe; the following March, Albania held its first multi-party elections and the Hoxha-era one-party state ended. Who was Hoxha's successor who allowed the opening?
context: Alia had been Hoxha's designated heir and party first secretary from 1985. His decision not to shoot the December 1990 student demonstrators ended the regime. The March 1991 elections were the first multi-party vote in Albanian communist history. Source: grokipedia.com/page/History_of_Albania.

question: A high-school student compares Albania's 173,000 concrete bunkers to the modern economy the same national labor and cement could have built. A Bastiatian economist points to a specific reasoning move to describe what happened. Which is it?
answer: The opportunity cost: every ton of cement in a bunker was a ton not in a house, school, or factory
choices: The opportunity cost: every ton of cement in a bunker was a ton not in a house, school, or factory
The Laffer curve: high taxes reduced total revenue
The Coase theorem: property rights would have solved the externality
The Phillips curve: unemployment traded off against inflation
context: By the end of the regime Albania had the lowest per-capita income in Europe and the most decayed infrastructure -- and 173,000 bunkers for an invasion that never came. The reasoning move is Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen applied to state investment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Albanian_bunkers.

question: A young Berkeley-trained mathematician had helped organize the Oakland meetings that became the cypherpunk mailing list in fall 1992. On March 9, 1993 he posted a short manifesto to the list that gave the movement its philosophical anchor. Which mathematician wrote it?
context: Eric Hughes wrote 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' on March 9, 1993. Timothy May wrote the earlier 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto; John Gilmore ran toad.com; Phil Zimmermann wrote PGP. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: The essay Eric Hughes posted on March 9, 1993 -- less than two pages long -- carries a title that names the movement whose founding text it became. What was it called?
context: 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' by Eric Hughes, March 9, 1993. Tim May wrote the earlier Crypto Anarchist Manifesto (1988); the Communist Manifesto (Marx-Engels 1848) and The Sovereign Individual (Davidson-Rees-Mogg 1997) are unrelated. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: The most-quoted line of Eric Hughes's 1993 manifesto draws a specific distinction between privacy and secrecy. Which sentence sets up privacy as an act of individual choice rather than concealment of wrongdoing?
answer: 'Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.'
choices: 'Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.'
'Privacy is the right to be let alone in every part of one's own life.'
'Privacy is a fundamental human right recognized in every free nation.'
'Privacy is the absence of observation by anyone else without consent.'
context: Hughes's line defines privacy as choice, not concealment. 'The right to be let alone' is Warren & Brandeis 1890; the other two are generic paraphrases from later privacy discourse. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Hughes drew a sharp line inside the 1993 essay against a certain kind of privacy advocate -- someone who wrote op-eds and held conferences but produced no working software. The line became the cypherpunk movement's operative motto. Which three-word phrase captured his rule?
context: 'Cypherpunks write code' is Hughes's operative motto -- privacy would only exist in the world if someone actually built and shipped the software. The other slogans circulate in adjacent movements but are not Hughes's line. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Hughes distinguished privacy from a related concept that his manifesto argued gets confused with it in ordinary usage -- something that hides wrongdoing rather than protects choice. Which concept did Hughes contrast against privacy?
context: Hughes: 'Privacy is not secrecy. A private matter is something one doesn't want the whole world to know, but a secret matter is something one doesn't want anybody to know.' Anonymity, encryption, and free speech are related tools or rights but not what Hughes contrasted here. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: The 1993 manifesto Eric Hughes wrote was distributed on the mailing list run by another cypherpunk out of his personal server. Which cypherpunk hosted the toad.com mailing list where Hughes's essay circulated?
context: John Gilmore -- Sun Microsystems's fifth employee, EFF co-founder -- hosted the cypherpunk mailing list at toad.com. Timothy May co-founded the meetings but did not host the list; Adam Back and Julian Assange were later members. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Eric Hughes was one of the original developers of a specific class of software the cypherpunk community used to route email untraceably -- essential infrastructure for the anonymity tools they were building. Which category of tool did Hughes help build?
context: Hughes co-authored anonymous remailer software (e.g., type-1 remailers of the early 1990s) that stripped headers and re-forwarded email to hide the original sender. Encryption libraries like PGP were built by others (Zimmermann); browsers were the province of Netscape; shipping software is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Hughes's 1993 manifesto identified a specific actor he believed would NOT build privacy tools for ordinary people -- so cypherpunks would have to build them themselves. Which actor did the essay explicitly rule out as the source of everyday privacy?
context: Hughes explicitly wrote that we cannot expect governments, corporations, or other large faceless organizations to grant us privacy out of their beneficence; we must build it ourselves. Mathematicians, free-software developers, and ISPs were tools or allies, not the actor being ruled out. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Fifteen years after Hughes's 1993 manifesto, an unknown developer publishing under the name Satoshi Nakamoto followed almost exactly the sequence Hughes's essay had laid out for how a privacy technology should reach the world. Which specific pattern did Satoshi enact from Hughes's operating manual?
answer: publish a paper, ship working code, deploy a live network, then step aside
choices: publish a paper, ship working code, deploy a live network, then step aside
petition governments to legalize the technology first
sell the technology to a large corporation for integration
form a nonprofit foundation to lobby for adoption
context: Satoshi followed the Hughes pattern precisely: October 2008 paper, January 2009 running network, April 2011 disappearance. Petitioning, corporate sale, and nonprofit lobbying are precisely the paths Hughes ruled out as sources of everyday privacy. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html; Nakamoto white paper 2008.

question: A modern cypherpunk historian argues that Hughes's 1993 manifesto did not merely describe an aspiration -- it functioned as a specific procedural instruction for the next generation of privacy technologies. Which reasoning move does the argument press?
answer: That 'cypherpunks write code' is a rule about proof: aspiration without a shipping working tool is not itself a privacy technology at all
choices: That 'cypherpunks write code' is a rule about proof: aspiration without a shipping working tool is not itself a privacy technology at all
That academic publication of privacy research alone is sufficient to protect ordinary users without any actual software being written or deployed
That waiting for privacy-protective legislation to pass is the correct path for cryptographers, and shipping software prematurely is counterproductive
That privacy tools must be sold in a competitive marketplace to be legitimate, and free-of-charge distribution undermines the professionalism of the field
context: The Hughes argument treats shipping software as the only proof that a privacy technology actually exists in the world for ordinary users. Academic publication, legislative advocacy, and commercial sale can all coexist with zero privacy actually reaching users. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Three US asset managers together control the largest share of the S&P 500 through index funds and thus cast approximately a quarter of votes at most major American corporate meetings. Which three firms make up this 'Big Three'?
choices: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Morgan Stanley
context: As of the mid-2020s, BlackRock (~$10T+ AUM), Vanguard (~$8T+), and State Street (~$4T+) collectively manage more than $22 trillion and hold roughly 20-25% of the average S&P 500 company's shares. Source: Bebchuk + Hirst, 'The Specter of the Giant Three' (Boston University Law Review, 2019).

question: The acronym ESG, central to a $20-trillion-plus investment-labeling movement peaking around 2022, stands for three word-categories used to evaluate corporate behavior against non-financial criteria. What do the three letters stand for?
context: ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) frameworks became a dominant investment-labeling convention 2015-22. Counting methodology is contested, but nominal 'ESG AUM' peaked around $20 trillion globally. Source: Grokipedia 'Environmental, social, and corporate governance.'

question: The 2019 Boston University Law Review paper by Lucian Bebchuk and Scott Hirst that documented the Big Three's aggregate voting power gave the phenomenon a memorable specter-themed title. What was the paper called?
answer: The Specter of the Giant Three
choices: The Specter of the Giant Three
The Rise of the Index Titans
The Age of the Asset Manager
context: Bebchuk + Hirst, 'The Specter of the Giant Three' (Boston University Law Review, 2019). The paper documented that Big Three ownership of the S&P 500 had roughly quadrupled since 1998 and would continue growing under passive-fund trends. Source: bu.edu/bulawreview (Bebchuk-Hirst 2019).

question: Beginning in 2018, Larry Fink began sending an annual public letter to corporate leaders calling on companies to take action on climate, DEI, and other ESG themes. What was Larry Fink's job title at BlackRock at that time?
context: Larry Fink co-founded BlackRock in 1988 and has been its Chief Executive Officer since. His annual CEO letters became one of the most-read documents in institutional finance. Source: blackrock.com (Fink annual letters archive).

question: The public-choice concern about the Big Three is that a small number of asset-manager decision-makers cast proxy votes on behalf of tens of millions of dispersed retirement-account holders whose consent is inferred rather than solicited. What kind of pattern does this look like in public-choice terms?
answer: Regulatory-style capture operating through private fiduciary infrastructure
choices: Regulatory-style capture operating through private fiduciary infrastructure
context: Capture need not require formal government regulators. When a small group of intermediaries makes decisions on behalf of many principals whose preferences are neither known nor consulted, the same alignment failure appears in private financial infrastructure. Source: Bebchuk + Hirst (2019); Boettke and various commentary in Cato Regulation (2022-24).

question: In August 2022 the governor of one large US state led the first prominent state-level pushback against BlackRock's ESG-voting posture by ordering a divestment of $2 billion in state pension assets. Which governor led that move?
context: Governor Ron DeSantis announced the Florida divestment in August 2022, followed by a coalition of state attorneys general in similar comment letters and, in some cases, further divestment action. Source: flgov.com (August 23, 2022 press release).

question: In September 1970 the New York Times Magazine published an essay by the Chicago economist Milton Friedman that has served as the founding statement of the shareholder-primacy position ESG explicitly rejects. What was the essay's title, as printed?
answer: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
choices: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
The Business of America Is Business
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits' (New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970). It argued that corporate managers are agents of shareholders and should not divert corporate resources to personal political preferences. Source: nytimes.com/1970/09/13/archives.

question: In response to political pressure over ESG proxy behavior, BlackRock began offering large institutional clients the ability to direct their own share votes rather than have BlackRock cast them centrally. What single two-word program name did BlackRock give this initiative?
context: BlackRock introduced 'Voting Choice' programs starting in 2022, allowing eligible institutional clients to select their own voting policies or vote shares directly. Retail 401(k) holders remain largely unable to direct their votes. Source: blackrock.com/corporate/about-us/investment-stewardship/voting-choice.

question: The Big Three story teaches a general lesson about who can be captured, in the sense George Stigler introduced for regulators. What is the expanded lesson?
answer: Capture can operate through private financial gatekeepers, not only government regulators
choices: Capture can operate through private financial gatekeepers, not only government regulators
Capture can only occur in government agencies
Capture is prevented by any private-sector alternative
context: Stigler's 1971 regulatory-capture framework identified the pattern. Bebchuk-Hirst extends the recognition to private financial infrastructure that operates on behalf of dispersed principals. Same alignment problem, different institutional venue. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Bebchuk + Hirst (2019).

question: The reasoning-move for policy analysis that the Big Three case illustrates is a Sowell-style comparative habit. Whenever intermediaries make decisions on behalf of dispersed principals whose preferences are not solicited, what should the analyst ask?
answer: Whether the intermediaries' incentives align with the principals' interests
choices: Whether the intermediaries' incentives align with the principals' interests
Whether the intermediaries have appropriate advanced degrees
Whether the intermediaries publish annual sustainability reports
Whether the intermediaries are located in the correct time zone
context: The principal-agent test: absent alignment, expect the agents to pursue their own preferences at principals' expense. The Bebchuk-Hirst paper's diagnostic move applies whether the agent is a regulator, a legislator, or a fund manager. Source: Bebchuk + Hirst (2019).

question: An Austrian Finance Minister resigns from cabinet in 1904 rather than sign off on further deficit spending, then returns to a full-time chair at the University of Vienna, where his seminar becomes the training ground for the next generation of Austrian-school economists. Who is he?
context: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) served three separate stints as Austrian Finance Minister (briefly in 1895, again in 1897, and 1900-1904), resigned in 1904 rather than approve further deficits, and returned to Vienna where his 1905-06 seminar became the training ground for the next generation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk was born on 12 February 1851 in a Moravian city that was then part of the Austrian Empire and is today the second-largest city in the Czech Republic. Which city?
context: Brno, in Moravia (then Austrian Empire, today the Czech Republic), was Boehm-Bawerk's birthplace on 12 February 1851. Prague was in Bohemia; Vienna the imperial capital where he later worked; Krakow in Galicia where Menger took his 1867 doctorate. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Boehm-Bawerk served three separate times as Austrian Minister of Finance -- briefly in 1895, again in 1897, and continuously from 1900 to 1904. In 1904 he resigned outright rather than sign off on further deficit spending. Whose spending demands was he refusing to accommodate?
context: Boehm-Bawerk resigned as Austrian Finance Minister in 1904 when the army's demand for increased military expenditure threatened to unbalance the budget beyond what he thought fiscally sustainable.
