The imperial court, pensions, and state railway were all separate calls on the budget of the era; but the specific breaking point in 1904 was army spending. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Boehm-Bawerk married a woman who was also the sister of another founding Austrian-school economist. He and that fellow economist thus became brothers-in-law and together carried Menger's project into its second generation. Who was Boehm-Bawerk's brother-in-law?
context: Boehm-Bawerk married Paula von Wieser, whose brother Friedrich von Wieser (1851-1926) had also studied under Menger and developed the Austrian theory of imputation and opportunity cost. The two brothers-in-law between them wrote the second-generation Austrian curriculum. Menger was their teacher; Mises and Schumpeter were their students. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: In 1896 Boehm-Bawerk published an essay attacking the labor theory of value defended in Capital Volume 1 (1867), on the ground that its author's own posthumously published Capital Volume 3 (edited by Friedrich Engels, 1894) could not be reconciled with Volume 1. What English title does that 1896 essay carry?
answer: Karl Marx and the Close of His System
choices: Karl Marx and the Close of His System
The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay 'Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems' -- translated as 'Karl Marx and the Close of His System' -- showed that Capital Volume 3, edited by Engels in 1894, contradicted the labor theory of value defended in Volume 1, opening a gap Marxists have argued about ever since. The Positive Theory of Capital (1889) was Boehm-Bawerk's own Volume 2 on capital; Principles of Economics (1871) was Menger's; The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was Mises's early book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: After his 1904 resignation as Finance Minister, Boehm-Bawerk returned to a full-time chair. His graduate seminar there ran 1905-06 and became historically famous because its students on the Austrian side went on to become the school's next great figures. Two attendees became household names in 20th-century economics. Who were they?
answer: Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter
choices: Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter
context: The 1905-06 Boehm-Bawerk seminar took a leading target of Austrian criticism as its topic and drew Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter from the Austrian side alongside two future Marxist statesmen. Hayek, Kirzner, and Rothbard came in later generations; the Chicago-school figures Friedman and Stigler were a different tradition. Source: Mises Institute, 'Uncovered Audio of Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk from 1905' (https://mises.org/power-market/uncovered-audio-eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-1905).

question: The 1905-06 Boehm-Bawerk seminar drew as much attention for its Marxist attendees as for its Austrian ones -- the room debated Marx's own theory week after week, with Boehm-Bawerk pressing his 1896 critique and the young Marxists defending. Two Austro-Marxist students in particular acted as the professor's principal adversaries. Who were the two?
context: Austro-Marxists Otto Bauer (1881-1938, later Foreign Minister of Austria 1918-19) and Rudolf Hilferding (1877-1941, later Reich Finance Minister of Weimar Germany 1923 and 1928-29) both attended Boehm-Bawerk's 1905-06 seminar as young students defending the Marxian position. Kautsky, Bernstein, Luxemburg, Liebknecht, Gramsci and Lukacs were separately famous Marxist theorists of the era who did not attend the seminar. Source: Wikipedia, 'Otto Bauer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Bauer).

question: Volume 3 of Boehm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest -- a set of long excursions and replies to critics that had piled up in the decades since Volume 2 -- appeared only after his death. In what year did that third volume finally reach print?
context: Volume 3 of Kapital und Kapitalzins, titled 'Exkurse' (Further Essays on Capital and Interest), was published in 1921, seven years after Boehm-Bawerk's death; the material had accumulated as appendices to Volume 2 (1889) and grew large enough to require a separate volume. 1896 was his Marx essay; 1914 the year of his death and of the First World War's outbreak. Source: Wikipedia, 'Capital and Interest' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest).

question: Boehm-Bawerk died on 27 August 1914. The date is remembered by economic historians because it fell just weeks after another event that would consume the empire he had served as Finance Minister. What had just happened?
answer: The First World War had broken out
choices: The First World War had broken out
The Austrian schilling had been introduced
The Federal Reserve had opened its doors
context: The First World War began on 28 July 1914 when Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; Boehm-Bawerk died a month later on 27 August 1914, having spent his final years watching the fiscal discipline he had defended in cabinet dissolve into war finance. The Austrian schilling was introduced in 1924; the Habsburg monarchy abdicated in November 1918; the US Federal Reserve had opened in November 1914. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay pressed a specific internal-contradiction argument against Marx: prices in Capital Volume 1 are said to reflect labor-hours embodied, but prices in Capital Volume 3 have to reflect equal profit rates across industries with different labor intensities, and the two accounts cannot both be true. Marxists have argued about the gap ever since under a specific name. What is the argument that Boehm-Bawerk sharpened usually called today?
context: The 'transformation problem' names the gap Boehm-Bawerk sharpened in 1896: Marx's Volume 1 labor-theory-of-value prices cannot be transformed into Volume 3's equal-rate-of-profit prices without inconsistency. Marxists have proposed rescues for a century. The knowledge problem (Hayek 1945), calculation debate (Mises 1920), and impossibility theorem (Arrow 1951) are separate Austrian and welfare-economics critiques of central planning and social choice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Transformation problem' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_problem).

question: The world's first widely-circulated government paper money was issued in 11th-century Sichuan province during a specific Chinese dynasty. Which dynasty issued the paper?
context: The Song dynasty took over jiaozi paper-money issuance around 1023 AD in Sichuan. The Han (206 BC-220 AD), Tang (618-907), and Ming (1368-1644) belong to other centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: Between 1716 and 1720 -- just four years -- a French monetary experiment run by a Scottish financier at the Banque Royale printed itself to collapse. What was the paper currency called?
context: John Law's system at the Banque Royale (1716-1720) issued livre notes that hyperinflated in four years. The assignat was a separate 1789-96 French Revolution experiment; the Weimar papermark was Germany 1914-23; the Continental dollar was America's 1775-81 revolutionary currency -- all real fiat failures but from other decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Law_(economist).

question: One 20th-century hyperinflation set an all-time world record for the speed of currency destruction, ending in 1946 with a currency in which prices doubled every 15 hours. Which country's currency holds that record?
context: The Hungarian pengő (1946) holds the world record for hyperinflation speed. The German papermark (1923), Zimbabwean dollar (2008), and Venezuelan bolívar (2016-) also hyperinflated but at slower peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Hungary.

question: One specific African country's hyperinflation in the late 2000s produced a banknote whose face value became a global punchline -- issued in 2008 as a single note whose denomination reached the hundred-trillion mark. Which country?
context: Zimbabwe issued a Z$100 trillion note in 2008-09 during its hyperinflation; the currency was formally demonetized in 2015. Nigeria, South Africa, and Ghana have had significant inflation but not this class of note. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: The current major fiat currencies -- the US dollar, the euro, the Japanese yen, the British pound -- all became purely political-promise currencies with no gold anchor after one specific 20th-century event. Which event ended the last real gold-money link?
answer: the August 15, 1971 Nixon shock closing the gold window
choices: the August 15, 1971 Nixon shock closing the gold window
context: The Nixon shock (August 15, 1971) closed the last gold link (dollar-to-gold redemption for foreign central banks). Bretton Woods CREATED the gold-exchange standard; the 1913 Fed Act founded the central bank; the 1985 Plaza Accord coordinated exchange-rate policy but did not involve gold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: Since the founding of the Federal Reserve in 1913, the US dollar has lost roughly what fraction of its purchasing power measured in gold?
context: In gold terms the US dollar has lost about 98-99% of its purchasing power since the Fed's 1913 founding (from ~$20.67/oz to $2,400+/oz); about 86% just since the Nixon shock 1971 (from $35/oz). 15% and 50% understate; 200% is not a purchasing-power figure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve.

question: Defenders of fiat currencies sometimes cite the British pound sterling as evidence that fiat money can survive for a very long time -- '1,300 years old'. What is the standard Austrian counter-argument about the modern paper pound?
answer: it has lost about 99.5% of its purchasing power since 1750, and its physical composition has repeatedly changed
choices: it has lost about 99.5% of its purchasing power since 1750, and its physical composition has repeatedly changed
the pound has held its value steadily against gold since the early 1900s and remains a reference standard for stability
the modern pound has never been formally debased or inflated by the Bank of England in its 300-year history of issuing paper
the British pound was formally re-linked to gold in the 2000s and now sits under a working gold-exchange standard again
context: The counter: the modern paper pound has lost about 99.5% of purchasing power since 1750; its coin composition changed from silver to nickel; the medieval silver penny and today's paper pound are different monetary regimes with a shared name. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: The 1997 book that documented and totaled the death tolls of communist regimes -- and became a key reference point in the sound-money case against political money -- is called what?
context: 'The Black Book of Communism' (Stéphane Courtois et al., 1997) totals 65-100M deaths across communist regimes. Marx's Das Kapital and the Communist Manifesto are 19th-century Marxist texts; Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) is unrelated to the death-toll accounting. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: Austrian economists (Mises, Rothbard, Salerno, Ammous) argue that the 5,000-year pattern of fiat-currency failure is not accidental but flows from a specific structural incentive that faces any monetary authority. Which incentive does the argument identify as the mechanism of failure?
answer: politicians promise citizens more than tax revenue supports, monetary authorities close the gap by printing, printing debases the currency, savers absorb the loss, and the cycle accumulates until confidence breaks
choices: politicians promise citizens more than tax revenue supports, monetary authorities close the gap by printing, printing debases the currency, savers absorb the loss, and the cycle accumulates until confidence breaks
monetary authorities in every country are secretly controlled by foreign powers who force them to overprint the domestic currency for their own competitive advantage over generations of policy
central bankers in every generation are personally corrupt and enrich themselves through undisclosed transactions before the currency they oversee inevitably loses its value against real goods
ordinary citizens demand ever-higher wages that force the money supply to grow to accommodate them, and the resulting debasement is a downstream effect of labor rather than monetary decisions
context: The Austrian pattern-claim: fiat failure is structural, not personal. Politicians overspend; the central bank prints; savers pay for it through debasement; the pattern accumulates. The other options are conspiracy or personal-corruption theories the argument specifically rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021); Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?.

question: The Austrian claim that no fiat currency in 5,000 years has escaped debasement or collapse is presented as the empirical case for a specific reframing of the sound-money problem. Which reasoning move does the argument press about the nature of monetary reform?
answer: That sound money is an engineering problem to be solved with fixed rules, not a political problem to be solved with better leaders
choices: That sound money is an engineering problem to be solved with fixed rules, not a political problem to be solved with better leaders
That sound money requires only better central-bank governance and improved appointment processes for the officials who run the system
That sound money is fundamentally a matter of tax policy alone, so fiscal reform inside each government can restore monetary discipline
That sound money will emerge automatically over time without any deliberate change in monetary institutions or protocols by anyone
context: The 5,000-year pattern-argument culminates in Satoshi's 2008 Bitcoin white paper: solve the political-money problem with cryptography and consensus rather than with trust in better leaders. Better central-bank governance, tax policy alone, and passive emergence are precisely what the argument denies is sufficient. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018); The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Since the 1971 Nixon shock, the US dollar has lost roughly what fraction of its purchasing power measured in gold?
context: From $35/oz in 1971 to $2,400+/oz by the mid-2020s is roughly an 86%+ loss in the dollar's purchasing power measured in gold. 25%, 40%, and 5% are all significant understatements. Source: London Bullion Market Association historical gold prices.

question: On February 2, 1934 President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6581 creating a federal agency to provide loans and guarantees to foreign buyers of US-manufactured goods. Which agency?
answer: The Export-Import Bank of the United States (Ex-Im Bank)
choices: The Export-Import Bank of the United States (Ex-Im Bank)
context: Ex-Im's stated mission is to level the playing field for US exporters competing against foreign firms whose governments provide similar export credits. FDIC, RFC, and OPIC were other 1930s-1970s federal financial vehicles for different purposes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: Mercatus Center analysis of Ex-Im Bank filings for 2007-2013 identified a specific single company as the largest beneficiary of the agency's lending. Which company received roughly 40 percent of all Ex-Im support in that period?
context: Boeing's foreign airline customers used Ex-Im-guaranteed financing to buy commercial aircraft. Critics call Ex-Im the 'Boeing Bank' because of this concentration. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: On June 30, 2015 something rare happened to the US Export-Import Bank -- a coalition of Heritage Foundation, Club for Growth, and FreedomWorks temporarily won a public-choice fight against Boeing and other concentrated beneficiaries. What happened?
answer: Congress declined to renew the bank's charter and it lapsed for about five months
choices: Congress declined to renew the bank's charter and it lapsed for about five months
The Supreme Court struck down the bank as unconstitutional
The bank formally merged with the Federal Reserve
The Treasury Department transferred all Ex-Im loans to the World Bank
context: The lapse was a rare successful mobilization of dispersed opposition against a concentrated-benefit program. Ex-Im's authority to finance new deals was suspended from June 30 to December 2015. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: The US Ex-Im Bank's charter was restored in December 2015 through a specific legislative technique that made it hard for individual members of Congress to vote against the bank without voting against something else. What was the technique?
answer: The renewal was bundled into a highway-bill omnibus (the FAST Act)
choices: The renewal was bundled into a highway-bill omnibus (the FAST Act)
The renewal was passed as a stand-alone emergency measure with a two-thirds majority
The renewal was enacted by executive order without Congressional action
The renewal was included in a formal treaty ratified by the Senate
context: Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act. The bundling demonstrated the Buchanan-Tullock logrolling mechanism: pair a concentrated-benefit program with widely-popular legislation so opposing it becomes politically costly. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: During the five-month 2015 lapse of the US Ex-Im Bank, its defenders had warned that US exports would collapse without it. What actually happened to US export volume during the lapse?
answer: It did not measurably decline; Boeing continued selling aircraft using commercial bank financing
choices: It did not measurably decline; Boeing continued selling aircraft using commercial bank financing
It fell by roughly 40 percent as predicted by Ex-Im's supporters
It doubled as foreign buyers rushed to sign contracts before the lapse ended
It was diverted almost entirely to European Union export-credit agencies
context: The counterfactual case for the bank's necessity was weaker than its proponents had claimed. Commercial bank financing was slightly more expensive than Ex-Im guarantees, but not by enough to collapse export flows. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: A high-school student asks a Mercatus-influenced economist why the US Ex-Im Bank keeps getting renewed despite the Boeing-heavy concentration and the empirical evidence that its absence did not collapse US exports. He points to a specific 1965 book that predicted exactly this. Which book?
answer: Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action'
choices: Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action'
context: Olson predicted that programs with large concentrated benefits to a small number of firms would attract intense organized lobbying, while the dispersed cost to taxpayers, competitor firms, and foreign consumers would not organize against it. Boeing spent millions annually lobbying to preserve Ex-Im. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: Thalidomide, a sedative sold across Europe and given to pregnant women for morning sickness, left thousands of babies with severe deformities. It never went on sale in the United States, because one reviewer at the Food and Drug Administration kept refusing to clear it for want of evidence. On August 7, 1962 President Kennedy handed her the highest honour America gives a civilian. Who was she?
context: Kelsey received the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service from John F. Kennedy on August 7, 1962, only the second woman to be given it; Kennedy said her judgment 'has prevented a major tragedy of birth deformities in the United States.' Samples distributed to American physicians were still linked to 17 birth defects. Sources: JFK Library; Wikipedia 'Frances Oldham Kelsey'; NLM.

question: Estes Kefauver had spent two years pressing for tighter rules on new medicines, with no interest from Congress. Thalidomide changed that in July 1962, and Kennedy signed the Kefauver-Harris Amendments that October. Before them, a maker had only to show the FDA a drug was safe. What did the law add?
choices: Proof that it cost less than older treatments
Proof that it had been tested abroad first
Proof that the maker could supply the country
context: The 1962 amendments introduced a proof-of-efficacy requirement for the first time in American law: safety was no longer enough, and a manufacturer now had to satisfy the FDA that a drug worked before selling it. The amendments also set rules for advertising and labelling. Source: Wikipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment'.

question: In 1973 an economist at the University of Chicago published a study in the Journal of Political Economy that asked about the 1962 drug amendments a question nobody in Washington had put: what did the new rule cost? He answered it by counting how many genuinely new medicines reached the American market before the law and after it. Which economist was he?
context: Sam Peltzman, 'An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments', Journal of Political Economy 81, no. 5 (September-October 1973). Peltzman took his Chicago PhD in 1965 and edited the JPE from 1974 to 1989. Stigler, Becker and Coase were Chicago colleagues working on regulation, human capital and social cost respectively. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sam Peltzman'; journals.uchicago.edu.

question: Sam Peltzman counted new chemical entities -- medicines built on a molecule never sold before -- arriving on the American market. In the years before the 1962 amendments the count ran at roughly 40 a year, and his statistical model said 41 a year would have kept arriving had the law not passed. What did the yearly figure actually become afterwards?
context: Peltzman found pre-1962 introductions averaging about 40 new chemical entities a year against about 16 afterwards, with his model predicting 41 absent the amendments -- roughly a 60 percent reduction in the flow of new medicines. Source: Peltzman (1973), JPE 81(5), summarised at fdareview.org.

question: Sam Peltzman did not stop at counting. He set the gain from keeping useless medicines off the shelves against the loss from good ones that never arrived, then stated the net result in a form any shopper would recognise. What did he say the 1962 amendments came to?
answer: A 5 to 10 percent tax on every prescription sold
choices: A 5 to 10 percent tax on every prescription sold
A delay of one year in every patient's access to new medicine
A transfer of about a billion dollars a year to the largest makers
A doubling of the price of the average brand-name medicine
context: Peltzman concluded the efficacy amendment imposed a net consumer cost comparable to a 5-10 percent excise tax on all prescriptions sold, and judged that 'the penalties imposed by the marketplace on sellers of ineffective drugs prior to 1962 seem to have been enough of a deterrent to have left little room for improvement.' Source: Peltzman (1973), p.1086; fdareview.org.

question: Alexander Schmidt ran the Food and Drug Administration from 1973 to 1976, and he explained the political weather his staff worked in by counting congressional hearings. Hearings attacking the FDA for having cleared a medicine, he said, were too frequent for his people to tally. What did he say about hearings of the opposite kind?
answer: In the agency's whole history he could not find one
choices: In the agency's whole history he could not find one
They came roughly once a decade, always after a lawsuit
They were held in closed session and never entered the record
They came only from members whose states had lost a factory
context: Schmidt, FDA Commissioner 1973-76: 'In all our FDA history, we are unable to find a single instance where a congressional committee investigated the failure of FDA to approve a new drug. But the times when hearings have been held to criticize our approval of a new drug have been so frequent that we have not been able to count them.' The asymmetry is the point: one kind of mistake summons a hearing, the other summons nothing. Source: quoted in Hoover Institution, 'The FDA at 100'.

question: A regulator judging medicines can go wrong twice over: it can clear one that turns out to harm people, or it can hold back one that would have helped them. The first mistake produces a name, a face and a hearing. Alex Tabarrok of George Mason University argues the second produces something just as real, and he coined a phrase for where those people end up. What did he call it?
context: Tabarrok's term: when a regulator fails to approve a good drug, people die, but the bodies are buried in an 'invisible graveyard' -- the deaths look like ordinary deaths from the disease, so nobody records them as an outcome of the decision. The regulatory ratchet is Robert Higgs's term; the precautionary principle is a real doctrine of erring toward caution. Sources: marginalrevolution.com, 'The Invisible Graveyard is Invisible No More' (2021); Wikipedia 'Alex Tabarrok'.

question: A senator proposes lengthening the FDA's review period so that no unsafe medicine ever reaches an American pharmacy again. Sam Peltzman and Alex Tabarrok would not answer that the proposal is wrong, and neither of them would call the senator's goal a bad one. They would put one particular question to the proposal. Which question?
answer: What happens to the patients still waiting in the queue, and who is counting them?
choices: What happens to the patients still waiting in the queue, and who is counting them?
Which companies helped write the review standards now in force?
How much will the extra months of review cost the taxpayer each year?
Why do European regulators reach other conclusions from the same trials?
context: This is Bastiat's method at the level of institutional design. The seen: a harmful medicine kept off the shelf, with a headline attached. The unseen: people dying of a disease whose treatment is still in the queue. Peltzman quantified the second in 1973; Tabarrok named it. The other three questions are real lines of criticism -- regulatory capture, budget cost, international comparison -- but none of them is the seen-versus-unseen move. Casey Mulligan's 'Peltzman Revisited' (NBER, 2021-22) redid the calculation for the COVID vaccine approval process and put the cost of a half-year delay at roughly a trillion dollars in the US alone.

question: In May 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression, President Franklin Roosevelt signed a landmark New Deal law designed to raise farm prices by reducing crop and livestock output. What was the law called?
context: The Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) of May 12, 1933 paid farmers to plow up crops already planted, kill livestock, and leave acreage idle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Adjustment_Act.

question: The most famous single case under the AAA's emergency hog program in the fall of 1933 was the government-directed slaughter of a huge number of animals -- many purchased from farmers specifically to destroy. Roughly how many pigs?
context: Roughly 6 million pigs were slaughtered under the AAA hog program in fall 1933. Millions of pounds of pork were rendered into fertilizer or dumped rather than shipped to the tens of millions of unemployed Americans in breadlines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Adjustment_Act.

question: The Roosevelt Secretary of Agriculture who publicly defended the pig-slaughter program on the radio -- and was booed for it -- was later Roosevelt's third-term vice president. What was his surname?
context: Henry Wallace (Secretary of Agriculture 1933-40, Vice President 1941-45) had to publicly defend the pig-slaughter policy on national radio. He was booed at speeches and the AAA became a national embarrassment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Wallace.

question: The Bastiat seen-versus-unseen reading of the 1933 pig slaughter is the archetype of the New Deal. SEEN was the higher price for surviving hogs, benefiting the farmer's cash flow. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The food itself -- pork rendered into fertilizer while children in breadlines went hungry
choices: The food itself -- pork rendered into fertilizer while children in breadlines went hungry
The federal tax revenue lost on the destroyed animals
The soil quality improvement from fewer hogs
The reduced water consumption on farms
context: Bastiat's method: the visible benefit was to farm cash flow; the hidden destruction was food that never reached the millions of hungry Americans in the same cities. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The Supreme Court struck down the original 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act in January 1936 as an unconstitutional use of the taxing power. What was the case name?
choices: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States
context: US v. Butler (297 US 1, January 6, 1936) struck down the AAA's processing tax as beyond Congress's taxing power. Congress passed a modified version in 1938 that survived and still forms the skeleton of US farm-subsidy programs today. Source: supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/297/1.

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued in 'A Monetary History of the United States' that New Deal supply-restriction programs like the AAA and NRA did what to the Great Depression?
answer: Prolonged it by raising costs during a monetary contraction
choices: Prolonged it by raising costs during a monetary contraction
Had no measurable effect on employment
context: Friedman + Schwartz's Monetary History argued the AAA and National Recovery Administration price supports artificially raised costs and prices during a period of monetary contraction, extending the depression. This is the mainstream monetarist reading. Source: Friedman + Schwartz (1963).

question: The AAA is often cited as the founding case for a specific Mancur-Olson-style political-economy dynamic: benefits concentrated on producers, costs spread across everyone else. What is the standard shorthand for this pattern?
context: Farm subsidy programs benefit a relatively small number of producers substantially while raising prices and taxes for everyone else diffusely. Olson's Logic of Collective Action theorized why the concentrated-benefit group organizes and the dispersed-cost group does not. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: A 2007 popular retelling of the AAA and other New Deal programs as economically damaging was written by an American economic journalist. What is the book called?
context: Amity Shlaes's The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression (HarperCollins, 2007) reintroduced the Rothbard-Friedman critique of the New Deal to a general audience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Forgotten_Man_(Shlaes_book).

question: The AAA's 1938 successor law survived the Supreme Court challenge and still forms the backbone of US federal farm-subsidy programs today. What is the modern general term for the periodic federal legislation that reauthorizes and modifies these programs?
context: The 'Farm Bill' is the general shorthand for the omnibus agricultural legislation Congress reauthorizes roughly every five years (most recently the 2018 Agriculture Improvement Act and its 2024 continuing resolution). The programs descend directly from the 1938 AAA. Source: usda.gov farm bill.

question: On April 5 1933, five weeks after his inauguration, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed an executive order requiring all US citizens to turn in their gold coins, gold bullion, and gold certificates to the Federal Reserve by May 1 1933 in exchange for paper Federal Reserve Notes. What is that order numbered?
context: Executive Order 6102 required Americans to turn in gold at the official rate of $20.67 per troy ounce. It was signed under authority of the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 (a wartime law) as amended by the March 9 1933 Emergency Banking Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: The penalty for refusing to turn in gold under the April 1933 order was severe. What did Americans who kept significant gold holdings face?
answer: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
choices: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
A fine of $500 and community service
A tax surcharge of 20% on all income
Loss of voting rights for the remainder of Roosevelt's term
context: $10,000 in 1933 dollars is roughly $240,000 in 2026 dollars. Citizens could keep small amounts (up to $100 face value in coins) and coins of recognized numismatic value. Bulk holdings were confiscated. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: On January 31 1934, less than a year after the gold seizure, Roosevelt issued a proclamation raising the official gold price to a new figure. What was the new official rate?
context: The January 31 1934 proclamation raised the official gold price from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce -- a 40.94% devaluation of the dollar against gold. Anyone who had turned in gold the previous year could not buy it back at the new rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The January 1934 gold revaluation was enabled by a specific new statute signed the day before. Which 1934 Act formalized the gold devaluation?
context: The Gold Reserve Act was signed January 30 1934. Roosevelt's proclamation raising the gold price to $35 followed the next day, January 31 1934. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1934 gold devaluation implicitly redistributed wealth by a specific percentage from Americans who had held gold to the US Treasury. What was the approximate implicit transfer?
answer: Roughly 77% of the purchasing power of savers who had held gold
choices: Roughly 77% of the purchasing power of savers who had held gold
context: A $20.67 dollar bought only 59% of what a $35 gold ounce did -- an implicit 77% devaluation of purchasing power measured against the gold citizens had been forced to sell at the lower rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1934 gold devaluation was upheld by a 5-4 Supreme Court ruling in 1935. What group of cases decided the constitutional challenge?
context: The 1935 Gold Clause Cases (5-4) upheld the seizure and devaluation while declaring unconstitutional the government's abrogation of gold-clause obligations in its own bonds. But the Court also held that bondholders were not entitled to damages -- a limited victory that was in practice a full defeat. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Clause Cases' (2026-09-05).

question: The prohibition on private gold ownership imposed in 1933 remained legally in force for four decades. When was it repealed?
choices: October 3 2008, under President George W. Bush
context: Congress repealed the ban on private gold ownership effective December 31 1974. Americans could once again legally own gold bullion for the first time in over 40 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold ownership laws in the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: The seized gold from the 1933 order needed a secure home. The federal government built a specific new secure vault in 1936 to house it. What is that facility called?
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Vault
context: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository was completed in 1936 in Kentucky to house the seized gold. It remains one of the most secure facilities in the world and holds the majority of official US gold reserves. Source: Grokipedia 'United States Bullion Depository' (2026-09-05).

question: Bastiat would describe the 1933-34 gold seizure and devaluation as a case where a stated policy purpose hides a systematic wealth transfer. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures its structure?
answer: Seen: strengthening the banking system by preventing gold hoarding; Unseen: American middle-class savers who had prudently held gold were transferred wealth to the US Treasury via the devaluation
choices: Seen: strengthening the banking system by preventing gold hoarding; Unseen: American middle-class savers who had prudently held gold were transferred wealth to the US Treasury via the devaluation
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: full employment; Unseen: rising real wages
Seen: growing federal revenue; Unseen: shrinking bureaucratic overhead
context: The stated purpose was banking stability. The invisible mechanism was a targeted wealth transfer from the group that had chosen the specifically prudent monetary asset. Bastiat's frame fits the episode exactly. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The 1933 gold seizure teaches a specific recognition move about the enforcement mechanisms available to a state that wants to break its citizens' hard-money alternatives. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: A determined state can criminalize private holding of hard money, seize existing holdings, and then devalue the currency at the new prices -- and this pattern has been used repeatedly across modern history
choices: A determined state can criminalize private holding of hard money, seize existing holdings, and then devalue the currency at the new prices -- and this pattern has been used repeatedly across modern history
States never take direct action against citizens' monetary choices
Democratic states are constitutionally unable to seize private property
Executive orders cannot legally override Article I Section 8 monetary powers
context: The 1933 US precedent is not unique. John Law tried to ban private gold ownership in 1720; the French Revolution imposed the death penalty for gold hoarding; multiple modern hyperinflators (Zimbabwe, Venezuela) have used similar mechanisms. The pattern is a standard tool. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold ownership laws by country' (2026-09-05).

question: During World War II and after, the Fed had agreed to peg US Treasury bond prices at levels the Treasury wanted -- effectively financing the war effort by keeping government borrowing costs artificially low. By 1951 this arrangement was fueling inflation. On March 4 1951 the two institutions announced a formal restoration of Fed independence. What is this restoration called?
context: The March 4 1951 Accord restored the Fed's independence to set monetary policy without pegging Treasury bond prices. Historians consider it the moment the modern independent Fed was born -- 38 years after the Federal Reserve Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: Shortly after the Accord, President Truman appointed a new Fed chairman in April 1951 who would go on to serve the longest of any modern Fed chair. Who was that appointee?
context: Martin served as Fed chairman for nearly 19 years (April 1951 to January 1970) under presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1951 Fed chair appointment had an ironic twist. The new chairman had actually helped negotiate the Fed-Treasury Accord from a specific institutional side, and Truman appointed him hoping he would prove loyal. What side had he been on during the negotiation?
choices: The Council of Economic Advisers side
context: Martin had negotiated the Accord as a Treasury official. Truman assumed a Treasury man would keep monetary policy accommodating to fiscal needs. Instead Martin became a fierce defender of Fed independence. Truman later said Martin 'double-crossed' him. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: In an October 19 1955 speech to the New York Group of the Investment Bankers Association of America, Martin used a memorable metaphor for the Fed's job that made his career. The Fed's role, he said, was to be the specific figure at a party. Which figure?
answer: The chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up
choices: The chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up
The bartender who refuses to serve one more drink
The host who quietly turns down the music
The doorman who admits only sober guests
context: Martin's 1955 punchbowl metaphor became the classic description of anti-inflationary central banking. The Fed's job, he said, is to be unpopular precisely when the boom feels best. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1955 punchbowl metaphor became so iconic that it entered financial journalism as the shorthand for a specific Fed function. What function does 'take away the punchbowl' name?
answer: Restrictive monetary policy imposed against political pressure during an economic boom
choices: Restrictive monetary policy imposed against political pressure during an economic boom
Rate cuts that stimulate the economy during a recession
Emergency lending to specific failing banks
Coordinated policy with foreign central banks during a currency crisis
context: 'Take away the punchbowl' means: raise rates when everyone wants easy money because the party is fun. It captures the political-economy tension every anti-inflationary Fed chair faces. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Martin served under a specific sequence of presidents across nearly 19 years. Which sequence covers his full tenure?
answer: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
choices: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Ford
Roosevelt, Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson
Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, and Ford
context: Martin's tenure ran from April 1951 through January 1970. He served under five presidents across three decades -- the longest continuous Fed chairmanship in modern history. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Martin's father held a specific earlier position in the Federal Reserve System, making the Martins one of very few father-son central bankers in US history. What was the father's role?
answer: First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
choices: First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
First chairman of the Federal Reserve Board
First governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York
First president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston
context: William McChesney Martin Sr. was the first governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis when the Fed opened for business in 1914. His son led the whole system 37 years later. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Martin's near-two-decade tenure faced increasing political pressure in his later years from a specific 1960s spending initiative. Which president's Great Society programs, alongside Vietnam War costs, put the toughest inflationary pressure on Martin's later years?
context: LBJ's Great Society programs and Vietnam War spending combined to test Martin's resolve. He eventually gave in to some inflationary policy, contributing to the setup for the 1970s Great Inflation that Arthur Burns then made worse. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed-Treasury Accord teaches a specific recognition move about the relationship between wartime finance and monetary independence. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: During wars central banks lose their independence to fiscal financing; the reassertion of independence afterward is a political fight that must be won explicitly, not assumed
choices: During wars central banks lose their independence to fiscal financing; the reassertion of independence afterward is a political fight that must be won explicitly, not assumed
Central bank independence is automatic and does not require political defense
Wars have no effect on central-bank monetary policy
Fiscal deficits are always neutralized by market interest-rate discipline
context: The 1951 Accord was a political victory hard-won by insiders who understood the inflationary consequences of continued Treasury-bond pegging. Fed independence is not a natural equilibrium; it is a political achievement that must be actively maintained. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: Martin's punchbowl metaphor teaches a specific recognition move about how difficult anti-inflationary central banking is politically. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The Fed's most important tightening decisions are always politically unpopular precisely because they arrive just when everyone is enjoying the boom
choices: The Fed's most important tightening decisions are always politically unpopular precisely because they arrive just when everyone is enjoying the boom
The Fed's tightening decisions are always politically popular during booms
The public consistently supports early anti-inflationary action
The Fed's decisions are politically neutral because they are technical
context: The Martin insight explains why Burns caved to Nixon in 1971-72, why Greenspan avoided the 1996 warning follow-through, and why every subsequent chair has struggled with the same tension. Anti-inflationary policy is unpopular when it matters most. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 1946 a former Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce executive founded an educational nonprofit in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York to keep classical-liberal economic writing in print. Who was the founder?
context: Leonard E. Read (1898-1983) founded the Foundation for Economic Education in March 1946 as the first American institutional home of the classical-liberal reading tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_for_Economic_Education.

question: Read named his 1946 nonprofit as the first American institutional home for classical-liberal educational work. What was the organization called?
context: FEE, founded 1946, preceded the Reason Foundation (1968), the Cato Institute (1977), and the Mises Institute (1982). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_for_Economic_Education.

question: In 1950 FEE re-published Bastiat's most-quoted pamphlet in a new American translation by Dean Russell. Which Bastiat pamphlet did the 1950 FEE edition carry?
context: La Loi (1850) as The Law, translated by Dean Russell, was the 1950 FEE edition that reintroduced Bastiat to English-language American readers. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Leonard Read's most famous essay, published in FEE's magazine The Freeman in December 1958, is narrated in the first person by an unusual speaker. Who or what narrates the essay?
context: 'I, Pencil' has an ordinary pencil describe the millions of coordinated market actions -- lumbering, mining graphite, refining rubber, mining zinc for brass ferrules -- required to make it, illustrating that no single actor holds the whole recipe. Source: fee.org/resources/i-pencil.

question: The argument of 'I, Pencil' -- that no single person on earth knows how to make even a common wooden pencil from scratch -- was built into an episode of a specific 1980 PBS television series. Which economist hosted that series?
context: Free to Choose (PBS, 1980), hosted by Milton and Rose Friedman, built its second episode around 'I, Pencil'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: FEE published two further Bastiat volumes in 1964 -- Selected Essays on Political Economy and an English edition of Economic Sophisms. Who edited the Selected Essays volume?
context: George B. de Huszar's 1964 FEE edition of Bastiat's Selected Essays on Political Economy became a standard American teaching text. Source: fee.org.

question: The most-read popular introduction to Austrian-flavored economics in American English was published by Harper in 1946 and long carried in FEE's catalog. Who was its author?
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) was published the same year as FEE's founding and became the paired popular introduction to the tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: FEE outlasted its Irvington-on-Hudson founding home and today operates from a specific American city where it continues to publish The Freeman and run student educational programs. Which city is FEE based in today?
context: FEE moved its offices to Atlanta, Georgia in the 21st century and continues its student-education mission from there. Source: fee.org.

question: The Cuban revolutionary who entered Havana on January 1, 1959 overthrew the previous strongman Fulgencio Batista and ran the island for nearly half a century. Who was he?
context: Fidel Castro's July 26 Movement entered Havana on January 1, 1959. He served as Prime Minister from February 1959, First Secretary of the Cuban Communist Party from 1965, and President 1976-2008. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro.

question: In April 1980 six Cubans crashed a bus through the fence of a foreign embassy in Havana asking for asylum. When Castro withdrew the embassy guards, more than 10,000 people poured onto the grounds within 48 hours. Which embassy?
context: On April 1, 1980 six Cubans drove a bus through the Peruvian embassy gates in Havana. When Castro withdrew the Cuban security guards for 48 hours, 10,800 Cubans poured into the embassy grounds asking for asylum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: Castro's response to the Peruvian embassy stampede in April 1980 was to open a specific Cuban harbor for a mass sea-crossing to Florida. What is that sudden exodus called?
context: Castro announced that Cubans who wished to leave could sail from Mariel harbor. From April through October 1980 about 125,000 Cubans crossed to Florida. Castro emptied several prisons and mental hospitals into the flow to embarrass the US. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: Roughly how many Cubans crossed to Florida during the April-October 1980 boatlift from Mariel harbor?
context: About 125,000 Cubans left Mariel between April and October 1980. The exodus overwhelmed South Florida's absorption capacity and became a defining political event of the Carter presidency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: After the USSR collapsed in 1991 and its subsidies ended, Cuba entered a severe economic contraction the government named with a euphemistic label. What did the state call this crisis?
context: The 'Special Period in Time of Peace' (1990-95) saw Cuban GDP fall about 35 percent in three years and average daily calorie intake fall from ~2,900 to ~1,800. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Period.

question: During six weeks in August-September 1994 the Special Period drove another mass exodus -- roughly 35,000 Cubans fled on rafts made from tires, wood, and scavenged materials. What was this exodus called?
context: 'Balseros' means raft-people. About 35,000 crossed to Florida in six weeks in 1994 aboard improvised rafts (balsas). The US shifted policy afterward to the 'wet foot / dry foot' rule that stood until 2017. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Cuban_rafter_crisis.

question: The 1960s Cuban political-prisoner memoir that opened the world's eyes to Castro's prison system was written by a poet who spent 22 years in confinement. Who wrote it?
context: Armando Valladares was arrested in 1960 and released in 1982 after French intervention. His memoir Against All Hope (1985) documented the Cuban prison system for a global readership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armando_Valladares.

question: In the first few years of the Cuban revolution, the head of the National Bank of Cuba and later Minister of Industry was a foreign-born revolutionary who oversaw the early nationalizations and the collapse of Cuban sugar output. Who was he?
context: Ernesto 'Che' Guevara ran the National Bank of Cuba 1959-61 and the Ministry of Industry 1961-65. Cuban sugar output fell sharply during his industrial-diversification push. He left Cuba in 1965 and was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara.

question: The Cuban diaspora total by 2016 -- including those born in the US to Cuban-American parents -- reached roughly what fraction of the island's population of about 11 million?
context: The 2010 US Census counted 1.79 million Cuban-Americans (immigrants plus US-born descendants), roughly a seventh of the island's population. Miami-Dade County alone had over 850,000. Source: US Census Bureau American Community Survey.

question: Fidel Castro handed provisional power to his brother Raul during a 2006 illness and then formally in 2008. In what year did Fidel die?
context: Fidel Castro died November 25, 2016 at age 90. Raul Castro remained head of state until 2018 and party first secretary until 2021. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro.

question: In January 2009 the incoming Obama administration's Council of Economic Advisers published a memo predicting that if Congress passed the $787B American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, unemployment would peak below a specific rate. Which peak rate did the memo predict?
context: The Romer-Bernstein memo of January 2009 ('The Job Impact of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan') published a chart showing unemployment peaking below 8%. In fact it reached 10.0% in October 2009, with ARRA fully in effect. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Recovery_and_Reinvestment_Act.

question: The two economists who signed the January 2009 CEA memo predicting an under-8% unemployment peak from the ARRA stimulus were the incoming CEA chair and vice-chair. Which pair signed it?
context: Christina Romer chaired the CEA; Jared Bernstein was Vice President Biden's chief economist. Their multiplier assumption of about 1.55 (each stimulus dollar raising GDP by $1.55) drove the under-8% forecast. Source: whitehouse.archives.gov (Romer-Bernstein memo, January 9 2009).

question: The Romer-Bernstein CEA memo of January 2009 rested on a specific numerical assumption about how much GDP each dollar of federal stimulus spending would generate. What size multiplier did the memo assume?
context: The 1.55 multiplier assumption is what generated the sub-8% unemployment forecast; recalculated with standard New-Keynesian frictions and crowding-out, the same models produce multipliers in the 0.6-0.7 range. Source: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland, Journal of Economic Dynamics 2010.

question: Robert Barro's Mercatus paper 'Government Spending, Taxation, and the Multiplier' (2011), using WWII as the biggest natural-experiment shock, estimated the peacetime US federal spending multiplier in what range?
context: Barro's estimate below 1 means: for every additional dollar of federal spending, private spending falls by MORE than the injected dollar, and total output rises by less than the dollar spent -- a net loss. Source: mercatus.org/publications/government-spending.

question: The Bastiat-style objection to any government spending multiplier above 1 is that the spent dollar had to come from somewhere. Bastiat's method names three possible sources for a stimulus dollar. Which triple is the correct list?
answer: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
choices: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
Confiscated from a corporation, appropriated from foreign trade, or drawn from reserves
Levied on tariffs, extracted from monopoly rents, or issued as certificates
Deducted from savings, garnisheed from wages, or redistributed from land
context: Bastiat's method: whatever the government spends, that dollar came from a taxpayer's foregone consumption, a lender's foregone loan to a private borrower, or a printed dollar whose Cantillon-effect winners capture it before prices adjust. The SEEN is the road crew; the UNSEEN is the private capital that dollar would have financed. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Valerie Ramey's 2011 JEL paper 'Can Government Purchases Stimulate the Economy?' uses vector-autoregression methods and finds that peacetime CIVILIAN federal spending multipliers cluster in what general range?
context: Ramey's careful VAR estimates find defense multipliers of 0.6-1.1 depending on specification, and civilian peacetime multipliers below 1. Sub-1 means net crowding-out of private activity. Source: Journal of Economic Literature 49(3), 2011.

question: The single Bastiat-style unseen effect at the core of the government-spending multiplier debate is that private borrowers or savers cannot use the same dollar the government has taxed or borrowed. What is the standard modern textbook name for this effect?
context: 'Crowding-out' is the modern name for Bastiat's UNSEEN: the private investment the government's borrowing displaces. If crowding-out is large, the stimulus multiplier falls below 1. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowding_out_(economics).

question: Cogan, Cwik, Taylor, and Wieland recalculated the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 multiplier in a 2010 Journal of Economic Dynamics paper. When they added standard New-Keynesian frictions and crowding-out, what multiplier did the same models produce?
context: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland showed the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 assumed away the crowding-out; realistic frictions bring the multiplier below 1. Source: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 34(3), 2010.

question: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) contains a single chapter whose title states the Bastiat objection to fiscal stimulus in one four-word phrase. Which chapter title states it?
context: Hazlitt's chapter 4 title, 'Public Works Mean Taxes,' compresses the whole Bastiat objection: the ribbon-cutting is seen; the tax that paid for it is unseen. Every 2009 ARRA critique is an application. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: The Bastiat objection to Keynesian public-works spending had a precedent in a 1932 letter to a British newspaper co-signed by four economists including F.A. Hayek, warning against Keynes-style deficit spending as a cure for the Depression. Which newspaper carried the letter?
context: The October 19 1932 letter to The Times, signed by Hayek, T.E. Gregory, Lionel Robbins, and Arnold Plant, objected to Keynes's proposed public-works program on classical / Austrian grounds; Keynes and Pigou replied five days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynes-Hayek_letters.

question: In 1973 the Bronx-born Mises disciple Murray Rothbard published his popular-audience libertarian manifesto with a major New York trade publisher. Which publisher issued it?
context: Macmillan editor Tom Mandel offered Rothbard the contract after reading his 1971 New York Times op-ed titled The New Libertarian Creed. The book, 327 pages in first edition, was Rothbard's first commercial book contract with a major trade house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: Rothbard's 1973 book with Macmillan was subtitled 'The Libertarian Manifesto.' What was its short main title?
context: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto (Macmillan, 1973) was Rothbard's popular-audience movement statement, distinct from his systematic 1982 political ethics and his 1962 economic treatise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard built his entire 1973 libertarian manifesto on one organizing axiom. Which axiom does it state?
answer: No person or group may aggress against the person or property of another
choices: No person or group may aggress against the person or property of another
Every person owes society a positive duty to reduce inequality where able
Government exists by the consent of the governed and rules only within that consent
The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right action
context: Rothbard called this the non-aggression axiom. He argued the whole libertarian program, on schools, roads, police, courts, and foreign policy, is what you get when you apply the axiom to state action as consistently as to private crime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard is credited with coining and popularizing a distinctive label for the stateless-society position he defended, one he began developing in the 1950s from an earlier phrase 'private-property anarchism'. What label did he coin?
context: Minarchism is the minimal-state position of Hayek and Milton Friedman. Classical liberalism dates to Adam Smith and the eighteenth century. Objectivism is Ayn Rand's philosophy. Rothbard's coinage set his position apart from all three by rejecting even a minimal state. Source: britannica.com/money/anarcho-capitalism.

question: A parent hears 'anarcho-capitalism' and pictures lawlessness. Murray Rothbard's 1973 book presses a specific correction: what does he say fills the role a state now plays for protection, courts, roads, and defense?
answer: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
choices: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
Voluntary local militias governed by direct town-hall vote
A single elected but powerless minimal state of night-watchman scope
International arbitration panels enforcing global common law
context: Rothbard's central move: not the ABSENCE of law but the private-market PROVISION of it. The famous test case in the book is his chapter on private roads. Source: mises.org/library/book/for-new-liberty-libertarian-manifesto.

question: Nine years after his 1973 manifesto, Murray Rothbard published a systematic philosophical treatise stating the same position from a Lockean natural-rights foundation. In what year did that treatise appear?
context: The Ethics of Liberty was published in 1982 by Humanities Press of Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey. If For a New Liberty was the popular manifesto, The Ethics of Liberty was the systematic treatise. A later edition (1998, NYU Press) carried an introduction by Hans-Hermann Hoppe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard's 1982 systematic ethics grounds the entire libertarian position in a secularized reading of one seventeenth-century political philosopher. Which philosopher's Second Treatise supplies the foundation?
context: Rothbard secularizes Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689): self-ownership, the labor theory of homesteading, and the strict limits on legitimate coercion. Rothbard drops Locke's theological grounding but keeps the natural-rights framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In the same year Murray Rothbard published For a New Liberty (1973), another American writer published a parallel anarcho-capitalist manifesto called The Machinery of Freedom, arguing for the same institutions from a consequentialist rather than natural-rights basis. Who wrote that parallel book?
context: David D. Friedman's The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism (Harper and Row, 1973) argued anarcho-capitalism on results-oriented grounds. The two 1973 manifestos, published within months of each other, defined the two branches of the modern anarcho-capitalist tradition, deontological (Rothbard) and consequentialist (Friedman). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: Robert Nozick's 1974 Harvard treatise Anarchy, State, and Utopia is often paired with Murray Rothbard's 1973 For a New Liberty as a rival libertarian statement. What position does Nozick DEFEND against Rothbard's anarcho-capitalism?
answer: A minimal night-watchman state, no more but no less
choices: A minimal night-watchman state, no more but no less
A stateless society organized by voluntary contracts
A liberal welfare state redistributing according to fair-share principles
A Rawlsian scheme maximizing the position of the least advantaged
context: Nozick argued that a minimal state limited to protecting rights against force and fraud would arise from an anarchic starting point without violating anyone's rights, but that anything more would. Rothbard rejected the derivation and insisted the state itself is a rights-violation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy,_State,_and_Utopia.

question: A student reads that The Ethics of Liberty devotes an entire Part IV to critical review of rival theories. Which four theorists does Murray Rothbard critique in that Part IV?
answer: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
choices: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
Milton Friedman, James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Ronald Coase
John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, and Michael Sandel
Ayn Rand, Nathaniel Branden, Leonard Peikoff, and Tibor Machan
context: Rothbard reviews Mises's utilitarianism, Hayek's rule-of-law liberalism, Berlin's two-concepts-of-liberty essay, and Nozick's minimal-state derivation, and argues each falls short of a fully consistent libertarian position. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: In the 1820s a young man on an inherited farm in the village of Mugron, in the Landes region of southwestern France, was teaching himself political economy by reading Adam Smith and Jean-Baptiste Say aloud in the evenings with his neighbour Felix Coudroy. His name was Frederic Bastiat. In which small Atlantic port had he been born in 1801?
context: Bastiat was born in Bayonne on 30 June 1801 to a merchant family, orphaned by tuberculosis at nine, and raised by his grandfather on the family estate near Mugron. Bordeaux, Nantes and La Rochelle are the other three major French Atlantic ports of the period. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: For twenty years Frederic Bastiat lived quietly on his grandfather's estate near Mugron, running the farm and reading political economy on his own. In October 1844 a Paris periodical published a first article of his, on English and French tariffs, and made his name overnight. Which one?
context: The Journal des Economistes was founded in 1841 by the Guillaumin house as the flagship of the French free-trade school. Bastiat's article 'The Influence of English and French Tariffs on the Future of the Two Peoples' appeared in the October 1844 issue. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frederic Bastiat wrote his economic essays in short, plain French that a shopkeeper or a farmer could follow -- deliberately, in conscious opposition to the continental economists of his day. Which stylistic choice did he most consistently reject?
context: Bastiat wanted his readers to be able to check the argument at each step without algebra. He used satirical dialogue (the Candlemakers' Petition), historical narration (the Sophisms), and first-person voice (Ce qu'on voit) freely; the one continental fashion he refused was the equation. Source: fee.org 'The Life of Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In 1846 Frederic Bastiat founded a national French free-trade organisation, the Association pour la Liberte des Echanges. He built it explicitly on a British campaign that Richard Cobden had just used to force through the 1846 repeal of the British grain tariffs. Which body did Bastiat copy?
context: Cobden's Anti-Corn Law League was founded in Manchester in 1838 and secured repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846. Bastiat visited England, met Cobden, and returned to Paris to build a French version of the League structure -- provincial chapters, a weekly paper, and public lectures. The Cobden Club came later (1866). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: After the February Revolution of 1848 Frederic Bastiat was elected to the French Constituent Assembly, and re-elected to the Legislative Assembly the following year. He sat on the finance committee, and the parliamentary speeches he chose to make there were mostly aimed at ONE set of opponents. Which?
answer: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
choices: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
The legitimists of Henri de Chambord and Berryer
The Bonapartists of Louis-Napoleon and Persigny
The Orleanists of Thiers and the Duke de Broglie
context: Bastiat's parliamentary speeches, published in the Assembly journals of 1848-49, mostly opposed Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux and Proudhon's Bank of the People. He was not primarily engaged with the royalist, Bonapartist or Orleanist blocs. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In June and July 1850, dying of tuberculosis in Paris, Frederic Bastiat sent two short pamphlets to the printer in the space of a few weeks. Together they became the most-quoted pages he ever wrote and remain his two best-known short works. Name the pair.
answer: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
choices: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
Sophismes economiques and Petition des fabricants de chandelles
Harmonies economiques and Cobden et la Ligue
Propriete et loi and Capital et rente
context: La Loi (The Law) appeared in June 1850 and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen) in July 1850. The Sophismes had appeared as two earlier collections (1845, 1848); Harmonies was his unfinished positive treatise; Propriete et loi and Capital et rente were earlier short pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: In the autumn of 1850 Frederic Bastiat's doctors sent him south, hoping the warm winter climate would ease his failing lungs. He travelled first to Pisa in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Which second Italian city did he then move to, and where he died on Christmas Eve?
context: Bastiat left Pisa for Rome in the late autumn of 1850 and lodged near the Piazza di Spagna. He died there on 24 December 1850 and is buried in the French national church of San Luigi dei Francesi. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frederic Bastiat's positive treatise, meant to answer the socialists on their own terms by showing that free exchange produces spontaneous cooperation rather than class conflict, went to press incomplete in the year he died. Only the first part appeared in his lifetime; the rest was assembled from his notebooks by his editors. What is the book called?
context: Harmonies economiques was Bastiat's attempt at a systematic positive doctrine, and he considered it the work he would be remembered for; only about half was in print at his death. Traite d'economie politique was Jean-Baptiste Say's 1803 textbook; Cours and Principes are common French treatise titles used by others. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: According to the friends who kept vigil at his bedside, Frederic Bastiat spent his last hour on 24 December 1850 murmuring the same two-word French phrase over and over, as if to remind them what he had spent his life defending. The phrase was:
context: The account of the deathbed scene comes from Prosper Paillottet, one of the editors of the posthumous Oeuvres completes, who was in the room. Bastiat had built his method around the discipline of not lying about consequences; the reported dying words -- 'the truth, the truth' -- were taken by his friends as the summary of that vocation. Legend, but well-attested. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Two economic concepts still standard in every modern textbook were introduced by Frederic Bastiat in the essays of 1848-1850. One is the parable of the broken window, which teaches the student to count what a policy destroys as well as what it creates. What is the OTHER concept?
context: Bastiat argued that every choice must be judged against the foregone alternative -- what the broken-window essay calls 'that which is not seen' -- and modern textbooks credit him with the first clear statement of opportunity cost. Comparative advantage is Ricardo (1817); marginal utility is Menger, Jevons and Walras (1871-74); the velocity of money goes back to the classical quantity theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: On September 13, 1970 the New York Times Magazine published a Milton Friedman essay that has become one of the most-cited business-ethics articles in history. What title did the magazine print above it?
answer: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
choices: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
The Corporation as a Moral Agent
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits' (New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970). Often called the Friedman Doctrine. Source: nytimes.com/1970/09/13/archives.

question: Friedman's 1970 argument frames the corporate executive as an employee of one specific group whose interests define his responsibilities. Which group?
context: Friedman: the executive is an employee of the shareholders and should generally maximize corporate profits within the rules of law and ethical custom. Any expenditure of shareholder money on the executive's own social projects is other people's money on his priorities. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (September 13, 1970).

question: Friedman's 1970 essay distinguishes what an executive may legitimately do with his SALARY from what he may do with CORPORATE resources. Which activity is the executive free to do with his own salary, but constrained from doing with the company's money?
answer: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
choices: Donate to whatever cause he chooses
Deposit it in a personal bank account
Buy shares in his own employer
context: Friedman's careful distinction: private-individual charity is voluntary and comes from one's own money; corporate-resource philanthropy uses shareholders' money for the executive's own priorities without their consent. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Friedman's 1970 essay explicitly permits executives to conform to two categories of societal rule while pursuing profit. Which pair is he willing to require the executive to follow?
choices: Only the letter of federal statutes
Only the moral code of the CEO's church
context: Friedman's precise phrasing: the executive should run the business to make as much money as possible 'while conforming to the basic rules of the society, both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom.' He is not defending fraud or predation. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Friedman's central move in the 1970 essay is not primarily moral -- it is an INSTITUTIONAL-DESIGN argument about accountability. When executives declare themselves representatives of workers, community, environment, and shareholders simultaneously, what specific problem arises?
answer: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
choices: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
They must consult a national advisory panel
They automatically qualify for federal subsidies
They lose access to corporate liability protection
context: Friedman's institutional-design point: multi-stakeholder mandates leave the executive without a specific principal to answer to. Any decision can be justified by naming which stakeholder it served. The shareholder-only mandate is disciplining precisely because it names one clear principal. Source: Friedman (1970); Jensen + Meckling, 'Theory of the Firm' (JFE 1976).

question: The Friedman doctrine was expanded from a chapter in an earlier Friedman book that had been published eight years before the New York Times essay. Which book was that?
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 8, made the shareholder-primacy argument that the 1970 NYT essay condensed and popularized. Friedman had been making the argument for at least a decade before the magazine version. Source: Friedman (1962), Chapter 8.

question: The Friedman doctrine has become the intellectual point of contact for the modern debate over ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) frameworks in investing. What is Friedman's specific critique of ESG in one phrase?
answer: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
choices: Other people's money charity by executives with no shareholder mandate
A regressive tax on middle-class households
A violation of federal antitrust law
An invitation to hostile foreign takeover
context: Classical-liberal critics of ESG apply the Friedman 1970 frame directly: fund managers directing corporate votes toward ESG goals are spending beneficiaries' assets to pursue the managers' own values without explicit consent. Source: Friedman (1970) as applied in Fink CEO-letter debates 2018-24.

question: In August 2019 the Business Roundtable, an association of nearly 200 large-corporation CEOs, released a Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation that explicitly broke from the Friedman doctrine. How many CEOs signed that 2019 statement?
context: The Business Roundtable's Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation (August 19, 2019) was signed by 181 CEOs and formally endorsed stakeholder capitalism over pure shareholder primacy. It was widely read as a direct response to renewed attention to the Friedman doctrine. Source: businessroundtable.org (August 2019).

question: Friedman's 1970 essay is often summarized in a memorable phrase capturing the objection when executives spend corporate resources on their own social preferences without shareholder consent. Which phrase captures the objection?
answer: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
choices: Spending other people's money on his own priorities
context: The Friedman phrase focuses attention on WHOSE money is being spent and WHOSE priorities are being served. Even a well-meaning executive-imposed cause is a use of shareholder assets without shareholder mandate. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Modern rebuttals of the Friedman doctrine include Michael Porter's 'shared value,' Colin Mayer's 'purpose of corporations,' and Rebecca Henderson's 'reimagining capitalism.' What structural claim do they all make against Friedman?
answer: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
choices: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
That the shareholder-only mandate should be criminalized federally
That the shareholder-only mandate applies only to European firms
That the shareholder-only mandate is unconstitutional under state law
context: The pro-stakeholder rebuttal, in various forms: attending to environmental, social, and community outcomes builds long-term corporate value that shareholder-narrow maximization misses. Friedman's response is that such considerations can be voluntarily adopted by shareholders themselves; executive imposition still lacks mandate. Source: Porter + Kramer, HBR (2011); Mayer, Prosperity (Oxford 2018); Henderson, Reimagining Capitalism (Public Affairs 2020).

question: In 1963 two economists published an 860-page monetary study of a century of American monetary events -- a book so influential that Ben Bernanke would later call it 'the leading and most persuasive explanation of the worst economic disaster in American history.' Which two economists coauthored it?
choices: John Maynard Keynes and Roy Harrod
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
