context: Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research through Princeton University Press. It became one of the most influential economics books of the 20th century. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: Chapter 7 of the 1963 book, titled 'The Great Contraction 1929-1933,' argued the Great Depression was fundamentally a monetary failure. By roughly what percentage did the M2 money supply contract during those four years -- a collapse the Fed had tools to prevent?
context: The M2 money supply contracted roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933. Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have prevented this by acting as lender of last resort during bank failures. It did not. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: Between 1930 and 1933 a specific catastrophic number of US banks failed out of roughly 25,000 in operation in 1929. How many banks collapsed during the Great Contraction?
context: Roughly 9,000 US banks failed 1930-33 -- about a third of all banks. Each failure destroyed the deposits held there (no FDIC until 1933), further contracting the money supply. The Fed, chartered specifically to be lender of last resort, mostly stood aside. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed's failure to act had specific institutional causes. One key cause was the 1928 death of the dominant Fed policymaker who had led the New York Fed since 1914. Whose death left the Fed rudderless?
context: Strong died in October 1928, less than a year before the crash. His absence left the Fed without a dominant voice able to force the system into aggressive lender-of-last-resort action during the 1930-33 bank failures. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: The Friedman-Schwartz analysis identified an internal Fed doctrine that became a suicide pact for the whole banking system: the doctrine held the Fed should not 'bail out' banks it judged unsound. What is this rescue-averse doctrine informally called?
answer: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
choices: The real-bills doctrine (in its liquidationist form)
context: The real-bills doctrine's liquidationist descendant held that the Fed should not lend to banks whose portfolios contained questionable loans -- exactly the banks needing rescue in 1930-33. The doctrine ensured the Fed refused to provide the liquidity that could have stopped the cascade. Source: Grokipedia 'Real bills doctrine' (2026-09-05).

question: On November 8 2002 the Fed governor who had trained as an academic historian of the Great Depression gave a speech at the University of Chicago concluding with a direct address to the aged authors of the 1963 book. What specific concession did he close with?
answer: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
choices: You're right, we did it, we're very sorry, but thanks to you we won't do it again
You were partly right, we admit some errors were made
You were largely wrong, but your work provoked useful thinking
You were right about the mechanics but wrong about the ultimate cause
context: Bernanke's November 8 2002 speech at Friedman's 90th-birthday conference conceded institutional Fed responsibility for the Great Depression -- an extraordinary public admission that made the Friedman-Schwartz thesis officially accepted. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: The Austrian critique of the 1963 book (Rothbard's counter-thesis in his own 1963 America's Great Depression) went further than the monetarist argument. What specifically did the Austrian critique add?
answer: The 1920s credit expansion Friedman-Schwartz downplayed was itself the seed of the 1929 crash
choices: The 1920s credit expansion Friedman-Schwartz downplayed was itself the seed of the 1929 crash
The Fed's contraction of 1929-33 had no relationship to the depth of the Depression
The Great Depression was primarily caused by protective tariffs and immigration policy
The Great Depression was primarily a natural business-cycle event unrelated to money
context: The Austrian addition: the 1929 bust was not just an accident that the Fed mishandled; it was the necessary correction of the malinvestment the Fed's own 1921-29 easing had produced. The two 1963 books agree that the Fed erred; they disagree about which decade's error was primary. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Milton Friedman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976. His coauthor Anna Schwartz, who continued working into her 90s and died in 2012 at age 96, never won the Nobel despite coauthoring the definitive American monetary history. Which Nobel year did Friedman receive?
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on monetary theory and consumption analysis. Schwartz's absence from the prize list is often cited as an example of the discipline's gender-biased recognition practices. Source: Grokipedia 'Anna Schwartz' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1963 book's core point -- that the Fed's monetary contraction 1929-33 caused the Depression -- has become mainstream doctrine even inside the Fed itself. Which recognition move does the ladder press about the political-economy significance of Bernanke's 2002 concession?
answer: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
choices: Institutional acceptance of a critical thesis by the very institution being criticized changes how that institution thinks about its own crisis responses -- for better or worse
Institutional acceptance of criticism has no effect on future policy
The Fed rarely acknowledges past errors publicly
Fed doctrine is entirely determined by whoever chairs the FOMC
context: The 2002 concession shaped Bernanke's own 2008 response (aggressive lender-of-last-resort action, massive QE). Austrian critics argue that by avoiding the 1930s error Bernanke created a different error -- long-lasting cheap money that seeded the 2020-24 inflation. Institutional learning has costs as well as benefits. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: Anna Schwartz, in a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview at age 92, gave a striking verdict on Ben Bernanke's crisis response -- effectively reversing the endorsement he had claimed six years earlier at Friedman's birthday party. What did she say about him?
answer: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
choices: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
That he was implementing exactly the policy she and Friedman had recommended
That his response would restore price stability within one year
That she remained firmly in agreement with his approach
context: Schwartz's October 2008 Wall Street Journal interview sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response. Six years after Bernanke had claimed the Friedman-Schwartz mantle at the birthday party, the surviving coauthor publicly withdrew the endorsement. Source: Wall Street Journal (October 18 2008).

question: In March 1975 Milton Friedman made a six-day trip to a South American country at the invitation of a private foundation. He met the country's ruler for about 45 minutes and gave public lectures in the capital on inflation policy. Which country was that?
context: Friedman visited Chile March 1975 at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He met Augusto Pinochet briefly and wrote one follow-up letter with monetary and economic recommendations. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The group of Chilean economists whose free-market reforms transformed Chile in the late 1970s and 1980s had studied at the University of Chicago under an exchange program with the Catholic University of Chile that began in 1955. What nickname did they acquire?
context: 'The Chicago Boys' were about 25 Chilean economists trained at Chicago under a 1955-founded exchange with the Catholic University of Chile. Their leaders included Sergio de Castro (Finance Minister 1976-82) and Hernan Buchi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Boys.

question: Friedman's 1975 Chile visit became controversial because Chile at that moment was under a military government that had taken power on September 11, 1973. Who ruled the country when Friedman visited?
context: Augusto Pinochet came to power in the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew the elected socialist president Salvador Allende. He ruled until 1990. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet.

question: Friedman was accused of endorsing Pinochet by his visit. In a 1976 letter to Newsweek he replied with a specific phrase about Pinochet's government. Which of the following captures his stated view?
answer: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
choices: A regime that I have nothing but dislike for
A shining example of Latin American governance
The best hope for South American development
A necessary transitional phase toward liberty
context: In his 1976 Newsweek letter Friedman described the Pinochet regime as 'one that I have nothing but dislike for.' He compared his visit to a doctor treating a patient in a country whose government he disapproved of. Source: Friedman, Newsweek (1976); Two Lucky People (1998).

question: Friedman also visited a large Marxist-Leninist state in 1980, giving similar economic advice to its leaders without generating comparable protest. Which country was that?
context: Friedman visited China in 1980, meeting Chinese leaders including Zhao Ziyang. He argued the selective outrage over his Chile visit reflected a political double standard, since the China visit went uncontested. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The Chicago Boys' economic reforms in Chile from 1975 onward included privatization of state industries, cuts in tariffs, opening to foreign investment, and price deregulation. Chile's poverty rate over the following decades moved from about 45% in 1973 to what level by 2010?
context: Chilean poverty fell from ~45% (1973) to ~10% (2010) as measured by the Chilean national statistics agency and the World Bank. Chile went from poorest to richest per-capita economy in South America. Source: worldbank.org (Chile poverty and inequality data).

question: On October 5, 1988 Chileans voted in a plebiscite on whether General Augusto Pinochet should remain in power. What was the outcome?
answer: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
choices: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
Pinochet won and remained in power for another decade
The plebiscite was cancelled by the military
Pinochet abdicated before the vote was counted
context: The October 5, 1988 plebiscite voted Pinochet out. Free elections in December 1989 chose Patricio Aylwin as president; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Chilean_national_plebiscite.

question: Chile's return to democracy in 1990 brought a series of center-left governments to power (Christian Democrats then Socialist-led coalitions). What did those elected governments do about the Chicago Boys' free-market reforms?
answer: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
choices: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
They reversed nearly every reform within the first two years
They nationalized every privatized industry immediately
context: Successor democratic governments in Chile substantially retained the market-economy framework across three decades of alternating center-left and center-right rule. Chile continued as the wealthiest South American economy per capita through the 2010s. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run macro data).

question: Friedman's 1975 Chile visit generated protests at his 1976 Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm. Which specific prize did Friedman win that year?
answer: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economic Sciences 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Protests at the Stockholm ceremony centered on the Chile visit. Source: nobelprize.org (Friedman 1976).

question: The Chile episode is often used to argue that free-market economics was inseparable from military dictatorship. Friedman rejected that argument by pointing to a specific pattern of his other visits to authoritarian countries. What was that pattern?
answer: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
choices: He also visited China, the USSR, and Yugoslavia without comparable protest
He refused ever to enter any country ruled by a dictator
He only visited democracies aligned with the US
He limited his travel exclusively to Western Europe
context: Friedman visited Communist China (1980), the Soviet Union, and Yugoslavia in earlier years, giving similar advice without generating comparable protests. He argued the selective outrage over Chile reflected political, not analytical, judgment. Source: Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The full Chile story from 1973 to the 2010s is often cited as a real-world natural experiment in economic-reform outcomes. Which one-sentence summary is most accurate to the record?
answer: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
choices: Chile went from poorest to richest South American economy while eventually returning to peaceful democracy
Chile remained the poorest South American economy throughout the entire period
Chile experienced total economic collapse and mass emigration
Chile abandoned all market reforms within five years of democratization
context: The record: Chile in 1973 was the poorest large South American economy; by the 2000s it was the richest per capita; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful and free-market reforms were substantially retained by successor democratic governments. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run data).

question: On December 29, 1967 in Washington, D.C., Milton Friedman delivered a presidential address to the American Economic Association that has been called the single most important paper in postwar macroeconomics. What was its title when published in the AER in March 1968?
choices: The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (American Economic Review, March 1968), from his December 29, 1967 AEA presidential address. Source: jstor.org (Friedman AER 1968).

question: Friedman's 1968 address argued that the long-run US jobless rate is anchored by real, non-monetary factors -- labor-market frictions, worker preferences, minimum-wage laws, unionization, information costs. What name did he give to this long-run anchor?
context: Friedman's natural-rate hypothesis: there is a rate of unemployment determined by real, non-monetary factors. Monetary policy cannot push unemployment permanently below it; it can only produce temporary reductions at the cost of accelerating inflation. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: In the mid-1960s the Keynesian macroeconomic consensus treated the Phillips Curve as a stable trade-off between inflation and unemployment. Friedman's 1968 address argued that this trade-off would eventually do what in the long run?
context: Friedman argued that once workers expected 4% inflation, they would demand 4% higher nominal wages, and unemployment would return to the natural rate -- with 4% inflation now baked in. The trade-off vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: Friedman developed the natural-rate hypothesis roughly simultaneously and independently with another economist -- a Columbia scholar whose 1967 Economica paper on the same topic actually preceded Friedman's AER paper by a few months. Who was that co-discoverer?
context: Edmund Phelps published 'Phillips Curves, Expectations of Inflation and Optimal Unemployment over Time' (Economica, August 1967) shortly before Friedman's AER paper. Phelps won the Nobel in 2006 specifically for this work. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Phelps 1967).

question: The Friedman-Phelps analysis of the Phillips curve modified it by adding a specific variable that had been absent from the standard 1960s treatment. What did they add to the analytical framework?
context: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve: workers demand nominal wages that account for expected inflation. Once expectations adjust, the trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman (1968); Phelps (1967).

question: Friedman's 1968 address predicted that attempts to keep unemployment permanently below the natural rate would produce accelerating inflation. Through the 1970s the US saw exactly this pattern: what did the annual US CPI inflation rate reach by 1980?
context: US CPI inflation ran ~2% in 1965, rising to ~13% by 1980. Unemployment did not fall permanently; both inflation and unemployment were high (stagflation) -- exactly what Friedman's 1968 address had predicted twelve years earlier. Source: bls.gov (CPI historical).

question: The joint condition -- high inflation AND high unemployment at the same time -- was the specific macroeconomic pathology of the 1970s that vindicated Friedman's 1968 prediction and shattered the stable-Phillips-curve consensus. What one-word name did the economics profession give this pathology?
context: Stagflation (stagnation + inflation) is the name for the 1970s combination of high unemployment and high inflation. The word was coined by British politician Iain Macleod in 1965. It marked the failure of the stable-Phillips-curve consensus. Source: Grokipedia 'Stagflation.'

question: Edmund Phelps received the 2006 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences citing his work on the natural-rate hypothesis and expectations-augmented Phillips curve. In what year had Milton Friedman received his Nobel, in part for related monetary-and-consumption work?
context: Friedman received the 1976 Nobel 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Phelps received the 2006 Nobel specifically for the natural-rate work. Source: nobelprize.org.

question: The natural-rate hypothesis carries a specific policy implication for central banks operating monetary policy. What is the accelerationist implication for keeping unemployment below the natural rate?
answer: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
choices: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
Doing so requires only a one-time inflation shock
Doing so is impossible without changing the natural rate itself
Doing so imposes no long-run inflation cost at all
context: The accelerationist implication: if the Fed keeps trying to push unemployment below natural, it must keep raising expected inflation to keep workers surprised. 4% then 8% then 16% -- eventually the monetary system breaks down. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: Friedman's 1968 address underlies a specific modern central-bank practice adopted in most developed economies since the early 1990s. What practice?
answer: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
choices: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
Complete abandonment of any monetary rule
context: Modern inflation targeting (New Zealand 1990, then dozens of countries) rests on the Friedman-Phelps insight: keep inflation expectations stable and the economy tends toward the natural rate. Wandering targets undermine expectations and produce accelerationist dynamics. Source: rbnz.govt.nz (New Zealand inflation-targeting history).

question: A boy born in Vienna in May 1899 grows up to become one of the twentieth century's most famous defenders of free markets, wins the 1974 Nobel in Economics, and dies in Germany in 1992. Which Austrian economist is he?
context: Friedrich August von Hayek (May 8, 1899 -- March 23, 1992). Mises was his teacher (born 1881); Menger founded the Austrian school in 1871 (born 1840); Rothbard was an American disciple (born 1926). Source: Wikipedia, Friedrich Hayek; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Which older Austrian economist ran the private Vienna seminar of the 1920s that Friedrich Hayek always credited as the man who taught him economics?
context: Hayek attended Mises's Privatseminar (Mises-Kreis) in Vienna throughout the 1920s. Bohm-Bawerk (1851-1914) had died before Hayek's student years; Menger (1840-1921) was gone from teaching; Schumpeter was contemporary but not Hayek's teacher. Source: mises.org profile.

question: In January 1931 an English economist invited a young Viennese researcher to give four lectures in London; the lectures were published that year as Prices and Production. Which host arranged the invitation that launched Hayek's English career?
context: Robbins was building up LSE's economics department and had read a Hayek article on underconsumption theory. Keynes was at Cambridge (and Hayek's later intellectual opponent); Pigou also at Cambridge; Marshall had died in 1924. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A von Hayek (1899-1992) at LSE'.

question: On the strength of his 1931 London lectures Hayek was offered a permanent chair. Which university housed the Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics that Hayek held from 1931 to 1950?
context: The Tooke Chair, named for Thomas Tooke, was LSE's senior economic-statistics post. Cambridge was the Keynesian citadel Hayek argued against; Oxford and UCL had different appointments. Source: LSE History blog on Hayek at LSE.

question: Hayek's 1944 polemic argued that central economic planning, however well-intentioned, tends to concentrate power in ways that erode political freedom. What is the title of the book that made Hayek famous outside academic economics?
context: Published 1944, the book was a wartime bestseller in Britain and the United States. Human Action (1949) was Mises's magnum opus; Man, Economy, and State (1962) was Rothbard's; The General Theory (1936) was Keynes's. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: When Hayek moved to the United States in 1950 he joined the University of Chicago -- but not the famous economics department, which refused to appoint him. Which interdisciplinary unit made him a professor instead?
context: The economics department found The Road to Serfdom too politically radioactive; the William Volker Fund financed his chair on the Committee. The Cowles Commission was the mathematical-economics group; Booth (then GSB) and the Law School were separate schools. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: In April 1947 an international society of classical-liberal scholars was founded at a Swiss mountain resort, with Hayek as its first president. Which forum -- named after the mountain that hosted the meeting -- did Hayek convene to keep the classical-liberal tradition alive after the war?
context: The founding meeting was April 1-10, 1947, at Mont Pelerin above Lake Geneva. The Fabian Society was the older British socialist group Hayek argued against; Cato (1977) and the IEA (1955) came later, both influenced by Mont Pelerin alumni. Source: Mont Pelerin Society, Friedrich Hayek page.

question: In 1974 the Nobel committee gave the Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Hayek jointly with a co-laureate whose politics were the opposite of Hayek's -- a Swedish social-democratic economist. Who shared the 1974 Nobel with Hayek?
context: The committee paired Hayek and Myrdal deliberately to honor both traditions. Samuelson won in 1970, Kuznets in 1971, Leontief in 1973 -- neighboring but not co-laureates. Source: Wikipedia, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Accepting the 1974 Nobel, Hayek delivered a lecture warning that economists had adopted the outward form of the natural sciences without the underlying knowledge such methods presuppose. Which title -- itself a rebuke to his own profession -- did Hayek give the Stockholm lecture?
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The General Theory of Second Best
context: Delivered December 11, 1974. 'The End of Laissez-Faire' was Keynes's 1926 essay; 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' was Hayek's 1945 American Economic Review paper (the same theme but a different work); the theory of second best was Lipsey and Lancaster 1956. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Hayek's final book, published in 1988 when he was 89, argued that morals and institutions have evolved through cultural selection rather than deliberate design, and that reason's ambition to redesign them is a mistake -- captured in a two-word title. Which late book presented Hayek's evolutionary case?
context: The Fatal Conceit (1988) was edited by W. W. Bartley III as the first volume of Hayek's Collected Works. The Sensory Order (1952) was his cognitive-psychology book; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected earlier essays; The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) was his methodology book. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Asked late in life how he would describe his own political tradition, Hayek rejected both 'conservative' and 'libertarian' and chose an older English label he traced back to Edmund Burke. Which self-description did Hayek adopt in his final decades?
context: Hayek explained the choice in the postscript to The Constitution of Liberty (1960), 'Why I Am Not a Conservative,' invoking Burke's use of the term. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Vienna, 1903. The founder of the Austrian school of economics, Carl Menger, retires from his university chair. The man chosen to take that seat is a former Menger student, born in Vienna in 1851, who will go on to be counted with Menger and Boehm-Bawerk as one of the three founding-generation Austrians. Which economist stepped into Menger's chair?
context: Friedrich von Wieser (1851 Vienna - 1926 St. Gilgen) succeeded Menger at the University of Vienna in 1903 and held the chair until 1922. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser and Eugen Boehm-Bawerk are the two most important Austrian economists of the generation after Menger. They also share a family tie: Wieser's sister Paula married Boehm-Bawerk. So the two founding-generation Austrians shared what family relationship?
context: Paula Wieser's marriage to Eugen Boehm-Bawerk made Boehm-Bawerk Friedrich Wieser's brother-in-law. The two studied together as students and worked in parallel for the rest of their careers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Before he returned to Vienna in 1903 to succeed Menger, Friedrich Wieser spent nearly twenty years (from 1884) as a professor at the German-language university in another Habsburg imperial capital. Where did Wieser teach for those two decades?
context: Wieser held the chair at the German-language Charles University in Prague from 1884 until his 1903 move to Vienna. Prague was then the second university city of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: August 30, 1917. World War One is grinding into its fourth year. Kaiser Karl I of Austria-Hungary appoints the sixty-six-year-old Vienna economics professor Friedrich Wieser to a cabinet position, which Wieser holds until the empire collapses on November 11, 1918. Which ministry did Wieser run in that last year of the empire?
context: Wieser served as Austro-Hungarian Minister of Commerce from August 30, 1917 to November 11, 1918, spanning the empire's collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A hungry man eats one apple, then a second, then a third. The pleasure the third apple gives him is less than the pleasure the first one did. Nineteenth-century economists needed a word for the extra usefulness of that LAST unit added. In 1884 a Vienna economist coined the German compound Grenznutzen for it -- and its English translation is now the load-bearing concept of modern price theory. Which term is the English translation of Wieser's 1884 coinage?
context: Grenznutzen = MARGINAL UTILITY -- the value of the last (marginal) unit consumed, and the reason a thirsty man in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and nothing for the tenth. Alfred Marshall coined 'consumer surplus' and 'producer surplus'; 'elasticity of demand' is also Marshall. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A farmer stares at his field in early spring. He can plant it with wheat or with barley -- not both. If he plants wheat, the real cost he bears is not the money for the seed; it is the barley crop he could have grown on that same field and now will not. Friedrich Wieser coined a German word for exactly this idea (Alternativkosten), and the English translation is now standard in every economics textbook. What is the English name for the cost the farmer bears?
context: Wieser's Alternativkosten translates as OPPORTUNITY COST -- the value of the next-best alternative use foregone. Sunk cost is spent-and-unrecoverable; marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; fixed cost does not vary with output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A German-speaking student in 1892 wants to learn the new marginalist economics but finds Carl Menger's 1871 Principles hard to read. He picks up a much more accessible marginalist treatise, published in 1889 under the title Der natuerliche Wert (Natural Value). Who wrote the 1889 book that taught marginalism to a generation of German-language readers?
context: Der natuerliche Wert (1889) was Wieser's more readable systematic restatement of Mengerian marginalism. For many 1890s German readers, Wieser -- not Menger -- was HOW they first met the theory. Karl Menger the mathematician was Carl Menger's son. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A steel mill produces train wheels using iron ore, coke, and skilled labor together. Classical economists (Ricardo, Marx) asked what gives the FACTORS -- ore, coke, labor -- their value, and answered with a labor theory built up from the bottom. Wieser rejected the classical bottom-up route: instead, WORK BACK from the final wheels' consumer value and attribute a share to each factor. Wieser named this top-down method with the German word Zurechnung. What is the English name for Wieser's method?
context: Wieser's IMPUTATION THEORY (Zurechnung) determines factor values by attributing back to each an appropriate share of the final product's utility -- a marginalist answer to the classical labor-theory question, from the top down. Arbitrage is exploiting price gaps; aggregation adds micro-quantities; depreciation reduces capital value over time. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser held the Vienna economics chair from 1903 to 1922. Sitting in his lecture hall at various points were three future giants of twentieth-century economics: Joseph Schumpeter, Ludwig Mises, and one man who would eventually win the 1974 Nobel Prize and write The Road to Serfdom. Which of Wieser's Vienna students was the future 1974 Nobel laureate?
context: Hayek attended Wieser's Vienna seminars in the early 1920s; he later wrote a warm memorial essay on his old teacher. Friedman, Rothbard, and Kirzner were all Americans of the next generation. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: In 1914 Friedrich Wieser published his mature synthesis, Theorie der gesellschaftlichen Wirtschaft (Social Economics) -- often called the only systematic treatise any of the older Austrians produced. Its most famous reader was a former Wieser student at Vienna who went on to write Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942) and to give economics the phrase 'creative destruction'. Which Wieser student did the 1914 book most influence?
context: Schumpeter was Wieser's Vienna student and always named the 1914 Social Economics as a formative influence on his own systematic ambitions. Boehm-Bawerk was Wieser's brother-in-law, not his student. Haberler and Machlup were later Vienna alumni. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser was born a commoner (plain 'Friedrich Wieser') but died a nobleman ('Friedrich von Wieser'). The particle 'von' was not birthright; it was awarded to him personally in 1917, the same year Kaiser Karl I put him in the cabinet and seated him in the upper chamber. Into which Austro-Hungarian body was Wieser seated on his 1917 ennoblement?
context: Wieser was elevated to hereditary nobility (Freiherr, Baron) in 1917 and appointed to the Austrian House of Lords (Herrenhaus) the same year, alongside his Ministry of Commerce cabinet role -- an unusually rapid political promotion for an academic. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: An Austrian-born economist who came up in the Mises Privatseminar in Vienna in the 1920s emigrated to America in 1933 and eventually held a chair at Princeton starting in 1960. Who was he?
context: Fritz Machlup (1902-1983) took his Vienna doctorate in 1923 with Mises's help, joined the Privatseminar, and moved to America in 1933 as a Rockefeller research fellow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: Machlup's most famous book was published by Princeton University Press in 1962 and pioneered a systematic count of a whole sector of American output no one had previously measured. What is the book's title?
answer: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
choices: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
context: The 1962 Princeton book coined and measured what Machlup called the knowledge industry: schools, research and development, media, communication, and information services. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: Machlup's 1962 book gave a headline figure that startled the mainstream profession: the knowledge industry already produced roughly what share of US GDP in 1958?
context: Machlup's 29% estimate for 1958 was published fifteen years before 'the information economy' became a business-magazine cliche. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: Machlup was a founding member in 1947 of Friedrich Hayek's classical-liberal scholarly society, which continues to meet today. What is that society called?
context: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded by Hayek in 1947 at Mont Pelerin, Switzerland; Machlup was a founding member and served as President 1966-1968. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: In 1966 Machlup was elected to the top professional office in his discipline, the highest honor an American economist can receive from peers. Which office was it?
answer: President of the American Economic Association
choices: President of the American Economic Association
Director of the National Bureau of Economic Research
Chief Economist of the World Bank
context: Machlup's 1966 AEA presidency was a rare case of a Mises-trained Austrian reaching the summit of the American mainstream without abandoning his tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/American_Economic_Association.

question: Machlup's later, much larger multi-volume treatise on the same topic as his 1962 breakthrough ran to eight volumes and appeared from Princeton University Press between 1980 and 1984. What was the collective title?
answer: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
choices: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
A Monetary History of the United States
context: The eight-volume series was completed posthumously by Machlup's colleagues and remains the most exhaustive academic treatment of the knowledge-industry idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: Machlup held his Princeton chair from 1960 to a specific year, after which he moved to New York University for his final active years. In what year did he move from Princeton to NYU?
context: Machlup's academic path ran Buffalo (1935) - Johns Hopkins (1947) - Princeton (1960) - NYU (1971 until his death in 1983). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: Machlup's own doctoral advisor at the University of Vienna in 1923 was the founding figure of the entire Austrian tradition Machlup carried to America. Who supervised the 1923 doctorate?
context: Machlup took his Vienna doctorate in 1923 under Mises and became one of the youngest members of the Mises Privatseminar. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: In November 2022 the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange stopped honoring customer withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy days later, headquartered in the Bahamas. What was the exchange's name?
context: FTX, founded 2019 by Sam Bankman-Fried, filed for Chapter 11 on November 11 2022 after a run triggered by a CoinDesk leak about its sister trading firm Alameda Research. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: FTX's founder was a former Jane Street quant trader in his late twenties, widely known by his initials 'SBF'. What is his full name?
context: Sam Bankman-Fried, MIT-educated, worked at Jane Street before founding Alameda Research (2017) and then FTX (2019). Arrested in the Bahamas December 12 2022. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: FTX had a sister trading firm run at various times by Caroline Ellison, whose losing trading positions were later shown to have been covered with FTX customer deposits. What was the trading firm's name?
context: Alameda Research, founded by SBF in 2017, was FTX's linked market-making and prop-trading arm. Its balance-sheet reliance on FTT triggered the November 2022 run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alameda_Research.

question: At its 2022 peak FTX was valued at $32 billion and sponsored a named professional-basketball venue in Miami. Which arena carried the FTX naming rights?
answer: FTX Arena (home of the Miami Heat)
choices: FTX Arena (home of the Miami Heat)
FTX Center (home of the Orlando Magic)
FTX Stadium (home of the Miami Dolphins)
FTX Field (home of the Tampa Bay Rays)
context: FTX bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's arena in a 2021 19-year, $135M deal. The naming reverted after the bankruptcy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaseya_Center.

question: On November 2 2022 CoinDesk published a leaked balance sheet that triggered the FTX bank run. The leak showed that Alameda Research's largest asset was not a normal reserve asset but a token issued by FTX itself. What was the token?
context: FTT was FTX's own exchange token. Alameda's balance sheet holding its sister exchange's own token as its largest asset was the market signal that led competitor Binance to announce it would sell its FTT holdings -- and that triggered the run. Source: coindesk.com (November 2 2022 report).

question: The competitor exchange whose CEO announced on November 6 2022 that it was selling its FTT holdings -- triggering the FTX run -- was the world's largest by trading volume. Which exchange was it?
context: Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao's November 6 2022 announcement that Binance would sell its FTT holdings after the CoinDesk leak triggered mass customer withdrawals from FTX; the run began within hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: The core operational fact that made FTX's collapse a fraud rather than just a bankruptcy was documented after the failure: customer funds had been treated in one specific unauthorized way. What had FTX done with customer deposits?
answer: Commingled them with Alameda's trading positions and used them to cover Alameda's losses
choices: Commingled them with Alameda's trading positions and used them to cover Alameda's losses
Wired them to overseas shell accounts to avoid US tax reporting
Loaned them to Binance to secure preferential trading terms
Used them to buy US government bonds without disclosure
context: The commingling-and-use of customer funds was the criminal act; it is the same failure mode as Mt Gox (2014) and MF Global (2011). Every exchange collapse of this shape has taught the same lesson: not your keys, not your coins. Source: cnbc.com (FTX bankruptcy filings coverage).

question: Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on all seven counts of fraud and conspiracy on November 2 2023. On March 28 2024 the federal judge Lewis Kaplan handed down his sentence. What was the sentence?
choices: Five years in federal prison and a fine
context: Kaplan's 25-year sentence covered wire fraud, securities fraud, and money-laundering conspiracy. FTX creditors were later paid back close to dollar-value on their claims by the bankruptcy estate, but of course missed the Bitcoin appreciation over the recovery years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried publicly identified his personal ethics with a specific movement whose stated aim was 'do the most good possible with your resources.' What was the movement called?
context: SBF had been publicly associated with 'effective altruism' since his Jane Street days; his stated ethic was that he would earn as much as possible and give it away. He then stole billions from his own customers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism.

question: FTX taught the same lesson as Mt Gox eight years earlier: an exchange that holds your Bitcoin can lose it, freeze it, or steal it. What Bitcoin-community slogan compresses that lesson?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
context: Every FTX customer who had trusted the exchange lost access; every customer who had self-custodied was untouched. The slogan predates FTX by years and got its clearest 21st-century test in November 2022. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Cold_storage.

question: In 1971 a Chicago School economist published a Bell Journal paper that stunned the profession by arguing regulation is generally acquired by the industry it supposedly restrains, and operated primarily for that industry's benefit. Who wrote that paper?
context: George Stigler (1911-1991) won the 1982 Nobel in economic sciences for his work on industrial structure and regulation. The 1971 paper is his most-cited contribution. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stigler.

question: George Stigler's foundational 1971 paper on regulatory capture appeared in a Bell Labs-sponsored economics journal that carried a specific mission-defining title. Which journal published 'The Theory of Economic Regulation'?
answer: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science
choices: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science
context: The Bell Journal (Spring 1971, volume 2 issue 1) published Stigler's paper. The journal is now the RAND Journal of Economics. Source: jstor.org (Stigler, Bell Journal 1971).

question: Stigler's one-line summary of his 1971 thesis flipped the standard public-interest story of regulation on its head. As he put it, regulation is 'acquired by the industry' and 'designed and operated primarily' for what purpose?
context: The exact phrasing: 'As a rule, regulation is acquired by the industry and is designed and operated primarily for its benefit.' Stigler documented this pattern across occupational licensing, trucking, and utilities. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal Spring 1971.

question: Stigler explained regulatory capture by pointing to an asymmetry of interest between two groups. On one side is the industry, with a large per-firm gain from favorable rules. On the other side is the general public, with a much smaller per-person loss. What word describes the shape of the public's costs in his analysis?
context: Stigler's concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern: a few firms gain a lot, millions lose a little each, so the concentrated side is worth organizing around and the dispersed side is not. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: A state legislature considers a new occupational-licensing law for interior designers. Stigler's 1971 analysis predicts which group will show up to lobby MOST enthusiastically IN FAVOR of the new requirement?
answer: Established interior designers already in the field
choices: Established interior designers already in the field
Prospective new entrants to the profession
context: Occupational licenses raise incumbents' incomes by restricting entry, so incumbent designers gain and future entrants lose. Stigler documented this pattern across barbers, morticians, accountants, and dozens of other licensed trades. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: Five years after Stigler's paper, another Chicago-trained economist formalized the theory into a mathematical model of interest-group competition over regulation in a 1976 Journal of Law and Economics article. Who wrote the model that became known as the second-generation capture theory?
context: Sam Peltzman, 'Toward a More General Theory of Regulation' (Journal of Law and Economics, 1976), generalized Stigler's insight into a formal model in which regulators balance pressure from multiple interest groups. Source: jstor.org (Peltzman 1976).

question: Stigler's theory made a testable prediction about the outcomes of rate regulation set by state utility commissions. Comparing the pattern across states, which side did his empirical work find those commissions consistently favored?
context: Stigler's electricity-rate case studies showed regulated rates systematically higher than they would have been under competition -- benefiting utility shareholders at consumer expense. Source: Stigler + Friedland, Journal of Law and Economics (1962) and Stigler 1971.

question: Stigler's 1971 analysis of federal trucking regulation named a specific agency that had spent decades setting rates and routes in a way that protected incumbent trucking firms from new competition. Which agency was that?
context: The ICC had regulated interstate trucking rates and routes since the Motor Carrier Act of 1935. Stigler's analysis anticipated the 1980 Motor Carrier Act deregulation. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971).

question: Stigler's research on capture led directly to a policy response: two waves of federal deregulation of transportation industries in the late 1970s. Which two industries were deregulated by acts signed in 1978 and 1980?
context: The Airline Deregulation Act (October 24, 1978, Carter) and Motor Carrier Act (July 1, 1980, Carter) were direct policy responses to Stigler-Peltzman capture analysis. Alfred Kahn led the airline deregulation as CAB chairman. Source: brookings.edu (transportation deregulation history).

question: Stigler's 1971 paper reframed a policy debate that had been mostly moral. Where welfare economics had asked 'what regulation SHOULD society want?', Stigler applied an economic method that asked a different question. Which question did his analytical move press?
answer: What regulation do interest groups actually DEMAND, and what does government SUPPLY?
choices: What regulation do interest groups actually DEMAND, and what does government SUPPLY?
What regulation would maximize national income under central planning?
What regulation would emerge from a Rawlsian veil of ignorance?
What regulation would satisfy median-voter theorem predictions?
context: Stigler's move: treat regulation as a PRODUCT with a market of its own. Industries demand it; politicians supply it in exchange for votes, contributions, and future employment. The public-interest justification is often a story told afterwards. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971), section II.

question: A high-school student asks how to test regulatory-capture theory. Stigler's own 1971 paper offered a specific empirical case where the theory made a distinctive prediction that public-interest theory did not. Which case did he treat as his sharpest test?
answer: Occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes without measurable quality gains
choices: Occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes without measurable quality gains
Antitrust litigation always benefits the largest firms
Central bank independence produces lower inflation
context: If licensing existed to protect consumers, quality should rise sharply relative to unlicensed states. Stigler and later Morris Kleiner found instead that incumbent wages rose and quality effects were small or nonexistent -- the pattern predicted by capture theory. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: One of the most-cited economists of the twentieth century co-founded a whole branch of economics without ever holding a PhD -- his highest earned degree was a University of Chicago law degree from 1947. Who was he?
context: Gordon Tullock (born February 13, 1922, Rockford, Illinois; died November 3, 2014) took a JD from Chicago in 1947 and never earned a PhD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Tullock.

question: Gordon Tullock spent nearly a decade after law school abroad in the US Foreign Service, and the postings colored his later economics. Which diplomatic posting during the Communist takeover of China gave him a firsthand look at bureaucratic maneuvering?
context: Tullock served in the US Foreign Service 1947-1956, with postings in Tianjin (during the Communist takeover), Hong Kong, and Korea. He later credited the experience with teaching him more about political incentives than any economics course. Source: Tullock, Selected Works (Liberty Fund, 2004).

question: Tullock and James Buchanan met at the University of Virginia and launched a founding book of public choice in 1962. What was the title of the treatise they co-authored that year?
context: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy (University of Michigan Press, 1962) is Buchanan-Tullock's founding text. Tullock arrived at Virginia in 1958. Source: press.umich.edu (Calculus of Consent).

question: In 1966 Gordon Tullock founded the discipline-defining journal for the field he had helped create, initially calling it 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making' before renaming it. What is the journal's current name?
context: Tullock founded 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making' in 1966 and renamed it Public Choice in 1968. He edited it for more than three decades. Source: springer.com/journal/11127.

question: In 1965 Tullock published a slim book with Public Affairs Press applying economic reasoning to how bureaucrats actually behave -- promoting their careers, expanding their agencies, protecting turf against rival departments. What did he call the book?
context: The Politics of Bureaucracy (Public Affairs Press, 1965) was Tullock's application of economic reasoning to bureau behavior. William Niskanen's 1971 Bureaucracy and Representative Government built directly on it. Source: mises.org (Tullock, Politics of Bureaucracy PDF).

question: Tullock's 1967 Western Economic Journal paper 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' launched a whole new subfield of economics. What one-word concept, formalized later by Anne Krueger in 1974, did that paper originate?
context: Tullock's 1967 paper introduced the idea; Anne Krueger's 1974 paper on Indian import licenses gave 'rent-seeking' its modern name. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: In 1983 Tullock moved to a Virginia university where he would spend the rest of his career and help make its economics department the world capital of public-choice research. Which institution was that?
context: Tullock and Buchanan moved the Center for Study of Public Choice to George Mason University in 1983. Tullock retired from GMU in 2008. Source: mercatus.org (Tullock biographical note).

question: Tullock's 1987 book applied public-choice reasoning to dictators, treating them as self-interested actors bargaining with courtiers and rival power centers. What one-word title did he give that book?
context: Autocracy (Kluwer Academic, 1987) extended the public-choice framework to dictatorships. Tullock argued dictators face the same rational-actor incentives as democratic politicians, only within different constraints. Source: springer.com (Autocracy 1987).

question: When James Buchanan won the economics Nobel in 1986 for the Calculus of Consent framework, Tullock -- his co-author on that book -- was pointedly not included in the prize. What was Tullock's widely-quoted quip about the omission?
answer: Being co-author of the Calculus of Consent apparently did not count
choices: Being co-author of the Calculus of Consent apparently did not count
The Nobel committee had confused public choice with social choice
The Foreign Service ruined his chances by delaying his degree
He should have insisted on the PhD after all
context: Tullock expected to share every public-choice-related Nobel and never won one. He was famously acerbic about the 1986 omission; the quote is well-attested by GMU colleagues. Source: Kliemt + Boettke, obituaries in Public Choice (2015).

question: Tullock spent nearly a decade in the Foreign Service before he ever wrote economics, yet his own account credited that experience with a very specific pedagogical role in his intellectual formation. What did he say the diplomatic posting had taught him?
answer: More about political incentives than any economics course could have
choices: More about political incentives than any economics course could have
The importance of Keynesian aggregate-demand management
The mathematical foundations of general equilibrium
That bureaucracy could not be modeled economically
context: In his autobiographical essays Tullock repeatedly credited Tianjin, Hong Kong, and Korea postings with teaching him how real bureaucracies actually work -- the raw material for his later economics of politics. Source: Tullock, Selected Works vol. 1 (Liberty Fund 2004).

question: In 1937 the League of Nations in Geneva commissioned an Austrian-born economist to survey every existing theory of the business cycle. Which Mises-Kreis alumnus took the commission?
context: Gottfried Haberler (1900-1995), a Vienna doctorate under Wieser and Mises and a Mises-Kreis member, was commissioned by the League of Nations to write the standard cross-theory survey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: Haberler's 1937 survey book for the League of Nations carried a two-word main title referencing the peak and trough of the trade cycle. What was the title?
context: Prosperity and Depression: A Theoretical Analysis of Cyclical Movements (Geneva, 1937) became the standard reference book on business-cycle theories for a generation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Prosperity_and_Depression.

question: In 1936 Haberler emigrated to America and took a professorial chair he would hold for 35 years, at one of the country's oldest universities. At which university did he hold the chair?
context: Haberler emigrated to the United States in 1936 and held his Harvard chair until retiring in 1971. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: Prosperity and Depression made a specific methodological move that more purist Austrians (especially Mises himself) saw as a first step toward compromise with the mainstream. What was Haberler's move?
answer: He treated the Austrian theory as one theory among several equally worth surveying
choices: He treated the Austrian theory as one theory among several equally worth surveying
He refused to include the Austrian theory in the survey at all
He argued the Austrian theory alone was correct and dismissed all others
He translated the Austrian theory into full Keynesian aggregate-demand language
context: By presenting Austrian ABCT alongside Mitchell, Keynes, Schumpeter and the classical purely-real theories without a strong methodological commitment, Haberler softened the strict Austrian position. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Prosperity_and_Depression.

question: Haberler's earlier 1933 book (translated 1936) on international trade formalized the Ricardian idea of comparative advantage in specifically Austrian-friendly terms. What was Haberler's key reformulation?
answer: Comparative advantage restated using opportunity cost
choices: Comparative advantage restated using opportunity cost
Comparative advantage restated using capital-labor ratios
Comparative advantage restated using the Cobb-Douglas function
context: Der internationale Handel (1933) reformulated Ricardo's original labor-theory formulation into the modern opportunity-cost version taught in trade textbooks today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: In 1947 Haberler joined a specific classical-liberal international scholarly society at its founding, alongside Hayek, Mises, Machlup, and Milton Friedman. Which society was it?
context: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded by Hayek in April 1947; Haberler was among its founding members and remained a lifelong participant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: After his 1971 Harvard retirement Haberler moved to a specific Washington DC think tank where he wrote policy pamphlets attacking wage-and-price controls, monetary inflation, and protectionism. Which institution did he join?
context: Haberler moved to AEI after his Harvard retirement in 1971 and wrote there until near his death in 1995. His policy convictions stayed classical-liberal even as his theoretical framework had softened. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: Haberler's original Vienna doctoral supervisors were two founding-generation Austrians. Which pair supervised him?
answer: Friedrich von Wieser and Ludwig von Mises
choices: Friedrich von Wieser and Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger and Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
context: Haberler took his Vienna doctorate under Wieser and Mises and joined the Mises Privatseminar. Wieser had been Menger's direct successor at Vienna. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gottfried_Haberler.

question: On August 11 1987 President Reagan appointed a new Fed chairman succeeding Paul Volcker. The appointee was a private economic consultant with unusually close ties to Wall Street and had briefly chaired the Council of Economic Advisers under Ford (1974-77). Who was he?
context: Greenspan took the Fed chair on August 11 1987. He was well-known for his admirer's relationship to Ayn Rand -- he had been a member of her Collective in the 1950s and contributed essays to her 1966 book Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: Only two months into the new Fed chair's tenure, on a specific day in October 1987 the US stock market crashed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points -- 22.6% in one day, still the largest single-day percentage decline in Dow history. What is this day remembered as?
context: October 19 1987 -- Black Monday -- saw the Dow fall 22.6% in a single trading day. It remains the largest single-day percentage decline in Dow history, exceeding even the worst individual days of 1929 and 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Black Monday (1987)' (2026-09-05).

question: The specific automated-trading strategy that contributed most to the cascading sell orders of Black Monday was a hedging technique developed by academics at UC Berkeley. What was this trading strategy called?
context: Portfolio insurance -- developed by Berkeley academics Hayne Leland and Mark Rubinstein -- used dynamic hedging with futures to protect portfolios from downside. In practice, during a sharp decline, the strategy triggered cascading sell orders that amplified the crash. Source: Grokipedia 'Portfolio insurance (finance)' (2026-09-05).

question: On the morning of Tuesday October 20 1987, the new Fed chair's Fed issued a one-sentence statement that stabilized the market within days. What was the substance of the statement?
answer: The Fed was ready to serve as a source of liquidity to support the economic and financial system
choices: The Fed was ready to serve as a source of liquidity to support the economic and financial system
The Fed would raise interest rates to defend the dollar
The Fed would suspend all open market operations pending review
The Fed would close the Discount Window until markets recovered
context: Greenspan's Fed statement of October 20 1987 committed to unlimited liquidity to prevent cascading bank failures from margin-call liquidations. Rates were cut. Markets stabilized within days. Source: federalreserve.gov (statement October 20 1987).

question: The new Fed chair's rapid October 1987 intervention became the template for what would soon be called a specific eponymous protection -- the pattern of Fed rate cuts and liquidity injections whenever asset prices fell sharply. What is this pattern called?
context: The 'Greenspan put' is an options-market metaphor. A put option protects the holder against downside. Markets learned in 1987 that the Fed would provide that protection whenever asset prices fell sharply. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: In March 1988, four months after the 1987 crash, an executive order created an interagency group to coordinate emergency responses to market instability. The group has an official name and a colorful informal nickname. What is the informal nickname?
context: The Working Group on Financial Markets -- created by executive order in March 1988 after Black Monday -- was quickly nicknamed the 'Plunge Protection Team' in financial press. It coordinates emergency responses across the Treasury, Fed, SEC, and CFTC. Source: Grokipedia 'Working Group on Financial Markets' (2026-09-05).

question: From an Austrian and moral-hazard perspective the successful defense of asset prices in 1987 taught investors a specific lesson that shaped subsequent decades. Which lesson did the market learn?
answer: The Fed would step in during major declines, creating the risk-taking incentive that drove the 1990s dot-com and 2000s housing bubbles
choices: The Fed would step in during major declines, creating the risk-taking incentive that drove the 1990s dot-com and 2000s housing bubbles
Portfolio insurance was too dangerous and would never be used again
Cash equities would trade only between 9:30 AM and 4:00 PM Eastern
The Fed's discount window would no longer accept commercial paper
context: The 1987 intervention 'worked' brilliantly in the short run. Its long-run effect was to train markets to price in Fed backstops, encouraging progressively larger risk-taking. The 1987 template is the parent of every subsequent bubble. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: The specific S&P 500 return to its pre-crash level took a particular length of time after Black Monday. How long did the index need to recover its September 1987 peak?
context: The S&P 500 recovered its pre-Black Monday level within about two years. The rapid recovery was itself part of the 'Greenspan put' lesson -- crashes that appear catastrophic in the moment could be reversed quickly if the Fed acted decisively. Source: Grokipedia 'Black Monday (1987)' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1987 intervention teaches a specific recognition move about the tension between short-run stabilization and long-run moral hazard. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: A rescue that succeeds brilliantly in the short run can teach markets exactly the wrong risk-taking lesson for the long run
choices: A rescue that succeeds brilliantly in the short run can teach markets exactly the wrong risk-taking lesson for the long run
Rescues always fail to stabilize markets
Short-run and long-run effects of rescues are always aligned
Markets never learn from prior rescue precedents
context: The 1987 intervention was a technical success. Its cost was expectational, arriving over years as markets priced in the implicit Fed backstop for every subsequent decline. The tension between short-run stabilization and long-run moral hazard is the deepest problem in discretionary central-bank policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Greenspan put' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1987 chair had a specific pre-Fed intellectual history that made his subsequent policy record striking. Which movement had he been intellectually associated with before joining the Fed?
answer: Ayn Rand's Objectivist circle and his 1966 essay Gold and Economic Freedom
choices: Ayn Rand's Objectivist circle and his 1966 essay Gold and Economic Freedom
The Chicago-school monetarist movement led by Milton Friedman
The Austrian-school movement led by Ludwig von Mises
context: Greenspan had contributed 'Gold and Economic Freedom' to Rand's 1966 book Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, defending the gold standard. His shift to a discretionary Fed chair who orchestrated the Greenspan put is one of the most striking intellectual reversals in American economic policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: The longest-serving Fed chairman in modern history served from August 11 1987 through January 31 2006 -- more than eighteen years across four US presidents. Who was he?
context: Greenspan served under Reagan, Bush 41, Clinton, and Bush 43. His nickname 'The Maestro' captured the cult of technocratic control that surrounded him at his peak. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: After the dot-com crash of 2000-01, the Greenspan Fed cut the federal funds rate from 6.5% in December 2000 down to a specific historic low. By June 2003 the funds rate reached what floor -- and stayed there for a full year?
context: The 1% federal funds rate held from June 2003 through June 2004 -- at the time the lowest US policy rate in 46 years. Cheap credit flowed into interest-rate-sensitive sectors, especially housing. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The extended 1% funds-rate policy poured cash into the American housing market, where prices had risen at roughly the rate of general inflation for decades. Once artificially cheap credit hit, what began happening in coastal markets like California, Florida, and Nevada?
choices: Home prices fell as builders overbuilt
Home prices held flat as buyer demand softened
Home prices rose only in high-tech cities
context: Coastal metros saw double-digit annual price gains through 2004-2006. Mortgage originators wrote enormous volumes of subprime loans -- no-doc 'liar loans,' 2/28 adjustable-rate mortgages, negative-amortization products -- to feed the demand. Source: Grokipedia 'United States housing bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: Two large subprime originators wrote enormous volumes of the exotic mortgages that fueled the mid-2000s housing boom. One was Angelo Mozilo's California-based firm; the other was an Orange County giant. Which two firms led subprime origination?
choices: Wells Fargo and Bank of America
context: Countrywide (Mozilo) and Ameriquest were the largest subprime originators through the mid-2000s boom. Both failed or were absorbed during 2007-2008 as the underlying loans defaulted at accelerating rates. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 27 2005, at a specific industry conference, the Fed chair publicly dismissed housing-bubble concerns, acknowledging some local 'froth' but arguing a national bubble was implausible. Which industry conference hosted the speech?
context: Greenspan's October 27 2005 ABA speech argued that housing markets were fundamentally local and heterogeneous, so a coordinated national bubble was unlikely. Two years later the national market entered the collapse that triggered the Global Financial Crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian analysts had been warning since 2003 that the low-rate policy was creating an unsustainable housing boom via a specific mechanism from Austrian business-cycle theory. Which mechanism did they name?
answer: Artificially low interest rates cause capital to be misallocated into interest-sensitive sectors, and the bust is inevitable when the underlying savings do not exist
choices: Artificially low interest rates cause capital to be misallocated into interest-sensitive sectors, and the bust is inevitable when the underlying savings do not exist
Rapid deflation forces creditors to seize collateral en masse
Foreign capital inflows always cause housing bubbles
Full employment always triggers wage inflation
context: Austrian business-cycle theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929): rates set below the natural rate mislead entrepreneurs into long-duration projects (like housing) that the real savings pool cannot sustain. When the mismatch resolves, the malinvestment liquidates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Three specific Austrian-tradition voices publicly warned about the housing boom on cable television, in Congress, and at the Mises Institute between 2003 and 2007. Which trio is standardly cited?
answer: Peter Schiff on CNBC, Ron Paul in Congress, and Mark Thornton at Mises
choices: Peter Schiff on CNBC, Ron Paul in Congress, and Mark Thornton at Mises
Larry Summers, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Nouriel Roubini
Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Alan Blinder
context: Schiff's CNBC appearances 2005-07 predicting the collapse are widely circulated on YouTube ('Peter Schiff was right' compilations). Ron Paul warned in congressional hearings; Mark Thornton wrote at mises.org. All three were dismissed at the time. Source: Grokipedia 'Peter Schiff' (2026-09-05).

question: In October 2008 congressional testimony, after the crisis had struck, the retired Fed chair made an extraordinary admission about his own economic worldview. What did he say he had found?
answer: A flaw in his worldview about how markets self-regulate
choices: A flaw in his worldview about how markets self-regulate
That interest-rate policy had no effect on housing prices
That subprime lending had been entirely responsible without any Fed role
That the crisis had been predicted only by leftist economists
context: Greenspan's October 23 2008 testimony to the House Oversight Committee: he had found 'a flaw' in his belief that self-interested bankers would protect their institutions from ruin. The admission stunned Congress. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: The Greenspan era teaches a specific recognition move about what happens when a central bank holds interest rates below the market-clearing level for years at a time. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: Cheap credit misallocates capital into interest-sensitive sectors; the bust that follows is not a market failure but the correction of the earlier distortion
choices: Cheap credit misallocates capital into interest-sensitive sectors; the bust that follows is not a market failure but the correction of the earlier distortion
Central banks always time interest-rate cuts correctly
Housing markets are immune to interest-rate policy because they are local
Deregulation is the sole cause of asset-price bubbles
context: The Austrian read of 2000-2008: the 2007-09 crash was the necessary liquidation of the malinvestment the 2003-06 cheap credit had produced. The bust was the market working, not failing. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: In a 1966 essay published in Ayn Rand's Objectivist newsletter, the man who would later chair the Fed argued explicitly for a return to a gold-based monetary system. What was the title of that essay?
choices: The Case for a Sound Dollar
Monetary Policy in a Free Society
context: Greenspan's 1966 essay is one of the sharpest short defenses of the gold standard ever published. He abandoned that view when he took the Fed chairmanship in 1987. The gap between the 1966 Greenspan and the 2003-06 Greenspan is one of the most striking intellectual reversals in American economic policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1560 an English merchant and financial advisor wrote to the newly-crowned Queen Elizabeth I explaining why England's coinage was in trouble. His formulation became one of the oldest named laws in economics. Who was he?
context: Thomas Gresham advised Elizabeth I on the crown's finances and founded the Royal Exchange in London in 1571. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Gresham.

question: Gresham's Law is remembered by a short six-word maxim describing what happens when two coins of the same face value but different metal content are both declared legal tender. What is the maxim?
choices: Inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
context: The formulation, later shortened to 'bad money drives out good,' is Gresham's core observation about circulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: When a full-silver shilling and a half-silver shilling both circulate as legal tender at one shilling, Gresham's Law says a rational spender behaves in one specific way at every transaction. What does the spender do?
answer: Pays with the half-silver coin and keeps the full-silver coin
choices: Pays with the half-silver coin and keeps the full-silver coin
Pays with the full-silver coin and keeps the half-silver coin
Pays with whichever coin is nearest to hand
Melts both coins into a single new shilling
context: The rational spender unloads the worth-less coin and retains the worth-more coin. Merchants receive only debased coin; full-silver coins get hoarded, melted for bullion, or exported. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: The astronomer Nicholas Copernicus also served as a monetary advisor to the Prussian estates. His 1526 treatise Monetae cudendae ratio contains an early statement of the same 'bad money drives out good' observation. In which year did Copernicus write it?
context: Copernicus's Monetae cudendae ratio (1526) noted that when better coin is introduced, the old is not withdrawn but hoarded. He beat Gresham by 34 years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Monetae_cudendae_ratio.

question: Even before Copernicus and Gresham, a 14th-century French bishop had already written up the same monetary insight in his treatise De Moneta (about 1360). Who was that earlier writer?
context: Nicole Oresme's De Moneta (about 1360) preceded Gresham's 1560 letter by roughly 200 years. The observation, in short, is far older than the name attached to it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nicole_Oresme.

question: Given that Oresme (about 1360) and Copernicus (1526) both wrote the insight before Gresham (1560), the modern textbook attribution to Gresham comes from a specific 19th-century economist who found Gresham's letter in the archives. Who attached Gresham's name to the law?
context: Macleod's 1858 book The Elements of Political Economy attached Gresham's name to the maxim. Naming honors are downstream of who happens to publish the compilation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Dunning_Macleod.

question: In 1965 the United States passed a Coinage Act that removed one specific metal from newly minted dimes and quarters, replacing it with a copper-nickel clad composition. Which metal did the 1965 act remove?
context: The Coinage Act 1965 removed silver from dimes and quarters and clad them in copper-nickel; Americans quickly pulled the pre-1965 silver coins out of pocket circulation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Coinage_Act_of_1965.

question: Within a few years of the 1965 US Coinage Act, pre-1965 US silver dimes and quarters largely vanished from pocket change. Gresham's Law names the specific mechanism that made them disappear. What did Americans do with the silver coins?
answer: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
choices: They pulled them from circulation and hoarded or melted them
They deposited them at the Federal Reserve to be re-issued
They mailed them to the US Treasury for silver certificates
They exchanged them at banks for the new clad coins
context: The classic modern instance of Gresham's Law: as soon as the copper-nickel dime and quarter appeared, ordinary savers pulled pre-1965 silver coins from change and kept them for their metal value. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: Gresham's Law depends on one very specific legal condition being in force. Without that condition, the mechanism does not fire. Which condition must be present?
answer: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
choices: Both coins are declared legal tender at the same face value
One coin is manufactured by a foreign mint
The economy is under a fixed gold standard
The central bank is targeting a specific inflation rate
context: The law's engine is legal-tender equality: only when the state forces the two coins to trade at the same face value will spenders unload the worth-less coin and hoard the worth-more one. Without that fiat equality, they would simply trade at their true weights. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gresham%27s_law.

question: On January 11 2009, days after the Bitcoin network went live, a cryptographer tweeted two words that became one of the most famous two-word tweets in tech history. Who typed the tweet?
context: Hal Finney (1956-2014) was a cryptographer at PGP Corporation who had spent the 1990s and 2000s writing PGP's encryption code. His January 11 2009 tweet: 'Running bitcoin.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney's famous January 11 2009 tweet was exactly two words describing what his computer was doing. What did the tweet say?
context: 'Running bitcoin.' Finney was the second-ever Bitcoin node operator, running the software days after Satoshi's own machine started the network. Source: twitter.com/halfin (January 11 2009).

question: On January 12 2009, one day after his 'Running bitcoin' tweet, Hal Finney received 10 BTC from Satoshi Nakamoto in what became the first Bitcoin transaction ever recorded between two different people. Which block on the block chain records that first person-to-person transaction?
context: Block 170 contains the first Bitcoin transaction between two distinct parties (Satoshi to Finney, 10 BTC). Every earlier transaction had been Satoshi mining and paying himself. Source: blockchain.info/block-height/170.

question: Before Bitcoin, Hal Finney was famous in cryptography circles for his contributions to a specific email-encryption tool that journalists, dissidents, and cypherpunks used worldwide through the 1990s. What was the tool?
context: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), designed by Phil Zimmermann and developed at PGP Corporation, was Finney's day job through the 1990s and 2000s. He wrote much of the code behind PGP as journalists and dissidents relied on it worldwide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy.

question: Later in 2009 Hal Finney was diagnosed with a specific neurodegenerative disease. It progressively paralyzed him, and by 2013 he was typing with eye-tracking software. Which disease?
context: ALS -- Lou Gehrig's disease -- progressively paralyzed Finney. His 2013 bitcointalk.org essay 'Bitcoin and Me' was typed with eye-tracking software when almost all voluntary movement was gone. Source: bitcointalk.org (Bitcoin and Me, 2013).
