question: Hal Finney's 2013 bitcointalk.org essay recounts running the second Bitcoin node, receiving the first person-to-person transaction, and watching Bitcoin grow while his body failed. What is the essay's title?
context: 'Bitcoin and Me' (bitcointalk.org, March 19 2013) is Finney's own account of everything from the first mailing-list post to his ALS diagnosis. It reads as a plain first-person history from inside the earliest Bitcoin community. Source: bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=155054.

question: Hal Finney died on August 28 2014. Per an arrangement he had had for years, his body was preserved by a specific Arizona-based life-extension organization. Which organization performed the cryopreservation?
context: Alcor (Scottsdale, Arizona) performed Finney's cryopreservation; Finney had been a long-term life-extension advocate. Bitcoin was one of many long-view bets in his life. Source: alcor.org (case report A-2643).

question: Hal Finney's 2004 paper 'Reusable Proofs of Work' was one of the direct technical antecedents Satoshi Nakamoto cited when publishing the Bitcoin white paper. What was the short name of Finney's system?
context: RPOW (Reusable Proofs of Work), 2004, built on Adam Back's earlier hashcash and pushed the idea toward a spendable digital token. Satoshi cited RPOW as prior art in the Bitcoin white paper. Source: rpow.net.

question: For years Hal Finney was one of the small handful of people accused of being Satoshi Nakamoto. Two lines of evidence rule out that theory. Which pair?
answer: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
choices: His own explicit denial, plus timeline evidence that he was training for a marathon while Satoshi was posting
His documented US citizenship, plus the fact that Satoshi's writing style was clearly non-American
His public retirement announcement, plus his stated preference for gold-backed money over digital cash
His employer's NDA obligations, plus his lack of interest in cryptographic proofs
context: Finney explicitly denied being Satoshi. Timing evidence: he was training for a marathon and posting run-times during periods Satoshi was posting emails elsewhere; forensic-text analysis has not matched. Source: newyorker.com (Andy Greenberg profile, 2014).

question: In the Bitcoin community Hal Finney is remembered as the first person besides Satoshi to see clearly what Bitcoin was going to be. What specific role did he play in the first weeks of the network?
answer: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
choices: He ran the second-ever Bitcoin node, one day after the network went live
He wrote the first Bitcoin exchange to trade coins for dollars
He mined the very first block, the genesis block, before Satoshi did
He edited the final draft of the Bitcoin white paper for Satoshi
context: Satoshi's own machine was Bitcoin node 1; Finney's was node 2, running January 11 2009. He received the first person-to-person transaction on Block 170 the following day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Adam Back's 1997 Hashcash system required a small proof-of-work stamp to be attached to every email, discouraging spam. But each stamp had a strict limitation compared to money. What was it?
answer: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
choices: Each stamp was single-use and could not be transferred like a coin
Each stamp had a fixed expiration date measured in seconds
Each stamp required a live connection to a central bank server
Each stamp was only redeemable on Microsoft-issued hardware
context: Hashcash proved you had done real computational work, but the stamp was spent after one use. Making stamps transferable required solving double-spending -- the same problem Bitcoin later solved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hashcash.

question: In 2004 a cryptographer built a system to make Hashcash-style proof-of-work stamps into transferable tokens -- something you could pass to another person, who could pass again. What did he call the system?
context: The cryptographer was Hal Finney. The RPOW acronym stands for Reusable Proofs of Work (plural of 'proof'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney's 2004 Reusable Proofs of Work system needed some way to prevent a token holder from spending the same token twice. What architectural choice did Finney make to solve that problem?
answer: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
choices: A trusted server that tracked which stamps had been spent and issued replacements
A blockchain distributed across thousands of independent nodes
A cryptographic zero-knowledge proof stored on every user's device
A quorum vote among the top 21 stamp holders
context: Finney ran the server himself on an IBM 4758 secure coprocessor, whose signed open-source code could be audited. But the trusted server was still a single point of failure. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Hal Finney's RPOW ran on cutting-edge trusted hardware whose signed code could be audited to prove it was doing what it claimed. Which specific hardware did he choose?
context: The 4758 was a tamper-resistant special-purpose chip designed for cryptographic key storage. Finney used it to prove the RPOW server code was the audited version -- but the trusted-server architecture itself remained a weakness. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Finney knew RPOW had a specific architectural weakness that his trusted-hardware approach could not fully eliminate. Which was it?
answer: The trusted server itself was a single point of failure -- if it went down or was corrupted, RPOW failed
choices: The trusted server itself was a single point of failure -- if it went down or was corrupted, RPOW failed
The proof-of-work puzzles could be solved instantly by any modern laptop
The stamps expired within twenty-four hours of issuance
The system required every user to hold a Federal Reserve routing number
context: This is the weakness Satoshi's proof-of-work + longest-chain rule solved four years later -- consensus without a trusted third party. Finney's own public writings had named the problem he could not solve. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: In late 2008 the Bitcoin white paper appeared, solving exactly the problem RPOW's trusted server had left unsolved. Because Hal Finney had spent four years thinking about that problem, he became one of the very first outsiders to run the software. Which two-word tweet did he post on January 11, 2009?
context: One of the earliest public traces of anyone besides Satoshi running the Bitcoin software. Finney had downloaded the software the day after Christmas 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: On January 12 2009 Hal Finney received the first person-to-person Bitcoin transaction, sent directly to him by Satoshi Nakamoto and recorded in block 170. How much Bitcoin did the transaction transfer?
context: Block 170 was the first Bitcoin transaction between two people (rather than a miner's block reward paying itself). Finney had answered Satoshi's forum post volunteering to test the network. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hal_Finney_(computer_scientist).

question: Every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years) a specific event in Bitcoin's protocol cuts the reward miners receive per new block exactly in half. What is this event called?
context: The halvings occurred in November 2012 (50 to 25 BTC per block), July 2016 (25 to 12.5), May 2020 (12.5 to 6.25), and April 2024 (6.25 to 3.125). The schedule caps the total supply at 21 million. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_halving.

question: Bitcoin's price history shows a rough four-year pattern of bull peaks. Which sequence gives the approximate peaks in order?
context: Each peak followed a halving by roughly 12-18 months, until the 2024-25 cycle, which peaked faster (about 8 months after the April 2024 halving) partly due to spot ETF flows. Source: grokipedia.com/page/History_of_Bitcoin.

question: Analysts describe Bitcoin's rough four-year cycle in four phases: capitulation after a peak, quiet buying at the low, price rising back as awareness returns, and a parabolic top before the next cycle. Which classical Austrian shape does this pattern resemble?
answer: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
choices: The boom-bust cycle Mises and Hayek attributed to monetary supply shocks
The permanent-income consumption smoothing hypothesis of Milton Friedman
The animal-spirits investment theory of John Maynard Keynes
The productivity-growth model of Robert Solow
context: Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT) treats booms and busts as monetary phenomena rather than psychological ones. Bitcoin's cycles have been interpreted as this shape applied to a monetary asset in an early-adoption phase. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: A Palestinian-American economist published a 2018 book making the Austrian case for Bitcoin as sound money, argued the halving schedule imposes hard monetary discipline, and became one of the movement's most-read authors. Who was he and what was the book?
choices: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan
context: Ammous made the argument that Bitcoin's programmatic supply schedule and its historical price cycles fit an Austrian monetary framework. Vijay Boyapati (The Bullish Case for Bitcoin) and Lyn Alden made related arguments. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: An anonymous analyst using the handle 'PlanB' published a 2019 Medium post proposing a model that claimed to predict Bitcoin prices from the halving schedule alone. What is the model called, and how has it held up?
answer: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
choices: The stock-to-flow model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
The stock-to-flow model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024
The Elliott wave model; it has tracked actual prices exactly through 2024
The efficient-markets model; it has significantly diverged from actual prices since roughly 2021
context: PlanB's model became famous during the 2020-21 bull market but has failed as a forecast since. The Austrian recognition move survives -- past cycles are real -- but the specific PlanB quantitative claim did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: The 2024-25 Bitcoin cycle broke $100,000 in December 2024, only about eight months after the April 2024 halving. Prior cycles had taken 12-18 months to peak. A specific new source of demand introduced in January 2024 helps explain the compressed timing. What was it?
answer: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, approved by the SEC on January 10, 2024
choices: US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, approved by the SEC on January 10, 2024
Widespread retail adoption of a new El Salvador wallet app
A Chinese central-bank purchase program for Bitcoin reserves
A European Central Bank digital-currency swap facility
context: Spot Bitcoin ETFs let institutional and retail buyers hold Bitcoin exposure through ordinary brokerage accounts. Inflows in early 2024 totaled tens of billions of dollars and preceded the December 2024 six-figure breakthrough. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_exchange-traded_fund.

question: A first-time Bitcoin holder in 2025 wants to know whether the past cycle pattern guarantees a next four-year peak. What is the honest analytical answer?
answer: The past cycles are real observations, but the 2024-25 cycle already broke the pattern -- past patterns do not guarantee future ones
choices: The past cycles are real observations, but the 2024-25 cycle already broke the pattern -- past patterns do not guarantee future ones
The pattern is mathematically certain and holders can time purchases from the halving date
The pattern was refuted by the stock-to-flow model and Bitcoin is now in permanent decline
The pattern only applies to gold, not to Bitcoin, so no forecast is possible
context: Recognizing the historical shape is teachable; treating it as a guaranteed forecast is not. The 2024-25 cycle compressed the timing and added spot-ETF demand as a structural factor prior cycles lacked. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: A German-born economist emigrated to the United States in 1986 to work with Murray Rothbard at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and became the leading modern voice of the Rothbardian anarcho-capitalist tradition. Who is he?
context: Hoppe was born September 2, 1949 in Peine, West Germany; joined Rothbard at UNLV in 1986; taught there until retiring in 2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: Hoppe's most-cited book was published in 2001 by Transaction Publishers and argues that hereditary rule creates better long-run governance incentives than a competing modern form. What is the book's title?
context: Democracy: The God That Failed (Transaction Publishers, 2001) is Hoppe's best-known book and the flagship of his controversial-within-Austrian argument. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Hoppe took his 1974 doctorate at the University of Frankfurt am Main under a specific leading left-wing philosopher of the Frankfurt School, before moving right and emigrating to America. Under whom did Hoppe study?
context: Hoppe's PhD in philosophy (Frankfurt, 1974) was supervised by Habermas, then the leading exponent of Frankfurt-School critical theory. It is an unusual training path for an Austrian economist. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: In 2006 Hoppe founded an annual libertarian conference held each summer in a specific Turkish coastal resort town. What is the town?
context: The Property and Freedom Society, founded by Hoppe in 2006, meets each year in Bodrum, Turkey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Property_and_Freedom_Society.

question: Democracy: The God That Failed compares monarchy and democracy through one specific incentive concept. Which concept anchors Hoppe's comparison?
context: Hoppe's argument turns on time-preference: how heavily an officeholder weighs the present against the future, given his tenure horizon. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Hoppe frames the difference between a monarch and a democratic politician through one specific property-rights analogy about the state itself. Which analogy captures his move?
answer: A monarch owns the country; a democratic politician rents it
choices: A monarch owns the country; a democratic politician rents it
A monarch leases the country; a democratic politician homesteads it
A monarch mortgages the country; a democratic politician insures it
A monarch inherits the country; a democratic politician sub-lets it
context: Owner-vs-renter is Hoppe's core analogy: an owner protects the long-term value of an asset; a renter has an incentive to extract before the lease expires. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Hoppe's argument predicts that a democratic officeholder facing a fixed term will handle public borrowing in a specific way that a hereditary monarch would not. What does the argument predict about borrowing?
answer: He borrows heavily against future taxpayers he will not answer to
choices: He borrows heavily against future taxpayers he will not answer to
He avoids borrowing to keep his term's balance sheet clean
He borrows only from citizens who voted for him
He borrows against his own private estate rather than the state's
context: In Hoppe's incentive analysis a term-limited politician is rewarded for pulling forward spending and pushing costs onto successors and their taxpayers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: In 1988 Hoppe published an argument that the very ACT of arguing already presupposes property rights, so any argument denying self-ownership contradicts itself. What is that argument called?
context: Hoppe's argumentation-ethics move (1988) claims performative contradiction: to argue at all, one must already exercise property in one's own body. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Argumentation_ethics.

question: Hoppe's Democracy: The God That Failed is controversial within the Austrian tradition itself. Two named Austrians who ACCEPT parts of his incentive analysis while REJECTING his anti-democratic conclusion are often cited. Which pair?
context: Boettke (George Mason) and Salerno (Pace, later Mises Institute) are prominent modern Austrians who engage Hoppe's incentive analysis critically without endorsing his political conclusion. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: Beyond Democracy: The God That Failed, Hoppe wrote an earlier 1989 book that laid out his praxeological-ethics defense of private property against socialism. What is that earlier book?
answer: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism
choices: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism
The Economics and Ethics of Private Property
context: A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism (Kluwer, 1989) is Hoppe's systematic praxeological-ethics treatise, four years before The Economics and Ethics of Private Property (Kluwer, 1993). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans-Hermann_Hoppe.

question: In 1935 an Austrian economist teaching at the London School of Economics edited a Routledge essay collection that carried the calculation problem to English-language readers for the first time. Which Austrian edited the volume?
context: Hayek, teaching at LSE since 1931, assembled and edited the volume Collectivist Economic Planning (Routledge, 1935) to bring the German-language debate into English. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: Hayek's 1935 Routledge collection had a two-word subject followed by a colon and a longer subtitle. What was the collection's main title?
context: Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism, edited by F. A. Hayek (Routledge, 1935). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: The centerpiece of the 1935 volume was the first English translation of an obscure 1920 German essay that had barely reached Anglo-American economists. Whose essay was newly translated?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Ludwig von Mises's Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
Karl Marx's Critique of the Gotha Program
Vilfredo Pareto's Manual of Political Economy
Leon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics
context: S. Adler's translation of Mises's 1920 essay became the volume's centerpiece; before 1935 the argument had circulated only in German-language economic journals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: One of the 1935 volume's translated foreign essays was by an Italian economist whose own 1908 paper 'The Ministry of Production in the Collectivist State' had actually PREDATED Mises 1920 and had argued an equilibrium theory of a planned economy. Who was the Italian?
context: Enrico Barone's 1908 essay outlined an equilibrium theory of a planned economy that Lange would later develop; Barone was actually closer to the eventual market-socialist reply than to Mises's position. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: Hayek contributed two of his own essays to the 1935 volume. The introductory piece surveyed the debate's origins; the closing piece reviewed the 1920s German-language literature. What is the shorter title of the closing survey?
answer: The Present State of the Debate
choices: The Present State of the Debate
The Nature and History of the Problem
The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: Hayek's two 1935 contributions were 'The Nature and History of the Problem' (introduction) and 'The Present State of the Debate' (survey of the 1920s German-language exchanges). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Collectivist_Economic_Planning.

question: The mid-1930s market-socialist reply to Mises came from a Polish-born economist whose 1936-1937 Review of Economic Studies papers were a direct answer to Hayek's 1935 volume. Who wrote that reply?
context: Lange's 'On the Economic Theory of Socialism' Parts I and II (Review of Economic Studies, 1936-1937) is the founding market-socialist reply to Mises and to the 1935 Hayek volume. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: Hayek collected his own later essays on the calculation and knowledge problem in a 1948 University of Chicago Press book. What is its title?
context: Individualism and Economic Order (Chicago, 1948) collects Hayek's 1930s-1940s essays, including 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) and 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Individualism_and_Economic_Order.

question: In 1934 a self-taught journalist who had left college early for money reasons joined The New York Times as its financial columnist, a post he would hold for twelve years. Which classical-liberal writer was he?
context: Henry Hazlitt (1894-1993) had already edited economics at The Nation before the NYT job; he left the Times in 1946 for a Newsweek column he kept for twenty years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hazlitt.

question: Henry Hazlitt spent twenty years, 1946 to 1966, writing a classical-liberal financial column inside a major mass-market American weekly, a lonely voice through the New Deal and Great Society years. Which magazine ran his column?
context: Hazlitt's 'Business Tides' column ran in Newsweek from 1946 to 1966; Milton Friedman later took a similar Newsweek slot in 1966, calling Hazlitt the model. Source: mises.org/library/portrait-henry-hazlitt.

question: In 1946 Henry Hazlitt published a short book that has never gone out of print and has sold over one million copies, dedicated on its title page to a French pamphleteer dead 100 years. Which book was it?
choices: The Failure of the New Economics
context: First issued by Harper & Brothers in 1946, then Arlington House in 1979; the dedication reads 'To Frederic Bastiat, 1801-1850.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: The 1946 book Economics in One Lesson carries a title-page dedication to a single 19th-century French classical-liberal economist whose seen/unseen method the book restates for American readers. Whom did Hazlitt name?
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' is the essay Economics in One Lesson expands, chapter by chapter, into a mid-20th-century American application. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Chapter 1 of Economics in One Lesson states the whole book's method in one sentence: 'The art of economics consists in looking not merely at the immediate but at the longer effects of any act or policy; it consists in tracing the consequences of that policy not merely for one group but for all groups.' What is Hazlitt's name for this method inside the book?
context: Every remaining chapter is a worked example of 'the one lesson' applied to a specific New Deal or postwar policy (public works, price fixing, tariffs, minimum wage). Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: In 1946, the same year Economics in One Lesson appeared, Henry Hazlitt co-founded America's first free-market think tank with Leonard Read in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Which organization did they start?
context: FEE (1946) predates Cato (1977), the Mises Institute (1982), and Reason Foundation (1978); Read was president, Hazlitt sat on the founding board. Source: fee.org/about/our-history.

question: In 1959 Henry Hazlitt published a book-length reply to John Maynard Keynes, working chapter by chapter through Keynes's 1936 General Theory and answering each argument in order. Which Hazlitt book was that?
answer: The Failure of the New Economics
choices: The Failure of the New Economics
context: The 1959 book is the closest thing to a full Austrian-tradition rebuttal of the General Theory, section by section; Hazlitt also edited The Critics of Keynesian Economics (1960), an anthology of every major published critique. Source: mises.org/library/failure-new-economics.

question: Friedrich Hayek publicly praised Economics in One Lesson in one short line printed on later editions of the book. Which two-word verdict did Hayek deliver?
context: John Chamberlain gave it the Wall Street Journal review; F.A. Hayek's 'a brilliant performance' has adorned the back cover of most editions since. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson takes a French pamphleteer's 1850 essay and turns it into a mid-20th-century American book. The essay it restates was written by a dying tuberculosis patient months before his death. Which essay did Hazlitt restate?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
context: Bastiat published the essay in July 1850 and died that December. Hazlitt's book applies its seen/unseen method to public works, tariffs, minimum wage, rent control, and every other 1946 American policy in turn. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Milton Friedman and Ron Paul both put Economics in One Lesson at the top of their recommended first-books-in-economics lists, and generations of American libertarians read it as their entry point to the classical-liberal tradition. What single method does the book teach a reader to apply to any proposed policy?
answer: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
choices: Trace the consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups over time
Sum the private benefits and subtract them from the private costs the sponsors disclose in advance
Compare the proposed policy against a randomly-selected historical policy of the same category
Accept the sponsors' stated aggregate multiplier and evaluate against that benchmark
context: This is Hazlitt's 'one lesson' verbatim from chapter 1: extend the analysis in TIME (past the immediate effect) and in SCOPE (past the visible group). Every remaining chapter applies it. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: On November 21 2002, a Fed governor gave a speech to the National Economists Club in Washington titled 'Deflation: Making Sure It Doesn't Happen Here.' Which Fed governor gave it?
context: Bernanke was a Fed governor from 2002 to 2005, then Council of Economic Advisers chair in 2005-06, then Fed chair from February 2006. The 2002 speech previewed nearly every unconventional tool he later deployed. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 Bernanke speech invoked a famous thought experiment first published by Milton Friedman in 1969, in which a central bank facing deflation could in principle create money in an extreme way. What was the pedagogical image?
choices: Burying coins in bottles for people to dig up
Buying every unsold house in the country
context: Friedman used the helicopter image in his 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' as a pedagogical device -- not as policy advocacy. Bernanke's citation converted the device into a proposed toolkit. Source: Grokipedia 'Helicopter money' (2026-09-05).

question: The nickname 'Helicopter Ben' stuck to the future Fed chair for the rest of his career. It came from his citation of a specific 1969 essay by Milton Friedman that used the helicopter image. What is that essay called?
context: Friedman's 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' used the helicopter as a thought experiment for a one-time increase in the money stock. Bernanke's 2002 reuse of the image gave him a nickname that outlasted his tenure. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 Bernanke speech listed several concrete unconventional tools a central bank could use once short-term rates hit zero. Which specific asset purchase headed the list of tools he named?
answer: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
choices: Buying long-term Treasuries to lower long-term yields
Buying gold bullion at fixed prices
Selling foreign-currency reserves against domestic bonds
Issuing zero-coupon perpetual bonds directly to the public

question: Nearly every tool listed in the 2002 speech was deployed between 2008 and 2014 under three named Fed programs. Which trio corresponds to what Bernanke had previewed?
context: QE1 (November 2008-March 2010, $1.75T), QE2 (November 2010-June 2011, $600B), Operation Twist (September 2011-December 2012), and QE3 (September 2012-October 2014) implemented in reality what Bernanke had merely sketched in 2002. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 speech's core argument was a claim about what a specific kind of central bank can always do to fight deflation, regardless of how low interest rates already are. What was the claim?
answer: A central bank with a fiat currency can always create money at zero marginal cost

A central bank must always coordinate with the fiscal authority
A central bank cannot inflate without abandoning its inflation target
A central bank must convert to a gold standard to maintain credibility

This was reassurance to markets facing deflation risk; it was warning to Austrians. Source: Grokipedia 'Fiat money' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian critics of the 2002 speech immediately called it a blueprint for eventual currency debasement. Three specific Austrian-tradition voices attacked the speech in real time. Which trio is standardly cited?
answer: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
choices: Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, and Jim Rogers
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Larry Summers
Alan Greenspan, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz, and Karl Brunner

question: Exactly six years after the 2002 speech, in November 2008, the same figure -- now Fed chair -- launched the first program of asset purchases at unprecedented scale. What was the first program called?
context: QE1, launched November 25 2008, initially bought $600 billion of mortgage-backed securities and $300 billion of Treasuries. It grew from there. The 2002 speech now reads as the most accurate preview of Fed crisis policy ever given -- everything Bernanke said the Fed could do, he did. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 speech included a concession about the ultimate reach of monetary policy that critics called 'monetary financing of fiscal policy.' What did Bernanke concede a central bank could always do?
answer: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
choices: Fund direct tax cuts by printing money if necessary
Freeze all commercial bank deposits by decree
Impose negative interest rates on retail savings

Critics said this was the door to 'helicopter money' in the literal sense: government spending funded directly by the printing press, bypassing bond markets. Source: federalreserve.gov (Bernanke 2002 speech text).

question: The 2002 Bernanke speech teaches a specific recognition move about how central-bank crisis rhetoric relates to future policy. Which move?
answer: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
choices: Public speeches by central bankers about what they could do in a hypothetical crisis often preview exactly what they will do in a real one
Central bank speeches are cheap talk and rarely predict actual future policy
Central banks always follow through on rate cuts announced in advance
Central bank crisis toolkits are never used because they exist to reassure
context: Read carefully, the 2002 speech told a listener exactly what would happen if a large financial crisis struck. Six years later it did, and the toolkit was deployed. Austrians took the speech seriously; most others did not. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1949 Yale University Press published a nine-hundred-page treatise by a 68-year-old Vienna-born economist who had been running an unpaid seminar at New York University since the end of 1945. The book put the whole Austrian system on one shelf. Which book did Ludwig von Mises publish in 1949?
choices: The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics (Yale University Press, 1949), roughly 881 pages. Socialism (1922, English 1936), The Theory of Money and Credit (1912), and Bureaucracy (1944) were the earlier Mises books it drew together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Mises opened Human Action (1949) with a single seven-word declaration that told the reader the whole book would rest on it. Which sentence begins Human Action?
choices: In the long run we are all dead.
The proper study of mankind is man.
There is no such thing as society.
context: The line is the opening of Chapter I, Section 1 -- and the axiom from which the entire treatise is deduced. The Keynes line, Pope line, and Thatcher line were all real but from other authors. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: Human Action calls its method 'praxeology' -- from the Greek word praxis, action -- and treats economic laws the way Euclid treated geometry: as theorems deduced from a starting axiom, illustrated but not verified by history. Against which rival method was Mises setting praxeology?
answer: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
choices: Positivism, which models economics on natural-science hypothesis testing
Scholasticism, which grounds economics in medieval theology
Historicism, which denies any general economic laws at all
Mercantilism, which measures national wealth by the trade balance
context: Mises's target was the mid-20th-century positivist program (later associated with Milton Friedman's 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics') that wanted economics to work like physics -- form hypotheses, test them statistically, discard the failed ones. Praxeology instead deduces laws from the action axiom and uses history only to illustrate. Historicism was the OLDER German quarrel with Menger; mercantilism was pre-Smithian; scholasticism belonged to an earlier era. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Human Action insists that only one kind of entity actually chooses in economics -- and that markets, societies, and economies are the un-designed by-product of countless such choices, none of which the whole ever made. Which methodological principle does Mises call this?
context: 'The market' does not act; only Alice at the fruit stall and Bob at the cash register act. A price, a boom, a shortage are the aggregate outcome no individual planned. Methodological holism (the whole society acts as a unit) was the position Mises rejected; the other two are unrelated terms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Human Action was NOT written from scratch in America. Mises had already published a 756-page German-language predecessor in exile in Geneva in 1940, whose appearance was announced in the Tribune de Geneve on June 16 and 17 of that year. Which title did the German precursor bear?
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens (Union, Geneva, 1940) was completed in the spring of 1940, weeks before the fall of France. Mises rewrote and expanded it into English as Human Action. Gemeinwirtschaft (1922) was his book on socialism; Kapital und Kapitalzins was Boehm-Bawerk; Grundsaetze was Menger's 1871 founding text. Source: mises.org/library/book/nationalokonomie-theorie-des-handelns-und-wirtschaftens.

question: Chapter 26 of Human Action folded a much older Mises argument -- an essay he had first published in a German journal in 1920 -- into the whole system as one theorem of the treatise. Which argument was Chapter 26 the mature statement of?
answer: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
choices: That rational calculation under socialism is impossible without market prices
That business cycles are caused by central-bank credit expansion
That the value of money regresses back to a prior barter demand
That interest rates reflect the community's time preference
context: Mises's 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' became Chapter 26 of Human Action ('The Impossibility of Economic Calculation Under Socialism'). The credit-expansion theory of the cycle became Chapter 20; the regression theorem for money is Chapter 17; the time-preference theory of interest is Chapter 19. Each has its own chapter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: For the entire twenty-four years of the NYU seminar that produced Human Action's American readership -- 1945 to 1969 -- New York University paid Mises exactly zero. His salary was funded by an anonymous private-donor institution (and by NYU board member Lawrence Fertig). Which foundation covered Mises's chair?
context: The Kansas City-based William Volker Fund quietly financed several classical-liberal appointments (Hayek at Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, Mises at NYU) that the mainstream foundations would not touch. The Rockefeller, Ford, and Carnegie foundations were the era's dominant funders but tilted toward the postwar Keynesian and behavioral-science consensus. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/anonymous-funding-academic-right-william-volker-and-henry-earhart.

question: In 1962 a young NYU-seminar graduate published his own thousand-page Austrian treatise, originally commissioned by the Volker Fund as a textbook version of Human Action but growing under his hand into an independent work. Which book stands as the standard companion volume to Mises's treatise?
context: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (1962) was the direct fruit of the NYU seminar and the Volker commission. The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was Hayek's; Prices and Production (1931) was Hayek's LSE lectures; Capital and Interest (1884-1889) was Boehm-Bawerk's earlier three-volume work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: Human Action appeared in a second edition in 1963 (Yale) and a third revised edition in 1966. The 1966 edition, brought out by a Chicago-based publisher, has been the standard scholarly text ever since. Which house published the 1966 third revised edition of Human Action?
context: The 1963 second edition (still Yale) was marred by typographical errors, which the 1966 Regnery edition corrected. Regnery had been publishing conservative and classical-liberal titles from Chicago since 1947. The Mises Institute's current scholar's edition (1998, Auburn) is set from the Regnery text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Inside the Austrian tradition, Mises's students and later Austrian economists refer to Human Action by a nickname so short it needs no adjective. Which one-word label do Austrians use when they say 'go read the ___' and mean Human Action?
context: The book's subtitle already announced it ('A Treatise on Economics'); inside the tradition the definite article is enough. Ayn Rand's Atlas Shrugged is 'the novel'; Marx's Capital is 'Kapital'; Mises's Human Action is 'the treatise.' Source: fee.org/articles/ludwig-von-misess-human-action-a-50th-anniversary-appreciation.

question: In May 1981 the Reagan administration negotiated an agreement with Japan capping Japanese passenger-car exports to the US at 1.68 million vehicles per year, on the argument that Detroit's Big Three needed relief from Japanese competition. What was the instrument called?
context: Called 'voluntary' because Japan self-imposed the cap under diplomatic pressure, avoiding a formal US tariff. The cap was renegotiated upward through the 1980s and formally ended in 1994. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: The 1981 US-Japan auto Voluntary Export Restraint capped Japanese passenger-car exports to the United States at how many vehicles per year?
context: Below the roughly 1.9 million Japanese cars sold in the US in 1980. The cap was raised to 1.85 million in 1984 and to 2.3 million in 1985 as Detroit stabilized. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: The 1981 auto Voluntary Export Restraint was designed to protect a specific set of American manufacturers who had been losing market share to Japanese imports. Which manufacturers?
context: Detroit's Big Three. United Auto Workers jobs in Michigan, Ohio, and Indiana were the politically visible beneficiaries; the Reagan administration framed the deal as breathing space for domestic industry. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trade_policy_of_the_Reagan_administration.

question: Robert Crandall of the Brookings Institution studied the 1981 Voluntary Export Restraint on Japanese cars and estimated in a 1987 Brookings paper that it raised the average US car price by roughly what amount (in 1983 dollars), for both Japanese and American vehicles?
context: Later Feenstra work and the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1999 AER paper put the total consumer cost at $5-8 billion per year. Domestic makers raised prices under the umbrella of reduced import competition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Crandall.

question: During the 1980s Japanese auto Voluntary Export Restraint, models like the Honda Accord, Toyota Camry, and Nissan Maxima grew larger, better-equipped, and more expensive; the cheap economy hatchback essentially disappeared. Which specific feature of the quota created that response?
answer: The cap was set in vehicles rather than in dollars, so each unit had to earn more profit
choices: The cap was set in vehicles rather than in dollars, so each unit had to earn more profit
A separate side-agreement banned imports below a set retail price
American dealers refused to stock any small Japanese cars
The Reagan administration imposed emissions rules only on smaller vehicles
context: This is the quality-upgrading response Robert Feenstra documented in his 1988 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper 'Quality Change Under Trade Restraints.' A per-unit cap rewards higher-margin models; a value-cap or tariff would not have. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Feenstra.

question: A high-school student says the 1981 Voluntary Export Restraint at least raised money for the US Treasury. Robert Feenstra's research showed the opposite: because the VER was a quantitative cap rather than a tariff, the price markup on each Japanese car went somewhere else entirely. Where?
answer: To Toyota, Honda, and Nissan as extra profit on each car sold
choices: To Toyota, Honda, and Nissan as extra profit on each car sold
To the American dealerships as higher sales commissions
To the state governments as import processing fees
To the United Auto Workers as a job-training levy
context: This is called quota rent. Feenstra estimated roughly $2,000 of quota rent per car flowed to the Japanese producers. An equivalent tariff would have collected the same revenue for the US Treasury; the VER simply transferred it to the foreign producers the policy claimed to punish. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Voluntary_export_restraint.

question: A senator in 1985 defends the auto Voluntary Export Restraint by pointing to United Auto Workers members in Michigan and Ohio whose jobs it protected. A Brookings economist counters that the seen worker in Michigan was purchased at the price of an unseen American buyer priced out of a $4,500 Japanese economy car. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Frederic Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen: name the invisible victim
choices: Frederic Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen: name the invisible victim
Ronald Coase's transaction-cost analysis of externalities
Milton Friedman's monetary theory of nominal-price inflation
John Maynard Keynes's argument for aggregate-demand stimulus
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' set the pattern: any policy has a visible beneficiary and an invisible one who bears the cost. The auto VER had three unseens (buyer, low-income buyer priced out of the small-car segment, quota rent to Japan). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: From independence in 1947 to 1991, India ran its economy on Nehru-era Fabian-socialist principles that required firms to obtain government permits for almost every business decision. What did economists nickname this regime?
context: 'License Raj' -- 'rule by permits' -- described the system in which Indian firms needed government approval to open a factory, expand capacity, import a machine, hire above a certain scale, produce a new product, or set prices. Often 80 or more separate approvals were required. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licence_Raj.

question: Economists coined a specific sardonic phrase for India's per-capita output rate of roughly 1 percent per year during the License Raj decades. What is the term?
context: 'Hindu rate of growth' was coined by economist Raj Krishna as a self-critical analytic term (not a slur) for the roughly 1% per-capita growth rate India averaged 1950-80 while its Asian neighbors grew 5-8x faster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_rate_of_growth.

question: While India averaged around 1 percent per-capita growth during the License Raj decades, a specific cluster of Asian economies -- South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong -- grew much faster from similar postwar baselines. What are these four economies collectively called?
context: The 'Four Asian Tigers' -- South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong -- averaged 5-8x India's per-capita growth rate over 1950-80. Their more open trade regimes are the standard counterfactual for the License Raj's opportunity cost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Asian_Tigers.

question: The economist who coined the term 'rent-seeking' in her 1974 American Economic Review paper drew directly on Indian License-Raj empirical work. Who was she?
context: Anne Krueger's 1974 AER paper 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' introduced the term based on Indian and Turkish empirical work. Krueger later served as World Bank Chief Economist 1982-86 and IMF Deputy Managing Director 2001-06. Source: aeaweb.org (AER June 1974).

question: The specific reasoning-move Krueger identified in her 1974 paper: because a government-issued license was worth more than the underlying resource, firms spent vast effort chasing licenses instead of producing goods. What is that phenomenon now called?
context: Rent-seeking: dissipation of real resources in pursuit of state-created privileges rather than value-creation. Krueger estimated License-Raj rent-seeking dissipation at up to 7% of Indian GDP. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: On July 24, 1991, facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India's Finance Minister delivered a landmark budget that dismantled the License Raj -- ending most industrial-licensing requirements, cutting tariffs, and permitting foreign investment. Who was the Finance Minister?
context: Manmohan Singh (Finance Minister 1991-96, later Prime Minister 2004-14) worked with Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to enact the reforms. The July 24, 1991 budget speech is the landmark. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh.

question: Following the 1991 reforms, India's per-capita income showed dramatic real-terms improvement over the next three decades. Roughly what multiple did real per-capita income reach by 2020?
answer: More than four times its 1991 level
choices: More than four times its 1991 level
context: India's real per-capita income more than quadrupled 1991-2020. Growth rates approximately doubled after 1991 and accelerated further in the 2000s. Hundreds of millions rose out of extreme poverty. Source: World Bank India data.

question: A 2008 scholarly synthesis of India's post-1991 reform-to-growth chain was written by an Indian-American economist based at Columbia. What is the book's title?
context: Arvind Panagariya's India: The Emerging Giant (Oxford UP, 2008) documents the reform-to-growth chain in detail. Panagariya later served as vice-chairman of NITI Aayog under PM Modi. Source: global.oup.com.

question: The 1991 reforms did NOT immediately eliminate all Indian bureaucracy. What is the more accurate description of the reform's effect?
answer: Growth accelerated dramatically without overnight transformation
choices: Growth accelerated dramatically without overnight transformation
The economy became fully deregulated within a year
All state industry was privatized within eighteen months
Tariffs went to zero within a decade
context: The reforms opened investment, cut tariffs, ended most industrial licensing -- but many state enterprises, banking regulations, and labor rules remained. The pattern is reform-and-growth-acceleration, not overnight transformation. Source: Panagariya, India: The Emerging Giant.

question: The License Raj's teaching for the political economy of regulation is that permits, licenses, and mandatory approvals impose a specific kind of hidden tax on production. What is the standard analytic name for this hidden burden?
context: Krueger's founding measurement: the real resources spent chasing state-created privileges are pure dissipation, adding nothing to output. This is why License-Raj-style regimes underperform: production is not just taxed but partially redirected into unproductive lobbying. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: In his 1845-1848 satirical series, Frederic Bastiat wrote a famous line about how a good cause can lose an argument. He said the worst thing that can happen to a good cause is not to be skillfully attacked but rather to be what?
context: The full line: 'The worst thing that can happen to a good cause is not to be skillfully attacked but to be ineptly defended.' Bastiat had watched French classical liberals lose public arguments through bad advocacy. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: Bastiat drew a practical rule from his 'ineptly defended' observation. What was the rule his own essays followed?
answer: First state the opposing case in its strongest form, then answer it
choices: First state the opposing case in its strongest form, then answer it
First denounce the opposition, then argue your own case
First appeal to authority, then invoke tradition
First mock the opponent, then move on quickly
context: Nearly every essay in Economic Sophisms first states the protectionist argument fairly, even sympathetically, then dismantles it. Anything less discredits the defender's cause. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: The 20th-century American economist most identified with the 'first state the opposing case fairly' discipline is a Hoover Institution senior fellow born in 1930. Who is he?
context: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930 in Gastonia, North Carolina) has repeatedly cited Bastiat as a formative influence on his method. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Sowell's 2000 Basic Books introduction to the field, now in its 5th edition, systematically steelmans policy arguments before answering them. What is the book's title?
context: Basic Economics: A Citizen's Guide to the Economy (Basic Books, 2000; 5th ed. 2014) is Sowell's most widely-read book. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Sowell's 1987 William Morrow book presents two opposing political worldviews in their strongest form and then traces where each leads. What is the book's short title?
context: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles (1987) presents the 'constrained' and 'unconstrained' visions each in the strongest terms before analyzing the resulting policy disagreements. Source: grokipedia.com/page/A_Conflict_of_Visions.

question: Sowell explicitly credits Bastiat as a formative influence in a specific 2000 Free Press memoir. What is the memoir's title?
context: Thomas Sowell's memoir A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) traces his intellectual formation and lists Bastiat among the formative early influences. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: In 21st-century rationalist internet writing, the same discipline Bastiat named has acquired a specific one-word verb. What is that modern coinage?
context: 'Steelman' entered the rationalist vocabulary around 2010 (LessWrong, Slate Star Codex) meaning to state the opponent's view in its strongest form before responding -- essentially Bastiat's 1845 rule with a new label. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Steelman_argument.

question: Milton Friedman's single most-quoted sentence declares that inflation always and everywhere has one and only one cause. He used it in a 1963 lecture, in Free to Choose, in Money Mischief, and in countless columns. Which cause does that sentence name?
context: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' -- Milton Friedman's most-repeated sentence, first delivered in his 1963 LSE lecture 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory,' repeated across three decades. Source: Friedman, 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory' (IEA 1970 publication of 1963 lecture).

question: Friedman's monetarist framing is not that inflation is caused by greedy businesses, unions demanding wages, oil cartels, or consumer psychology. What variable does he say drives inflation always and everywhere?
answer: The money supply growing faster than real output
choices: The money supply growing faster than real output
context: Friedman's monetarist move: inflation is caused by the money supply growing faster than real economic output. Every historical inflation tracks the monetary expansion; no lasting inflation has ever occurred without it. Source: Friedman (1963); Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (Princeton 1963).

question: The 1963 book that provided the empirical foundation for Friedman's monetarist claim was co-authored with a National Bureau of Economic Research colleague and traced a century of US monetary data. Who was the co-author?
context: Milton Friedman + Anna Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton University Press, 1963). It documented that changes in the money supply preceded and predicted changes in nominal income and inflation across a century of data. Source: press.princeton.edu (Friedman + Schwartz 1963).

question: The Friedman-Schwartz Monetary History has one especially famous chapter interpretation of a specific historical episode: the US decline in the money supply of roughly one-third from 1929 to 1933 as the cause of the depth of the Depression. Which chapter is that?
context: Chapter 7 of A Monetary History, titled 'The Great Contraction,' documented that the US money supply fell by roughly one-third between 1929 and 1933 -- a Fed failure Friedman argued caused the depth of the Depression. Source: Friedman + Schwartz (1963), Chapter 7.

question: Friedman's 1963 lecture 'The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory' was a deliberate call to overturn a mid-century economic-policy consensus. Which school of thought was he seeking to displace?
context: Friedman's 1963 LSE lecture called for overturning the Keynesian consensus that had governed US monetary policy since WWII. Keynesians treated the money supply as mostly passive; Friedman argued it was the driver. Source: Friedman, IEA (1970) publication of 1963 lecture.

question: The 1970s stagflation -- rising inflation AND rising unemployment simultaneously -- became the classic empirical case that shattered the Keynesian Phillips-curve consensus and vindicated Friedman's monetarist critique. In which decade did the profession substantially accept the monetarist framework?
context: By the mid-1980s the economics profession had substantially accepted the monetarist critique of the stable Phillips curve, though not every technical detail. Friedman was the intellectual victor of the 1960s-80s macroeconomic debate. Source: Blinder, 'The Monetarist Counterrevolution' (JEP 2001).

question: Friedman explicitly did NOT claim to invent monetarism. He credited earlier economists for elements of the framework. Which trio of predecessors did he most often name?
answer: Henry Simons, Clark Warburton, and Anna Schwartz
choices: Henry Simons, Clark Warburton, and Anna Schwartz
John Maynard Keynes, Michal Kalecki, and Piero Sraffa
Karl Marx, Rosa Luxemburg, and Louis Althusser
context: Friedman credited his Chicago mentor Henry Simons, Clark Warburton (a pre-Friedman quantitative monetarist), and his co-author Anna Schwartz for pieces of the framework. His claim was demonstration with US century-long data, not invention. Source: Friedman, autobiographical Nobel essay (1976); IEA 1970 lecture.

question: Friedman's monetarism is distinct from Austrian business cycle theory, though both frameworks agree that inflation is monetary in origin. Which one specific claim best distinguishes Friedman's monetarism from Mises-Hayek Austrian macro?
answer: Friedman focuses on aggregate money supply growth; Austrians focus on credit-driven malinvestment structure
choices: Friedman focuses on aggregate money supply growth; Austrians focus on credit-driven malinvestment structure
Friedman believes inflation is caused by unions; Austrians believe it is caused by monopolies
Friedman rejects the concept of money supply entirely
context: Both traditions agree on the monetary origin of inflation. They differ on transmission and business-cycle dynamics: Friedman focuses on aggregate M vs Y; Austrian ABCT (Mises-Hayek-Rothbard) focuses on the structure of malinvestment produced by artificially low interest rates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963); Friedman, IEA (1970).

question: Friedman's monetarist framework gives citizens a diagnostic to apply when a politician blames rising prices on a specific group. In the 1970s, whom did politicians and journalists routinely blame for inflation?
answer: Greedy businesses, unions demanding wages, and oil sheikhs
choices: Greedy businesses, unions demanding wages, and oil sheikhs
The Federal Reserve and its monetary expansion
Consumer preference shifts toward domestic products
The gold standard's restrictions on money supply
context: Popular explanations in the 1970s recycled corporate greed, union wage demands, and OPEC as inflation causes. Friedman's move: point at the multi-year monetary expansion behind them all. The specific blame targets are effects, not causes. Source: Friedman, IEA (1970).

question: The 'always and everywhere' phrase is a strong empirical claim. Friedman meant it not as a metaphysical truth but as a hypothesis supported by which specific body of evidence?
answer: A century of US money-supply-and-inflation data documented in A Monetary History
choices: A century of US money-supply-and-inflation data documented in A Monetary History
A single laboratory experiment run in Chicago in 1961
A theological argument from natural law
A survey of contemporary US Federal Reserve staff
context: Friedman's empirical basis was the 1867-1960 US data he and Anna Schwartz assembled and analyzed in A Monetary History. That century of correlation is the evidentiary claim behind 'always and everywhere.' Source: Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History (Princeton 1963).

question: A London-born economist takes his Ph.D. at New York University in 1957 under Ludwig von Mises, joins the NYU faculty the same day, and remains the Austrian school's leading American figure into the twenty-first century. Which Austrian economist -- born February 13, 1930 -- is he?
context: Israel Meir Kirzner, born London 1930, moved to South Africa at age 10, then to the United States for graduate work at NYU. Rothbard took his Ph.D. at Columbia in 1956 (under Arthur Burns, not Mises); Boettke and Hoppe are younger scholars trained in the Kirzner-Rothbard generation's wake. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: In 1957 Israel Kirzner completed his Ph.D. dissertation, writing under his teacher's supervision at New York University. Which older Austrian economist -- himself an emigre from Vienna -- was Kirzner's doctoral supervisor?
context: Mises had joined NYU as a visiting professor in 1945 and ran a graduate seminar there for two decades; Kirzner was his most consequential doctoral student. Hayek was at Chicago from 1950; Schumpeter had died at Harvard in 1950; Machlup was a Vienna-circle friend but at Johns Hopkins and Princeton. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: In 1973 Israel Kirzner published the book that made his name -- a University of Chicago Press monograph founding what is now the standard modern Austrian account of the market process. Which title did that 1973 book bear?
context: Competition and Entrepreneurship, University of Chicago Press, 1973. Human Action (1949) was Mises's; Man, Economy, and State (1962) was Rothbard's; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected essays by Hayek. Source: Econlib, 'Competition and Entrepreneurship: The Fountainhead of the Contemporary Austrian School'.

question: For Kirzner, the entrepreneur is not primarily an inventor, a risk-bearer, or a capital-owner; he is the person who NOTICES something others have missed. Which single word does Kirzner use for the entrepreneur's defining trait?
context: Alertness -- attention to hitherto-unnoticed opportunities -- is the load-bearing concept in Competition and Entrepreneurship. Innovation is Schumpeter's key term; prudence is Aristotelian; foresight belongs to Frank Knight's risk-bearing entrepreneur. Source: Econlib biography, Israel Kirzner.

question: Kirzner's alert entrepreneur spots a real profit opportunity, acts on it, and in the process moves market prices toward what economists call an equilibrium. Which OTHER Austrian-tradition theorist described entrepreneurial activity in the OPPOSITE way -- as disruption that shatters equilibrium through 'creative destruction'?
context: Schumpeter's Theory of Economic Development (1911) and Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942) present the entrepreneur as disruptive innovator; Kirzner's 1973 book is the deliberate Austrian counter-account. Knight (1921) emphasized uncertainty-bearing; Drucker was a management theorist; Coase worked on transaction costs. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: Schumpeter said entrepreneurs CREATE new opportunities by inventing new products and methods. Kirzner said, on the contrary, that opportunities are already there, latent in the market, waiting to be seen. Which single verb captures the Kirznerian entrepreneur's act -- opportunities are what?
context: Kirzner's language of DISCOVERY versus Schumpeter's CREATION is the standard shorthand for the two accounts in the entrepreneurship literature. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: For his lifetime contribution to the economic study of enterprise, Israel Kirzner was awarded in 2006 the field's most senior international honor. Which prize -- the top award in entrepreneurship research -- did Kirzner receive that year?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
context: Awarded in Stockholm 2006 by the Global Award Foundation -- the entrepreneurship field's senior prize, sometimes called 'the Nobel of entrepreneurship.' The John Bates Clark Medal is for American economists under 40; the Adam Smith Prize is a Cambridge undergraduate award; the Bank of Sweden Prize is the Nobel in Economics itself. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: Unlike most twentieth-century American economists of comparable stature, Israel Kirzner spent his entire fifty-year academic career at a single institution -- and, following the pattern set by Mises and Rothbard in the United States, never held a chair in its ECONOMICS department. Which university housed Kirzner throughout his career, in its business school?
context: Kirzner joined NYU on completing his Ph.D. in 1957 and remained until his 2002 retirement, based in the business school (later Stern). Chicago was the mainstream free-market department; Columbia was Rothbard's Ph.D. institution; George Mason became the leading Austrian department AFTER Kirzner's generation, largely staffed by his students. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: For decades at NYU, Israel Kirzner ran a weekly graduate seminar that trained a generation of Austrian scholars -- Peter Boettke and Sanford Ikeda among them -- and became the institutional heart of American Austrian economics after Mises's death. Which name did the seminar carry?
context: Kirzner's NYU Austrian Economics Colloquium ran for decades and produced Peter Boettke (now at George Mason), Sanford Ikeda, and many others. The Mises Circle was the Vienna Privatseminar of the 1920s; the Bastiat Society and FEE are separate American educational organizations. Source: Econlib, 'Competition and Entrepreneurship: The Fountainhead of the Contemporary Austrian School'.

question: In 1960 Israel Kirzner published his first book -- a revised version of his 1957 doctoral thesis under Mises, treating the history of economic thought and the question of what economics IS. Which title did Kirzner give this first monograph?
choices: The Theory of Money and Credit
The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science
context: The Economic Point of View (1960) was Kirzner's revised dissertation, a history of how economists have defined their own field. The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was Mises's; The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science (1962) was Mises's late methodological book; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was Hayek's. Source: EconJournalWatch author page, Israel M. Kirzner.

question: Kirzner is unusual among leading twentieth-century economists in a second respect: alongside his academic career he is an ordained clergyman, a lifelong practitioner and teacher of the tradition of his father. Which religious tradition does Kirzner belong to as a rabbi?
context: Kirzner is an Orthodox rabbi; his father was a well-known rabbi and Talmudist, and Kirzner has written on ethics and enterprise from within that tradition. The other three are distinct American Jewish movements. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Kirzner, Israel M(ayer) 1930-'.

question: The economist who would go on to found the public-choice school was born in October 1919 on a small farm outside Murfreesboro, Tennessee, and paid his way through teachers college by milking dairy cows. Who was he?
context: James McGill Buchanan (October 3, 1919 - January 9, 2013) was born on a Tennessee farm, the grandson of a Reconstruction-era governor. Middle Tennessee State Teachers College was his undergraduate school. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_M._Buchanan.

question: James Buchanan entered the University of Chicago for graduate school in 1945 on the GI Bill, after wartime Navy service on Admiral Nimitz's staff in Honolulu. By his own account, one Chicago economics professor converted him from what he called 'libertarian socialism' to a market-order view in a single course. Who was that professor?
context: Buchanan later insisted that six weeks in Frank Knight's price-theory course flipped his intellectual orientation. He took his 1948 Chicago PhD under Knight's supervision. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: Buchanan's first academic institution-building project was co-founding a research center at the University of Virginia in 1957 with G. Warren Nutter. What name did they give this early center?
answer: The Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy
choices: The Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy
The Center for Study of Public Choice
context: Buchanan and Nutter founded the Thomas Jefferson Center at UVa in 1957. It was Buchanan's first institutional home before Tullock arrived and the two founded the Public Choice Society together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_Center_for_Political_Economy.

question: In 1969 Buchanan and Gordon Tullock founded a new research center at a different Virginia university, the institution that would host public-choice research for the next fifteen years. Which university was that?
context: The Center for Study of Public Choice was founded at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg in 1969. It moved with Buchanan and Tullock to George Mason University in 1983. Source: mercatus.org (Center biographical history).

question: In October 1986 the Royal Swedish Academy named James Buchanan the year's laureate in economic sciences, the first Nobel ever given for work in this specific field. The citation named his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for what?
answer: The theory of economic and political decision-making
choices: The theory of economic and political decision-making
context: The 1986 Nobel citation, October 16, 1986: 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The committee generalized rather than saying 'public choice.' Source: nobelprize.org (Buchanan 1986).

question: Buchanan and Tullock moved their Center for Study of Public Choice from Virginia Tech to a third Virginia institution in 1983, where Buchanan spent the rest of his career and the discipline effectively made its permanent home. Which university did they move to?
context: The Center moved to George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, in 1983. GMU has hosted public-choice research ever since, alongside the Mercatus Center. Source: gmu.edu (public choice program history).

question: During a 1955-56 Fulbright year abroad, Buchanan spent time in Rome studying with an economist whose classical-liberal fiscal-constitution work shaped Buchanan's own interest in constitutional constraints on government. Which Italian scholar was his host?
context: Buchanan spent 1955-56 in Italy on a Fulbright, working with Luigi Einaudi (former President of Italy 1948-55) and the Italian public-finance tradition. He credited that year with shaping his constitutional-fiscal focus. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: At his 1986 Nobel ceremony in Stockholm, Buchanan insisted on displaying a specific tribute to his Chicago mentor alongside his own materials, in gratitude for the conversion that had reshaped his career. What did Buchanan present alongside himself?
choices: A page from Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations
A copy of the Constitution of the United States
context: Buchanan brought Frank Knight's portrait to the Stockholm ceremonies and referred to Knight as his intellectual father. The gesture was widely reported. Source: Buchanan Nobel-week press coverage; Boettke + Marciano biography.

question: Buchanan's grandfather had been a Reconstruction-era Tennessee political figure whose name the young James inherited. What high office had grandfather John Price Buchanan held in the state?
choices: Chief Justice of the Tennessee Supreme Court
context: John Price Buchanan served as Governor of Tennessee from 1891 to 1893, elected on a Farmers' Alliance platform. James Buchanan often noted the family political inheritance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_P._Buchanan.

question: Buchanan often described his own intellectual conversion at Chicago as changing from 'libertarian socialist' to a market-order view. What does that phrase tell us about the political ground he actually STARTED from, before Frank Knight's course?
answer: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
choices: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
He was a Chicago-machine urban liberal
He was already a doctrinaire Austrian
He was a Trotskyist committed to permanent revolution
context: Buchanan was the son of Tennessee farming Democrats, sympathetic to New Deal redistribution when he arrived at Chicago. The 'libertarian socialist' label was his own description of that starting point. Do not overstate an early conservatism -- he had none. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: Buchanan's biographical arc runs from a Tennessee dairy farm to the Royal Swedish Academy. In shaping the whole field of public choice from that unlikely path, what did the man do in a single sentence?
answer: He taught the world that politicians are self-interested actors, not benevolent planners
choices: He taught the world that politicians are self-interested actors, not benevolent planners
He proved mathematically that market prices reflect all available information
He founded the doctrine of comparative advantage in international trade
He reformed monetary policy by inventing the money-supply target rule
context: Public choice is politics without romance. Buchanan's contribution: strip the assumption that politicians act from pure public spirit; treat them as ordinary humans responding to ordinary incentives. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: In 2020, during the COVID lockdown period, a Canadian technology entrepreneur published a book making the case that falling prices from technology are a good thing that central banks are hiding. The book became one of the most-read modern Bitcoin books alongside Saifedean Ammous's. What was it titled?
answer: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
choices: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Sovereign Individual: Mastering the Transition to the Information Age
The Ascent of Money: A Financial History of the World
context: Written by Jeff Booth, formerly the founder of BuildDirect, an online building-materials company. He had spent 30 years building and selling companies before turning to monetary writing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth's 2020 book argues that a specific empirical property of the technology industry is misunderstood as bad news when it is actually a gift to ordinary people. Which property?
answer: Technology naturally cheapens things over time (computing power, solar energy, storage all fall in cost)
choices: Technology naturally cheapens things over time (computing power, solar energy, storage all fall in cost)
Technology always requires a government subsidy to develop
Technology inherently favors older workers over younger ones
Technology can only be produced by monopolies
context: Moore's Law (Gordon Moore, 1965) captures the classical case: the number of transistors on a chip doubles every two years for the same cost. Solar photovoltaics, LEDs, memory, and storage follow parallel curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moore%27s_law.

question: In Booth's account, central banks respond to technology's natural cheapening effect in a specific way that hides the gift from savers and workers. What does he say central banks do?
answer: Expand the money supply, letting asset prices rise instead of consumer prices falling
choices: Expand the money supply, letting asset prices rise instead of consumer prices falling
Buy technology stocks directly on the open market to raise their share prices
Print physical dollar bills at a fixed rate matching Moore's Law
Ban the sale of foreign-made technology to protect national producers
context: The technology-deflation benefit gets absorbed into rising stock, real-estate, and bond prices. Owners of assets gain; workers and savers whose wages and cash holdings should have bought more each year do not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: A saver in 2025 asks why her wages have risen only modestly since 2010 while the S&P 500 has more than tripled. A Booth-influenced analyst points to a specific Bastiat-style unseen. Which is it?
answer: The technology-cheapening she should have seen in her cost of living was absorbed into asset prices instead
choices: The technology-cheapening she should have seen in her cost of living was absorbed into asset prices instead
The Federal Reserve directly transferred wages from workers to investors by executive order
Chinese manufacturing subsidies alone explain the entire stock-market rise
European Central Bank interest-rate cuts caused the entire US wage stagnation
context: The seen: relatively stable consumer prices, a 'successful' Fed inflation target. The unseen: the prices should have fallen substantially given the underlying productivity gains. The gap accrues to asset holders. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Booth argues that a specific monetary technology can let holders capture the technology-deflation benefit that central banks otherwise erase. Which one?
answer: Bitcoin, whose 21 million cap prevents any authority from expanding the supply to hide falling prices
choices: Bitcoin, whose 21 million cap prevents any authority from expanding the supply to hide falling prices
The US dollar, backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government
The euro, coordinated by the European Central Bank across 20 nations
context: Booth's argument connects Bitcoin to technology-optimism in a way that reaches audiences who resist harder Austrian or goldbug framings. The point is monetary design, not price prediction. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth is often interviewed as one of a three-voice synthesis of modern Bitcoin monetary theory, alongside two other prominent figures. Who are the other two?
context: Saylor (MicroStrategy chairman, corporate-treasury Bitcoin advocate) and Ammous ('The Bitcoin Standard') provide the corporate and Austrian frames; Booth provides the technology-optimist frame. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: In November 1910 six men boarded a Republican senator's private railcar in New Jersey, told to bring hunting clothes and use only first names in front of servants. They travelled south to a private hunting retreat off the coast of Georgia. Which island were they traveling to?
context: The Jekyll Island Club, off the Georgia coast, was owned by a small group of America's richest families. The November 1910 meeting produced the blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve. Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island Club' (2026-09-05).

question: The Republican senator whose private railcar carried the group south was from Rhode Island and was the father-in-law of John D. Rockefeller Jr. Who convened the November 1910 meeting?
context: Nelson Aldrich (R-Rhode Island) chaired the National Monetary Commission and was the political sponsor of the plan that emerged from the meeting. His daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1901. Source: Grokipedia 'Nelson Aldrich' (2026-09-05).

question: One of the six attendees at Jekyll Island was a German-born banker who was a partner at Kuhn Loeb and Company and the family expert on European central banks. Who was he?
context: Warburg (1868-1932) brought the expertise on European central-banking design that shaped the American plan. He later became one of the first members of the Federal Reserve Board. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Warburg' (2026-09-05).

question: Another Jekyll Island attendee was president of a specific New York bank associated with the Rockefeller interests. Which bank did Frank Vanderlip lead?
answer: National City Bank of New York
choices: National City Bank of New York
