First National Bank of New York
context: Frank Vanderlip led National City Bank of New York -- the Rockefeller bank, later Citibank and eventually Citigroup. His Jekyll Island participation was carefully hidden until his 1935 confession. Source: Grokipedia 'Frank Vanderlip' (2026-09-05).

question: Two additional Jekyll Island attendees represented specific major New York financial institutions. One was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company; another was Benjamin Strong, then president of Bankers Trust. What was Henry Davison's affiliation?
answer: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
choices: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
Chairman of Kuhn Loeb and Company
President of First National Bank of New York
context: Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company. The Jekyll Island meeting essentially assembled the leadership of the New York financial establishment plus one German-American central-banking specialist. Source: Grokipedia 'Henry Pomeroy Davison' (2026-09-05).

question: The sixth Jekyll Island attendee was an academic economist serving in the Taft administration. What was A. Piatt Andrew's federal role?
context: A. Piatt Andrew was serving as Assistant Treasury Secretary under Franklin MacVeagh. His presence gave the meeting official Treasury representation without formal Treasury endorsement. Source: Grokipedia 'A. Piatt Andrew' (2026-09-05).

question: For roughly ten days the six men worked in secret at Jekyll Island to draft what became known as the Aldrich Plan. When did Frank Vanderlip publicly acknowledge the meeting for the first time?
answer: 1935, in a Saturday Evening Post article
choices: 1935, in a Saturday Evening Post article
1913, at the passage of the Federal Reserve Act
context: Vanderlip's 1935 Saturday Evening Post article 'From Farm Boy to Financier' was the first public acknowledgment of the meeting -- 25 years after it happened. The other participants had died or maintained the sworn secrecy. Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island (Federal Reserve)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Aldrich Plan itself was politically dead because of Aldrich's association with Wall Street. But when Democrats took Congress in 1912 and Wilson took the White House, the same basic structure was passed under a Democratic bill signed in December 1913. What was that bill?
context: The Federal Reserve Act was signed by Wilson on December 23 1913. It preserved the Aldrich Plan's essential structure (regional banks, note-issue power, private-bank ownership of regional-bank stock) with cosmetic changes for political viability. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In his 1935 confession Vanderlip described his own participation using specific language that captured the meeting's atmosphere. What word did he use to describe how the group behaved?
context: Vanderlip's 1935 article: 'I was as secretive -- indeed as furtive -- as any conspirator... our secret expedition to Jekyll Island as the occasion of the actual conception of what eventually became the Federal Reserve System.' Source: Grokipedia 'Jekyll Island (Federal Reserve)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Jekyll Island meeting teaches a specific recognition move about the political economy of central-bank design. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The specific individuals who design a central bank tend to be the very people whose institutions and dynasties will benefit from its structure
choices: The specific individuals who design a central bank tend to be the very people whose institutions and dynasties will benefit from its structure
Central banks are always designed by disinterested academic economists
Central-bank design is a purely technical question with no distributional implications
Public participation in central-bank design has been the norm throughout American history
context: The men at Jekyll Island were the leaders of the very New York financial establishment whose banks would become primary dealers to the new central bank. G. Edward Griffin's 1994 book The Creature from Jekyll Island popularized this line of critique for a mass audience. Source: Grokipedia 'The Creature from Jekyll Island' (2026-09-05).

question: In an 11th-century Chinese province, merchants began issuing paper receipts backed by deposits of iron coins, because the iron coins were too bulky and heavy for large transactions. In which province did the paper receipts first circulate?
context: Iron-coin-backed paper receipts (later called jiaozi) first circulated in Sichuan province during the Song dynasty. Guangdong, Yunnan, and Zhejiang are other Chinese provinces without the same paper-money origin story. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: The world's first widely-circulated government paper money, issued when the Song dynasty took over the Sichuan merchant paper around 1023 AD, has a specific name. What was it called?
context: Jiaozi was the Song dynasty government paper (from ~1023 AD). Chao was the later Mongol Yuan dynasty paper; yuan is the modern name for the Chinese currency unit; 'cash' is the English name for old Chinese round coins with a square hole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: The discipline behind the Song dynasty's jiaozi held for about 40 years, then began breaking down. Which specific fiscal pressure drove the government to issue paper faster than its specie backing could support?
answer: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
choices: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
the construction of the Great Wall extensions
irrigation projects in the Yangtze delta
silk trade with the Roman Empire
context: Late-Song military spending against the Jin (northern rival) and later the Mongols drove the fatal jiaozi over-issuance; by the early 13th century the currency had lost most of its value. Great Wall extension (Ming era), Yangtze irrigation, and Roman silk trade are the wrong causes or wrong eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: After the Mongols conquered Song China, one Mongol emperor issued his own paper currency, the chao, that -- unlike Song paper -- had no metal backing at all and was declared legal tender by imperial decree. Which Mongol emperor issued the chao?
context: Kublai Khan (reigned 1260-94) issued the chao. Genghis Khan (1162-1227) founded the Mongol empire but did not issue Chinese paper money; Timur was the later Turco-Mongol ruler (1370-1405); Möngke Khan was Kublai's brother. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kublai_Khan.

question: According to Marco Polo's Travels, Kublai Khan enforced acceptance of the chao paper currency under a specific extreme penalty. Which punishment did Polo report Kublai used to keep the paper in circulation?
answer: death for refusing to accept the notes
choices: death for refusing to accept the notes
a fine of one hundred silver taels
context: Marco Polo reported that refusing the chao was punishable by death under Kublai. Banishment, fines, and flogging were common Mongol punishments for other offenses but Polo specifies death for chao refusal. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels of Marco Polo (c. 1298), Book II ch 24.

question: Marco Polo devoted a whole chapter of his 1298 Travels to describing Kublai Khan's paper currency. He described the notes as being made from the bark of a specific tree stamped with imperial vermilion. Which tree's bark did Polo describe the chao being made from?
context: Polo described the chao as being made from mulberry bark. Oak, willow, and birch bark have been used for other papers in other places but Polo specifies mulberry for the chao. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: Marco Polo, coming from a Europe where money was gold and silver, described Kublai Khan's paper-money system in terms that captured his astonishment. Which specific comparison did Polo use in the Travels to describe how the paper worked?
answer: a kind of alchemy -- the Khan's magic that turns bark into wealth
choices: a kind of alchemy -- the Khan's magic that turns bark into wealth
a form of taxation the citizens paid willingly
a religious offering the citizens made to the Khan
a military tribute the conquered peoples paid
context: Polo compared the chao system to alchemy: bark being transmuted into wealth by the Khan's stamp. He did not frame it as tax, offering, or tribute in the passage. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: The chao paper currency held its value only while Kublai lived and his empire could project force. What happened to the chao within a generation of Kublai's death in 1294?
answer: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
choices: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
the chao was formally backed by silver and stabilized for another two centuries
the Ming dynasty adopted it as their own currency in 1368
Marco Polo returned to enforce its acceptance
context: After Kublai, later Yuan emperors printed chao at will; by the 1350s it was worthless and the Yuan dynasty was collapsing. The Ming (founded 1368) inherited the ruin, not the currency; silver backing did not stabilize it; Polo had died in 1324. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty.

question: The 11th-century jiaozi and the 13th-century chao together give the world its first two hyperinflations of paper money -- both in China, both within a few centuries of each other. Which specific reasoning move do modern Austrian economists press about this early Chinese paper-money record?
answer: That the very first two government paper currencies in world history hyperinflated, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
choices: That the very first two government paper currencies in world history hyperinflated, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
That Chinese culture was uniquely unsuited to paper money, so the Song and Yuan collapses tell us nothing about later fiat currencies elsewhere in the world
That the paper-money failure in both dynasties was caused primarily by insufficient literacy among the population handling the notes rather than by over-issuance
That the Song and Yuan governments simply lacked modern accounting tools, so a modern central bank with proper spreadsheets would not repeat the same mistake
context: The Austrian move: paper money is nine hundred years old and hyperinflated the first two times anyone tried it; the failure pattern is structural, not modern-specific. Cultural, literacy, and accounting explanations are the alternative arguments the Austrian analysis specifically rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021); Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?.

question: A Bastiat-pattern retelling of the Kublai Khan chao story presses one specific reasoning move about what Marco Polo actually witnessed when he called the paper 'alchemy'. Which move does the argument make about the mechanism behind the Khan's 'magic'?
answer: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
choices: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
That Marco Polo simply misunderstood Chinese economics and misreported what Kublai's paper system actually did in daily commerce inside the Mongol empire
That paper money worked reliably in Kublai's China as long as the Khan personally guaranteed it, and no monetary lesson generalizes to any later fiat system elsewhere
That the chao would have lasted indefinitely if the Mongol empire had lasted longer, and the collapse says nothing about paper money's structural incentive to over-issue
context: The Bastiat move: SEEN (the wealth Kublai's paper appeared to create); UNSEEN (the future currency collapse quietly transferring that wealth away from every holder). Personal guarantee, imperial duration, and mistaken observer are the standard alternative theories the argument rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: France in 1715 was nearly bankrupt from the wars of Louis XIV. A Scottish gambler and monetary theorist arrived in Paris and offered a plan to the regent, the Duke of Orleans, to solve the crisis using a new kind of money. What was his name?
context: John Law (1671-1729), a Scot who had fled London after killing a man in a duel, arrived in France in 1715 and won the ear of Philippe, Duke of Orleans, regent for the child-king Louis XV. Source: Antoin Murphy, John Law: Economic Theorist and Policy-Maker (1997).

question: In 1717 the Scottish monetary projector who had gained the trust of the French regent founded a trading company holding France's monopoly over its Louisiana colony. The company's name reflected the river running through those lands. What was the company called?
context: Founded in 1717 as the Compagnie d'Occident and quickly known as the Compagnie du Mississippi, it held the exclusive right to develop the vast French Louisiana territory. Source: Grokipedia 'Mississippi Company' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1716 the Scottish theorist founded a private bank in Paris that could issue paper banknotes. Two years later, in 1718, the French crown took the bank over and gave it state backing, transforming it into what was effectively France's first central bank. Under what name did it operate after 1718?
context: Law founded the Banque Generale in 1716. In 1718 the crown nationalized it and renamed it the Banque Royale, guaranteeing its notes as legal tender. Banque de France (a different institution) was founded by Napoleon in 1800. Source: Grokipedia 'Banque Royale' (2026-09-05).

question: During the Mississippi Company boom of 1719-1720 in Paris, so many ordinary shareholders got rich on paper that a new French word was coined for people worth a million livres. Which word entered the language in this bubble?
context: The word 'millionaire' first appears in French in about 1719 to describe the newly rich shareholders in Law's Mississippi Company. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Oxford English Dictionary etymology entry.

question: Between 1719 and early 1720 shares in the Scottish theorist's Louisiana trading company rose from about 500 livres each to a peak that made the whole scheme famous. Roughly what peak did the share price reach?
context: Mississippi Company shares climbed roughly twenty-fold from about 500 livres in mid-1719 to around 10,000 livres by early 1720 -- one of the sharpest speculative rises in monetary history. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: The Scottish projector's scheme in France rested on a self-reinforcing loop tying his state-backed bank to his Louisiana trading company. Which loop did he construct?
answer: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
choices: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
The bank taxed foreign trade and used the revenue to buy shares back from the public at a fixed price
The company shipped Louisiana silver to France, and the bank issued notes backed 100 percent by that silver
The bank borrowed from Dutch and English merchants and lent the proceeds to the company at low interest
context: The circular mechanism was the core of Law's scheme: paper money financed share purchases, rising share prices created demand for more paper, and the bank obliged. This is the shape every asset-inflation bubble since has followed. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997).

question: In February 1720, as large shareholders began cashing in Mississippi Company stock and demanding gold coin instead of the bank's paper, the Scottish controller-general reached for a desperate legal weapon. What did he try to do to gold?
answer: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
choices: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
He fixed the price of gold at half its market rate
He required all gold to be deposited with the Mississippi Company
He nationalized every French goldsmith's shop
context: Law's February 1720 edict forbade private holdings of gold and silver bullion above small amounts, hoping to force the public back into paper. It failed within weeks. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: By late 1720 the Mississippi Company shares and the paper money issued to buy them had both collapsed, and the Scottish projector fled France in disgrace. Where did he end his days, dying poor in 1729?
context: Law fled France in December 1720, drifted through European cities, and died in Venice in March 1729, largely forgotten and in poverty. Source: Grokipedia 'John Law (economist)' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1720 French collapse damaged confidence in paper money so severely that the country resisted a national paper currency for roughly seventy years. When France finally tried paper money again, in the Revolution, the second attempt ended the same way. What was that second experiment called?
context: The 1789-1796 Assignat was the second modern paper-money experiment in France, backed by seized Church lands. It hyperinflated just as Law's system had, confirming the pattern. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian economists point to the 1719-1720 French episode as the first modern case of the boom-bust pattern their theory describes. Which specific Austrian move fits Law's scheme most exactly?
answer: Credit expansion produces malinvestment concentrated in one sector, then collapses when redemption is demanded
choices: Credit expansion produces malinvestment concentrated in one sector, then collapses when redemption is demanded
Government spending stimulates aggregate demand and drives permanent growth
A fixed money supply causes deflation and long-run unemployment
Free banking causes an excess of small denominations to circulate
context: The Austrian business-cycle pattern: newly created money distorts capital toward a favored project (Louisiana), the boom looks like prosperity, and when holders of the new money try to convert it back to real goods or hard money, the whole edifice collapses. Ludwig von Mises named the mechanism in 1912. Source: Mises, Theory of Money and Credit (1912).

question: A Brooklyn-born Pace University economist has been the most persistent modern scholar of the 1920 Mises calculation debate, arguing for a strict reading against the more common Hayek-influenced view. Who is he?
context: Joseph T. Salerno (born 1950 in Brooklyn, New York) is professor emeritus at Pace University and academic vice president of the Ludwig von Mises Institute. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Salerno.

question: Salerno edits the flagship modern Austrian scholarly journal, published by the Mises Institute since 1998. What is its title?
context: Salerno has edited the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics since its founding in 1998; the older Review of Austrian Economics (edited by Boettke) is a separate journal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_Salerno.

question: There is a live intra-Austrian dispute about how to READ Mises's 1920 essay on socialism. Salerno's position holds that Mises's core argument was strictly about which specific problem?
answer: Monetary calculation without exchange-generated prices for capital goods
choices: Monetary calculation without exchange-generated prices for capital goods
Dispersed knowledge that no planner could aggregate
Political incentive of central planners to maximize personal power
The absence of a functioning banking system
context: Salerno's strict-Misesian reading: without real market prices for producer goods, no cost comparison is possible; the calculation problem is a monetary problem, not primarily a knowledge problem. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Socialist_calculation_debate.

question: The alternative reading of Mises 1920 that Salerno pushes back against is most closely associated with a different Austrian giant. Whose interpretation emphasizes DISPERSED KNOWLEDGE as the primary obstacle?
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' framed the calculation debate in knowledge-problem terms; Israel Kirzner and Don Lavoie extended this reading. Salerno argues it displaces Mises's original monetary-calculation point. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Socialist_calculation_debate.

question: Salerno's decisive intervention in the intra-Austrian dispute was a 1990 article in the Review of Austrian Economics that made the case for his strict-Misesian reading. What was the article's short title?
answer: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
choices: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
The Use of Knowledge in Society
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
context: 'Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist' (Review of Austrian Economics, 1990) is the paper that shifted majority Austrian opinion within the Mises Institute tradition toward Salerno's reading. Source: mises.org/library/ludwig-von-mises-social-rationalist.

question: Salerno's 2010 book from the Mises Institute collects his essays applying strict Misesian monetary theory to the Federal Reserve and the 2008 crisis. What is the book's title?
choices: The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Money: Sound and Unsound (Mises Institute, 2010) is Salerno's applied-Misesian essay collection on monetary policy. Source: mises.org/library/money-sound-and-unsound.

question: In 2004 Salerno edited the standard modern scholar's edition of a Rothbard treatise, published by the Mises Institute with the two volumes reunited. Which Rothbard treatise did he edit?
answer: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
choices: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
context: Salerno's 2004 scholar's edition finally reunited Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (1962) with its originally-excised political-economy volume Power and Market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: Mises's 1920 founding essay of the calculation debate ran under a specific title in the journal Archiv fur Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik. In English translation, what is the essay's title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Nature and Significance of Economic Science
context: 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' (1920) is Mises's founding contribution; the entire subsequent Austrian tradition, including the intra-tradition dispute Salerno intervened in, argues about how to read it. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: One of Milton Friedman's most-quoted maxims warns against judging policies by their announced good motives instead of by what they actually do to people over time. Which sentence best captures this Friedman maxim?
answer: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
choices: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
Judge policies by the party that sponsors them
Judge policies by their popularity in the polls
Judge policies by their moral rhetoric
context: 'One of the great mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results' -- Milton Friedman, spoken repeatedly in interviews including the 1975 Richard Heffner Open Mind interview, and written in Free to Choose (1980). Source: pbs.org (Free to Choose archive).

question: Friedman applied the results-not-intentions move sharply to a specific labor-market policy. Which policy did he describe with the blunt paraphrase that it was really a law requiring employers to discriminate against people who have low skills?
choices: The Fair Labor Standards Act as a whole
context: Friedman: 'The minimum wage law is most properly described as a law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills.' It appears repeatedly in his columns and in Free to Choose Chapter 8. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (Harcourt 1980), Chapter 8.

question: Friedman's minimum-wage critique distinguishes between two workers affected by a legal wage floor. Which worker is the SEEN beneficiary and which is the UNSEEN cost?
answer: SEEN: the worker who keeps the job. UNSEEN: the worker whose job is priced out of existence
choices: SEEN: the worker who keeps the job. UNSEEN: the worker whose job is priced out of existence
SEEN: the employer who pays the wage. UNSEEN: the government that collects payroll tax
SEEN: the union that negotiated the wage. UNSEEN: the pension fund that received the dues
SEEN: the retailer's customers. UNSEEN: the retailer's shareholders
context: The Bastiat SEEN vs UNSEEN move applied to the minimum wage: the worker who keeps the job at the higher wage is visible; the marginal worker whose job is automated away or moved offshore is invisible. Friedman presses attention to the invisible category. Source: Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), Chapter 8.

question: Friedman's rent-control critique appeared before he was famous, in a 1946 pamphlet he co-wrote with another future Chicago Nobel laureate about post-war US housing shortages. Who was his co-author?
context: Milton Friedman + George Stigler, 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem' (Foundation for Economic Education, 1946). It was Friedman and Stigler's first major joint work, before both became Chicago-school leaders. Source: fee.org (Roofs or Ceilings 1946 reprint).

question: Applied to rent control, the results-not-intentions move identifies a specific consequence for the affected housing stock. What does the empirical literature consistently find happens to buildings under rent control?
answer: Landlords let them decay and new construction stops
choices: Landlords let them decay and new construction stops
Landlords invest heavily in luxury upgrades
The buildings receive federal subsidies for maintenance
Occupancy drops sharply as tenants vacate
context: Rent-controlled buildings suffer deferred maintenance and the housing stock stops growing because new construction is unprofitable at the controlled rate. Existing tenants stay for decades because leaving means losing the rate. Source: Friedman + Stigler (1946); Diamond + McQuade + Qian, AER (2019) on San Francisco.

question: The results-not-intentions move sits alongside another Thomas Sowell diagnostic that pairs naturally with it in policy analysis. What is Sowell's paired two-word question?
context: Sowell's 'compared to what?' presses the alternative any proposed reform is being measured against. Combined with Friedman's 'judge by results,' the pair produces a mature policy-analysis toolkit: what does the policy actually do, and compared to what alternative? Source: Sowell, Knowledge and Decisions (Basic 1980).

question: Friedman's results-not-intentions move applied to occupational-licensing rules identifies a specific incumbent-benefit pattern. Whose incomes do state hairdressing, cosmetology, and interior-design licenses primarily protect?
context: Friedman + Kleiner: occupational licensing raises incumbent incomes by restricting entry, with little measurable consumer-safety benefit. The stated intent is consumer protection; the result is incumbent rent extraction. Source: Friedman (1962) Chapter 9; Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: Friedman applied the results-not-intentions move to the mid-20th-century US welfare system's family-structure consequences. What specific disincentive did the pre-reform welfare structure impose?
answer: A marriage penalty embedded in household-income aggregation rules
choices: A marriage penalty embedded in household-income aggregation rules
A required 40-hour work week for all beneficiaries
A ban on any bank account with a balance over one dollar
A prohibition on private tutoring for beneficiaries' children
context: The pre-reform welfare system counted household income for eligibility; a two-parent household could lose more benefits from marrying than the added income was worth. Friedman documented this in Capitalism and Freedom and Free to Choose. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), Chapter 4.

question: The results-not-intentions move gives the policy analyst a specific empiricist habit against accepting a policy's own theory. What should the analyst do instead of taking the policy's advertised justification at face value?
answer: Look at what actually happened when the policy was applied
choices: Look at what actually happened when the policy was applied
Look at the political party that sponsored the policy
Look at whether the policy was passed unanimously
Look at whether the policy has a memorable acronym
context: The Friedman move is a form of empiricism: policies come with their own theories about how they work; the honest analyst compares the theory to the observed outcome. This is what unites the minimum-wage, rent-control, and welfare cases. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (1980).

question: The Friedman results-not-intentions move fuses with Sowell's two questions ('compared to what?' and 'at what cost?') into a three-part diagnostic. Which sentence best captures what a responsible policy analysis asks?
answer: What does the policy INTEND, what does it actually DO, and at what COST compared to what alternative
choices: What does the policy INTEND, what does it actually DO, and at what COST compared to what alternative
Which political party sponsors it, which lobbyists supported it, and which president signed it
How long is the statute, who wrote it, and when was it introduced
How much does it cost, how much does it raise in revenue, and how much does the CBO score it
context: The Friedman-Sowell three-part diagnostic: (a) intended outcome; (b) actual result; (c) cost, compared to the honest alternative. Skipping any of the three is standard practice in unserious policy debate. Source: Sowell + Friedman across their popular books.

question: In July 2019 President Trump announced his intent to nominate a specific economist to the Federal Reserve Board of Governors -- a woman with a 1994 book titled Money Meltdown that argued for a return to a gold-linked international monetary system. Who is she?
context: Judy Shelton (born 1954) had served in the US delegation to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Her nomination was formally submitted January 16 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Judy Shelton was widely characterized during her nomination fight as belonging to a particular tradition of monetary thought that is skeptical of central-bank discretion and sympathetic to a metallic monetary anchor. Which tradition?
context: Shelton's public paper trail argued against Fed discretionary policy. She was described in both defense and attack coverage as Austrian-tradition and gold-curious -- an unusual combination for a Fed nominee. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Shelton's nomination attracted unusually broad opposition. Over 100 former officials -- including several former Fed chairs and vice chairs -- signed a letter opposing her confirmation. Roughly how many former Fed chairs and vice chairs signed?
context: The seven signatories included every living former Fed chair and several former vice chairs. The letter was extraordinary; former Fed leaders almost never intervene in a sitting nomination. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: The Senate cloture vote on Shelton's confirmation failed 47-50 on November 17 2020. Three Republican senators voted against her. Which trio of GOP senators broke ranks?
answer: Susan Collins, Mitt Romney, and Lamar Alexander
choices: Susan Collins, Mitt Romney, and Lamar Alexander
Rand Paul, Ted Cruz, and Josh Hawley
Mitch McConnell, John Thune, and Roy Blunt
Lisa Murkowski, Ben Sasse, and Pat Toomey
context: Collins, Romney, and Alexander joined all Democrats in voting against cloture. Two absent Republicans plus VP-elect Kamala Harris on the Biden transition meant the vote could not be salvaged. Trump did not re-nominate her. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Shelton's mentor for her 1994 book Money Meltdown was a former US Treasury Secretary who had served under President Reagan. Who mentored her?
context: James Baker served as Reagan's Treasury Secretary from 1985 to 1988 and later as Secretary of State under Bush 41. His mentorship placed Shelton in a Reagan-era hard-money lineage. Source: Grokipedia 'James Baker' (2026-09-05).

question: Shelton's 1998 book made a strikingly accurate prediction about the impending collapse of the Soviet economy, arguing from a specific tradition of economic reasoning. Which book was it?
context: Shelton's 1998 The Coming Soviet Crash predicted USSR economic collapse from the calculation-debate perspective -- the same Mises 1920 argument that Venezuela later illustrated in real time. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Had Shelton been confirmed in early 2020, she would have been an FOMC voting member during a specific set of consequential 2020-2021 decisions. Which set do Austrian-tradition analysts most often cite as lost oversight opportunities?
answer: The March 2020 unlimited-QE decision, the 2020-21 M2 explosion, and the 2021 transitory-inflation call
choices: The March 2020 unlimited-QE decision, the 2020-21 M2 explosion, and the 2021 transitory-inflation call
The 2008 Lehman decision and the AIG rescue
The 1998 LTCM rescue and the 1999 Glass-Steagall repeal
The 2015 first rate hike and the 2018 quantitative tightening
context: All three unfolded in the 15 months after her rejection. Her published writings had specifically warned about central-bank-driven asset inflation and currency debasement -- the very phenomena that then materialized. Whether one dissenting vote would have changed policy is unknowable. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: Democratic opposition to Shelton focused on her writings expressing skepticism about a specific institutional norm that has protected the Fed from political pressure since the 1951 Fed-Treasury Accord. What norm did she publicly question?
answer: Federal Reserve independence from the executive branch
choices: Federal Reserve independence from the executive branch
The dual mandate for employment and price stability
The rotation of regional Fed presidents on the FOMC
The publication of FOMC minutes with a lag
context: Shelton had questioned whether the Fed should be as insulated from elected oversight as the current norm makes it. Democrats framed this as a threat to the Fed's political neutrality; Republicans on the fence were nervous about her gold-standard sympathies. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: The Shelton rejection is often described by Austrian-tradition analysts as the closest the Fed has come to seating an explicit hard-money voice in a generation. Which recognition move does the ladder press about the political economy of central-bank appointments?
answer: A candidate who explicitly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's alumni network
choices: A candidate who explicitly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's alumni network
Senate cloture votes are always decided on strictly ideological grounds
Fed nominees are always approved regardless of controversy
Central bank independence is unrelated to appointment politics
context: The seven-former-chair opposition letter is the visible mechanism. An institution defends itself against reform-minded appointees by mobilizing its retired officials. The Fed alumni network functions as an implicit veto. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: The Shelton episode is the first Fed appointment fight of the modern era to turn substantively on a specific monetary-doctrine question rather than the usual technocratic vetting. Which question dominated the fight?
answer: Whether a gold-linked international monetary system is a legitimate policy option
choices: Whether a gold-linked international monetary system is a legitimate policy option
Whether the Federal Reserve should hire economists over lawyers
Whether regional Fed banks should be reorganized
Whether the FOMC should meet monthly instead of every six weeks
context: Shelton's gold-curious writings put a live monetary-doctrine question at the center of a modern Fed nomination for the first time in decades. The rejection settled the political question; the intellectual question survives in the growing Austrian-tradition public sphere. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: In the mid-1990s a young Melbourne programmer, born 1971 in Townsville, joined the cypherpunk mailing list and corresponded for years with cryptographers like Tim May, John Gilmore, and Adam Back about tools governments could not seize. Who was he?
context: Assange had already been convicted of hacking in Australia in 1996. His decade on the cypherpunk list predated WikiLeaks by roughly ten years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: In 1997 Julian Assange and collaborators released a file-encryption system named for the joke term 'rubber-hose cryptanalysis' -- extracting a password by beating someone with a hose. What was the system called?
context: Rubberhose was written in Melbourne. TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013) later adopted similar deniable-encryption designs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rubberhose_(file_system).

question: Rubberhose introduced a specific kind of encryption designed to protect users who might be tortured for their passwords. What was the key idea?
answer: Multiple hidden encrypted volumes on one disk, so revealing one password does not prove other volumes do not exist
choices: Multiple hidden encrypted volumes on one disk, so revealing one password does not prove other volumes do not exist
A single very long password that took decades to memorize but was impossible to guess
A one-time-pad shared physically with a trusted friend
Automatic deletion of all data after a wrong password attempt
context: The attacker cannot tell how many volumes exist -- only how many the victim has chosen to reveal. This is called plausibly-deniable encryption. Assange said the target user was a human-rights worker whose sources could die if the wrong files were found. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rubberhose_(file_system).

question: Rubberhose's deniable-encryption idea proved important enough to be adopted by later widely-used disk-encryption software. Which two systems inherited the design?
context: TrueCrypt became the standard cross-platform disk-encryption tool of the 2000s; VeraCrypt is its actively-maintained successor. Both borrowed Rubberhose's hidden-volume idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/TrueCrypt.

question: Julian Assange founded WikiLeaks in 2006 and applied the cypherpunk mailing-list principles to publishing leaked documents. What specific technical design let WikiLeaks resist government shutdown attempts?
answer: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
choices: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
Documents were stored only on physical media in Assange's home
Documents required an in-person appointment with WikiLeaks staff to access
Documents were held in escrow by the United Nations
context: A direct scale-up of 1990s cypherpunk censorship-resistance principles. No single government could shut all the mirrors down without cross-border legal cooperation that was often unavailable. Source: grokipedia.com/page/WikiLeaks.

question: Julian Assange spent seven years inside a specific diplomatic building in London (2012-2019) after taking asylum there to avoid extradition, and then years in a British high-security prison. Which embassy hosted him?
context: Ecuador granted him asylum in 2012; the asylum was revoked in April 2019 and British police arrested him inside the embassy the same day. He was then held in Belmarsh prison until his 2024 plea deal and release. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: A high-school student asks how the 1990s cypherpunk mailing list turned into 21st-century geopolitics. A cryptographer points to a specific principle that connected the two eras: the same technique used to protect one human-rights worker's files can also scale up to mirror thousands of classified documents across many jurisdictions. Which principle?
answer: Distributed censorship-resistance: no single actor can seize what many independent copies preserve
choices: Distributed censorship-resistance: no single actor can seize what many independent copies preserve
Central authorization: a single trusted third party must approve every access
Physical secrecy: sensitive information must be stored on paper only
Legal compliance: encryption must obey all national import-export restrictions
context: The principle traces from the cypherpunk mailing list through Rubberhose to WikiLeaks to Bitcoin. The same design property -- deniability of destruction -- is what makes both a private encrypted disk and a public censorship-resistant ledger work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cypherpunk.

question: In 1981 Princeton University Press published a University of Maryland economist's book arguing that human ingenuity, not any specific commodity, is the true bottleneck on human progress. What single phrase names the book's central claim about that ingenuity?
context: Julian L. Simon (1932-1998), The Ultimate Resource (Princeton University Press, 1981; reissued as The Ultimate Resource 2 in 1996). Source: press.princeton.edu (Simon 1981/1996).

question: Julian Simon's core empirical claim was that the real (inflation-adjusted) prices of most commodities have moved in a specific direction over the long run, despite world population growth. In which direction?
context: Simon documented that real prices of copper, tin, wheat, aluminum, and iron were cheaper in 2000 than in 1800 even as world population sextupled. If resources were becoming scarcer, prices would rise; they did not. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Simon's principal Malthusian intellectual opponent was a Stanford biologist whose 1968 book The Population Bomb predicted mass famines that would kill hundreds of millions in the 1970s. Who was that opponent?
context: Paul Ehrlich, The Population Bomb (Ballantine, 1968), predicted global famines in the 1970s. The predicted famines did not occur; food supply per capita rose. Simon spent much of his career debating Ehrlich. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Population_Bomb.

question: In 1980 Julian Simon publicly offered any Malthusian a bet: pick any five commodities, any duration 1-100 years, and Simon would bet their real prices would fall. Paul Ehrlich accepted with two colleagues -- John Harte and John Holdren -- and picked which five metals?
answer: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
choices: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
Gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and rhodium
Iron, aluminum, lead, zinc, and magnesium
Uranium, plutonium, thorium, cesium, and radium
context: Ehrlich, Harte, and Holdren chose chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten for a 10-year wager ending September 1990, totaling $1,000 ($200 per metal). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: The Simon-Ehrlich wager ran from September 1980 to September 1990. On October 10, 1990, John Holdren mailed Simon a check for a specific amount. Who won each metal?
choices: Simon won three; Ehrlich won two
The bet ended in an exact draw across the five
context: All five metals had fallen in real (inflation-adjusted) price over the wager decade. Some had also fallen in nominal terms. Simon won every commodity -- a total refutation of the Malthusian pricing prediction over the wager decade. Source: nyt.com (Simon-Ehrlich wager coverage 1990).

question: Ehrlich's Malthusian view held that population growth would exhaust resources. Simon's counter-view has been popularized in subsequent decades by writers like Matt Ridley and Hans Rosling. Which of the following was NOT part of the Simon counter-argument?
answer: That governments should impose one-child policies
choices: That governments should impose one-child policies
That people are producers as well as consumers
That human ingenuity finds substitutes as scarcity rises
That real prices are the honest measure of scarcity
context: Simon's argument is anti-Malthusian, not pro-population-control. He argued people are producers of ideas as well as consumers, that ingenuity finds substitutes, and that real prices are the honest scarcity measure. One-child policies belong to the opposing Ehrlich tradition. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: One of Simon's Malthusian wager partners went on to a prominent US government position under President Barack Obama in the 2010s. Which of the three -- Ehrlich, Harte, or Holdren -- served as White House science advisor?
choices: None of them held any government post
context: John Holdren served as Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and science advisor to President Obama from 2009 to 2017. He had signed onto the losing Ehrlich side of the 1980 Simon wager. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holdren.

question: Julian Simon's intellectual heirs in the 21st century include a British popularizer whose 2010 book The Rational Optimist and 2020 book How Innovation Works extend the ingenuity-as-ultimate-resource case. Who is that writer?
context: Matt Ridley, The Rational Optimist (Harper 2010) and How Innovation Works (Harper 2020), popularizes the Simon case for continued improvement in human welfare through ingenuity. Hans Rosling's Factfulness (2018) also fits the tradition. Source: mattridley.co.uk.

question: The Simon-Ehrlich wager is often cited as the closest thing to an empirical decision on late-20th-century population-resource pessimism. What specific reasoning move about scarcity does the wager illustrate?
answer: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
choices: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
Rising real prices always indicate that resources are getting rarer
Government subsidies always distort scarcity signals beyond usefulness
Commodity markets are irrelevant to any long-run resource question
context: The Simon move: real prices, not headlines, are the honest scarcity measure. Falling real prices for a commodity mean it is becoming LESS scarce, not more. This is the empirical test that decides the population-resource debate. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Paul Ehrlich has continued into the 2010s and 2020s to argue that the 1980-90 wager decade was atypical and that his broader Malthusian predictions remain correct. Which best characterizes the honest state of the specific 1980-90 empirical outcome?
answer: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
choices: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
The metals rose in real price; Simon lost every commodity
The outcome was too close to call between the two
The metals were not actually tracked over the decade
context: The record on the specific wager: all five metals fell in real price over 1980-90; Holdren wrote the check. Ehrlich's continuing broader argument is separable from that specific outcome; the specific outcome is unambiguous. Source: Simon 1990 correspondence; Sabin, The Bet (Yale 2013).

question: London, 1883. Karl Marx dies without finishing his masterwork Das Kapital. Only Volume 1 (1867) is in print; Volumes 2 and 3 exist as boxes of handwritten manuscripts and notes. Marx's lifelong collaborator inherits the boxes and spends the rest of his own life editing them into publishable form. Who was the collaborator who edited and published Marx's unfinished volumes after his death?
context: Engels published Volume 2 in 1885 and Volume 3 in 1894 (eleven years after Marx's death) from the scattered manuscripts Marx left behind. The manuscript pages Engels used for Volume 3 were themselves drafted 1863-1883. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital.

question: Volume 1 of Marx's Das Kapital (1867) laid down a single, sharply-stated principle: when two goods exchange for each other in a market, the ratio between their prices reflects the ratio of one specific input each contains. Which input did Volume 1 say determined exchange ratios?
context: This is the LABOR THEORY OF VALUE: a coat that took twice as many socially necessary labor-hours to make as a pair of shoes should exchange for two pairs of shoes. Marx inherited the theory from Ricardo and made it the foundation of Volume 1. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital.

question: Every attentive reader of Volume 1 (1867) noticed the same problem: real market prices do NOT match the labor-hours in goods. A capital-heavy factory's products sell for more than their labor-hours would predict; a labor-heavy workshop's products sell for less. Marx promised readers he would solve this in a later volume. The puzzle was named for the operation he still owed them -- converting labor-values into actual market prices. What did the Marxist tradition come to call this problem?
context: The transformation problem = converting Volume 1's labor-values into Volume 3's actual prices of production. Mises's later calculation problem is a DIFFERENT critique (no market prices at all under socialism); the socialization and accumulation problems are further-downstream Marxist debates. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: The Austrian economist Eugen Boehm-Bawerk (who would answer two years later in his famous 1896 essay 'Karl Marx and the Close of His System') had waited nearly three decades for Marx to reconcile the price-vs-value objection raised by Volume 1 (1867). In 1894 Engels finally published the volume that was supposed to contain Marx's answer. Which volume of Das Kapital did Engels publish in 1894?
context: Volume 3 (1894) was expected to contain Marx's promised transformation of labor-values into market prices. Volume 1 (1867) posed the problem; Volume 2 (Engels 1885) covered the circulation of capital; there is no completed Volume 4 (Kautsky later assembled Theories of Surplus Value from Marx's notes and gave it that number). Source: marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1894-c3/editorial/heinrich.htm.

question: In 1896 Eugen Boehm-Bawerk published his scorching answer to Marx's Volume 3 as an essay in a festschrift honoring an older German-tradition economist -- the same man who had helped train the whole late-nineteenth-century generation of German-language economists. In whose honor was the festschrift published?
context: Karl Knies (1821-1898) was one of the founding generation of the German Historical School. Boehm-Bawerk's essay first appeared in the 1896 festschrift for Knies before being reissued as a standalone book the same year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay pressed one central charge against Marx: the labor-hour equation stated in Volume 1 (1867) and the price-of-production equation stated in Volume 3 (1894) cannot both hold in the same economy. Which specific analytical failing did Boehm-Bawerk say the two volumes together suffered?
context: Boehm-Bawerk's charge was NOT that Marx failed a data test; it was that Marx's own two volumes CONTRADICT each other. Volume 3 quietly drops what Volume 1 confidently asserted -- and no data are needed to see the internal inconsistency. This is why his essay is called the CLASSICAL critique of Kapital: the flaw is logical, not empirical. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: In 1904 a young Marxist economist named Rudolf Hilferding published the definitive Marxist reply to Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay. Hilferding's book Boehm-Bawerks Marx-Kritik had an awkward biographical twist for its author: Hilferding had once sat in Boehm-Bawerk's own Vienna seminar as a student. Later in his career, Hilferding served twice in one European government as its Finance Minister. Which government did Hilferding serve twice as Finance Minister?
context: Rudolf Hilferding (1877-1941) served as Weimar Germany's Finance Minister in 1923 and again in 1928-29. He fled the Nazis in 1933, was captured in Vichy France in 1941, and was murdered by the Gestapo the same year. Source: hetwebsite.net/het/profiles/hilferding.htm.

question: Boehm-Bawerk read Marx's Volume 3 attempt to solve the transformation and delivered a specific and cutting diagnosis: Marx does not really convert the labor-hour equation into a price equation at all. Instead, Marx QUIETLY DROPS the labor theory of value and substitutes an older, rival theory of price -- dressed up as if it were the solution. Which older theory did Boehm-Bawerk accuse Marx of smuggling in?
choices: a subjective marginal utility theory of price
context: Boehm-Bawerk showed that Marx's Volume 3 prices are effectively determined by the sum of costs (wages plus capital-input costs plus average profit) -- the classical COST-OF-PRODUCTION theory of price associated with Adam Smith. That is not a transformation of the labor theory; it is a quiet substitution for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: In 1949 an American Marxist economist compiled Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay and Hilferding's 1904 reply into a single English-language volume that finally put the whole debate in front of Anglo-American readers. The compiler was himself the most influential twentieth-century American Marxist economist and a co-founder of the Monthly Review. Which economist edited the 1949 English compilation?
context: Paul Sweezy's 1949 combined volume (Karl Marx and the Close of His System, by Boehm-Bawerk, plus Boehm-Bawerk's Criticism of Marx, by Hilferding) is the standard English-language source for the whole debate. Baran was Sweezy's later Monopoly Capital co-author; Dobb the leading British Marxist economist; Mandel the Belgian trotskyist economist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: Since the 1970s a group of Marxist economists (Duncan Foley, Fred Moseley, and others) have offered what they call the NEW INTERPRETATION of Marxian value theory. Rather than defending Marx's Volume 3 solution as it was written, they OFFER A NEW ONE that produces different equations from different assumptions. Which reasoning move does the New Interpretation project itself amount to?
answer: conceding the 1896 charge and rebuilding from other passages
choices: conceding the 1896 charge and rebuilding from other passages
reproducing the 1894 solution with better mathematics
abandoning the labor theory of value entirely
context: The New Interpretation does not defend Volume 3's original transformation equation (that would be reproducing Marx's math); it builds a substitute from a different reading of scattered Marx passages -- which is a concession that Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 diagnostic held for the printed text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: By the 1920s Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay had produced a striking result in one specific arena. Which arena did the essay effectively close for a generation?
answer: academic defense of Marxian value theory in German universities
choices: academic defense of Marxian value theory in German universities
political influence of the European socialist parties
public sales of Das Kapital across the continent
translation of Marx into non-German European languages
context: Boehm-Bawerk's essay did not damage socialist party politics (which grew rapidly after 1900) or public sales of Marx (which continued). What it ended for a generation was serious ACADEMIC defense of the Volume 1 labor-value equation inside German-language universities; that defense only resumed with the Anglo-American revival in the 1940s-70s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: The founder of the Austrian School of economics had a son born in Vienna in 1902 who became a first-rank mathematician rather than an economist. What was the son's first name?
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) was born when his father Carl Menger was 62. Father became the economist; son became the mathematician. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: One of the standard textbook fractals is a solid cube from which smaller cubes are recursively drilled out at every scale. What is that fractal called?
context: Karl Menger the younger described the sponge in 1926. It is a 3-dimensional analogue of the 1D Cantor set. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: Karl Menger the younger took his doctorate under Hans Hahn at the University of Vienna in a specific area of mathematics that studies how many parameters are needed to describe a space. What was his area?
context: Menger's 1924 doctorate under Hans Hahn produced original work on the topological definition of what it means for a space to be n-dimensional. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: From 1928 to 1936 Menger ran a fortnightly mathematics seminar at the University of Vienna. What was the seminar called?
context: Menger's Mathematical Colloquium was one of the most important mathematics seminars of the interwar era. Kurt Godel presented parts of his incompleteness work through it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: Menger's fractal has a Hausdorff dimension that is neither 2 nor 3 but strictly between them, reflecting its infinitely-pocked structure. What is the approximate value of that dimension?
context: The Menger sponge's Hausdorff dimension is log(20)/log(3), approximately 2.727 -- a solid cube that is dimensionally between a 2D surface and a full 3D volume. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: Alongside his own math colloquium, Menger attended the philosophical seminar of the logical positivists in Vienna, associated with Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, and Otto Neurath. What was that seminar's shorthand name?
context: The Vienna Circle of logical positivists was the philosophy scene through which Menger's mathematics work interacted with Godel, Carnap, and Wittgenstein-as-influence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Reading the direction of Central European politics, Karl Menger the younger left Austria in 1937 for a Catholic research university in Indiana. Which American university did he accept a chair at?
context: Menger accepted a Notre Dame chair in 1937, moving permanently to America a year before the March 1938 Anschluss. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: Menger's autobiographical memoir of both the mathematical seminar he ran and the philosophy seminar he attended in interwar Vienna was published posthumously in 1994. What is its title?
answer: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium
choices: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium
The Open Society and Its Enemies
context: Menger's 1994 memoir is one of the best insider accounts of Vienna's twin scientific-philosophical circles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: On August 23, 1939 the foreign ministers of two states signed a treaty in Moscow that publicly promised non-aggression and secretly divided Eastern Europe between them. Which two states?
answer: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union
choices: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union
The Soviet Union and Republican Spain
The Soviet Union and the United Kingdom
context: The signers were Nazi Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov; the treaty is universally known as the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: Nazi Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939 -- the accepted start of World War II in Europe. Sixteen days later, on September 17, 1939, another power invaded Poland from the opposite direction, acting on the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact's secret protocol. Which power?
context: The USSR annexed eastern Poland immediately, and in June 1940 annexed the three Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), all consistent with the pact's secret territorial protocol. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: In April and May 1940 the Soviet NKVD executed roughly 22,000 Polish military officers, police, and educated professionals, most by pistol shot to the back of the head. What is the massacre named for?
context: Katyn was one of three main execution sites; the other two were the NKVD facilities at Kalinin and Kharkiv. The category of victim was deliberately chosen to decapitate Polish national leadership. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: The 1940 Katyn massacre took approximately how many lives, drawn from the Polish military officer corps, police, and educated professional class?
context: The victims were specifically the categories most likely to lead a Polish national resistance or postwar state. The class-decapitation intent is what NKVD execution lists document. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: From 1943 to 1990 the Soviet Union publicly denied its own responsibility for Katyn and blamed Nazi Germany. On April 13, 1990 the Soviet government finally acknowledged the truth. Which Soviet leader was in office at the acknowledgment?
context: Gorbachev's glasnost policy made possible the archival admission that Stalin's Politburo, not Nazi Germany, had ordered the Katyn executions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: On October 14, 1992 Russian President Boris Yeltsin handed Polish leaders the original Politburo documents on Katyn -- including a specific piece of physical evidence dated March 5, 1940 that named the ordering authority. What did the document carry?
answer: Stalin's own signature on the execution order
choices: Stalin's own signature on the execution order
Molotov's diplomatic notes on the Ribbentrop pact
context: The Politburo order of March 5, 1940 was signed by Stalin personally. Its transfer to Poland closed a fifty-year denial. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: In 2007 the Polish director Andrzej Wajda released a film about the Katyn massacre told from the perspective of Polish families searching for missing officers. What personal history gave the director a direct claim to the story?
answer: Wajda's own father, an officer, had been killed at Kharkiv
choices: Wajda's own father, an officer, had been killed at Kharkiv
Wajda had served in the NKVD before defecting to Poland
Wajda had personally filmed the German 1943 exhumations
Wajda had led the March 1990 protests demanding acknowledgment
context: Wajda was one of Poland's most decorated filmmakers (director of 'Man of Iron' and 'Man of Marble'). The 2007 'Katyn' won multiple international awards. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_(film).

question: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact plus Katyn together illustrate a specific historical fact about the two-year period from August 1939 to June 1941, when Hitler broke the pact by invading the USSR. Which fact does the pair establish?
answer: The Soviet Union was a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany from August 1939 to June 1941
choices: The Soviet Union was a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany from August 1939 to June 1941
The Soviet Union was neutral throughout World War II
The Soviet Union was allied with the United Kingdom throughout 1939-41
The Soviet Union invaded no other country between 1939 and 1945
context: The pact and its secret territorial protocol, the September 1939 Soviet invasion of Poland, the June 1940 annexation of the Baltics, and the 1940 Katyn massacre are one continuous historical arc. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: In the late 1990s a Connecticut woman named Susette Kelo bought and renovated a small pink house at 8 East Street in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood, only to find her home sat in the footprint of a planned redevelopment centered on a new $300 million Pfizer research campus. In which city did her house stand?
context: Kelo's pink house was in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood of New London, Connecticut. The city and New London Development Corporation adopted a plan to build offices, retail, and residential development around the Pfizer campus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelo_v._City_of_New_London.

question: When Susette Kelo refused to sell her New London home, the city moved to seize it under the Fifth Amendment power to take private property for 'public use' with just compensation. What is the name of that constitutional power?
context: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause authorizes eminent domain -- government seizure of private property for public use, with just compensation. Historically 'public use' meant roads, schools, or military bases. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Fifth Amendment).

question: The Kelo case reached the Supreme Court, and on June 23, 2005, the justices held 5-4 that economic development satisfies the 'public use' requirement of the Fifth Amendment. Which justice wrote the majority opinion?
context: Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the majority in Kelo v. City of New London, 545 US 469 (2005), joined by Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Source: supremecourt.gov (Kelo 545 US 469).

question: The principal dissent in Kelo warned in a famous passage that 'nothing is to prevent the State from replacing any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton, any home with a shopping mall, or any farm with a factory.' Which justice wrote that dissent?
context: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor's principal dissent was joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas. The Motel-6-to-Ritz-Carlton passage became the most-quoted line of the case. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), dissent.

question: Susette Kelo lost her house, but what happened to the Pfizer research campus that had been the redevelopment plan's anchor?
answer: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
choices: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
Pfizer moved its global headquarters there
Pfizer converted it to an art museum
context: Pfizer closed the New London research facility in 2009-10. The cleared land where Kelo's house and her neighbors' homes had stood then remained vacant for more than a decade. Source: nytimes.com and courant.com (Pfizer New London closure coverage).

question: In the decade after the Kelo decision, most US states enacted state-constitutional or statutory reforms restricting private-to-private eminent-domain takings for economic development. Roughly how many states passed such reforms?
context: Roughly 45 states enacted post-Kelo constitutional amendments or statutes restricting economic-development takings, largely driven by campaigns from the Institute for Justice, Kelo's counsel. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo state legislation tracker).

question: Kelo's legal team came from a public-interest law firm founded in 1991 by Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick that has become the leading American property-rights litigation vehicle. What is its name?
context: The Institute for Justice, founded in 1991, represented Susette Kelo and has litigated dozens of eminent-domain cases since. Source: ij.org.

question: The Kelo redevelopment illustrates a specific public-choice diagnosis of why private-to-private takings persist despite constitutional tension. Which combined analysis best captures the structural pattern?
answer: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
choices: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
A benevolent city planner balances competing public interests
A federal environmental review paralyzes local government
A random judicial error assigns rights inefficiently
context: The public-choice reading combines Tullock 1967 rent-seeking (real resources burned on the political process) with Olson 1965 concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost (one organized developer versus many un-organized neighbors). Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: A supporter of the majority ruling in Kelo would defend the outcome by pointing to a specific stated public purpose the redevelopment plan named. What was that stated purpose?
answer: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
choices: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
Federal defense readiness in New England
Access to a natural harbor for shipping
Preservation of a historic Colonial neighborhood
context: The New London plan's stated purpose was economic development -- jobs and tax base -- which the Kelo majority accepted as satisfying 'public use' under the Fifth Amendment. The public-choice reading focuses on WHO actually benefited concentrated-ly, and how organized they were. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), majority opinion.

question: The Kelo case teaches a general reasoning move public-choice analysts should apply whenever government coercion transfers resources between private parties. What should the analyst look for behind the stated public-purpose justification?
answer: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
choices: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
Which political party holds the mayor's office
How large the total municipal budget is
Whether the seized property is above or below the median value
context: The stated public purpose is often sincere but incomplete. The public-choice reading identifies the concentrated beneficiary (developer) and concentrated cost-bearers (individual homeowners) whose organizational asymmetry drives the outcome. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965); Kelo (2005) as case study.

question: The post-Kelo state-reform wave is unusual in the public-choice literature because it is a rare case where the dispersed victim interest actually organized successfully to reverse a concentrated-benefit outcome. Which condition made that reversal possible?
answer: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
choices: Sustained litigation and advocacy by the Institute for Justice organized the dispersed interest
The federal government abolished eminent domain entirely
Insurance companies refused to insure any seized property
The Supreme Court reversed itself in a follow-up case
context: IJ served as the selective-incentive engine (documentation, model legislation, media) that turned diffuse public concern into effective 45-state legislative action. This is Olson's own solution to the collective-action problem in action. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo advocacy history).

question: In 1951 a young Columbia doctoral student published a slim book whose central mathematical result would eventually earn him the Nobel Prize at age 51 -- then the youngest economics Nobel ever. He proved that no fair method exists for turning individual votes into a coherent group preference. Who was he?
context: Kenneth Arrow (1921-2017) won the 1972 Nobel jointly with John Hicks. He was 51 -- then the youngest economics Nobel. His doctoral book Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951) contained the impossibility result. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Arrow.

question: Kenneth Arrow's 1951 book -- his Columbia doctoral dissertation adapted -- carried a title that named its two-part concern: how to combine what individuals want into what society chooses. What was the book's title?
context: Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951; second edition 1963). The book launched the modern field of social-choice theory. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (2012 reprint of the second edition).

question: Arrow's theorem imposes a short list of fairness criteria on any voting method and asks whether all can be satisfied at once. One criterion insists that if every voter prefers option A to option B, then the group must too. By what name is this basic requirement known?
context: Arrow's five criteria include unanimity (if all voters rank A above B, so does the group), independence of irrelevant alternatives, universal domain, transitivity, and non-dictatorship. The theorem proves no method satisfies all simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963).

question: Another of Arrow's fairness criteria says that no single voter's preference should determine the group outcome irrespective of everyone else's. What is this criterion called?
context: The non-dictatorship condition rules out any voting method that always follows one specified voter. Arrow proved that dropping this condition is the only way to make the other criteria consistent -- which is why the theorem is so provocative. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Kenneth Arrow's central result about voting-method fairness has come to be known by a specific two-word name that captures what the theorem proves cannot be built. What is the theorem called?
context: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem: for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives, no method can satisfy the five fairness criteria simultaneously. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Arrow's result kicks in only above a specific threshold of voters and options. Below that threshold, majority rule can behave perfectly well. What is the smallest number of alternatives at which the impossibility bites?
context: With only two alternatives, majority rule satisfies every Arrow criterion. The impossibility applies for any group of three or more voters facing three or more alternatives. The classic Condorcet paradox is a three-voter, three-option case. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Three years before Arrow's book appeared, a Scottish-Welsh economist had published a partial escape from the impossibility problem: majority rule DOES produce a stable outcome when voter preferences line up along a single ideological dimension. Which theorem did he prove in 1948?
context: Duncan Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making' (Journal of Political Economy, 1948), showed that if preferences are single-peaked on one dimension, majority rule picks the median voter's preferred option. It is the narrow exception to Arrow's impossibility. Source: jstor.org (Black 1948).

question: Arrow shared his 1972 Nobel with a British economist whose Value and Capital (1939) had done for consumer theory what Arrow's own work did for welfare economics. Who was Arrow's co-laureate?
context: John Hicks and Kenneth Arrow shared the 1972 Nobel 'for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory.' Source: nobelprize.org (1972 Economic Sciences).

question: The most sweeping implication of Arrow's theorem for democratic theory is that a familiar phrase used every election night does not describe any coherent object at all. Which phrase does his mathematics dissolve?
context: If different voting methods produce different winners from the same voter preferences, there is no method-independent 'will of the people' waiting to be discovered. The winner is jointly produced by voters AND the aggregation rule. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (Freeman 1982).

question: Arrow's theorem strengthens a specific move public choice already wanted to make about political institutions. Given that no method-independent group preference exists, what added weight does the theorem give to which set of choices?
answer: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
choices: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
The particular slate of candidates matters more than the rules
Party discipline can substitute for any voting-method choice
Judicial review can always correct impossibility results
context: James Buchanan built on this insight: rules that determine HOW votes are aggregated do not merely process a preexisting will; they partly DEFINE what the aggregate looks like. Constitutional political economy takes the rules-choice question with new seriousness. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (1982).

question: In 1973 the University of Chicago Press published a book by a New York University Austrian economist that defined the entrepreneur as the person who is ALERT to profit opportunities other market participants have missed. Who was the author?
context: Israel Kirzner (b. February 13, 1930), Competition and Entrepreneurship (University of Chicago Press, 1973). Kirzner was a student of Ludwig von Mises at NYU. Source: press.uchicago.edu (Kirzner 1973).

question: Kirzner's 1973 theory distinguishes the entrepreneur from two rival theories of the same figure. Frank Knight said the entrepreneur was principally a risk-bearer; Joseph Schumpeter said the entrepreneur was principally an innovator. What did Kirzner say the entrepreneur principally is?
answer: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
choices: Someone alert to profit opportunities others missed
Someone who assembles the largest possible capital
Someone who lobbies government for protective regulation
Someone who monopolizes an existing market
context: Kirzner separates alertness from Knight's risk-bearing and Schumpeter's creative-destruction innovation. The entrepreneur perceives an opportunity in the flow of prices and technology that competitors with the same information failed to see. Source: Kirzner, Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago 1973).

question: Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997 and led the launch of the iPhone in June 2007. In Kirznerian terms, what did Jobs see that his rivals at BlackBerry, Nokia, and Motorola did not act on?
answer: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
choices: That touchscreens, music players, and phones could be integrated into one mass-market product
That mobile phones should be limited to voice calls only
That physical keyboards would dominate for the next thirty years
That personal computers should replace all mobile devices
context: Jobs saw the integration opportunity. Touchscreens (LG Prada 2006), music players (Apple's iPod since 2001), and phones (Nokia, BlackBerry, Motorola) all existed. The Kirznerian alertness was seeing they could combine. BlackBerry's Jim Balsillie publicly derided the iPhone in 2007. Source: Isaacson, Steve Jobs (Simon & Schuster 2011).

question: In 2002 Elon Musk founded SpaceX to pursue a Kirznerian opportunity that NASA and the incumbent contractors Boeing and Lockheed Martin had missed for forty years. What was that opportunity?
answer: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
choices: Reusable orbital rockets that land and fly again
Traditional expendable rockets built cheaper offshore
