context: The launch industry had assumed rockets were disposable for decades. Musk's insight was that per-launch cost drops dramatically if the first stage lands and is reused. Falcon 9's first successful landing was December 21, 2015. Source: spacex.com (Falcon 9 mission archive).

question: As of the mid-2020s SpaceX has landed and reused first-stage boosters an unprecedented number of times, validating Musk's Kirznerian bet that the launch industry's disposability assumption was wrong. Roughly how many first-stage landings and reuses had SpaceX accomplished?
context: By 2024 SpaceX had landed and reused Falcon 9 first stages over 300 times, some individual boosters twenty times or more. It has driven launch prices down substantially and captured most of the commercial launch market. Source: spacex.com (launch archive).

question: On July 5, 1994 Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in Seattle, starting with one specific product category. In Kirznerian terms, what made this category the perfect place to start an internet-scale retailer?
answer: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
choices: Books are standardized, durable, easily shipped, with a long-tail catalog
Books have the highest per-unit profit margins in all of retail
Books face no competition from physical bookstores
Books are exempt from state sales tax on federal statute
context: Bezos's Kirznerian alertness: books were the perfect starting product for internet-scale retail. No physical bookstore could stock the long-tail catalog. Chain bookstores had the same information but did not move decisively online. Source: Stone, The Everything Store (Little Brown 2013).

question: Kirzner's mentor at New York University, whose economics of human action shaped Kirzner's whole framework, was one of the twentieth century's leading Austrian economists. Who was that mentor?
context: Ludwig von Mises taught at NYU from 1945 to his death in 1973. Kirzner was among his most prominent students and inherited the Austrian entrepreneurship-and-market-process tradition. Source: mises.org (Mises + Kirzner biographical materials).

question: Kirzner received a major international honor in 2006 for his contributions to entrepreneurship research, though he never received a Nobel. What prize did he win in 2006?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
context: Israel Kirzner received the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research (Swedish Entrepreneurship Forum) in 2006 for his lifetime work. He is widely regarded as the leading Austrian theorist of the entrepreneurial function. Source: e-award.org (Kirzner 2006 laureate).

question: Kirznerian analysis of a spectacular new company asks a specific diagnostic question about the founder. What is the question the framework tells the analyst to press when explaining a modern success like Amazon, SpaceX, or the iPhone?
answer: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
choices: What did the founder see that competitors with the same technology and capital did not act on
How much capital did the founder inherit from family
Which lobbying firm secured the founder's early contracts
How many patents did the founder personally hold
context: Kirznerian analysis: technology and capital are usually accessible to many; alertness is not. The reason a new firm succeeds where competitors failed is usually a specific perception of an integration or application others considered impossible. Source: Kirzner (1973), Chapter 2.

question: Real entrepreneurs typically mix elements of all three Austrian-tradition theories -- Kirznerian alertness, Knightian risk-bearing, Schumpeterian innovation. What is the pedagogical value of separating the three when analyzing a specific founder?
answer: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
choices: It clarifies which theory fits which specific move being analyzed
It proves one of the three theories is always correct
It refutes the other two theories permanently
It replaces the need to look at any actual data
context: The point is not that a founder is 'a Kirznerian' or 'a Schumpeterian' in every action. The point is that different moves within a founder's career fit different theories: Bezos's book-choice was Kirznerian alertness; Musk's Mars ambition is Schumpeterian innovation; both took Knightian risks. Source: Kirzner (1973); Schumpeter (1911); Knight (1921).

question: In 1980 Basic Books published a 422-page book arguing that the knowledge an economy runs on is scattered across millions of separate people, so the real question to ask about any institution is what it can find out. Its author had taught at Cornell and UCLA and would later write the bestselling primer Basic Economics. Who wrote it?
context: Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions with Basic Books in 1980; it ran 422 pages in hardcover and won that year's Law and Economics Center Prize. Stigler, Becker and Friedman were all Chicago colleagues of his, which is why they make honest distractors. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Knowledge_and_Decisions); Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: Thomas Sowell built Knowledge and Decisions out of a single journal article F.A. Hayek had published in the American Economic Review in September 1945 -- the article arguing that prices carry information no central office could ever collect for itself. Which Hayek article?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review 35(4), September 1945. 'Economics and Knowledge' is his 1937 lecture, 'The Pretence of Knowledge' his 1974 Nobel lecture, and The Road to Serfdom the 1944 book. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions' and 'Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Tin grows scarce -- maybe a mine floods, maybe a new use for it is found -- and the price rises. Manufacturers in a dozen industries economize on tin; none ever learns which cause it was. F.A. Hayek built his 1945 argument on this example, and Sowell built Knowledge and Decisions on Hayek's. What does Hayek say no central planning board could manage here?
answer: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
choices: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
Proving in advance that the scarcity was real and not a speculator's rumour
Keeping its own officials honest once tin was valuable enough to bribe over
Matching the speed with which foreign factories would switch to substitutes
context: Hayek's point is not that planners are stupid but that the knowledge is not theirs to have: it exists only as millions of particular circumstances of time and place. The price is not a summary of that knowledge -- it is the only form in which it can travel. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hayek' and 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: Asked in a 2018 Reason interview whether Knowledge and Decisions was the achievement he was proudest of, Thomas Sowell said it certainly had been at the time and was still among them -- then named a different book of his own as his personal favourite, about a third the length and, he said, more readable. Which book?
context: Sowell to Reason, November 26 2018: Knowledge and Decisions 'certainly was at the time, and it's certainly among the books that I'm proudest of now,' but his 'own personal favorite is Conflict of Visions, which is perhaps a third of the size and more readable.' Source: Reason, 'Thomas Sowell Returns' (https://reason.com/2018/11/26/thomas-sowell-returns/).

question: Knowledge and Decisions had rested its entire case on one 1945 essay by F.A. Hayek. In December 1981 Hayek, then 82 and seven years past his Nobel, took up Sowell's book himself in the pages of Reason magazine. What did he do there?
answer: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
choices: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
Objected in a letter to the editor that his 1945 essay had been flattened into slogans
Listed it among ten books he wished that he had written himself before the war
Warned readers that Sowell had confused his 1945 essay with Mises's 1920 one
context: Hayek's review ran in Reason, December 1981, under exactly that title. He wrote that Sowell had expanded admirably on his original concepts and made them clear to lay readers, with examples of economic activity drawn from the real world. Sources: Reason, December 1981 (https://reason.com/1981/12/01/the-best-book-on-general-econo/); Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: In the autumn of 1973 the pump price of American gasoline was held down by federal ceilings while queues at filling stations ran for hours. Oregon's Governor Tom McCall had no power to move the price, so he changed the rule about who could fill up -- the first state scheme of its kind, and other states soon copied it. What was Oregon's rule?
answer: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
choices: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
Every registered household received a coupon book good for a fixed number of gallons
The first two hours of every morning were reserved for commercial and farm vehicles
Each station auctioned off its remaining supply to the highest bidders at opening time
context: Oregon adopted odd-even rationing in the autumn of 1973, Governor Tom McCall urging stations to sell by the last digit of the plate. It is the clean illustration of Sowell's point: stop the price from rationing scarce gasoline and something else must ration it -- a queue, a coupon, a calendar. Source: Grokipedia, 'Odd-even rationing' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Odd-even_rationing) and '1970s energy crisis'.

question: The Law and Economics Center gave its 1980 prize to Knowledge and Decisions, calling the book a landmark work. The citation did not praise it in general terms; it named one specific thing the book had helped its readers understand. What did the committee name?
answer: The differences between the market process and the process of government
choices: The differences between the market process and the process of government
The reasons wage and price controls had failed in every decade since 1940
The drift of American courts away from the intentions of the Constitution's framers
The gap between what academic economists publish and what voters actually believe
context: The Law and Economics Center called Knowledge and Decisions a landmark work, chosen 'because of its cogent contribution to our understanding of the differences between the market process and the process of government.' Sources: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions); ContemporaryThinkers.org, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Through the winter of 1973-74 American drivers queued for hours at filling stations, and much of the coverage treated those queues as proof that the oil had simply run out. National inventories in fact remained adequate. Washington had capped the price of domestic oil and refined products. On Sowell's account, what did that cap do?
answer: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
choices: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
Moved the shortage from the pump back to the refinery, where it could be managed out of public sight
Raised the cost of hoarding so sharply that drivers ran their tanks down to fumes before refilling
Concentrated the loss on the oil companies while spreading the gain thinly across every single driver
context: The 1973 Arab embargo was a real supply shock -- crude went from about $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Sowell's argument is not that the controls caused the shortage but that they made it far worse: with the price frozen, refiners had little reason to produce more, drivers little reason to buy less, and hoarding paid. Source: Grokipedia, '1970s energy crisis' (https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s_energy_crisis) and 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Sowell opens Knowledge and Decisions not with a complaint about any single policy but with a structural worry about modern societies -- one he says threatens economic efficiency, political effectiveness and personal freedom all at once, as concrete understanding gets displaced by abstract assumptions about how society ought to work. What widening gap does he describe?
answer: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
choices: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
Between what a government promises at election time and what it can actually afford to pay for later
Between the wealth held by a country's oldest households and the wealth held by its youngest ones
Between the speed at which a society's technology changes and the speed at which its laws get rewritten
context: Sowell's framing worry is a widening gap between firsthand knowledge and decision-making authority: the further a decision travels from the person who knows the particulars, the more it must run on somebody's general theory instead. Source: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: A student sums up Knowledge and Decisions as 'markets good, government bad.' Sowell's actual structure is different: he takes markets with their prices and profits, elected legislatures with their votes and lobbying, and courts with their rules of evidence, and runs every one of them through the same single test. What is that test?
answer: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
choices: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
Whether the people who designed the process meant well by those it would govern
How thinly the process spreads its costs and how narrowly it piles up its benefits
Which rival process would otherwise do the same job, and how badly it would do it
context: This is why the book is not a market-versus-state pamphlet: Sowell asks the identical question of every institution, markets included, and the answers come out different by institution rather than by team. The other three choices are real analytic moves too -- Sowell's own 'compared to what?', Mancur Olson's dispersed costs and concentrated benefits, and Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: An admissions office admits a student under a racial preference into a programme where nearly every classmate has arrived with far stronger preparation. Thomas Sowell argued from the 1970s onward that placements like this systematically fail the very students they were meant to help, and he is explicit that his complaint is not about those students' ability. What does he say the admissions process never actually finds out?
answer: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
choices: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
Whether this particular student's own high school was underfunded next to its neighbours
Whether the programme's faculty would end up marking this student harder than the others
How many students from the same background that programme had already admitted before
context: Sowell calls this mismatch. It grew out of what he saw teaching at Cornell in the late 1960s, where students admitted under preferences were disproportionately on academic probation -- not, he argued, because they could not do college work, but because the fit was wrong. He made the case at book length in Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study (Yale University Press, 2004). Note carefully what the argument is and is not: it is a claim about what admissions data can and cannot tell you, not a claim about who deserves a place. Sources: H-Net Reviews, DasGupta on Sowell, 'Affirmative Action Around the World'; Claremont Review of Books, Sowell, 'The Perversity of Diversity'.

question: In 1997 the economist Thomas Sowell -- better known for 'Basic Economics' and 'A Conflict of Visions' -- published a book on a subject far outside economics: bright toddlers who begin speaking much later than typical peers but develop normally or exceptionally afterward. What was the book called?
context: Basic Books published it. Sowell followed it in 2001 with 'The Einstein Syndrome: Bright Children Who Talk Late.' The subject was well outside his usual economics beat and became his most personal work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: The personal event that drove Thomas Sowell to spend years researching bright children who talk late was one specific family experience. What was it?
answer: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
choices: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
Sowell's own younger brother had been misdiagnosed as deaf
Sowell had witnessed a neighbor's child undergo similar mislabeling
Sowell had been asked to consult by a Stanford developmental clinic
context: When John was young, doctors and specialists variously diagnosed him as autistic, mentally retarded, or hearing-impaired -- all of which turned out to be wrong. John talked late and grew into a highly intelligent adult with a technical career. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Thomas Sowell coined a name for the recurring cluster of characteristics he found in his research -- late talking, unusually strong analytic ability once speech developed, musicality, engineering or mathematical relatives -- naming it for a famously late-talking physicist. What did he call it?
context: Albert Einstein was reported to have been a late talker (his family said he did not speak in sentences until about age 3). The 2001 book carried the name in its title: 'The Einstein Syndrome: Bright Children Who Talk Late.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Thomas Sowell argued that the diagnostic institutions treating late-talking children -- pediatricians, speech pathologists, special-education programs -- had a specific structural incentive that biased the diagnostic process. What did he identify?
answer: Institutions had incentives to categorize children into named conditions with named interventions and named funding
choices: Institutions had incentives to categorize children into named conditions with named interventions and named funding
Institutions had a legal obligation to diagnose all children with a specific developmental syndrome
Institutions had a financial incentive to refuse to diagnose any child under age 5
Institutions had no diagnostic incentive of any kind
context: Sowell's argument is a Hayekian knowledge-problem move applied to a medical-institutional case. No single specialist could see the pattern because it crossed specialties, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded diagnosis-and-treatment over watchful waiting. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: A Vanderbilt speech-pathologist independently studied the same population as Thomas Sowell and later wrote his own 2014 book on late-talking children (published by Broadway). Who was he?
context: Camarata's academic research provided a scholarly counterpart to Sowell's more accessible books. His own 'Late-Talking Children' (Broadway, 2014) drew on his Vanderbilt clinical practice. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Sowell's late-talking-children books represent a specific kind of methodological demonstration -- his analytic style applied to a subject far outside economics. What is the underlying reasoning move that carries across?
answer: The knowledge-problem move: no single specialist could see the cross-specialty pattern, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over waiting
choices: The knowledge-problem move: no single specialist could see the cross-specialty pattern, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over waiting
The revealed-preference move: parents' choice of schools reveals their true valuation of education
The comparative-advantage move: economies specialize according to relative production costs
The efficient-markets move: all public information is instantly priced in
context: The same Hayekian analytical style Sowell applies to economic-policy questions carries over to a medical-institutional question. The books are often the first Sowell book recommended to non-economists because they show his method on a subject no one has a political axe about. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: In his seventies at Freiburg, Friedrich Hayek published a three-volume treatise over the 1970s -- Volume 1 in 1973, Volume 2 in 1976, Volume 3 in 1979 -- offering his mature statement on rules, freedom, and the limits of legislation. What is the overall title of the trilogy?
context: Law, Legislation and Liberty, Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1973 / 1976 / 1979. The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is a distinct earlier single-volume work; The Road to Serfdom (1944) is the wartime polemic; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected essays. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: Hayek borrows two Greek words to name a distinction he uses throughout the trilogy: TAXIS for a deliberately arranged order (a garden laid out by a gardener) and KOSMOS for what kind of order?
answer: A grown order, ordered but not designed
choices: A grown order, ordered but not designed
A hierarchical order commanded from the top
A legally codified order backed by force
context: Kosmos (grown) versus taxis (made) is Hayek's central pair -- a forest is a kosmos, a garden is a taxis. Hierarchical command is a species of taxis; randomness is Hayek's opposite of both; legal codification is legislative taxis. Source: Knowledge Problem blog, 'Hayek on Order: Cosmos and Taxis'.

question: Hayek reserves a specific term for kosmos-in-society -- for the kinds of orders that emerge from countless individual actions without anyone intending or designing the pattern that results. Which two-word phrase names such orders?
context: Hayek's canonical Kosmos examples of spontaneous order: language, the common law, market prices, and cultural norms. Central planning is the opposite; constructivist rationalism is the intellectual error Hayek attacks; positive liberty is Isaiah Berlin's concept, not Hayek's. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: Volume 1 of the trilogy (Rules and Order, 1973) applies the kosmos-versus-taxis distinction to the legal system, contrasting THESIS -- deliberately drafted statutory legislation -- with a rival tradition Hayek treats as a kosmos: a legal order that grows precedent by precedent without any single author. Which legal tradition is Hayek's paradigm case of the GROWN kind of law?
context: Common law grows precedent by precedent through judicial decision, without any single legislator; continental codes (Napoleonic Code 1804 and its successors) are deliberate taxis; Roman edicts and sharia have their own histories but are not Hayek's paradigm of a Kosmos-legal-order. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: In Volume 2 (The Mirage of Social Justice, 1976) Hayek argues that a widely used phrase applied to the market's outcomes is not just wrong but a CATEGORY MISTAKE -- because a Kosmos has no author to be praised or blamed. Which phrase does Hayek target as a category mistake?
context: Hayek's argument: justice is a property of intentional individual conduct; the distribution that emerges from millions of separate voluntary acts is un-designed, so calling it 'just' or 'unjust' misapplies the concept. Economic freedom, political liberty, and public reason are terms Hayek uses positively or neutrally. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Volume 2.

question: Hayek illustrates his 'category mistake' argument with a homely analogy: an unwelcome natural event that spoils an ordinary human plan cannot be called MORALLY unjust, however bad the outcome, because there is no agent to have chosen it. Which everyday scene does Hayek use to make the point?
choices: A wolf carrying off a lamb
A river flooding a farmer's field
A rockfall blocking a mountain path
context: Hayek's picnic-and-rainstorm illustration: no one designed the weather to spoil your afternoon, so calling it 'unjust' misuses the concept of justice; his claim is that market outcomes are analogous. The wolf-and-lamb is Aesop and La Fontaine; river and traveler examples belong to other authors. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Volume 2.

question: Hayek's language of 'the result of human action but not of human design' -- the tag line of the whole spontaneous-order tradition -- comes directly from a Scottish Enlightenment writer whose 1767 Essay on the History of Civil Society Hayek quotes at length. Which eighteenth-century Scot coined the phrase?
context: The exact phrase comes from Part III of Ferguson's 1767 Essay: nations 'stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design.' Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776); Hume died 1776; Hutcheson was Smith's teacher but did not coin this phrase. Source: Online Library of Liberty, Adam Ferguson quote page.

question: Volume 3 (The Political Order of a Free People, 1979) is Hayek's most explicitly institutional volume: it proposes a constitutional reform intended to slow the drift toward unlimited majoritarianism that Hayek believed was making the rule of law impossible in modern welfare states. What structural reform does Volume 3 propose?
answer: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
choices: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
A single-chamber assembly directly elected by universal proportional franchise
The abolition of parliament in favor of binding national referenda on major questions
The devolution of central authority to autonomous chartered city-states of Swiss size
context: Hayek's design: a rule-making chamber elected on a long, lifetime-scale franchise to insulate it from short-term political pressures, and a separate government-making chamber on ordinary franchises -- an explicit bicameral proposal to protect the rule of law from majoritarian drift. Source: University of Chicago Law Review, review of Volume 3.

question: Late in the trilogy Hayek names what he considered the fundamental intellectual error of the twentieth century: the belief that a Kosmos -- an order that GREW -- can be treated as a Taxis, redesigned like a machine by planners. Which name does Hayek give to that error?
context: Constructivist (or naive) rationalism is Hayek's label for the mistake of thinking that reason can design social institutions from scratch, as against evolutionary rationalism which recognizes tested-through-time rules. Methodological individualism is a separate Austrian commitment; analytic positivism belongs to the Vienna Circle Hayek argued against. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: When Hayek published Volume 2 of the trilogy in 1976, the mainstream Anglophone philosophical work that had made 'social justice' the field's central concept had appeared just five years earlier at Harvard. Which 1971 book was Volume 2 written partly to answer?
answer: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
choices: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
Anarchy, State, and Utopia by Robert Nozick
The Open Society and Its Enemies by Karl Popper
The Concept of Law by H. L. A. Hart
context: Rawls's A Theory of Justice (Harvard, 1971) put social justice at the center of Anglophone political philosophy; Hayek's 1976 argument is the counter-tradition's reply. Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) was itself a reply to Rawls; Popper (1945) and Hart (1961) are earlier works Hayek shared intellectual ground with. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: Hayek's spontaneous-order argument stands in a lineage that runs through the eighteenth-century Scots, through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees, and forward into the twentieth century to a Hungarian-British chemist-turned-philosopher who argued that much of what we know cannot be spoken. Which twentieth-century thinker's concept of TACIT KNOWLEDGE parallels Hayek's argument that dispersed knowledge is irreducibly distributed?
context: Michael Polanyi (1891-1976), in Personal Knowledge (1958) and The Tacit Dimension (1966), argued that we know more than we can tell -- a claim Hayek treated as complementary to his own case that dispersed knowledge cannot be aggregated by a central planner. Popper, Berlin, and Russell were contemporaries in Hayek's circle but on other questions. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty; standard secondary literature on Hayek and Polanyi.

question: On September 15 2008 the fourth-largest US investment bank, founded in 1850 and holding $639 billion in assets, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy -- the largest bankruptcy in American history. Which firm filed?
context: Lehman Brothers filed at 1:45 AM on September 15 2008 with $639 billion in assets, primarily mortgage-backed securities and commercial real estate. The S&P 500 fell 4.7% that day. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: The CEO of Lehman Brothers for the 14 years leading up to its collapse was known on Wall Street for aggressive expansion. He was reportedly worth about $500 million when the firm collapsed and lost most of it in the wipeout. Who was he?
context: Fuld led Lehman from 1994 through the 2008 collapse. His stock holdings represented most of his personal wealth. When Lehman shares went to zero, roughly $450 million of his paper wealth was destroyed. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Fuld' (2026-09-05).

question: Through the summer of 2008, Lehman attempted to sell itself to two specific rescuers. Both talks failed. Which pair of potential buyers walked away?
answer: Korea Development Bank in July and Bank of America in early September
choices: Korea Development Bank in July and Bank of America in early September
Wells Fargo in July and Deutsche Bank in September
HSBC in June and Barclays in August
Citigroup in July and Nomura in September
context: Korea Development Bank walked away in July over price. Bank of America talks collapsed in early September when a better opportunity to buy Merrill Lynch presented itself. Both losses left Lehman without an exit. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Over the weekend of September 13-14 2008, the Treasury Secretary and the Fed Chair gathered the heads of every major Wall Street bank at the New York Fed to arrange a private rescue. Who were the two officials leading that weekend?
context: Paulson (former Goldman Sachs CEO, now Treasury Secretary) and Bernanke (Fed chair) worked with New York Fed president Tim Geithner over that weekend. The private-rescue attempt failed when the strongest candidate buyer walked away. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Unlike the March 2008 Bear Stearns rescue, Paulson and Bernanke announced over the September 13-14 weekend that they would NOT use taxpayer money to guarantee Lehman's assets for a buyer. Which named bank then backed away from the deal?
context: Barclays was the last serious buyer standing. British regulators refused to bless the deal without a US backstop, and Paulson would not provide one. Barclays walked away on Sunday, September 14. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: The day after Lehman filed, a money-market mutual fund with heavy Lehman commercial paper exposure had to write down its net asset value below the traditional par of $1.00 -- an event known on Wall Street as 'breaking the buck.' Which fund did it?
choices: The Vanguard Prime Money Market Fund
The Dreyfus Basic Money Market Fund
context: The Reserve Primary Fund held over $700 million in Lehman commercial paper. It broke the buck on September 16 2008, triggering a broad run on money-market funds and forcing the Treasury to guarantee the whole sector. Source: Grokipedia 'Reserve Primary Fund' (2026-09-05).

question: Both Paulson's and Bernanke's memoirs argued that the Fed had a specific legal reason for not lending to Lehman. What did they claim as their legal constraint?
answer: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
choices: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
The Fed was prohibited by the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act
The Fed needed prior congressional approval for the specific loan
The Fed's charter forbade any loan to an investment bank
context: Paulson and Bernanke both maintained that Lehman lacked the good collateral required under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act. Whether this claim was accurate has been sharply disputed by later historians. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: In a 2018 book, an economist at Johns Hopkins made a detailed case that the Fed HAD legal authority to lend to Lehman and simply chose not to use it -- directly contradicting the official memoirs. Which economist wrote the book?
context: Larry Ball's The Fed and Lehman Brothers (Cambridge, 2018) built on years of archival research to argue that the collateral was adequate and the Fed's refusal was a political choice, not a legal necessity. Source: Grokipedia 'Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: The Lehman decision is the most debated single Fed action of the modern era. Austrian critics argue the failure proved a specific point about the March 2008 Bear rescue and the moral-hazard structure it created. Which point do they press?
answer: Markets had priced in a rescue based on Bear; the sudden removal of that expectation caused the panic that followed
choices: Markets had priced in a rescue based on Bear; the sudden removal of that expectation caused the panic that followed
The Fed's refusal to lend was economically correct and stabilized markets
Lehman's collapse was unrelated to the earlier Bear precedent
Only fiscal policy could have prevented the September 2008 panic
context: The March Bear rescue trained counterparties to expect similar treatment for Lehman. When the trained expectation was violated overnight, the panic that swept the system was exactly the outcome the earlier rescue had trained people not to expect. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012).

question: The Lehman decision teaches a specific recognition move about discretionary central-bank interventions and the crises that follow them. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: Discretionary rescues alter market expectations, and the alteration itself becomes a source of future instability
choices: Discretionary rescues alter market expectations, and the alteration itself becomes a source of future instability
Discretionary rescues always stabilize markets in the long run
Discretionary rescues are neutral because markets absorb them quickly
Discretionary rescues are effective only when applied uniformly to every failing firm
context: The Bear-then-Lehman sequence shows the trap: rescue creates expectation, non-rescue violates expectation, both generate systemic effects. Discretionary policy is not a neutral fallback -- each intervention rewrites the script for the next crisis. Source: Selgin, Money: Free and Unfree (2017).

question: Bitcoin's main chain adds one block every ten minutes and each block holds only a few thousand transactions -- fine for large transfers but slow and costly for small everyday purchases. A second-layer system was designed to handle those small payments off the base layer. What is it called?
context: Lightning is a layer built on top of Bitcoin, not a separate cryptocurrency. Base-layer Bitcoin remains the settlement rail; Lightning handles the fast, cheap, off-chain payments. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Two Bitcoin developers published the original Lightning Network white paper in January 2016, titled 'The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments.' Who were they?
context: The paper proposed payment channels secured by Bitcoin smart contracts. The mainnet went live in March 2018 with implementations from Lightning Labs (LND), Blockstream (c-lightning), and ACINQ (Eclair). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Two parties who want to transact repeatedly on the Lightning Network first perform a specific setup step on the Bitcoin base chain, then send payments back and forth off-chain many times, and only settle the net balance on-chain when they finish. What is the setup step called?
answer: Opening a payment channel with a funding transaction
choices: Opening a payment channel with a funding transaction
context: The funding transaction commits Bitcoin to a two-party multisignature address. Off-chain updates rebalance the split without touching the chain. When the channel closes, only the final balance is settled on-chain. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: On the Lightning Network, if Alice has a channel with Bob and Bob has a channel with Carol, Alice can pay Carol without ever opening a direct channel to Carol. What compensates Bob for passing the payment along?
answer: A small routing fee, paid by the sender to each intermediary along the path
choices: A small routing fee, paid by the sender to each intermediary along the path
A block reward paid out of Bitcoin's monetary base
A transaction subsidy from the Lightning Labs company
An interest charge added to Carol's balance at settlement
context: Routing fees are voluntary market prices set by each node. The network structure depends on nodes with well-funded channels making themselves available for routing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: On September 7, 2021, one country made Bitcoin legal tender alongside the US dollar and launched a government-issued wallet that used Lightning to enable small everyday purchases (like a pupusa) at almost no fee. Which country?
context: The wallet was called Chivo. Same-day the government issued each adult citizen a $30 Bitcoin allocation to encourage adoption. The rollout had bugs but demonstrated Lightning at national retail scale for the first time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: An American Bitcoin developer founded Strike (formerly Zap), a Lightning-based payments app that helped drive Lightning adoption in El Salvador and was a visible advocate during the 2021 legal-tender rollout. Who was he?
context: Mallers appeared alongside President Nayib Bukele at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference where the legal-tender law was announced. Strike allowed US-El Salvador remittances via Lightning at negligible cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Mallers.

question: A high-school student in 2025 buys a $2 coffee in San Salvador using a Bitcoin app on her phone; the transaction settles in under a second for a fraction of a cent. A Hayekian economist notes that the Lightning Network solves a specific problem that a central authority could not have solved by fiat. Which problem?
answer: How to preserve auditable Bitcoin settlement while enabling coffee-sized payments no central rate-setter could price
choices: How to preserve auditable Bitcoin settlement while enabling coffee-sized payments no central rate-setter could price
How to eliminate all fees on international wire transfers by legislative decree
How to guarantee a fixed exchange rate between Bitcoin and the US dollar
How to compel merchants worldwide to accept a single national currency
context: Lightning fees are set by node operators competing for routing volume, not by any central body. Bitcoin's settlement layer stays fully auditable. The design is analogous to how the internet has TCP/IP at the base and higher-level protocols on top. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: In 1994 a Greenwich, Connecticut hedge fund was founded by John Meriwether (former head of Salomon Brothers bond arbitrage) and staffed with prominent traders and academics including two Nobel laureates. What was the fund called?
context: LTCM's founder team included Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who had won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on options pricing (the Black-Scholes model). Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: LTCM used sophisticated mathematical models to identify small pricing anomalies in fixed-income securities. To make small anomalies profitable, they used a specific tool at extreme scale. At peak, roughly what was their leverage ratio (positions to capital)?
context: LTCM held roughly $125 billion in positions against only $4.7 billion in capital -- a leverage ratio of about 27 to 1 (and much higher when derivative exposures were counted). For four years (1994-97) the strategy produced spectacular returns of 40%+ annually. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: LTCM's strategy of arbitraging tiny pricing gaps between related securities blew up in August 1998 when a specific foreign country's default triggered a global 'flight to quality' that made all their convergence trades diverge instead. Which country defaulted?
context: The Russian government defaulted on August 17 1998, devaluing the ruble and defaulting on domestic debt. The resulting flight to quality made LTCM's leveraged spread bets go against them across every desk. Source: Grokipedia '1998 Russian financial crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: On September 23 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York convened the CEOs of 14 major banks in a conference room and coordinated a specific dollar-amount rescue -- entirely privately-funded. What was the rescue size?
context: The $3.6 billion September 23 1998 rescue was entirely privately funded. Each of the 14 banks contributed and took a stake in the fund's positions, unwinding them slowly over months. No federal money was used, but the Fed's coordination power was central. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York president who oversaw the September 1998 rescue coordination was a specific figure. Who was he?
context: William McDonough led the New York Fed 1993-2003. Peter Fisher ran the actual operation of coordinating the private banks. The rescue was a formative moment in Fed practice of coordinating rescues without directly using federal funds. Source: Grokipedia 'William McDonough' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed's justification for coordinating a rescue of a purely private hedge fund with no depositors and no explicit regulatory oversight was a specific risk-management argument. What did the Fed cite?
answer: LTCM's counterparty banks were so exposed that a disorderly unwind could cascade into the banking system
choices: LTCM's counterparty banks were so exposed that a disorderly unwind could cascade into the banking system
LTCM held over $10 billion in FDIC-insured deposits
LTCM's Nobel-laureate advisors deserved public defense
LTCM's collapse would trigger a Russian government invasion of Ukraine
context: The 1998 justification: LTCM's counterparties (the 14 banks that would organize the rescue) were also its potential victims. A disorderly unwind of $125 billion in leveraged positions could damage them enough to trigger a broader crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: The LTCM rescue extended a specific existing regulatory doctrine beyond regulated banks. Which category of institution now became implicitly protected by the Fed's coordination power?
answer: Hedge funds -- purely private investment vehicles with no depositors and no explicit regulatory oversight
choices: Hedge funds -- purely private investment vehicles with no depositors and no explicit regulatory oversight
context: The LTCM precedent extended too-big-to-fail protection beyond commercial and investment banks to any purely private vehicle sufficiently interconnected with the banking system. The 2008 AIG rescue and 2008 money-market fund guarantees extended the pattern further. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: Three weeks before the September 23 1998 Fed-coordinated rescue, a specific well-known investor had offered $250 million for LTCM's positions, but the negotiations broke down. Which investor made that offer?
context: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, together with AIG and Goldman Sachs, offered $250 million for LTCM's positions in early September 1998. The offer would have wiped out the LTCM partners entirely. Negotiations broke down; the Fed rescue came days later. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: One striking coincidence of the LTCM affair is that its two Nobel-laureate advisors had won their Nobel Prize only one year before the fund's near-collapse. In which year did Myron Scholes and Robert Merton win the Nobel?
context: Scholes and Merton won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for the Black-Scholes options-pricing model. Less than a year later, the fund they advised was near-insolvent. It is one of the most-cited coincidences in modern finance. Source: Grokipedia 'Myron Scholes' (2026-09-05).

question: The LTCM rescue teaches a specific recognition move about how too-big-to-fail protection spreads across institutional categories over time. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: Any sufficiently interconnected financial entity will eventually be rescued; the moral-hazard incentive spreads beyond banks to hedge funds, insurance companies, and money-market funds
choices: Any sufficiently interconnected financial entity will eventually be rescued; the moral-hazard incentive spreads beyond banks to hedge funds, insurance companies, and money-market funds
Too-big-to-fail applies only to FDIC-insured commercial banks
The Fed can protect the financial system while preventing all future risk-taking
Purely private investment vehicles are never protected by federal regulators
context: The LTCM pattern extended through AIG (2008), the Reserve Primary Fund (2008), and eventually to any entity whose failure would cascade into the banking system. The Continental Illinois principle grew steadily across categories over four decades. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: A German-born Austrian-tradition economist held a chair in Johannesburg from 1948 and became famous for pressing subjectivism further than either Mises or Hayek. Who was he?
context: Ludwig Lachmann (1906-1990) taught at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg from 1948 and became the leading voice of what is now called radical-subjectivist Austrian economics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Lachmann's 1956 book, published by Bell and Sons in London, treated a specific category of goods as fundamentally heterogeneous rather than as a single aggregate. What was the book's short title?
choices: The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Capital and Its Structure (Bell, London, 1956) argued that a lathe is not a truck is not a factory building, and that aggregating them into a single 'K' hides the actual complementarities the cycle disrupts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Lachmann's argument about capital cuts directly against a specific mainstream macro assumption. Which assumption did he attack?
answer: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
choices: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
That capital is always privately owned
That capital depreciates at a constant rate
That capital is measured in labor-hours
context: The heterogeneous-capital claim: because specific goods have specific complementarities, adding them into aggregate K erases the very structure that matters to production and to booms and busts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Lachmann's more radical claim was about how entrepreneurs face the future. Which position did he defend against the rational-expectations movement of the 1970s?
answer: The future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs form different expectations
choices: The future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs form different expectations
The future is a well-defined probability distribution known to all entrepreneurs
The future is known perfectly through central-planner announcements
The future is irrelevant because entrepreneurs only respond to present prices
context: Lachmann invoked Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between measurable risk and genuine uncertainty; there is no such thing as 'the' rational expectation of a market participant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Lachmann's most-cited essay in the Journal of Economic Literature (1976) declared that the tradition should align with a British Post-Keynesian economist's picture of radical uncertainty. Whose picture did Lachmann want to align with?
context: 'From Mises to Shackle: An Essay on Austrian Economics and the Kaleidic Society' (JEL, 1976) argued the tradition should follow Shackle's radical-uncertainty picture rather than any equilibration story. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: Lachmann's 1976 essay coined a picture of markets as constantly shifting patterns, borrowing a term from Shackle. Which two-word phrase became the label for Lachmann's position?
context: 'Kaleidic' -- from kaleidoscope -- captures Lachmann's picture of markets in constant pattern-shifting flux, as opposed to any tendency toward stable equilibrium. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: From 1975 Lachmann split time between Johannesburg and a specific American university where the modern Austrian revival was centered under Mises's disciple Israel Kirzner. Which American university?
context: The NYU Austrian program under Kirzner and Rothbard was the principal American training ground for the modern tradition; Lachmann's visiting stint made him one of its senior figures. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Lachmann's second major book (1971) applied Austrian ideas to the sociology of a specific German thinker known for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. Whose sociology did Lachmann engage?
context: The Legacy of Max Weber (1971) applied Austrian ideas about individual choice under uncertainty to Weberian action-theory sociology. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: A Viennese economist arrives in New York in August 1940 after a train ride across occupied France and a ship from Lisbon. Ninety-two years old at his death in 1973, he will spend twenty-four years running an unpaid seminar at NYU because the postwar economics profession, swinging Keynesian, will not give him a paid chair. Who was he?
context: Mises (1881-1973) fled Vienna via Geneva in 1934 and Europe in 1940. Hayek left Vienna for London in 1931, not New York; Schumpeter had moved to Harvard in 1932 with a full professorship; Machlup emigrated in 1933 and held paid chairs at Buffalo, Johns Hopkins, and Princeton. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises was born on September 29, 1881 in a Habsburg provincial capital -- a city that changed hands and names many times in the twentieth century. Which modern country's second-largest city now stands where Mises was born?
context: Mises was born in Lemberg, then the capital of Austrian Galicia -- today Lviv, western Ukraine's largest city. The city was Polish (Lwow) between the wars, Soviet after 1945, and Ukrainian since 1991. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Mises studied at the University of Vienna and earned his doctorate there in 1906. The two teachers who shaped him were the founder of the Austrian School and the tradition's greatest capital theorist. Which pair taught the young Mises?
answer: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
context: Menger (1840-1921) had founded the school with his 1871 Principles of Economics; Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) developed the theory of capital and interest and demolished the Marxian labor theory of value. Marx and Engels were Vienna's ideological opponents, not teachers; the other two pairs were English and Franco-Italian schools respectively. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: From roughly 1909 onward Mises's day job was chief economist for a large Vienna institution -- NOT the university, which gave him only an unpaid Privatdozent title. Which body actually employed him and paid his salary for a quarter century?
context: The Kammer fuer Handel, Gewerbe und Industrie (Chamber of Commerce, Trade and Industry) paid Mises to draft economic policy briefs on tariffs, labor law, and monetary reform. He held his unpaid University of Vienna Privatdozent title from 1913 to 1938 in parallel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Between 1920 and 1934 Mises hosted a fortnightly invitation-only Vienna gathering that ran from 7:30pm in his Chamber of Commerce office to an after-dinner coffee at Cafe Kuenstler at 1am. One young attendee would go on to share the 1974 Nobel Prize in Economics. Which attendee?
context: Hayek (1899-1992) attended the Vienna seminar throughout the 1920s and shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal. Schumpeter (1883-1950) belonged to an older Vienna cohort and never received a Nobel (he died 19 years before the prize was created). Machlup and Morgenstern also attended the seminar but neither won a Nobel; Morgenstern is better remembered for co-authoring the 1944 Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with von Neumann. Source: mises.at/en/denker/ludwig-von-mises.

question: In 1934, seeing the Vienna atmosphere darken, Mises left Austria for a research-and-teaching post at a Swiss postgraduate institute. Which Swiss city hosted the Graduate Institute of International Studies that gave Mises his 1934-1940 chair?
context: The Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales (IUHEI) in Geneva was one of the few European institutions still hiring Vienna-Jewish scholars in the mid-1930s. Zurich, Bern, and Basel all had universities but not the IUHEI. Mises left Geneva in 1940 when the fall of France made continental Europe untenable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Mises married for the first time on July 6, 1938, at the age of 56 -- just months after the Anschluss. His bride was a widow he had known in Vienna since 1925: a former Hamburg stage actress who would outlive him by twenty years and, at 103, would still be a trustee of the institute bearing his name. What was her name?
context: Margit Sereny (1890-1993) had been a Hamburg actress before her first marriage; she met Ludwig in Vienna in 1925 and married him in 1938 as Nazi pressure closed in. She wrote the 1976 memoir 'My Years With Ludwig von Mises' (Arlington House) and helped Lew Rockwell found the Mises Institute in 1982. The other three names are inventions. Source: mises.org/library/book/my-years-ludwig-von-mises.

question: In 1927 Mises founded a Vienna research body -- with Rockefeller Foundation funding -- devoted to a single technical question that would preoccupy Austrian economists for the next decade: why capitalist economies swing between boom and bust. Which institute did Mises establish in 1927?
answer: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
choices: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
The Vienna School of Political Economy
context: The Oesterreichisches Institut fuer Konjunkturforschung was directed by Mises's young protege Friedrich Hayek from its founding; Hayek's monthly reports on the American boom made his name in Britain and led to Lionel Robbins's 1931 invitation to the LSE. The other three are inventions or unrelated institutions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Nine years after Mises's 1973 death, an American classical-liberal organizer founded a research institute bearing Mises's name -- with the blessing of Margit von Mises, Murray Rothbard, Henry Hazlitt, and Ron Paul -- and located it at a small Southern university town. Which town in Alabama has been the Ludwig von Mises Institute's home since October 1982?
context: Llewellyn H. Rockwell Jr. founded the Mises Institute in October 1982 and placed it in Auburn, home of Auburn University, whose economics department at the time had several Austrian-friendly faculty. Tuscaloosa is Alabama's other main university town; Birmingham is the largest city; Montgomery is the state capital. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/story-mises-institute.

question: Mises rejected the label 'economist' as too narrow for his method. He held that economics was only one branch of a wider deductive science of purposeful human action, and he preferred to describe himself using its Greek-derived name. Which self-description did Mises prefer?
context: Praxeology (from Greek praxis, action) was Mises's own coinage for the general science of purposive action; economics is the best-developed branch of it. Monetarism was Milton Friedman's Chicago-school program; microeconomist and econometrician are 20th-century academic labels Mises specifically resisted. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: Murray Rothbard, then 36 years old and the leading American disciple of Ludwig von Mises, publishes a two-volume, thousand-page systematic treatise of Austrian economics in 1962. What is the book called?
context: Published 1962 by D. Van Nostrand of Princeton, New Jersey, in two volumes running 987 pages. Human Action (1949) is Mises's own treatise; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) is Hayek; Principles of Economics (1871) is Menger. Source: Wikipedia, Man, Economy, and State.

question: Rothbard's 1962 treatise Man, Economy, and State was originally commissioned as a textbook version of an earlier 1949 Austrian magnum opus. Whose earlier book was Rothbard asked to render into textbook form?
choices: Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest
context: The William Volker Fund gave Rothbard the assignment in the mid-1950s. Under his hand the textbook grew into a full original treatise. Road to Serfdom (1944) is a political tract, not a treatise; Menger 1871 and Bohm-Bawerk 1884-89 predate the assignment. Source: FEE, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State at 50'.

question: The donor network that paid for Rothbard to write Man, Economy, and State had also underwritten Mises's private NYU seminar and other classical-liberal scholarship after 1947 under director Harold Luhnow. Which fund was it?
context: The Kansas-City-based Volker Fund, run by Luhnow after 1947, was the single largest financier of American classical-liberal scholarship in the postwar decades. The three larger foundations funded almost exclusively mainstream progressive research. Source: Gary North, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State: A Memoir', Mises Institute.

question: Rothbard opens Man, Economy, and State with a chapter titled 'The Fundamentals of Human Action', from which every later theorem in the book is logically derived. Which starting move does that chapter make?
answer: It takes as its axiom that human beings act -- consciously choosing means to reach chosen ends -- and deduces economic law from there
choices: It takes as its axiom that human beings act -- consciously choosing means to reach chosen ends -- and deduces economic law from there
It gathers price-and-quantity time series and infers regularities by statistical induction
It postulates a representative agent maximizing utility subject to a budget constraint
It begins with the equilibrium condition that aggregate supply equals aggregate demand
context: This is the Misesian method Rothbard calls praxeology: the science of human action, developed by deduction, not by econometric induction. The other three describe mainstream methodological rivals -- positivism, neoclassical utility maximization, and Keynesian aggregate equilibrium. Source: FEE, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State at 50'.

question: As Rothbard finished the manuscript of Man, Economy, and State, the publisher D. Van Nostrand made a decision that materially changed what appeared in the 1962 first edition. What did the publisher require?
answer: That the final eight chapters -- the systematic analysis of government intervention -- be cut before printing, as too politically radical
choices: That the final eight chapters -- the systematic analysis of government intervention -- be cut before printing, as too politically radical
That the entire manuscript be rewritten in the third person to sound less polemical
That the footnotes citing Ludwig von Mises be removed to avoid appearing derivative
That the two-volume format be compressed into a single introductory paperback
context: The cut section became a separate book eight years later. The 1962 first edition ran to 987 pages across two volumes even after the excision; the restored full text runs 1,506 pages. Source: Wikipedia, Man, Economy, and State.

question: The chapters cut from Rothbard's 1962 treatise were published as a stand-alone book in 1970, brought out by F.A. Harper's Institute for Humane Studies under a title that named its subject directly. What was the 1970 book called?
answer: Power and Market: Government and the Economy
choices: Power and Market: Government and the Economy
context: Rothbard's other books listed here are all real: America's Great Depression (1963), For a New Liberty (1973), The Ethics of Liberty (1982). Only Power and Market is the specific rescue-in-print of the excised chapters. Source: Mises Institute library, Power and Market.

question: In Power and Market Rothbard groups every act of state intervention into three exhaustive categories by WHO is being coerced into WHAT. Which taxonomy did he propose?
context: The scheme is original to Rothbard and is the analytic backbone of Power and Market. The three-name scheme lets him treat drug bans, taxes, and rent control as three structurally different coercions rather than one blurry 'government activity'. The other groupings are real but describe different distinctions (kind of instrument, tax shape, branch of government). Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: Rothbard's category of TRIANGULAR intervention names cases where the state stands outside a proposed exchange between two private parties and forces or forbids the terms. Which policy is a textbook triangular intervention in his scheme?
answer: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
choices: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
A federal income tax withheld from a worker's paycheck
A statute making private possession of a drug a crime
A conscription order drafting a citizen into the army
context: Triangular intervention: state + two private parties whose exchange is dictated (rent controls, minimum wages, tariffs, licensing). Income tax and conscription are BINARY interventions (state extracts from the individual directly). A private-drug ban is AUTISTIC intervention (state forbids a solitary act, no exchange). Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: In 2004 the Ludwig von Mises Institute reunited Rothbard's 1962 treatise with the 1970 cut section into a single 1,500-page Scholar's Edition -- the volume Rothbard had wanted in the first place. Which longtime Rothbard student edited it?
context: Salerno, a senior Mises Institute scholar and Rothbard student, restored the original architecture: pure market theory (Man, Economy, and State) plus the intervention analysis (Power and Market) in one framework. Friedman was Chicago School (Rothbard's methodological opposite); Kirzner was a Mises-seminar contemporary; Buchanan founded public choice. Source: Mises Institute, Scholar's Edition listing.

question: 1962 shipped two rival flagship books for the market-liberal side of American economics: Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (Austrian praxeology, deduced from the action axiom) and one from a Chicago economist arguing the same politics from a positivist, empirical method. Which was the Chicago counterpart?
choices: Paul Samuelson, Economics: An Introductory Analysis
John Maynard Keynes, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
John Kenneth Galbraith, The Affluent Society
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago, 1962) and Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) reach overlapping political conclusions from opposite methodological traditions -- Chicago positivism vs Austrian praxeology. Samuelson (1948) is the flagship neo-Keynesian textbook; Keynes (1936) is what both books are arguing against; Galbraith (1958) is the progressive counterpoint. Source: Wikipedia, Capitalism and Freedom.

question: In 1965 Harvard University Press published a North Dakota farm boy's PhD dissertation, a slim book that explained why bad policies with concentrated beneficiaries so often survive. What was the author's name?
context: Mancur Olson Jr. (1932-1998) earned his PhD at Harvard and taught for most of his career at the University of Maryland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancur_Olson.

question: Mancur Olson's 1965 Harvard book carried a full title naming both its topic and its central concept. Which title did he give the book?
choices: The Rise and Decline of Nations
context: The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of Groups (Harvard University Press, 1965). Source: hup.harvard.edu (Logic of Collective Action).

question: Ten million taxpayers each stand to save $10 if a certain subsidy is defeated. On the other side, a small few each stand to gain a million dollars if it passes. Olson's Logic of Collective Action predicts a clear outcome. Which side will organize a serious lobbying campaign?
choices: A neutral consumer coalition organizes both
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern. Each farmer has $1M at stake; each taxpayer has $10. The math of individual incentives, not moral character, produces the asymmetric lobbying. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965).

question: Olson's argument turned on a specific game-theoretic problem where each individual has an incentive to let others bear the cost of producing a shared benefit. What is the name of that problem?
context: Free-riding is central to Olson's account: in large groups no individual has enough at stake to bear the cost of organizing, so each rationally hopes others will do it. The result is under-organization. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 1.

question: Olson's book was widely misread as claiming large groups NEVER organize. His actual argument identified one mechanism that lets some large groups succeed despite the free-rider problem. What did he call this mechanism?
context: Selective incentives are private benefits available only to members: union-negotiated contracts, professional certifications, discount insurance for AARP members. They give individuals a private reason to join what would otherwise be an under-organized group. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 6.

question: A classic textbook Olson example of selective incentives is a large voluntary organization whose members join partly to get discounted insurance, hotel rates, and prescriptions. Which American membership organization is the standard case?
context: AARP offers its members insurance and travel discounts as selective incentives; these private benefits sustain what would otherwise be an under-organized dispersed group of older Americans. Source: Olson, Logic (1965); Skocpol, Diminished Democracy (Oklahoma 2003).

question: Olson wrote three great books in his career. His 1965 Logic and 2000 posthumous Power and Prosperity bracket a middle work published by Yale University Press in 1982 that extended the collective-action idea to comparative national economic growth. What was the middle book called?
answer: The Rise and Decline of Nations
choices: The Rise and Decline of Nations
context: The Rise and Decline of Nations: Economic Growth, Stagflation, and Social Rigidities (Yale University Press, 1982). It applied the Logic to macro-history. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (Rise and Decline).

question: Olson's account of concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs politics offers a structural explanation for why certain policies persist even when the total social cost clearly exceeds the total social benefit. In one word, what happens to those policies over time under Olson's mechanism?
context: The beneficiaries organize to defend the policy; the victims never organize to oppose it. Farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, occupational licensing, and thousands of similar policies survive for decades despite failing cost-benefit tests. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: Olson's third and final book, published posthumously in 2000 by Basic Books, extended his political-economy framework to explain the large gaps between rich and poor nations. What was that book called?
choices: The Wealth and Poverty of Nations
context: Power and Prosperity: Outgrowing Communist and Capitalist Dictatorships (Basic Books, 2000) was completed by Olson's students after his 1998 death. It introduced his 'stationary bandit' / 'roving bandit' framework. Source: basicbooks.com (Power and Prosperity).

question: A high school student watches Congress pass a $50-per-family tariff on a foreign import while opposition to the tariff never materializes. Applying Olson's 1965 analysis, which structural feature best explains the passage?
answer: A hundred domestic producers each gain millions; a hundred million consumers each lose a little
choices: A hundred domestic producers each gain millions; a hundred million consumers each lose a little
Congress overwhelmingly cares about consumer welfare on tariffs
The domestic producers spontaneously coordinate without lobbying
The consumers spontaneously organize but are overruled by judges
context: Olson's structural mechanism: the beneficiary side has enough per-capita stake to bear the cost of organizing; the victim side does not. The rest is arithmetic. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), applied throughout Rise and Decline (1982).

question: Olson's 1965 argument overturned a widely-held assumption in mid-century political theory about large groups with shared interests. Which older assumption did his logic dispose of?
answer: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
choices: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
Small groups always fail against large coalitions
Politicians act from pure public spirit rather than self-interest
Voting systems always produce coherent group preferences
context: Pre-Olson pluralist theory (David Truman, Arthur Bentley) assumed shared interests produce organization. Olson showed the opposite: shared interest is not enough; you need selective incentives OR small numbers OR compulsion. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), preface.

question: On Tuesday March 3 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic reached the United States, the Fed made its first emergency inter-meeting rate cut since October 2008. By how much did it cut the federal funds rate in that surprise move?
context: The March 3 2020 emergency cut moved the target range from 1.50-1.75% to 1.00-1.25%. It was the first out-of-meeting emergency cut in 12 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: Twelve days after the first March 2020 emergency cut, the Fed acted again on a Sunday -- another emergency, out-of-meeting move. This time it cut the funds rate down to a specific floor and left it there for two years. What was the floor?
context: The Sunday March 15 2020 emergency action cut an additional 100 basis points to a range of 0.00-0.25%. It also announced $700 billion in initial asset purchases. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: On March 23 2020 the Fed announced asset purchases 'in the amounts needed' -- with no fixed cap. What is the informal name financial markets used for this unbounded new program?
context: The March 23 2020 announcement removed any dollar cap on Treasury and mortgage-backed-security purchases. It also launched unprecedented new lending facilities. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The March 23 2020 package included two new facilities that let the Fed buy something it had never bought before in its history. What did the PMCCF and SMCCF allow the Fed to purchase?
context: The Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility allowed the Fed to buy corporate bonds directly for the first time. Previously the Fed had bought only Treasuries and agency debt. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: On April 9 2020 the Fed expanded its corporate-bond facilities to include a specific new category of debt: bonds that had been investment-grade before the crisis but had since been downgraded to junk. What was the informal name for these bonds?
context: The April 9 2020 expansion covered 'fallen angels' -- formerly investment-grade debt now trading as high yield. The Fed had crossed the line from Treasury-and-agency-only purchases into direct corporate credit allocation, including junk. Source: Grokipedia 'Fallen angel (finance)' (2026-09-05).

question: The same April 9 2020 announcement created a Municipal Liquidity Facility to buy state and local government bonds. Combined with the corporate-bond facilities, this represented a significant expansion of Fed activity. What line did the Fed cross with the muni and corporate purchases?
answer: Direct corporate and municipal credit allocation by the central bank
choices: Direct corporate and municipal credit allocation by the central bank
Setting long-term interest rates directly by yield-curve control
Issuing central-bank digital currency to households
context: For the first time in its history the Fed was directly choosing which private and municipal borrowers received support. This is credit allocation -- traditionally a legislative function, not a central-bank function. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed's balance sheet expanded from $4.2 trillion in early March 2020 to a peak in April 2022. What was the approximate peak size?
context: The Fed's assets peaked at roughly $8.9 trillion in April 2022 -- larger in dollar terms than QE1 plus QE2 plus QE3 plus Operation Twist combined. It was the largest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-22).

question: The Fed's decision to buy corporate bonds in 2020 was administered by an outside asset-management contractor -- a hire that drew criticism as a regulator-industry-contractor conflict. Which firm ran the program?
context: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, was hired by the Fed to administer the corporate-bond-buying program. Critics noted BlackRock was also managing enormous corporate-bond portfolios for private clients at the same time. Source: Grokipedia 'BlackRock' (2026-09-05).

question: The emergency lending programs of March 2020 were established under a specific section of the Federal Reserve Act that requires 'unusual and exigent circumstances' before use. Which section is this?
context: Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, dating to 1932, allows the Fed to lend to non-bank borrowers in emergencies. Its 2020 use was the broadest invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The March 2020 monetary response set a precedent that Austrian critics warned would apply at double the scale every Cantillon-effect prediction they had made about the 2008-14 programs. What is the recognition move the ladder presses?
answer: Emergency-era programs establish new institutional baselines, and next-crisis responses start from the elevated baseline rather than returning to normal
choices: Emergency-era programs establish new institutional baselines, and next-crisis responses start from the elevated baseline rather than returning to normal
Emergency-era programs are always fully unwound within two years
Emergency-era programs affect only asset prices, not consumer prices
Emergency-era programs are politically neutral and do not affect distribution
context: The Fed's 2020 balance sheet ($8.9T peak) is now the reference point. Any future crisis will be met with something at least as large. The Cantillon-effect distribution to first receivers -- asset holders, primary dealers, government contractors -- was correspondingly larger. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: On August 21, 2003 two economics professors at George Mason University launched a daily economics blog that became one of the longest continuously-posted economics blogs in the world. Who founded marginalrevolution.com?
context: Cowen (born 1962) and Tabarrok (born 1966) both teach economics at GMU, where they succeeded the Buchanan-Tullock generation as the public face of the George Mason public-choice and Austrian-adjacent tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_Revolution_(blog).

question: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok teach at a specific US university whose economics department is closely identified with public choice and Austrian-adjacent traditions. Which university?
context: GMU became the successor institutional home of James Buchanan's Center for Study of Public Choice in 1983. Cowen directs the Mercatus Center at GMU; Tabarrok holds the Bartley J. Madden chair at Mercatus. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: In 2012 Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok launched a free online economics course library at mru.org, covering principles, macroeconomics, development economics, monetary policy, and public choice through short video lessons. What is the platform called?
context: MRU has millions of enrolled students as of the 2020s and is widely used in home-school and secondary-school economics. Its scene-led case-study style is directly modeled on Sowell's Basic Economics approach. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_Revolution_(blog).

question: Tyler Cowen's most-cited 2011 book argued that US productivity growth had slowed dramatically since the 1970s, ending a long period of easy-to-pick technological 'low-hanging fruit.' What was the book called?
