context: The F. A. Hayek Program for Advanced Study in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics is the principal graduate training site for young Austrian scholars in America. Source: mercatus.org/hayek-program.

question: Boettke edited a major reference volume that serves as the standard modern one-volume introduction to the field. Published by Edward Elgar in 2010, what is its title?
context: Boettke's edited Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics (Edward Elgar, 2010) collects the leading modern voices of the tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Boettke.

question: The George Mason faculty is unusual in mainstream American academia because it hosts BOTH major Nobel-winning heterodox schools in one department. Which two schools?
context: James Buchanan's public-choice Nobel (1986) and Vernon Smith's experimental-economics Nobel (2002) both grew at GMU, alongside its Austrian tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/George_Mason_University.

question: An American stockbroker who runs the firm Euro Pacific Capital and has been publicly bullish on gold since the early 2000s has become the best-known Bitcoin critic in the sound-money tradition. Who is he?
context: Peter Schiff runs Euro Pacific Capital and has been a public gold-bull since the early 2000s. Michael Saylor is Bitcoin's most prominent corporate advocate; Cramer runs Mad Money on CNBC; Buffett is a Bitcoin skeptic but not from the sound-money-Austrian tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: Peter Schiff's father was a well-known American Austrian-economics writer and tax-protester who died while serving a federal prison sentence in 2015. Which economist was Peter's father?
context: Irwin Schiff (1928-2015) was an Austrian-economics writer whose tax-protester positions led to his imprisonment; he died in federal custody in 2015. Ron Paul, Murray Rothbard, and Lew Rockwell are separate Austrian figures unrelated by family to Peter. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: Peter Schiff became widely known outside the gold community after making one specific correct prediction, on live television, in the years just before it came true. Which market crash did Schiff repeatedly warn about on CNBC in 2006-07, while other on-air guests laughed at his forecast?
context: Schiff warned about the coming US housing crash repeatedly on 2006-07 CNBC panels; the videos went viral after the crash arrived in 2007-08. His book 'Crash Proof' (2007) laid out the argument in detail. The other crashes predate or postdate the specific prediction videos. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schiff.

question: Peter Schiff's 2007 book laid out the housing-crash prediction he had been making on television. What was the book called?
context: Peter Schiff, 'Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse' (2007). Michael Lewis wrote 'The Big Short' (2010) about the same crash from a different angle; Nassim Taleb wrote 'The Black Swan' (2007) and 'Fooled by Randomness' (2001) on general market unpredictability. Source: https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Crash+Proof-p-9780470043608.

question: From 2013 onward Peter Schiff has been Bitcoin's most persistent critic in the sound-money community. His central argument against Bitcoin points to one specific property that he believes gold has and Bitcoin lacks. Which property does Schiff say Bitcoin is missing?
answer: intrinsic non-monetary value: gold has jewelry and industrial uses, Bitcoin has none of that
choices: intrinsic non-monetary value: gold has jewelry and industrial uses, Bitcoin has none of that
cryptographic security against tampering, forgery, or double-spending in the underlying ledger
portability across international borders without triggering physical searches or seizure risk
recognizability by international courts as a legally protected form of property in every jurisdiction
context: Schiff's central claim is that gold has intrinsic value (jewelry, industrial uses, 5,000 years of recognition) while Bitcoin has none, so Bitcoin is a pure speculative bubble. He does not dispute Bitcoin's cryptographic security, portability, or courtroom recognition -- he argues those are insufficient without intrinsic value. Source: https://www.schiffgold.com/; various Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: Since 2020 Peter Schiff has repeatedly debated the CEO of the company that made the largest corporate-treasury Bitcoin purchases in history. Which Bitcoin executive is Schiff's usual debate opponent on the gold-versus-Bitcoin question?
choices: Vitalik Buterin of the Ethereum Foundation
context: Michael Saylor of MicroStrategy (renamed Strategy) is Schiff's usual debate opponent since 2020, when Saylor began the corporate treasury Bitcoin accumulation. Armstrong runs an exchange; CZ runs another exchange; Buterin runs Ethereum, not a Bitcoin-focused position. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Saylor.

question: Michael Saylor's central counter-argument in the Schiff-Saylor debates concedes that Bitcoin is new but denies that intrinsic value is what actually determines what becomes money. Which specific move does Saylor press against Schiff's argument?
answer: that monetary value comes from properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability and verifiability, and Bitcoin dominates gold on each of those measures except historical duration
choices: that monetary value comes from properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability and verifiability, and Bitcoin dominates gold on each of those measures except historical duration
that intrinsic value is entirely irrelevant to all economic reasoning about money, so gold's jewelry and industrial uses have never mattered to its role as a store of wealth
that gold has no non-monetary uses of significance and never has, so the whole gold-vs-Bitcoin debate is really about which useless object is scarcer
that only government-issued money can serve as a durable store of value, so both gold and Bitcoin will eventually be replaced by state currency systems
context: Saylor's argument: monetary properties (scarcity, divisibility, portability, verifiability, durability) determine what becomes money, not jewelry uses; on those measures Bitcoin dominates gold, with duration the one property gold currently leads on. He does not deny gold's non-monetary uses or dismiss intrinsic-value theory categorically. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts 2021-24.

question: One of Saylor's most repeated debate lines invokes a specific comparison about what happens when a holder crosses an international border with each form of wealth. What does Saylor say gold cannot do that Bitcoin can?
context: Saylor's line: gold cannot be sent over the internet; Bitcoin can. This is the network-transmission property he uses to argue Bitcoin dominates gold on portability. Weighing, minting, and banking are not what the specific rhetorical move disputes. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: As of 2026 the Schiff-Saylor debate is unresolved at market level, though both gold and Bitcoin have appreciated substantially since 2020. Which specific reason does a Bitcoin educator most often give for why the whole debate has been valuable, regardless of who is right?
answer: That both men articulate their arguments honestly, in public, in a financial-media environment where that is unusually rare
choices: That both men articulate their arguments honestly, in public, in a financial-media environment where that is unusually rare
That the debate has convinced most governments to accept Bitcoin as legal tender
That the debate has been settled definitively by peer-reviewed economics papers
That the debate has ended with a formal apology from Schiff
context: The bank's stance (honest-debate rung): the value of the Schiff-Saylor exchange is that both men state and defend their positions publicly rather than through carefully-cropped soundbites. No government adoption cascade, definitive academic resolution, or Schiff apology has occurred. Source: Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: A student watching the Schiff-Saylor debates in 2026 asks which specific Austrian-tradition reasoning move Schiff most reliably brings that Saylor concedes is a legitimate consideration -- even where they disagree on how it applies to Bitcoin. Which move does Schiff press that Saylor treats as serious rather than dismissing?
answer: the Mises regression theorem: a money must be traceable to a prior non-monetary demand
choices: the Mises regression theorem: a money must be traceable to a prior non-monetary demand
the Keynesian aggregate-demand model: the general price level tracks total spending
the Chicago-school efficient-markets hypothesis: prices always reflect all known info
the MMT sovereign-currency thesis: a state issuer can never involuntarily default
context: Schiff's substantive move is the Mises Regression Theorem. Saylor treats it seriously and answers with an account of Bitcoin's early cypherpunk-collectible use (following Ammous). The Keynesian, Chicago-school, and MMT frames are not Schiff's ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem; Schiff-Saylor debate transcripts.

question: In 1991 an American programmer, worried that pending US legislation would ban strong encryption for ordinary citizens, wrote a program that let anyone encrypt email so only the intended recipient could read it. Who wrote it?
context: Phil Zimmermann wrote PGP in 1991. Gates and Wozniak were building operating systems and personal computers; Torvalds released the Linux kernel that same year but did not write PGP. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: Phil Zimmermann's 1991 email-encryption program has a name that sounds intentionally understated -- three words, one an adjective meaning 'fair-to-good', the other two the value the software delivers. What was the program called?
context: PGP stands for Pretty Good Privacy -- Zimmermann's deliberately modest name for a program that gave ordinary users email cryptography previously available only to governments. The other expansions are fabrications. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy.

question: To keep PGP from being blocked before it could spread, Phil Zimmermann took a specific action in 1991 that guaranteed the software could no longer be stopped by any single government. What did he do with it?
answer: uploaded it to the internet where it circulated worldwide within weeks
choices: uploaded it to the internet where it circulated worldwide within weeks
sold the rights to the US Department of Defense
patented it and licensed only US citizens
distributed it exclusively on floppy disks inside the US
context: Zimmermann uploaded PGP to the internet in 1991; within weeks it was on servers in every country including US-embargoed states. Selling to DoD, patenting for US-only licensing, or floppy-only distribution are the opposite of what he did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: In 1993 the United States government opened a criminal investigation of Phil Zimmermann under a specific federal statute that treated strong cryptography as a category of weapon. Which act was Zimmermann investigated under?
choices: the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
context: The 1993 US investigation treated strong cryptography as a munition under the Arms Export Control Act; PGP appeared on the US Munitions List alongside tanks and missiles. Espionage Act (1917) covers classified information; CFAA (1986) covers computer intrusion; Patriot Act (2001) postdates the investigation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: The US government's specific theory in 1993 was that by uploading PGP to a server foreigners could download from, Phil Zimmermann had 'exported' something the government classified as a weapon. On which specific list was PGP-strength cryptography classified?
context: Strong cryptography above certain key lengths appeared on the US Munitions List (USML) governed by the Arms Export Control Act. The Entity List (Commerce Department), SDN (Treasury), and OFAC country sanctions are different and specifically about persons, entities, and territories. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_of_cryptography_from_the_United_States.

question: Phil Zimmermann's response to the export-control investigation was a piece of legal-technical theater. In 1995 MIT Press published a specific object that could not be regulated as a weapon under US law. What did MIT Press publish?
answer: a book containing PGP's entire source code, printed on paper
choices: a book containing PGP's entire source code, printed on paper
a documentary film about Zimmermann's fight
an unclassified summary of the Arms Export Control Act
a public directory of PGP users worldwide
context: MIT Press published PGP's entire source code as a printed book in 1995 -- because books, as speech, are protected by the First Amendment. A foreign purchaser could scan or OCR the pages to recover the software. The other options were not the specific counter-move. Source: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262240390/pgp-source-code-and-internals/.

question: The whole point of MIT Press's 1995 PGP-source-code book was to force a specific US constitutional question about the difference between electronic export and print. Which constitutional principle did the book invoke to route around the Arms Export Control Act?
answer: First Amendment protection of speech, applied to source code as speech
choices: First Amendment protection of speech, applied to source code as speech
Second Amendment protection of arms, applied to source code as an arm
Fourth Amendment protection against search, applied to encrypted content
context: The book strategy tested whether printed source code was First-Amendment-protected speech even when the same code as an electronic download was a Munitions List item. The stunt was central to the later Bernstein v US and Junger v Daley cases that ultimately held source code as speech. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_v._United_States.

question: The US Department of Justice ended its investigation of Phil Zimmermann without charges. In which year did DOJ drop the case?
context: DOJ dropped the investigation in January 1996 without charges. The 1993 date is when the investigation opened; the US relaxed cryptography export controls in 1999; and 2001 is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: The PGP export-control fight is a load-bearing precedent for every later open-source cryptography project -- including Bitcoin. Which specific legal ground did PGP's outcome establish that Bitcoin's 2008 publication would rely on to be released openly without government approval?
answer: that cryptographic source code counts as speech protected by the First Amendment
choices: that cryptographic source code counts as speech protected by the First Amendment
that all software must be reviewed by the Department of Defense before release
that only US citizens may write and publish cryptography
that any distributed system requires a special license
context: The PGP episode helped establish that source code is speech (later confirmed by Bernstein v US, Junger v Daley). Without that precedent, Satoshi's 2008 open publication of Bitcoin source code would have faced a version of the same 1993 investigation. The other options are the opposite of what the fight settled. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein_v._United_States.

question: A cypherpunk historian looking back on the PGP fight often presses one specific reasoning move about what made Zimmermann's approach effective against a much larger adversary. Which move does the argument press?
answer: That making the software already widely distributed before the state could act removes the state's leverage to suppress it
choices: That making the software already widely distributed before the state could act removes the state's leverage to suppress it
That petitioning legislators one at a time is the correct path for privacy tools
That a well-funded lobbying group is needed before shipping cryptography
That patent protection is the crucial defense for open-source privacy code
context: The PGP argument: releasing the software worldwide before the state could stop it removed the state's suppression leverage; you cannot un-publish a program on ten thousand servers. Legislative petitioning, lobbying groups, and patents are the opposite of the shipping-first strategy the fight vindicated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann.

question: The 18th-century French economic-reform school that preceded Bastiat's classical liberalism was led by a physician to Louis XV who also wrote about the circular flow of wealth. Who led it?
context: Francois Quesnay (1694-1774), physician to Louis XV, led the Physiocrats and published the Tableau economique in 1758. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Physiocracy.

question: Quesnay's most famous work, published in 1758, was the first attempt to trace the movement of wealth through an economy as a diagram. What is the work's title?
choices: Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth
context: The Tableau economique (1758) diagrammed the circulation of wealth between farming, artisanal, and landowning classes -- the first such macroeconomic model. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tableau_%C3%A9conomique.

question: The Physiocrats coined a two-part policy motto in French, arguing government should not obstruct trade or production. What was the motto?
choices: Vive la France, vive la republique
context: 'Laissez faire, laissez passer' -- let it be done, let it pass -- is the Physiocrats' motto, later adopted more broadly as a shorthand for the classical-liberal policy stance. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Laissez-faire.

question: The Physiocrats' central theoretical claim, now recognized as wrong, held that only one specific sector of the economy produced new NET wealth. Which sector did they hold to be the sole source of net wealth?
context: The produit-net doctrine held that only agriculture produced new net wealth; manufacturing and commerce merely transformed it. The claim is now recognized as mistaken, but the free-trade policy conclusions largely stood. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Physiocracy.

question: A Physiocrat served briefly as controller-general of finance under Louis XVI from 1774 to 1776, attempting to abolish internal grain tariffs, guild monopolies, and the corvee. Who was he?
context: Turgot's brief tenure (1774-1776) was a rare case of a Physiocrat actually running economic policy; his 1776 fall under noble pressure is a canonical example of reform blocked by concentrated interests. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anne-Robert-Jacques_Turgot.

question: The intellectual bridge between the Physiocrats and Bastiat was a French economist who in 1803 published a Traite d'economie politique giving the French version of Adam Smith. Who was he?
context: Jean-Baptiste Say (1767-1832) systematized classical-liberal economics for French readers and formulated what came to be called Say's Law. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jean-Baptiste_Say.

question: Say's Law is often summarized in a four-word English phrase, though Say's actual formulation was more nuanced. What is the common four-word summary?
context: The compressed English form 'supply creates its own demand' was attacked by Keynes and defended by the Austrians; Say's own version emphasized that products offered on a market create the purchasing power that buys other products. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Say%27s_law.

question: The traditional origin story of 'laissez-nous faire' has it as an answer given by a specific 17th-century French merchant to the finance minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. What was the merchant's name?
context: Around 1680 the merchant Le Gendre reportedly answered Colbert's question 'What should we do to help you?' with 'Laissez-nous faire' -- leave us alone. The phrase then spread through economic writing via the Physiocrats around 1750-1760. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Laissez-faire.

question: After Solidarity's June 1989 election victory, Poland's new government appointed a Warsaw School of Economics professor as finance minister to design the post-communist reform package. What was his surname?
context: Leszek Balcerowicz, a Warsaw School of Economics professor, was named finance minister and deputy prime minister in the Mazowiecki government of August 1989. He assembled the reform package by end-1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leszek_Balcerowicz.

question: Balcerowicz's reform package took effect on January 1, 1990 and came to be called by two names -- one after him, one describing the speed of the transition. What is the second name?
context: 'Shock therapy' captured the speed of Poland's turn from central planning to market pricing overnight -- as distinct from the gradual approaches other post-communist states attempted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_therapy_(economics).

question: The Balcerowicz Plan's core move on prices was to end Communist-era controls immediately -- not gradually. What did Poland do to prices on January 1, 1990?
answer: Liberalized prices on almost all goods overnight
choices: Liberalized prices on almost all goods overnight
Fixed all prices at the previous month's levels
Doubled all prices to reflect shortages
context: The immediate price liberalization was the sharpest single move. Alongside it: hard-budget constraints on state enterprises, currency convertibility, foreign trade opening, and privatization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balcerowicz_Plan.

question: The first year of Balcerowicz-era reform was painful. Roughly what happened to Polish GDP in 1990?
context: GDP contracted about 12% in 1990 and again in 1991. Unemployment rose from nominal Communist-era full employment to over 12%. Inflation initially spiked. Political heat was intense. Source: World Bank Poland historical data.

question: From 1992 onwards Poland achieved something no other European economy matched for the following 16 years: no year of GDP contraction until the 2008 global crisis. What is the standard shorthand for this stretch of expansion?
context: Poland grew continuously 1992-2008, an unmatched European record. By 2019 real per-capita GDP had roughly tripled from its 1990 low. Warsaw modernized; the country joined the EU in 2004. Source: World Bank Poland data.

question: The Harvard economist who advised Balcerowicz's reform team and became closely associated with the 'shock therapy' approach was a young rising star in international development economics. Who was he?
context: Jeffrey Sachs advised Poland, Russia, and other post-communist countries on stabilization. His association with shock therapy became foundational -- and controversial when Russia's later reforms produced different results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Sachs.

question: By 2019 Poland's real GDP per capita had roughly what multiple of its 1990 low?
context: Poland's real per-capita GDP had roughly tripled from its 1990 low by 2019. The stretch of continuous growth 1992-2008 and steady recovery after the 2008 crisis produced the largest sustained gain among post-communist economies. Source: World Bank Poland data.

question: Russia's post-communist reform, run under Yeltsin from 1992-95 with voucher privatization, produced a different outcome than Poland's. What is the standard critique of the Russian sequence?
answer: Gradual measures were captured by insiders, producing the oligarch collapse
choices: Gradual measures were captured by insiders, producing the oligarch collapse
The reforms were too fast, producing hyperinflation
The government stayed too socialist, producing shortage
The state privatized only strategic industries, producing distortion
context: Russia's voucher privatization was captured by well-positioned insiders who accumulated stakes cheaply. Without hard-budget discipline, the result was oligarch-owned enterprises rather than a genuine market. The comparison with Poland became the standard case for the coherent-package view. Source: aslund.org, Russia After Communism.

question: For the calculation debate, the Balcerowicz Plan's teaching is that half-measures fail while a coherent package works. What set of ingredients did Balcerowicz insist go together?
answer: Price liberalization plus hard-budget constraints plus currency convertibility plus trade opening
choices: Price liberalization plus hard-budget constraints plus currency convertibility plus trade opening
Price liberalization alone plus foreign aid
Currency convertibility plus state industrial policy
Trade opening plus continued state pricing
context: Balcerowicz's insight: nominal price liberalization without hard-budget constraints (no state bailouts of failing SOEs) does not produce market discipline. A coherent package with all four elements enables the Mises-Hayek mechanism to work. Source: Balcerowicz, Socialism, Capitalism, Transformation (1995).

question: In 1975 a young Yale economist published a Review of Economic Studies paper that formalized the idea that fiscal and monetary authorities under political pressure will time expansionary policy to precede elections. Who was the author?
context: William Nordhaus, 'The Political Business Cycle' (Review of Economic Studies, April 1975). Nordhaus later shared the 2018 Nobel for work on climate integrated assessment. Source: jstor.org (Nordhaus 1975).

question: Nordhaus's 1975 model treats politicians and central bankers as strategic actors optimizing for what specific objective, rather than for long-run welfare?
context: Nordhaus's model: an incumbent seeking reelection benefits from a pre-election boom (voters observe strong economy, incumbent gets credit) and can defer the post-election bust past the election-day judgment. Source: Nordhaus, Review of Economic Studies (1975).

question: In 1971-72, President Richard Nixon personally pressured the Federal Reserve Chair to loosen monetary policy ahead of his November 1972 reelection campaign. Which Fed Chair received that pressure, as documented in the Nixon White House tapes?
context: Arthur Burns chaired the Federal Reserve from February 1970 through January 1978. The Nixon White House tapes -- partially transcribed in Burton Abrams's 2006 Journal of Economic Perspectives article -- document Nixon pressing Burns for easier money before the 1972 election. Source: aeaweb.org (Abrams 2006).

question: Fed funds rates fell from about 9% in mid-1969 to about 3.3% by early 1972, and M1 growth accelerated to about 9% for 1972 -- consistent with an incumbent-friendly loosening ahead of the November vote. What was the November 1972 election outcome for Nixon?
choices: A defeat by a third-party candidate
context: Nixon carried 49 states on November 7, 1972 (losing only Massachusetts and DC). CPI inflation then ran ~3.2% (1972), ~6.2% (1973), ~11.0% (1974) -- the beginning of the stagflation decade Volcker would eventually crush. Source: uselectionatlas.org; bls.gov (CPI historical).

question: In June 2003, Alan Greenspan cut the Fed funds rate to a specific low level and held it there for a full year. What was that low rate, then the lowest since 1958?
context: The Fed cut its target rate to 1.00% by June 2003 and held it there until June 30, 2004 -- when the FOMC began a slow tightening cycle just after the summer political conventions and before the November 2004 election. Source: federalreserve.gov (FOMC historical decisions).

question: The 2003-04 low-rate period ended with a slow tightening cycle that began after the summer political conventions and before the November 2004 election, when George W. Bush was seeking reelection. What broader real-estate consequence did economists in the Austrian tradition predict would follow the extended low-rate environment?
answer: A housing bubble that would eventually burst
choices: A housing bubble that would eventually burst
A permanent halt to residential construction
A boom in agricultural land prices only
A collapse in urban land values
context: US housing prices continued rising through 2006. Austrian-tradition economists like Roger Garrison (Time and Money, Routledge 2001) and Mark Thornton predicted the bubble in real time. The 2008 GFC followed. Source: Case-Shiller US National Home Price Index; Thornton, Mises Institute writings 2004-06.

question: Empirical evidence has been mixed on the STRONG version of political business cycles (proving intent from data alone is hard) but robust on the WEAK version. What does the weak version predict about central-bank behavior under political pressure?
answer: Systematically pro-cyclical policy relative to a fully independent central bank
choices: Systematically pro-cyclical policy relative to a fully independent central bank
Systematically pro-recession policy in election years
Randomized changes uncorrelated with political events
context: The Alesina + Roubini + Cohen synthesis (Political Cycles and the Macroeconomy, MIT Press 1997) finds pro-cyclical bias under political pressure -- easier money before elections, tighter after -- relative to an independent counterfactual. Source: mitpress.mit.edu (Alesina 1997).

question: The dramatic counter-example to a political-business-cycle pattern came in the early 1980s when a Fed Chair knowingly pursued a tightening that would cost the incumbent president reelection. Which Fed Chair took that course?
context: Paul Volcker's 1979-82 tightening produced a deep recession that helped defeat Jimmy Carter in 1980. Volcker's willingness to accept that cost is the counter-example that shows independent-central-banker behavior is possible when the incentives allow it. Source: Volcker, Keeping At It (Public Affairs 2018).

question: Between 2018 and 2019 a sitting US president repeatedly, publicly, and personally pressured his appointed Fed Chair to cut rates faster. Which Fed Chair received that pressure from President Trump?
context: Jerome Powell (appointed by Trump in November 2017, sworn in February 2018) faced repeated public pressure from President Trump in 2018-19 to cut rates. It is the modern echo of the Nixon-Burns pressure documented in the tapes. Source: contemporary Wall Street Journal and New York Times coverage 2018-19.

question: The reasoning move the political-business-cycle literature teaches is not a conspiracy theory about the Fed. What is the actual analytical move Buchanan's 'politics without romance' applied to central banks?
answer: Fed independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure
choices: Fed independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure
The Fed is always corrupt regardless of who chairs it
Fed independence is a myth invented after 1913
The Fed is always politically neutral in practice
context: Buchanan's move: examine the specific chair's reappointment prospects, congressional-relationship incentives, and post-Fed career prospects. Legal independence is compatible with substantial de facto political responsiveness. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979) applied.

question: When James Buchanan sat down to describe what the public-choice school actually did, he coined a three-word phrase that has served as its shorthand ever since. What was that phrase?
context: 'Politics without romance' is Buchanan's own three-word summary of the public-choice program. He used it as the title of a widely-cited 1979 lecture and returned to it in his Nobel-era writings. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (IHS Vienna, 1979).

question: James Buchanan's 1979 lecture 'Politics Without Romance' was delivered at a Vienna research institute and then widely reprinted. What was the ROMANTIC assumption that Buchanan's phrase was written to strip away?
answer: That politicians and bureaucrats act from pure public spirit
choices: That politicians and bureaucrats act from pure public spirit
That elections are decided by campaign advertising
That voters read platforms carefully before voting
That parties always keep their platform promises
context: The romance to be stripped: that political actors somehow escape the ordinary self-interest that economics assumes for consumers and firms. Public choice treats them as ordinary humans facing ordinary incentives. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: Buchanan's phrase was a critique of a widespread mid-century way of doing welfare economics: comparing imperfect REAL markets against IDEALIZED government intervention. What did Buchanan say the honest comparison had to be?
answer: Real market failure against real government failure
choices: Real market failure against real government failure
Ideal market outcomes against ideal government outcomes
The best market case against the worst government case
The worst market case against the best government case
context: Buchanan's move: welfare economics had compared apples to angels -- imperfect markets to perfect government. Compare like to like, and the case for intervention becomes far less obvious. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: Thomas Sowell, writing across many books, condensed Buchanan's whole comparative move into a two-word question a critic should always ask when someone claims 'the market has failed, so government must act.' What is Sowell's two-word question?
context: Sowell's 'compared to what?' recurs across Knowledge and Decisions (1980), The Vision of the Anointed (1995), and other books. It is his shorthand for the Buchanan comparative move. Source: Sowell, Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books 1980).

question: Because public choice takes the incentive structures of political actors seriously, it identifies a category of policy breakdown that mirrors the market pathology economists had long studied. Which two-word term names this new category?
context: Government failure is public choice's response to the market-failure literature: not that market failures do not exist, but that government intervention has its own systematic failure modes -- capture, rent-seeking, budget maximization, rational ignorance. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: Public choice identifies several specific mechanisms of government failure produced by identifiable incentives. Which of the following is NOT one of the standard mechanisms in the Buchanan-Tullock-Olson toolkit?
answer: The invisible hand of consumer sovereignty
choices: The invisible hand of consumer sovereignty
Rent-seeking by lobbyists competing for privilege
Rational ignorance by voters with low per-capita stakes
context: The invisible hand describes a MARKET mechanism, not a government-failure mode. The other three -- capture (Stigler), rent-seeking (Tullock), rational ignorance (Downs) -- are core public-choice mechanisms. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: Buchanan credited a Hungarian-born economist for coining the closely-related phrase 'the romantic view of the state' well before Buchanan wrote 'Politics Without Romance.' Which development economist did Buchanan cite for that phrase?
context: Peter Bauer (1915-2002) was a Hungarian-born LSE development economist who spent decades attacking the romantic view of the state that underpinned post-war aid programs. Buchanan credited Bauer with the phrase. Source: Bauer, Dissent on Development (Harvard 1972).

question: The reasoning move behind 'politics without romance' is best characterized as SYMMETRIC treatment. What exactly must be treated symmetrically in Buchanan's frame?
answer: Political actors and market actors, both as self-interested humans
choices: Political actors and market actors, both as self-interested humans
Winners and losers, both as morally equivalent
Small government and big government, both as equally efficient
Voters and non-voters, both as equally informed
context: The move: if we assume ordinary self-interest for consumers and firms, we must assume it for politicians and bureaucrats too. Asymmetric assumptions (angels in government, humans in markets) built the pre-Buchanan case for intervention. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: The phrase 'politics without romance' functions as a diagnostic test in public-choice argument. Whenever an advocate says 'the market has failed, so GOVERNMENT must act,' which specific counter-question does the diagnostic require the analyst to ask?
answer: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
choices: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
What percentage of GDP will the new agency consume?
Which political party currently controls the executive branch?
How much did the market failure cost in dollar terms?
context: The public-choice discipline: never compare a REAL failure to an IDEALIZED alternative. Given the actual incentive structure facing the people who would design and administer the fix, is there reason to expect improvement? Often the answer is no. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: 'Politics without romance' is Buchanan's own three-word slogan for the whole discipline. Which of the following slogans is NOT Buchanan's but belongs to a different public-choice or Chicago-school figure?
answer: There are no solutions, only trade-offs (Sowell)
choices: There are no solutions, only trade-offs (Sowell)
context: Thomas Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only trade-offs' recurs across his books. Buchanan's own slogans include 'politics without romance,' 'constitutional political economy,' and 'the samaritan's dilemma.' Source: Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (Morrow 1987).

question: In 1545 an Andean local led Spanish colonists to a mountain of ore in the highlands of what is now Bolivia. Within a generation the town below it was the largest city in the Americas, producing roughly 60% of world silver output. What was the town's name?
context: Potosi (Cerro Rico) was discovered in 1545 and by 1600 held perhaps 200,000 residents, making it larger than any European city apart from Paris and London. Source: Grokipedia 'Potosi' (2026-09-05).

question: For a century after 1550 the Spanish crown moved American bullion to Europe by twice-yearly armed convoys sailing from Havana to Seville. What were these convoys called?
context: The Flota de Indias sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana and then across the Atlantic, carrying the world's largest sustained cross-oceanic flow of precious metal. Source: Grokipedia 'Spanish treasure fleet' (2026-09-05).

question: Between 1500 and 1650, as bullion from the New World spread through European commerce, a sustained continent-wide rise in prices occurred that historians estimate at roughly 500%. What is this era conventionally called?
context: Modern estimates put the general European price level in 1650 at roughly six times its 1500 level, with the acceleration tracking the arrival of American silver. Source: Grokipedia 'Price revolution' (2026-09-05).

question: Spain in 1600 held more bullion than any nation in Europe, yet its industry was hollowing out, its treasury was chronically bankrupt to Genoese bankers, and its farmers were being priced out of foreign markets. What is the paradox this ladder points at?
answer: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
choices: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
The country with the most silver could not defend its ships
The country with the most silver refused to trade with its colonies
The country with the most silver banned interest on loans
context: The bullion inflow raised prices in Spain faster than in its trading partners, so Spanish goods became uncompetitive. Real wealth flowed abroad while nominal money piled up. Source: Grokipedia 'Economic history of Spain' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1556 a Spanish theologian at the University of Salamanca wrote the first clear European statement of what became the quantity theory of money: that money is worth less where and when it is abundant. Which theologian was he?
context: Azpilcueta's 1556 Commentary on the Resolution of Money linked the arrival of American bullion to rising Spanish prices, publishing the insight roughly 220 years before Adam Smith. Source: Grokipedia 'Martin de Azpilcueta' (2026-09-05).

question: The 16th-century Spanish scholastic thinkers who were reasoning about money, prices, and interest 200 years before Adam Smith are grouped by historians of thought under a name taken from their university. What is the group called?
context: The School of Salamanca (Azpilcueta, Luis de Molina, Domingo de Soto, Francisco de Vitoria) is now recognized by Austrian economists such as Rothbard and Huerta de Soto as a genuine predecessor to modern economics. Source: Grokipedia 'School of Salamanca' (2026-09-05).

question: In its abundance-and-scarcity form the Salamanca insight -- more money in circulation raises prices, less money lowers them -- is the same reasoning modern economists apply when they warn about central banks expanding the money supply. What is the modern label for that argument?
context: The quantity theory (money supply times velocity equals prices times output) was formalized by Irving Fisher in 1911, but its European roots go back to Azpilcueta and the Salamanca scholastics in the 1550s. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantity theory of money' (2026-09-05).

question: The standard textbook claim that economics began with Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations in 1776 was challenged by Austrian historians of thought pointing to the Salamancans as a genuine earlier school. Which 20th-century Austrian economist made that case most forcefully?
context: Rothbard's 1995 An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought traced pre-classical economics back to the Salamancans and the medieval scholastics, undoing the Smith-as-founder story. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought.

question: The Salamanca argument, applied to a modern central bank, teaches the reader to look past a specific misleading appearance in monetary policy. Which appearance does it teach the reader to distrust?
answer: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
choices: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
That international trade always benefits the exporting country
That taxation is always preferable to borrowing
That war spending stimulates long-run growth
context: The Salamanca-to-Austrian line: nominal money and real wealth are different things. Printing more units of currency raises prices, redistributes purchasing power to the first receivers, and leaves the underlying productive capacity unchanged. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective (1995).

question: Bastiat would frame the 1600 Spanish paradox as a contrast between what is visible in Seville and what is invisible across the whole economy. Which pairing best captures that contrast?
answer: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savers debased
choices: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savers debased
Seen: high consumer spending; Unseen: rising farmer productivity
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: rising imports
Seen: growing armies; Unseen: shrinking population
context: Bastiat's 'seen and unseen' fits the Spanish silver flood exactly: what looks like national wealth (bullion arriving) hides the destruction of domestic industry and the debasement of every existing peseta of savings. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The CARES Act, signed March 27 2020 during the COVID lockdowns, created a forgivable-loan mechanism that ultimately disbursed roughly $800 billion to US small businesses conditioned on their maintaining payroll. What was it called?
context: PPP was administered by the Small Business Administration through private banks. Loans were forgiven if the borrower spent them mostly on payroll within a set window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: The Paycheck Protection Program was created as part of a broader roughly $2.2 trillion emergency package Congress passed in late March 2020. What was that package's name?
context: The Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act was signed March 27, 2020, and was the largest single US relief bill at that time. The American Rescue Plan came later in March 2021 under President Biden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/CARES_Act.

question: David Autor of MIT and coauthors evaluated the Paycheck Protection Program in a January 2022 NBER working paper using administrative payroll microdata. They estimated the program preserved roughly 2-3 million job-years. Roughly what did each preserved job cost?
context: Autor et al, 'An Evaluation of the Paycheck Protection Program Using Administrative Payroll Microdata,' NBER Working Paper 29669. The figure came out far higher than the pre-COVID annual wage of the workers whose jobs were preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_Autor.

question: David Autor's team also calculated the share of Paycheck Protection Program funds that actually reached workers versus the share captured by business owners and shareholders. Which figure did they report?
answer: About 72 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
choices: About 72 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 30 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 5 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
About 95 percent went to owners and shareholders, not workers
context: The bulk of the money flowed to firms that would not have laid off workers even without PPP. Autor and coauthors published the finding in the Journal of Economic Perspectives Spring 2022 and NBER 29669. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: The Small Business Administration distributed the Paycheck Protection Program in April 2020 through existing bank relationships. As a result, minority-owned and rural firms disproportionately missed the first tranche of loans while long-standing corporate clients of large banks got funded in days. Which Austrian reasoning move does this pattern illustrate?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: no central agency knew which firms actually needed relief
choices: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: no central agency knew which firms actually needed relief
Milton Friedman's monetary theory that inflation is a purely monetary phenomenon
John Kenneth Galbraith's conventional-wisdom theory of institutional inertia
John Maynard Keynes's animal-spirits theory of investment
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' argued that the specific knowledge of who needs help, at what price, and in what shape is dispersed across millions of local actors and irreducible to any central authority. PPP defaulted to whoever had a bank relationship because the agency had no other way to allocate the money at speed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: In 2022 Cato and Mercatus economists argued that a different existing program, which the CARES Act had also expanded, would have preserved the same COVID-era jobs as PPP at a small fraction of the per-job cost by paying only workers whose employers actually needed to reduce payroll. Which program did they point to?
context: The CARES Act had raised UI benefits by $600 per week. Because UI pays only workers actually displaced, it avoids paying firms whose employees would have kept their jobs anyway -- addressing the 72 percent leakage documented by Autor and coauthors. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: A congressman in 2021 defends the Paycheck Protection Program by pointing to the millions of small-business owners who received forgivable loans during the lockdowns. A Bastiatian critic responds that the seen beneficiaries were real, but so was an invisible cost future taxpayers now carry. Which specific unseen does that critic press?
answer: Roughly $600 billion in debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs without PPP
choices: Roughly $600 billion in debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs without PPP
The immediate loss of federal tax revenue from small-business income during lockdowns
The direct destruction of small-business inventories during the closure period
A permanent shortage of qualified accountants to administer future federal relief
context: Applied Bastiat: the seen preserved payroll is real; the unseen is the taxpayer liability for the inframarginal share (Autor's 72 percent leakage) that funded no additional employment. Cato and Mercatus economists made the argument most forcefully. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: Ludwig von Mises borrowed a term from a French social philosopher and made it the name of his whole method: the general logical science of human action, of which economics is the most fully developed branch. From what Greek word does that term derive?
context: Praxeology (praxis + -logia) was coined in its modern sense by the French sociologist Alfred Espinas in an 1890 essay in the Revue Philosophique. Mises adopted it in the 1940s for the science that starts from human action as its single axiom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: In 1949 Ludwig von Mises published his English-language treatise laying out praxeology in full. It became the single most systematic Austrian statement of the method, running to nearly a thousand pages. What is the book's one-phrase title?
choices: The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics was published by Yale University Press in September 1949. It rebuilt Mises's German-language Nationaloekonomie (1940) for an American audience and defined praxeology as the general theory of action, with economics as its most developed branch. Source: Grokipedia, 'Human Action'.

question: Praxeology in Ludwig von Mises's system rests on a single starting proposition, which Mises called self-evident because trying to deny it would itself be a purposeful act. In one sentence, what does that starting proposition assert?
answer: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
choices: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
Every good has a market price equal to its cost of production
The general price level moves in proportion to the money supply
Individuals choose the option that maximizes measurable utility
context: This is the action axiom. Mises treated it as apodictic: the very effort to argue against it is a means-and-ends act, so the axiom cannot be coherently rejected. From it he deduced the whole cascade of Austrian economics. Source: Grokipedia, 'action axiom'.

question: In 1953 the University of Chicago economist Milton Friedman published a famous essay laying out the mainstream methodology that Austrians reject. Friedman argued economic theories should be judged only by the accuracy of the predictions they generate, not by the realism of their assumptions. What was the title of the essay?
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
context: Friedman's 1953 essay is often called the most influential piece of methodological writing in twentieth-century economics. It set out the positivist alternative to praxeology: economics as an empirical predictive science whose theorems stand or fall by out-of-sample data, not deduction. Source: Western Sydney University, 'Friedman 1953: The Methodology of Positive Economics'.

question: When a mainstream economist objects that Austrian claims cannot be tested by out-of-sample data the way physics is tested, Ludwig von Mises has a stock reply, which he repeats through Human Action and Theory and History. Which analogy does he press?
answer: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- you cannot re-run 1929 with the money supply held constant
choices: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- you cannot re-run 1929 with the money supply held constant
Economics is not astronomy -- there are no cycles regular enough to fit an equation
Human action is not biology -- there are no species-level laws below the individual
Economics is not engineering -- there is no fixed material to be shaped
context: The point is not that historical evidence is worthless but that no economic episode is ever a controlled experiment: every other variable moves at the same time as the one under study. Mises concluded that economic laws have to be established by deduction from the action axiom, with history supplying cases the laws help interpret. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: In Theory and History (1957) Ludwig von Mises paired praxeology with a second discipline that he said supplies what praxeology does not: the historical understanding of why particular actors chose the specific ends and means they did in a specific time and place. What is the name of this companion discipline?
context: Thymology (from Greek 'thymos', the seat of feeling) is for Mises a historical branch of the sciences of human action. Praxeology tells you WHAT it means to act; thymology tells you WHY this actor, in these circumstances, chose those ends and reached for those means. Source: Wikipedia, 'Thymology'.

question: In 1962 a young American student of Ludwig von Mises published what has come to be regarded as the most extensive systematic treatise in the praxeological tradition. It was originally begun as a textbook version of Human Action and ballooned into a full treatise of its own. Which book?
answer: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State
choices: Murray Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State
Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson
Ludwig Lachmann's Capital and Its Structure
context: The William Volker Fund commissioned Rothbard in 1952 to condense Human Action for classroom use. Ten years later he handed in Man, Economy, and State: A Treatise on Economic Principles instead, running to over a thousand pages and covering the whole of praxeological economics from consumer theory through money and banking. Source: Wikipedia, 'Man, Economy, and State'.

question: In 1995 the Mises Institute published the modern epistemological defense of praxeology against Popperian and positivist objections. The author, a German-born student of Juergen Habermas turned Austrian economist, grounded the action axiom in Immanuel Kant's synthetic a priori. Who was the author, and what was the book?
answer: Hans-Hermann Hoppe, Economic Science and the Austrian Method
choices: Hans-Hermann Hoppe, Economic Science and the Austrian Method
Joseph Salerno, Money, Sound and Unsound
Israel Kirzner, The Economic Point of View
context: Hoppe's lectures at the Mises University argued that the action axiom is a synthetic a priori proposition in Kant's sense -- informative about the world but true by the structure of thought, not by empirical test. The book has been the standard defense of praxeological method for a generation of Austrian graduate students. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: One consequence of grounding Austrian economics in praxeology rather than in data has a specific historical bite. Because Ludwig von Mises's 1920 calculation argument was deduced from the action axiom rather than derived from statistics, Austrians characterized the 1989 collapse of Soviet central planning in a very particular way. How did Austrians frame that collapse in relation to the 1920 argument?
answer: As historical confirmation of a theorem that had already been logically settled in 1920
choices: As historical confirmation of a theorem that had already been logically settled in 1920
As the first genuine empirical test the socialist calculation argument had ever received
As a refutation of the Lange-Lerner reply that the argument had been superseded
As proof that Austrian predictions had at last passed a Popperian falsification
context: The distinction is methodological, not rhetorical. If the calculation problem is a deduced law of action under conditions of no market prices, then the USSR could no more disprove it than a falling apple could disprove gravity; the Soviet experience showed the law working, it did not test whether the law is true. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: At the core of praxeological reasoning is a rule about which entities can be the subject of an economic law. Ludwig von Mises insisted that only one kind of entity ever actually chooses, values, and acts -- and that every claim about 'the state', 'society', or 'the class' has to be traced back to that entity or it is meaningless. What is the one-phrase name for this rule?
context: The doctrine goes back through Mises's teacher Carl Menger and forward to Hayek and Buchanan. Methodological individualism does not deny that groups exist; it insists only that groups do not act -- individuals within them do -- so an economic law that skips the individual is a category error. Source: Grokipedia, 'Human Action'.

question: In 301 AD a Roman emperor issued an edict setting maximum prices for more than 1,200 goods and services, with the death penalty for sellers who charged more. Which emperor?
context: Emperor Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) covered over 1,200 goods and services and hundreds of occupations, with death for overcharging. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: The writer Lactantius, in a work composed not long after Diocletian's edict, reported that its enforcement caused goods to disappear from markets and 'many died on trifling and small accounts'. What kind of author was Lactantius?
context: Lactantius (c. 240-320 AD) was an early Christian rhetorician; his De Mortibus Persecutorum (c. 315 AD) covers Diocletian's reign. He describes the edict as counter-productive from the outset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactantius.

question: On August 15, 1971 an American president announced a 90-day wage-and-price freeze -- the first peacetime price controls in US history -- as part of a broader Sunday-night economic broadcast. Which president?
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 broadcast (which also closed the gold window) imposed a 90-day freeze extended in later Phases through April 1974. Once controls lapsed, the 1973-75 inflation acceleration followed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: In October 1973 the Nixon-Ford administration's price cap on domestic crude oil, combined with the OAPEC embargo, produced a widely photographed shortage in a specific everyday commodity. What shortage image defined the crisis?
answer: Fuel lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing
choices: Fuel lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing
context: Winter 1973-74 gas lines with odd-and-even license-plate rationing became the visual argument for a generation that price caps produce shortages. The controls were partially lifted in 1974 but full oil-price decontrol did not come until 1981 under Reagan. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: A Swedish social-democrat economist famously said in 1971 that a specific housing policy was 'the best way to destroy a city, other than bombing'. Which policy was he criticizing?
context: Assar Lindbeck (1930-2020), a leading Swedish social-democrat economist, made the observation in 1971 and repeated it in many later publications. He was not a libertarian; the line is widely cited across the political spectrum. Source: Lindbeck, The Political Economy of the New Left (1971).

question: In April 2021 Germany's Constitutional Court struck down a controversial Berlin rent-cap law that had been in force since 2020. What was that Berlin cap called?
context: Berlin's Mietendeckel froze most residential rents from February 2020. The federal Constitutional Court struck it down as beyond state competence in April 2021, requiring landlords to be repaid the difference. Source: bundesverfassungsgericht.de (BVerfG 2 BvF 1/20).

question: New York City has had some form of residential-rent regulation continuously since a specific WWII-era year, making it the longest continuous rent-regulation program in the US. In what year did NYC rent regulation begin?
context: NYC rent control began in 1943 under wartime federal price controls and continued in state and city form after the war. Rent stabilization (a distinct, larger program) began 1969. Source: hcr.ny.gov (rent regulation history).

question: The reasoning move at the heart of every price-control failure -- from Diocletian to Nixon to Berlin -- is that a ceiling set below the market clearing price produces one of a specific set of outcomes. Which outcome pattern?
answer: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
choices: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
Higher taxes, lower wages, and unemployment
context: When the state sets a price below what buyers would pay, demand exceeds supply. The gap is filled by non-price rationing (queues), by illegal secondary markets, or by suppliers exiting entirely (landlords convert to condos, sellers hoard, farmers plant less). Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: The Austrian reading of price controls connects them directly to Mises's 1920 argument: the state does not need to abolish exchange to suppress the price signal. What is that connection?
answer: A ceiling below market suffices to break the local signal, the way full central planning breaks it economy-wide
choices: A ceiling below market suffices to break the local signal, the way full central planning breaks it economy-wide
Price controls create genuinely new information the market lacks
Ceilings work perfectly if enforcement is strict enough
Ceilings raise supply by lowering prices
context: Mises's 1920 argument applied at smaller scale: whether by abolishing exchange or by capping the price, if the market-clearing signal is suppressed the allocation goes wrong. Same mechanism, different scale. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The modern textbook exposition of the price-control-produces-shortage argument -- combining Diocletian, Nixon, and rent control cases in a single narrative -- is a widely-adopted introductory text by an American economist. Which book?
choices: The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith
The Undercover Economist by Tim Harford
context: Sowell's Basic Economics (first edition 2000; multiple later editions) is the standard introductory exposition that runs the price-control-produces-shortage argument across centuries of cases. Source: tsowell.com.

question: Hurricane Fran cut power to a million people around Raleigh, North Carolina in September 1996. Four men trucked in bagged ice from Goldsboro and sold it at several times the pre-storm price. Police arrested them and impounded a truck. What did the customers waiting in the line do?
answer: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
choices: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
Blocked the police cars until the ice was freed
Emptied the truck while the officers wrote tickets
Chipped in for the sellers' bail
context: Michael Munger, who teaches political science and economics at Duke University, wrote the night up for the Library of Economics and Liberty on January 8, 2007 under the title 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' His line: 'They clapped. I can't for the life of me understand why the people would clap.' The four men had rented two freezer trucks, paid $1.70 a bag for 500 bags per truck, and chain-sawed fallen logs off the road to get in. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: Most American states punish merchants who raise prices on water, fuel and generators after a disaster. Florida's statute does not run all the time: it switches on at one moment and then measures a price against the thirty days before it. What switches Florida's law on?
answer: The governor declaring a state of emergency
choices: The governor declaring a state of emergency
A hurricane making landfall inside the state
A county sheriff reporting a supply shortage
The attorney general opening an investigation
context: Florida Statute 501.160 forbids an 'unconscionable' price during a declared state of emergency, defining it as a 'gross disparity' with the average price charged in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately before the declaration. Penalties run to $1,000 per violation and up to $25,000 for violations inside a single 24-hour period. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.myfloridalegal.com/price-gouging-hotline/price-gouging-statute.

question: John Shepperson of Kentucky watched the Hurricane Katrina coverage in 2005, bought nineteen generators, rented a truck and drove about six hundred miles to Mississippi, where buyers were waiting and willing to pay roughly double what he had paid. What happened to Shepperson and to the generators?
answer: Police jailed him for four days and kept the generators
choices: Police jailed him for four days and kept the generators
The state bought his whole load at the price he had paid
A judge cleared the sale once he agreed to halve his price
FEMA hired him to haul relief supplies for the next month
context: Shepperson was arrested for price gouging, held four days, and the nineteen generators remained in police custody rather than in the hands of anyone in Mississippi. John Stossel used the case on ABC's 20/20; Mark Perry has cited it repeatedly. Sources: https://abcnews.com/2020/Stossel/story?id=1954352 ; https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/dear-la-times-reporter-your-lack-of-understanding-of-economics-doesnt-mean-that-price-gouging-is-a-bad-thing/.

question: F. A. Hayek published 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' in the American Economic Review in September 1945. He asked readers to suppose that tin has suddenly grown scarce, and that tens of thousands of people who use tin must now use less of it. Hayek's whole argument turns on what those users have to be told first. What did Hayek say they need to know?
answer: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
choices: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
Which mine closed or which war caused it
How long the shortage is expected to last
Which uses of tin the state ranks highest
context: Hayek's marvel was that 'without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' He added that it does not matter which cause made tin scarcer, and called the price system 'a system of telecommunications' whose users watch a few pointers as an engineer watches dials. Sources: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html ; https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/hayek-the-use-of-knowledge-in-society-1945.

question: Michael Munger gave his account of the Raleigh ice night a two-word title taken from what the crowd did. The subtitle that followed it was a question, and that question is the argument of the whole essay in six words. What did Munger's subtitle ask?
choices: Can a state legislate a fair price?
Does the law owe disaster victims a queue?
Should a state ration what a storm spared?
context: 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?', Library of Economics and Liberty, January 8, 2007. Munger's answer is no: a statute can forbid a price, but the ice, generators and chain saws are no less scarce for the ban. As he put it, 'all a state accomplishes by passing an anti-gouging law is to ensure that there is no ice.' Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: A state attorney general announces that any merchant who sells a generator above its pre-storm price once the hurricane has passed will be prosecuted. The stated aim is to keep generators within reach of families who have just lost everything, and the first prosecutions are still weeks away. A critic working in Frederic Bastiat's tradition does not dispute the aim. Which cost does the critic say the announcement has already imposed?
answer: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
choices: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
The state's own emergency stockpile is drawn down faster than planned
Retailers raise prices on unrelated goods to make up the lost margin
Insurance premiums across the state rise for the following season
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' asks, after any law, what does not happen because of it. The prosecuted merchant is seen; the trucker who never loads, never drives and never arrives is not. John Shepperson's nineteen generators reached Mississippi and ended up in an impound lot; the ones that stayed in Georgia never made the news at all. Sources: Bastiat, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (1850) (https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss.html); https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: Florida's statute makes a post-disaster price unlawful when it shows a 'gross disparity' with the average price the merchant charged during the thirty days before the governor declared the emergency. A Hayekian critic reads that definition and says the drafters quietly assumed away the very event the statute exists to address. What does the definition assume?
answer: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
choices: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
That merchants can compute their own thirty-day averages precisely
That every merchant in the state buys from the same wholesale supplier
That governors declare emergencies at the same point in every storm
context: The benchmark in Florida Statute 501.160 is the average price in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately preceding the emergency declaration. On Hayek's account a price is a piece of information about present conditions, so freezing the benchmark at the pre-storm figure instructs the market to behave as though the storm carried no information at all. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html.

question: Michael Munger has argued against anti-gouging statutes for two decades, and on EconTalk he reduced the whole position to one sentence about what a state has to permit if it wants a well-supplied city after a disaster. How did Munger put it?
answer: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
choices: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
The only way to protect the poor is to ration essentials by household size
The only way to stop hoarding is to cap what any single buyer may carry away
The only way to speed relief is to suspend the state's transport licensing rules
context: Munger's point is that the high price is the thing that pulls supply toward the disaster: it tells a trucker eight hundred miles away that this city is where his load is worth most, it moves the scarce stock toward the buyers who need it most, and it makes the people already holding ice or fuel stretch it. A cap removes all three at once, and the shortage the cap was meant to soften simply lasts longer. The distractors here are real positions people hold in this debate, not straw men. Source: https://www.econtalk.org/munger-on-price-gouging/.

question: A 31-year-old Viennese economist gives four guest lectures at the London School of Economics from 27 to 30 January 1931, at the invitation of Lionel Robbins. Which named economist was the invited lecturer?
context: Robbins had read Hayek's article 'The Paradox of Saving' and brought him to LSE. Mises never took an English professorship; Schumpeter was at Bonn (and later Harvard); Machlup was another Vienna-Circle Austrian but was not the invited lecturer that January. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Hayek's four LSE lectures of January 1931 were published later that year as a short book by George Routledge & Sons. What was the book titled?
context: Prices and Production is Hayek's monetary-theory book; Road to Serfdom (1944) is his popular political tract; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) is an essay collection; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is his mature political philosophy. Source: LSE History blog.

question: Robbins was so impressed by the four January-1931 lectures that he offered Hayek a permanent LSE chair the same year, which Hayek accepted and held until 1950. Which named chair did Hayek take?
answer: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
choices: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
The Cassel Professorship of Economics at Stockholm
The Drummond Chair of Political Economy at Oxford
The Alfred Marshall Professorship at Cambridge
context: The Tooke Chair, endowed in memory of the 19th-century monetary economist Thomas Tooke, was Hayek's home at LSE for nearly two decades. The three distractors are real named chairs at rival departments Hayek never held. Source: LSE History blog.

question: The central claim of Hayek's Prices and Production is that the ordinary boom-and-bust of a modern economy is not an unexplained psychological swing but a specific KIND of phenomenon. Which kind does Hayek argue it is?
answer: A MONETARY phenomenon caused by artificial credit expansion
choices: A MONETARY phenomenon caused by artificial credit expansion
A collapse of aggregate consumer demand and animal spirits
A shortfall of real technology shocks in a productive economy
A financial-instability spiral built into every capitalist system
context: Hayek's answer is monetary and Austrian. The three distractors are the three main rival theories that would dominate the 20th century: Keynes's aggregate-demand-plus-animal-spirits view, the real-business-cycle school of Kydland and Prescott, and Hyman Minsky's financial-instability hypothesis. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: In Hayek's Prices and Production the specific damage of artificial credit expansion is not that prices rise across the board but that the CAPITAL STRUCTURE is distorted. What does Hayek argue actually happens to the pattern of production?
answer: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
choices: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
Consumer-goods factories are shuttered as households divert spending toward government bonds
Money velocity collapses and idle cash balances swell across every stage of production
Nominal wages become sticky downward and unemployment jumps immediately in every sector
context: Artificially low interest rates falsify the natural rate of interest -- the rate at which voluntary saving would match investment demand. Firms respond as if saving were plentiful and start long-horizon capital projects that must later be abandoned. The other three describe rival theories (crowding out, Keynesian liquidity trap, Keynesian sticky-wage unemployment). Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: To display his theory of the temporal structure of production -- stages running from higher-order capital goods down to final consumer goods -- Hayek introduced a diagram in Prices and Production that has carried his name in Austrian economics ever since. What is the diagram called?
context: The Hayekian triangle organizes all spending in the economy as a triangle whose base measures time-to-consumer-good; artificial credit tilts the triangle to a longer, capital-heavy shape it cannot sustain. Phillips (1958), Laffer (1974), and Kondratiev (1920s) are all real diagrams from unrelated traditions. Source: Mises Wiki, 'Hayekian triangle'.

question: For Hayek in Prices and Production the crash at the end of a credit-driven boom is not the underlying illness -- something else was. Which is his view of where the disease actually sat?
answer: The BOOM was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
choices: The BOOM was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
The bust was the disease and the boom had been a healthy real expansion
Both boom and bust are neutral psychological fluctuations around a stable trend
The whole cycle is a statistical artefact with no underlying economic cause
context: This is Hayek's core diagnostic move against Keynes: the mistakes were made during the artificial boom (wrong capital projects, wrong worker locations); the bust is the market discovering the errors and reallocating resources. Stimulus that prolongs the boom prolongs the disease. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: The core cycle theory Hayek presented at LSE was not new with him -- it had first been laid out two decades earlier by his own teacher, in the book that founded modern Austrian monetary theory. Which earlier work is the doctrinal source?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's The Theory of Money and Credit
choices: Ludwig von Mises's The Theory of Money and Credit
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest
context: Mises's 1912 book applied Menger's marginalism to money and introduced the credit-expansion account of the cycle; Hayek's 1931 lectures are the mature LSE presentation. Bohm-Bawerk supplied the capital-theory backdrop; Menger the value theory; Wicksell the natural-rate-of-interest concept Mises then used -- all real, all upstream, but not the direct doctrinal source of ABCT. Source: Mises Institute, Prices and Production and Other Works.

question: Hayek's Prices and Production sparked the most famous methodological duel of interwar economics: Hayek's two-part review of a two-volume 1930 monetary treatise, then a counter-attack aimed at Hayek's own book. Which economist's treatise was Hayek reviewing?
answer: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
Irving Fisher's The Purchasing Power of Money
Arthur Pigou's The Economics of Welfare
context: Hayek's two-part critique of Keynes's Treatise on Money (1930) appeared in Economica in August 1931 and February 1932. Keynes's reply attacked Prices and Production rather than defending his Treatise, and in 1932 he abandoned the debate to write what became the 1936 General Theory. Fisher, Pigou, and Marshall are all real monetary or welfare theorists of the previous generation. Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: Rather than answer Hayek's critique of the Treatise on Money point-for-point, Keynes withdrew from the direct exchange in 1932 and spent the next four years rebuilding his monetary theory into a new book. Which book was the eventual result?
answer: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
The Economic Consequences of the Peace
How to Pay for the War
context: The General Theory (1936) replaced the Treatise as Keynes's monetary statement and became the founding text of Keynesian macroeconomics. The three distractors are all real Keynes works from other decades: Economic Consequences (1919), Tract (1923), How to Pay for the War (1940).
