Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: In September 1945 Friedrich A. Hayek published a short essay in the American Economic Review that has since become one of the most cited papers in the discipline. Its subject was how a market economy uses information that no single person possesses. What is the title of that essay?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: American Economic Review 35:4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London against the Central Planning Board scheme of Oskar Lange, and he made the case that the market's own prices carry knowledge no planner ever holds. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' turns on a single running parable: a shortage of one raw material suddenly arises somewhere in the world, and every user of that material across the globe economizes on it within days, without anyone giving an order and without more than a handful of people knowing the cause. Which raw material did Hayek choose for the parable?
context: Hayek picked tin because it was a genuine commodity of the day whose supply chain crossed empires -- the miner in Bolivia, the smelter in Malaya, the canner in Chicago. A single rising price on the London Metal Exchange told them all what a central planner could never have compiled: use less tin. Source: FEE, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay opens by rejecting the way most economists of his day framed the economic problem. They assumed, he wrote, that a competent authority already had all the relevant data. Hayek's counterclaim was that no such authority ever does, because of the specific character of the knowledge that economic decisions actually require. What one-word Hayek adjective describes that character of the knowledge?
context: Hayek's exact phrasing: the knowledge relevant to economic decisions 'never exists in concentrated or integrated form but solely as the dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals possess.' The point runs through the whole essay. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay coined a compact phrase for the individual actor who holds the immediately relevant local knowledge -- the mechanic who knows this particular lathe, the shopkeeper who knows the buyers on this particular street, the ship's captain who knows the loading conditions in this particular port. Which three-word phrase did he coin?
context: Hayek's argument: it is the man on the spot who has the knowledge of time and place that matters; even a perfectly benevolent central board cannot substitute for him, because his knowledge is precisely the sort that cannot be written up in a report and mailed to headquarters in time. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay was written explicitly as the answer to another economist who had claimed nine years earlier, in an essay in the Review of Economic Studies, that a Central Planning Board could 'play at markets' -- posting prices, raising them when queues form and lowering them when goods pile up -- and match a real market economy. Whose 1936 essay was Hayek answering?
answer: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
choices: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
Abba Lerner, The Economics of Control
Maurice Dobb, Political Economy and Capitalism
Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition
context: Lange's Part I appeared in RES in October 1936, Part II in February 1937. He famously opened with an ironic tribute to Ludwig von Mises as 'the great advocatus diaboli' of socialism. Hayek's 1945 answer was that Lange had missed the point: the market's prices aggregate knowledge that was never centrally gathered, so no board can duplicate them by trial-and-error alone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar R. Lange'.

question: The Mises 1920 formulation of the calculation problem and the Hayek 1945 formulation of the knowledge problem are usually described as two sides of the same coin. Mises's side emphasized what socialism lacks in institutions; Hayek's side emphasized what it lacks in information. What did Mises argue socialism specifically has no basis to do, because there are no market prices for the means of production?
answer: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
choices: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
Reward its most productive workers fairly
Distribute consumer goods on a per capita basis
context: Mises's 1920 essay Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen argued that without private ownership of the means of production there are no exchanges of them, so no prices, so no way to answer 'is it cheaper to build the railway of steel or of aluminium?' Hayek added: even if you tried to set trial-and-error prices, you would still not have the dispersed knowledge those prices normally aggregate. Source: Mises Institute, 'The End of Socialism and the Calculation Debate Revisited'.

question: On October 9, 1974 the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced that Friedrich A. Hayek would share that year's Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences with an economist whose views on central planning were nearly the opposite of his own. Who was the co-recipient?
context: The joint citation honoured 'pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations' and 'penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena'. Myrdal was a leading Swedish social-democratic policy intellectual; the Academy paired the two deliberately, and each spent his Nobel lecture disagreeing with the other. Source: NobelPrize.org, 'The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1974'.

question: In the summer of 1979 American drivers waited in queues that snaked around city blocks to buy gasoline; many states rationed by license-plate parity. From the standpoint of Friedrich Hayek's 1945 argument, what specifically had gone wrong at the pump?
answer: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
choices: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
The OPEC cartel had unilaterally halted all crude oil exports to the American market
The Federal Reserve had refused to expand the money supply enough to accommodate demand
The Environmental Protection Agency had banned all leaded gasoline sales without notice
context: The Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act of 1973 held domestic gasoline prices below the world price for the rest of the 1970s; the 1979 lines were the shortage the cap guaranteed. President Reagan lifted the controls in January 1981 and the queues vanished within weeks -- exactly the Hayekian prediction. Source: Institute for Energy Research, 'Price Controls and the 1970s Oil Crisis'.

question: In 1980 the American economist Thomas Sowell published a book-length restatement of Friedrich Hayek's three-page 1945 essay, extending the price-signal argument across politics, law, science, and everyday institutions. Hayek himself reviewed it as 'the best book on economics in many a year'. What was the title of the book?
context: Sowell wrote in the acknowledgements that no other single source had shaped his framework more than the 1945 Hayek essay. Knowledge and Decisions became the standard American undergraduate route into Hayekian economics, precisely because it puts the dispersed-knowledge point in terms an 18-year-old can grasp in one sitting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Austrian economists apply Friedrich Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument not only to visible price ceilings on goods but to a much larger and less visible price control -- the one that runs through the whole of modern finance. Which price do Austrians identify as itself being under a form of central price control by a national committee?
answer: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
choices: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
The retail price of gasoline, capped by the Department of Energy
The wage of federal contractors, floored by the Davis-Bacon Act
The exchange rate of the dollar, pegged by the Treasury
context: The Austrian argument, from Mises through Hayek to Rothbard: the interest rate is a price like any other -- the price of present goods in terms of future goods -- and when a central bank pushes it below the rate that would clear the loanable-funds market, it breaks the signal that would tell entrepreneurs whether long-lived projects can be sustained. This is the mechanism behind Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek reprinted his 1945 essay as the centerpiece of a 1948 University of Chicago Press collection, placing it alongside his earlier 1937 essay 'Economics and Knowledge' -- the more technical statement of the same argument, delivered originally as a Presidential Address to the London Economic Club. What was the one-word title of the 1948 collection?
choices: Studies in Philosophy, Politics and Economics
context: The 1948 volume was Hayek's own bid to fix the shape of the argument for postwar economists: 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) framed the problem, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) delivered it in a form any working economist could read in a lunch break, and the surrounding essays applied it to markets and planning. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Hayek: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)'.

question: In 1871 a 31-year-old Vienna civil servant who had spent the 1860s writing market news for the Wiener Zeitung published a slim book he hoped would win him a university chair. Two years later, in 1873, the University of Vienna handed him its chair of economic theory. Who was he?
context: Menger (1840-1921) reported on grain and stock prices for the Lemberger Zeitung and then the Wiener Zeitung in the 1860s -- watching real traders form prices in real time is where his subjective-value instinct came from. He joined the University of Vienna law faculty in 1872 and won the economic-theory chair in 1873. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Carl Menger's 1871 founding book of the Austrian School bore the German title Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre. What is its standard English title?
context: Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre translates literally as 'Foundations of the Theory of the National Economy,' but the standard English rendering has always been Principles of Economics -- confusingly sharing a title with Alfred Marshall's 1890 book. The English translation by James Dingwall and Bert F. Hoselitz did not appear until 1950. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Menger's 1871 Principles was published in Vienna by which German-language house?
context: Braumueller was a mid-sized Vienna academic publisher; Menger paid for the printing himself in the hope the book would open the university door -- which it did, two years later. Duncker und Humblot was the Berlin house of Schmoller and the German Historical School; Gustav Fischer of Jena published much of the later German-language economics literature. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: The same year Menger's Principles appeared in Vienna, an English economist independently published The Theory of Political Economy making the same core marginal-utility argument. Three years later, in 1874, a French economist teaching in Lausanne published Elements of Pure Economics doing the same again. Historians call the whole 1871-1874 cluster of THREE independent inventions by what name?
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none of the three knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection (1858) and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of history's clearest cases of parallel scientific invention. The Methodenstreit was Menger's LATER 1883 methodological quarrel with Schmoller; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalism; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: A student asks Menger why classical economists from Adam Smith to Karl Marx held that a good's value comes from the labor-hours it took to produce. Menger answers that they were looking in the wrong place -- value does not live in the good, it lives in the mind of a chooser at a moment ranking specific means against specific ends; the same loaf is worth more to a hungry man than to a full one. Which reasoning move does Menger press?
context: Menger's move was not to REFINE the labor theory but to REPLACE it. Adam Smith, David Ricardo, and Karl Marx all held labor-embodied theories in some form; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced them with subjective valuation. The quantity theory of money (Hume, Fisher, Friedman) explains price levels; comparative advantage (Ricardo 1817) explains trade -- neither is what Menger contributes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Classical economists were long puzzled that diamonds command a huge price while water, without which no one lives, commands almost none. Menger's marginal move dissolves the paradox by looking not at the total stock but at what?
answer: The next specific unit a chooser is ranking
choices: The next specific unit a chooser is ranking
The average labor-hours across all producers
The total quantity supplied in a year
The moral desert of the buyer
context: A chooser never ranks 'all water' against 'all diamonds'; he ranks the NEXT glass against the NEXT stone. Water is so abundant that the marginal glass is nearly worthless; diamonds are so scarce that the marginal stone is very valuable. Total utility is enormous for water and tiny for diamonds; the MARGINAL utility is the reverse -- and price tracks the margin. Adam Smith noticed the paradox in Wealth of Nations (1776); it took Menger, Jevons, and Walras 95 years to solve it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalism.

question: The German word Grenznutzen -- the label the whole tradition would carry -- appears nowhere in Menger's 1871 Principles. Who actually coined it, building on von Thuenen's earlier Grenzkosten (marginal cost)?
context: Wieser (1851-1926), one of Menger's two most important students, coined Grenznutzen to name a concept his teacher had already articulated in prose. Boehm-Bawerk, the other great student, developed capital and interest theory instead. The English 'marginal utility' is a direct translation of Wieser's German. So the school's most famous term was named by the pupil, not the founder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Menger wrote his 1871 Principles in continuous prose, with no equations, no graphs, and no curves -- a choice he defended as fitting the subject: economics investigates the essences of human choice, not their specific quantities. His pupils and their pupils (Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Rothbard) all kept this style. Which permanent marker of the Austrian tradition did that founding choice set?
answer: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
choices: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
Founding the discipline of experimental economics
Grounding claims in national statistical surveys
context: Menger's rejection of mathematical economics was not incidental; it was a claim about the SUBJECT -- since valuation is subjective and preferences are ordinal, false precision misleads more than it clarifies. Walras and Jevons, the co-inventors of marginalism, went the other way and built the mathematical tradition. Experimental economics (Vernon Smith, Nobel 2002) came a century later; large econometric models are Cowles Commission and Klein 1940s-60s; national statistical surveys are the German Historical School Menger's 1883 Methodenstreit book attacked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Menger drafted but never published a Volume 2 of Principles, intended to cover capital and interest. The book that occupies that missing volume's place in the Austrian corpus was written by his student instead, appearing as Kapital und Kapitalzins in the 1880s. Who filled the gap?
context: Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) wrote Kapital und Kapitalzins (Capital and Interest) in three volumes 1884-1889 -- history and critique of interest theories, positive theory of capital, and further essays -- effectively the Volume 2 Menger never produced. Boehm-Bawerk also served three terms as Austrian finance minister and taught the young Mises. Wieser wrote on marginal utility and social economics rather than capital; Mises and Machlup were of later generations. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: Menger's 1871 Principles founded the Austrian School in German. For 79 years there was no English edition -- the tradition traveled to America through Mises's students, not through the book itself. When did James Dingwall and Bert F. Hoselitz's English translation finally reach print through the Free Press?
context: The 1950 Free Press edition, with an introduction by Frank Knight, appeared 29 years after Menger's death (1921) and only after his student Hayek had already moved to LSE (1931) and then Chicago (1950). Frank Knight -- the great Chicago economist and Milton Friedman's teacher -- wrote the introduction. The 79-year gap is a measure of how far the German-speaking Austrian tradition had traveled before English-speaking economics noticed the founding text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: The founder of the Austrian School had a son named Karl who became a first-rate mathematician, belonged to the Vienna Circle of logical positivists, ran his own Mathematical Colloquium in interwar Vienna, and later spent decades teaching at the Illinois Institute of Technology. Which specific relationship did that son carry?
answer: Son of Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian School
choices: Son of Carl Menger, founder of the Austrian School
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985) did not follow his father into economics; he did mathematics, contributed to dimension theory, edited the Mathematical Colloquium proceedings that included work by Kurt Goedel and John von Neumann, and belonged to the Vienna Circle. So the Menger name reaches into TWO of interwar Vienna's great intellectual traditions -- Austrian economics through the father, mathematical positivism through the son. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: A Bitcoin miner's computer, trying to add a new block to the block chain, must find a specific number that, when combined with the block's contents, produces a scrambled fingerprint starting with a required number of zeros. What is the name of that specific number?
context: The 'nonce' (number-used-once) is what miners search for. Trillions of guesses per second per machine try different nonces until one produces a hash below the required difficulty target. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nonce.

question: There is only one way a miner's computer can find a valid nonce for a Bitcoin block: by trial and error at enormous speed. What is the everyday analogy Bitcoin educators use for this process?
context: Every guess is a lottery ticket; more hashing power means more tickets per second; the miner with the most tickets wins most often. First to find a valid nonce broadcasts the block and other miners immediately begin building on top of it. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: The specific cryptographic hash function Bitcoin uses to scramble each candidate block into its fingerprint was designed by the US National Security Agency and standardized in 2001. Which hash function is it?
context: SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) is a member of the SHA-2 family, published by NIST in 2001. Litecoin uses Scrypt; Ethereum used Ethash before the Merge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2.

question: The Bitcoin network adjusts the difficulty of the mining puzzle at a fixed schedule to keep block times close to ten minutes on average. At what interval does the difficulty adjust?
context: Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks (roughly two weeks at 10-minute blocks). If blocks came faster than expected, difficulty rises; slower, it falls. This is how Bitcoin auto-regulates against changes in aggregate mining power. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Difficulty.

question: To rewrite the Bitcoin block chain and reverse past transactions, an attacker would have to redo the proof-of-work of every block being rewritten AND keep outpacing the honest network going forward. In one shorthand, what share of network hashing power would the attacker have to command?
context: The classic 51% attack: an attacker with more hashing power than the rest of the network combined can, in principle, rewrite recent history. The energy is what makes such an attack expensive; that is the security. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-spending.

question: The energy Bitcoin miners burn is not incidental to the security of the network. In one shorthand, what specific role does that electricity play?
answer: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
choices: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
It is a byproduct of the transaction-processing bandwidth
It is a subsidy that pays for the developer-team infrastructure
It is the cooling cost of the servers that broadcast transactions
context: The economic barrier to attack is what real-world energy an attacker would have to burn to redo the work faster than the honest network. Defenders call this 'the energy IS the security.' Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: The specific consensus design Satoshi Nakamoto invented -- proof-of-work plus longest-chain rule -- is named for him and treated in computer-science literature as the first solution to a classic distributed-agreement problem. What is that classic problem called?
context: Byzantine Generals (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, 1982): how do untrusted, distributed parties reach agreement on a shared record without a central authority? Nakamoto Consensus is the first known solution using proof-of-work as the coordinating mechanism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault.

question: The named consensus design that combines proof-of-work with the rule that the honest chain is the one with the most cumulative work is called after Bitcoin's pseudonymous founder. What is it called?
context: 'Nakamoto Consensus' is the standard name in cryptography and computer-science literature for the proof-of-work + longest-chain rule Satoshi introduced with Bitcoin. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nakamoto_consensus.

question: When critics call Bitcoin mining 'wasteful,' defenders often reply that fiat-currency systems also cost enormous energy that is simply less visible. Which set of fiat-system energy costs do defenders typically point at?
answer: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
choices: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
Central bank cooling systems, satellite payment routing, and mint-vault air handling
Government subsidies to Bitcoin miners built into monetary policy operations
Federal Reserve academic research on money-supply forecasting
context: The defender's move: fiat's energy cost is spread across every branch, every armored truck, every printing plant, every ATM, every regulatory apparatus. Bitcoin makes its energy cost visible and concentrated; fiat hides its energy cost. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: A Bitcoin miner who finds a valid nonce and broadcasts a valid block collects a compound payment made of newly-issued coins plus fees on the transactions the block carries. What is the standard name for this payment?
context: 'Block reward' = newly-issued coins from the current issuance schedule plus fees on the transactions the miner has included in the block. Issuance falls to zero around 2140; by then miners live on fees alone. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Block_reward.

question: On September 15 2022 Ethereum completed the largest scheduled software upgrade ever performed on a live financial network, transitioning off proof-of-work. The upgrade has a one-word name in the Ethereum community. What is it?
context: The Merge (September 15 2022) joined Ethereum's execution layer with its already-live proof-of-stake beacon chain. Ethereum's energy consumption dropped by roughly 99.95% overnight. Source: ethereum.org/en/roadmap/merge.

question: The consensus mechanism Ethereum adopted at the Merge assigns the right to add the next block not by burning electricity but by locking up an amount of the cryptocurrency as collateral. What is this alternative consensus called?
context: Proof-of-stake (PoS): the right to propose the next block is assigned in proportion to staked collateral, not to burned electricity. Cardano, Solana, and most post-2018 chains launched with PoS from the start. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake.

question: Ethereum Foundation figures put the energy reduction from the September 15 2022 Merge at a very high specific percentage. About how much did Ethereum's energy consumption drop overnight?
context: The Ethereum Foundation's post-Merge figure is a roughly 99.95% cut in network electricity use. That is the strongest engineering argument PoS supporters make for the switch. Source: ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption.

question: Ethereum's founder has publicly favored proof-of-stake since roughly 2014, well before the Merge itself. Which founder is he?
context: Vitalik Buterin published the Ethereum white paper in late 2013 and has argued for proof-of-stake since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The Merge was the culmination of an eight-year design goal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin.

question: The most common Bitcoin-community critique of proof-of-stake is that it recreates a specific pre-Bitcoin monetary property that proof-of-work explicitly rejects. What is the property?
answer: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
choices: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
Requirement of a central government treasury for issuance
Dependence on trusted third-party settlement rails
Delegation of block production to a small licensed authority
context: The Bitcoin-community argument: whoever starts with the most tokens has the most power to add blocks, entrench their position, and shape network rules, without an external check equivalent to the electricity a PoW miner must burn. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: The Bitcoin-community critique of proof-of-stake as 'permissioned in disguise' rests on a specific attack economists call the 'nothing-at-stake' problem. What is that attack about?
answer: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
choices: Validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once, since no real-world resource is spent per signature
Validators can rewrite the block chain to their advantage without incurring any staking penalty
Validators can drop their staked collateral before their signatures are recorded
Validators can vote in proportion to their trading volume rather than their staked balance
context: Under PoW a miner can only mine one chain at a time (electricity is a real resource). Under naive PoS a validator can sign every fork simultaneously; the defense requires trusted checkpoints or slashing penalties that add complexity and trust assumptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake#Attacks.

question: In 2023 the chair of a specific US financial regulator suggested that many proof-of-stake tokens could fall under US investor-protection statutes because staking looks like an investment contract. Which US regulator was that?
context: Gary Gensler, then SEC chair, made this suggestion in public testimony in 2023; the SEC's PoS-token stance has since become a running legal question for Ethereum and other PoS chains. Source: sec.gov (Gensler public testimony 2023).

question: Bitcoin remains on proof-of-work as a core design principle. In the Bitcoin-community argument, the electricity cost is not a bug but which specific kind of feature?
answer: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
choices: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
A regulatory-compliance cost that satisfies environmental disclosure rules
A liquidity provision that reduces short-run mining-fee volatility
A payment to network engineers who maintain node infrastructure
context: The Nakamoto-Consensus defense: the electricity is what makes Bitcoin's security depend on something outside the network's own token economics. Proof-of-stake keeps costs internal and depends on economic incentives among token holders. Source: mises.org/library/proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake.

question: The proof-of-work vs proof-of-stake debate is one of the largest live economic-engineering contrasts in cryptocurrency. Both sides made real bets in 2022. In one sentence, what will decide which was right?
answer: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
choices: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
Whether central banks issue their own digital currencies competing with both
Whether the SEC issues a definitive ruling on token classification
Whether major derivative exchanges list futures on both consensus mechanisms
context: The empirical verdict on PoW vs PoS security will require decades of live operation across real attacks, market crashes, and regulatory pressure. Bitcoin has fifteen years of proof-of-work data; Ethereum's proof-of-stake has three post-Merge years. Source: mises.org/library/pow-pos-empirical.

question: Two named cryptocurrencies persisted on proof-of-work well past the 2022 Merge, both technical descendants of Bitcoin. Which pair are they?
context: Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee) and Dogecoin (2013, Billy Markus & Jackson Palmer) are Scrypt-based PoW coins descended from Bitcoin's codebase. Cardano, Solana, Polkadot, and Avalanche all use PoS variants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litecoin.

question: In 1966 an economist at the University of Virginia founded a small scholarly journal to publish work that mainstream economics journals were reluctant to touch -- namely the economic analysis of political actors. Who was the founder?
context: Tullock, a lawyer by training, was one of the founders of public choice theory alongside James Buchanan. Buchanan would later win the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics for the field's development. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Gordon Tullock's 1966 journal originally carried a longer descriptive title before being renamed to the two-word name that would attach to the entire discipline. What was the ORIGINAL title?
context: The journal renamed itself 'Public Choice' in 1969, and the new name became the label for the whole scholarly field. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Gordon Tullock's journal Public Choice was originally published under the auspices of the Center for Study of Public Choice, which he and James Buchanan led. Which university hosted the center at the journal's founding?
context: The center was originally at the University of Virginia, moved to Virginia Tech, and then followed Buchanan to George Mason in 1983 -- an unusual case of a research center migrating with its founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: One year before Gordon Tullock founded his journal in 1966, he and James Buchanan founded a scholarly society to convene public-choice researchers. What is its current name?
choices: The National Bureau of Economic Research
context: Founded 1965 as the Committee on Non-Market Decision Making. The society hosts an annual conference; the European Public Choice Society (1972) and Public Choice Society of Japan (1996) followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: Public Choice as a discipline was ratified by a specific award to one of its co-founders in 1986. What was awarded, and to whom?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
The John Bates Clark Medal, to Gordon Tullock
The Presidential Medal of Freedom, to William Niskanen
The Manhattan Institute Hayek Prize, to Anthony de Jasay
context: The Nobel-adjacent prize (usually just called the Nobel Prize in Economics). Buchanan's citation credited his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for economic and political decision-making. Tullock never received the prize, an omission still noted by public-choice scholars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/James_M._Buchanan.

question: By 2020 Public Choice was cited across economics, political science, sociology, and law. Its early pages laid down the intellectual scaffolding of a whole field. Which cluster of concepts is characteristic of the field's contribution?
answer: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
choices: Rent-seeking, logrolling, bureaucratic behavior, constitutional political economy, expressive voting
Aggregate demand, marginal propensity to consume, Phillips curve, IS-LM
General equilibrium, comparative statics, Walrasian auctioneer, Edgeworth box
Mean-variance optimization, capital asset pricing model, efficient markets
context: Tullock coined 'rent-seeking' in 1967 in a Public Choice paper. Niskanen 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government' (1971) worked out bureaucratic behavior. Buchanan-Tullock 'The Calculus of Consent' (1962) had already introduced constitutional political economy. All worked out first in the journal before diffusing more widely. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_choice.

question: On August 16, 1937, a US president who had done more than any other to strengthen PRIVATE-sector unions -- signing the Wagner Act two years earlier -- wrote a letter warning that collective bargaining 'as usually understood, cannot be transplanted into the public service.' Which president wrote that letter?
context: Franklin D. Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, President of the National Federation of Federal Employees, on August 16, 1937. Roosevelt considered a public-sector strike 'unthinkable and intolerable.' Source: presidency.ucsb.edu (Roosevelt letter to Steward, 1937).

question: Franklin D. Roosevelt's 1937 argument against transplanting collective bargaining into government identified a specific structural difference across the two contexts. What kind of counterparty sits across the bargaining table in a commercial firm but is REPLACED in a public-sector negotiation?
context: In the private sector, wage demands trade off against the employer's profits and the firm's competitive survival. In the public sector, the employer is a taxpayer-funded entity whose ultimate check-writer is the same voter the union spends dues to influence. Source: Roosevelt letter (1937).

question: By 2010, US public-sector union density had reached a level more than four times that of the private sector. Roughly what share of public-sector workers were union members?
context: In 2010, public-sector union density was ~36% while private-sector density had fallen to ~7%. The gap reflects both public-sector expansion after Kennedy's Executive Order 10988 (1962) and long-running private-sector decline. Source: bls.gov (union-membership historical series).

question: In February-March 2011 the governor of Wisconsin proposed and the legislature enacted a state law sharply limiting public-sector collective bargaining, ending automatic dues deduction, and requiring annual union recertification. What was that governor's name?
context: Scott Walker's Act 10 passed in March 2011 after weeks of massive protest at the state capitol and a Democratic-senator walkout to Illinois to deny quorum. The Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the law in July 2014. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Wisconsin_Act_10.

question: During the fight over Wisconsin Act 10 in early 2011, Democratic state senators fled to Illinois to prevent a quorum from being reached on the bill. What was the immediate procedural purpose of that walkout?
answer: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
choices: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
To lobby the federal Department of Labor for intervention
To organize with unions on the Illinois-Wisconsin border
To evade personal fines imposed by Walker
context: The Wisconsin state constitution required a quorum for fiscal legislation. Democratic senators crossed the state line to make that quorum unreachable, delaying but not ultimately preventing passage. Source: madison.com and wisconsinwatch.org (2011 protest coverage).

question: In the years after Wisconsin Act 10 took effect, public-sector union membership in Wisconsin fell substantially. Which large state teachers' union lost most of its members within a few years?
choices: The New York State United Teachers
context: WEAC lost the majority of its members after the end of automatic dues deduction and mandatory annual recertification votes. It is the clearest measured effect of Act 10 on public-sector union density. Source: journalsentinel.com (WEAC membership coverage 2013-16).

question: On June 27, 2018 the Supreme Court decided a case holding that non-member public-sector employees could not be required to pay 'agency fees' to unions bargaining on their behalf. What was that case called?
choices: Abood v. Detroit Board of Education
context: Janus v. AFSCME Council 31, 585 US ___ (2018), overturned the 1977 Abood decision. Mandatory agency fees to public-sector unions violate the First Amendment because all public-sector collective bargaining is inherently political. Source: supremecourt.gov (Janus 585 US).

question: The California pension fund CalPERS holds pension assets for state employees and is the largest US public pension fund. Its unfunded pension liabilities have remained a genuine long-term fiscal concern for the state. Roughly what size of assets does it manage in the mid-2020s?
context: The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) manages approximately $460 billion in the mid-2020s. Its unfunded liabilities remain a fiscal concern reflecting the long-term public-sector-union bargaining pattern FDR warned about. Source: calpers.ca.gov (annual financial reports).

question: The FDR-1937 structural diagnosis, combined with Olson's collective-action framework, identifies a UNIQUE feature of public-sector union incentives that private-sector unions cannot replicate. What is that unique feature?
answer: The union spends dues to elect the officials who then negotiate with the union
choices: The union spends dues to elect the officials who then negotiate with the union
The union always represents a majority of workers by law
The union is prohibited from ever going on strike
The union receives federal matching funds automatically
context: Private-sector union dues cannot select the CEO across the bargaining table. Public-sector union dues can and do help select the mayor, governor, or school-board members who then negotiate. That is the circle FDR flagged in 1937. Source: Roosevelt letter (1937); Freeman + Ichniowski (1988).

question: The recognition-move the FDR-Wisconsin case teaches is a general principle about interest groups. Whenever a group spends resources both on political influence and on negotiation with a counterparty whose selection it partly determines, what happens to standard bargaining-model logic?
answer: It breaks down because the group is effectively bargaining with itself
choices: It breaks down because the group is effectively bargaining with itself
It becomes more efficient than any private negotiation
It always produces zero surplus for both sides
context: The Olson + Stigler combined diagnosis: concentrated interest + captured counterparty gives you a single institutional structure where standard adversarial-bargaining assumptions fail. FDR saw the shape in 1937; the modern literature formalized it. Source: Olson (1965); Stigler (1971); DiSalvo, Government Against Itself (Oxford 2015).

question: On November 25 2008, in the middle of the financial crisis, the Federal Reserve announced it would buy $500 billion of mortgage-backed securities and $100 billion of agency debt. This was the first large-scale asset-purchase program. What is it now called?
context: QE1 was launched November 25 2008 and expanded in March 2009. It ran until June 2010 at a total commitment of about $1.75 trillion. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The initial November 2008 program was expanded in March 2009 to include $300 billion in long-term Treasuries and to grow the mortgage-backed-security purchases to $1.25 trillion. What was the total commitment when the program ended in June 2010?
context: QE1's total commitment was $1.75 trillion when the program wound down in June 2010: $1.25T in MBS, $300B in Treasuries, and $200B in agency debt. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: Quantitative easing works mechanically by having the Fed pay for bond purchases with a specific kind of newly created liability on its own books. What does the Fed create when it buys a bond?
answer: New bank reserves credited to the seller's Fed account
choices: New bank reserves credited to the seller's Fed account
New Treasury bills issued alongside the purchase
New physical paper notes printed and shipped
context: When the Fed buys a bond from a primary dealer, it pays with newly created reserves credited to the dealer's Fed account -- reserves that did not exist before the purchase. This is monetary base expansion at its most direct. Source: federalreservehistory.org 'Quantitative Easing'.

question: The Fed's balance sheet grew from roughly $900 billion in September 2008 to a specific much larger figure by mid-2010, when QE1 wound down. What did it reach?
context: The Fed's balance sheet more than doubled from about $900 billion pre-crisis to about $2.3 trillion by mid-2010. This 150%+ expansion in two years was unprecedented in peacetime. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2010).

question: The Cantillon-effect insight -- that newly created money enters the economy at specific points and benefits the first recipients before it reaches later recipients -- was first published in the 1730s by a specific Irish-born banker who had traded John Law's Mississippi Bubble. Who was he?
context: Richard Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734), an Irish-born banker who shorted John Law's bubble before it collapsed, wrote his Essai in the 1730s. It was published posthumously in 1755. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: Applied to QE1, the Cantillon-effect analysis names a specific group as the first receivers of the newly created bank reserves. Who benefits first, at the Fed-dealer interface?
answer: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
choices: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
Low-income wage earners on fixed hourly rates
Retirees living on Social Security benefits
context: The new money enters at the Fed-dealer transaction. Asset prices (stocks, real estate, corporate bonds) rose sharply through 2009-10 while wages stagnated -- textbook first-receiver benefit. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Mainstream defenders of QE1 -- Bernanke's memoirs, Paul Krugman's blog commentary -- argued the program had a specific effect during 2008-09 that prevented a worse outcome. What did they credit it with?
answer: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
choices: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
Preventing the collapse of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
context: The defense: absent QE1, mortgage markets would have seized, rates would have spiked, and housing would have crashed further. Whether this defense holds up depends on counterfactuals nobody can run. Source: Bernanke, The Courage to Act (2015).

question: The term 'quantitative easing' was not invented by the Federal Reserve. It was borrowed from an earlier central-bank program in another country. Which country pioneered the term?
answer: Japan, in the Bank of Japan's 2001-06 program
choices: Japan, in the Bank of Japan's 2001-06 program
Switzerland, in a 1990s Swiss National Bank program
Sweden, in a Riksbank program of the 1980s
Britain, in a 1970s Bank of England program
context: The Bank of Japan ran quantitative easing 2001-2006 to fight deflation. Bernanke borrowed the label. He reportedly preferred 'credit easing' but the QE label stuck. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank of Japan' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian critics predicted throughout QE1 that the program was a monetary-financing operation whose consumer-price consequences would arrive on a delayed schedule. Which three Austrian-tradition voices most publicly made this prediction in 2008-2010?
answer: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
choices: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Ben Bernanke
Larry Summers, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz, and Alan Meltzer
context: Schiff on television, Murphy at the Mises Institute, and James Grant in Grant's Interest Rate Observer all publicly warned that the delay between monetary expansion and consumer-price adjustment did not mean the mechanism was broken. The 2021-23 wave was consistent with their long-horizon call. Source: mises.org and Grant's Interest Rate Observer archive.

question: The 2008 QE1 launch marks the start of what analysts now call the balance-sheet era of central banking. Which recognition move does the ladder press about this era?
answer: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
choices: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
Central banks always fully unwind emergency programs within two years
Balance-sheet expansion is neutral because commercial banks control final money creation
Central-bank asset purchases affect only bond markets and never asset prices generally
context: QE1 was framed as an emergency. Seventeen years later, three additional rounds have followed, along with two massive 2020 pandemic-era expansions. Emergency practice has become standing doctrine. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: On November 3 2010 the Federal Reserve announced a second round of large-scale asset purchases -- $600 billion in longer-term Treasury securities at a pace of $75 billion per month through June 2011. What is this second round known as?
context: QE2 pushed the Fed's balance sheet from about $2.3 trillion to about $2.9 trillion by mid-2011. It was the second round in what would become a multi-decade balance-sheet policy tool. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: One day after the November 3 2010 announcement, Ben Bernanke did something unusual for a Fed chair: he published an op-ed defending the new program directly to the general public. In which newspaper did he publish?
context: Bernanke's November 4 2010 op-ed in The Washington Post was titled 'What the Fed Did and Why: Supporting the Recovery and Sustaining Price Stability.' Using a newspaper op-ed to defend Fed policy was itself a break from tradition of speaking only through official channels. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: The most controversial passage in the 2010 op-ed explicitly named a market Bernanke expected the second round to boost as part of its transmission channel. Which market did he say the program would help?
answer: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
choices: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
The residential real-estate market, which he said would boost construction jobs
The commodity market, which he said would raise farm incomes
The auto market, which he said would help Detroit
context: Bernanke wrote: 'higher stock prices will boost consumer wealth and help increase confidence, which can also spur spending.' It was one of the first explicit public admissions that the Fed intended its policy to boost equity values. Source: Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: The transmission mechanism Bernanke named in his 2010 op-ed -- higher asset prices boosting consumer confidence and spending -- has a standard name in economics. What is it called?
context: The wealth effect is the standard economic label for higher household net worth leading to higher spending. Its invocation by Bernanke made explicit what critics had said was implicit in QE all along: the Fed was targeting asset prices. Source: Grokipedia 'Wealth effect' (2026-09-05).

question: In an unusually blunt German reaction to the 2010 Fed program, one specific Cabinet-level German official gave an interview calling QE2 'clueless.' Who called it that?
context: Schauble, then German Finance Minister under Angela Merkel, called QE2 'clueless' in a 2010 Der Spiegel interview. He argued the program would export inflation to Europe and destabilize the emerging-market dollar bloc. Source: Grokipedia 'Wolfgang Schauble' (2026-09-05).

question: In August 2011 the Texas governor and 2012 Republican presidential candidate attacked the Fed chair at a campaign event, calling his policy 'almost treasonous' if he printed more money before the election. Which governor said this?
context: Perry made the remark at an August 2011 campaign event in Iowa. It became one of the defining moments of Perry's brief 2012 run and marked one of the first times a Republican presidential candidate publicly attacked a sitting Fed chair by name. Source: Grokipedia 'Rick Perry' (2026-09-05).

question: The Cantillon-effect payoff of QE2 was visible on the tape between its November 2010 announcement and its June 2011 conclusion. What did the S&P 500 do over that seven-month window?
context: The S&P 500 gained roughly 24% from the November 3 2010 QE2 announcement through the program's June 2011 end. The wealth effect Bernanke had named publicly was operating exactly as promised -- for those who owned equities. Source: Grokipedia 'S&P 500' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2010 QE2 episode is a paradigmatic Bastiat-pattern moment. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures its structure?
answer: Seen: the recovery is strengthening; Unseen: the new reserves are flowing into asset prices, not wages or productive investment
choices: Seen: the recovery is strengthening; Unseen: the new reserves are flowing into asset prices, not wages or productive investment
Seen: full employment achieved; Unseen: currency devaluation abroad
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: rising savings; Unseen: falling consumption
context: The visible outcome (S&P 500 +24%) was framed as recovery. The invisible mechanism -- new reserves flowing directly to first-receivers who owned equities -- was the actual causal channel. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The 2010 op-ed set a template that every subsequent QE round would follow: publicly cite the wealth-effect channel as part of the justification. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: A central bank's public admission that it is targeting asset prices makes that goal a permanent, unhidden feature of policy
choices: A central bank's public admission that it is targeting asset prices makes that goal a permanent, unhidden feature of policy
Public op-eds by central bankers rarely reveal actual policy targets
Wealth-effect transmission has no long-term distributional consequences
Central bank asset-price targeting works best when kept secret
context: After the 2010 op-ed, no serious observer could claim the Fed was not targeting equity values. Every subsequent QE round openly invoked the wealth-effect channel. The distributional implications -- who owns stocks, who does not -- became visible and permanent. Source: Bernanke, Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: The 2010 op-ed is also notable as one of the first modern instances of a central-bank chair breaking from Fed tradition on public communications. Which tradition did he break?
answer: The Fed's tradition of speaking only through official statements and formal congressional testimony
choices: The Fed's tradition of speaking only through official statements and formal congressional testimony
The Fed's tradition of publishing monthly balance-sheet reports
The Fed's tradition of holding secret FOMC meetings
The Fed's tradition of coordinating with the European Central Bank
context: Prior Fed chairs generally avoided newspaper op-eds. Bernanke's decision to argue directly to the general public via the Washington Post marked a shift toward more overt political communication. Subsequent chairs (Yellen, Powell) have all made increasing use of public commentary channels. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve System' (2026-09-05).

question: For centuries, villagers on a Micronesian island used massive round limestone discs as their circulating money -- some over 12 feet across and weighing several tons. Which island is famous for this monetary system?
context: The Yap Islands are a small group in Micronesia. Their traditional currency, the rai, is one of the most distinctive monetary systems ever recorded. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: The limestone discs used as money on Yap had to be transported by outrigger canoe from a quarry on another island roughly 250 miles away. On which island were they quarried?
context: Yap has no limestone; the rai were carved from aragonite in Palau and transported by long open-ocean canoe voyage. The difficulty of transport was itself part of what made each stone valuable. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: Once a giant rai stone was installed on Yap, it was generally too heavy to move for later transactions. When ownership changed hands, how did the transfer actually take place?
answer: By public community agreement that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed put
choices: By public community agreement that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed put
By carving the new owner's name onto the stone's surface
By moving the stone to a central marketplace once a year
By breaking off a small piece and giving it to the new owner
context: The ledger was social memory: everyone in the village simply agreed, and the transfer was complete. Physical possession and ownership were decoupled. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: In a famous Yap incident, a canoe crew was bringing a particularly large rai back from the quarry when a storm arose and the stone slid into the sea, sinking to the bottom. What did the islanders subsequently decide about it?
answer: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
choices: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
They declared the crew liable for the full value in fish and taro
They dived down to retrieve fragments over the next generation
They classified it as destroyed and removed it from the record
context: The crew's testimony to the stone's exact size and quality was enough. The rai continued to circulate through community memory even though it was hundreds of feet under the Pacific. Source: William Henry Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: A famous American monetary economist retold the Yap sunken-stone story in a 1991 essay and drew a direct parallel to how the Federal Reserve holds gold at Fort Knox. Which economist wrote that essay?
context: Friedman's 1991 essay 'The Island of Stone Money' was later collected in his 1992 book Money Mischief. The Yap story became one of his favorite teaching devices. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: Friedman's Yap essay cited a real 1932-33 case in which one central bank shifted gold ownership across national accounts without the physical metal leaving a single building in New York. Whose vault was it?
answer: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
The Bank of England in London
The Bank for International Settlements in Basel
The Bank of France in Paris
context: When France wanted to convert dollar claims to gold, staff at the New York Fed simply moved gold bars from a drawer labeled 'US' to a drawer labeled 'France' inside the same vault. National ownership changed; the metal did not move. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: The deep lesson Milton Friedman drew from Yap -- and that the cypherpunks later drew -- was a specific claim about the fundamental nature of money. Which claim?
answer: Money is a ledger; the physical medium is only a container for social agreement about who owns what
choices: Money is a ledger; the physical medium is only a container for social agreement about who owns what
Money must be issued by a sovereign to have value
Money is worthless unless backed one-to-one by gold in a vault
Money is fundamentally a religious or ceremonial object
context: Once you accept that the ledger is the money, the shape of the container -- stone disc, gold bar, paper note, database entry -- is a secondary engineering choice. This is the conceptual bridge from rai to Bitcoin. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: In the Bitcoin architecture the community memory that Yap villagers held collectively is replaced by a specific technical mechanism -- a distributed ledger enforced not by memory but by mathematics. What is that ledger called?
context: Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 design replaces trusted human memory with a chain of cryptographically linked blocks that every node holds a copy of. The rai villagers' shared verbal record becomes a mathematical public record. Source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008).

question: The Yap-to-Bitcoin bridge that Friedman set up teaches a specific recognition move about monetary innovation. Which move?
answer: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
choices: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
Only physical scarcity can back a real currency
Cryptography cannot replace the role of a sovereign
Monetary systems always fail when the physical medium is lost
context: Once money is understood as a ledger, moving from community memory to cryptographic memory is a technology upgrade, not a change in category. The Yap sunken stone is functionally the same object as an unspent Bitcoin output on the blockchain. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out: The Origins of Money (2002).

question: One additional feature the rai system shared with Bitcoin, which most historical monies lack, is a specific kind of costly and verifiable production process. What did rai and Bitcoin both require?
answer: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
choices: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
A licensed sovereign mint to stamp each unit
A physical backing in an underlying commodity
Continuous inflation to keep supply growing
context: Nick Szabo argued that a rai's cost of production (quarry, carve, canoe across open ocean) is a physical analog of Bitcoin's proof-of-work (electricity spent on cryptographic hashing). Both systems make new supply hard, and past supply cheap to verify. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out (2002).

question: On December 10, 2008, in the middle of the financial crisis, the operator of the largest Ponzi scheme in US history -- worth about $65 billion in nominal value -- confessed to his sons and was arrested the next day. Who was he?
context: Bernard Madoff ran the largest financial fraud in US history through his investment-advisory business. He confessed on December 10, 2008, was arrested December 11, and sentenced to 150 years in June 2009. Source: sec.gov (Madoff litigation releases).

question: As early as May 2000 a quantitative analyst working for a Madoff competitor figured out that Madoff's reported returns were mathematically impossible and filed his first formal SEC complaint. Who was that whistleblower?
context: Harry Markopolos was a quantitative analyst at Rampart Investment Management. He determined by May 2000 that Madoff's steady ~1% monthly returns could not be produced by any real trading strategy. Source: Markopolos, No One Would Listen (Wiley 2010).

question: In November 2005 Harry Markopolos submitted his most detailed complaint yet to the SEC -- a 19-page filing running 29 numbered red flags. What title did he give the submission?
answer: The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud
choices: The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud
A Quantitative Investigation of Impossible Returns
context: Markopolos's November 7, 2005 submission was titled 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud,' 19 pages with 29 red flags and mathematical proofs. The SEC opened but did not adequately pursue the investigation. Source: sec.gov (Markopolos submissions).

question: Over eight years before Madoff's 2008 confession, Harry Markopolos filed multiple detailed complaints warning the SEC. Roughly how many substantive complaints did the SEC receive about Madoff between 1992 and 2008 without acting effectively on any of them?
context: The SEC Inspector General's 2009 post-mortem report found approximately six substantive complaints raising significant red flags about Madoff between 1992 and 2008. None was adequately investigated. Source: sec.gov (OIG Report No. 509, August 31, 2009).

question: The SEC's 2009 Office of Inspector General post-mortem report identified several specific failures in the agency's handling of the Madoff complaints. Which of the following was one of the standard failure modes named in the report?
answer: Junior staff assigned to complex complaints they lacked training to evaluate
choices: Junior staff assigned to complex complaints they lacked training to evaluate
Senior enforcement staff were fired for insubordination
The agency's Enforcement Division was disbanded
The complainant refused to speak to investigators
context: The OIG Report 509 (August 31, 2009) documented junior staff assignments, missed basic verification steps (a single call to DTCC would have revealed Madoff was not actually trading the volumes he claimed), and misunderstanding of the alleged strategy. Source: sec.gov OIG Report 509.

question: Bernard Madoff's establishment status in American finance was unusual for a Ponzi operator. What senior role had he held at a major US stock market in the early 1990s?
choices: President of the New York Stock Exchange
Head of the Chicago Board Options Exchange
context: Madoff served as chairman of NASDAQ in the early 1990s -- an establishment credential that made SEC skepticism of a whistleblower's complaint about him structurally harder. Stigler's capture theory predicts exactly this pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Madoff.

question: Harry Markopolos's book about the eight-year effort to get the SEC to investigate Madoff was published by Wiley in 2010. What title did Markopolos give the book?
context: Harry Markopolos, No One Would Listen: A True Financial Thriller (Wiley, 2010). The book documents the whole sequence from Markopolos's side, from his May 2000 discovery through Madoff's arrest. Source: wiley.com (Markopolos 2010).

question: The Madoff Ponzi's nominal value was reported as $65 billion, but this included fictitious returns credited to accounts. What was the approximate actual investor cash-in loss (principal) from the scheme?
context: Actual investor cash-in losses (principal) totaled approximately $18B, while the $65B figure included years of fictitious returns credited to statements. The Madoff Recovery Fund has recovered a substantial portion of the principal for victims. Source: madofftrustee.com (Picard trustee reports).

question: After the Madoff case exposed the SEC's failure to act on whistleblower tips, Congress created a new bounty program in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act to route around the capture problem. What percentage bounty range does the SEC Office of the Whistleblower offer on qualifying tips?
answer: Ten to thirty percent of monetary sanctions
choices: Ten to thirty percent of monetary sanctions
One to two percent of the fraud size
context: The SEC Office of the Whistleblower (created in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act) offers 10-30% of monetary sanctions above $1M for actionable tips leading to enforcement action. It is an institutional attempt to align incentives with fraud detection. Source: sec.gov/whistleblower.

question: The SEC-Madoff failure is not primarily a story of incompetence or of individual corruption. In George Stigler's 1971 framework, what best explains the pattern of ignored warnings?
answer: Staff incentives -- career, avoiding embarrassing establishment cases, revolving-door -- did not align with fraud detection
choices: Staff incentives -- career, avoiding embarrassing establishment cases, revolving-door -- did not align with fraud detection
The SEC was infiltrated by Madoff's family members
SEC staff genuinely believed Madoff's math was correct
The SEC lacked any legal authority to investigate Madoff
context: Stigler's 1971 capture theory predicts that regulators tend to identify with, defer to, and hire from established regulated figures. The SEC's staff incentive structure did not reward embarrassing a former NASDAQ chairman. Markopolos, an outsider, was on the wrong side of that capture. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); SEC OIG Report 509 (2009).

question: The recognition-move the Madoff case teaches applies whenever a regulator receives repeated warnings about a well-connected industry figure and repeatedly fails to act. What structural question should the analyst ask?
answer: Whose specific career interests are served by NOT investigating this figure
choices: Whose specific career interests are served by NOT investigating this figure
Whether the whistleblower is entitled to a share of any eventual fine
Whether the regulator's paint scheme is up to date
Whether the whistleblower's college degree is from the right school
context: Stigler-style capture analysis: work out which specific decision-makers stand to lose or gain from an investigation. When the answer is that the decision-makers see mostly downside from investigating a well-connected figure, expect systematic under-enforcement. Source: Stigler (1971); Kwak, 'Cultural Capture and the Financial Crisis' (2013).

question: For four decades one federal agency decided which American airlines could fly which routes at which fares, and never once let a new trunk-line carrier enter the market. In 1978 President Carter signed a law dismantling the agency's power. Which regulator had ruled the skies until then?
context: The CAB, created in 1938, controlled airline routes and fares until the Airline Deregulation Act (October 24, 1978, Carter). Real airfares fell dramatically over the next two decades. Source: brookings.edu (Kahn + Deregulation history).

question: The 1978 Airline Deregulation Act was championed by an economist President Carter appointed to chair the very agency he ended up dismantling. Which economist ran the CAB from 1977 to 1978?
context: Alfred Kahn (1917-2010), a Cornell regulatory economist, chaired the CAB 1977-78 and led its dismantling. He is remembered as the father of airline deregulation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_E._Kahn.

question: The oldest federal regulatory agency was created in 1887 to protect shippers from what were then called the railroad monopolies. Historian Gabriel Kolko's 1963 Triumph of Conservatism documented that the railroads themselves had lobbied to create it. Which agency was Kolko writing about?
context: The ICC (1887) was the first modern US regulatory agency. Kolko's Triumph of Conservatism (Free Press, 1963) argued incumbent railroads lobbied for it to stabilize rates and prevent price-cutting competition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission.

question: The 1934 Communications Act created a federal agency to allocate broadcast spectrum. Once granted, its broadcast licenses became worth millions, and holders lobbied fiercely to prevent competing licenses and to block new technologies like cable television. Which agency issued those licenses?
context: The FCC was created by the 1934 Communications Act, replacing the earlier 1927 Federal Radio Commission. Broadcast-license politics is a classic capture case: cable TV was delayed for years by broadcaster opposition mediated through the FCC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission.

question: Two years after airline deregulation, President Carter signed a second landmark law breaking up rate and route regulation of another transportation industry. The Motor Carrier Act of 1980 deregulated which sector?
context: The Motor Carrier Act of 1980, signed July 1, 1980, deregulated interstate trucking rates and routes, ending decades of ICC-set trucking rates. Truckload shipping costs fell substantially over the following decade. Source: brookings.edu (Motor Carrier Act history).

question: The Food and Drug Administration shows a somewhat different capture pattern -- not so much industry lobbying for the agency's creation as senior FDA officials leaving to work for the pharmaceutical companies they had regulated. What is the standard name for this pattern?
context: The revolving door: senior agency officials rotate into industry positions at companies they previously regulated. GAO studies (2007 and later) documented systematic migration between FDA reviewers and the pharmaceutical industry. Source: gao.gov (FDA post-employment reports).

question: Two federal bank regulators missed enormous accumulating risks in mortgage lending during the years leading up to the 2008 financial crisis. Post-crisis studies documented extensive personnel flow between their staff and the banks they regulated. Which pair of agencies is generally singled out in that critique?
answer: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC
choices: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC
The Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department
The Securities and Exchange Commission and the CFTC
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and HUD
context: The OCC (chartering and supervising national banks) and the FDIC (insuring deposits and supervising state non-Fed member banks) both faced heavy post-crisis criticism for capture and revolving-door personnel flows. Source: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report (2011).

question: The term 'regulatory capture' predates George Stigler's 1971 formal theory. Which political scientist used the phrase in a 1955 book on the life-cycle of American regulatory agencies?
context: Marver Bernstein, Regulating Business by Independent Commission (Princeton University Press, 1955), introduced the four-stage life cycle: gestation, youth, maturity, and old age -- with capture occurring in the maturity phase. Source: press.princeton.edu (Bernstein 1955).

question: By reputation the ICC, CAB, and FCC each fit the same historical pattern: an agency created to serve the public interest that ended up serving the industry it regulated. What single sentence best captures the shared story?
answer: Industry incumbents captured the agency and used it to restrict entry by new competitors
choices: Industry incumbents captured the agency and used it to restrict entry by new competitors
The agency's staff turned against the industry and imposed heavy fines each year
Congress abolished each agency within a decade of its founding
Consumers seized the regulatory process through mass grassroots organizing
context: The common thread across the ICC, CAB, and FCC: agencies whose original public-interest justification gradually gave way to protecting incumbent firms against new entrants. Stigler's 1971 paper formalized the pattern as theory. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kolko, Triumph of Conservatism (1963).

question: A high-school student asks how one would DETECT capture in a specific agency without relying on ideology. Which empirical marker does the Bernstein-Stigler-Peltzman tradition treat as the strongest single indicator?
answer: The agency systematically blocks new entrants while protecting incumbents' profits
choices: The agency systematically blocks new entrants while protecting incumbents' profits
The agency's budget grows year over year
The agency issues detailed technical regulations
The agency has a large research staff
context: Capture is measured by outcomes, not intent. If regulation systematically raises incumbent profits and blocks new competitors, the regulation is functioning like an industry-serving barrier, whatever its stated purpose. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006).

question: In the decades since Stigler's 1971 paper, empirical scholars have applied his capture theory across dozens of specific US regulatory agencies. What has the broad pattern of that literature been?
answer: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
choices: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
Stigler's theory holds only for transportation regulators, not others
Stigler's theory has been refuted by studies of environmental agencies
Stigler's theory applies only in states with weak public-service ethics
context: From transportation to broadcasting to banking to occupational licensing, empirical work has confirmed the Stigler-Peltzman pattern of incumbent-serving regulation. The theory is now standard even outside the Chicago tradition. Source: Levine + Forrence, Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization (1990); Carpenter + Moss, Preventing Regulatory Capture (Cambridge 2014).

question: A City Council proposes freezing rents on existing apartments to keep housing affordable. In Bastiat's framing, the seen effect is that current tenants pay less month to month. What is the primary unseen effect on the housing stock?
answer: Apartment buildings a developer would have built are never built because future rents are capped below construction cost
choices: Apartment buildings a developer would have built are never built because future rents are capped below construction cost
Apartment buildings already in place are seized by the state under compulsory-purchase orders
Apartment buildings switch to office use because commercial leases pay more per square foot
Apartment buildings raise their prices to cover a mandatory rent-control administrative fee
context: The classic price-ceiling result: capping future rents below construction cost stops the pipeline of new buildings; the units the city never gets are the Bastiat UNSEEN. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control.

question: The Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck, no libertarian, is famous for one deadpan comparison about rent control. In his line, rent control is the most efficient technique known to destroy a city, EXCEPT for what alternative?
context: Lindbeck's line: 'In many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city -- except for bombing.' The bite of it is that a socialist Swedish economist said it. Source: Lindbeck, The Political Economy of the New Left, 1971.

question: New York City's rent-stabilization system, in its current form, dates to a 1974 state law that layered on top of even older WWII-era controls. Which 1974 law is the current legal foundation?
context: The ETPA of 1974 is the legal foundation of NYC's modern rent-stabilization regime; roughly 966,000 apartments were covered as of the 2023 NYC Housing and Vacancy Survey. Source: NYC HPD 2023 Housing Vacancy Survey.

question: Stockholm's rent-control system produces a city-run public waiting list for a first-hand rental contract. By the mid-2010s the average wait for a first-hand rental in central Stockholm had reached what?
context: Stockholm's Bostadsformedlingen (municipal housing office) published waits above 20 years for central-city apartments through the mid-2010s; widely reported in SVT and The Economist 2015. Source: bostad.stockholm.se.

question: The 2019 Diamond, McQuade, and Qian paper in the American Economic Review studied San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion. Their headline finding was that affected landlords reduced their rental housing supply by what magnitude?
context: Diamond-McQuade-Qian, 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality,' AER 2019: San Francisco's 1994 expansion caused a 15% cut in rental supply from affected landlords, deepening the shortage the policy meant to fix. Source: American Economic Review 109(9).

question: In every serious rent-controlled market a specific kind of side-payment appears -- an up-front bribe a would-be tenant pays to a landlord or outgoing tenant to secure a covered lease. What is the standard name for this side payment?
context: 'Key money' is the standard term for the covert side payment used to acquire a rent-controlled lease; the Fraser Institute's 1981 collection Rent Control: Myths and Realities documents the pattern across cities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_money.

question: Berlin passed a five-year rent-control law in 2020 called the Mietendeckel that froze rents on roughly 1.5 million apartments. In April 2021 a specific German court struck down the law entirely as beyond the state's power. Which court struck it?
context: The Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe struck down Berlin's Mietendeckel on April 15 2021, ruling rent regulation was a federal not a state matter; Berlin tenants suddenly owed back-rent for the freeze period. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Mietendeckel.

question: Milton Friedman's Bastiat-style closing move on rent control names the specific reasoning fallacy behind the policy in one phrase. Friedman wrote: 'The most important single central fact about a free market is that no exchange takes place unless both parties benefit.' Applied to rent control, whom does the policy help and whom does it harm most?
answer: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
