choices: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
Helps all tenants equally; harms only speculators and non-resident landlords
Helps first-time buyers; harms only established homeowners
Helps landlords by stabilizing income; harms the general tax base
context: This is the classic seen/unseen split for a price ceiling: the incumbent tenant is SEEN paying less; the would-be tenant who never appears on any waiting list because the building was never built is UNSEEN. Source: Friedman & Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), price-ceilings chapter.

question: The Fraser Institute's 1981 collection Rent Control: Myths and Realities, edited by Walter Block and Edgar Olsen, argues that price ceilings on rent produce a predictable set of long-run outcomes in every city that tries them. Which outcome does the collection identify as most damaging over decades?
answer: Collapse of new rental construction combined with deteriorating maintenance of existing stock
choices: Collapse of new rental construction combined with deteriorating maintenance of existing stock
Immediate uniform reduction in average rents across all neighborhoods
Redistribution of rental supply toward higher-income neighborhoods
Complete elimination of the private rental market within five years
context: The Fraser collection's cross-country evidence: capped future rents kill new construction, and capped current rents remove the incentive for landlords to maintain existing units. The city ends the decade with a smaller and shabbier housing stock than it started with. Source: fraserinstitute.org (Block & Olsen, Rent Control: Myths and Realities, 1981).

question: In Bastiat's method the Stockholm 20-year waitlist and the New York cracked-plaster walk-up point at the same UNSEEN cost: the family that never got the apartment at all. What is the technical economics name for the queue-and-shortage outcome any binding price ceiling produces?
context: A binding price ceiling forces the market to allocate scarce units by NON-PRICE means: waiting lists, insider connections, key money, discrimination. The seen tenant paid less; the unseen family got nothing. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics, chapter on price ceilings.

question: An Irish-born banker who made a fortune in Paris financing John Law's Mississippi Company bubble -- and, crucially, shorted the bubble before it collapsed in 1720 -- later wrote a treatise that became a founding text of economic thought. Who was he?
context: Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734) was an Irish-born banker who lived in Paris. His trading in the Mississippi Bubble made his fortune; his shorting of it made him a rare survivor. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: Cantillon's treatise, written in French sometime in the 1730s and circulated in manuscript before publication in 1755, carries a title translated as 'Essay on the Nature of Trade in General.' What is its French title?
answer: Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General
choices: Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General
Reflexions sur la Formation des Richesses
context: The essay circulated in manuscript for two decades and was finally published in 1755, twenty-one years after Cantillon's mysterious 1734 death by house fire in London. Source: Grokipedia 'Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en General' (2026-09-05).

question: Cantillon's key insight was that money creation is not neutral -- new money does not raise all prices at the same time. Where does it enter, in his framing?
answer: At specific points, benefiting first-receivers who can spend at old prices
choices: At specific points, benefiting first-receivers who can spend at old prices
Uniformly across the whole economy in a single moment
Only in the country producing the precious metals
Only at the seasonal harvest time
context: In Cantillon's day, mines and government-favored merchants received new coins first. They could buy at old prices before prices adjusted. Late-receivers -- wage earners, savers -- paid the new higher prices with old wages. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: The wealth transfer Cantillon named -- from savers and wage-earners to those who received the newly created money first -- is what modern Austrian economists call by a specific eponymous label. What do they call it?
context: The Cantillon effect is the standard Austrian label for the redistribution from late-receivers to first-receivers of newly created money. Whether the money is 18th-century Peruvian silver or 21st-century Fed reserves, the mechanism is the same. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Applied to the modern quantitative-easing era, the Cantillon-effect analysis names a specific interface where the new money enters. Where do Fed-created reserves first arrive?
answer: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
choices: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
In Treasury tax-refund payments to individuals
In the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation reserves
context: When the Fed buys a bond it credits the primary dealer's reserve account. First-receivers are banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, asset holders. Consumer prices adjust years later when velocity recovers. Source: Grokipedia 'Primary dealer' (2026-09-05).

question: The specific 2020-24 pattern of asset-price inflation in 2020-21 followed by consumer-price inflation in 2021-23 is a textbook example of Cantillon-effect timing. Which feature of the modern pattern most exactly matches Cantillon's original 1730s description?
answer: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
choices: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
The complete absence of any asset-price effect
The immediate uniform response of all prices
The concentration of the effect on export prices only
context: Cantillon explicitly described the timing: new money enters at specific points, those points enjoy the old prices, prices then adjust over months and years, late-receivers pay the higher prices with wages set at the old level. The modern QE-then-CPI sequence follows the pattern precisely. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: Cantillon's essay was cited approvingly by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations (1776) and by later economists including John Stuart Mill, Carl Menger, and one 20th-century Austrian economist who called Cantillon 'the founder of economic science.' Which economist gave him that title?
context: Rothbard's 1995 An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought called Cantillon 'the founder of economic science' -- an unusual honor coming from an Austrian scholar, since it displaces both Adam Smith and Carl Menger from that title. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective (1995).

question: Cantillon originated a term still used in modern economics that describes the person who bears the risk of buying inputs at known prices to sell outputs at uncertain prices. Which term did he coin in its modern economic sense?
context: Cantillon's Essai introduced 'entrepreneur' as the systematic risk-bearer in the market. Modern Austrian economics -- especially Israel Kirzner -- treats this Cantillonian concept as central to how markets discover new information. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: Cantillon's 300-year-old insight explains a specific modern political-economy pattern the Austrian tradition presses hard about central-bank policy. Which pattern does the ladder press?
answer: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
choices: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
Central-bank money creation is distributionally neutral across all social groups
Central-bank money creation always causes immediate consumer-price inflation
Central-bank money creation has no effect on asset prices
context: The Cantillon-effect analysis explains why QE lifts asset prices for existing owners before consumer prices rise for everyone. It is not a bug of the modern system; it is a structural feature the Austrian tradition traces back to the 1730s. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995).

question: Cantillon died in 1734 under circumstances that historians still debate. His London townhouse burned in a fire that may have been an arson-cover for what murder. Which unresolved suspicion surrounds his death?
answer: An insurance-fraud murder by a dismissed servant
choices: An insurance-fraud murder by a dismissed servant
A political assassination by John Law loyalists
A heart attack while asleep unrelated to the fire
A duel gone wrong on the London docks
context: Cantillon's death by house fire remains unsolved. Contemporary accounts suggest a dismissed servant may have set the fire to cover an insurance-fraud murder. The economist most famous for shorting a bubble may have been killed for money by someone who worked for him. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1973 a Chicago-trained economist published a Journal of Political Economy paper studying the effects of the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which imposed new proof-of-efficacy requirements on FDA drug approvals. His finding: new drug flow fell by roughly half. Who wrote it?
context: Sam Peltzman, 'An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments' (Journal of Political Economy, September 1973). Peltzman estimated lives lost from delayed approval of effective drugs significantly exceeded lives saved from blocking ineffective ones. Source: jstor.org (Peltzman 1973).

question: The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act were passed in response to a specific tragedy in which a European sedative widely used off-label in pregnancy caused thousands of severe birth defects. What was the drug called?
context: The thalidomide birth-defect crisis (1957-62, mostly in Europe) prompted Congress to pass the Kefauver-Harris Amendments in 1962, requiring proof of efficacy for FDA approval. Source: fda.gov (Kefauver-Harris Amendments history).

question: Peltzman's 1973 analysis of the Kefauver-Harris Amendments identified a SEEN benefit (thalidomide-style tragedies prevented) and an UNSEEN cost. What is the UNSEEN cost his analysis named?
answer: Patients dying while safe-and-effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue
choices: Patients dying while safe-and-effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue
Government spending on FDA staff increased slightly
context: The Bastiat SEEN vs UNSEEN move applied to drug regulation: the prevented tragedies are visible; the patients who died waiting for approvals of drugs available in Europe or Japan are largely invisible. Peltzman argued the invisible category dominated in aggregate. Source: Peltzman, JPE (1973).

question: In May 2018 the federal Right-to-Try Act was signed into law, allowing terminally-ill patients access to drugs that had passed Phase I safety trials but not yet completed full FDA approval. A George Mason economist chaired the movement for years leading up to its passage. Who was that scholar?
context: Alex Tabarrok (George Mason University) has been a leading academic advocate for FDA reform, including chairing the right-to-try movement. The Right to Try Act was signed by President Trump on May 30, 2018. Source: fda.gov (Right to Try).

question: The core reasoning move behind the right-to-try argument reverses a common intuition about defaults. For a patient with a fatal diagnosis and no approved options, what does the default of 'wait for the FDA' actually mean?
context: The right-to-try move: absent right-to-try, a terminally-ill patient with no approved option is not being 'protected' by delay -- they are dying while decisions are made elsewhere. The default is death, not safety. Source: Tabarrok, 'Assessing the FDA via the Anomaly of Off-Label Drug Prescribing' (Independent Review 2000).

question: A prominent modern medical-establishment critic of the FDA is a UCSF hematologist-oncologist whose 2020 Johns Hopkins book argued that many drugs approved through FDA accelerated pathways never convert their surrogate-endpoint gains into actual survival benefit. Who is he?
context: Vinay Prasad's book Malignant: How Bad Policy and Bad Evidence Harm People with Cancer (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2020) argues that accelerated FDA approval on surrogate endpoints has often failed to deliver actual survival improvements. Source: jhupbooks.press.jhu.edu (Prasad 2020).

question: Vinay Prasad's critique of FDA accelerated approval is best summarized as applying a specific Thomas Sowell / Milton Friedman reasoning move to drug regulation. Which move?
answer: Judge drugs by results, not by intentions or surrogate markers
choices: Judge drugs by results, not by intentions or surrogate markers
Abolish the FDA and let markets rate every drug
Federalize drug regulation into the Department of Defense
Require unanimous physician consent for every prescription
context: Prasad's move is not 'less FDA' but 'better FDA': require the outcome that matters (survival for oncology drugs) rather than proxy measures (tumor shrinkage) that often do not translate. It is the results-not-intentions frame Friedman and Sowell repeatedly pressed. Source: Prasad, Malignant (JHU Press 2020).

question: The FDA's approach to drug approval sits inside a two-sided error problem. TYPE I errors (approving an unsafe drug) get front-page coverage; TYPE II errors (blocking an effective drug) are far harder to see. Which famous 2004 drug withdrawal is a Type-I-error case Congress remembers by name?
context: Merck withdrew Vioxx (rofecoxib) on September 30, 2004 after evidence of increased cardiovascular risk. It became the canonical Type-I error case in FDA reform debates. Source: fda.gov (Vioxx withdrawal history).

question: In December 2016 a bipartisan federal law significantly expanded FDA accelerated-approval pathways and modernized clinical-trial designs. What was that law called?
context: The 21st Century Cures Act was signed December 13, 2016. It broadened accelerated-approval pathways, modernized trial designs, and increased funding for the NIH and FDA. Source: congress.gov (Public Law 114-255).

question: The synthesis Peltzman, Tabarrok, and Prasad each press from different angles is not 'abolish the FDA' but a specific honest-cost-accounting move. What must an honest cost-benefit analysis of drug regulation account for?
answer: Both TYPE I and TYPE II errors, not only the seen error
choices: Both TYPE I and TYPE II errors, not only the seen error
Only the interests of pharmaceutical companies
Only the interests of currently-healthy voters
Only the fiscal cost of FDA staff salaries
context: The synthesis: the SEEN cost of approving a dangerous drug is politically overwhelming; the UNSEEN cost of not approving a lifesaving drug is politically invisible. Honest cost-benefit accounts for both, which is Peltzman 1973 as a live diagnostic in 2020s FDA debates. Source: Peltzman (1973); Prasad (2020); Tabarrok (2000-).

question: In December 2020 the FDA authorized the first COVID-19 vaccines under an emergency pathway that let them reach the population months before full approval would have been possible. What three-letter acronym names that pathway?
context: Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) allowed COVID-19 vaccines to reach the population starting December 11, 2020, months before full BLA approval. It is the highest-stakes real-world case of accelerated authorization in the FDA's history. Source: fda.gov (Emergency Use Authorization).

question: In 1968 an Anglo-American historian and former British Foreign Office intelligence officer published the first comprehensive Western scholarly account of Stalin's 1936-38 purge wave. Who was the author?
context: Conquest was born 1917 in Great Malvern, England, and died 2015 at Stanford, California. He had worked at the Foreign Office Information Research Department before turning to Sovietology in the 1950s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: Robert Conquest's 1968 book on Stalin's 1936-38 purge wave carried a title that became a standard shorthand for the entire period. What was the book called?
context: Published by Macmillan of London in 1968. The book drew on defector testimony, Soviet dissident samizdat, and close reading of the Soviet published record. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Great_Terror.

question: Robert Conquest's 1968 book estimated the number of executions during the 1937-38 peak years of Stalin's terror. What figure did he give?
context: Conquest also estimated about 1.5 million arrests in the same window, and specifically documented the targeting of the Old Bolsheviks and Red Army officer corps. The figures were treated as Cold War inflation by much of the Western academic establishment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Great_Terror.

question: Through the 1970s and 1980s a distinct academic school challenged Robert Conquest's numbers and his emphasis on Stalin's personal will. It was associated with Sheila Fitzpatrick and J. Arch Getty. What was this school of Sovietology called?
context: Getty's 1985 book 'Origins of the Great Purges' argued that lower-level party officials, not Stalin personally, drove much of the terror -- and that Conquest had over-counted. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Historiography_of_the_Great_Purge.

question: The Soviet archives opened after December 1991. What did they show about Robert Conquest's 1968 estimates versus the revisionist critics who had said he over-counted?
answer: The NKVD's own records vindicated Conquest's execution estimate within a rounding error
choices: The NKVD's own records vindicated Conquest's execution estimate within a rounding error
The NKVD's records showed Conquest had over-counted by roughly a factor of ten
The NKVD's records could not be located and the debate remains unresolved
The NKVD's records confirmed both sides were wrong by equal amounts
context: The archives also confirmed the personal-will attribution: Stalin's handwritten annotations appear on execution lists. Getty and other revisionists partially retracted; Conquest published a 1990 'Reassessment' folding in the new material. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Great_Terror.

question: Beyond 'The Great Terror,' Robert Conquest wrote a major 1986 book on the 1932-33 Ukrainian famine known as the Holodomor. What is that book's title?
context: 'The Harvest of Sorrow: Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine' (Oxford University Press, 1986) was the Western scholarly standard on the Holodomor before Snyder's 'Bloodlands' (2010). Conquest also wrote 'Reflections on a Ravaged Century' (1999). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: Robert Conquest taught for decades at a specific US research institute after 1981, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005 from President George W. Bush. Where did he teach in California?
context: The Hoover Institution is a policy research center on the Stanford campus. Conquest mentored a generation of Sovietologists there through the 1980s and 1990s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: A Texas congressman -- an obstetrician by training -- spent three separate stints in the US House and became the chamber's most consistent Federal Reserve critic across three decades. He ran for president once as a Libertarian in 1988 and twice more in Republican primaries. Who is he?
context: Ron Paul (born 1935), an OB-GYN physician, served in Congress 1976-77, 1979-85, and 1997-2013. He was called 'Dr. No' for casting the lone No vote on many bills. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: In September 2009, in the immediate aftermath of the 2008 crisis, the long-serving Texas Fed-critic congressman published a general-audience book that reached #6 on the New York Times bestseller list. What was its blunt three-word title?
context: End the Fed (Grand Central Publishing, September 2009) argued the Fed is unconstitutional, morally objectionable, and economically destructive. Its bestseller performance signaled Fed criticism had gone mainstream. Source: Grokipedia 'End the Fed' (2026-09-05).

question: The Texas congressman was one of the very few members of Congress reading a specific trio of Austrian-school economists throughout his career. Which trio's works did he draw on in his floor speeches?
context: Ron Paul was a personal friend of Murray Rothbard's. He made frequent floor speeches drawing on Mises's monetary theory and Hayek's calculation argument throughout the 1980s-2000s. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: In a 2003 floor speech in the House, the Texas congressman named the housing bubble by name and warned that a specific Fed policy would end in a crash. Whose interest-rate policy did he attack in that speech?
context: The 2003 speech, delivered as the funds rate was moving toward the 1% floor, predicted a housing bubble and eventual crash. Ron Paul was widely dismissed at the time. Five years later he was largely vindicated. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: In February 2009 the Texas congressman introduced a bill formally titled the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, informally known by a memorable three-word tagline. What was the tagline?
context: HR 1207, the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, was informally 'Audit the Fed.' It attracted 320 co-sponsors -- extraordinary bipartisan support -- but was gutted by Senate leadership. A limited one-time audit was included in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Transparency Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2009 Audit-the-Fed bill attracted unusually broad House support before being cut back in the Senate. Approximately how many House co-sponsors signed onto HR 1207?
context: 320 House co-sponsors is a supermajority -- extraordinary for any bill, unprecedented for a Fed-oversight bill. Democratic Senate leadership prevented a full vote, but a limited one-time audit of Fed emergency-lending programs made it into the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Transparency Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2009 End the Fed book made three arguments against the Federal Reserve. It said the Fed was unconstitutional (Article I Section 8 monetary authority cannot be delegated), morally objectionable (permits systemic debt creation), and economically destructive. Which specific Austrian-tradition economic critique did the book use for the third argument?
answer: The Fed creates the boom-bust cycles Austrian business-cycle theory predicts
choices: The Fed creates the boom-bust cycles Austrian business-cycle theory predicts
The Fed is unable to control the money supply during recessions
The Fed cannot coordinate with foreign central banks
The Fed's dot plot is inaccurate more than half the time
context: Ron Paul's economic argument was ABCT-driven: artificially low interest rates cause capital misallocation, and the resulting bust is inevitable. The 2008 crisis, arriving as the book was going to press, made the argument urgent. Source: Paul, End the Fed (2009).

question: In 2011 the Texas congressman received the Mises Institute's highest honor, an award named after the Austrian-school economist who was his personal friend. Which award did he receive?
context: Murray Rothbard died in 1995. The Mises Institute's Rothbard Medal of Freedom is awarded to those who have advanced Austrian economics and libertarian thought. Ron Paul received it in 2011. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: The Texas congressman's most consequential legacy is not any specific bill but a shift in what Republican politics considered a mainstream position on the Federal Reserve. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: Prior to Ron Paul, Fed-critical positions were confined to fringes; after Ron Paul, they became a mainstream Republican-primary position
choices: Prior to Ron Paul, Fed-critical positions were confined to fringes; after Ron Paul, they became a mainstream Republican-primary position
Ron Paul had no lasting effect on Republican monetary policy
Ron Paul's positions were adopted by Democrats but rejected by Republicans
Ron Paul's audit bills were fully enacted into law during the Obama presidency
context: Fed criticism before Ron Paul lived among monetarists and Ayn Rand followers. After his three decades in the House and three presidential runs, hard-money views became a normal Republican-primary stance. His son Rand Paul, a Kentucky senator since 2011, carries the campaign forward with HR 24 in the 118th Congress. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: The Texas congressman's audit-the-Fed campaign draws on a specific reading of the US Constitution about which body has authority over money. Which constitutional argument does he press?
answer: Congress's Article I Section 8 monetary authority cannot legitimately be delegated to an independent agency
choices: Congress's Article I Section 8 monetary authority cannot legitimately be delegated to an independent agency
The Federal Reserve was explicitly authorized by the Constitution's Preamble
The Tenth Amendment reserves monetary authority to the states
The Sixteenth Amendment implicitly authorizes central banking
context: The constitutional case: Article I Section 8 assigns to Congress the power 'to coin Money, regulate the Value thereof, and of foreign Coin.' Ron Paul argues this authority cannot be delegated wholesale to the Federal Reserve without amending the Constitution. Source: US Constitution, Article I Section 8; Paul, End the Fed (2009).

question: An English-born economist who lived to 102 and spent most of his career at the University of Chicago Law School won the 1991 Nobel for showing how transaction costs and property rights shape the economy. Who was he?
context: Ronald Coase (1910-2013) won the 1991 Nobel 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: In 1937 a 27-year-old English economist published his first great paper in Economica, opening with a question no one had thought to ask: why do FIRMS exist at all if markets are so good at coordinating economic activity? What was the paper called?
context: 'The Nature of the Firm' (Economica, November 1937), written while Coase was still at Dundee. It launched transaction-cost economics. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Coase 1937).

question: Coase's 1937 answer to why firms exist was that markets carry hidden costs: finding partners, negotiating contracts, monitoring performance, enforcing agreements. A firm exists when it is cheaper to organize an activity in-house than to buy it repeatedly on the market. What did Coase call these hidden costs?
context: Transaction costs is Coase's coinage for the costs of using the price mechanism. Where in-house costs are lower, firms replace market transactions with command relationships. The firm's size is where the two costs meet. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: Coase's second great paper appeared in 1960 in the Journal of Law and Economics and transformed the economics of externalities. What did he title that paper?
context: 'The Problem of Social Cost' (Journal of Law and Economics, October 1960) is one of the most-cited economics papers ever written. It launched law and economics as a field. Source: chicagounbound.uchicago.edu (Coase 1960).

question: The standard pre-1960 analysis of externalities came from the Cambridge economist Arthur Pigou: if a factory harms a neighbor, the state should tax the harm to internalize the externality. What was Coase's 1960 alternative claim, assuming transaction costs are low enough?
answer: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
choices: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
The state should immediately shut down the factory
The neighbor should be forced to move at government expense
The government should build a rival factory to compete on pollution
context: Coase's insight: when parties can negotiate, they will bargain to the outcome that maximizes joint value, regardless of who initially holds the legal right. The initial rights determine WHO PAYS, not the final allocation. Source: Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960).

question: The result at the heart of Coase's 1960 paper has come to be known as a theorem, though Coase himself never used the term. What is the standard name for the proposition that, under low transaction costs, initial property rights do not affect the efficient final allocation?
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase theorem' in his 1966 Theory of Price textbook. Coase himself was ambivalent about the honorific and worried the theorem was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: Coase repeatedly complained that his 1960 argument was misread as a claim that government intervention is unnecessary. What was his actual position when transaction costs are HIGH -- for instance, when many parties are affected and negotiation is prohibitive?
answer: Government intervention can be justified, but its own transaction costs must be included
choices: Government intervention can be justified, but its own transaction costs must be included
Nothing can be done and the parties must accept the outcome
The market always still finds an efficient solution regardless
Only judicial rulings, never legislation, are appropriate
context: Coase's actual argument: compare like to like. When private bargaining is too costly, government intervention may be superior -- provided the analysis honestly counts the transaction costs of government administration too. Source: Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960), final section.

question: At age 100, Coase co-authored his last major book with a younger colleague on the economic transformation of a specific country. Which country's post-1978 economic history was the subject of Coase's final book?
context: How China Became Capitalist (Palgrave Macmillan, 2012), co-authored with Ning Wang. Coase was 100 at publication and 102 at his death in 2013. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase.

question: Coase's insight in 'The Nature of the Firm' was to notice that economic activity happens inside two very different institutional environments: some coordinated by prices, others by command relationships. Which internal environment does the firm mostly use for its coordination?
answer: Command relationships between manager and employee
choices: Command relationships between manager and employee
Random assignment of tasks by lottery
context: Inside a firm a manager instructs an employee what to do. Between firms, prices coordinate. Coase's question: why draw the line here rather than there? His answer: transaction costs. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: Coase's two great papers -- 1937 and 1960 -- share a common analytical move that reframes debates that had seemed like a simple choice between markets and government. What move do they share?
answer: They compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
choices: They compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms
They assume all transaction costs are zero for tractability
They favor central planning over private ordering
They apply mathematical topology to price theory
context: The Coase move: never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative. Firms, markets, private bargains, and government all have their own transaction costs. Comparative institutional analysis must count them all. Source: Coase, Essays on Economics and Economists (Chicago 1994).

question: A young American libertarian, holding physics and materials-science degrees from Penn State, founded a website in 2011 that ran on the Tor anonymous network and used Bitcoin for payments. Who was the founder?
context: Ross Ulbricht (born 1984) founded Silk Road in early 2011. Charlie Shrem ran BitInstant and later served prison time on separate charges; Roger Ver was an early Bitcoin evangelist; Cody Wilson ran the 3D-printed-gun project Defense Distributed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: On the site he ran, Ross Ulbricht used a pseudonym borrowed from a 1980s film in which the pirate's title passes from person to person so that no single 'DPR' can ever be caught. Which pseudonym did he adopt?
context: Ulbricht used the pseudonym Dread Pirate Roberts (DPR), from The Princess Bride (1987), where the title passes between wearers. The other names are unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Federal agents arrested Ross Ulbricht in San Francisco on October 1, 2013 -- specifically in one particular room of a specific city institution, where they had to physically distract him and grab his open laptop before he could lock the screen. Where did the arrest happen?
answer: the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library
choices: the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library
the outdoor patio of the Bello Cafe coffee shop in the San Francisco Mission District
the third-floor entryway of his rented apartment on Hickory Street in San Francisco
the international-arrivals lobby at San Francisco International Airport terminal one
context: The arrest took place October 1, 2013 in the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library, with Ulbricht's laptop open and unencrypted. The coffee-shop and apartment guesses are common misremembers; the airport was not involved. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: The particular arrest technique used against Ross Ulbricht was chosen because his laptop's disk encryption would have been effectively unbreakable if he had time to close it. What did agents do to bypass the encryption at the moment of arrest?
answer: physically distracted him to keep him from locking the running laptop
choices: physically distracted him to keep him from locking the running laptop
used a court-ordered decryption key from Apple
captured the disk encryption key from the router
brute-forced the password over several days
context: Agents staged a couple's argument nearby to distract Ulbricht, then grabbed the running (logged-in-as-DPR) laptop before he could lock it. Apple decryption keys and router-side captures do not exist for this class of full-disk encryption; brute-force would not have succeeded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Ross Ulbricht was convicted at trial in February 2015 on multiple federal charges. On January 29, 2015 the judge in the case sentenced him to a specific and unusually severe punishment for a first-time nonviolent offender. What sentence did he receive?
answer: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
choices: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
a 20-year sentence with possibility of parole
a 10-year sentence in a minimum-security prison
a 5-year suspended sentence with community service
context: Judge Katherine Forrest sentenced Ulbricht to two life sentences plus 40 years without parole. The lesser sentences never applied. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: For eleven years after her son's sentencing, one woman ran the most sustained clemency campaign in modern Bitcoin history -- arguing that a two-life-plus-40 sentence was massively disproportionate for a first-time nonviolent offender. Which family member became the public face of the campaign?
context: Lyn Ulbricht ran the FreeRoss.org campaign for eleven years. Kirk (his father) and Cally (his sister) were supportive but did not lead the public campaign; Judith is not a named figure in the case. Source: https://freeross.org/.

question: Ross Ulbricht walked out of federal prison on January 21, 2025 after a full pardon signed by the US President on the second day of his second term. Which president signed the pardon Trump had promised at the 2024 Libertarian Party convention?
context: Donald Trump, having promised the pardon at the Libertarian Party's 2024 national convention, signed a full pardon for Ross Ulbricht on January 21, 2025 -- the second day of his second term. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Between January 2011 and October 2013, the Silk Road marketplace Ross Ulbricht ran operated for a specific duration on the Tor network. About how long did the site actually run before its shutdown?
context: Silk Road ran from January 2011 until the October 2013 shutdown -- roughly 2 years and 9 months. The alternative durations do not match the actual operating window. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: After the shutdown of Silk Road, the US Marshals Service auctioned the seized bitcoins in tranches beginning in 2014-15. Roughly how many bitcoins did the initial seizure at the site's takedown yield?
context: The initial October 2013 seizure at Silk Road's takedown was roughly 144,000 BTC (later seizures added more). The Marshals auctioned tranches through 2014-15, notably to buyer Tim Draper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: A libertarian commentator writing about Ross Ulbricht's pardon in 2025 argues that the eleven-year clemency campaign vindicated one specific proposition about how a movement should respond when its principles collide with prosecution. Which move does the argument press?
answer: That sustained public campaigning for a specific person can succeed where abstract advocacy fails, even against the largest legal apparatus
choices: That sustained public campaigning for a specific person can succeed where abstract advocacy fails, even against the largest legal apparatus
That accepting the original sentence quietly and trusting the appeals process is the only ethical response for a movement that respects the rule of law
That armed resistance is the appropriate remedy for perceived legal injustice when the sentence appears disproportionate on nonviolent charges
That prosecutorial verdicts on nonviolent first-time offenders are always correct in retrospect and public campaigning for clemency is always a mistake
context: The libertarian argument (Rand Paul, Roger Ver, Lyn Ulbricht's own writings): the eleven-year FreeRoss.org campaign shows that specific-person advocacy is the operative pressure. The other options are the opposite of the movement's approach. Source: https://freeross.org/; Rand Paul Senate statements 2019-25.

question: A Lebanese-Palestinian economist trained at Columbia University (PhD 2011) has become the most widely-read modern advocate for treating Bitcoin as sound money in the Austrian tradition. Who is he?
context: Saifedean Ammous holds a Columbia PhD (2011) and was for years a tenured economics professor at Lebanese American University in Beirut. Saylor runs a Bitcoin-heavy corporate treasury; Schiff is a gold advocate; Taleb writes on risk and is now Bitcoin-critical. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: In 2018 Saifedean Ammous published a book with the John Wiley publishing house that has since become the best-selling Bitcoin book of all time. What is the book's title?
answer: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
choices: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Bitcoin Way: A History of Digital Currency
The Bitcoin Manifesto: A New Financial Order
The Bitcoin Book: An Introduction for Investors
context: 'The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking' (Wiley, 2018) has been translated into 40+ languages. The other titles are fabrications. Source: https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Bitcoin+Standard%3A+The+Decentralized+Alternative+to+Central+Banking-p-9781119473862.

question: Saifedean Ammous's book argues that money emerges to whichever candidate has the highest value on a specific ratio -- one that measures how much of the thing already exists compared to how fast new units can be created. What is that ratio called?
context: Ammous uses the stock-to-flow ratio (existing supply divided by annual new production) to argue money gravitates to whatever has the highest S2F. Debt-to-equity, P/E, and current ratio are accounting metrics with no monetary-theory role in his argument. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 1-3.

question: Applied to Bitcoin, Ammous's stock-to-flow argument reaches one specific conclusion about Bitcoin's monetary properties over time. What does the book say happens to Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio because of the halving schedule?
answer: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
choices: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
it stays flat throughout Bitcoin's existence
it falls each cycle because miners create more coins
it is set annually by a Bitcoin holder vote
context: Ammous's argument: because the halving cuts new issuance in half every four years while stock keeps accumulating, Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio approximately doubles each cycle -- heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero. The other options misdescribe the halving schedule. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: In 2021 Saifedean Ammous published a sequel focused on what fiat currencies have DONE to the world since Nixon closed the gold window in 1971 -- inflation of the money supply, chronic misallocation of capital, sovereign debt bubbles. What is the sequel called?
context: 'The Fiat Standard' (Ammous, 2021) is the sequel to The Bitcoin Standard. The other titles are unrelated books or fabrications. Source: https://saifedean.com/tfs/.

question: Saifedean Ammous's stock-to-flow framework builds on an older tradition in monetary economics that classifies goods by how HARD they are to produce more of. Which term from that tradition does Ammous use for money whose supply is hard to expand?
context: 'Hard money' (money hard to produce more of) versus 'easy money' (money easy to produce more of) is the classical Austrian distinction Ammous inherits. Quick money, narrow money (M0/M1), and helicopter money are different concepts from other traditions. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 1.

question: In 2020, during COVID lockdowns, Saifedean Ammous parted company with the tenured position he had held at Lebanese American University in Beirut. What was the specific occasion of his separation from the university?
answer: he refused to comply with the university's online-teaching requirements during COVID lockdowns and was fired
choices: he refused to comply with the university's online-teaching requirements during COVID lockdowns and was fired
he was offered an endowed chair at Harvard's economics department and moved to Cambridge Massachusetts
he retired from academia to write books and produce his podcast full-time from Beirut
his university lost its formal accreditation during the Lebanese banking crisis and closed its doors
context: Ammous refused the mandatory online-teaching-with-lockdown regime, argued the lockdowns were themselves an example of the concentrated-power failure he had been writing about, and was dismissed from LAU in 2020. Source: Ammous public statements 2020-21; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: After leaving LAU, Saifedean Ammous did not seek another tenured post. Instead he built a specific kind of subscription platform to deliver his Austrian-economics teaching directly to paying students without any university mediation. Which platform did he create?
context: Ammous built saifhouse.com as a subscription platform for his Principles of Economics course and other material -- now with thousands of paying students. Khan Academy, Coursera, and Mises Institute are unrelated existing platforms. Source: https://saifhouse.com/.

question: The Bitcoin Standard's monetary-history arc argues that the reason Bitcoin's fixed 21-million cap matters is not primarily aesthetic but structural. Which specific reasoning move does the book press about what a fixed supply does to a currency over time?
answer: That a fixed supply removes the political discretion to debase, which historically is the mechanism by which every fiat currency has lost value
choices: That a fixed supply removes the political discretion to debase, which historically is the mechanism by which every fiat currency has lost value
That a fixed supply guarantees perpetual deflation of general prices regardless of what happens to real production or productivity growth
That a fixed supply requires a specific central authority to enforce the cap and defend it against political pressure to raise it
That a fixed supply automatically raises real interest rates in every credit market whenever borrowing demand rises against savings supply
context: The Ammous argument: fiat currencies have historically failed via political discretion to expand supply, and Bitcoin's fixed cap removes that specific mechanism. The other options misdescribe Ammous's actual claim about debasement as a political mechanism. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 4-5.

question: Saifedean Ammous's Principles of Economics course, taught outside any university, has been called by his students the modern Austrian answer to a real economics degree. Which historical Austrian institution is Ammous most often compared to as an educational model?
answer: the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama
choices: the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama
the Cato Institute in Washington DC
the Adam Smith Institute in London
context: Ammous's independent Austrian-economics teaching is most often compared to the Mises Institute (Lew Rockwell, Auburn AL, founded 1982), the modern American home of Rothbardian Austrian economics. The other institutions have different orientations and are not the standard comparison. Source: https://mises.org/; https://saifhouse.com/.

question: In 1994 San Francisco voters passed a ballot measure (Proposition I) that extended the city's rent control from pre-1980 buildings to small multi-family properties (2-4 units). Stanford economists later used this expansion as a natural experiment. Which trio published the classic study?
answer: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
choices: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, and Emmanuel Saez
Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, and John Van Reenen
Milton Friedman, George Stigler, and Rose Friedman
context: The 1994 expansion created a discontinuity that let economists compare almost-identical properties on either side of the cutoff. Diamond, McQuade, and Qian are mainstream Stanford scholars, not identified with the Austrian school. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: The Diamond-McQuade-Qian study of the 1994 San Francisco rent-control expansion appeared in one of economics' top journals in September 2019. Which journal?
context: Published as 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco.' The AER is the American Economic Association's flagship journal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: The Diamond-McQuade-Qian study measured what landlords of newly-controlled San Francisco properties did to the supply of rental housing on those buildings, relative to the counterfactual otherwise-identical uncontrolled buildings. What was the finding?
answer: Rental supply on the newly-controlled buildings fell by about 15 percent
choices: Rental supply on the newly-controlled buildings fell by about 15 percent
Rental supply rose by about 30 percent as landlords added units
Rental supply was unchanged either way
Rental supply doubled within five years
context: Landlords converted units to condominiums, demolished and rebuilt as unregulated new construction, or undertook renovations that removed units from the rental market. Every route around rent control that the law allowed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: The Diamond-McQuade-Qian study measured a second-order effect on city-wide San Francisco rents caused by the 15 percent supply reduction on newly-controlled buildings. What happened to average city-wide rents?
context: The city-wide supply reduction pushed up rents on the units that remained available to move-in tenants. The policy transferred wealth from future tenants (who face higher rents in a smaller market) to current protected tenants (who save on their own units). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: Rebecca Diamond herself, in subsequent interviews about her San Francisco study, characterized its central result in a specific way rather than as a housing-affordability solution. Which framing did she use?
answer: A wealth transfer from future tenants to current protected tenants
choices: A wealth transfer from future tenants to current protected tenants
A win-win outcome for both landlords and tenants
A vindication of increased federal housing subsidies
A demonstration that any regulation is inherently better than no regulation
context: Diamond's own framing matters: she is not an ideological opponent of the policy; she is a mainstream researcher whose finding was that the redistribution was intergenerational rather than tenant-versus-landlord. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rebecca_Diamond.

question: A housing advocate in 2020 dismisses the Diamond-McQuade-Qian study as ideological. A Sowell-influenced economist replies that the finding is empirically identical to a prediction two Chicago-school economists had made in a specific 1946 pamphlet. What was that pamphlet called?
answer: 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem'
choices: 'Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem'
context: Written by Milton Friedman and George Stigler in 1946, published by the Foundation for Economic Education. The pamphlet predicted the supply-response and quality-decay mechanisms Diamond-McQuade-Qian empirically measured 73 years later. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: On July 30 2002, months after Enron's December 2001 bankruptcy and WorldCom's July 2002 collapse, President George W. Bush signed a sweeping corporate-governance law imposing new financial-reporting and internal-control requirements on US publicly traded companies. What was the law's common name?
context: Named for Senator Paul Sarbanes (D-Maryland) and Representative Michael Oxley (R-Ohio), the chairs of the two committees that shaped the bill. Formally the Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 was passed directly in response to two accounting scandals: an energy-trading company that had collapsed in December 2001, and a long-distance telecommunications giant that filed for bankruptcy in July 2002. Which pair triggered the law?
context: Enron filed December 2, 2001; WorldCom filed July 21, 2002. WorldCom's collapse revealed roughly $11 billion in improperly capitalized expenses. Both scandals shattered public trust in audited financial statements. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enron.

question: One provision of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires the CEO and CFO of a publicly traded company to PERSONALLY certify the accuracy of the firm's financial statements, exposing them to criminal liability if they knowingly sign off on a materially false report. What is this provision commonly called?
context: Section 302 targeted the WorldCom shape of fraud, in which senior executives had claimed ignorance of accounting irregularities. Post-SOX, that defense is legally hollow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: One specific section of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) required management to establish and independently audit internal controls over financial reporting. It became the most expensive provision to implement, costing a small-cap public company roughly $1-2 million per year. Which section was it?
context: The Section 404 internal-controls attestation is the compliance cost that finance professionals name first when they discuss SOX. Its cost is largely fixed per firm rather than scaling with company size. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: The number of US publicly listed companies stood at roughly 7,300 in 1996. Twenty years later, in 2016, roughly how many US public companies were left, per Grullon-Larkin-Michaely and related research?
context: A roughly 40 percent decline. IPO activity in the same period fell from over 300 per year in the mid-1990s to about 100 per year post-SOX. Many small-cap firms went private or stayed private rather than face Section 404 compliance costs. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: A CFO at a $50 million-market-cap technology firm decides in 2004 not to take the company public because Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 compliance would cost roughly $1.5 million per year -- a small share of a $10 billion firm's revenue but a fatal share of hers. A Columbia banking economist points to this asymmetry as the same pattern he sees in Dodd-Frank. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Regulations with a large fixed compliance cost fall heaviest on the smallest firms
choices: Regulations with a large fixed compliance cost fall heaviest on the smallest firms
Regulations always fail because bureaucracies are inefficient by design
Regulations succeed when their costs are widely publicized in advance
Regulations improve competition by weeding out weak firms
context: The same reasoning move that Calomiris and Haber applied to Dodd-Frank in Fragile by Design (2014). Fixed compliance costs create an anti-competitive moat around large incumbents. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: A retail investor in 2015 wants to buy shares in a promising small-cap tech firm before it grows into the next Apple. She discovers the firm has stayed private, funded instead by venture capital and later private equity. A Bastiatian critic points to the seen benefit of Sarbanes-Oxley (fewer Enron-style frauds) and names an unseen cost specific to ordinary savers. What is that unseen cost?
answer: Retail investors have lost access to early-stage growth investing, which is now reserved for accredited private-equity clients
choices: Retail investors have lost access to early-stage growth investing, which is now reserved for accredited private-equity clients
Retail investors face higher brokerage commissions on the shares that remain publicly listed
Retail investors are barred by the SEC from owning any technology stocks
Retail investors have to pay more federal tax on capital gains from private companies
context: Peter Wallison of AEI has argued that SOX plus Dodd-Frank represents the biggest capital-formation regression in US history. A firm that stays private into a multi-billion valuation delivers those gains only to accredited investors; ordinary retail buyers get the shares only after most of the growth. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Wallison.

question: On the night of October 31 2008 -- Halloween -- someone using a pen name posted a message to the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list announcing 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.' What pen name was on the post?
context: The October 31 2008 post from 'Satoshi Nakamoto' to the metzdowd.com cryptography list -- run by Perry Metzger -- announced the Bitcoin white paper and linked to bitcoin.org. Source: metzdowd.com archives (October 31 2008).

question: Attached to the October 31 2008 mailing-list announcement was a nine-page technical paper describing the new system. What is the title of that paper?
answer: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
choices: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
A New Digital Money for the Twenty-First Century
On the Cryptographic Foundations of Trustless Value
context: Nine pages, twelve sections. The paper contained no mathematics more advanced than probability theory -- deliberately readable by any competent programmer, not just cryptographers. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The central technical problem Satoshi's 2008 white paper claims to solve had defeated every earlier attempt at electronic cash (DigiCash, e-gold, and others), each of which required a trusted issuer to prevent it. What problem?
context: Double-spending: how do you stop someone from spending the same digital coin twice, WITHOUT a central authority checking every transaction? Every prior digital-cash design had needed a trusted issuer (Chaum's DigiCash, e-gold, and others). Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi's white paper solves the double-spending problem by combining a public timestamped chain of transactions with a specific ordering-enforcement mechanism, so rewriting history would cost more computation than any attacker could afford. What is that mechanism called?
context: Proof-of-work enforces the ordering: each block requires real-world computation, and the honest chain is the one with the most cumulative work. Rewriting history requires redoing all that work faster than the honest network. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In Satoshi's white paper the rule for which chain is authoritative is stated in one line: whoever has the most computing power working honestly wins the race to add the next block. What is the standard name for the resulting design?
context: 'Nakamoto Consensus' is the cryptography-literature name for the proof-of-work plus longest-chain rule Satoshi introduced. It is the first known solution to the Byzantine Generals Problem for open, permissionless networks. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nakamoto_consensus.

question: The cryptography mailing list where Satoshi posted the Bitcoin white paper on October 31 2008 was run by a specific cypherpunk-adjacent moderator who had been running it for years. Who ran the list?
context: Perry Metzger ran the metzdowd.com cryptography list, a well-known venue for reviewing cryptographic proposals throughout the 1990s and 2000s. The Bitcoin white paper appeared as a normal posting on that list. Source: metzdowd.com archives.

question: The Bitcoin white paper is organized into a specific small number of numbered sections that build the argument from Transactions up through Network, Incentive, and Privacy to Conclusion. How many sections does the paper carry?
context: Twelve sections: Introduction, Transactions, Timestamp Server, Proof-of-Work, Network, Incentive, Reclaiming Disk Space, Simplified Payment Verification, Combining and Splitting Value, Privacy, Calculations, Conclusion. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: As of 2026 the real identity of Satoshi Nakamoto is still unknown, despite hundreds of accusations, lawsuits, and forensic-text analyses. Approximately how many bitcoins from the earliest days of the network sit in Satoshi's mined addresses, never having moved?
context: Chain analysis of the earliest-mined addresses (the 'Patoshi pattern' studied by Sergio Demian Lerner) places Satoshi's holdings at roughly one million BTC. Not one satoshi has moved from those addresses in more than fifteen years. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: The Bitcoin white paper reads as a purely technical proposal, but its unseen political implication only became visible over years. What was the unseen implication?
answer: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
choices: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
That programming languages could enforce contracts without courts
That cryptographic proofs could replace public identity verification
That the internet could function without private-sector service providers
context: The SEEN in 2008 was a paper about digital cash; the UNSEEN was that a working solution to double-spending meant money could exist without a bank, a central bank, or any political authority. That implication took years to become visible. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Satoshi's 2008 white paper cited a small number of specific prior works as technical antecedents for Bitcoin's design. One of the cited authors -- a cryptographer whose 2004 system was the closest predecessor -- also ran the second-ever Bitcoin node in January 2009. Who was he?
context: Hal Finney's 2004 'Reusable Proofs of Work' (RPOW), building on Adam Back's earlier hashcash, was cited in the Bitcoin white paper. Finney ran the second-ever Bitcoin node on January 11 2009 and received the first person-to-person transaction the next day. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: From October 2008 until early 2011 Satoshi Nakamoto was an active presence in the Bitcoin community, posting on bitcoin.org forums, patching the code, and emailing early developers. When did Satoshi make his last public forum post?
context: The last public bitcointalk.org post from Satoshi was on December 12 2010, on the technical topic of DDoS defenses. He never posted publicly again. Source: bitcointalk.org (Satoshi archive).

question: The final public Satoshi forum post on December 12 2010 was not a farewell but an ordinary mundane message about a specific technical topic. Which topic?
context: The December 12 2010 post concerned defenses against distributed denial-of-service attacks on Bitcoin nodes. Nothing in the message gave any hint that it would be Satoshi's last public communication. Source: bitcointalk.org (Satoshi's final post).

question: Satoshi's last known private email, sent to an early Bitcoin developer in April 2011, contained a specific short line handing off the project. To which developer did Satoshi write?
context: The April 23 2011 email to Mike Hearn read (in essence): 'I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Hearn published the exchange years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: In Satoshi's April 2011 email to Mike Hearn, he named the lead developer he was handing the project to. Who was that developer?
context: Satoshi's line: 'It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Gavin Andresen served as the lead maintainer of the Bitcoin reference client for the next several years before stepping back himself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Andresen.

question: Before disappearing, Satoshi mined roughly a specific number of Bitcoins in the earliest days of the network, when he was often the only miner running. Those coins now sit in thousands of early addresses. About how many BTC?
context: Chain analysis of the 'Patoshi pattern' by Sergio Demian Lerner places Satoshi's early-mined stash at roughly one million BTC. At $50,000/BTC that is $50 billion; at higher prices, far more. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: In the fifteen years since Satoshi's disappearance, one specific documented fact about his early-mined coins has become the strongest evidence that he genuinely walked away. What is that fact?
answer: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
choices: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
The coins have been repeatedly split across many new addresses
The coins have been used to pay Bitcoin Core developer salaries
The coins have been transferred to a charitable trust in the Cayman Islands
context: If Satoshi were alive and had access to the keys, he could have sold, borrowed against them, or moved them for privacy at any time in fifteen years. Instead, the coins sit untouched -- an unusually strong empirical signal that he truly walked away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: One consequence of Satoshi's non-selling of his roughly one million early-mined BTC is that he REMOVED an incentive conflict every prior monetary founder has faced. Which incentive conflict does Satoshi's silence remove?
answer: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
choices: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
The founder's temptation to give press interviews that move the currency's price
The founder's temptation to hire successors from his own family
The founder's temptation to relocate the project to a favorable tax jurisdiction
context: A central banker profits by inflating; a company founder profits by manipulating stock; Satoshi could have sold his million BTC at any time. His non-action is a KEPT PROMISE the design's story needed. Source: mises.org/library/satoshi-kept-promise.

question: As of 2026 not one person has been definitively identified as Satoshi Nakamoto, despite one Australian claimant who spent years pursuing lawsuits asserting the identity. Which claimant was legally rejected as Satoshi by the UK High Court in March 2024?
context: In the Crypto Open Patent Alliance v Wright case, the UK High Court ruled in March 2024 that Craig Wright is NOT Satoshi Nakamoto; the ruling cited his falsified documents and inconsistent testimony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright_(computer_scientist).

question: The theory that Satoshi may have died is one honest possibility among several for the fifteen-year silence, but none has ever been confirmed. In one line, what is the honest answer as of 2026 to why Satoshi vanished?
answer: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
choices: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
He confirmed his retirement in a signed 2015 essay published in Wired
He handed off his private keys to Gavin Andresen in a documented ceremony
He died of a documented illness in 2013, per public medical records
context: Illness, deliberate silence, prosecution fears, or death are all live theories; none has been confirmed. What IS documented: the coins have not moved in fifteen years, and no verified message from Satoshi has appeared since April 2011. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: In economic terms, Satoshi's disappearance and his untouched million BTC together form a specific rare achievement no other monetary founder has managed. What could Satoshi have become and chose not to?
choices: The chair of a major central bank
The head of a global banking consortium
The founder of a publicly-listed corporation
context: At various Bitcoin price levels, Satoshi's million-BTC stash has repeatedly ranked notionally at or above the world's wealthiest documented individual. He could have sold at any point and did not. The kept promise is unusual in the history of money. Source: mises.org/library/satoshi-kept-promise.

question: In 1955 the Chicago economist Milton Friedman published an essay titled 'The Role of Government in Education,' later reprinted as a chapter of his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom. What K-12 reform did the essay propose?
answer: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
choices: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
A federally-set minimum teacher salary schedule
A single national K-12 curriculum administered by the Department of Education
Direct federal ownership of all urban public schools
context: Friedman argued government financing might be justified on externality grounds, but government production of schooling did not follow. Vouchers separated the two: public money, private (or public) provider chosen by the family. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milton_Friedman.

question: Since 1970, real US K-12 per-pupil spending has approximately tripled. What has happened to National Assessment of Educational Progress reading and math scores for 17-year-olds over the same period?
choices: They have collapsed by more than a third
They have grown steadily at a compounded 2 percent per year
context: The NAEP long-term-trend data show the flat scores. Friedman-influenced reformers cite this as the empirical anomaly a monopoly-provider hypothesis would predict: spending rose without competitive pressure to convert it into learning gains. Source: grokipedia.com/page/National_Assessment_of_Educational_Progress.

question: The first urban voucher program in the United States launched in a specific Midwestern city in 1990, providing per-pupil grants to low-income families to attend participating private schools. Which city was it?
context: The Milwaukee Parental Choice Program was championed by Democratic state legislator Polly Williams, herself a former welfare mother, and signed into law by Republican Governor Tommy Thompson. The program was the model for later urban vouchers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milwaukee_Parental_Choice_Program.

question: In 2002 the US Supreme Court upheld a voucher program in a Rust Belt city, ruling that public dollars could flow to religious schools chosen by parents without violating the First Amendment. What was the case's name?
context: The 5-4 decision upheld Cleveland's voucher program on the reasoning that the aid flowed through private parental choice, not directly to religious institutions. The ruling opened the constitutional path for voucher programs to include religious schools. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zelman_v._Simmons-Harris.

question: A school-board member argues in 2023 that families should not be able to exit her district because rival options would drain enrollment. A Chicago-trained economist replies that a grocery store where 90 percent of customers were mandatorily assigned to its checkout would degrade over time -- and public K-12 is that grocery store. Which classical reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
choices: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
The externality move: education produces spillover benefits so government should fully fund it
The public-goods move: schools are non-rival non-excludable and must be publicly produced
The redistribution move: spending must equalize per-pupil funding across districts
context: This is the core Friedman-Chubb-Moe argument. John Chubb and Terry Moe developed the empirical case in Politics, Markets, and America's Schools (Brookings 1990), arguing that governance structures immune to exit block real reform. Source: grokipedia.com/page/John_Chubb.

question: Milton and Rose Friedman founded an organization in 1996, in the last decade of Milton's life, dedicated to a single policy application he considered his most important. The group was renamed EdChoice in 2016. What cause did it promote?
answer: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
choices: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
The abolition of the Federal Reserve System
Universal negative-income-tax replacement of welfare programs
context: Milton Friedman regarded vouchers as the single application of his method with the greatest human-welfare payoff. The Friedman Foundation for Educational Choice ran advocacy, research, and litigation support until it was renamed EdChoice in 2016. Source: grokipedia.com/page/EdChoice.

question: In 2023-2024 a wave of US states passed Education Savings Account laws making K-12 school choice broadly available for the first time in US history. Which set of states enacted UNIVERSAL programs (available to every family, not just the poor)?
answer: Arizona, West Virginia, Iowa, Arkansas, Florida, and Ohio
choices: Arizona, West Virginia, Iowa, Arkansas, Florida, and Ohio
California, New York, Massachusetts, Washington, and Illinois
Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Kentucky only
context: Arizona's 2022 expansion to universal eligibility set the model; the 2023-24 wave followed. The programs give parents a state-funded account they can spend on private-school tuition, tutoring, therapy, or curriculum -- broadening Friedman's original voucher into a broader family-choice instrument. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Education_savings_account.

question: Bitcoin protocol upgrades come in two flavors: one is backward-compatible (older software still accepts the new blocks), and one is breaking (older software rejects them, splitting the chain). Which is the term for the backward-compatible upgrade type?
context: Soft forks preserve one shared chain; hard forks can create two chains if any subset of nodes refuses the change. SegWit was a soft fork; Bitcoin Cash was a hard fork from Bitcoin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fork_(blockchain).

question: On August 24, 2017 Bitcoin activated a soft fork that moved transaction signatures (the 'witness') outside the main transaction body, effectively expanding block capacity and fixing an old technical flaw called transaction malleability. What was the upgrade called?
context: SegWit had been debated since 2015. Its activation followed a User-Activated Soft Fork (UASF) push (BIP148) that pressured miners to accept the upgrade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/SegWit.

question: The 2015-2017 dispute over how Bitcoin should scale is now known as the Block Size War. When the sides could not agree, one faction hard-forked on August 1, 2017 to create a separate cryptocurrency with a much larger base block size. What was the new coin called?
context: Bitcoin Cash launched with 8 MB blocks (vs Bitcoin's ~1 MB). Jonathan Bier's 2021 book 'The Blocksize War' is the standard chronicle of the dispute. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_Cash.

question: On November 14, 2021 (block 709,632) Bitcoin activated its largest upgrade since SegWit. It bundled a more efficient signature scheme, improved multisignature capability, and better smart-contract flexibility. What was the upgrade named?
context: Taproot's activation was notably drama-free after the SegWit years. Over 90 percent of mining hash power signaled support during the 'Speedy Trial' window in June-August 2021. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: The 2021 Taproot upgrade replaced Bitcoin's older ECDSA signature scheme with a more efficient and privacy-preserving alternative named for a German cryptographer. What is the new scheme called?
context: Named for Claus-Peter Schnorr, a German cryptographer. Schnorr signatures allow multiple signers to combine their signatures into one, saving block space and improving on-chain privacy for multisig transactions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Schnorr_signature.

question: A high-school student compares Bitcoin's upgrade path to Ethereum's frequent design changes and asks how Bitcoin's community decides. A veteran developer explains that Bitcoin's culture is deliberately conservative because the network coordinates thousands of independent operators. Which classical reasoning move describes his explanation?
answer: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
choices: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
The efficient-markets move: any upgrade will be priced in instantly
The aggregate-demand move: upgrades should follow monetary stimulus
The revealed-preference move: users always choose the fastest network
context: Hayek's 1945 argument applies to protocol governance as well as to prices. Bitcoin's slow, consensus-heavy upgrade process is the practical embodiment of that principle. Ethereum's alternative approach takes on more coordination risk. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: The 2017 Bitcoin Block Size War produced a hard fork, a civil-war-level community dispute, and a book-length postmortem. The 2021 Taproot activation, by contrast, was notably calm. What lesson do Bitcoin developers usually draw from the contrast?
answer: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
choices: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
Only hard forks work; soft forks always fail in the long run
The Bitcoin Foundation should have final authority over all upgrades
The US Securities and Exchange Commission should ratify each Bitcoin upgrade
context: The lesson is not that all disagreements can be avoided (Bitcoin Cash still exists) but that when the network is aligned, upgrades proceed smoothly without any central authority. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: In Bitcoin, a specific 256-bit random number lets its holder sign transactions and prove ownership of coins at a given address. Anyone who lacks this number cannot move the coins; anyone who has it can. What is this number called in Bitcoin?
context: The private key is the ~256-bit secret that authorizes spending from a Bitcoin address. The block hash is the miner-computed identifier of a completed block; the mempool is the pool of unconfirmed transactions; the nonce is the number miners adjust when hashing a candidate block. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/private-key.

question: A customer buys Bitcoin on a large exchange -- Coinbase, Kraken or Binance -- and leaves it in the exchange account. Legally and technically, what does the customer now hold?
answer: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
choices: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
the private keys to the coins
a share of the exchange company
context: The exchange holds the private keys; the customer holds an IOU denominated in Bitcoin. If the exchange fails, freezes accounts, or is hacked, the customer becomes an unsecured creditor. Bitcoin exchange balances are not FDIC-insured and are not equity in the exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange.

question: A Greek-British Bitcoin educator, author of the technical book Mastering Bitcoin, spent years traveling the conference circuit repeating one seven-word slogan that has become the Bitcoin community's shortest statement of the self-custody principle. Which sentence did Andreas Antonopoulos popularize?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins.
choices: Not your keys, not your coins.
Fix the money, fix the world.
context: Antonopoulos, author of Mastering Bitcoin (2014), popularized the phrase from stages in the 2010s. The other three slogans circulate in Bitcoin culture too -- 'fix the money, fix the world' is Saifedean Ammous-adjacent; 'don't trust, verify' is a general node-runner motto; 'be your own bank' is a marketing tagline -- but the pithy sovereignty rule the community drills newcomers with is Antonopoulos's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Antonopoulos.

question: The safest way to hold Bitcoin private keys is on a small dedicated device whose keys never touch an internet-connected computer -- brands like the Czech Trezor, the French Ledger, and the Canadian Coldcard. What is the general name for this class of device?
context: A hardware wallet stores keys on a secure chip that signs transactions offline; the private keys never leave the device.
