question: Thomas Sowell says the people he calls 'the anointed' have a characteristic substitute for policy analysis. When a hard problem resists them, they reach for something that costs nothing, commits nobody, and settles no part of the difficulty. What do they reach for?
answer: A slogan that denounces the problem
choices: A slogan that denounces the problem
A commission that studies the problem
A budget that under-prices the problem
A statistic that shrinks the problem
context: Sowell calls these 'verbal solutions' -- a public denunciation of poverty, say, standing in for any assessment of what a poverty programme costs or what it does to incentives. He treats the substitution as the signature move of The Vision of the Anointed (1995). Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A city caps what may legally be charged for a flat, and tenants in the capped flats do pay less -- that part is real, immediate and countable. Thomas Sowell's method says the sentence is only half written until a student names what the lower rent was bought with. Which cost does his analysis put first?
choices: Taxes that homeowners must now shoulder
Wages that construction crews must accept
Mortgages that banks now refuse to write
context: Sowell's argument is about incentives, not motives: rent-capped income will not cover upkeep, so upkeep stops, and the tenant's saving is paid for in decay, queues and substandard units. Whether that trade is worth making is the reader's call; the analysis only insists that a trade is being made. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell', on his price-control analysis.

question: Thomas Sowell argues that a legal ceiling on a price does not simply push the price down; it opens a second, illegal trade beside the lawful one. He then makes a claim about the prices charged in that illegal trade which startles most people who hear it for the first time. What does Sowell say about them?
answer: They run higher than a free market's prices would
choices: They run higher than a free market's prices would
They settle at almost exactly the legal ceiling
They swing far less than lawful prices do
They fall further the longer the shortage lasts
context: 'Price controls almost invariably produce black markets, where prices are not only higher than the legally permitted prices, but also higher than they would be in a free market, since the legal risks must also be compensated.' -- Thomas Sowell, Basic Economics. The seller is being paid for the risk of prosecution as well as for the goods. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A student prices out a proposed subsidy line by line, finds the bill steep, and knocks the proposal down. Pleased with himself, he then argues that an existing programme should be abolished outright. Thomas Sowell's own rule does not let him stop where he has stopped. What must the student now do?
answer: Name what abolishing it will cost, and who bears that
choices: Name what abolishing it will cost, and who bears that
Show that the programme was unpopular when it passed
Prove that the programme's budget has grown every year
Find a country that has already abolished the same thing
context: The move is symmetric or it is worthless. Repeal is a policy too, with its own costs falling on identifiable people; a student who applies the question only to proposals he dislikes has learned a debating trick, not a method. Sowell's rail is that intentions do not settle anything, in either direction. Source: Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (1987); Applied Economics (2003).

question: A student prices out a proposed programme down to the last line item and finds the total bearable -- the country can afford it. Thomas Sowell says the analysis is still unfinished, because an affordable price proves nothing whatever on its own. What has the student still not established?
answer: That no other real arrangement buys the same thing cheaper
choices: That no other real arrangement buys the same thing cheaper
That the programme's supporters have declared their interests
That the cost will not rise once the programme is running
That the people paying the cost are the people it helps
context: Sowell treats his two questions as one test with two halves: a cost you can bear is still a cost you may not have to pay. The pairing is why he insists that a policy argument surviving only one of the questions has not been tested at all. Source: Thomas Sowell, collected at quotefancy.com/quote/920957; A Conflict of Visions (1987).

question: Thomas Sowell has never claimed the six-word line as a discovery. He treats it as a slogan for a proposition that economics has rested on since the subject began, and that every first-year textbook still opens with. Which proposition is the slogan compressing?
answer: That resources are limited, so every use forgoes another
choices: That resources are limited, so every use forgoes another
That prices carry information no planner can gather
That people answer to incentives more than to orders
That money loses value when governments issue more
context: Opportunity cost under scarcity -- the idea that using a thing one way means not using it another -- is older than Sowell by a century and more, and older than the Austrian School that sharpened it. The three distractors are the knowledge problem, the incentive principle, and the quantity theory of money: all real, all somebody else's. Source: Sowell, Is Reality Optional? (1993).

question: Two economists whose long-running body of work is the leading academic reference for the near-unanimous finding that public subsidies for professional sports stadiums do not generate positive net regional economic effects are usually cited together. Which pair?
choices: Michael Leeds and Peter von Allmen
context: Dennis Coates + Brad Humphreys, especially their 2008 Econ Journal Watch survey 'Do Economists Reach a Conclusion on Subsidies for Sports Franchises, Stadiums, and Mega-Events?' The finding was near-unanimous across independent studies. Source: econjwatch.org (Coates + Humphreys 2008).

question: Modern American professional sports stadium projects typically carry several hundred million to over a billion dollars in public subsidy. Which mechanism accounts for a large share of this taxpayer contribution?
context: Federal tax exemption of municipal bond interest lowers borrowing costs on stadium bonds. A 2016 Brookings analysis estimated cumulative federal cost from 1986 to 2017 of over $3 billion in foregone federal tax revenue on stadium-related bonds. Source: brookings.edu (Long + Aizenman 2016).

question: The Bastiat SEEN vs UNSEEN move applied to stadium subsidies identifies a specific offset that supporters typically miss. When a family spends $200 at a baseball game, what likely happens to that spending in aggregate?
answer: It substitutes for other local entertainment spending
choices: It substitutes for other local entertainment spending
It generates entirely new economic activity
It exports to other regions permanently
It disappears from the local economy
context: The $200 that goes to the ballgame typically comes out of what the family would have spent at a restaurant, movie, or bowling alley. The visible stadium employment is real; the less-visible offsetting decline in other entertainment employment is the substitution effect. Source: Coates + Humphreys, Journal of Sports Economics (2002).

question: In Olson's concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost framework applied to stadium subsidies, who is the concentrated beneficiary that lobbies, funds campaigns, and threatens to relocate the team?
context: Team owners are typically billionaires whose franchise values rise substantially when public capital funds the stadium. They capture ticket, concession, and media revenue. Taxpayers bear the dispersed cost. Source: Olson (1965) applied; Coates + Humphreys (2008).

question: Cities considering whether to subsidize their local franchise face a specific game-theoretic problem. Any single city that refuses subsidies loses its team to a rival city that will subsidize. What game-theoretic structure best describes this dynamic across US cities?
choices: A coordination game with two equilibria
A repeated auction with cheap talk
context: The subsidy competition among US cities forms a prisoner's dilemma. Individually, each city rationally overpays because the alternative is losing the team; collectively, cities would be better off refusing to subsidize. Source: Rosentraub, Major League Losers (Basic 1999).

question: In 2009 the Dallas Cowboys opened a new stadium in Arlington, Texas, with roughly $325 million in public subsidy. In 2020 another major NFL project opened with roughly $750 million in public subsidy via a hotel-room tax. Which team's new stadium was that?
context: Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas opened in 2020 with about $750M in public subsidy funded largely by hotel-room tax revenue. The Raiders had relocated from Oakland to Las Vegas partly to capture the subsidy the Nevada government offered. Source: reviewjournal.com (Allegiant Stadium financing coverage).

question: The 2008 Coates-Humphreys survey Econ Journal Watch article asked whether professional economists reached a conclusion on stadium subsidies. What was the survey's headline finding about the range of independent (non-team-commissioned) studies?
answer: Near-unanimous agreement that subsidies do not produce positive net regional effects
choices: Near-unanimous agreement that subsidies do not produce positive net regional effects
Roughly evenly split between positive and negative findings
Overwhelming agreement that subsidies produce large positive effects
No independent studies had ever been conducted
context: Coates + Humphreys (2008) reviewed dozens of independent economist studies and found near-unanimous agreement that publicly-subsidized stadiums do not generate positive net economic effects. Team-commissioned studies of course reach different conclusions. Source: econjwatch.org (Coates + Humphreys 2008).

question: The persistence of stadium subsidies despite the professional-economist consensus that they don't produce positive net effects is a rare case where an entire academic consensus and popular support for the subsidy simultaneously exist. What is the STRUCTURAL explanation the ladder gives for that persistence?
answer: Concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost combined with a jurisdictional prisoner's dilemma
choices: Concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost combined with a jurisdictional prisoner's dilemma
Widespread economist confusion about the underlying data
Undocumented federal mandates requiring the subsidies
Unanimous voter belief in the accuracy of team-commissioned studies
context: Olson's collective-action framework (concentrated owners organize, dispersed taxpayers do not) plus the city-level prisoner's dilemma (any city that refuses loses the team) is the joint structural explanation. Source: Olson (1965); Rosentraub (1999) as applied.

question: The reasoning-move at the heart of the stadium-subsidy case gives the policy analyst a specific diagnostic to apply generally. When professional experts on a policy question reach near-unanimous agreement that a policy has negative net effects AND the policy nonetheless persists universally, what should the analyst look for?
choices: A single hidden constitutional prohibition on repeal
Random voter confusion equally distributed across parties
context: The stadium-subsidies case is a clean archetype: professional consensus is against; the policy persists because organized concentrated beneficiaries have overwhelming advantages against dispersed unorganized cost-bearers. The same diagnostic applies across policy domains. Source: Olson (1965); Stigler (1971).

question: The academic literature on stadium subsidies has been remarkably consistent for decades in describing the substitution effect at the heart of the Bastiat critique. Which broad claim about the substitution finding is honest to the literature?
answer: Sports spending substitutes for other local entertainment; the multiplier is small
choices: Sports spending substitutes for other local entertainment; the multiplier is small
Sports spending is entirely new economic activity with a huge multiplier
Sports spending has no measurable effect of any kind
Sports spending permanently exports wealth to other cities
context: The consistent independent-economist finding: sports-attendance spending is largely substituted from other local entertainment. Multipliers claimed by boosters (often 2-3x) systematically fail to appear in the data. Source: Coates + Humphreys (2008); Rosentraub (1999).

question: On January 10 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission approved eleven products of a specific new kind, allowing institutional pools direct access to Bitcoin through the regulated stock-exchange wrapper. What kind of product was approved?
context: Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds hold the actual asset rather than futures contracts. Applications had been filed with the SEC repeatedly since 2013 (starting with the Winklevoss twins) and had all been rejected until this batch approval. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: The largest of the eleven approved spot Bitcoin ETFs was issued by the world's largest asset manager, with the ticker IBIT. Which firm issued it?
context: BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (ticker IBIT) accumulated the largest ETF asset base in any category during its first year. Other issuers included Fidelity (FBTC), ARK Invest (ARKB), Bitwise (BITB), VanEck (HODL), and Grayscale (GBTC, a conversion from its existing trust). Source: Grokipedia 'iShares Bitcoin Trust' (2026-09-05).

question: The SEC's approval was effectively forced by an August 2023 federal appeals-court ruling that the agency's earlier rejection of one specific firm's spot-Bitcoin ETF conversion application was 'arbitrary and capricious.' Which firm won that case?
context: The DC Circuit's August 2023 ruling in Grayscale v SEC held that the SEC could not consistently approve Bitcoin futures ETFs (which it had done in 2021) while denying spot Bitcoin ETFs based on the same underlying market. The ruling essentially forced approval. Source: Grokipedia 'Grayscale v SEC' (2026-09-05).

question: The SEC vote to approve the spot Bitcoin ETFs on January 10 2024 was closely divided. What was the final vote count?
context: SEC Chair Gary Gensler joined the two Republican commissioners in the 3-2 approval, over the objections of two Democratic commissioners. Gensler's own public statement made clear he was voting yes reluctantly under the court ruling's pressure. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: By December 2024, eleven months after approval, the spot Bitcoin ETFs collectively held approximately how many bitcoin -- roughly 5% of total supply?
context: The 1.1 million BTC accumulated by ETFs in eleven months is about 5.2% of the total 21 million cap. It is the fastest institutional accumulation of any commodity via an ETF in history. Source: bitcointreasuries.net.

question: The Cantillon-effect analysis of the January 2024 spot Bitcoin ETF approval identifies the first receivers of the new institutional product. Who benefited first from the ETF wrapper?
answer: Institutional pools -- pensions, endowments, family offices, and RIA-managed retail
choices: Institutional pools -- pensions, endowments, family offices, and RIA-managed retail
Retail Bitcoin holders using cold-storage wallets
Small-country central banks holding Bitcoin as reserves
Bitcoin miners in Iceland and Kazakhstan
context: The ETF wrapper solved a regulatory-accessibility problem for fiduciary-constrained institutions. Individual holders who wanted Bitcoin already had it. The new demand came from pools that had been prohibited by fiduciary rules from direct custody. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: One prominent Bitcoin advocate has continued to criticize the ETF product as a trade of sovereignty for accessibility -- specifically arguing that fiduciary-approved wrappers replace the self-custody feature that makes Bitcoin distinctive. Which critic?
context: Andreas Antonopoulos is the definitive not-your-keys-not-your-coins Bitcoin educator (Mastering Bitcoin 2014); he consistently frames self-custody as the property that makes Bitcoin distinctive, and treats ETF wrappers as a return to the trusted-third-party model Bitcoin was designed to escape. Source: Grokipedia "Andreas Antonopoulos" (2026-09-05).

question: In contrast to critics who see the January 2024 ETF approval as an institutionalization compromise, the CEO who steered MicroStrategy's Bitcoin treasury has publicly welcomed the ETFs. Who welcomed them as broadening the base of Bitcoin adoption?
context: Saylor has publicly framed the spot ETFs as a positive structural event -- institutional pools now have a fiduciary-safe way to hold Bitcoin exposure. He and Antonopoulos-style critics agree on the fact of institutionalization while disagreeing on whether it is a net win. Source: Grokipedia 'Michael Saylor' (2026-09-05).

question: Bitcoin's price on the January 10 2024 spot ETF approval day was approximately $46,300. By December 2024 it had reached a specific milestone for the first time. What did it pass?
context: Bitcoin passed $100,000 for the first time in December 2024, roughly eleven months after the ETF approval. The ETF-driven demand was one contributor among several (the April 2024 halving, macro conditions, US election dynamics). Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin' (2026-09-05).

question: The January 2024 ETF approval is best understood as a specific kind of structural inflection rather than a monetary event. Which recognition move does the ladder press?
answer: It solved a regulatory-accessibility problem for institutional pools; it did not change Bitcoin's underlying monetary properties
choices: It solved a regulatory-accessibility problem for institutional pools; it did not change Bitcoin's underlying monetary properties
It changed Bitcoin's 21-million cap by allowing ETF issuers to create additional supply
It permanently converted Bitcoin into a purely institutional asset
It made self-custody legally impossible for US residents
context: The ETF wrapper is a regulatory technology, not a monetary change. Bitcoin's fixed supply, its self-custody option, and its underlying network operate identically before and after the ETF. What changed is the demand curve from previously constrained institutional buyers. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin ETF' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1997 book 'The Black Book of Communism' (Le Livre noir du communisme) documented approximately 85-100 million deaths across the communist regimes of the 20th century. Who edited the volume and wrote its introduction 'The Crimes of Communism'?
context: Courtois was born 1947 in Dreux, France. Solzhenitsyn was a Russian dissident writer, Furet a French historian of the French Revolution, Conquest an Anglo-American historian of the Soviet purges. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: As a young French intellectual in Paris during a specific 1968 event, Stephane Courtois was radicalized by China's Cultural Revolution and embraced a hard-left political stance he later spent his life documenting. Which ideology did he adopt as a student?
context: The May 1968 Paris upheavals radicalized many French students; Maoism was the fashionable variant among the most zealous. Courtois grew out of it in the 1970s as reports from Cambodia and the USSR made the ideology impossible to sustain intellectually. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: Stephane Courtois became a professional historian at France's national research center, specializing in the archives of the French Communist Party and the Comintern. Which institution employed him?
answer: The CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique)
choices: The CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique)
context: The CNRS is France's national research funding and employment body for permanent researchers. Courtois used the position to access the archives of the French Communist Party and the international communist movement, then the newly opened Soviet archives after 1991. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: Courtois's 1997 Black Book brought together country specialists to sum up the archival totals. Who wrote the USSR chapter (the largest section, given the Soviet share of the total)?
context: Werth was the French Sovietologist of his generation. Paczkowski covered Poland; Margolin covered Asia (China, Vietnam, Cambodia, North Korea); Bartosek covered Eastern Europe. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: Stephane Courtois's introduction to the 1997 Black Book made two of his own co-authors publicly dissent in a Le Monde letter. What specifically did they object to?
answer: His equating of communist and Nazi crimes in the introduction
choices: His equating of communist and Nazi crimes in the introduction
The USSR chapter's estimate of Gulag deaths
The China chapter's estimate of Great Leap Forward deaths
The Cambodia chapter's estimate of Khmer Rouge deaths
context: Nicolas Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin agreed with the country-by-country archival totals but not with Courtois's editorial framing that put communist and Nazi crimes on the same moral plane. The country chapters have held up thirty years later. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: The topline estimate in Stephane Courtois's introduction to the 1997 Black Book has become the standard scholarly figure for the total communist death toll of the 20th century. Approximately what range did he give?
context: The country breakdown: China ~65 million, USSR ~20 million, North Korea ~2 million, Cambodia ~2 million, Africa ~1.7 million, Afghanistan ~1.5 million, Vietnam ~1 million, Eastern Europe ~1 million, Latin America ~150 thousand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: The specific personal arc that lends Stephane Courtois's Black Book its intellectual force is not just his scholarship. It is a biographical fact about his own youth. What is that fact?
answer: Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-historian of communism
choices: Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-historian of communism
Courtois had himself served in the KGB before defecting to France
Courtois had himself survived a Chinese labor camp
Courtois had himself fought in the Spanish Civil War
context: The trajectory from believer to counter-historian gives the introduction a particular authority. It also explains the confrontational tone that his more cautious co-authors resisted in their Le Monde letter. Source: grokipedia.com/page/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: Sweden imposed nationwide rent control during World War II (1942) and extended it as permanent postwar policy; Stockholm centralized rental allocation through a public housing bureau. What is the Swedish name of that bureau?
context: 'Bostads' means housing, 'formedlingen' means bureau or agency. The bureau runs the queue by which most first-hand rental contracts in central Stockholm are allocated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: Swedish rents are not set by market prices; they are negotiated between the national tenant union (Hyresgastforeningen) and landlord associations under a specific pricing system. What is the Swedish name for the system?
context: Utility-value rents are set below what a market-clearing price would be, so demand for central-Stockholm rentals massively exceeds supply. Units are then allocated by time in the queue rather than by willingness to pay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: As of the early 2020s, the average waiting time for a first-hand rental contract in central Stockholm reached a specific figure that made international headlines. Roughly how long was the average wait?
context: The longest documented waits exceeded 30 years. Swedish parents commonly sign their children up to the queue at birth so the child has a chance of a first-hand contract by age 20. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: A specific practice among Swedish parents has become the most-cited illustration of how deep Stockholm's rental queue runs into everyday family life. What do many Swedish parents do the day a child is born?
answer: Enter the newborn into the Bostadsformedlingen housing queue
choices: Enter the newborn into the Bostadsformedlingen housing queue
Open a national retirement savings account for the newborn
Register the newborn for compulsory military service
Reserve a place in a Nobel-affiliated preschool
context: The queue is strictly first-come-first-served. By the time a child turns 18-20 and needs their own place, roughly two decades of queue time have accumulated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: A Swedish economist who chaired the Nobel prize committee in economics for many years -- writing about his own country -- named rent control as the primary cause of Stockholm's queue and rental-market dysfunction. Who was he?
context: Lindbeck (1930-2020) was the long-serving chair of the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences committee. His willingness to name his own country's policy publicly made his critique especially load-bearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Assar_Lindbeck.

question: Because Stockholm's official rental price does not clear the market, a specific parallel market emerged, often charging 3-5 times the controlled rent. Stockholm police reports and the housing think-tank Timbro have documented it. What is this market?
choices: A European Union subsidized rent-supplement system
context: Sitting tenants sublet their controlled units at multiples of the controlled rent. The practice is illegal but widespread, and one of several mechanisms that emerge whenever an official price does not equilibrate supply and demand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: A high-school student asks how a below-market apartment ever actually gets allocated in Stockholm if the price does not do the work. A Hayekian economist points to a broader principle. Which is it?
answer: When a price does not clear the market, some other mechanism must -- typically queueing, connections, black markets, or exit
choices: When a price does not clear the market, some other mechanism must -- typically queueing, connections, black markets, or exit
The Swedish central bank secretly assigns units to voters of the governing party
The European Union assigns units by lottery among all EU citizens
Stockholm's climate does the allocation by discouraging most residents
context: The pattern generalizes: Soviet bread lines, US 1973 gas queues, wartime rationing, and public-housing waiting lists all illustrate the same principle. Prices carry information; suppress them and the information reappears in another form, usually less efficient. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_control_in_Sweden.

question: In March 2018 the Trump administration announced two headline tariffs on imported metals, aimed at protecting US primary-metals jobs. On steel the tariff was 25 percent. On the second metal it was 10 percent. Which metal took the 10 percent rate?
context: March 8 2018 proclamations: 25% on imported steel and 10% on imported aluminum under Section 232 national-security authority; specific mill workers in Granite City IL and Ashland KY were cited by the administration as beneficiaries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_tariffs.

question: The 2018 US steel tariff was framed by its sponsors as protection for US steelworkers. Which unseen party did Bastiat's method identify as bearing the real cost?
answer: American consumers of goods that use steel as an input
choices: American consumers of goods that use steel as an input
Foreign steel exporters based in South Korea and Japan
US municipal governments that build public infrastructure
Investors in the emerging-markets exchange-traded funds
context: Bastiat's UNSEEN victim in a tariff: the American car buyer, appliance buyer, canned-food buyer, and construction customer whose prices rise because steel inputs cost more. Source: piie.com (Bown & Zhang, PIIE Working Paper 20-14).

question: A 2020 Peterson Institute for International Economics working paper by Chad Bown and Yilin Zhang calculated a per-job figure for the US 2018-19 steel and aluminum tariffs: dividing consumer cost by steel jobs saved gave roughly what annual cost per steel job?
context: The PIIE 2020 calculation: about $900,000 spent by US consumers per steel job protected per year, because the added cost is dispersed across every buyer of steel-intensive goods. Cato and PIIE both cite the same per-job figure. Source: piie.com (Bown & Zhang PIIE WP 20-14, 2020).

question: A December 2019 Federal Reserve Board staff paper by Aaron Flaaen and Justin Pierce calculated the net US manufacturing-employment effect of the 2018 tariffs on ALL manufacturing sectors combined. The paper's headline finding was a NET LOSS of how many jobs?
context: Flaaen & Pierce, FEDS 2019-086: about 1,000 primary-steel jobs added versus about 75,000 lost in steel-USING industries (autoparts, machinery, canned food, appliances) whose input costs jumped. Source: federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/2019-086.htm.

question: The classic historical anchor for the modern tariff-and-retaliation cycle is a June 1930 US law that raised average tariffs on dutiable imports to roughly 45 percent, over the signed objection of 1,028 economists. Which act did President Hoover sign?
context: Smoot-Hawley (June 1930): 1,028 economists led by Paul Douglas signed a petition against it; Hoover signed anyway. Foreign retaliation followed, US exports collapsed from $5.2B (1929) to $1.7B (1933). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: The petition signed by 1,028 US economists in 1930 asking Hoover to veto the Smoot-Hawley tariff was led by a University of Chicago economist who later became a US Senator from Illinois. Which economist led it?
context: Paul Douglas, University of Chicago economics professor before his Senate career, was the lead signatory; the petition ran the same day in the New York Times, May 5 1930. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Douglas.

question: Douglas Irwin's 2011 book Peddling Protectionism is the standard modern history of one specific US tariff act. Which act?
context: Irwin's Peddling Protectionism (Princeton, 2011) is the definitive history of Smoot-Hawley and the trade-collapse that followed; his Free Trade Under Fire (Yale, multiple editions) applies the same reasoning to modern trade debates. Source: press.princeton.edu/books/peddling-protectionism.

question: The Milton Friedman / Anna Schwartz Monetary History of the United States (1963) settled a specific historical question about the cause of the Great Depression's severity. Their conclusion was that the primary cause was NOT the Smoot-Hawley tariff but what?
answer: The Federal Reserve's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock
choices: The Federal Reserve's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock
The stock-market crash of October 1929 driving consumer confidence down
European war debts pulling gold reserves out of the American banking system
The Dust Bowl reducing agricultural productivity across the Great Plains
context: Friedman & Schwartz argued the Depression's severity was monetary: the Fed let the money stock collapse by about a third, 1929-33. Smoot-Hawley made a monetary contraction worse but did not cause it. Source: Friedman & Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1963.

question: Bastiat's 1845 candlemakers' petition is the classical reductio against protectionism, and 21st-century critics of the 2018 US steel tariff have cited it directly. In one shorthand, what asymmetric political feature does the tariff share with the candlemakers' argument?
answer: Concentrated benefit for a small named group; dispersed cost across every consumer
choices: Concentrated benefit for a small named group; dispersed cost across every consumer
Concentrated cost on foreign producers; dispersed benefit across all Americans
Concentrated fiscal revenue; dispersed regulatory-compliance cost
Concentrated pollution reduction; dispersed employment loss
context: Mancur Olson's Logic of Collective Action (1965) formalized this: concentrated benefits are politically loud (Granite City steelworkers), dispersed costs are politically quiet (every American who buys a car). The candlemakers' petition is the same shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentrated_benefits_and_diffuse_costs.

question: The 2018-19 US steel tariffs' clearest verdict in the Bastiat frame is that they cost more downstream manufacturing jobs than they saved upstream in primary steel. In one line, what did the Fed's Flaaen-Pierce study document as the ratio?
answer: About 75 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
choices: About 75 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
About 3 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added
About equal downstream losses and upstream gains
About 2 primary-steel jobs added per downstream job lost
context: Roughly 1,000 primary-steel jobs added versus roughly 75,000 downstream manufacturing jobs lost -- Flaaen & Pierce Federal Reserve FEDS 2019-086. The UNSEEN downstream employers were the Bastiat victim. Source: federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/2019-086.htm.

question: On Saturday September 20 2008 -- five days after Lehman Brothers filed bankruptcy -- the US Treasury Secretary sent Congress an unusually short proposal requesting $700 billion in authority to buy 'troubled assets' from banks. How long was the original draft?
context: The initial September 20 2008 proposal was three pages long. Its brevity became legendary; even members of Congress who supported the concept were startled by how little detail accompanied the request for $700 billion. Source: Grokipedia 'Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008' (2026-09-05).

question: The Treasury Secretary who wrote the three-page proposal was a former CEO of Goldman Sachs who had joined the Bush administration in June 2006. Who was he?
context: Henry 'Hank' Paulson was Goldman Sachs's CEO from 1999 to 2006, then Bush Treasury Secretary June 2006 through January 2009. His Wall Street background became one of the flashpoints in the political fight over TARP. Source: Grokipedia 'Henry Paulson' (2026-09-05).

question: The original three-page proposal included a clause that would have made all Treasury decisions non-reviewable by any court of law or administrative agency. Which section of the draft carried the language?
context: Section 8 of the original draft: 'decisions by the Secretary pursuant to the authority of this Act are non-reviewable and committed to agency discretion, and may not be reviewed by any court of law or any administrative agency.' Congress removed this language in the final bill. Source: Grokipedia 'Troubled Asset Relief Program' (2026-09-05).

question: The House rejected the first version of the bailout bill on Monday September 29 2008. What was the immediate stock-market reaction that day?
answer: The Dow Jones fell 777.68 points -- the largest single-day point drop in history to that date
choices: The Dow Jones fell 777.68 points -- the largest single-day point drop in history to that date
The Dow Jones rose 200 points on hopes for a better bill
The Dow Jones fell 50 points as traders had priced in the outcome
The Dow Jones was closed early due to circuit-breaker trips
context: The 777.68-point drop on September 29 2008 was the largest single-day point drop in Dow history to that date. Congress rewrote the bill with oversight provisions and executive-pay limits, and the revised version passed October 3 2008. Source: Grokipedia 'Dow Jones Industrial Average' (2026-09-05).

question: Congress rewrote the bill with oversight and pay limits and passed it on Friday October 3 2008. President George W. Bush signed it the same day under a new formal statutory title. What was the Act called?
context: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 authorized the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) with $700 billion in spending authority. The final bill included a Special Inspector General (SIGTARP) and a Congressional Oversight Panel chaired by Elizabeth Warren. Source: Grokipedia 'Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008' (2026-09-05).

question: TARP's original purpose was to buy toxic mortgage-backed securities off bank balance sheets. Within two weeks the Treasury Secretary pivoted to a different mechanism -- directly injecting government capital into the nine largest US banks on October 14 2008. How much did he push into those nine banks initially?
context: The October 14 2008 forced capital injections put $125 billion into the nine largest US banks -- whether they wanted it or not. The pivot from asset-purchase to capital-injection was made without seeking new congressional authorization. Source: Grokipedia 'Troubled Asset Relief Program' (2026-09-05).

question: TARP was later expanded to cover a specific non-financial sector after auto companies faced imminent failure in late 2008. Which two auto companies received TARP funds totaling roughly $80 billion?
context: General Motors and Chrysler received TARP funds totaling roughly $80 billion. Ford declined federal assistance. The auto rescue was controversial because it stretched TARP well beyond its originally stated financial-sector purpose. Source: Grokipedia 'Automotive industry crisis of 2008-2010' (2026-09-05).

question: The FDIC chair through the 2008 crisis later argued that the forced capital injections were 'the biggest bailout in history' precisely because they made no distinction between healthy and troubled banks. Who was that FDIC chair?
context: Sheila Bair, FDIC chair 2006-2011, argued the forced capital injections protected the too-big-to-fail structure itself by treating healthy and troubled banks identically. Her 2012 memoir Bull by the Horns tells the story from inside the crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Sheila Bair' (2026-09-05).

question: On paper TARP eventually recovered most of the money disbursed -- by 2015 the Treasury reported roughly $442 billion disbursed and $442+ billion recovered. Which recognition move does the ladder press about the interpretation of that recovery?
answer: The nominal financial recovery does not undo the permanent moral-hazard precedent that a large enough failure will always be met with public rescue
choices: The nominal financial recovery does not undo the permanent moral-hazard precedent that a large enough failure will always be met with public rescue
The nominal financial recovery proves the bailout was economically neutral
The nominal financial recovery means no future bank rescues will be needed
The nominal financial recovery included interest sufficient to cover all inflation losses
context: The dollar-for-dollar recovery is often cited as evidence TARP 'worked.' The Austrian point: the enduring effect is not financial but expectational. Every future risk-taker learned that too-big-to-fail is a real category. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012).

question: The Congressional Oversight Panel that monitored TARP was chaired by a Harvard Law professor who later became a Massachusetts senator and 2020 presidential candidate. Who chaired the panel?
context: Warren chaired the Congressional Oversight Panel for TARP from 2008. Her visibility on the panel launched her national political career; she was elected to the Senate in 2012 and ran for president in 2020. Source: Grokipedia 'Elizabeth Warren' (2026-09-05).

question: On October 3 2008 President George W. Bush signed a $700 billion program authorizing the US Treasury to buy troubled assets from major banks and to inject equity into them. What is the acronym for the program?
context: Troubled Asset Relief Program, October 3 2008; Treasury ended up injecting preferred stock into Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley among others. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubled_Asset_Relief_Program.

question: The 2008 bailout of major US banks under TARP has a specific name in economics for the behavioral distortion it creates in future creditors and borrowers. What is the standard term?
context: Moral hazard: once creditors and banks expect rescue in a crisis, they demand less risk premium and take more risk, making the system more fragile for the next crisis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard.

question: In the Bastiat framing of TARP, the SEEN benefit is preventing a cascading financial collapse in 2008. What is the UNSEEN cost the moral-hazard critique keeps pointing at?
answer: The changed behavior of every future creditor and every future bank, expecting rescue and taking more risk
choices: The changed behavior of every future creditor and every future bank, expecting rescue and taking more risk
The administrative overhead of the Treasury team that ran the program
The tax revenue foregone on the preferred-stock dividend payments
The regulatory-compliance burden imposed on smaller community banks
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN in a bailout is not in the year of the bailout; it is in the next crisis. The rescued creditors' expectation of rescue changes behavior going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/tarp-moral-hazard.

question: On March 10 2023 a specific California-headquartered bank failed after a classic bank run triggered by unrealized losses on its long-duration Treasury holdings, becoming the largest US bank failure since 2008. Which bank failed?
context: SVB failed March 10 2023 with roughly 93% of its deposits UNINSURED, mostly tech firms and venture-capital funds. Signature Bank followed days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank.

question: On March 12 2023 the Treasury, Federal Reserve, and FDIC jointly announced a bailout decision about Silicon Valley Bank depositors that broke a settled expectation about federal deposit insurance. What did they announce?
answer: All SVB depositors would be made whole, including uninsured ones above the $250,000 FDIC cap
choices: All SVB depositors would be made whole, including uninsured ones above the $250,000 FDIC cap
Only insured SVB depositors would be reimbursed, per the standard $250,000 FDIC limit
SVB depositors would be paid haircuts of 20 to 40 percent depending on account size
SVB depositors would be forced to convert their claims into equity in the receiving bank
context: The joint March 12 2023 announcement invoked the systemic-risk exception; Signature Bank got the same treatment days later. Uninsured depositors -- who had chosen to keep more than $250K in a single account -- were made whole at zero cost. Source: federalreserve.gov (joint press release, March 12 2023).

question: In Bastiat's framing of the SVB bailout, uninsured tech and venture-capital depositors had CHOSEN to keep more than $250,000 in a single account, betting against a run. What market signal did the bailout eliminate?
answer: Diversify your bank exposure across accounts or lose it when a run hits
choices: Diversify your bank exposure across accounts or lose it when a run hits
Bank only with federally-insured community banks in your local region
Convert cash holdings into short-duration Treasury bills below $250,000
Purchase supplemental private deposit insurance from a licensed carrier
context: The market's normal signal to a depositor over the FDIC cap: split your money across banks. The 2023 SVB rescue eliminated that signal for large uninsured depositors going forward. Source: cato.org/commentary/svb-bailout-moral-hazard.

question: The classic Victorian rule for a central bank's crisis response was written by Walter Bagehot in his 1873 book Lombard Street. In three phrases, Bagehot said the lender of last resort should lend freely, against good collateral, and at what kind of interest rate?
context: Bagehot's rule: 'lend freely, at high rates, against good collateral.' The punishing rate is the point -- banks would only draw the facility in true crisis, not because it was cheap. The 2023 SVB bailout gave uninsured depositors a FREE option instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street_(book).

question: The moral-hazard critique of federal bailouts has a specific Bastiat-style logical shape: an intervention in one crisis changes the expectations of every future actor, so the true cost is paid in later crises the current bailout invisibly enables. Which is the precedent-and-sequel pair that this ladder traces?
answer: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
choices: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization
Chrysler 1979 as precedent; TARP 2008 as reversal
LTCM 1998 as precedent; Chrysler 1979 as sequel
AIG 2008 as precedent; LTCM 1998 as sequel
context: The 2008 TARP established that the federal government would rescue major-bank creditors; the 2023 SVB action made the rescue apply to any deposit at any bank the regulators later name systemic. The UNSEEN cost of 2008 is paid in the changed behavior visible in 2023. Source: mercatus.org/publications/svb-bailout-changed-behavior.

question: Anna Schwartz, co-author with Milton Friedman of the 1963 Monetary History of the United States, delivered a one-line warning about the direction the Federal Reserve had taken by the 21st century. In her formulation, the Fed was now in the business of what?
answer: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
choices: Preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money
Fine-tuning the unemployment rate to a Phillips-curve target
Coordinating fiscal policy with the elected Treasury
Regulating derivatives markets under a systemic-risk mandate
context: Schwartz's warning, restated in her final years: the Fed's mission had drifted from monetary stability toward defending asset prices, and the moral hazard consequences would surface in the next crisis. Source: wsj.com/articles/anna-schwartz-1915-2012.

question: In 1955 Milton Friedman published an essay in a Rutgers University Press volume arguing that even if government should FUND schooling, it does not follow that government must PRODUCE it. What title did he give the essay that founded the modern school-choice movement?
answer: The Role of Government in Education
choices: The Role of Government in Education
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education,' in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest (Rutgers University Press, 1955). Friedman argued for funding pupils (via vouchers) rather than school buildings. Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: Between 2012 and 2022 one large American public-school teachers' union struck three times -- for 9 days in 2012, 11 days in 2019, and 5 days in 2022 -- each strike closing schools for roughly 300,000 K-12 children. Which city's teachers union is this?
context: The Chicago Teachers Union struck in 2012 (9 school days), 2019 (11 days), and 2022 (5 days) -- each closing schools for approximately 300,000 students, disproportionately low-income, whose parents cannot easily choose an alternative. Source: chicagotribune.com strike coverage.

question: In 2004 Congress enacted a targeted federal voucher program funded scholarships of about $8,000-$12,000 for low-income families in a single US city to attend private schools. What is this program called?
context: The DC Opportunity Scholarship Program was enacted in the 2004 DC School Choice Incentive Act. Multi-year IES / Patrick Wolf and Anna Kisida evaluations (US Department of Education 2010, 2018) found statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for scholarship recipients. Source: ed.gov (DC OSP evaluations).

question: Multi-year US Department of Education evaluations of the DC Opportunity Scholarship Program by Patrick Wolf and colleagues found a specific statistically-significant benefit for scholarship recipients relative to non-recipients. Which outcome did they document?
context: The IES evaluations (2010, 2018) documented statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for DC OSP scholarship recipients. Congressional attempts to shut the program down have come repeatedly from the DC teachers-union's allies. Source: ies.ed.gov (Wolf + Kisida evaluations).

question: In 2020 the Basic Books published a late-career book by an American economist comparing NYC charter-school and district-school test scores for demographically-matched cohorts of children in the SAME physical buildings, under NYC's charter co-location rules. Who wrote that book?
context: Thomas Sowell, Charter Schools and Their Enemies (Basic Books, 2020). Sowell used NYC co-location data to compare charter and district students in the same building. In every matched-building comparison, charter students outperformed. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 2020).

question: Sowell's 2020 book used a specific NYC building policy that let him compare charter and district students in the SAME physical structure with the SAME neighborhood demographics. What is that NYC policy called?
context: NYC co-location rules place charter schools and district schools inside the same physical building, allowing direct like-for-like comparison. Sowell used this data to build his 2020 book. Source: schools.nyc.gov (co-location policy history).

question: The standard academic reference for the public-choice analysis of teachers' unions in American K-12 policy is a 2011 Brookings Institution book titled 'Special Interest.' Who wrote it?
context: Terry Moe, Special Interest: Teachers Unions and America's Public Schools (Brookings Institution, 2011). Moe applied Olson-style analysis to teachers-union political power. Source: brookings.edu (Moe 2011).

question: In 1993-94 California voters faced Proposition 174, a ballot initiative to institute a statewide school-voucher system. The measure was defeated after one specific interest group massively outspent the pro-voucher side, by roughly ten to one. Which group led that spending effort?
context: The CTA spent tens of millions of dollars against Proposition 174 in 1993, outspending the pro-voucher side by roughly 10-to-1. The initiative failed. It is a textbook Olson concentrated-benefit case study. Source: California Secretary of State campaign-finance records; Moe (2011).

question: Applied to K-12 education, Olson's concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost framework identifies a specific concentrated interest that organizes, negotiates, endorses candidates, and staffs school-board elections. Who is that concentrated interest?
context: The teachers' union is the concentrated organized beneficiary with the resources and staff to shape school-board and legislative outcomes. Parents and children are the dispersed victim class that pays higher taxes and receives worse outcomes but does not systematically organize. Source: Moe, Special Interest (Brookings 2011).

question: The K-12 education case teaches a reasoning move about how to frame the education-policy debate. What is the honest structural question a public-choice reader should press, rather than 'are teachers bad'?
answer: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
choices: Which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules
Which political party spends more per capita on schools
Which state has the highest average teacher salary
Which district uses the newest textbooks
context: The Olson-Stigler applied move: individual educators are usually decent people; the rule-selection process is dominated by whichever organized interest has resources and staff. That is a structural analysis, not a moral one. Source: Olson (1965); Moe (2011).

question: Milton Friedman's 1955 essay was the founding modern statement of the school-choice movement. Its central design proposal separated two functions government had traditionally combined. Which pair of functions did Friedman propose separating?
context: Friedman's move: the state may legitimately fund a service without also being the exclusive producer of that service. Vouchers fund the pupil rather than the building; private, charter, magnet, and district schools then compete for that funded pupil. Source: Friedman, 'Role of Government in Education' (1955).

question: Fifteen US states have constitutional or statutory term limits on their state legislators, most enacted in the 1990-94 reform wave. The US Congress has none. The one American office where a two-term limit was formally added to the Constitution is the presidency. Which constitutional amendment imposed it?
context: The 22nd Amendment (ratified February 27, 1951) limits the president to two elected terms, passed in response to FDR's four elections. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Twenty-Second Amendment).

question: In 1995 the US Supreme Court decided a 5-4 case holding that only a constitutional amendment (not state action) can add qualifications for the US Congress, striking down state-imposed congressional term limits. What is that case called?
answer: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
choices: US Term Limits Inc. v. Thornton
context: US Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton, 514 US 779 (1995), decided 5-4 on May 22, 1995. States cannot impose term limits on federal congressional service; only a constitutional amendment can. Source: supremecourt.gov (514 US 779).

question: Public polling on a constitutional amendment for congressional term limits has been remarkably stable for decades. What is the approximate range of public support Gallup and Pew typically find for such an amendment?
context: Congressional term-limits polling has stayed in the ~75-83% range across decades of surveys by Gallup, Pew, and others. It has never come close to the two-thirds House and Senate majorities required to send an amendment to the states. Source: news.gallup.com (term-limits polling history).

question: The Buchanan-Tullock 1962 framework distinguishes two levels of political decision. At the higher, rules-of-the-game level, individuals rationally consent to constraints on future incumbents; at the lower level, sitting incumbents rationally resist those same constraints. What does Buchanan-Tullock call these two levels?
context: The constitutional level is where rules are chosen behind a veil of uncertainty about your own future position. The post-constitutional level is choices made within the rules by known-position actors. Term limits are the paradigmatic case of a rule desired at level one, resisted at level two. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 6.

question: In November 1990 California voters approved the first US state legislative term-limits initiative. What was that ballot proposition's number?
context: California Proposition 140 (November 1990) established term limits on state legislators, executive-branch officials, and staff. It launched the 1990-94 wave of state-level term-limit reforms. Source: California Secretary of State (Proposition 140 official election materials).

question: Studies of California and other state legislatures after term-limits reforms found the reforms had substantial but not entirely expected effects. Toward which actors did power shift after term limits reduced legislators' seniority and expertise?
answer: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
choices: The executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff
The judicial branch and state constitutional officers
Local school boards and city councils
context: Post-term-limits studies including Elhauge (1997) and Hansen on California pre-and-post-Proposition-140 found power shifted toward actors whose knowledge was not term-limited. The Virginia school's unintended-consequences prediction. Source: Elhauge, University of Chicago Law Review (1997).

question: One incumbent Democratic congressman offered a widely-quoted rhetorical parry to term-limits advocates in the 2010s: 'Congress has term limits: they're called elections.' Which congressman is famous for that line?
context: Alan Grayson (D-FL), a two-term House member, repeatedly used the 'elections are term limits' line as the standard incumbent parry. The line captures the post-constitutional logic Buchanan predicted. Source: contemporary press coverage 2010-16.

question: Switzerland's federal executive is a seven-member Federal Council whose presidency rotates yearly among its members, so no single person accumulates the perquisites of office long enough to entrench. What does the Swiss system illustrate?
answer: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
choices: A constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start
A recent reform in the wake of a scandal
A UN treaty obligation binding on European states
A holdover from medieval papal succession rules
context: Switzerland's rotating presidency is a constitutional-level structural rule adopted at foundation, so no sitting incumbent had to vote to shorten his own tenure. It illustrates the Buchanan point about which anti-incumbent rules can actually get chosen and stick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Council_(Switzerland).

question: The Buchanan-style diagnosis of congressional term-limits gridlock generalizes to other reforms of the same structural shape. Which of the following reforms shares the pattern where those who would lose from the reform are the ones whose votes would enact it?
answer: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
choices: Campaign-finance reform in the US Congress
Sunset provisions for expiring tax cuts
context: Campaign-finance reform, redistricting reform, gerrymandering reform, and term limits all share the losers-must-enact-the-reform pattern. Buchanan's constitutional-level analysis predicts these reforms will struggle regardless of majority popular support. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman + Handley on gerrymandering.

question: The reasoning-move the term-limits case teaches is a default expectation about reforms with a specific structure. Whenever a proposed reform requires the CURRENT incumbents to accept a cost to themselves for a benefit that flows to future citizens or challengers, what should the analyst expect?
answer: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
choices: The reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support
The reform will pass by acclamation within one session
The reform will pass automatically once polling exceeds sixty percent
The reform will pass only through executive order
context: The default is failure at the post-constitutional stage. Which is not cynicism -- it is Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy analysis of which rules survive democratic selection when the rule-writers themselves would bear the costs of the rule. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Grofman (2006).

question: Between May and July of 2022, three separate 'crypto' companies collapsed in a chain reaction that erased tens of billions in customer funds -- and had nothing to do with Bitcoin. Which of these three altcoin-space projects failed FIRST in that cascade?
context: Terra/LUNA collapsed May 9-12, 2022; Celsius froze withdrawals June 12 and filed for bankruptcy July 13; Voyager filed for bankruptcy July 5. FTX was a later collapse in November 2022 that traced back partly to the same contagion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_(blockchain).

question: The Terra project was run by a South Korean entrepreneur whose flagship 'algorithmic stablecoin' UST was supposed to hold a stable one-dollar value via a mathematical relationship with a sister token. Who was Terra's founder?
context: Do Kwon (born 1991, South Korean) co-founded Terraform Labs and led the Terra/LUNA project. SBF ran FTX; Mashinsky ran Celsius; Su Zhu ran Three Arrows Capital. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_Kwon.

question: Terra's UST 'stablecoin' offered users up to 20% yields via a related lending product. When UST lost its dollar peg in May 2022, the algorithm required minting massive amounts of the sister token LUNA to redeem the failing UST -- and the flood of new LUNA destroyed LUNA's own value. Roughly how much nominal value evaporated in days?
context: The May 9-12, 2022 collapse of Terra/LUNA evaporated roughly $40 billion in nominal market value. Multiple suicides among affected retail investors were reported in South Korea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_(blockchain).

question: A separate US-based 'crypto bank' run by Alex Mashinsky had been offering high yields on customer deposits before the Terra collapse triggered a run. On which date did that company freeze withdrawals and later file for bankruptcy?
answer: Celsius froze on June 12, 2022 and filed bankruptcy July 13
choices: Celsius froze on June 12, 2022 and filed bankruptcy July 13
Celsius froze on May 9, 2022 and filed bankruptcy May 12
Celsius froze on November 6, 2022 and filed bankruptcy November 11
Celsius froze on January 1, 2023 and filed bankruptcy February 1
context: Celsius Network froze all customer withdrawals on June 12, 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on July 13, 2022. The other dates correspond to unrelated collapses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius_Network.

question: The Celsius Network freeze on June 12, 2022 locked up customer funds while bankruptcy proceedings began. Roughly what dollar amount of customer deposits was trapped in Celsius when withdrawals were frozen?
context: Estimated customer funds locked in the Celsius bankruptcy were about $4.7 billion. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius_Network.

question: A third 'crypto broker' collapsed alongside Celsius in July 2022 after one of its biggest borrowers -- a hedge fund destroyed by the Terra collapse -- defaulted on hundreds of millions of dollars in loans. Which hedge fund's default destroyed Voyager Digital?
context: Three Arrows Capital (3AC), run by Su Zhu and Kyle Davies, was destroyed by the Terra/LUNA collapse and defaulted on Voyager's loans, forcing Voyager into bankruptcy July 5, 2022. Alameda Research was FTX's affiliated trading firm (later collapse); LTCM was a 1998 failure; Bridgewater is unrelated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_Digital.

question: Do Kwon fled South Korea after Terra's May 2022 collapse and was eventually arrested in a specific small European country in March 2023 while trying to travel on falsified documents. In which country was Kwon arrested?
context: Do Kwon was arrested at Podgorica airport in Montenegro in March 2023 with false Costa Rican documents; he was later extradited to the US in December 2024. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_Kwon.

question: Alex Mashinsky, the CEO of Celsius Network, was arrested after his firm's collapse and eventually convicted in a New York federal court in December 2024. What was the substance of his conviction?
answer: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
choices: fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL
context: Mashinsky was convicted December 2024 of fraud and market manipulation related to the Celsius native token CEL. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Mashinsky; US DOJ press releases.

question: In the 2022 collapse cascade -- Terra, Celsius, Voyager, and later FTX -- one specific class of customer was structurally unaffected in every case. Which decision distinguished the customers who kept their bitcoin from those who did not?
answer: holding their bitcoin in self-custody rather than trusting a third-party high-yield service
choices: holding their bitcoin in self-custody rather than trusting a third-party high-yield service
buying the failed exchange's native token before the collapse to unlock priority withdrawal
enabling two-factor authentication on the exchange account and using strong unique passwords
signing up for the exchange's advertised insurance program and paying the monthly premium fee
context: In every 2022 collapse the customers who had moved bitcoin to their own hardware wallets were unaffected; those who had trusted a third party for a promised yield lost access. 2FA does not protect against custodian insolvency; native tokens (LUNA, CEL, FTT) collapsed alongside their issuers; insurance programs were widely absent or hollow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_bubble.

question: A Bitcoin educator summarizing 2022 for a general audience presses one specific pedagogical distinction that Andreas Antonopoulos and others have taught for a decade. Which move does the argument press about how the failing 'crypto' companies structurally differed from Bitcoin itself?
answer: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
choices: That 'crypto' companies with an issuer or a promised-yield model can collapse, while Bitcoin held in self-custody has no counterparty to fail in the first place
That all cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin eventually collapse in the same way through cascading market losses and customer runs on custodial services
That Bitcoin itself failed as a protocol in 2022 alongside Terra and Celsius and only survived because major exchanges chose to keep supporting it
That regulators should treat Bitcoin and 'crypto' identically in every jurisdiction since the underlying mathematics is the same across the whole industry
context: The Antonopoulos/Ammous move: Terra, Celsius, Voyager and FTX all had issuers or promised-yield structures with counterparty risk; Bitcoin held on a hardware wallet has neither. Bitcoin itself did not collapse; its price fell but the protocol continued operating; equating 'crypto' with Bitcoin is exactly the confusion the argument refuses. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.); Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: In July 1850 a French classical-liberal writer, dying of tuberculosis at forty-nine, sent to press a sixty-page pamphlet of twelve short chapters, each a worked economic example. Which writer sent it?
context: Bastiat (1801-1850) published the pamphlet a few months before his December 1850 death in Rome; it is his last complete work. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: The 1850 Bastiat pamphlet carries a title, in the French original, that names the whole method in five words. What is that title, in English?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
A Petition of the Merchants of Bordeaux
context: French original: Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas. Standard English editions since 1859 keep the literal title. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: The opening sentence of Bastiat's 1850 essay states the whole method up front: 'In the economic sphere, an act, a habit, an institution, a law produces not only one effect, but a series of effects. Of these effects, the first alone is immediate ... the other effects emerge only subsequently; they are not seen; we are fortunate if we FORESEE them.' In one economist's-shorthand phrase, what distinction does this sentence draw?
answer: Between the seen and the unseen
choices: Between the seen and the unseen
context: The whole essay's method is a single move: name the visible first effect, then name the invisible later effects the visible one hid. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay draws its central contrast between two kinds of economist. 'The bad economist,' he writes, 'confines himself to the visible effect; the good economist' does what?
answer: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
choices: Takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen
Reports the aggregate government multiplier for each proposed policy
Consults the historical record for identical policies in prior centuries
Weighs the immediate winners against a randomly-drawn sample of losers
context: This is the essay's programmatic sentence: the good economist FORESEES the effects the bad economist misses because they haven't happened yet. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay is built as a sequence of twelve short chapters, each a worked example of the seen/unseen method applied to a specific French policy. Which chapter opens the sequence?
context: Chapter 1 is 'The Broken Window', built around James Goodfellow's careless son and the six-franc pane; every later chapter is another worked case. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay was not translated into English until nine years after his death, when a Scottish educator produced the first English version in 1859. Which translator brought it into English?
context: William Ballantyne Hodgson (1815-1880), Scottish educational reformer and free-trader, produced the 1859 English edition; George B. de Huszar's Liberty Fund translation (1964) is the modern standard. Source: oll.libertyfund.org/titles/bastiat-selected-essays-on-political-economy.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay was kept in continuous American print starting in 1946 by a New York classical-liberal institute co-founded that same year by Leonard Read and Henry Hazlitt. Which institute kept it in print?
context: FEE (Irvington-on-Hudson, 1946) has kept Bastiat's essays in print in America without a break for eighty years; Cato (1977), Mises Institute (1982), and Heritage (1973) all came later. Source: fee.org/about/our-history.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics rebrands Bastiat's 1850 seen/unseen move under a two-part label built around a single word repeated. Sowell says the bad economist stops at stage one. What is his term for what the good economist reaches?
context: Sowell uses 'stage-one vs stage-two thinking' throughout Basic Economics (2000-present) and Applied Economics; it is the same Bastiat method under a new name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Bastiat's 1850 essay found its most famous 20th-century restatement in a short American book of 1946, structured as a book-length application of the seen/unseen method to New Deal and postwar policies and explicitly dedicated to Bastiat on its title page. Which book was that?
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper & Brothers, 1946), dedicated 'To Frederic Bastiat, 1801-1850,' is the essay in modern American English; it has never gone out of print. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: Milton Friedman named a single 1850 French essay as a formative influence on his own economic writing, saying it taught him to look past the immediate visible effect of any policy. Which essay did Friedman credit?
answer: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
context: Friedman credited Bastiat's essay in interviews and in Free to Choose (1980); its influence on the seen/unseen habit runs through his Newsweek columns and TV series alike. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-frederic-bastiat.

question: A grocer's daughter from Grantham became leader of the Conservative Party in 1975 and served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 4 May 1979 to 28 November 1990 -- the longest-serving British PM of the twentieth century. Which Prime Minister?
context: Thatcher led the Conservative Party from 1975 and won three general elections (1979, 1983, 1987). The three distractors are all real prominent British women in politics of the same generation: Barbara Castle (Labour cabinet minister), Shirley Williams (Labour then SDP), Betty Boothroyd (Speaker of the House of Commons 1992-2000). None was Prime Minister. Source: Wikipedia, Margaret Thatcher.

question: An actor who had been Governor of California became the fortieth President of the United States, serving two terms from 20 January 1981 to 20 January 1989 and cutting the top federal income tax rate from 70% to 28% across two big tax acts. Which President?
context: Reagan's two terms overlapped almost exactly with Thatcher's middle and later years in office; the two governments consciously coordinated on tax cuts, deregulation, and Cold War strategy. Carter was Reagan's predecessor (1977-1981); Ford served 1974-1977; George H. W. Bush was Reagan's Vice President and successor (1989-1993). Source: Wikipedia, Ronald Reagan.

question: At a Conservative Research Department meeting in the summer of 1975 Margaret Thatcher interrupted a speaker urging a 'middle way' by pulling a book from her handbag, banging it on the table, and saying 'THIS is what we believe.' John Ranelagh, who was present, recorded the incident in his 1991 book Thatcher's People. Which book did Thatcher slam on the table?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty
choices: Friedrich Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty
Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations
Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France
Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies
context: The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is Hayek's mature political philosophy -- long, dense, and radical. The three distractors are all real classical-liberal or conservative touchstones Thatcher admired but did not brandish that day. The Ranelagh account is the founding anecdote of the intellectual side of Thatcherism. Source: Sotheby's, 'This is what we believe: Margaret Thatcher and F. A. Hayek.'

question: In April 1947 Friedrich Hayek gathered 36 like-minded classical-liberal scholars -- among them Ludwig von Mises, Milton Friedman, Karl Popper, and Lionel Robbins -- at a hotel in a Swiss mountain village to found a society that would connect free-market intellectuals across the next four decades. What is the society called?
context: The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS) met at the Hotel du Parc on Mont Pelerin, above Lake Geneva, in the first ten days of April 1947 and has met roughly biennially ever since. The three distractors are real organisations of very different politics: the Fabian Society is British democratic socialist (founded 1884), the Bilderberg Group is a private policy conference (founded 1954), and the Trilateral Commission is a US-Europe-Japan policy body (founded 1973). Source: Wikipedia, Mont Pelerin Society.

question: In November 1984 the Thatcher government privatised a state-owned monopoly by floating over 50% of it on the London Stock Exchange in the largest share offering in British history to that date; more than two million small investors bought shares. Which company was privatised?
context: British Telecom (BT) was valued at around £8 billion; the 51% flotation raised roughly £4 billion. British Rail, the Post Office, and the National Coal Board all remained in public ownership through the Thatcher years -- the coal board actively so, since it was the government's opponent in the miners' strike of 1984-85. British Gas followed in 1986 with the famous 'Tell Sid' campaign; British Airways in 1987. Source: Institute for Government, 'The Privatisation of British Telecom (1984).'

question: From 6 March 1984 to 3 March 1985 the National Union of Mineworkers waged a year-long strike against the Thatcher government's pit-closure programme; the union returned to work with no settlement, the government made no concessions, and the defeat effectively broke the industrial power of British trade unions for a generation. Which union president led the strike?
context: Scargill led the NUM from 1982 and was the strike's public face; the government had spent years stockpiling coal and had prepared for the confrontation. Jack Jones led the TGWU in the 1970s; Vic Feather was TUC general secretary; Rodney Bickerstaffe led NUPE and later UNISON. None led the 1984-85 miners' strike. Source: Wikipedia, 1984-1985 United Kingdom miners' strike.

question: On 27 October 1986 the Thatcher government pushed through a deregulation of the London Stock Exchange that abolished fixed commissions, opened membership to foreign firms, ended the separation of brokers and jobbers, and moved trading onto electronic screens. What is the reform commonly called?
context: The Big Bang is credited with making the City of London one of the two global financial centres of the following generation. The three distractors are all real financial-regulation events but from other countries and other decades: Glass-Steagall was a 1933 US bank-separation law; Bretton Woods was the 1944 international monetary conference; the Volcker Rule was a 2010 US restriction on bank proprietary trading. Source: Wikipedia, Big Bang (financial markets).

question: In 1988 the Chancellor of the Exchequer cut the UK top rate of income tax to 40% -- it had stood at 83% when Thatcher took office in 1979 -- and reduced the basic rate to 25%. Which Chancellor delivered the 1988 Budget?
context: Lawson was Chancellor from 1983 to 1989; the 1988 Budget is generally treated as the defining Thatcher-era tax reform. Denis Healey was Labour Chancellor (1974-1979); Geoffrey Howe was the Conservative Chancellor who cut the top rate from 83% to 60% in 1979 (Lawson took the further step to 40%); Norman Lamont was John Major's Chancellor (1990-1993), after Thatcher had left office. Source: OMFIF, 'Nigel Lawson: influential politician and architect of Thatcherism.'

question: On 17 November 1983 President Reagan invited an 84-year-old Vienna-born economist to the White House and wrote in his diary that night: 'Met 85 year old Frederick Von Hayek -- the great economist, a pupil of Von Mises.' The visit signalled that ideas long marginal in academic economics had reached the American presidency. Which economist did Reagan host?
context: Hayek's health had been fragile for years; the 1974 Nobel and the Reagan-Thatcher recognition of the following decade reinvigorated him and his final book, The Fatal Conceit, appeared in 1988. Milton Friedman was Reagan's other favourite economist and a frequent White House visitor; Samuelson and Galbraith were the leading American Keynesians of the era, neither aligned with Reagan. Source: Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation, Diary Entry 11/17/1983.

question: A former RAF pilot who read the Reader's Digest condensation of Hayek's Road to Serfdom in 1945 later visited Hayek at the LSE seeking political advice; Hayek told him not to go into party politics but to fight the war of ideas from outside, and in 1955 he founded a London think-tank that became the intellectual supply-line for the Thatcher revolution. Which think-tank did Antony Fisher found?
context: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) at 2 Lord North Street pumped out short, sharp free-market monographs from 1957 onwards and became the model for over 150 similar think-tanks Fisher would help seed worldwide. The three distractors are real organisations of adjacent politics: the Adam Smith Institute (founded 1977) was a later free-market think-tank; the Centre for Policy Studies was founded by Keith Joseph and Thatcher herself in 1974; the Fabian Society is the century-old British socialist think-tank.
