Source: Economic History Society, 'Waging the War of Ideas: the Institute of Economic Affairs.'

question: The American stock-market boom of the 1920s ended in a specific two-day panic on the New York Stock Exchange, remembered by the color-and-weekday nicknames of its worst sessions. Which pair of days marked the crash?
context: Black Thursday (October 24, 1929) began the panic; Black Tuesday (October 29, 1929) broke the market. Both names have been the standard shorthand ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929.

question: The 1920s American stock boom that ended in the October 1929 panic is remembered by a nickname evoking its wild energy and jazz-age culture. What is the era usually called?
context: The Dow Jones rose from about 63 in August 1921 to a peak of 381 on September 3, 1929 -- roughly a six-fold gain in eight years. Easy credit and margin buying drove the run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roaring_Twenties.

question: The famous stock index whose value tracked the 1920s boom hit its pre-crash peak of 381 in early September 1929 and did not regain that level until the mid-1950s. Which index?
context: The Dow peaked at 381.17 on September 3, 1929, then bottomed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932 -- an 89% peak-to-trough decline. The S&P 500 in modern form didn't exist yet, and NASDAQ was created in 1971. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: In the 1920s, ordinary investors could buy stock with borrowed money, putting up only a small fraction of the price in cash and financing the rest. Roughly what minimum cash fraction was common at the peak of the boom?
context: Ten-percent margin was widespread by 1929 -- an investor could hold a $1,000 position with $100 down. When prices fell, brokers issued margin calls, forcing cascading liquidation. Post-crash Regulation T set higher minimum margin. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/stock-market-crash-of-1929.

question: On the worst single day of the October 1929 panic, trading volume set a record that stood for decades. Roughly how many shares changed hands on that Tuesday?
context: October 29, 1929 saw about 16 million shares traded on the NYSE -- a volume record that held for nearly 40 years. The Dow fell nearly 12 percent that day. Source: nyse.com historical trading records.

question: The peak-to-trough decline of the Dow between September 1929 and July 1932 was extraordinary by any historical standard. Approximately what percentage did the index lose from top to bottom?
context: Peak 381.17 on September 3, 1929; trough 41.22 on July 8, 1932 -- roughly an 89% collapse. Compare: October 1987 crash ~22% in a day, 2008 GFC ~54% peak-to-trough. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: In mid-October 1929, just two weeks before the crash, Yale economist Irving Fisher made a public forecast that later became the emblematic bad prediction of the era. What did he say the stock market had reached?
choices: The end of its long bull run
context: Fisher's October 15, 1929 statement -- 'stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau' -- became a cautionary quote about expert overconfidence. Fisher lost most of his personal fortune in the crash. Source: New York Times, October 16, 1929.

question: Austrian and monetarist economists argue that the 1929 panic itself did not cause the decade of misery that followed; something else turned a market crash into a depression. On this view, what actually turned the crash into the Great Depression?
answer: The Federal Reserve allowing the money supply to collapse by about a third
choices: The Federal Reserve allowing the money supply to collapse by about a third
Excess consumer saving that starved industry of demand
A demographic bulge that shrank the working-age population
A sudden collapse in agricultural export prices alone
context: Friedman and Schwartz's Monetary History showed M2 fell about 33% between 1929 and 1933 as the Fed failed to counter bank runs. Recessions had followed earlier crashes (1907, 1920-21) without becoming decade-long depressions. Source: Friedman + Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (1963).

question: The 1920-21 American slump is the counterfactual case Austrians cite: a sharp downturn with roughly 12 percent unemployment and a 17 percent GNP drop, in which the federal government cut spending and let wages and prices adjust. Roughly how long did that earlier recession last?
context: The 1920-21 depression under Harding ended within about a year and a half despite being deeper on some measures than the 1929 crash's opening year. It is the natural-experiment case for the 'do less' policy response. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/forgotten-depression-1920.

question: The date the pre-crash Dow peak of 381 was first regained by the same index -- after the 1929 fall, the Depression years, World War II, and the postwar boom -- was a landmark for anyone who had held stocks since 1929. In what decade did the Dow finally recover to its September 1929 peak?
context: The Dow first closed above its September 1929 peak on November 23, 1954 -- more than 25 years after the crash. Investors who bought at the top and held through the crash needed a quarter-century to break even in nominal terms. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: On 9 October 1974 the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced that year's Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. One of the two joint recipients was a 75-year-old Vienna-born classical liberal whose 1944 book The Road to Serfdom was a household name on the political right. Which economist won a share of the 1974 prize?
context: The cable from Stockholm reached Hayek in Salzburg. Mises had died the year before, in 1973, and never received the prize. Roepke, another classical-liberal continental economist, died in 1966. Machlup was Hayek's fellow Vienna Circle Austrian and later Princeton economist, but was not the 1974 laureate. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1974 press release.

question: The 1974 economics prize was announced as a joint award to Hayek and a Swedish economist -- an odd-couple pairing widely read as a deliberate committee attempt to balance the honouring of a classical liberal by including a co-recipient from the socialist tradition. Who was Hayek's co-laureate?
context: Myrdal was a Swedish socialist economist, welfare-state architect, and author of An American Dilemma. He was reportedly furious to share the prize with an 'Austrian reactionary' and later argued the economics prize should be abolished. Ohlin was another Swedish laureate (1977); Leontief won in 1973; Kuznets in 1971. All are real Nobel names of the surrounding years. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1974 press release; FEE, 'Hayek's Rejuvenating Event.'

question: 1974 was the peak year of a phenomenon Anglo-American economies were then living through that the standard Keynesian Phillips-curve model had said was impossible: rising inflation AND rising unemployment at the same time. What is the phenomenon called?
context: Stagflation (stagnation + inflation) was the defining economic failure of the 1970s and the empirical event that broke the post-war Keynesian consensus. Deflation is falling prices; hyperinflation is very rapid inflation; recession is falling output. Only stagflation was the phenomenon the accepted macro model of the day said could not happen. Source: FFF, '50 Years Ago: Hayek's Nobel Lecture on The Pretence of Knowledge.'

question: On 11 December 1974 Hayek stepped to a lectern in Stockholm to deliver his Nobel lecture -- one of the most-cited Nobel lectures in the prize's history. What is its one-phrase title?
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: The lecture is short -- about fifteen minutes -- and reads as a compressed statement of the Hayekian critique of macroeconomics. The three distractors are all real Hayek works of other decades: Road to Serfdom (1944), 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (an American Economic Review article, 1945), Constitution of Liberty (1960). Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: The central charge of Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture is that economists have imitated the methods of the natural sciences -- pretending to a quantitative predictive power over aggregate variables that in principle they cannot have, because the underlying data are dispersed across millions of minds. Which one-word label did Hayek give to this false imitation?
context: Hayek had used 'scientism' as the target of an earlier essay, 'Scientism and the Study of Society' (1942); the Nobel lecture is the mature restatement. Positivism, empiricism, and rationalism are real philosophy-of-science labels for adjacent doctrines but are not the specific pejorative Hayek coined for the imitation move. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: In The Pretence of Knowledge Hayek argues that macroeconomic models pretend to predict aggregate variables that in principle they cannot, because the relevant information is not held by any single agency. Where does Hayek say the missing information actually sits?
answer: Dispersed across millions of individual minds
choices: Dispersed across millions of individual minds
In the hands of the central bank's research staff
Encoded in slowly-updating statistical time series
context: This is the direct application of Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' -- the knowledge relevant to allocation is the local, tacit, contextual knowledge of individuals, communicated through prices, not through any central agency. The three distractors describe the sources macro forecasters actually reach for; Hayek's point is that these are precisely NOT where the decision-relevant knowledge lives. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Hayek's target in The Pretence of Knowledge is explicitly the doctrine of aggregate-demand management that had dominated Anglo-American economics since the Second World War. Whose 1936 book is the founding text of that doctrine?
answer: John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Alvin Hansen's Fiscal Policy and Business Cycles
Joan Robinson's The Economics of Imperfect Competition
context: Keynes's General Theory (1936) reframed macroeconomics around aggregate demand and government fiscal management. The three distractors are all real texts of the Keynesian tradition -- Hansen (1941) popularised Keynes in America; Samuelson's textbook (1948) taught two generations; Robinson (1933) was a Cambridge Keynesian. Hayek's Nobel lecture is aimed at the whole tradition Keynes founded. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: The Pretence of Knowledge closes with a warning that the pretence itself has political costs. Hayek writes that the student of society must recognise the insuperable limits to his knowledge to guard him against becoming an accomplice in men's fatal striving to control society -- a striving which may make him the destroyer of a civilization which has this specific origin. Which origin does Hayek name?
answer: That has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals
choices: That has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals
That has been designed by the great political thinkers of the age
That has been built by the guiding hand of the modern state
That has been forged in the industrial revolutions of the nineteenth century
context: The full closing sentence: 'a striving which makes him not only a tyrant over his fellows, but which may well make him the destroyer of a civilization which no brain has designed but which has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals.' This is Hayek's spontaneous-order doctrine restated as a moral warning. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences that Hayek shared in 1974 was not one of the original Nobel prizes established in Alfred Nobel's 1895 will. It was funded by Sweden's central bank in memory of Nobel and first awarded in a specific later year, marking the first year an economics prize was given at all. Which year was the prize first awarded?
context: The first economics prize (1969) went jointly to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen for econometrics. 1901 was the first year of the ORIGINAL Nobel prizes -- physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace. 1945 and 1958 are distractor dates from unrelated Swedish-institutional history. The 1974 Hayek award was thus the sixth economics prize ever given. Source: NobelPrize.org, Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

question: The 1974 prize was widely seen as a turning point that made previously marginal free-market ideas respectable in mainstream economics. In the twelve years after Hayek's award, two other economists in the classical-liberal / public-choice tradition also won the same prize: Milton Friedman in 1976 and a Virginia professor in 1986 whose Calculus of Consent (with Gordon Tullock, 1962) founded public-choice theory. Who was the 1986 laureate?
context: Buchanan won in 1986 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The three distractors are all real Chicago-tradition laureates of the same decade: Stigler (1982) for regulatory-capture theory, Coase (1991) for the theory of social cost, Becker (1992) for the economic analysis of human behaviour. All belong to the same broader turn; only Buchanan won in 1986 for public choice. Source: NobelPrize.org, all prizes in economic sciences.

question: Hayek's health had been poor in the years before the 1974 prize, and friends reported the recognition genuinely reinvigorated him. His final book, published in 1988 when he was 89, is a sustained argument against socialism as an intellectual and moral system. What is the book titled?
answer: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
choices: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
context: The Fatal Conceit (1988) is Hayek's summary book of his ninth decade; it argues that socialism rests on a 'fatal conceit' -- the belief that a rational mind can design social institutions better than the trial-and-error evolution of the market order. The three distractors are all real Hayek titles from other decades: The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952), Individualism and Economic Order (1948), and The Sensory Order (1952, on cognitive psychology). Source: FEE, 'Hayek's Rejuvenating Event.'

question: In August 1980 a shipyard electrician led a strike at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk that founded the first independent trade union in the Warsaw Pact. What was that union called?
context: Solidarnosc was founded in August 1980 at the Gdansk shipyard strikes. It was the first independent trade union in the Warsaw Pact. Banned under martial law in December 1981, it survived underground through the 1980s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union).

question: The shipyard electrician who led the Solidarity strike in 1980 and later became President of Poland was known by his surname. Who was he?
context: Lech Walesa was a shipyard electrician who became Solidarity chairman, won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize, and served as President of Poland 1990-95. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lech_Wa%C5%82%C4%99sa.

question: On June 4, 1989 Solidarity's partly free elections in Poland produced a stunning result, forming the first non-communist government in the Warsaw Pact. Roughly how well did Solidarity do?
answer: It won 99 of 100 Senate seats and every contested Sejm seat
choices: It won 99 of 100 Senate seats and every contested Sejm seat
It won about half the seats up for election
It narrowly took a small opposition foothold
context: The Round Table Agreement allowed contested elections for the Senate and one-third of the Sejm. Solidarity won 99/100 Senate seats and swept the contested Sejm seats. The first Solidarity-led government followed in August 1989 under Prime Minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Polish_legislative_election.

question: On May 2, 1989 border guards of one country began dismantling the electrified fence along its Austrian border, opening the first practical route out of the Eastern Bloc. Which country cut the fence?
context: Hungarian border guards began cutting the barrier along the Austrian border on May 2, 1989. East Germans vacationing in Hungary began crossing on foot into Austria; the Pan-European Picnic of August 19, 1989 opened the flow to a torrent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Curtain.

question: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989 after a specific East German official misread a note at a press conference and told journalists new travel rules were 'in force, effective immediately'. Who made the mistake?
context: Schabowski, a Politburo spokesman, botched the answer at a press conference the evening of November 9, 1989. The border guards were not warned; East Berliners walked through and danced on the Wall that night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Schabowski.

question: The peaceful November-December 1989 revolution in Czechoslovakia, led by the Civic Forum coalition, produced a specific playwright as the country's new president on December 29. What is the revolution called?
context: The Velvet Revolution (November 17 - December 29, 1989) was led by the Civic Forum (Czech lands) and Public Against Violence (Slovakia). The playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on December 29. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_Revolution.

question: The Warsaw Pact collapse cascade reached Romania in the final weeks of 1989 with the trial and execution of Nicolae Ceausescu. On what specific date were the Ceausescus shot?
context: The Christmas Day execution at Targoviste military barracks made Ceausescu the only communist leader shot during the 1989 collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Nicolae_and_Elena_Ceausescu.

question: The Soviet Union itself formally dissolved on December 25, 1991 in a televised ceremony from a specific Moscow location. Where did the Soviet flag come down for the last time?
context: On December 25, 1991 the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin flagpole and the Russian tricolor raised. Gorbachev resigned as USSR President that evening; the Union formally ceased to exist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union.

question: A lifelong democratic-socialist economist at the New School wrote a September 1990 New Yorker essay titled 'After Communism' that included a famous three-word verdict on the calculation debate. What did Robert Heilbroner write?
context: Heilbroner's September 10, 1990 New Yorker essay 'After Communism' delivered the three-word verdict from a witness who had spent his life on the other side of the calculation debate. It became the epitaph of the debate. Source: The New Yorker, September 10 1990.

question: One 1989 event with the same date as the Polish elections gave the year an ironic pairing between the peaceful triumph of democracy in one country and its violent suppression in another. What was the other 1989 event on June 4?
choices: The fall of the Berlin Wall
context: June 4, 1989 saw both Solidarity's Polish election sweep and the People's Liberation Army's crackdown in Beijing. The two events on the same day frame Chinese and European responses to their 1980s reform pressures. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre.

question: The pace of the 1989-91 collapse surprised almost every Western academic Sovietologist. Which small group had predicted the system's ultimate calculation-driven unsustainability decades earlier?
context: Mises (1920, 1922), Hayek (1935, 1945), and Rothbard (1962) all argued the Soviet-style economy was calculation-impossible and therefore ultimately unsustainable. Robert Conquest, on separate grounds, made similar predictions. Most Western sovietology missed it. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: After holding the federal funds rate at 1% for a full year, the Fed began raising rates on June 30 2004 -- Chairman Greenspan's first hike in four years. By how much did it raise the rate in that first move?
context: The June 30 2004 quarter-point hike moved the funds rate from 1.00% to 1.25%. It began a tightening cycle that would prove one of the most consequential -- and most predictable in its consequences -- in Fed history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: Over the next two years the Fed hiked at each meeting -- seventeen consecutive 25-basis-point moves -- taking the federal funds rate to a specific peak by June 29 2006. What was the peak?
context: The last hike, June 29 2006, was Greenspan's successor Ben Bernanke's -- Bernanke had taken the chair February 1 2006. The seventeen consecutive quarter-point hikes ended at a 5.25% federal funds rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2004-06 tightening cycle used a specific FOMC coded phrase repeated in nearly every statement, signaling continued quarter-point hikes at each meeting. What was the phrase?
context: The phrase 'measured pace' meant '25 basis points per meeting.' It became a Wall Street cliche through 2004-06 as traders learned to expect the predictable quarter-point cadence. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2004-06 rate hikes triggered a cascade in the housing market as adjustable-rate mortgages written at 2003-04 teaser rates began resetting to the new higher rates. What happened to many households' monthly payments overnight?
context: Adjustable-rate mortgages with 2-year teaser periods reset in 2006-07 to the new market rates. Many households saw payments double or triple. Subprime foreclosure notices climbed sharply in the second half of 2006. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: By late 2006 the US Treasury yield curve was inverted -- short-term 2-year yields were higher than long-term 10-year yields. In modern US data, an inverted yield curve for a full quarter has been the single most reliable predictor of what?
answer: A US recession within the next 12-18 months
choices: A US recession within the next 12-18 months
A stock-market melt-up in the next quarter
A dollar appreciation of at least 10 percent
A commodity-price collapse of at least 20 percent
context: The yield-curve inversion signal comes from Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 New York Fed research paper. Every US recession since 1968 has been preceded by a sustained inversion. The 2006 signal was accurate: NBER dated the recession start December 2007. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: The two New York Fed researchers whose 1996 paper established the yield-curve inversion as the most reliable recession predictor made their finding a standard reference in later crisis warnings. Which two economists co-authored that paper?
context: Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 paper 'The Yield Curve as a Predictor of US Recessions' documented the empirical reliability of the signal across every US recession since 1968. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2006 yield-curve inversion held through most of 2007. When did the National Bureau of Economic Research subsequently date the recession's start?
context: The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee later fixed the recession start at December 2007. Bear Stearns's hedge funds had collapsed July-August 2007; Lehman failed September 15 2008. The Fed's own recession-warning tool had rung the bell for two years before the crisis fully arrived. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Recession' (2026-09-05).

question: Through 2007, as the yield-curve signal held and mortgage-related stresses mounted, the Federal Reserve leadership repeatedly used a specific reassuring phrase to describe the subprime stress. What phrase did they use?
choices: The stress was normal seasonal noise
context: Bernanke and other Fed officials used 'contained' repeatedly through 2007 to describe subprime stress. The phrase would join 'transitory' in the museum of Fed forecasting errors. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: The former FDIC chair through the 2008 crisis later called the 2004-2008 cycle by a distinctive phrase capturing how visible the warning signs had been in real time. What did Sheila Bair call this crisis?
answer: The most predictable financial crisis in American history
choices: The most predictable financial crisis in American history
The most sudden and unforeseeable crisis in American history
The inevitable result of foreign meddling
context: Bair's phrase captured what many observers had warned about in real time: the yield curve had inverted, subprime foreclosures were climbing, and Fed officials were dismissing both signals. Source: Bair, Bull by the Horns (2012).

question: The 2004-06 rate hikes and the yield-curve inversion together teach a specific recognition move about how central banks respond to signals from their own monetary tools. Which move does the ladder press?
answer: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
choices: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
The Fed always acts immediately on yield-curve inversion signals
Yield-curve signals are unreliable in modern markets
Central banks always respond correctly to market-based recession warnings
context: The full pattern is comic if it were not so damaging: cheap money 2003-04 built the housing bubble; tight money 2004-06 popped it; the yield-curve inversion warned of recession from late 2006; Fed leadership called the stress 'contained' through 2007. The tool rang the bell; the institution ignored the bell. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: On 15 September 2008 a 158-year-old Wall Street investment bank filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection listing about $613 billion in liabilities -- the largest bankruptcy filing in United States history. Which bank collapsed?
context: Lehman had 25,000 employees worldwide and was the country's fourth-largest investment bank. Bear Stearns had already been swallowed by JPMorgan in a rescue that March; Merrill Lynch was sold to Bank of America on the same weekend Lehman failed; Goldman Sachs converted to a bank holding company a week later to survive. Only Lehman was allowed to fail outright. Source: Wikipedia, Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers.

question: A stockbroker who ran the small firm Euro Pacific Capital went on cable news through 2006 and 2007 warning that the American housing boom was a Federal-Reserve-fueled bubble that would end in a housing crash, a banking crisis, and a dollar decline; CNBC nicknamed him 'Dr. Doom'. Which stockbroker?
context: The three distractors are all real 2008-crisis callers, but from other backgrounds: Roubini was an NYU economics professor, Shiller a Yale housing-index economist, and Burry the physician-turned-hedge-fund manager of The Big Short. Schiff was the Austrian-influenced STOCKBROKER whose television appearances -- and the mocking laughter of the panelists sharing his studio -- became the viral post-crash montage. Source: NPR, 'The Man Who Predicted the Economic Meltdown.'

question: Peter Schiff's 2007 book, published by John Wiley & Sons and released just before the crash, predicted a housing collapse, a banking crisis, and a dollar decline before any of them had arrived. What is the book titled?
answer: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
choices: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
Too Big to Fail: The Inside Story of How Wall Street and Washington Fought to Save the Financial System
House of Cards: A Tale of Hubris and Wretched Excess on Wall Street
context: Crash Proof appeared in early 2007 and reads today as an eerie sequential forecast of the events of 2007-08. The three distractors are all real 2010-11 books ABOUT the crisis after the fact -- Michael Lewis (The Big Short, 2010), Andrew Ross Sorkin (Too Big to Fail, 2009), William Cohan (House of Cards, 2009). Only Schiff wrote his book BEFORE the crash. Source: Wikipedia, Crash Proof.

question: After the crash a YouTube compilation went viral. It intercut cable-news interviews from 2006 and 2007 in which Peter Schiff warned of a housing collapse, a banking crisis, and a dollar decline, alongside the on-air LAUGHTER of the panelists sharing his studio; the events he predicted then appeared on the screen. What was the compilation titled?
context: 'Peter Schiff Was Right' was uploaded in late 2008 and racked up millions of views. The three distractors are real 2009 documentary films about the crash -- Frontline's Inside the Meltdown, Frontline's The Warning (on Brooksley Born and derivatives), Niall Ferguson's The Ascent of Money -- all serious, but none is the specific mockery-then-vindication YouTube montage. Source: NPR, 'The Man Who Predicted the Economic Meltdown.'

question: Under Alan Greenspan the Federal Reserve cut its benchmark federal funds rate to a specific low in response to the dot-com bust and held it there for a year, from June 2003 to June 2004 -- feeding the mortgage boom that peaked in 2006. What level did Greenspan cut the funds rate to in June 2003?
context: One percent was, at the time, the lowest federal funds rate in nearly half a century; it made adjustable-rate mortgages and long-duration housing bets look permanently affordable. 3 percent was closer to the Taylor-rule level economists like John Taylor said would have been appropriate; 5.25 percent was the peak the Fed later raised to in 2006; the ZIRP era of a zero-percent rate arrived only after the 2008 crash. Source: FEE, 'A Tale of Two Bubbles.'

question: From June 2004 the Fed raised the funds rate in seventeen quarter-point steps, reaching 5.25% by June 2006. The rate rises reset tens of billions of dollars of adjustable-rate mortgages upward, and by 2006 housing prices began to fall and mortgage default rates rose sharply. Which Austrian-tradition mechanism does this pattern illustrate?
answer: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
choices: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
Minsky's financial-instability hypothesis of endogenous fragility
Real business cycle theory of exogenous technology shocks
context: The Austrian claim: cheap credit made long-duration projects (in this case housing developments and mortgage assets) look profitable; when rates returned to something like the natural rate, the mismatch between the projects started and the saving to sustain them was revealed and collapsed. The three distractors are real rival cycle theories from Keynes (liquidity trap), Hyman Minsky (financial instability), and Kydland-Prescott (real-business-cycle) -- all applied to the same crisis by their proponents. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations.'

question: On 28 March 2007 the Fed Chairman told the Joint Economic Committee of Congress: 'At this juncture, however, the impact on the broader economy and financial markets of the problems in the subprime market seems likely to be contained.' Eighteen months later Lehman failed and the broader financial system nearly collapsed. Which Fed Chairman gave the 'contained' testimony?
context: Bernanke chaired the Fed from February 2006 to January 2014. Greenspan retired in January 2006 (a month before the housing peak); Yellen chaired the Fed 2014-2018 after the crash; Volcker had been Fed chairman 1979-1987, a generation earlier. Only Bernanke was in the chair on 28 March 2007. Source: Yahoo Finance, 'This Day in Market History.'

question: On 10 September 2003 a Texas congressman testified to the House Financial Services Committee warning that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's implicit government backing had created an artificial housing bubble: 'like all artificially created bubbles, the boom in housing prices cannot last forever.' Which congressman?
context: Paul introduced the Free Housing Market Enhancement Act that year to strip Fannie and Freddie of their government sponsorship; the bill went nowhere. Barney Frank was the ranking Democrat on the same committee and defended the GSEs against Paul's warnings. Sanders was a House member during those years but was not the author of this specific testimony; Schumer was a senator, not a House committee witness. Source: RonPaulQuotes, 2003 testimony.

question: The Austrian critique of the Fed's cheap-credit policy of 2003-06 uses exactly the mechanism a Vienna-born economist had described in his 1931 LSE lectures Prices and Production: artificially low interest rates tilt the CAPITAL STRUCTURE toward long-duration projects that voluntary saving cannot sustain. Which economist authored Prices and Production?
context: Hayek delivered the four LSE lectures in January 1931 at Lionel Robbins's invitation; George Routledge published them the same year. Mises founded the theory in his 1912 Theory of Money and Credit; Rothbard wrote the mature Austrian textbook Man, Economy, and State (1962); Friedman was the Chicago monetarist, not Austrian. Only Hayek wrote Prices and Production. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations.'

question: The Federal Reserve's response to the 2008 crash was to cut the federal funds rate to zero (December 2008) and launch three successive rounds of large-scale asset purchases beginning November 2008, November 2010, and September 2012, growing the Fed's balance sheet from under $1 trillion to over $4 trillion by 2014. What is the one-phrase name for this asset-purchase program?
context: Quantitative easing (QE) was the label the Fed adopted for buying long-dated Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities directly with newly-created reserves, once the funds rate had hit its zero lower bound. The three distractors are all real, older Fed policy tools: open-market operations (routine short-Treasury buying and selling), the discount window (direct emergency lending to banks), and reserve-requirement adjustment (changing the fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves). QE was the historically new instrument. Source: Brookings, 'The Fed's Balance Sheet.'

question: The mature Austrian post-mortem of the 2008 crisis was written by a historian at the Mises Institute; his 2009 book from Regnery Publishing reached number one on the New York Times bestseller list and became the standard free-market retelling of the crash. What is the book titled?
answer: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
choices: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
Stress Test: Reflections on Financial Crises
context: Thomas E. Woods Jr.'s Meltdown (February 2009) frames the crash as a straight Austrian-Business-Cycle case study -- Fed cheap credit, malinvestment in housing, inevitable liquidation, bailouts prolonging the disease. The three distractors are all real bestsellers about the crisis: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010), Reinhart and Rogoff's This Time is Different (2009), and Timothy Geithner's Stress Test (2014). Only Woods's book is the Austrian one. Source: Wikipedia, Meltdown (Woods book).

question: In the years just before the COVID-19 pandemic, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet -- the assets it holds against the dollars it has issued -- stood at roughly $4.2 trillion. In the 27 months from March 2020 to June 2022, that number more than doubled. Roughly what size did the Fed's balance sheet reach at its 2022 peak?
context: The Fed balance sheet peaked at $8.97 trillion as of June 8, 2022, up about $4.25 trillion from March 18, 2020. Source: Peter G. Peterson Foundation summary of Federal Reserve data (https://www.pgpf.org/article/the-federal-reserve-will-begin-reducing-its-holdings-of-treasury-notes-and-bonds/).

question: M2 is the broad measure of the dollars circulating in the American economy -- checking accounts, savings, small time deposits, money-market balances. In February 2020, M2 stood at about $15.4 trillion. By April 2022, this number had jumped roughly 40 percent to a peak that no peacetime American expansion had ever matched. About what did M2 reach at its April 2022 peak?
context: M2 rose from about $15.4T in February 2020 to a peak near $21.7T in April 2022 -- a 40%+ jump in about two years, the fastest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2023/may/the-rise-and-fall-of-m2).

question: In January 2021, US consumer prices were rising at 1.4 percent year over year -- the quiet baseline before the surge. Chair Jerome Powell and the Federal Open Market Committee spent 2021 telling the public that any rise from that baseline would be brief and self-correcting, driven by supply chains rather than money creation. Which single word did Powell use again and again in his 2021 press conferences to describe that inflation?
context: Powell used 'transitory' repeatedly through 2021; on November 30 he told Congress it was 'probably a good time to retire that word.' At his August 2021 Jackson Hole speech he used 'transitory' and 'temporary' five times each defending the call. Sources: Federal Reserve press conference transcripts; Bloomberg 'Powell Ditches Transitory Inflation Tag' (Nov 30 2021).

question: By spring 2020, one small group of American analysts was already publishing charts of the Federal Reserve's exploding balance sheet and warning that persistent, not brief, inflation was coming on a roughly two-year lag. Peter Schiff and the hard-money commentators around him were making the same call: expand the money supply that fast and general prices must follow. Which school of economics were those analysts drawing on to make that call in real time?
choices: The Modern Monetary Theory school (Kelton, Wray)
context: Schiff and other hard-money analysts used Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1931) to argue in 2020-21 that the Fed's monetary expansion would produce persistent inflation on a two-year lag. Milton Friedman's monetarist tradition, though not strictly Austrian, made a parallel prediction. Source: SchiffGold podcast archive 2020-21 (https://www.schiffgold.com/peters-podcast/peter-schiff-2021-the-year-of-inflation).

question: In February 2020, before the pandemic, the M2 dollar supply was about $15.4 trillion. Twenty-six months later, in April 2022, it peaked near $21.7 trillion -- a roughly 40% expansion. Milton Friedman, in a famous 1963 talk in India, had summarized his answer to what happens next in a single sentence about inflation and money. What conclusion does Friedman's sentence draw about what causes persistent inflation?
answer: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output
choices: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output
It is always the result of workers demanding wages ahead of productivity
It is always driven by corporate market power and price gouging
It is always the consequence of oil shocks and other supply disruptions
context: From Friedman's 1963 talk 'Inflation: Causes and Consequences' delivered in India: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon in the sense that it is and can be produced only by a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output.' Source: Wikiquote / Hoover Institution reprints.

question: In January 2021, US CPI was rising at 1.4% year over year. Eighteen months later -- June 2022 -- it printed the highest 12-month reading in 40 years, since November 1981. Chair Powell had been calling the run-up 'transitory' throughout 2021. What was that June 2022 peak year-over-year CPI reading?
context: US CPI peaked at 9.1% year over year in June 2022, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics -- the largest 12-month increase since November 1981. Source: BLS, 'Consumer prices up 9.1 percent over the year ended June 2022' (https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2022/consumer-prices-up-9-1-percent-over-the-year-ended-june-2022-largest-increase-in-40-years.htm).

question: Once the June 2022 inflation reading came in, the Federal Reserve reversed course and began raising its policy rate faster than at any time since the early 1980s. Between March 2022 and July 2023, the fed funds target rose from 0-0.25% to 5.25-5.5% -- 525 basis points in roughly sixteen months. Which earlier Federal Reserve chair's tightening cycle -- the only comparable one in modern history -- was Powell's 2022-23 campaign most often compared to?
context: The FOMC raised its target 525 bp between March 2022 and July 2023, the fastest tightening cycle in four decades -- rivalled in pace only by Paul Volcker's 1979-82 campaign, which pushed rates near 20% to crush inflation. Sources: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter June 2024; Richmond Fed Economic Brief 23-26.

question: In the single month of April 2020, the Federal Reserve executed asset purchases -- Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities -- at a pace unprecedented in its 107-year history. This one month alone accounted for a large chunk of the total monetary expansion that would follow. Roughly what dollar amount of assets did the Fed purchase in that single month?
context: April 2020 Treasury and agency-MBS purchases by the Federal Reserve exceeded $1 trillion in that single month -- a single-month pace that the previous eleven decades of the Fed's history had never approached. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (July 2020, 'A New Reserves Regime? COVID-19 and the Federal Reserve Balance Sheet').

question: In her 2020 book 'The Deficit Myth,' Stephanie Kelton laid out the Modern Monetary Theory case: because the US issues its own currency, its real constraint is not deficits but the availability of real resources -- and inflation was decades of overreaction ago. In 2021-23, US CPI ran from 1.4% year over year to 9.1% while the Fed's balance sheet had just doubled. Which MMT claim did that outcome most directly falsify in real time?
answer: That the binding constraint on money-financed spending is real resources, not the political willingness to print
choices: That the binding constraint on money-financed spending is real resources, not the political willingness to print
That the federal government must always balance its budget over the business cycle
That central banks should target a specific level of the nominal exchange rate
That commercial banks alone determine the money supply, not the central bank
context: Kelton's 2020 book argued the binding constraint on federal spending was not deficits but real resources and inflation; critics point to 2021-23 CPI running 1.4% -> 9.1% as real-time falsification of the practical judgment that the resource constraint was not yet close. Source: 'The Deficit Myth' (2020); Mises Institute review (https://mises.org/mises-wire/review-stephanie-keltons-deficit-myth).

question: For most of 2021, Chair Jerome Powell had defended the Federal Reserve's inflation forecast with a single reassuring adjective. Then on November 30, 2021 he appeared before a Senate committee and told the senators it was 'probably a good time to retire that word.' In the same appearance he began preparing markets for the aggressive rate-hike campaign that would begin the following March. Which month's testimony did Powell use to formally drop his earlier inflation adjective?
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30, 2021 that it was 'probably a good time to retire that word' -- formally dropping the earlier framing. The FOMC began its rate-hike campaign in March 2022. Source: Bloomberg 'Powell Ditches Transitory Inflation Tag, Paves Way for Rate Hike' (Nov 30 2021).

question: In 2020-21, a small group of hard-money analysts -- Austrian economists, monetarists in Milton Friedman's tradition, and Bitcoin sound-money commentators -- publicly predicted that the Fed's balance sheet doubling would produce persistent inflation on a two-year lag. The Fed and most mainstream commentators throughout 2021 argued the price pressures would be brief supply-chain effects. CPI then ran from 1.4% year over year to 9.1% eighteen months later. Which reasoning move about money and prices did the critics press against the Fed's 2021 framing?
answer: That a large enough expansion of the money supply drives the general price level on a lag, whatever supply-side story runs alongside
choices: That a large enough expansion of the money supply drives the general price level on a lag, whatever supply-side story runs alongside
That regulatory capture of the Fed by the banks it supervises made the 2020-21 emergency programs politically unavoidable
That dispersed costs and concentrated benefits explain why farm-subsidy programs survive changes of administration
That the calculation problem prevents a central planner from setting relative prices efficiently in a moneyless economy
context: The Austrian and monetarist critics pressed Friedman's line -- persistent inflation is a monetary phenomenon -- against the Fed's supply-chain framing. Supply and demand shocks can shift the SHAPE of the inflation but a 40% M2 expansion drives the general price level on a lag. Powell dropped 'transitory' Nov 30 2021; CPI peaked at 9.1% June 2022. Sources: Friedman 1963; SchiffGold; BLS; Bloomberg Nov 30 2021.

question: A phrase popularized by hedge-fund manager Jesse Felder around 2018 describes simultaneous price inflation across multiple asset classes -- housing, equities, private credit, art, collectibles -- driven by a common monetary cause. What is the phrase?
context: Felder popularized the 'everything bubble' label to distinguish the modern QE-era pattern from single-asset bubbles like the dot-com or 1980s Japan. It was expanded by Vincent Deluard and Grant Williams. Source: Grokipedia 'Everything bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: The Case-Shiller US National Home Price Index rose approximately 45% between January 2020 and June 2022 -- the fastest 30-month gain in the index's history since it began in 1987. What was the peak monthly year-over-year gain during that stretch?
context: The 20.8% year-over-year gain in April 2022 is the highest reading in the Case-Shiller series. Housing was the single most visible of the everything-bubble asset classes. Source: S&P/Case-Shiller US National Home Price Index (fred.stlouisfed.org).

question: From its March 23 2020 pandemic low to its December 2021 peak, the S&P 500 rose by approximately what percentage?
context: The S&P 500 nearly doubled from its March 23 2020 low of about 2,237 to its December 2021 peak of about 4,796. The NASDAQ Composite roughly 2.3-doubled over the same window. Source: Grokipedia 'S&P 500' (2026-09-05).

question: Bitcoin's price rose from about $4,000 at its March 2020 low to a November 2021 peak. What was the November 2021 peak?
context: Bitcoin peaked at roughly $69,000 in November 2021 -- a 17-fold rise from the March 2020 low. It was among the most extreme moves in the everything-bubble asset complex. Source: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin' (2026-09-05).

question: Two speculative meme-stock episodes in early 2021 saw stocks disconnect dramatically from any traditional fundamental valuation -- driven by Reddit-coordinated retail buying. Which two stocks became emblematic of the meme-stock frenzy?
context: GameStop surged in January 2021 after r/wallstreetbets coordination against short-sellers; AMC Entertainment followed later that year. Both episodes were symptoms of the broader liquidity flood into speculative assets. Source: Grokipedia 'GameStop short squeeze' (2026-09-05).

question: Non-fungible token sales -- essentially digital art authenticated by blockchain -- exploded from near-zero in 2019 to a peak market volume in 2021 before collapsing 97% by later years. Roughly what did 2021 total NFT sales reach?
context: Total NFT sales hit about $25 billion in 2021. By 2023 volumes had fallen 97% from peak. The rise-and-collapse pattern is a textbook Cantillon-first-receiver liquidity spike. Source: Grokipedia 'Non-fungible token' (2026-09-05).

question: A specific class of cash-shell corporate vehicles used to take private firms public by merging with them raised an enormous total in 2020-21 before nearly disappearing by 2023. What are they called?
context: SPACs raised about $162 billion in 2020-21, matching the entire prior decade combined. Volumes collapsed as rates rose in 2022. The SPAC boom was a paradigmatic Cantillon-effect speculative excess. Source: Grokipedia 'Special-purpose acquisition company' (2026-09-05).

question: The most-cited exchange-traded fund symbolizing the long-duration growth-stock cycle of the everything-bubble era rose sharply through 2021 and then fell approximately 80% from peak to trough by 2022-23. Which ETF and its manager are the poster-child?
answer: ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK), managed by Cathie Wood
choices: ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK), managed by Cathie Wood
SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), managed by State Street
iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), managed by BlackRock
Vanguard Total Stock Market Index (VTI), managed by Vanguard
context: Cathie Wood's ARKK peaked in February 2021 and lost about 80% peak-to-trough by 2022-23. It was the poster-child of long-duration growth-stock cycle exposure to rate policy. Source: Grokipedia 'ARK Investment Management' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2020-24 pattern -- asset-price inflation in 2020-21, consumer-price inflation in 2021-23, then a speculative bust in 2022-23 -- fits a specific Austrian-tradition analytic framework. Which framework identifies the pattern as it unfolded?
answer: The Cantillon-effect pattern of first-receiver benefits followed by later-receiver adjustment
choices: The Cantillon-effect pattern of first-receiver benefits followed by later-receiver adjustment
The Keynesian animal-spirits framework of investor sentiment
The efficient-markets hypothesis of neutral price discovery
The random-walk model of stock-market behavior
context: The Austrian intellectual contribution to the 2020s: identifying the pattern as a Cantillon-effect sequence rather than as 'irrational exuberance' or 'animal spirits.' The specific rise-then-fall timing across asset classes tracks the theory precisely. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: The 2022-23 bust for the most speculative tier of the everything bubble was concentrated in specific asset classes. Which trio saw the sharpest peak-to-trough drops?
answer: Bitcoin -78%, ARK Innovation ETF -80%, and the meme-stock complex -90%+
choices: Bitcoin -78%, ARK Innovation ETF -80%, and the meme-stock complex -90%+
S&P 500 -70%, Case-Shiller Home Price Index -60%, and Treasury bonds -50%
Investment-grade bonds -75%, corporate credit -70%, and municipal bonds -65%
context: The speculative-asset tier -- long-duration growth stocks, crypto, meme stocks -- corrected hardest as rates rose. Real estate and broad equities were stickier because Powell's 2022-23 hikes came after the peak and did not fully unwind earlier gains. Source: Grokipedia 'Everything bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 1789 the revolutionary National Assembly in France needed money to run the state and had none. It seized about 15% of French land -- the estates of one large institutional owner -- as collateral for a new paper currency. Whose lands were seized?
context: The Assembly's November 2 1789 decree nationalized the property of the Church in France to serve as backing for a new currency. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: The new paper currency the French revolutionary Assembly issued in 1789, each note legally a claim on future sales of confiscated Church land, took a single distinctive name. What was it called?
context: The name came from the French verb 'assigner' -- each note was assigned against specific land parcels for redemption. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: The first issue of assignats in December 1789 was 400 million livres, and the Assembly promised solemnly it would be the ONLY issue. By 1795 the total in circulation had risen to a very different figure. What did the total reach?
answer: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
choices: Over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit
About 2 billion livres, roughly 5 times the promised limit
About 800 million livres, roughly double the promised limit
Just under 400 million livres, exactly the promised limit
context: Every subsequent Convention and Directory added new issues to cover expenses. By late 1795 the outstanding stock exceeded 40 billion livres of face value. Source: Grokipedia 'Assignat' (2026-09-05).

question: When peasants and merchants began refusing assignats and demanding gold coin, the revolutionary government responded not by reducing paper issues but by escalating legal penalties. What was the ultimate penalty enacted for treating gold as more valuable than paper?
context: The Convention's 1793-94 anti-hoarding laws carried capital punishment for those who refused assignats at face value or hoarded specie. Legal coercion did not restore confidence in the paper. Source: Andrew Dickson White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: By 1796 an assignat was worth about one thousandth of its face value. The Directory withdrew the currency and attempted a fresh start with a new paper money supposedly backed by the same land. What was the replacement called?
context: The mandats territoriaux were introduced in March 1796 and collapsed even faster than the assignats they replaced, losing 97% of value within months. Napoleon later restored specie-based currency with the franc germinal in 1803. Source: Grokipedia 'Mandat territorial' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1789-1796 Assignat episode was actually France's second attempt at a national paper money in less than a century -- the first had ended in the 1720 collapse of a Scottish projector's scheme in Paris. Whose scheme was that first attempt?
answer: John Law's Banque Royale and Mississippi Company
choices: John Law's Banque Royale and Mississippi Company
context: France tried paper money in 1716-1720 under John Law, saw it collapse, and stayed off paper for the next seventy years. The Assignat was the second full experiment -- same country, same result. Source: Grokipedia 'John Law (economist)' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1912 an American historian and educator wrote a slim but definitive account of the Assignat collapse as a warning to his own era's paper-money advocates. He was also the first president of a major American university. Which university?
context: Andrew Dickson White was Cornell's co-founder and first president, and his 1912 book Fiat Money Inflation in France has been in print continuously since. Source: Grokipedia 'Andrew Dickson White' (2026-09-05).

question: Andrew Dickson White's 1912 study of the Assignat episode concluded with a line still quoted by Austrian economists. Which conclusion did he draw?
answer: No government could make paper worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem
choices: No government could make paper worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem
Paper money can succeed if backed by patriotic sentiment
Only unlimited legal-tender enforcement can preserve currency value
The failure of paper money in France was due to foreign interference
context: White's book documented every mechanism the Revolution used -- legal tender laws, price controls, capital punishment for speculators -- and their uniform failure once the paper supply outran the backing. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: The mechanisms the French Revolution used to try to prop up the assignat -- legal tender coercion, price controls, capital punishment for hoarders -- had already been tried by the Continental Congress a decade earlier and would be tried again in a 20th-century episode. Which later episode reused the same playbook?
context: Every hyperinflating government reaches for the same tools: legal tender laws, wage and price controls, criminal penalties for currency skepticism. And every one fails for the same reason -- the underlying money-printing is untouched. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: Bastiat would read the Assignat episode as a case where a visible near-term gain hides a systematic destruction that shows up later. Which pairing best captures the seen-and-unseen contrast?
answer: Seen: legal-tender laws and price controls; Unseen: goods vanishing from shops and savers wiped out
choices: Seen: legal-tender laws and price controls; Unseen: goods vanishing from shops and savers wiped out
Seen: rising real wages; Unseen: falling unemployment
Seen: increased tax revenue; Unseen: lower interest rates
Seen: growing exports; Unseen: falling imports
context: Bastiat's frame: the visible policy tools look decisive; the invisible costs -- black markets, empty shelves, evaporated savings -- are the actual result. The Assignat is a textbook illustration published 40 years after Bastiat's death. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In his 1912 book on the theory of money, an Austrian economist argued that any successful money must have had some prior non-monetary demand before it became money -- otherwise nobody would have known what its exchange value should be on its first day of use. Which Austrian economist proposed this argument?
context: Mises presented the Regression Theorem in 'The Theory of Money and Credit' (1912). Menger had proposed the general theory of money's emergence (1892); Hayek and Rothbard later extended Mises's work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: The Mises argument that any successful money must have had a prior non-monetary demand has a distinctive name in Austrian economics. What is the argument called?
context: The Regression Theorem is Mises's 1912 argument. The Calculation Debate is Mises's separate 1920 case against socialism; praxeology is his general methodology; time-preference is a distinct concept in Bohm-Bawerkian capital theory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: In the early 2010s several old-guard Rothbardian economists -- most prominently one senior scholar at the Mises Institute -- argued that Bitcoin FAILED the Regression Theorem because it had no prior non-monetary use, and therefore Bitcoin should not have been able to become money in the first place. Which senior Mises Institute economist pressed this argument?
context: Frank Shostak, longtime Mises Institute scholar, argued Bitcoin failed the Regression Theorem and was therefore a bubble. Robert Murphy later took the opposite (pro-Bitcoin) side; Peter Boettke is at George Mason; Israel Kirzner works on entrepreneurship not monetary theory. Source: https://mises.org/profile/frank-shostak.

question: Frank Shostak's specific conclusion from his 2010s Regression-Theorem-vs-Bitcoin analysis was direct. Which prediction did Shostak draw about Bitcoin's future?
answer: that Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse
choices: that Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse
that Bitcoin would become the world's dominant reserve currency by 2020
that Bitcoin should be adopted by central banks as a reserve asset
that Bitcoin's value was purely a matter of government regulation
context: Shostak's conclusion from applying the Regression Theorem as he read it: Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that must eventually collapse. He did not predict reserve-currency status, central-bank adoption, or a regulation-only explanation. Source: Shostak Mises Wire articles 2013-15.

question: Younger Austrian economists -- most influentially Saifedean Ammous, alongside Peter St Onge and others -- pushed back against Frank Shostak's reading. Which specific move did the Ammous side make about Bitcoin's actual earliest history that they argued Shostak had missed?
answer: that Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use -- a cypherpunk collectible cryptographers valued for the technical achievement itself
choices: that Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use -- a cypherpunk collectible cryptographers valued for the technical achievement itself
that the Regression Theorem does not apply to any digital currency by definition, so Bitcoin sits outside its scope
that Bitcoin had an implicit government-backing guarantee from the start through federal law-enforcement action
that Mises himself would have retracted the Regression Theorem if he had lived to see Bitcoin's first two years
context: The Ammous/St Onge response: in Bitcoin's earliest days it functioned as a cypherpunk collectible whose non-monetary use was the technical curiosity itself; that initial demand satisfied the theorem's requirement. The other options are not what the pro-Bitcoin Austrians argued. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8-9.

question: Ammous's argument for how Bitcoin satisfies the Regression Theorem points to one specific transaction as the moment Bitcoin can be dated to have crossed from cypherpunk collectible to medium of exchange for goods. Which transaction serves as that dateable turning point in his analysis?
context: Ammous points to Laszlo Hanyecz's May 22, 2010 pizza trade as the dateable transition point from cypherpunk collectible to medium of exchange for physical goods. The genesis block and white paper are pre-money events; the Cyprus crisis (March 2013) is later. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: By roughly what year had the Austrian community broadly resolved the dispute in favor of the Ammous side -- with most working Austrian economists accepting Bitcoin as compatible with the Regression Theorem correctly understood?
context: The dispute was broadly resolved in the modern Austrian community by around 2018-2020, with working economists like Ammous, Bob Murphy, Peter St Onge, Vijay Boyapati having converged on the pro-Bitcoin reading. Shostak has kept his position. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers 2015-20; Bob Murphy Show archive.

question: One American Austrian economist -- host of a long-running podcast on Austrian topics -- has hosted the Bitcoin-Regression-Theorem debate on his show multiple times, giving both sides extended time. Which economist runs the podcast that hosted the debate?
context: Robert Murphy hosts the Bob Murphy Show and has featured the Bitcoin/Regression Theorem debate extensively. Sowell is not an Austrian and does not run a Bitcoin podcast; Friedman was a monetarist, died 2006; Samuelson was a Keynesian, died 2009. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_P._Murphy.

question: A pedagogical writer looking back at the Shostak-Ammous dispute argues that the lesson runs beyond Bitcoin itself. Which broader reasoning move does the story teach about how a rigorous theoretical tradition should handle a new empirical case?
answer: That even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record
choices: That even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record
That any internal disagreement inside a school of thought discredits the whole tradition and reveals its foundational theorems as unable to survive scrutiny
That founding texts should be treated as fixed and never re-examined against new empirical cases, since re-examination undermines the tradition's authority
That new empirical cases should always be rejected if they conflict with existing theory, since preserving theoretical purity is more valuable than case-by-case revision
context: The dispute-recognition move: internal disagreement is a sign of a live tradition; the resolution came from re-examining Bitcoin's actual early history rather than reinterpreting Mises's 1912 text. The other options are opposite reasoning moves that would have prevented the resolution. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard.

question: A Bitcoin-friendly Rothbardian writing in 2026 identifies one specific academic figure whose bridge between the Mises-Rothbard tradition and modern Bitcoin economics is the strongest in the literature. Which Austrian scholar's work is most often cited as that bridge?
context: Peter St Onge's academic writing (papers 2015 onward) is the standard bridge between the Mises-Rothbard tradition and modern Bitcoin economics. Shostak took the opposite position; Block and Hulsmann have been publicly ambivalent. Source: Peter St Onge academic papers; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_St._Onge.

question: On Sunday March 12 2023 -- the same weekend Signature Bank was seized -- the Federal Reserve announced an emergency lending facility for banks facing bond-loss stress from the rate-hike cycle. What is the facility called?
context: The BTFP was announced March 12 2023 as part of the emergency response to the SVB and Signature failures. It offered one-year loans to US-chartered banks against posted collateral of Treasuries, agency debt, or MBS. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: The distinctive feature that made the BTFP unusual -- and that critics called 'stealth QE' -- was how it valued the collateral banks pledged. How was collateral valued at the BTFP window?
answer: At par (face value), not at market value
choices: At par (face value), not at market value
At market value with a 10% haircut
At market value plus a 5% premium
At a rolling three-month moving average of market prices
context: Par valuation meant a 10-year Treasury bought at 1.5% yield when 10-year yields were 4% could be pledged at 100 cents on the dollar rather than roughly 80 cents. The Fed was accepting underwater bonds at their pre-loss face value. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: The BTFP's par-valuation mechanic represented a departure from how the Fed normally values collateral at its lending facilities. What is the standard valuation practice at the traditional Discount Window?
answer: Collateral is valued at market price, typically with a haircut
choices: Collateral is valued at market price, typically with a haircut
Collateral is valued at book value with no haircut
Collateral is valued at par regardless of market conditions
Collateral is valued at whichever is lower of book or market
context: The traditional Discount Window values collateral at market minus a haircut, ensuring the Fed is over-collateralized. BTFP's departure from this norm was explicit -- and explicitly a subsidy to banks whose portfolios had lost value. Source: Grokipedia 'Discount window' (2026-09-05).

question: Because the BTFP accepted underwater collateral at pre-loss face value, it functioned as a specific implicit subsidy to banks that had loaded up on long-duration bonds during the QE era. Analysts flagged the program by a specific three-word informal label. What did they call it?
context: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, Lyn Alden, Jim Bianco and other analysts publicly called BTFP 'QE by another name.' The Fed's balance sheet was rising against the announced quantitative tightening program because banks were borrowing directly from the BTFP window. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: Borrowings under the BTFP grew rapidly through 2023 and peaked in early 2024. Approximately what did the peak balance reach?
context: BTFP borrowings peaked at roughly $167 billion in early 2024. Every dollar borrowed under BTFP was a dollar of implicit rate-cycle-loss coverage for the borrowing bank. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 releases 2024).

question: The BTFP was authorized under a specific section of the Federal Reserve Act -- the same section that had been used for the March 2020 emergency facilities. Which section?
context: Section 13(3), dating to 1932, permits Fed lending to non-bank borrowers in 'unusual and exigent circumstances.' Its 2020 and 2023 uses established the highest cadence of invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: The BTFP was designed to end at a specific date in 2024. The Fed did not extend the facility. When did it expire?
context: BTFP expired on March 11 2024, one year after its launch. Outstanding balances continued to be paid down, but no new borrowings were permitted after that date. The precedent, however, stands. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: The last time before BTFP that the Fed had accepted collateral at above market value was during the 2008 crisis. Which 2008-era facility set that earlier precedent?
choices: The Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF)
context: The 2008 Term Auction Facility (TAF) was the previous precedent for accepting collateral at above market value. BTFP was in effect a re-run of that mechanism, calibrated to bond-loss stress rather than to broader liquidity strain. Source: Grokipedia 'Term Auction Facility' (2026-09-05).

question: The BTFP is a paradigmatic Bastiat move -- the visible policy achievement hides an invisible transfer. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures its structure?
answer: Seen: stability for the banking system; Unseen: par-valuation on underwater collateral is a subsidy to banks whose duration mismatches were created by the Fed's own earlier zero-rate policy
choices: Seen: stability for the banking system; Unseen: par-valuation on underwater collateral is a subsidy to banks whose duration mismatches were created by the Fed's own earlier zero-rate policy
Seen: rising rates; Unseen: falling exports
Seen: growing employment; Unseen: shrinking productivity
Seen: a broad recovery; Unseen: a narrow crisis in one region
context: The banks had bought long bonds at low rates because the Fed's earlier policy made them attractive. When the same Fed's tightening exposed those bonds to loss, the BTFP quietly reimbursed the losses. The whole cycle -- create the incentive, expose the loss, cover the loss -- was internal to Fed choices. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The BTFP's expiration in March 2024 does not remove the precedent it set. Which recognition move does the ladder press about the political-economy meaning of the program's end?
answer: When banks lose on rate-cycle bond exposures, the Fed will provide non-market-priced collateralized lending -- and every future risk manager now knows it
choices: When banks lose on rate-cycle bond exposures, the Fed will provide non-market-priced collateralized lending -- and every future risk manager now knows it
The Fed will never again offer emergency facilities to commercial banks
Future rate cycles will not produce bank bond losses
The end of BTFP proves the Fed has abandoned discretionary rescues permanently
context: The BTFP ran its course but its precedent is now baked into every bank's implicit risk framework. Duration mismatch is less risky when the central bank has demonstrated willingness to cover the loss. Moral hazard accumulates one precedent at a time. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: On February 18, 1987, the sitting US Secretary of Education published a New York Times essay titled 'Our Greedy Colleges' arguing that federal financial-aid increases do not primarily reduce net cost for students -- they primarily enable colleges to raise tuition and capture the aid as revenue. Who was that secretary?
context: William Bennett was Reagan's Secretary of Education (1985-88). His 1987 NYT essay 'Our Greedy Colleges' launched what came to be called the Bennett Hypothesis. Source: nytimes.com/1987/02/18 (Bennett op-ed).

question: William Bennett's 1987 claim, which came to be known by his name as a hypothesis, is that increases in federal student aid primarily flow to which party?
context: The Bennett Hypothesis: subsidies to a demand-side party (student) can be substantially captured by the supply-side party (college) when supply is constrained and demand is inelastic. Source: Bennett, NYT (1987).

question: Federal student loan debt in the United States grew dramatically from the early 1990s through 2023. Approximately what dollar figure does the total stand at in the mid-2020s?
context: Total federal student loan debt grew from ~$100B in the 1990s to ~$1.7T in the early-to-mid 2020s. The debt is largely the mirror image of the tuition inflation the Bennett Hypothesis predicts. Source: newyorkfed.org (Household Debt and Credit Report).

question: Between 1978 and 2018 average US public four-year college tuition rose approximately 213% in real terms, and private four-year tuition rose approximately 129% in real terms. This growth happened alongside sustained increases in a specific category of federal funding. Which category?
answer: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
choices: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
context: The tuition rise tracks federal aid expansion tightly -- the 1965 Higher Education Act reauthorizations, the 1992 direct-loan program, and the 2010 elimination of private-lender intermediation each expanded federal aid. Source: nces.ed.gov (tuition historical series); collegeboard.org (Trends in Student Aid).

question: A 2015 New York Fed staff report by David Lucca, Taylor Nadauld, and Karen Shen exploited discontinuities in federal loan limits to estimate the causal effect of expanded student loan access on college tuition. What was their headline finding?
answer: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
choices: A $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $0.05 decrease in tuition
A $1 increase in loans led to about a $2 decrease in net cost
A $1 increase in loans produced no measurable tuition change
context: Lucca + Nadauld + Shen, New York Fed Staff Report 733 (2015, revised 2019). The 60-cent tuition pass-through is a direct market-mechanism confirmation of the Bennett Hypothesis using discontinuities in loan-limit rules. Source: newyorkfed.org (staff report 733).

question: A 2016 NBER working paper by Grey Gordon and Aaron Hedlund built a structural model to attribute observed 1987-2010 US college tuition inflation to expanded federal financial aid. Roughly what share of the tuition rise did their model attribute to aid expansion?
context: Gordon + Hedlund's model attribution was approximately 106% of the observed rise -- essentially all of it, with a slight overshoot other model features offset. Note the model dependency in interpreting the exact number. Source: NBER Working Paper 21967 (Gordon + Hedlund 2016).

question: One driver of the tuition-inflation pattern was that aid-funded revenue supported administrative expansion rather than instructional capacity. Between 1987 and 2011 US higher-education administrative staff grew by approximately what percentage, versus a 50% rise in students?
context: The Delta Cost Project and GAO documented administrative-staff growth of ~87% from 1987 to 2011, well ahead of the ~50% student-enrollment rise. The aid revenue built bureaucracy rather than classrooms. Source: deltacostproject.org (Trends in College Spending reports).

question: A 2004 AEI book by Ohio University economist Richard Vedder was one of the earliest sustained academic syntheses of the college-cost / student-debt escalator. What was the book's title?
context: Richard Vedder, Going Broke by Degree: Why College Costs Too Much (AEI Press, 2004). Vedder's book presented the tuition-inflation / administrative-bloat pattern years before the Lucca and Gordon-Hedlund quantitative work. Source: aei.org (Vedder 2004).

question: The Bennett Hypothesis pattern is not unique to higher education. Where else does the same demand-subsidy-captured-by-constrained-supply mechanism appear in US policy?
answer: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
choices: Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets
context: Section 8 vouchers substantially raise landlord rent capture in constrained markets. Similar mechanisms operate in health-insurance subsidies (premium inflation) and the 2008-10 first-time homebuyer credit (largely captured in seller prices). Source: Collinson + Ganong on Section 8; Zwick + Malani on homebuyer credit.

question: The Bennett Hypothesis gives the policy analyst a general diagnostic to apply BEFORE approving any new demand-side subsidy. What question should the analyst ask about the supply side?
answer: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
choices: Who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity
Whether the supplier's headquarters is unionized
Whether the supplier accepts credit cards
Whether the supplier files its taxes electronically
context: The reasoning move: when a subsidy is proposed, ask whether the supply side is constrained and whether the specific suppliers have pricing power. If yes, expect substantial subsidy capture through prices. Source: Bennett (1987); Lucca + Nadauld + Shen (2015).

question: The three mechanisms by which the Bennett Hypothesis operates in higher education can be summarized in a single sentence. Which sentence best captures what federal student aid does at the aggregate level?
answer: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
choices: It builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity
It reduces the total price paid per credit hour
It shifts students into cheaper community colleges
It eliminates the need for private philanthropy
context: The three-part mechanism: demand-side pricing effect, administrative expansion of aid-funded revenue, and amenity-competition arms race in place of price competition. All three point in the same direction. Source: Gordon + Hedlund (2016); Vedder (2004); Delta Cost Project reports.

question: On the night of August 12-13, 1961 the East German government sealed the boundary between East and West Berlin, first with barbed wire and then with a concrete structure that stood for 28 years. What structure did they build?
context: Walter Ulbricht's East German government built the initial barrier overnight August 12-13, 1961. It grew into a concrete wall encircling West Berlin, standing until November 9, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: The Berlin Wall ran for a substantial distance around West Berlin. Roughly how long was the full barrier?
context: The Wall was roughly 155 km (96 miles) long, encircling West Berlin -- not running along the East-West German border. It included concrete, watchtowers, a 'death strip', anti-vehicle trenches, and patrol roads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.
