question: The most telling design fact about the Berlin Wall from an economics perspective is the direction its watchtower guns pointed -- not west at NATO, but the other way. Which direction did the guns point?
context: The Wall's fortifications faced INWARD -- guns and mines directed at East Germans trying to leave, not westward at any invading force. The design fact is the argument: the state had to wall its own citizens in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: The reason the East German state built the Wall in 1961 was that its citizens had been walking out. Between 1949 and 1961, roughly how many East Germans had left for the West through open Berlin -- more than a fifth of the East German population?
context: About 3.5 million East Germans left through Berlin between 1949 and August 1961 -- roughly a fifth of the country's population. The Wall was built to stop the flow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: During the 28 years the Wall stood, people died trying to cross it. What is the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented figure for confirmed deaths at the Wall itself?
context: The Berlin Wall Memorial documents about 140 confirmed deaths at the Wall itself; several hundred more died at the wider inter-German border. The first was Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961); the last was Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989). Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: The East German secret police, at the regime's fall in 1989, employed about 91,000 full-time officers and had roughly 189,000 unofficial informants in a country of 16.4 million. What was the German name of that police?
context: Ministerium fuer Staatssicherheit -- Ministry for State Security -- gave East Germany the highest surveillance-to-population ratio of any modern state. Source: bstu.de (Stasi Records Archive).

question: The first person killed trying to escape the Wall died within ten days of its construction, jumping from an apartment window in the border zone. What was her name?
context: Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961) died jumping from her fourth-floor Bernauer Strasse apartment on the border. She is the first of the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented victims. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: The last person to die trying to escape the Wall was killed by border guards in February 1989, less than nine months before the Wall fell. Who was he?
context: Chris Gueffroy (February 5, 1989) was shot trying to cross to West Berlin. His death drew international protest and East German policy shifted; his was the last shooting fatality at the Wall. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: After the 1990 German reunification, ordinary East Germans gained the right to read their own Stasi files under a specific 1991 law. What is this transparency law commonly called?
context: The Stasi Unterlagen Gesetz (Stasi Records Act, December 1991) established the office administering the archive and gave individuals the right to read their own files. The former ministry headquarters at Normannenstrasse is now the Stasi Museum. Source: bstu.de.

question: The Wall physically illustrated one core Austrian argument about the calculation debate. Which argument does 3.5 million pre-1961 East German exits and the inward-facing wall demonstrate at physical scale?
answer: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
choices: When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in
The market side always subsidizes the planned side
Planning works well as long as walls are built early
Cold War rivalry drove all migration flows
context: The argument is exit-as-verdict: given free comparison across an open border for twelve years, the population had voted with its feet. The Wall's inward-facing design is the calculation-debate answer made physical. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: The Wall's construction and dismantling frame the exact 28-year interval when Berlin was a divided city. In what years did the Wall stand?
context: The Wall was built August 12-13, 1961 and fell November 9, 1989 -- 28 years and 3 months. The demolition was completed by the early 1990s; small segments remain as memorials, and a double-cobblestone line traces the former path across the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: A three-word meme sentence emerged on Twitter around 2019 and became the Bitcoin community's dismissive response to almost every headline about monetary debasement, bank freezes, or currency collapse. Which phrase?
context: Popularized by Michael Saylor and thousands of others. Half meme, half genuine argument that most modern financial pathologies trace to monetary debasement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: The Bitcoin community deliberately distinguishes itself from a broader online scene it treats as a source of confusion and grift. Which broader label does the community actively distance itself FROM?
answer: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
choices: 'Crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins
context: Bitcoin advocates argue Bitcoin is monetary infrastructure with a specific design; altcoins are, in their view, mostly speculative tokens or venture-capital exit vehicles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A 'sat' or satoshi is Bitcoin's smallest divisible unit. How many satoshis make up one Bitcoin?
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC. Named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto. Naming the smallest unit for the creator is analogous to naming a small currency unit for a founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Satoshi_(unit).

question: The practice of buying a small fixed amount of Bitcoin on a regular schedule (daily, weekly, or monthly) regardless of the current price has a specific community name. What is it called?
context: Formally this is dollar-cost averaging. The community identity built around stacking emphasizes the discipline of not trying to time the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: The dismissive four-word community slogan 'Have Fun Staying Poor' (often abbreviated HFSP) was popularized by an anonymous British trader and podcaster who uses a specific pseudonym. What is his handle?
context: Cobie is the pseudonym of Jordan Fish, a British Bitcoin and altcoin trader who co-hosts the UpOnly podcast. The slogan expresses the impatience of holders who have watched skeptics predict Bitcoin's death for years while the network keeps functioning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A Nobel-winning economist would recognize the Bitcoin community's shared norms and practices (stacking sats, running nodes, meetup networks, conference culture) as a modern example of a concept he defined. Which concept?
context: Spontaneous order is Hayek's term for shared norms and institutions -- like language, common law, and open-source software -- that arise without any central planner. Bitcoin culture emerged with no central architect. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: Bitcoin conferences in cities like Nashville, Miami, Prague, and Riga draw tens of thousands of attendees each year. Compared to a Wall Street investment conference, what specifically dominates the keynote programming?
answer: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
choices: Talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips
Presentations of specific-price Bitcoin forecasts by regulated broker-dealers
Endorsements of specific altcoins by government regulators
context: The culture's emphasis on long time preference (deferring consumption today for a stronger monetary position later) and monetary-history education distinguishes the Bitcoin conference circuit from the mainstream investment-conference culture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_conference.

question: In May 2010, a Florida programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz posted on the bitcointalk.org forum offering 10,000 bitcoins to anyone who would arrange food delivery to his house. What ordinary meal did he ask for?
context: Hanyecz wrote 'I'll pay 10,000 bitcoins for a couple of pizzas... like maybe 2 large ones so I have some left over for the next day.' The transaction settled on May 22, 2010. Source: https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=137.0.

question: A British forum member accepted Laszlo Hanyecz's 10,000-BTC offer and had the two large pizzas delivered from an American chain that had nothing to do with Bitcoin. Which pizza chain delivered the pies?
context: The pizzas were ordered from Papa John's through its normal website by a UK forum user with the handle 'jercos'; Papa John's had no direct involvement with the crypto side of the deal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: On May 22, 2010, when Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 BTC for two Papa John's pizzas, Bitcoin was trading at fractions of a cent. Roughly what was the US-dollar value of 10,000 BTC that day?
context: 10,000 BTC at the prevailing rate of roughly $0.004 per BTC came to approximately $41 -- so Hanyecz paid about $20 per pizza in dollar terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: The Bitcoin community treats May 22, 2010 as the moment Bitcoin crossed a specific line -- not the first ever Bitcoin transaction, but the first of a specific commercial kind. Which milestone did Hanyecz's pizza order set?
answer: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
choices: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
the first Bitcoin mined by a home computer
the first Bitcoin transaction between two people who had never met
context: Bitcoin had been mined, sent between hobbyists, and traded for other cryptocurrencies before May 22, 2010 -- but Hanyecz's pizzas were the first documented exchange of BTC for a real physical good, marking Bitcoin's crossing from experiment to money. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Before he became famous for buying pizza, Laszlo Hanyecz had already made a separate technical contribution that arguably reshaped Bitcoin mining forever. Which piece of code did he write and share on the bitcointalk forum in 2010?
answer: the first software that let a graphics card (GPU) mine Bitcoin
choices: the first software that let a graphics card (GPU) mine Bitcoin
the first mixing service to anonymize transactions
the first Lightning Network channel implementation
context: Hanyecz worked out that a GPU could hash far faster than any CPU and wrote and shared the code, inadvertently starting the mining arms race that led to FPGAs, then ASICs. Mobile wallets came later; mixing services and Lightning are unrelated projects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Every May 22, Bitcoin holders around the world post pictures of their lunch on social media to commemorate Hanyecz's 2010 trade. What is the informal holiday called?
context: The community holiday Bitcoin Pizza Day is celebrated every May 22. Genesis Day (January 3) marks the mining of Block 0; Satoshi has no official birthday; the halving happens roughly every four years, not annually. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: By Bitcoin's later peaks the 10,000 BTC Laszlo Hanyecz spent on two pizzas would have grown to an eye-watering nominal fortune. At Bitcoin's cycle highs the same 10,000 BTC crossed which threshold?
choices: about one hundred million US dollars
context: 10,000 BTC at prices above $100,000 -- reached in Bitcoin's 2024-25 cycle -- crosses the one-billion-dollar mark. At earlier peaks the figure was measured in hundreds of millions; by any 2020s-era peak the paper value ran well into the ten-figure range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Asked in later interviews whether he regrets the 10,000-BTC pizza trade, Laszlo Hanyecz has consistently given the same answer, framed around what the trade did for Bitcoin rather than for his personal fortune. Which position does he take publicly on the deal?
answer: That he does not regret it; the trade was proof Bitcoin could be spent on real goods
choices: That he does not regret it; the trade was proof Bitcoin could be spent on real goods
That the trade was a mistake he has spent years trying to unwind
That the coins were never really his and belonged to the network
That he was pressured into the trade by other developers
context: Hanyecz has said in multiple interviews that Bitcoin needed to be spent before it could be money, and that being the first person to spend it on a physical good was worth more to him than the coins were then. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day; Cointelegraph interview archives.

question: The 2022 Austrian dispute about whether Bitcoin satisfies Mises's Regression Theorem -- the requirement that money must have some prior non-monetary use -- often points to the Hanyecz pizza trade as the specific dateable moment when one thing became another. Which transition does Bitcoin Pizza Day mark in that argument?
answer: the moment Bitcoin crossed from cypherpunk collectible to a medium of exchange for goods
choices: the moment Bitcoin crossed from cypherpunk collectible to a medium of exchange for goods
the moment Bitcoin's supply first hit the halving schedule
the moment Bitcoin's block reward first dropped below one bitcoin
the moment Bitcoin was first regulated as a security
context: In the Ammous-vs-Shostak debate, Bitcoin's early non-monetary use as a cypherpunk collectible satisfies the Regression Theorem; the pizza trade is the dateable moment (May 22, 2010) when it began being used to acquire ordinary goods. Halving schedule and reward cuts are separate mechanical events; Bitcoin's US legal status was settled much later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: In 1997 a French university press published a landmark 900-page collaborative work by six European historians on the death tolls of 20th-century communist regimes. What is the book's short name?
context: Le Livre noir du communisme was published by Editions Robert Laffont, Paris, in 1997. Harvard University Press released the English translation in 1999. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: The lead editor of the 1997 Black Book was a French CNRS historian who had begun his career as a Maoist student in 1968. What was his surname?
context: Stephane Courtois, historian at the CNRS (French national research center), spent three decades reading the archives that opened after 1991. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Courtois.

question: The Black Book's total for 20th-century communist death tolls -- assembled country by country from the newly opened post-1991 archives -- was a range. What is the range Courtois documented?
context: The Black Book's totals: about 65M in China, 20M in the USSR, 2M in Cambodia, 2M in North Korea, 1.7M in Africa, 1.5M in Afghanistan, ~1M in Vietnam, 150K in Eastern Europe. Aggregate 85-100M. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1997/1999).

question: The English translation of the Black Book was published by a specific major US academic press in 1999, bringing the totals into standard scholarly circulation in the Anglophone world. Which press?
context: Harvard University Press published the English edition in 1999 under the title The Black Book of Communism: Crimes, Terror, Repression. Source: hup.harvard.edu.

question: The Black Book's Soviet-Union chapter -- by a French historian who had specialized in Soviet archives -- documented the roughly 20 million figure for USSR deaths across Gulag, famines, purges, and executions. Which historian wrote it?
context: Nicolas Werth (CNRS) wrote the USSR chapter based on Soviet archival access after 1991. His later monograph Cannibal Island (2007) covered a specific 1930s Siberian deportation atrocity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Werth.

question: Courtois's introduction to the Black Book -- 'The Crimes of Communism' -- made an argument that generated a famous internal dispute. What was the specific claim two co-authors publicly protested?
answer: The equation of communist and Nazi crimes
choices: The equation of communist and Nazi crimes
The specific China total of 65 million
The framing of Ceausescu's execution as justified
The inclusion of Ethiopia in the totals
context: Nicolas Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin signed a Le Monde letter distancing themselves from Courtois's equation of communist and Nazi crimes, while standing by the country chapters they had written. The country totals were not disputed. Source: Le Monde (November 1997 letter).

question: The Black Book's China chapter documented a specific enormous figure driven by the Great Leap Forward famine of 1959-61 plus the Cultural Revolution 1966-76 plus the laogai prison-labor system. What is the standard total for China?
context: The Black Book's China total of ~65M has been refined by later Chinese archival scholarship. Yang Jisheng's Tombstone (2008) estimates the Great Leap famine alone at ~36M. Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine (2010) argues for a higher famine total. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: The Black Book's China total dwarfs the widely-cited figure for a comparable 20th-century atrocity. Roughly what fraction was the Nazi total in comparison to the aggregate communist total in the Black Book?
context: The Nazi total is ~25 million dead (military and civilian, per standard scholarly figures). The Black Book's ~85-100M communist total is roughly four times as large. Courtois's introduction asked why the two totals had such asymmetric public memory. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: Beyond the Black Book, several major single-country scholarly volumes documented specific pieces of the same total. Which 2003 Pulitzer-winning work by an American journalist covered the Soviet Gulag in detail?
context: Applebaum's Gulag: A History (Doubleday, 2003) won the 2004 Pulitzer for General Nonfiction. It uses newly opened Soviet archives to tell the camp system's history from Solovki 1918 through the post-Stalin dismantling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag:_A_History.

question: The 2008 scholarly volume documenting the Great Leap Forward famine at roughly 36 million dead, written by a Chinese journalist based on archival access inside China, is now the standard single-work source. What is its English title?
context: Yang Jisheng's Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962 was first published in Hong Kong in 2008; the English edition was released by Farrar Straus and Giroux in 2012. Yang was a lifelong Xinhua journalist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tombstone_(book).

question: The Black Book was translated into an unusually large number of languages, driven by both scholarly and popular interest. Roughly how many translations were published in the years after 1997?
context: About 26 language editions were published, and French sales alone exceeded 200,000 copies in the first year. The book triggered national black-books for individual regimes (Cuba, Vietnam, Poland). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: At the end of World War II the US had roughly 12 million men under arms. By June 1946 more than 8 million had been demobilized. The Harvard Keynesian economist Alvin Hansen predicted the US economy would react to this by doing what?
answer: Slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn
choices: Slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn
Sustaining wartime full employment for at least another decade
Entering a mild recession that would end within six months
Experiencing runaway inflation as pent-up demand met limited supply
context: Hansen and other 'secular stagnation' Keynesians argued the war had 'lifted' the US out of the 1930s and removing wartime spending would collapse it back. Every major Keynesian forecast in 1945-46 predicted renewed depression. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Hansen.

question: Federal spending in the immediate US postwar transition fell from $84B in 1945 to $30B in 1946 to $34B in 1947. Over the same 1946-47 stretch, with 8 million soldiers returning to the labor force, what did the US unemployment rate do?
choices: Rose to about 25 percent as in 1933
Stayed exactly at wartime levels near 1 percent
context: Despite the Keynesian prediction of depression, unemployment averaged around 4% in 1946-47 as private demand and investment absorbed the released wartime resources within months. Source: bls.gov historical LFS series.

question: Henry Hazlitt in Economics in One Lesson (1946) called the postwar demobilization the definitive real-world test of one specific Bastiat argument, since the massive wartime spending had NOT been what kept the country prosperous. Which Bastiat argument did Hazlitt say the demobilization vindicated?
choices: The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: The postwar experience was Bastiat's broken-window in reverse: the destruction (of massive government spending) did not impoverish the country because the released resources were used privately. Hazlitt makes this the anchor chapter of Economics in One Lesson. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: On September 14 2001 a specific Nobel laureate published a New York Times column arguing that the 9/11 attacks might 'do some economic good' via reconstruction spending. Which columnist wrote it?
context: Krugman's September 14 2001 NYT column, and follow-ups on Hurricane Katrina and the 2011 Japan earthquake, applied broken-window logic to disasters and terrorist attacks. He later walked the framing back. Source: nytimes.com (Krugman archive, September 14 2001).

question: Bastiat's method identifies the UNSEEN cost that any 'destruction stimulates the economy' claim ignores. Applied to Hurricane Katrina's ~$100B rebuild, what did Louisianans and Mississippians end 2006 with, relative to what they had had in mid-2005?
answer: The same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries
choices: The same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries
Better houses than before, thanks to the stimulus multiplier on federal spending
The same houses they had before, plus a year of higher aggregate income
Fewer houses than before, but with matching insurance-industry compensation
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN: the resources that rebuilt destroyed homes could not build new homes elsewhere. The Gulf ended 2006 no better off in housing stock than it had been in mid-2005, minus everything the same labor and capital could have produced instead. Source: cato.org/commentary/broken-window-fallacy-still-fooling-people.

question: Applied to the 9/11 attacks, Bastiat's method surfaces one specific unseen cost of the World Trade Center reconstruction. What could not be built because those resources went to the WTC rebuild?
answer: Other new office buildings and other homes those workers and materials could have produced instead
choices: Other new office buildings and other homes those workers and materials could have produced instead
The federal defense-spending programs Congress passed later in 2001
The airport-security infrastructure the TSA needed to hire staff for
The insurance-industry reserves needed to cover future terror events
context: The classic seen/unseen split for reconstruction: the WTC rebuild used labor and materials that would otherwise have built new offices in Queens or new homes on Long Island. The rebuild is SEEN; those other buildings are UNSEEN because they never got built. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/broken-window-fallacy-and-911.

question: The US postwar demobilization of 1945-46 is the largest peacetime natural-experiment shock in the federal-spending series ever recorded. About how large was the drop in federal spending, 1945 to 1946?
context: Federal outlays fell from $84B (1945) to $30B (1946), a two-thirds cut in a single year, at the same time as 8M soldiers returned to the labor force. The Austrian-Bastiat prediction (private demand absorbs the released resources) beat the Keynesian one on the largest peacetime test available. Source: whitehouse.gov OMB historical tables.

question: The 1946 postwar transition is the historical vindication of one specific 1946 American book that laid out the seen/unseen method for a mass audience the same year the demobilization ran. Which book was it?
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper & Brothers, 1946) appeared alongside the demobilization it explained: the broken-window and public-works chapters map directly onto the postwar reallocation. Source: fee.org/resources/economics-in-one-lesson.

question: The general Bastiat-method lesson of the 1946 postwar demobilization can be stated in one sentence about released resources and private demand. In its cleanest form, what did the released 12 million soldiers and $54B of released federal spending do?
answer: Were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition
choices: Were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition
Were absorbed by state and local government spending that replaced federal outlays
Were absorbed by an inflation surge that ate the released resources' real value
Were absorbed by involuntary unemployment for a full decade after 1946
context: The Austrian-Bastiat prediction: released resources go back into private hands and are put to their next-best use quickly. Empirically, 1946-47 US private consumption and private nonresidential investment surged as government spending fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-World_War_II_economic_expansion.

question: The whole 'wrecking things stimulates the economy' family of claims, from Krugman on 9/11 to WWII 'ending the Depression' to Hurricane Katrina 'boosting the Gulf,' shares one Bastiat-style diagnostic error. What are they treating as economically equivalent?
context: Bastiat's one-line diagnosis in the broken-window chapter: 'Destruction is not profit.' Every destruction-as-stimulus claim collapses the difference between a country that built new things and a country that rebuilt destroyed things. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Chapter 1 of Frederic Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' opens with a specific French shopkeeper whose careless son has just smashed a pane of glass. What is the shopkeeper's name in standard English editions?
context: Bastiat's French uses Jacques Bonhomme as the everyman placeholder; Hodgson's 1859 English translation renders him James Goodfellow, and every American edition since has followed. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: In the broken-window chapter of Bastiat's 1850 essay, the shopkeeper's smashed pane of glass gives the local glazier a specific number of francs of new business. Which number does Bastiat name?
context: Bastiat specifies six francs, and the whole rest of the chapter turns on those exact six francs and where they came from. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: In the broken-window scene, bystanders console the shopkeeper by pointing at a specific trade the smashed pane has just fed. Which trade do they say has been given six francs of business?
context: The glazier's six-franc replacement job is the SEEN benefit; the bystanders' whole consoling argument is that if panes were never broken, glaziers would starve. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Bastiat's punchline in the broken-window chapter rests on what the shopkeeper CANNOT now buy, because his six francs went to the glazier. Bastiat names one specific purchase the shopkeeper had planned. What was he going to buy?
answer: A new coat from the tailor
choices: A new coat from the tailor
A cask of wine from the vintner
A brass lamp from the tinsmith
context: The tailor's foregone coat is Bastiat's chosen UNSEEN alternative: 'It is not seen that as our shopkeeper has spent six francs upon one thing, he cannot spend them upon another.' Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Bastiat closes the broken-window chapter with a net-accounting line: BEFORE the break the shopkeeper had a window AND six francs; AFTER the break he has only a window. What single-sentence summary does Bastiat give for the community as a whole?
answer: The community is exactly one window poorer
choices: The community is exactly one window poorer
The community is exactly six francs richer
The community is no better and no worse off
The community has traded consumption for investment
context: Bastiat's summary line: 'Destruction is not profit.' The community's total wealth is one pane of glass smaller than it was five minutes earlier, and that is the whole result. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: The consoling bystanders in Bastiat's broken-window chapter open their comforting speech with a proverb about wind and misfortune, which is now the folk-name of the fallacy Bastiat is refuting. Which proverb do they cite?
answer: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good
choices: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good
Every cloud has a silver lining
One man's loss is another man's gain
Necessity is the mother of invention
context: The bystanders' opening line: 'It is an ill wind that blows nobody good. Everybody must live, and what would become of the glaziers if panes of glass were never broken?' Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: In September 2001 Paul Krugman published a New York Times column arguing that the 9/11 attacks might 'do some economic good' by generating reconstruction spending. Which Bastiat-based objection did Austrian economists and libertarian columnists immediately press against the piece?
answer: The resources spent rebuilding could no longer be spent on other new construction
choices: The resources spent rebuilding could no longer be spent on other new construction
The reconstruction would depress interest rates below their natural equilibrium
The insurance-industry payouts would fail to trigger a Keynesian multiplier
The federal deficit would rise faster than the private-sector recovery
context: The classic seen/unseen objection: the labor and capital that rebuilt lower Manhattan could not simultaneously build new offices in Queens. Krugman later walked the framing back; the objection has been standard Austrian-classroom material ever since. Source: cato.org/commentary/broken-window-fallacy-still-fooling-people.

question: In 2009 the federal government paid buyers a rebate to trade in older vehicles for new ones, but required the trade-ins be destroyed by pouring sodium silicate into the engine. Which 2009 program was the textbook 21st-century broken-window case?
choices: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act
context: Formally the Car Allowance Rebate System (CARS Act, June-August 2009): roughly 690,000 running used cars were destroyed to qualify buyers for a $3,500-$4,500 rebate on a new one. Source: brookings.edu/articles/cash-for-clunkers-an-evaluation-of-the-car-allowance-rebate-system.

question: In one economist's-shorthand phrase, Bastiat's whole broken-window argument teaches the reader to trace what beyond the immediate visible effect of any policy?
context: The essay's title is the whole method: what is SEEN vs what is NOT SEEN. Every worked example in Bastiat, Hazlitt, Sowell, and Friedman since is another application of that single move. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Milton Friedman's 1980 book and PBS television series, co-authored with Rose Friedman, brought Bastiat's seen/unseen method to a mass American audience in the same decade Ronald Reagan came to office. Which Friedman book made the case?
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
context: Free to Choose (Harcourt, 1980) applies the Bastiat move across public education, welfare, consumer protection, and inflation; the ten-part PBS series aired the same year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_to_Choose.

question: The founding text of public choice as a discipline was co-authored by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock and published by the University of Michigan Press in 1962. What was the book's title?
context: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy (University of Michigan Press, 1962). Both authors were then at the University of Virginia. Source: press.umich.edu (Calculus of Consent).

question: The Calculus of Consent applied standard economic reasoning -- self-interest, marginal analysis, opportunity cost -- to a set of decision-makers that welfare economics had traditionally assumed were BENEVOLENT SOCIAL PLANNERS. Which decision-makers were being reinterpreted?
choices: Consumers and firms in competitive markets
context: The Calculus of Consent's central methodological move: treat political actors with the same self-interest assumption economics uses for consumers and firms. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 1.

question: Buchanan and Tullock distinguished two levels of political decision. The lower level was choices made within the rules -- votes on tariffs, taxes, subsidies. What did they call the upper level, where the rules themselves are chosen?
context: The constitutional level is where individuals choose the rules that will bind all subsequent political choices. Buchanan's whole later career built out this idea as 'constitutional political economy.' Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: Buchanan and Tullock argued that at the constitutional level, an individual reasoning about the rules cannot know whether he or she will be in the majority or minority on future issues. What phrase did they use for this reasoning stance?
context: The 'veil of uncertainty' is Buchanan-Tullock's term. Individuals reasoning about future political outcomes rationally consent to rules that limit majority power. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: Nine years after the Calculus of Consent, a Harvard philosopher published a book that made a similar move under a different name: reason about principles of justice from behind a veil that hides your future position. Who was that philosopher?
context: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard 1971), asked what redistributive principles rational agents would choose from behind a 'veil of ignorance.' Buchanan reached the parallel constitutional move nine years earlier from an independent starting point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Theory_of_Justice.

question: The Calculus of Consent explicitly attacked what Buchanan-Tullock called the ROMANCE view of majority voting -- the assumption that if a policy is chosen by majority vote, it must reflect 'the will of the people.' Their book replaced this romance with an analysis of what real determinants of majority outcomes?
answer: Interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance
choices: Interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance
The moral wisdom of the median voter
The efficient aggregation of correct beliefs
The natural convergence of common purposes
context: Once you model voters, politicians, and bureaucrats as self-interested individuals, majority outcomes reflect the balance of organized pressures, vote-trading across issues, and voter apathy on issues with low per-capita stakes. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 10.

question: The Calculus of Consent argued that individuals behind the veil of uncertainty would prefer decision rules that require more than a simple majority for certain especially consequential choices. What term describes the higher-than-majority thresholds they analyzed?
context: Buchanan + Tullock analyzed the trade-off between decision costs (higher thresholds are harder to reach) and external costs (lower thresholds impose more harm on losing minorities). Supermajority rules for consequential choices minimize expected total cost. Source: Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: Buchanan and Tullock met at the University of Virginia after Tullock arrived from the Foreign Service in 1958. Which US foundation provided a key early grant that funded the research leading to the Calculus of Consent?
context: Buchanan's autobiographical essays document early Ford Foundation support for the Virginia research program that produced the Calculus of Consent. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (Chicago 1992).

question: The Calculus of Consent gave the entire discipline of public choice its foundational vocabulary. Which of the following ideas did the book NOT introduce, but instead borrow from a different foundational text?
answer: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern of collective action
choices: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern of collective action
The veil of uncertainty behind rule choice
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern comes from Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965) -- three years after the Calculus. The other three are all in the Calculus. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Olson (1965).

question: The Calculus of Consent's most durable analytical achievement was a distinction that reframed how political theory could argue with itself. Which distinction did the book put at the center of public-choice reasoning?
answer: The distinction between the RULES of the game and the choices WITHIN the rules
choices: The distinction between the RULES of the game and the choices WITHIN the rules
The distinction between right-wing and left-wing voters
The distinction between economic policy and social policy
The distinction between elected and appointed officials
context: The constitutional / post-constitutional distinction is Buchanan's most enduring contribution. Individuals may agree on the rules (constitutional consent) while disagreeing on the choices made under the rules (post-constitutional politics). Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), preface and Chapter 6.

question: Half a century after the Calculus of Consent appeared, its influence extended well beyond formal public-choice scholarship. In what single sentence is the book's abiding lesson best summarized?
answer: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
choices: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
The bigger the majority, the wiser the decision
Politicians are always more knowledgeable than voters
Economic policy should never be constrained by any constitution
context: Buchanan's whole later career built out this insight. Constitutional rules that bind majorities are the deepest form of consent, because they are agreed to when the future distribution of winners and losers is still unknown. Source: Buchanan, The Reason of Rules (Cambridge 1985).

question: In 1821 Britain formally committed that its central bank would redeem paper pound notes for gold at a fixed price -- about 4.86 pounds per troy ounce, the informal rate since 1717. This launched a monetary system that would become the model for the industrial world. What is that system called?
context: The 1821 resumption of gold payments by the Bank of England is the conventional start of the classical gold standard, a system Britain led until 1914. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Under the classical gold standard, exchange rates between the major currencies were fixed because each currency was fixed to gold at a stated ratio. A pound was consistently equal to what number of dollars for most of the pre-1914 era?
context: The pound-dollar rate stayed at 4.8665 for decades before 1914, held there by the two currencies' independent gold parities. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Germany adopted the gold standard in 1871, funding the transition with a large indemnity paid by another European power that had just lost a war. Which indemnity funded the German conversion?
answer: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
choices: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
The Austrian tribute after the Austro-Prussian War
The Ottoman payment for the Berlin conference
context: France paid Germany 5 billion francs in gold after its 1871 defeat, giving Chancellor Bismarck the reserves he needed to move Germany to the mark on a full gold basis. Source: Grokipedia 'Franco-Prussian War' (2026-09-05).

question: One of the most striking economic features of Britain under the classical gold standard was that its general price level in 1914 was roughly the same as in 1821 -- despite a century of industrial expansion. What word describes that kind of long-run price behavior?
choices: Volatile in a wide upward trend
context: The British price level fluctuated within a range but showed no sustained trend across the 93 years of the classical gold standard. A pound in 1914 bought roughly what a pound in 1821 bought. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Under the classical gold standard a working-class Italian family could receive remittances from a son working in London without exchange-rate risk, and the wages he sent would keep their value across the trip. What specific technical feature of the system made that possible?
answer: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
choices: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
The Bank of England guaranteed all foreign remittances at face value
The Italian government subsidized the Lira-Pound conversion
International trade unions negotiated the exchange rates
context: The pound was fixed to gold at one ratio, the Italian lira at another; their cross-rate followed mechanically. A worker's remittance kept its purchasing power across borders because both currencies shared a real anchor. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises later wrote about the classical gold standard in political terms, describing it not primarily as an economic arrangement but as something else. How did he characterize it?
answer: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
choices: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
The unavoidable relic of a pre-industrial economy
A middle-class conspiracy against wage earners
A technical convenience of no political significance
context: Mises argued that gold discipline restrained state power more effectively than any written constitution. Governments unable to inflate had to persuade taxpayers or lenders to fund their projects. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: The most consequential constraint the classical gold standard imposed on governments was budgetary. What specific state activity did the gold discipline make unaffordable when honestly paid for?
answer: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
choices: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
context: Under gold, wars had to be paid for by taxes or borrowing. Neither scaled to modern industrial slaughter. Governments could inflate only by first suspending convertibility -- which is what all major belligerents did within days in August 1914. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: The 1871-1914 stretch of European history that ran on the classical gold standard is remembered by a specific French phrase capturing its cross-border investment, expanding middle class, and rising life expectancy. Which phrase?
context: The Belle Epoque -- 'beautiful era' -- runs from roughly 1871 to 1914. Its economic character (free capital movement, stable prices, mass migration funded by private savings) was inseparable from the shared gold basis of world money. Source: Grokipedia 'Belle Epoque' (2026-09-05).

question: The classical gold standard ended in the first week of a specific month in 1914, when every major belligerent suspended gold convertibility so it could print money to fund the coming war. Which month?
context: Germany suspended gold payments August 4 1914; Britain effectively followed within days; France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary within the week. The century of stable prices ended not because gold discipline failed but because states wanted to fight a war that gold discipline would have made unaffordable. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: The classical gold standard was celebrated by Austrian economists not because the money supply was rigid but because of the specific political effect that rigidity had. Which effect do they emphasize?
answer: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
choices: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
It ensured full employment across the developed world
It equalized income across social classes
context: The Austrian point: the value of gold discipline is not perfect stability -- there were still recessions and shocks -- but the constraint it placed on government power. Every 20th-century abandonment of gold was driven by governments that wanted to be freed from that constraint. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: German economist Horst Siebert coined a parable-name in his 2001 book Der Kobra-Effekt (The Cobra Effect), drawn from a widely-retold story about British colonial administration in a particular Indian city. Which city is the story set in?
context: The parable is traditionally set in British colonial Delhi in the late 19th century. The historical base is disputed; Siebert used it as an illustrative parable in 2001 for the general perverse-incentive pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: In the standard telling of the Cobra Effect, the colonial government wanted to reduce the venomous-cobra population in the city and offered a specific type of payment scheme. What did the government offer?
answer: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
choices: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
A tax rebate for landowners who eradicated cobras from their plots
A trained mongoose delivered to each household that requested one
A public-works job for anyone willing to clear cobra dens
context: The bounty was the seen policy: kill more cobras, get paid, cobra population should fall. Straight, intuitive, and completely wrong once the incentive was actually running. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: The Cobra Effect got its name because Delhi residents responded to the bounty with a specific unintended entrepreneurial move. What did they do?
answer: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
choices: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
Began smuggling cobras in from neighboring provinces
Began stealing cobras from public zoo enclosures
Began falsely reporting non-cobra snakes as cobras
context: Farming dead cobras in the back yard was more profitable than hunting wild ones. The bounty had created a farming operation, not a hunting one -- exactly the unseen behavioral response the policy did not price in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: The second-order twist in the Cobra Effect story explains why the parable is memorable. When the government eventually noticed the perverse incentive and cancelled the bounty, what did the cobra-breeders do?
answer: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
choices: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
Petitioned the government for a compensation payment
Killed and buried their cobra stock privately
Sold the cobras through underground exotic-pet markets
context: Delhi's cobra population ended the program HIGHER than it started; the released breeder-stock hit the streets after the bounty ended. The parable's whole punch is this cancellation-worse-than-nothing outcome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: A better-documented parallel case to the Cobra Effect is a rat-bounty scheme run by the French colonial administration in a specific Southeast Asian city; the historian Michael Vann described it in French Colonial Studies (2003). Which city did the French pay a bounty on rat tails in?
context: The French Hanoi rat-bounty (1902) is better historically documented than the Delhi cobra story. Rat-catchers began FARMING rats and turning in the tails while releasing the tail-less rats to breed more. Source: Michael Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race,' French Colonial History 4 (2003).

question: In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart wrote a one-line formulation of the general perverse-incentive pattern the Cobra Effect illustrates. In its most common paraphrase, when a measure becomes what, it ceases to be a good measure?
context: Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Originally a Bank of England paper on monetary aggregates, it generalized to name the whole pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law.

question: In 2016 a specific US retail bank was fined for a Cobra-Effect-style scandal: employees under pressure to hit a cross-sell bounty opened millions of accounts customers had never asked for. Which bank was fined?
context: Wells Fargo's 2016 cross-sell fake-accounts scandal: employees hit incentive targets by opening real accounts customers had not requested. The bounty on 'accounts opened' produced accounts, not customer value. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo_cross-selling_scandal.

question: The 2001-2015 US federal education law tied school funding partly to standardized test scores, producing a documented Cobra-Effect pattern that critics called 'teaching to the test.' What was the law's popular name?
context: NCLB (2001), signed by George W. Bush, made federal funds contingent on test-score improvements; schools optimized on the specific tested items, sometimes at the expense of everything else. The 2015 Every Student Succeeds Act replaced it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act.

question: The Cobra Effect, Goodhart's Law, and the Hanoi rat-bounty all illustrate the same Bastiat-style unseen effect: policy sets an incentive, and the unseen behavioral response drives the outcome. The 2010 US health law added a specific example when it imposed penalties on hospitals for excessive 30-day readmissions. What did hospitals do in response?
answer: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
choices: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
Refused to accept transfers from other hospitals with high readmission rates
Reduced the length of stay for all admitted patients uniformly
Charged patients directly for care that would trigger a readmission classification
context: The ACA's CMS 30-day-readmission penalties incentivized hospitals to keep returning patients in ED observation status (which is not counted as an admission), reducing the measure without necessarily improving the outcome. Standard Cobra-Effect / Goodhart pattern. Source: healthaffairs.org/do/10.1377/hpb20180216.35660.

question: In February 1960, the University of Chicago Press brought out a 500-page defense of the classical-liberal social order, written by a Viennese emigre professor across the second half of the 1950s. The book would later be slammed on a table in London by Margaret Thatcher as a manifesto. Which economist wrote it?
context: F. A. Hayek completed the manuscript in May 1959; University of Chicago Press published it as 'The Constitution of Liberty' in February 1960. Source: Wikipedia article on The Constitution of Liberty (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constitution_of_Liberty).

question: Friedrich Hayek wrote his big 1960 defense of classical-liberal principles while holding a professorial chair at the University of Chicago -- not in the Economics Department but in an interdisciplinary program known for Saul Bellow and Allan Bloom. What was that program called?
context: Hayek held the Committee on Social Thought chair at Chicago from 1950 through the late 1950s; The Constitution of Liberty was written there. Source: University of Chicago Press catalog listing (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo9253956.html).

question: Early in 'The Constitution of Liberty' (1960), Hayek insists on a precise definition. He rejects the loose modern usage in which liberty can mean political participation, or economic power, or wealth. In Hayek's usage, liberty is one specific thing -- the absence of being made to serve another's will. What does Hayek call that specific thing?
answer: The absence of coercion by another person
choices: The absence of coercion by another person
The satisfaction of one's most fundamental preferences
The equal exercise of political voice in the public sphere
The material means to pursue one's chosen ends
context: Hayek: liberty is the absence of coercion by another person -- being made to serve another's will. Not power, not wealth, not political participation. Source: Cato Institute review and Online Library of Liberty essay by Ronald Hamowy (https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/hamowy-s-critique-of-hayek-s-concept-of-freedom).

question: Hayek's 1960 book is organized in three named parts. Part I lays the philosophical groundwork; Part II turns to the legal framework; Part III applies the principles to specific 20th-century policies. What is Part I -- the opening third of the book -- titled?
context: The book runs Part I 'The Value of Freedom,' Part II 'Freedom and the Law,' Part III 'Freedom in the Welfare State.' Source: BiblioVault edition listing (https://www.bibliovault.org/BV.book.epl?ISBN=9780226315393).

question: In Part II of 'The Constitution of Liberty,' Hayek argues that even the same practical outcome differs in kind when produced by a policeman citing a published traffic code versus a policeman saying 'you are fined because I said so.' Which classical legal distinction is Hayek pressing to explain that difference in kind?
answer: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
choices: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
context: Hayek's core Part II thesis: the rule of law -- general, prospective, equal, published in advance -- is a distinct kind of political order from administrative discretion, even when the practical results coincide. Source: True North Ideas summary (https://truenorthideas.org/the-constitution-of-liberty-hayeks-lessons-for-today-and-tomorrow/).

question: Hayek's central argument for a free society in 'The Constitution of Liberty' does not rest on the claim that individuals are always wise -- he explicitly says they are not. Instead, he defends freedom on the ground that a society organized around it will produce discoveries -- in law, science, technology, and culture -- that a designed order could not. Which specific claim about knowledge does that argument turn on?
answer: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
choices: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
That elected representatives are systematically better informed than administrators
That most citizens correctly rank their long-term interests over short-term ones
That common law judges reason more reliably than legislators about complex trade-offs
context: Hayek's argument: freedom matters because we do not know in advance what discoveries a free society will make; only a free order can produce them, precisely because a planner would have to know them already to permit them. Source: Cato Institute Regulation review (https://www.cato.org/regulation/spring-2026/book-review-constitution-liberty).

question: Friedrich Hayek closes 'The Constitution of Liberty' with a postscript in which he refuses a political label many readers had assumed applied to him. Instead he takes the older British label that Edmund Burke had also claimed for himself. Which chapter title Hayek uses for that closing essay?
answer: Why I Am Not a Conservative
choices: Why I Am Not a Conservative
context: The postscript is titled 'Why I Am Not a Conservative.' Hayek identifies himself as an 'Old Whig,' the term Burke had used for himself. Source: Hayek, postscript, reprinted at Cato (https://www.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/articles/hayek-why-i-am-not-conservative.pdf).

question: In the 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' postscript to his 1960 book, Hayek explains why conservatism cannot be a genuine alternative to socialism. Conservatives, he says, want to keep things as they are; he himself wants to move somewhere. Which reasoning move against the conservative label is Hayek pressing?
answer: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
choices: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
That conservatism has always been captured by throne-and-altar aristocracy and cannot be democratized
That conservatism confuses the value of tradition with the value of the particular customs it inherits
That conservatism is incompatible with the constitutional limits on royal power the Whigs defended
context: Hayek: conservatives want to keep things as they are; he wants to move toward greater freedom -- so conservatism cannot be a real alternative to socialism, only a brake on it. Source: Hayek, 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' (https://soonersentinel.substack.com/p/fa-hayek-why-i-am-not-a-conservative).

question: In summer 1975, the newly elected Conservative Party leader interrupted a Research Department speaker urging a moderate 'middle way' policy. She reached into her briefcase, pulled out a five-hundred-page 1960 academic book by an Austrian economist, slammed it on the table, and declared 'This is what we believe.' The book, per John Ranelagh's 1991 account, was Hayek's 'Constitution of Liberty.' Which party leader was it?
context: The anecdote is told in John Ranelagh's 'Thatcher's People' (1991); the Margaret Thatcher Foundation itself calls it 'perhaps a little too perfect to be actually true,' so it should be treated as reported testimony rather than settled fact. Sources: Sotheby's essay (https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/this-is-what-we-believe-margaret-thatcher-and-f-a-hayek); Margaret Thatcher Foundation archive note.  (Legend.)

question: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation's own archive note on the 1975 'this is what we believe' anecdote -- Thatcher slamming Hayek's 'Constitution of Liberty' on a Conservative Research Department table -- cautions that the story is beloved of biographers and 'perhaps a little too perfect to be actually true.' What kind of source discipline does that Foundation caution point to?
answer: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
choices: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
That John Ranelagh's 1991 book was later fully retracted by its publisher
That Margaret Thatcher denied the anecdote in her own memoirs
That Hayek himself in the 1980s explicitly denied ever meeting Thatcher
context: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation records the anecdote as beloved-of-biographers but cautions it may be too perfect to be true; Ranelagh 1991 is the source, not a contemporaneous document. Neither Thatcher's memoirs nor Hayek's biography retracts the story -- the Foundation simply flags it as unverified testimony. Source: Margaret Thatcher Foundation Hayek archive (https://www.margaretthatcher.org/archive/Hayek).  (Legend.)

question: In June 1775 the Continental Congress voted for war against Britain but had no power to tax -- only the individual colonies did. To pay for soldiers and gunpowder, Congress authorized a new paper money. What was it called?
context: The June 22 1775 resolution authorized $2 million in bills of credit -- soon known as 'Continentals' -- to fund the Revolutionary War effort. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: Over the six years of the Revolutionary War the Continental Congress printed issue after issue of paper money, totaling about $241 million. At the war's start, the total gold and silver coin circulating in the colonies was estimated at what much smaller figure?
context: Estimates of specie in the colonies at 1775 hover around $6 million. Printing $241 million against a $6 million specie base guaranteed collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: By the summer of 1781 a Continental paper dollar was worth about one hundredth of a silver dollar, and by the end of that year it was effectively worthless. A folk phrase from that collapse entered American English and stayed current for a century. Which phrase?
context: The phrase 'not worth a Continental' became the standard American idiom for anything valueless. Barbers reportedly papered their shops with unwanted Continentals as decoration. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: Continental soldiers were paid in Continentals, and the paper's collapse hit a specific group hardest. Who suffered most from the collapse of the American Revolution's paper money?
answer: Soldiers' families and small savers who held Continentals as savings
choices: Soldiers' families and small savers who held Continentals as savings
context: Soldiers who earned in Continentals watched the paper their families held evaporate. Farmers who accepted Continentals for grain became poor; those who insisted on gold were denounced as gougers. This asymmetric destruction became a Founding-era grievance. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: In 1777 and 1778 the Continental Congress tried to slow the collapse of its paper money by decreeing legal ceilings on what merchants and farmers could charge for goods. What are these decrees called?
context: Congress and several state governments imposed wage and price controls in 1777-78, hoping to freeze the visible collapse. The controls were widely evaded and abandoned within about a year. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: Beyond price controls, several states also tried a legal mechanism forcing shopkeepers to accept Continentals at face value on pain of penalty. What are laws of this kind called?
context: Legal-tender laws penalize refusal of a specific currency at face value. In the Continental case they were widely evaded -- sellers demanded gold or fled the market rather than accept the paper. Source: Grokipedia 'Legal tender' (2026-09-05).

question: When the US Constitution was drafted in 1787, delegates who had watched the Continental collapse specifically forbade the states from issuing paper money, using a phrase from the era. Which phrase does Article I Section 10 use?
context: Article I Section 10 forbids any state to 'emit Bills of Credit'. Article I Section 8 confines federal monetary power to 'coin Money, regulate the Value thereof'. Both clauses were drafted with the Continental collapse in living memory. Source: US Constitution, Article I.

question: The 1787 Constitution's tight monetary language -- forbidding state paper money and restricting federal power to coinage -- reflected a specific attitude toward hard money on the part of the framers. What best describes that attitude?
answer: An empirical lesson drawn from a catastrophe they had personally lived through
choices: An empirical lesson drawn from a catastrophe they had personally lived through
A theoretical preference borrowed from Adam Smith's 1776 book
A concession to British commercial interests
A late compromise proposed by Alexander Hamilton alone
context: Madison, Hamilton, and every other delegate had watched the Continental hyperinflate. Their hard-money bias was earned firsthand, not imported from any theorist. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: The mechanisms tried during the Continental collapse -- legal-tender laws, wage and price controls, criminal penalties for refusing paper -- were the same ones later used in the French Revolution's paper-money episode a decade later. Which French currency followed the same failed script?
context: The 1789-1796 French assignat episode reached for the same legal tools (with the death penalty on top). It collapsed for the same reason: the underlying paper-printing was untouched. Every hyperinflation reruns the same playbook. Source: White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912).

question: Bastiat would describe the Continental collapse using a contrast between what appeared to be happening and what actually happened to real people. Which pairing best captures that seen-and-unseen structure?
answer: Seen: government paying soldiers; Unseen: soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed
choices: Seen: government paying soldiers; Unseen: soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed
Seen: rising retail sales; Unseen: falling personal debt
Seen: growing agricultural output; Unseen: falling immigration
Seen: new colonial banks opening; Unseen: British trade barriers
context: Bastiat's frame: the visible act (payment) hides the invisible destruction (evaporation of the recipient's savings). The Continental is the earliest well-documented American case of the Cantillon-effect asymmetric damage every paper-money collapse produces. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: In 1873 the US Coinage Act quietly ended the free coinage of silver, effectively moving the country to a pure gold standard. Silver-mining states and agricultural debtors gave the change a bitter nickname that would echo through the 1890s. What did they call it?
context: Silver interests alleged the change was a conspiracy by Eastern bankers to enrich creditors. Most historians think the decision was not a conspiracy, but the political label stuck for a generation. Source: Grokipedia 'Coinage Act of 1873' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1873 shift toward a stronger dollar made an existing group of Americans suffer immediately because it changed the real weight of their obligations. Which group did it hurt most?
answer: Farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks
choices: Farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks
context: Farmers borrowed money in the plentiful greenback dollars of the 1860s and had to repay in the harder-to-earn gold-standard dollars of the 1870s and 1880s. Falling crop prices with fixed debts transferred wealth from debtors to creditors. Source: Grokipedia 'Crime of 1873' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1890s political movement demanding the US resume unlimited coinage of one specific metal at the traditional 16-to-1 ratio to gold -- effectively re-monetizing it to help agricultural debtors -- had a single memorable slogan. What was the movement called?
context: The Free Silver campaign argued for unrestricted minting of silver dollars alongside gold, at a legal ratio that would have inflated the money supply and eased farm debts. Source: Grokipedia 'Free silver' (2026-09-05).

question: The Free Silver movement split the Democratic Party in the mid-1890s. The 'Gold Democrats' backed the sitting president Grover Cleveland. The 'Silver Democrats' rallied around a 36-year-old congressman from Nebraska. What was his name?
context: Bryan was 36 at the 1896 Democratic National Convention. His silver-currency populism galvanized rural voters and defined the Democratic Party for a generation. Source: Grokipedia 'William Jennings Bryan' (2026-09-05).

question: On July 8 1896 at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, the young Nebraskan closed his address with a line that named the entire hard-money system as an instrument of religious torture. Which phrase did he end on?
answer: You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold
choices: You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold
Give me liberty or give me death
Malice toward none, charity for all
The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
context: Bryan's peroration -- 'you shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns; you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold' -- won him the nomination that afternoon and became one of the most quoted political speeches in American history. Source: Grokipedia 'Cross of Gold speech' (2026-09-05).

question: Bryan won the Democratic nomination in July 1896 but lost the general election in November to the Republican candidate. Which Ohio Republican defeated him?
context: McKinley, backed by industrialist Marcus Hanna's fundraising machine, won 271 electoral votes to Bryan's 176 in the 1896 election. Source: Grokipedia '1896 United States presidential election' (2026-09-05).

question: The Free Silver question quietly died in the decade after Bryan's 1896 defeat because a specific external event organically inflated the world's gold money supply, easing farm debts without a legal change. What happened?
answer: Major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado
choices: Major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado
The Federal Reserve began open-market operations
European nations shipped gold reserves to New York for safekeeping
A cyanide-leaching breakthrough doubled US silver output
context: The Klondike strike (1896), the Witwatersrand gold rush in South Africa (1886 onward, expanding through the 1890s), and Colorado mining organically expanded the gold money supply. Prices rose, debtors were relieved, and Congress passed the Gold Standard Act in 1900. Source: Grokipedia 'Klondike Gold Rush' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1873-1896 US money debate teaches a specific reasoning move about who benefits from hard money and who benefits from inflation. Which pairing best summarizes that move?
answer: Hard money benefits savers and creditors; inflation benefits debtors
choices: Hard money benefits savers and creditors; inflation benefits debtors
Hard money benefits urban workers; inflation benefits rural landowners
Hard money benefits banks only; inflation benefits governments only
Hard money benefits importers; inflation benefits exporters
context: The distributional effect is symmetric and unavoidable. Inflating the money supply erodes the real value of nominal debts, transferring wealth from lenders to borrowers. Both effects are real and both are political. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: The Austrian preference in the 19th-century American money debate was not for permanent deflation. What Austrian arrangement did economists like Rothbard actually favor?
answer: A market-determined money supply that neither government nor lobby can inflate to redistribute wealth by decree
choices: A market-determined money supply that neither government nor lobby can inflate to redistribute wealth by decree
A permanent legal peg to silver at 20 to 1
A government fiat money with a 3% annual growth rule
A single global central bank issuing a shared currency
context: The Austrian move: the problem with Free Silver was not that it would have inflated, but that it would have inflated by government decree at a legislated ratio. A market-selected commodity money removes both discretion and lobbying. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: The 1896 Cross of Gold campaign was the first American presidential contest fought explicitly and openly on a monetary policy question. Which recognition move does the ladder press on the reader?
answer: Money policy is always distributional -- there is no neutral choice between hard and soft money
choices: Money policy is always distributional -- there is no neutral choice between hard and soft money
Politicians can always neutralize the effects of monetary policy with fiscal measures
Elections rarely turn on economic issues alone
The gold standard was universally supported across all US regions in 1896
context: Every monetary regime enriches one group and disadvantages another. The Cantillon effect makes this unavoidable. The Austrian argument is not that hard money is neutral but that market-determined money removes the political discretion that lobbies compete for. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: From 1966 to 1976 Mao Zedong ran a decade-long campaign against alleged class enemies inside the Communist Party of China. What is that campaign called?
context: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution ran 1966-76, formally launched with the May 16, 1966 Notification declaring class enemies had infiltrated the party at every level. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution.

question: Mao's instrument for the Cultural Revolution was a mass movement of university and high-school students given armbands and permission to attack teachers, party officials, and professionals. What were these young enforcers called?
context: The Red Guards were students mobilized in the millions from summer 1966. They attacked the 'Four Olds' (old ideas, culture, customs, habits) and denounced teachers and officials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards.

question: The public accusation ritual of the Cultural Revolution required the target to stand or kneel before a crowd, wear a placard listing accusations, and be shouted at for hours. What was this ritual called?
context: Struggle sessions (pi dou hui) targeted teachers, doctors, engineers, party rivals, and Buddhist monks. Humiliation-to-suicide was a routine outcome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_session.

question: The Cultural Revolution targeted a specific list of things the Red Guards were to destroy: old ideas, old culture, old customs, old habits. What is the shorthand name for this list?
context: The 'Four Olds' (Si Jiu) framed the destruction of historic buildings, temples, books, artworks, and traditional practices during the campaign's peak in 1966-67. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Olds.

question: The Cultural Revolution's most prominent victim was the sitting state president of the People's Republic, denounced as the 'number-one capitalist roader' and arrested in 1967. Who died in prison of untreated pneumonia in November 1969?
context: Liu Shaoqi, state president of the PRC, had helped organize the retreat from the Great Leap famine. Denounced by Mao, he died in prison November 12, 1969 of untreated pneumonia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Shaoqi.

question: Another prominent Cultural Revolution victim was purged twice -- once in 1966 and again in April 1976 -- and then returned to power after Mao's death to lead the 1978 economic reforms. Who was he?
context: Deng was purged in 1966, rehabilitated briefly by Zhou Enlai in 1973, purged again April 1976 after the Tiananmen protests over Zhou's death, then fully rehabilitated after Mao's death. He launched Reform and Opening in December 1978. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping.

question: The Cultural Revolution formally ended with the arrest in October 1976 of a small group headed by Mao's widow. What was the group called?
context: The Gang of Four -- Jiang Qing (Mao's widow), Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen -- were arrested one month after Mao's death on September 9, 1976. Their trial in 1980-81 blamed them for the excesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_of_Four.

question: Scholarly death-toll estimates for the Cultural Revolution proper (1966-76) span a range, with millions more imprisoned or exiled to the countryside in the 'send-down' movement. What is the standard range for direct deaths?
context: Direct Cultural Revolution death estimates range from ~500,000 to ~2 million. Millions more were imprisoned or sent down to the countryside for reeducation through manual labor. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: The party's own 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party gave the Cultural Revolution a specific formal judgment. What did the resolution say?
answer: It was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the PRC
choices: It was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the PRC
It was a necessary period of ideological cleansing
It was largely misled by foreign interference
It was a success in mobilizing the countryside
context: The 1981 Resolution formalized the party's judgment that the Cultural Revolution was catastrophic, though it did not indict Mao personally to the same degree. The judgment remains formal party doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_on_Certain_Questions_in_the_History_of_Our_Party_since_the_Founding_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China.

question: A leading figure of 21st-century Chinese politics grew up during the Cultural Revolution as the son of a purged party elder -- Xi Zhongxun -- and was himself sent down to the countryside as a boy. Who is that current leader?
context: Xi Jinping, born 1953, spent years in a rural Shaanxi village during the Cultural Revolution after his father Xi Zhongxun was purged. He became General Secretary of the CPC in 2012 and President in 2013. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping.

question: In the early 1990s a mailing-list movement of cryptographers and privacy advocates coalesced in the San Francisco Bay Area, dedicated to building working software that would give ordinary people privacy the state could not take away. What name did this movement take?
context: The name -- a pun on 'cipher' and 'cyberpunk' -- was coined by hacker Jude Milhon at an early meeting hosted by Eric Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore. The FSF (founded 1985 by Stallman) and EFF (founded 1990 by Kapor and Barlow) were older sibling movements; CCC is the German hacker collective. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: In 1989 an American cryptographer -- often called the father of digital cash -- founded an Amsterdam company to commercialize his invention of blind signatures, an anonymous digital-money technology. Which cypherpunk-era company did he build?
context: David Chaum founded DigiCash in Amsterdam in 1989 to license his 1982 blind-signatures work as an anonymous digital cash system. PayPal (1998, Confinity) was e-mail money for eBay; Silk Road (2011) was a Tor darknet market; Coinbase (2012) is a modern Bitcoin exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: In November 1998 a Chinese-American cryptographer, active on the cypherpunk mailing list and author of the Crypto++ library, posted a two-page proposal describing a decentralized digital cash where every user maintains their own copy of the ledger. What was the proposal called?
context: Wei Dai posted 'b-money' to the cypherpunk list in November 1998.
