Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman'; Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: The Statement of Aims signed on 8 April 1947 opened not with a policy but with an alarm: over large stretches of the Earth's surface, it said, three things were already threatened. Two of them were individual liberty and human cooperation by voluntary agreement. What was the third?
context: The Statement of Aims warned that 'the central values of civilization are in danger,' naming individual liberty, human cooperation by voluntary agreement, and private property, 'together with the institutions necessary to maintain these.' It went on to blame a decline of belief in private property and the rule of law. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: The ten days at Mont Pelerin in 1947 came to 18,062.08 Swiss francs, and 93 per cent of that bill was settled not by the scholars, nor by their universities, nor by any of the American foundations that chipped in, but by one institution alone. What kind of institution paid the overwhelming share?
context: The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt -- today Credit Suisse -- paid 93 per cent of the conference costs. Smaller sums came from the William Volker Fund via Harold Luhnow, from the Bank of England via Alfred Suenson-Taylor, and from the Foundation for Economic Education. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society', citing Mirowski and Plehwe (2009), p. 15.

question: In 1950 Friedrich Hayek left the London School of Economics for the University of Chicago, where Milton Friedman had been teaching since 1946. For the twelve years that followed the two men worked on the same campus -- yet Hayek never held a post in Friedman's department. Where at Chicago was Hayek appointed?
context: Hayek was Professor of Social and Moral Science on the Committee on Social Thought from 1950 to 1962 -- an interdisciplinary body, not the Economics Department -- and his salary was funded in part by outside grants including the Volker Fund. Aaron Director, another Mont Pelerin founder, was the one at the Law School. Source: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Milton Friedman's 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics' held that a theory earns its keep by the accuracy of its predictions, however unrealistic its assumptions may look. Friedrich Hayek would not accept that test for his subject, and spent decades saying why. What was Hayek's objection to it?
answer: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
choices: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
That predictions in economics can never be made short-run enough
That an economist's assumptions matter more than any test can show
That economics should be studied as a branch of law and history
context: Hayek attacked what he called scientism in The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) and returned to it in his 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretence of Knowledge': an economics that counts only what it can count will quietly drop the dispersed, local, tacit knowledge that makes markets work at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Milton Friedman wrote the introduction to the fiftieth-anniversary edition of Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom, and admired the man for half a century. On one piece of Hayek's economics he was blunt to the point of rudeness, and said so in print more than once. Which part of Hayek's work did Friedman call false?
answer: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
choices: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
Hayek's account of how prices carry information
Hayek's account of how legal rules evolve
Hayek's account of how planning erodes liberty
context: 'The Hayek-Mises explanation of the business cycle is contradicted by the evidence. It is, I believe, false.' Friedman first pressed the objection in a 1964 NBER article and again in Economic Inquiry in 1993, examining U.S. cycles from 1879 to 1988 and finding no significant link between the length of an expansion and the severity of the contraction after it. Source: Mark Skousen, 'Economics on Trial', The Freeman (FEE), March 1, 1995.

question: Both men wanted money taken out of politicians' hands, and each published an answer. Milton Friedman's, set out in 1959, was a rule for the central bank: raise the money supply by a fixed few per cent a year and stop meddling. Friedrich Hayek's answer of 1976 was more radical still. What did Hayek propose?
answer: Letting private banks compete to issue currencies
choices: Letting private banks compete to issue currencies
Fixing the currency's value to a basket of goods
Returning the currency to a gold coin standard
Handing note issue to an international authority
context: Friedman's k-percent rule appeared in A Program for Monetary Stability (1959): fix money growth at roughly 3 to 5 per cent a year. Hayek's Denationalisation of Money (1976) would not tie the monopoly down but abolish it, letting users walk away from any currency being debased. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Milton Friedman'; Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Friedrich Hayek took the economics Nobel in 1974 and Milton Friedman in 1976 -- two men who had sat in the same Swiss hotel twenty-seven years earlier. But 1974 was no victory lap: the committee split that year's prize, and the man who shared it had spent his career arguing for the very planning Hayek attacked. Who shared Hayek's prize?
context: The 1974 prize went jointly to Hayek and the Swedish social-democrat Gunnar Myrdal 'for their pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations and for their penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena.' Tinbergen won in 1969, Kuznets in 1971, Leontief in 1973. Eight Mont Pelerin members have taken the prize in all: Hayek, Friedman, Stigler, Allais, Buchanan, Coase, Becker and Vernon Smith. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: On January 3, 2009, an unknown developer using the name Satoshi Nakamoto mined the first block of the Bitcoin block chain on his own computer. What is that first block conventionally called?
context: The first block is 'the genesis block' or 'Block 0'; it was mined January 3, 2009. 'Coinbase' names the special transaction inside each block that mints new coins to the miner; the halving is a recurring reward-cut event; SegWit was a 2017 protocol upgrade. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: The genesis block that Satoshi mined on January 3, 2009 rewarded him with 50 BTC sent to a Bitcoin address. Because of a quirk in Satoshi's original code, that particular 50-BTC reward has one strange property. What can never happen to it?
answer: it can never be spent or moved to another address
choices: it can never be spent or moved to another address
it can never be seen by other nodes
it can never be used as a mining reward
it can never be counted in the total supply
context: By a quirk of the original code, the genesis-block coinbase output was written such that it is unspendable -- the 50 BTC exists in the chain but can never be moved. Every full node sees it; miners still get later rewards; supply totals do include it. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Inside the coinbase transaction of the genesis block -- the first transaction of the whole Bitcoin chain -- Satoshi embedded a short line of text that had no technical purpose. It was a message meant to be read. What did that message quote?
answer: a January 3, 2009 headline from The Times of London
choices: a January 3, 2009 headline from The Times of London
a Bible verse from the book of Revelation
a passage from Ayn Rand's Atlas Shrugged
context: The embedded text reads 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' -- the actual front-page headline of the London Times that day. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: The exact newspaper headline Satoshi encoded in the January 3, 2009 genesis block described a political action against a specific institution. Which subject did the headline address?
answer: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
choices: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates
the European Central Bank launching the euro
the Bank of Japan announcing quantitative easing
context: The Times, January 3, 2009 front page: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' referred to Alistair Darling, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, preparing to rescue major British banks a second time following the 2008 financial crisis. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Times archive.

question: The Times headline Satoshi embedded in the genesis block was doing two jobs at once. The first was cryptographic: because the block hash includes that text, the block could not possibly have been mined earlier than the day the headline was printed. What was that first function called?
answer: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
choices: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
an encryption key preventing later modification
a signature identifying Satoshi's private key
context: Including a January 3, 2009 headline proves the block could not have been mined earlier -- the same trick newspaper hostages hold up dated papers to prove the video is current. The Bitcoin protocol has separate difficulty and signature machinery. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: The second job the embedded Times headline was doing was political. Alongside timestamping, the headline choice sent a specific message about what Bitcoin was launching in opposition to. Which stance does the community read into Satoshi's choice of that headline?
answer: a direct protest against the 2008-09 bank-bailout culture
choices: a direct protest against the 2008-09 bank-bailout culture
a celebration of British monetary tradition
a warning about Chinese currency manipulation
an endorsement of European monetary union
context: The headline referenced a second bailout of failing UK banks weeks after the first; embedding it in Bitcoin's founding block was widely read as naming the political enemy: a monetary system in which banks fail and the state prints to rescue them. The other options are not supported by the text. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: After mining the genesis block on January 3, 2009, Satoshi did not immediately mine block 1. He paused, presumably to check that the software actually worked as designed on a live network. Roughly how long was the gap before Block 1 appeared?
context: Block 0 was mined January 3, 2009; Block 1 was mined January 9, 2009 -- a gap of about six days. From that point on, blocks arrived on roughly the ten-minute schedule that has held ever since. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Bitcoin block chain.

question: No previous currency in modern history has launched with a message quoting a specific news headline about the ruling political class embedded permanently into its founding document. Which comparison do Bitcoin writers most often use for the role that embedded Times headline plays in Bitcoin's history?
answer: a declaration of independence naming the adversary in one sentence
choices: a declaration of independence naming the adversary in one sentence
a corporate mission statement filed with regulators
a monetary policy target set by a central bank
an academic dedication to a favorite teacher
context: The comparison in the Bitcoin literature (Ammous, Antonopoulos, Song, others) is to a declaration of independence: an act that both timestamps itself and names its adversary explicitly. No corporate filing, central-bank target, or academic dedication had ever served that purpose in a monetary system. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) chapter on Bitcoin.

question: The 50-BTC reward Satoshi minted to himself in the January 3, 2009 genesis block, because of the code quirk that makes it unspendable, has one specific consequence for Bitcoin's aggregate supply. What effect does that quirk have on the coins that will ever actually circulate?
answer: it permanently removes 50 BTC from the effective circulating supply
choices: it permanently removes 50 BTC from the effective circulating supply
it doubles the block reward of the next block
it delays the first halving by 210,000 blocks
it lowers the 21-million supply cap by 50 BTC
context: The 50 BTC of the genesis reward can never be moved, so the coins nominally exist in the chain but can never enter circulation. The supply cap arithmetic is not adjusted (21M is a mathematical limit from halving geometry); block-reward and halving schedule are unchanged. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Austrians who write about Bitcoin as a monetary innovation often press one specific reasoning move about what the embedded Times headline signals a monetary system CAN do that fiat systems structurally cannot. Which move does the argument make?
answer: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule at issuance and refuse the political discretion to rescue any subsequent bank failure
choices: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule at issuance and refuse the political discretion to rescue any subsequent bank failure
That a monetary system can be democratically voted into and out of existence each cycle
That a monetary system's founder must remain publicly known to legitimize it
That a monetary system requires state backing to be trusted
context: The genesis-headline argument (Ammous, Song, Antonopoulos) is a rules-vs-discretion move: Bitcoin binds itself at issuance to a fixed schedule with no bailout discretion. Democratic overturning, publicly-known founder, and state backing are precisely what Bitcoin does NOT rely on. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: From 1958 to 1962 Mao Zedong drove the People's Republic of China through a crash campaign of forced agricultural collectivization plus small-scale rural industrialization. What was the campaign called?
context: The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) was Mao's attempt to overtake Britain in steel output within 15 years through people's communes and backyard industrial furnaces. It produced the deadliest famine in history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward.

question: The Great Leap Forward organized rural Chinese into massive agricultural units of thousands of households each. What were these units called?
context: People's communes of 5,000 households or more replaced smaller cooperatives in 1958. Private plots, tools, and cookware were absorbed. The commune was both economic unit and local government. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_commune.

question: The Great Leap's industrial-side gimmick asked peasants to melt down their own cookware, farm tools, and door hinges to hit district steel quotas. What were these village-scale kilns called?
context: Backyard furnaces (tulufeng) produced mostly unusable pig iron. The destruction of farm implements happened exactly as collectives needed them for the harvest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward.

question: The Great Leap's agricultural side rested on state-endorsed pseudoscience borrowed from a Soviet biologist who had rejected Mendelian genetics. Whose ideas produced the disastrous 'close planting' and 'deep plowing' techniques?
context: Lysenko's rejection of Mendelian genetics had been imposed on Soviet agriculture by Stalin. Chinese agriculture adopted Lysenkoist close-planting and deep-plowing techniques during the Great Leap, with disastrous results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysenkoism.

question: Grain reports from Chinese communes to Beijing during the Great Leap were systematically inflated because commune officials feared reporting shortfalls. What did the state do with the reported 'surplus' grain?
answer: Exported it to earn foreign currency
choices: Exported it to earn foreign currency
Distributed it back to the communes
context: Beijing exported grain based on the inflated commune reports, drawing on 'reserves' that did not exist. This continued as village granaries emptied and peasants starved. Source: Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (2008).

question: At the July-August 1959 Lushan Conference a specific People's Liberation Army marshal wrote Mao a private letter criticizing the Great Leap's failures. Which marshal?
context: Peng Dehuai's private letter at Lushan warned of the campaign's failure. Mao circulated it publicly, had Peng denounced and purged; Peng was later beaten to death during the Cultural Revolution. The moment Mao chose to defend the campaign over fixing it cost tens of millions more deaths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Dehuai.

question: The 2008 scholarly volume that gave the most-cited modern figure of about 36 million famine dead -- based on provincial-level Chinese archives -- was written by a Chinese journalist. What is its English title?
context: Yang Jisheng's Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962 was first published in Hong Kong in 2008; the English edition (FSG) appeared in 2012. Yang was a longtime Xinhua journalist who accessed provincial archives across China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tombstone_(book).

question: A 2010 scholarly volume by a Dutch historian, using more provincial archives, argued for the upper end of Great Leap famine death estimates at roughly 45 million. Who wrote 'Mao's Great Famine'?
context: Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine (Bloomsbury, 2010) drew on party archives to argue for a 45-million total. It won the Samuel Johnson Prize for non-fiction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao%27s_Great_Famine.

question: Estimates for Great Leap Forward excess deaths span a wide range depending on demographic method. What is the standard scholarly range across the leading recent studies?
context: Yang Jisheng estimates ~36 million; Dikotter ~45 million; Jasper Becker's Hungry Ghosts (1996) synthesized earlier work in a 15-30 million range. The lower bound is ~15M, the upper ~45M. Source: aggregation of Yang, Dikotter, Becker.

question: For Ludwig von Mises's 1920 calculation argument, the Great Leap Forward is the largest single vindication in history. What mechanism did it demonstrate?
answer: Without market prices there was no signal that the commune grain reports were fantasy until the granaries were empty
choices: Without market prices there was no signal that the commune grain reports were fantasy until the granaries were empty
Without market prices industrial planning was more efficient than under capitalism
Without market prices agricultural output naturally rose
Without market prices international trade solved local shortages
context: Mises's 1920 argument at the largest possible scale: no market prices meant no way to correct commune-level lies about production before the empty stomachs did the correcting. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The Great Leap was formally ended in January 1961; the more moderate party leadership then ran a partial retreat 1961-65 that Mao would answer with the Cultural Revolution five years later. Who ran that partial retreat?
context: Liu Shaoqi (as state president) and Deng Xiaoping led the 1961-65 recovery, restoring some private plots and market allocation. Mao's answer was the 1966 Cultural Revolution, which purged both. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931976).

question: Stalin's peak mass-execution wave from mid-1937 through late 1938 is remembered by an English name and a Russian personal name (after the NKVD chief). What is the English name for this campaign?
context: The Great Terror (Bolshoy terror), July 1937 - November 1938, executed about 750,000 people in 18 months. Also called the Yezhovshchina after NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge.

question: The Great Terror is sometimes named after the head of the NKVD who ran it from 1936 to 1938 (as a Russian personal adjective). What was his surname?
context: Nikolai Yezhov ran the NKVD 1936-38. He was replaced by Lavrentiy Beria in November 1938, arrested in April 1939, and shot on February 4, 1940. His name was erased from photographs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Yezhov.

question: On July 30, 1937 the NKVD issued a specific numbered order giving every regional office quotas for executions and Gulag sentences. What number is the order known by?
context: NKVD Order 00447 (July 30, 1937) established 'first category' (execution) and 'second category' (10-year camp) quotas by region. Local officers were rewarded for exceeding the quota. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NKVD_Order_No._00447.

question: Post-1991 archive access gave the definitive figure for the Great Terror's 18 months. Roughly how many people did the NKVD shoot between July 1937 and November 1938?
context: About 750,000 shot -- roughly 1,000 per day for 18 months. About 1.5 million total were arrested. Figures are from opened NKVD archives after 1991. Source: memo.ru (Memorial archives).

question: The Great Terror included a series of Moscow Show Trials that destroyed the surviving Old Bolsheviks who had made the 1917 Revolution. Which Bolshevik -- called by Lenin the 'darling of the party' -- was tried and shot in March 1938?
context: Bukharin was tried in the March 1938 Trial of the Twenty-One and shot. He had been Lenin's designated 'darling of the party'. Trotsky had already been exiled (1929) and was assassinated in Mexico in 1940. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_the_Twenty-One.

question: The 1968 pioneering Western scholarly account of Stalin's purges, treated with academic-left disdain at publication and wholly vindicated by the archives that opened after 1991, was written by a British-American historian. Who wrote 'The Great Terror'?
context: Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (Macmillan, 1968) was the pioneering account. A 1990 revised edition (Oxford UP) folded in the archival numbers. Conquest reportedly suggested titling the new edition 'I Told You So, You Fucking Fools'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Conquest.

question: The Great Terror deliberately targeted the Red Army officer corps in 1937-38, weakening the Soviet military just before World War II. Of the five Marshals of the Soviet Union, how many were shot?
context: Three of five marshals (Tukhachevsky, Blyukher, Yegorov) were shot; also 13 of 15 army commanders, 8 of 9 fleet admirals, and roughly half the officer corps. The Red Army was still recovering when Germany invaded in June 1941. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_of_Trotskyist_Anti-Soviet_Military_Organization.

question: Yezhov himself was executed by his successor's NKVD in early 1940 -- the standard fate of the enforcer once his campaign had done its work. Who replaced Yezhov and oversaw his execution?
context: Beria replaced Yezhov in November 1938 and ran the NKVD (later MVD) through Stalin's death in 1953. Beria himself was arrested and shot in December 1953. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria.

question: The Great Terror also included ethnic-targeted operations within the wider campaign, killing disproportionately in specific border-nation communities. Which ethnic 'operation' was among the deadliest per capita?
context: NKVD Order 00485 (August 11, 1937) targeted ethnic Poles across the USSR. About 111,000 were shot in the Polish Operation. Similar orders targeted Germans, Latvians, Greeks, and other border-nation communities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Operation_of_the_NKVD.

question: Timothy Snyder's 2010 scholarly work integrating the Great Terror with the parallel Nazi killings of the same period is now the standard integrated account of the two regimes' crimes. What is its title?
context: Bloodlands: Europe Between Hitler and Stalin (Basic Books, 2010) covers the 14 million civilians deliberately killed in the region between 1933 and 1945. It won the 2013 Hannah Arendt Prize. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodlands.

question: When Bitcoin launched on January 3, 2009, every time a miner successfully added a new block to the chain they were rewarded with a fixed number of newly created bitcoins. What was that initial per-block reward?
context: The initial block reward was 50 BTC per block. 25 BTC was the reward after the first halving in 2012; 6.25 BTC applied 2020-24; 1 BTC has never been a block-reward value. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Satoshi wrote a rule into the original Bitcoin code that cuts the per-block reward in half after a fixed number of blocks have been mined. What is this scheduled event called in the community?
context: 'The halving' (early forum slang 'halvening') is the scheduled event that cuts the block reward in half. A fork is a protocol change or chain split; an airdrop is a token giveaway on other networks; a burn is destroying tokens by sending them to an unspendable address. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin's halving is not calendar-based but block-based: it happens after a specific fixed number of blocks have been mined. Because Bitcoin targets one block roughly every ten minutes, that block interval works out to roughly one halving every four years. How many blocks separate one halving from the next?
context: The halving happens every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years at ~10-minute block times). Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin's first halving arrived roughly four years after launch and dropped the block reward from 50 BTC down to 25 BTC. In which month did the first halving occur?
context: The first halving cut the reward from 50 BTC to 25 BTC in November 2012. The second (25 -> 12.5) came July 2016; the third (12.5 -> 6.25) May 2020; the fourth (6.25 -> 3.125) April 2024. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: After the fourth halving in April 2024, the block reward that Bitcoin miners collect for adding a valid block dropped from 6.25 BTC to what new value?
context: The April 2024 halving cut the reward to 3.125 BTC per block. The 2028 halving is expected to cut it to 1.5625 BTC. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Because each halving cuts issuance in half, the total number of bitcoins that will ever be created converges on a specific mathematical limit -- the number that the code has enforced from day one. What is Bitcoin's ultimate total supply cap?
context: The geometric halving series sums to 21 million BTC -- the fixed hard cap, expected to be effectively reached around 2140. After that miners earn only transaction fees, not new coins. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: The smallest denomination of Bitcoin -- named for its inventor -- is one hundred-millionth of a whole bitcoin. What is this smallest unit called?
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC (10^-8 BTC), named for Satoshi Nakamoto. 'Bit' and 'millibit' are informal larger sub-units (1 bit = 100 satoshis); 'wei' is Ethereum's smallest unit, named for cypherpunk Wei Dai, not a Bitcoin unit. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Units.

question: The halving cascade is written to end at the 21-million cap not by an executive decision but by the arithmetic of the geometric series itself. Around which future year is that final coin scheduled to be mined?
context: The geometric issuance schedule -- 50 -> 25 -> 12.5 -> ... -- exhausts at approximately the year 2140 assuming the ~10-minute average block time holds. From that point on miners are compensated only by transaction fees. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Milton Friedman spent his career pressing a single-sentence view on what causes persistent inflation: expand the supply of money faster than the supply of goods, and prices must rise. Bitcoin's 21-million cap is the sharpest possible engineering answer to that view. Which specific property of the cap makes it structurally different from any prior monetary regime?
answer: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
choices: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
the cap doubles automatically whenever the block-time drifts
the cap adjusts based on global GDP growth
the cap is set by an annual vote of Bitcoin holders
context: The 21M cap is enforced by every node's software; raising it would require every user to accept a protocol change that would fork Bitcoin. It cannot be adjusted for GDP, drift, or voter preference. Every fiat central bank has discretion to expand; Bitcoin has none. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: The Keynesian tradition and the Austrian tradition disagree about whether a fixed supply cap is a monetary virtue or a monetary flaw. Austrian sound-money advocates point to Friedman's line about inflation to argue the cap is a virtue; Keynesian aggregate-demand advocates argue it is a flaw. Which specific Keynesian objection do critics of a fixed cap most often press?
answer: That a truly fixed supply forces the general price level to adjust downward during a recession, worsening debt burdens
choices: That a truly fixed supply forces the general price level to adjust downward during a recession, worsening debt burdens
That a fixed supply automatically triggers hyperinflation whenever velocity falls
That a fixed supply cannot be divided into small enough units for retail commerce
That a fixed supply requires a central bank to enforce it
context: The standard Keynesian critique -- Krugman, DeLong, Summers -- is that a fixed-supply currency has no elastic response to demand shocks, so nominal prices and wages must fall (Fisher's debt-deflation). Hyperinflation is by definition monetary expansion, not fixed supply; Bitcoin divides to 10^-8; a fixed cap is what removes any need for a central issuer. Source: Ammous vs Krugman debates; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_deflation.

question: In August 1931 the London School of Economics journal Economica published a long two-part review essay by a young Austrian economist attacking a book Cambridge's most famous economist had just published in 1930. Which two economists were the review's author and its target?
answer: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
choices: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
Ludwig von Mises reviewing Alfred Marshall
context: Hayek published Part I of his review of Keynes's A Treatise on Money (1930) in the August 1931 issue of Economica; Keynes replied and Hayek rejoined in November 1931; Hayek's Part II appeared in February 1932. Source: The Coolidge Review, 'Why the Keynes-Hayek Clash Endures' (https://www.coolidgereview.com/articles/keynes-hayek-debate-endures).

question: The famous 1931-1932 review exchange between F. A. Hayek at LSE and John Maynard Keynes at Cambridge appeared in the pages of ONE journal, run out of LSE. Which journal ran the exchange?
context: Economica was the LSE journal that ran the Hayek review, Keynes's reply, and Hayek's rejoinder across four issues from August 1931 to February 1932. Keynes's own Cambridge-based Economic Journal ran a separate front in the debate (Sraffa's 1932 review of Hayek). Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: F. A. Hayek's 1931 Economica review of Keynes's Treatise on Money was a ferocious paragraph-by-paragraph technical attack. Hayek's headline charge was that Keynes had built a monetary theory disconnected from capital theory and had ignored an older continental school. Which school did Hayek accuse Keynes of ignoring?
answer: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
choices: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
The Marshall-Pigou tradition on partial equilibrium welfare economics
The Marx-Engels tradition on the falling rate of profit
The Walras-Pareto tradition on general equilibrium mathematics
context: Hayek's central technical charge against Keynes's Treatise was that Keynes had a monetary theory disconnected from capital theory and had ignored the continental (Knut Wicksell in Sweden, Ludwig von Mises in Vienna) tradition on the natural rate of interest -- the foundation Hayek's own business-cycle theory was built on. Source: Mises Institute, Hayek's 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J. M. Keynes.'

question: When John Maynard Keynes replied to F. A. Hayek's 1931 Economica review of his Treatise on Money, he mostly refused to answer Hayek's technical points. Instead he pivoted to attack Hayek's OWN 1931 book on business cycles, calling it 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read.' Which book of Hayek's was Keynes attacking?
choices: Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle
context: Keynes wrote that Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) was 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read' and 'an extraordinary example of how, starting with a mistake, a remorseless logician can end up in Bedlam.' Keynes's move -- attack the OTHER book rather than defend his own -- became famous for its aggression. Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: In 1932 John Maynard Keynes, as editor of Cambridge's Economic Journal, opened a second front against Hayek by commissioning a Cambridge colleague to review Hayek's Prices and Production. The reviewer's attack on Hayek's concept of a single natural rate of interest is credited with turning professional opinion against Hayek's business-cycle theory. Who was the Cambridge reviewer Keynes enlisted?
context: Piero Sraffa was an Italian-born Cambridge economist and a Keynes ally. His hostile 1932 review argued that without money there is a MULTIPLICITY of commodity own-rates and no unique natural rate of interest can be identified -- the concept of the 'own-rate of interest' was introduced (unnamed) in that review. Hayek replied in the Economic Journal in June 1932 with 'Money and Capital: A Reply to Mr. Sraffa.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Sraffa-Hayek debate' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sraffa%E2%80%93Hayek_debate).

question: In the 1930s a single professional rivalry dominated British economics: Keynes and his students on one side, Hayek and Lionel Robbins on the other, each side working out of a different university. Which two British universities framed the 1930s Keynes-vs-Hayek clash?
answer: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
choices: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
Oxford and the London School of Economics
context: Keynes was at King's College, Cambridge; Hayek had arrived at the London School of Economics on Houghton Street in 1931. The 1930s Cambridge-vs-LSE feud framed the whole landscape of British economics until the war. Source: Adam Smith Institute review, 'Keynes Hayek: The Clash That Defined Modern Economics' (https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/thinkpieces/review-keynes-hayek-the-clash-that-defined-modern-economics).

question: In 1936 John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money -- the book that would reshape twentieth-century macroeconomics. F. A. Hayek, Keynes's most technical Austrian critic, made a choice about the General Theory that he later called one of the great professional regrets of his life. What did Hayek do?
answer: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
choices: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
He wrote a hostile Economica review that Keynes never answered
He co-authored a rebuttal book with Ludwig von Mises
He challenged Keynes to a public debate at Cambridge
context: Hayek chose not to review the General Theory in 1936. He gave several reasons later, including that Keynes was notorious for changing his mind, so Hayek expected the position would soon be revised again; by the time it was clear Keynes was serious, the Keynesian revolution had swept the profession with no serious Austrian rebuttal in print for a generation. Source: Bruce Caldwell, 'Why Didn't Hayek Review Keynes's General Theory?' Duke University (https://public.econ.duke.edu/~bjc18/docs/Why%20Didn't%20Hayek%20Review%20General%20Theory.pdf).

question: F. A. Hayek later gave a specific reason for not reviewing Keynes's 1936 General Theory: he had watched Keynes revise his positions before and expected another revision was coming. Which recurring habit of Keynes did Hayek cite?
answer: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
choices: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
Keynes refused to engage in print with any Austrian economist
Keynes had privately told Hayek the General Theory was a joke
Keynes had already promised a full retraction in a coming article
context: Hayek said in interviews that Keynes had a well-known propensity to change his positions, so writing a long technical review of one Keynes book seemed likely to be answered by yet another Keynes book that revised everything -- as had partly happened with the Treatise on Money after Hayek's 1931 review. Source: Caldwell, Duke University essay.

question: The 1931-1932 Hayek and Keynes review essays, later correspondence between the two men, and Piero Sraffa's 1932 attack were collected together and published as one volume of the University of Chicago Press's Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. Bruce Caldwell edited the collection in 1995 under a pointed title. What is the volume titled?
choices: Studies in Philosophy Politics and Economics
context: Contra Keynes and Cambridge, edited by Bruce Caldwell, was published in 1995 as Volume 9 of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. Its three parts cover Hayek's 1930s arrival at LSE, the direct exchanges with Keynes and Sraffa, and later essays -- including Hayek's previously unpublished 1963 memoir 'The Economics of the 1930s as Seen from London.' Source: University of Chicago Press catalog (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo3614356.html).

question: F. A. Hayek and John Maynard Keynes fought a bitter public argument in the pages of Economica in 1931-1932, but their personal relationship stayed cordial. When the London School of Economics was evacuated to Cambridge during the Blitz, Keynes personally helped Hayek find accommodation at ONE Cambridge college -- his own -- and even shared fire-watch duty with Hayek on its roof. Which college?
context: Keynes was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge; when LSE was evacuated to Cambridge in 1940, Keynes found Hayek a place at King's and Hayek's son Laurence a place at King's College School. Hayek and Keynes shared night fire-watch duty on the King's chapel roofs, and Hayek later called the wartime Cambridge hospitality one of the pleasantest memories of his life -- a striking coda to the 1931-1932 attack in Economica. Source: University of Cambridge Alumni magazine, 'City of refuge' (https://www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/magazine/issue-98/city-of-refuge).

question: A Ukrainian word meaning 'death by hunger' is now used specifically for the famine Stalin's grain-requisition policy inflicted on Soviet Ukraine in 1932-33. What is that word?
context: Holodomor combines the Ukrainian holod (hunger) and mor (mortality, plague). It is used specifically for the 1932-33 famine as a policy-driven catastrophe distinct from natural crop failure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: The Holodomor was not a natural harvest failure -- the state deliberately set an unfillable requisition target and sent brigades to search peasant houses. What did the brigades take?
answer: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
choices: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
Only what was above household needs
context: Requisition brigades searched houses and took stored food, cured meat, and seed grain. Peasants with no reserves and no seed for next year starved by early 1933. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: On January 22, 1933 Stalin and Molotov personally signed an order sealing the borders of Ukraine and the Kuban so starving peasants could not leave to buy food elsewhere in the USSR. What did the order do to those who tried to leave?
answer: They were turned back or arrested
choices: They were turned back or arrested
They received travel permits and rations
They were resettled in Siberia with food
They were allowed passage but taxed heavily
context: The January 22, 1933 order sealed Ukraine and the Kuban internally, stopping the peasant escape that had helped during earlier famines. It converted a policy-caused shortage into a policy-caused mass death. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: Ukrainian rural settlements that failed their grain quotas were placed on a specific state list -- with all trade cut off, remaining reserves confiscated, and residents not allowed to leave. What were these communities called?
context: 'Blacklisted villages' (chorna doshka villages) were targeted for full economic isolation and starvation. Signs marked the boundaries. The mechanism killed by community, not by household. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: Scholarly death-toll estimates for the Holodomor by Ukrainian and Western historians using post-1991 archives cluster in a specific range. What is the standard range?
context: Most peer-reviewed studies (Snyder's Bloodlands 2010, Ukrainian government 2008 study, Andriewsky, Graziosi) cluster at 3.5-5 million; the upper bound reaches ~7.5 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: In November 2006 Ukraine's parliament formally recognized the Holodomor as a specific legal category of state crime. What did the Verkhovna Rada declare it to be?
context: The Verkhovna Rada's November 28, 2006 law recognized the Holodomor as a genocide of the Ukrainian people. The European Parliament followed with a similar resolution in December 2022 during Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor_genocide_question.

question: The first major Western scholarly account of the Holodomor was published by Oxford University Press in 1986. What was its title?
context: Robert Conquest's The Harvest of Sorrow: Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine (Oxford UP, 1986) was the first major Western scholarly synthesis. It was funded partly by the Ukrainian diaspora and treated with skepticism by academic sovietology until the archives opened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvest_of_Sorrow.

question: A 2017 scholarly account of the Holodomor by an American journalist-historian using newly opened Ukrainian and Russian archives is the current standard modern reference. Who wrote 'Red Famine'?
context: Anne Applebaum's Red Famine: Stalin's War on Ukraine (Doubleday, 2017) is the standard modern reference. Serhii Plokhy's The Man with the Poison Gun and other work cover adjacent Ukrainian history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Famine.

question: The parallel 1932-33 famine in Soviet Kazakhstan, produced by forced collectivization of nomadic herds, is called Asharshylyk. Roughly what proportion of the ethnic Kazakh population died?
context: About 1.5 million Kazakhs died (roughly 40% of the ethnic Kazakh population). The famine transformed Kazakhstan's demographic balance for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakh_famine_of_1930%E2%80%931933.

question: The Holodomor's core mechanism was distinct from a natural famine. Which best describes the policy mechanism that turned crop shortfall into mass death?
answer: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
choices: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
An early frost combined with a locust plague
A blockade by Western powers restricting food imports
A Ukrainian nationalist boycott of Soviet economic institutions
context: The three-step policy mechanism -- impossible quotas, sealed borders, blacklisting -- converted a policy-induced shortage into targeted mass death. This is what distinguishes the Holodomor from natural famine. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: In December 2022, at a specific moment during Russia's invasion of Ukraine, another major European legislature formally recognized the Holodomor as a genocide. Which legislature followed Ukraine's 2006 recognition?
context: The European Parliament passed a December 15, 2022 resolution recognizing the Holodomor as genocide. The timing during Russia's invasion of Ukraine added political weight to the recognition. Source: europarl.europa.eu (2022/2988 RSP).

question: On April 17, 1975 a communist movement led by Pol Pot captured the capital of Cambodia and began a four-year rule of extreme social erasure. What was the movement called?
context: The Khmer Rouge (Communist Party of Kampuchea), led by Pol Pot (born Saloth Sar), captured Phnom Penh April 17, 1975. Their rule ended with a Vietnamese invasion in December 1978 - January 1979. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Rouge.

question: The Khmer Rouge declared their April 1975 victory the beginning of a new era in which history itself would restart from that day. What did they call this restart?
context: Year Zero meant every trace of the previous urban-professional society was to be erased. Money was abolished, the central bank building blown up, private property abolished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Zero_(political_notion).

question: Within 72 hours of capturing Phnom Penh, the Khmer Rouge did something unprecedented to the city's 2 million inhabitants. What did they do?
answer: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
choices: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
Confined them to reeducation blocks by street
Deported them by rail to Vietnam
context: Hospitals were emptied of patients, monasteries of monks, universities of professors -- all forced out on foot within days. This is the first act of the Year Zero policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Phnom_Penh.

question: The Khmer Rouge target category was extended to any Cambodian bearing marks of urban education. Wearing what item was enough to be marked for execution?
context: Wearing glasses marked a Cambodian as educated. Speaking French, having soft hands, or having worked in a profession similarly marked people for execution or death by forced labor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_genocide.

question: The central Khmer Rouge interrogation facility in Phnom Penh -- located in a former high school -- processed roughly 14,000-20,000 prisoners; only about a dozen are known to have survived. What was the facility called?
context: S-21, in a former Phnom Penh high school, was chief Kaing Guek Eav ('Duch')'s facility. The photographic and confession archive he kept became the evidence base for later trials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuol_Sleng_Genocide_Museum.

question: The trucked-in victims of the Khmer Rouge were killed at hundreds of execution sites, of which the largest and most photographed lies about 10 miles from Phnom Penh. What are these sites collectively called?
context: The Killing Fields at Choeung Ek is the most-visited memorial site. Hundreds of similar sites across Cambodia together hold the remains of roughly 1.5-2 million victims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_Fields.

question: Death-toll estimates for the Khmer Rouge's four-year rule (1975-79), out of a pre-1975 Cambodian population of about 7-8 million, make it proportionally the worst genocide of the 20th century. What is the standard range?
context: About 1.5-2 million Cambodians died -- roughly a fifth to a quarter of the entire population. Nazi Germany killed a smaller fraction of its own population than the Khmer Rouge killed of theirs. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: The Khmer Rouge leadership had been radicalized as students together in a specific European city in the early 1950s. Which capital produced Pol Pot, Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, and Son Sen?
context: The Cercle Marxiste-Leniniste in Paris in the early 1950s included Saloth Sar (later Pol Pot), Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, and Son Sen. They returned home with the pure-agrarian-utopia idea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Pot.

question: The Khmer Rouge regime fell to a specific foreign invasion in December 1978 - January 1979 -- a war between two communist regimes. Which country invaded Cambodia and ended the Khmer Rouge?
context: The Vietnamese invasion began December 25, 1978 and captured Phnom Penh on January 7, 1979. Vietnam installed the Kampuchean People's Republic and occupied the country until 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian%E2%80%93Vietnamese_War.

question: The chief of Khmer Rouge prison S-21 was convicted of crimes against humanity by a specific UN-backed tribunal in Cambodia in 2010. What was the tribunal called?
answer: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
choices: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
The International Criminal Tribunal for Cambodia
The Phnom Penh War Crimes Court
context: The ECCC (Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia) convicted Duch (Kaing Guek Eav) in July 2010 and later convicted senior leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan. Pol Pot died under house arrest in 1998 without trial. Source: eccc.gov.kh.

question: In August 1982, one of the biggest borrowing nations in the Western Hemisphere told the US Treasury it could no longer pay its foreign debts, opening a sovereign-debt crisis across an entire continent. Which country's default touched off the crisis?
context: Finance Minister Jesus Silva Herzog called the US Treasury on August 12, 1982 to say Mexico could not service its dollar debt. Brazil, Argentina, and others followed within months. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: Through the 1970s a leading US commercial bank chairman was famous for a confident line about the safety of lending to foreign governments -- a line he repeated in a 1982 New York Times op-ed just before the Latin American default cascade. What was the essence of Walter Wriston's line?
context: Walter Wriston, Citibank chairman 1967-84, argued sovereigns could always repay because they could tax and print. His September 1982 op-ed in the New York Times crystallized the doctrine -- just as the crisis was breaking. Source: nytimes.com Wriston 'Banking Against Disaster', September 14 1982.

question: The chair of the Federal Reserve whose 1979-81 rate hikes drove up interest costs on Latin American dollar debt was the same chair remembered for defeating US inflation. Who was he?
context: Volcker (Fed chair 1979-87) pushed the fed funds rate above 19 percent in 1981 to break US inflation. The rate spike also blew up dollar-denominated foreign loans across Latin America. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/anti-inflation-measures.

question: By 1982 the nine largest US commercial banks held Latin American loans equal to nearly what fraction of their combined equity, according to FDIC official history?
context: The FDIC's 'History of the Eighties' documents the exposure. Marked to market, several of the largest US banks would have been technically insolvent had the Latin American loans been written down at the time. Source: fdic.gov/bank/historical/history.

question: Rather than let the sovereign loans default in 1982, the Fed and IMF pressured banks into a strategy of keeping loans current while stretching out repayments. What did contemporaries call this coordinated approach?
context: 'Concerted lending' meant banks were pressured to keep extending fresh credit so that old loans could technically stay current. This bought time for bank balance sheets at the cost of years of Latin American recession. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: The 1980s in Latin America came to be summed up by a single dismal label reflecting ten years of stagnation, hyperinflation, and social upheaval across the region. What is the standard shorthand?
context: Per-capita GDP in Mexico did not regain 1981 levels until the mid-1990s. Inflation ran into the thousands of percent in Argentina, Brazil, and Peru during the 1980s. The World Bank and IDB use 'Lost Decade' as the standard term. Source: World Bank data.

question: In 1989 a Treasury Secretary under George H.W. Bush proposed a new instrument that let banks finally convert old sovereign loans into tradable, partially-collateralized bonds. What are those bonds now called?
context: Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady's 1989 plan converted the old loans into new tradable bonds partially backed by zero-coupon US Treasuries as collateral. This finally let banks acknowledge and market-price losses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: The Brady Plan's essential financial engineering used a specific type of US government security as collateral against the new sovereign bonds -- a security that pays no coupon and matures at face value. What was the collateral?
context: Countries bought long-dated US Treasury zeros with a portion of new-loan proceeds; the zeros' face value at maturity guaranteed the principal on the Brady bonds. This gave holders a hard collateral floor while letting the coupon on the sovereign portion trade at deep discount. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: From an Austrian and moral-hazard perspective, the 1980s Latin American workout is the archetype of a specific pattern -- who bore the concentrated cost, and who was spared the consequences of the original lending decision?
answer: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
choices: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
Latin American publics bore currency gains; US banks paid full losses
European banks bore the losses; US banks were untouched
The IMF absorbed the losses through direct grants
context: The Austrian reading: the workout socialized the costs of bad lending onto Latin American publics via the Lost Decade, while US bank creditors were rescued from the market discipline that would have failed several of them. This is the template that repeated in 1998, 2008, and 2010. Source: mises.org/library/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: The 1980s Latin American debt cycle drew its US banking exposure largely from a wave of aggressive foreign lending in the 1970s -- one Wriston-era Citibank policy in particular. Which foreign-currency lending practice made the crisis's damage so severe?
choices: Local-currency loans with fixed exchange rates
context: The Latin American loans were mostly dollar-denominated. When US rates spiked under Volcker, sovereign borrowers owed more dollars in interest than their export earnings could cover, and had no domestic monetary tool to help. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: In June 1850, six months before he died of tuberculosis in Rome, Frederic Bastiat sent to press a seventy-five-page political-economy pamphlet whose one-word French title is a single common noun. What was the pamphlet called, in English?
context: French original: La Loi. Published June 1850, six months before Bastiat's death in December; his most widely-read work in English by a wide margin. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Bastiat's 1850 pamphlet The Law names three pre-existing individual rights it says the law's legitimate function is to defend. Which three does he name?
choices: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
context: 'The law is the collective organization of the individual right to lawful defense.' Bastiat's triad is nearly Lockean; he says these three exist BEFORE any law and give the law its purpose. Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: In The Law Bastiat gives a two-word name to what happens when the law, instead of defending property, is used to take from some people and give to others. His French term is spoliation legale. What is it in English?
context: Bastiat's spoliation legale becomes 'legal plunder' in every standard English edition since Hodgson 1859; the term is Bastiat's own coinage for the phenomenon. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Bastiat's The Law offers a specific diagnostic test to determine whether a given statute is legal plunder. According to Bastiat, one asks whether the law does what?
answer: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
choices: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
Fails to secure a positive right to housing or employment for every citizen
Was passed by a majority smaller than two-thirds of the elected assembly
Diverges from the natural-law tradition articulated by medieval theologians
context: Bastiat's second test in the paragraph: 'See if the law benefits one citizen at the expense of another by doing what the citizen himself cannot do without committing a crime.' Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: In The Law Bastiat identifies two large categories of 1850 French policy as legal plunder. One is socialism (the National Workshops, guaranteed jobs, guaranteed credit). What is the other?
context: The two French policies Bastiat names as legal plunder: PROTECTIONISM (tariffs transferring wealth from consumers to sheltered producers) and SOCIALISM (transfers from taxpayers to National Workshop beneficiaries). Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Bastiat, in The Law, worries that once the law is regularly used to take from some and give to others, ordinary people stop distinguishing right from wrong and begin distinguishing legal from illegal. What word does he use for this effect on public morality?
context: Bastiat treats moral CORRUPTION as the largest unseen cost of legal plunder: legality replaces morality in the citizen's daily judgments. Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: The Law contains a single sentence that libertarian readers ever since have quoted like scripture, describing what the state becomes when legal plunder is systematic. Which sentence carries that line?
answer: The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else
choices: The state is the great fictitious entity by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else
Society exists for the benefit of its members and not the members for society
Politics is the art of the possible in an age of impossible expectations
The government is best which governs least, because the people discipline themselves
context: French: L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde. From Bastiat's 1848 essay 'The State' and echoed inside The Law. Source: bastiat.org/en/state.html.

question: Since 1950, The Law has been kept continuously in American print in a translation issued by the New York classical-liberal institute Leonard Read and Henry Hazlitt founded in 1946. Which institute publishes the standard American edition?
context: FEE (Irvington-on-Hudson) has issued The Law without a break since 1950; Cato (1977), the Mises Institute (1982), and Heritage (1973) came later. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: In his 2011 book Liberty Defined the former Texas congressman Ron Paul names one single economics-adjacent text as his most-recommended reading for anyone new to classical-liberal ideas. Which 1850 Bastiat pamphlet does Paul name?
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
context: Paul's Liberty Defined (2011) cites The Law as the single best entry point; the pamphlet is, by wide margin, the first Austrian-adjacent text most American libertarian teenagers ever read. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Defined.

question: For most of the 20th century, English readers of Frederic Bastiat depended on three incomplete translations from a single New York libertarian foundation -- Dean Russell's 1950 The Law, de Huszar's 1964 Selected Essays, Goddard's 1964 Economic Sophisms. Which foundation published these?
context: FEE was founded 1946 by Leonard Read in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Its editions were excellent for their day but covered only a fraction of Bastiat's actual output; most of his correspondence, journalism, and Assembly speeches had never been translated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Starting in the 2000s, an Indianapolis-based classical-liberal educational foundation (founded 1960 by Pierre F. Goodrich) undertook the first complete English edition of Frederic Bastiat's works. Which foundation?
context: Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat is projected to run to six volumes. Goodrich, an Indiana lawyer and businessman, endowed the foundation specifically to sustain the classical-liberal scholarly tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: The Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat is led by a specific general-editor team plus a distinct English editor who oversees the translations. Who is the English editor?
context: Hart works alongside general editors Jacques de Guenin and Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean. He also maintains the Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org), a free online archive of classical-liberal texts that includes all the Bastiat volumes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Volume 3 of the Liberty Fund Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat, published in 2017, contains what is arguably Bastiat's most famous essay -- his 1850 discussion of hidden versus visible economic consequences. What essay is included in Volume 3?
answer: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
choices: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
context: 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas' (1850). Volume 3 also contains the Economic Sophisms, Bastiat's satirical essays including the Petition of the Candlemakers demanding a law against the sun. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: The Liberty Fund edition of Bastiat differs from the older FEE translations in a specific set of scholarly apparatus that lets a modern reader place each essay in context. Which set of features is characteristic?
answer: Full introductions locating each essay in the French context, glossaries of French political figures, and modern translations restoring passages older editions had softened
choices: Full introductions locating each essay in the French context, glossaries of French political figures, and modern translations restoring passages older editions had softened
Chapter-by-chapter mathematical proofs of every argument
Adjacent Chinese translations for every French passage
A comic-book version of each essay for younger readers
context: The scholarly apparatus is what distinguishes a modern scholarly Collected Works from older enthusiast translations. The Liberty Fund edition provides tools for a serious 21st-century reader that the mid-century FEE editions could not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: David M. Hart, the Liberty Fund's English editor for the Bastiat Collected Works, has also built and maintained a free online resource that makes the whole Bastiat corpus (and hundreds of other classical-liberal texts) available at zero cost to any 21st-century reader with internet access. What is the resource called?
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute online archive
context: Any curious kid with internet access can now read every essay Bastiat ever wrote, in modern English, on a free website funded by a classical-liberal foundation. The tradition is being actively cultivated, not just preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Since 1998 the total dollars spent on US federal lobbying have roughly tripled in nominal terms and doubled in real terms. Approximately how much did federal lobbying cost in 2023, per OpenSecrets.org?
context: Federal lobbying spending grew from ~$1.44B in 1998 to ~$4.1B in 2023 per opensecrets.org (Center for Responsive Politics). Registered federal lobbyists number ~11,000-14,000. Source: opensecrets.org (Lobbying Data).

question: Gordon Tullock's 1967 Western Economic Journal paper introduced the concept later named 'rent-seeking' by Anne Krueger in 1974. In Tullock's framework, resources devoted to capturing government privileges -- lobbying, campaign spending, litigation for regulatory advantage -- are what specific kind of loss?
context: Tullock's move: resources burned in the competition for privilege produce no goods or services; they only reshuffle existing wealth. The whole rectangle of resources burned is deadweight loss to society. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (June 1967).

question: In 2023 the top-spending US industry on federal lobbying spent approximately $385 million. Which industry led the ranking?
context: Pharmaceuticals/health products led at ~$385M in 2023, followed by electronics manufacturing and equipment (~$228M) and insurance (~$164M). Source: opensecrets.org (Top Industries 2023).

question: The individual organization that has ranked as the largest single US federal lobbying spender in most recent years spent about $68 million in 2023. Which organization is it?
context: The US Chamber of Commerce has been the largest single-organization federal lobbying spender for most recent years -- ~$68M in 2023. National Association of Realtors (~$52M) and Meta Platforms (~$20M) round out the top individual spenders. Source: opensecrets.org (Top Organizations 2023).

question: The 2014 American Economic Review paper by Bertrand, Bombardini, and Trebbi took a specific empirical approach to distinguishing lobbying that works through information versus lobbying that works through connections. What was the paper's memorable title?
answer: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
choices: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
context: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi, 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? An Empirical Assessment of the Lobbying Process' (American Economic Review, December 2014). Answer: mostly whom. Source: aeaweb.org (Bertrand et al. 2014).

question: The market prices ex-Members of Congress and ex-senior congressional staff who move to lobbying at large multiples of their public-sector pay. Which range best captures the observed premium over government pay?
context: Ex-Members and ex-senior staffers who become lobbyists command salary premiums of ~500-1000% over their government pay, consistent with a market pricing their capture-value. Source: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi (2014); Blanes i Vidal + Draca + Fons-Rosen, American Economic Review (2012).

question: The federal statute passed in 1938 requires disclosure of lobbying on behalf of foreign governments and corporations to influence US public opinion and policy. What is its acronym?
context: The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), passed 1938, requires disclosure of foreign-government-directed lobbying. FARA disclosures in recent years total ~$500M/year, on top of the ~$4B/year in domestic-lobbying disclosure. Source: justice.gov/nsd-fara.

question: Washington DC has a physical geographic corridor whose name has become shorthand for the industry itself -- a specific downtown thoroughfare where many top lobbying firms and trade associations have offices. What street is that?
context: K Street NW in downtown Washington DC hosts many of the largest lobbying firms and trade associations. 'K Street' has become synonymous with the lobbying industry as an American shorthand. Source: Grokipedia 'K Street (Washington, D.C.)'.

question: Tullock's 1967 paper and the modern lobbying-industry aggregate data point to the same conclusion about how the $4B/year in federal lobbying is best characterized. Which sentence best captures the Tullock reading?
answer: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
choices: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
Money is spent purely to educate legislators about general policy tradeoffs
Money is spent on ceremonial political events with no material effect
Money is spent solely to comply with existing legal disclosures
context: Tullock's rent-seeking framework: $4B/year is not being spent to persuade Congress of general truths. It is being spent to capture concrete, industry-specific policy outcomes. The stated purpose (democratic participation) is not always false; the aggregate spending is not consistent with it either. Source: Tullock (1967); opensecrets.org.

question: The reasoning-move the lobbying-industry-aggregate case teaches is a diagnostic habit for any policy analyst evaluating a proposed complex, industry-specific statute. What should the default suspicion be?
answer: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
choices: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
The beneficiaries are always the retail voters who elected the sponsors
The statute is copied verbatim from a Nordic model
The statute was drafted overnight by a single ideologue
context: When a proposed statute is complex, industry-specific, and heavily lobbied, the Tullock-Olson default is that the concentrated organized interests are the primary beneficiaries. The First Amendment protects petition; the ladder analyzes the aggregate incentive structure. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: In 1871 a junior lecturer at the University of Vienna named Carl Menger published a slender book that founded a whole school of economics. Its central move was to reject the classical claim that value came from embodied labour or cost of production. What did Menger say value came from instead?
answer: The marginal utility of the next unit to a specific chooser
choices: The marginal utility of the next unit to a specific chooser
The average labour-time embodied in producing the good
The gold price of the raw materials used
The political power of the merchant class
context: Menger's Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre insisted that value is subjective, ranked by an individual chooser, and always applies to a specific additional unit rather than to a good as a class. That single move dissolved a hundred years of classical puzzles. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger and the Sesquicentennial Founding of the Austrian School'.

question: Carl Menger's 1871 marginalist book was published in German in Vienna. In the very same year, another economist in England published a book making essentially the same core argument. Who was he?
context: Jevons's The Theory of Political Economy appeared in London in 1871, the same year as Menger's Grundsaetze. Marshall would not publish his Principles until 1890; Mill and Senior belonged to the earlier classical generation. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: William Stanley Jevons had held a chair of political economy since 1866 at the university where he wrote his 1871 book, on the subjective 'final degree of utility' of an added unit. In which English city did he teach?
context: Jevons was Professor of Political Economy at Owens College, Manchester -- the institution that later became the University of Manchester. He wrote The Theory of Political Economy while holding that chair. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: Three years after Menger and Jevons a third economist independently arrived at the marginal-utility insight, and pushed it further into a mathematical model in which every price in every market is determined jointly, as a system of simultaneous equations. He published the first part of his Elements d'economie politique pure in 1874. Who was he?
context: Walras published in Lausanne, using the French word 'rarete' for what English readers called marginal utility. Cournot preceded him with 1838 mathematical duopoly; Pareto succeeded him in the Lausanne chair after 1893; Bastiat was of an older generation and no marginalist. Source: Britannica, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Leon Walras spent his career at a Swiss academy where he took the chair of political economy in 1870 and printed his Elements four years later. The school of general-equilibrium theory that grew out of his work is still named for this city. Which is it?
context: Walras held the chair of political economy at the Academie de Lausanne (later the University of Lausanne) from 1870; his book was printed there in 1874. The Lausanne School of general equilibrium takes its name from the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Historians of economic thought describe the cluster of independent 1871-1874 marginalist publications by Menger, Jevons and Walras as one of the tightest parallel-invention events in intellectual history. What name do they give to this cluster?
context: The Methodenstreit was the later Menger-Schmoller quarrel over historicist versus analytic method; the neoclassical synthesis was the mid-twentieth-century Samuelson fusion of Keynes and Walras; the Keynesian revolution was the 1930s reversal against neoclassical orthodoxy. Only the 1871-1874 cluster is called the marginal revolution. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: The three parallel-invention roads diverged into three enduring schools of economics. Menger's Vienna road became the Austrian School. Walras's Lausanne road became mathematical general-equilibrium theory. Whose road, mediated by Alfred Marshall's 1890 Principles of Economics, became the mainstream neoclassical microeconomics still taught today?
context: Marshall married Jevons's marginal-utility insight to partial-equilibrium supply-and-demand diagrams, adding elasticity of demand, consumer surplus and the representative firm. The Cambridge School he founded dominated English-speaking economics for the next half century. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alfred Marshall'.

question: Carl Menger himself thought the Walrasian project of modelling the whole economy as a system of simultaneous equations was misconceived at the philosophical level, not merely at the technical level. What was Menger's objection?
answer: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
choices: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
The mathematics of 1874 was not yet advanced enough for the task
General-equilibrium models understate the importance of labour-time in value
Walras had rejected marginal utility in favour of pure cost-of-production
context: Menger accepted the marginal-utility insight the three founders shared; his disagreement was about method. This methodological gap between the Austrian and Lausanne roads persists to the present day and underlies the Austrian critique of modern DSGE modelling. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: The marginal-utility principle was actually stated seventeen years before 1871, in a German book that sold so badly its author had the remaining edition destroyed before dying in 1858. His priority was recovered only in 1878 when a Manchester professor tracked down a surviving copy in a German antiquarian bookshop. Name the forgotten precursor.
context: Gossen's 1854 Entwickelung der Gesetze des menschlichen Verkehrs laid down what are still called Gossen's Laws of diminishing marginal utility and equimarginal allocation. Robert Adamson of Manchester found the surviving copy in 1878 and Jevons publicly acknowledged Gossen's priority in the second edition of his own book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gossen's laws'.

question: Once the marginal-unit move was on the table, an entire class of classical value theories collapsed at one stroke. Which theory did it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
choices: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
The quantity theory of money later revived by Milton Friedman
The theory of comparative advantage stated by David Ricardo
context: Every rung of the labour-theory chain assumed value was a property of the good, fixed by its cost or labour input. The marginalist move denies the assumption: value is a ranking of the next unit by a specific chooser. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus were unaffected -- each addressed a different question. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: That three economists in three different countries independently converged on the same core insight in a three-year window suggests the marginal move was, in some sense, ripe by 1870. That the three roads diverged so sharply into the Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools -- differing in method, style and eventual influence -- suggests what about economics?
answer: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
choices: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
It is primarily an empirical laboratory science like chemistry
It is settled by mathematical proof once its axioms are stated
It has no genuine intellectual disagreements after 1874
context: The Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools agreed on the marginal-utility insight but disagreed sharply about whether economics should be prose-based praxeology, partial-equilibrium diagrams, or systems of simultaneous equations. Those methodological choices still divide the profession. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: In 1883, twelve years after his founding Principles and ten years into his Vienna chair, Carl Menger published a second book with a very different purpose: to argue how economics OUGHT TO BE DONE. Which target did he pick a fight with?
answer: The German Historical School led by Gustav von Schmoller in Berlin
choices: The German Historical School led by Gustav von Schmoller in Berlin
The English classical tradition of David Ricardo
The French physiocrats of the eighteenth century
The American institutionalists led by Thorstein Veblen
context: The book was Untersuchungen ueber die Methode der Socialwissenschaften (Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences, with Special Reference to Political Economics), 1883. Schmoller held the chair at the University of Berlin from 1882 and led what economists call the 'younger' German Historical School. Ricardo was 60 years dead; the physiocrats a century earlier; Veblen and the American institutionalists would come after 1899. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: The German Historical School around Gustav von Schmoller held that a serious economist must first gather masses of national statistics, study specific historical periods, and document institutional details -- and only then, very cautiously, generalize. What is the name for a method that reasons from many collected observations up to a rule?
context: Induction moves from cases to a general rule; deduction moves from general premises to specific conclusions (like geometry proving a theorem from axioms). The German Historical School was inductive-first; Menger's Austrians were deductive-first. This deductive-vs-inductive split is what a 'method-war' -- a Methodenstreit -- is FOUGHT OVER. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Menger's 1883 method book carried a German title. Which German word gave the whole ten-year quarrel the name it wears in every history of economics?
