context: Methodenstreit literally means 'method-fight' or 'quarrel over method' -- Streit is the German for a dispute or fight. Kulturkampf was Bismarck's 1870s fight with the Catholic Church; Klassenkampf is Marx's class struggle; Vernunftstreit is not a standard historical term. The word Methodenstreit is now used by historians for any deep methodological quarrel, but by default it means THIS ONE. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Menger argued in 1883 that economics is like geometry -- it has universal laws that hold in every time and place, and those laws can be derived from a small number of self-evident starting points about human choice. From which base does a geometry-like science reason?
answer: From general first principles down to specific cases
choices: From general first principles down to specific cases
From specific cases up to tentative rules
From surveys of the general population
From statistical patterns in historical data
context: This is deduction: axioms first, theorems derived. Menger's atom was the individual acting to satisfy a want; from that atom he derived subjective value, marginal ranking, price formation. Ludwig von Mises would later name the method PRAXEOLOGY (Human Action, 1949). The Historical School's method -- from cases up to tentative rules -- is induction; surveys and statistical patterns are its tools. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In 1883, Gustav von Schmoller wrote a scorching review of Menger's method book in his own Berlin journal. In it he first used a two-word label meaning 'the Vienna sect that had failed to catch up with proper German methods.' It was intended as an insult. Menger's followers later wore it as a badge and it stuck for good. What was the label?
context: The very name 'Austrian School' was invented by an opponent as a put-down and adopted by the accused as a name of honor. The Manchester School was the free-trade movement around Cobden and Bright (1830s-60s); the Lausanne School was Walras and Pareto's mathematical-equilibrium tradition; the Cambridge School was Alfred Marshall's neoclassical mainstream. Schmoller's slur is now the name of a Nobel-decorated tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: In 1884 Menger answered Schmoller's review with a passionate short book written as a series of open letters to a friend -- Die Irrthuemer des Historismus in der deutschen Nationaloekonomie (The Errors of Historicism in German Economics). Which reasoning move did Menger press against the Historical School?
answer: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
choices: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
That economic laws depend entirely on the historical period, so no universal science of economics is possible
That only mathematical models can settle economic questions
That government must collect national statistics before any economic argument is legitimate
context: Hayek later said Menger 'ruthlessly demolished Schmoller's position' in the 1884 pamphlet. The point is exact: a scarce means will still be economized in ancient Rome and in modern Vienna; a chooser will rank in every century. History is DATA, not the SOURCE. Menger did not reject historical study; he denied it could replace theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: The insult 'Austrian School' was one weapon; the professional freeze was the other. From his chair at the University of Berlin, Schmoller publicly declared members of the abstract Vienna school unfit for German university positions. What concrete consequence did that declaration have across Germany?
answer: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
choices: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
An immediate ban on Menger's Principles being sold in Germany
Menger's removal from his chair at the University of Vienna
The dissolution of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik
context: Schmoller controlled Prussian academic appointments through his Berlin chair, his editorship of the leading journal, and his chairmanship of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik. His public verdict effectively closed the German academic market to Austrians well into the 1900s -- a professional freeze, not a book ban. Menger kept his Vienna chair; the Verein continued and Schmoller kept chairing it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: The generation of Menger's students continued the methodological fight after 1884, arguing back against Schmoller and defending the deductive Austrian method. Which pair of Menger's Vienna pupils carried the school forward?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
John Maynard Keynes and Joan Robinson
context: Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) and Wieser (1851-1926) were Menger's direct pupils and the school's second generation. Mises and Hayek were the THIRD generation (Mises studied under Boehm-Bawerk; Hayek under Wieser and then Mises). Machlup and Haberler were the fourth. Keynes and Joan Robinson were the Cambridge tradition Austrians would fight NEXT. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: The personal quarrel ended when Gustav von Schmoller died on June 27, 1917, at age 79 -- but the METHODOLOGICAL split it opened stayed permanent. Which lasting division in twentieth-century economics traces straight back to Berlin 1883?
context: The Austrian line (Menger, Boehm-Bawerk, Wieser, Mises, Hayek) kept methodological individualism -- the individual choosing actor as the atom of analysis. The descendants of the German Historical School (Veblen, Commons, and later institutional, behavioural, and evolutionary economics) kept the historical-institutional focus on how rules, habits, and organizations shape choice. Both traditions still argue the 1883 quarrel every generation. Free trade vs protectionism, gold vs fiat, and micro vs macro are separate debates. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: The Methodenstreit gave the Austrian School its name; it did not give it its most famous positive doctrines. Which specific pillar of Austrian economics was NOT born in the 1883 method quarrel, but developed later by the school's successors?
answer: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
choices: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
The rejection of the labor theory of value
The claim that value is subjective
The insistence on universal deductive laws
context: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' -- the argument that without market prices no rational allocation is possible -- came in 1920, thirty-seven years after Menger's method book. Subjective value, the rejection of labor value, and universal deductive laws were all Menger 1871 and 1883 -- the founding moves. The calculation critique is the DAUGHTER of the founding method, not the mother. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: From 1920 to 1934, on every other Friday evening at 7 p.m. from October to June, a group of Vienna scholars climbed the stairs of the Austrian Chamber of Commerce on the Ring to a working economist's office and argued for three hours about economics, philosophy, sociology, and history. There were no fees, no exams, no degree. Whose invitation-only private seminar was it?
context: Mises (1881-1973) worked at the Handelskammer -- the Austrian Chamber of Commerce -- as an economic policy adviser from 1909 onwards, and used his office there as the meeting room. The seminar is remembered as the Mises-Kreis or the Privatseminar. Menger had retired in 1903 and died in 1921; Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914; Schumpeter had left Austria for Bonn and would soon leave for Harvard. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/ludwig-mises-and-the-vienna-private-archive/.

question: The Mises private seminar was called by a German word that literally means 'private seminar.' Which word?
context: Privatseminar (private + seminar) marks its outside-the-university status; Hauptseminar means main university seminar; Kolloquium is a formal academic colloquium (Karl Menger the younger ran a Mathematical Colloquium in the same Vienna years); Lehrstuhl means academic chair. The Privatseminar had no institutional home -- that was the point. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: Two of the fortnightly regulars at Mises's Vienna office in the 1920s would each later hold Nobel-level standing in economics -- one won the Nobel Prize in 1974, the other co-founded a whole new field of analysis in 1944. Which pair?
choices: Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard
John Maynard Keynes and Joan Robinson
context: Hayek shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal for his work on money and business cycles. Morgenstern co-authored Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with John von Neumann in 1944 -- the founding book of game theory. Both cut their teeth in Mises's Vienna office in the 1920s. Rothbard was Mises's New York student decades later; Keynes and Robinson were the Cambridge tradition; Friedman and Schwartz met at NBER in America. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: The Privatseminar met inside which Vienna institution's building -- the workplace where Mises earned his living as an economic policy adviser?
choices: The University of Vienna Faculty of Law
context: Mises never held a paid university chair in Vienna; the Faculty of Law let him teach as an unsalaried Privatdozent, but his day job -- and the seminar's meeting room -- was at the Handelskammer. The Austrian National Bank and the Ministry of Finance were separate institutions Mises advised as an outside expert. The choice of the Chamber of Commerce, not the university, was itself an emblem of the seminar's independent, non-academic character. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: The Vienna Privatseminar was famous not only for its members but for who visited from abroad. One visitor from the London School of Economics was so struck by what he saw and by the young Friedrich Hayek in particular that in 1931 he arranged for Hayek to come to LSE as a professor, opening the door that would bring Austrian economics to England. Who was the LSE visitor?
context: Robbins was head of the LSE economics department and the author of An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science (1932), which carried strong Austrian influence. His invitation brought Hayek to LSE in 1931 and set up the famous Hayek-Keynes debates of the 1930s. Keynes was at Cambridge, not LSE; Pigou held the Cambridge chair; Beveridge was LSE Director but not the economist who spotted Hayek. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Beyond economists, the Privatseminar drew philosophers and sociologists. One member was the sociologist and philosopher who would later flee to New York and become a founder of phenomenological sociology at the New School for Social Research. Which Privatseminar regular was he?
context: Schuetz (1899-1959) worked days as a bank lawyer and joined the Privatseminar in the 1920s; his book The Phenomenology of the Social World (1932) argued that economics rests on the meanings actors give their own actions -- a philosophical fit with Mises's methodological individualism. He escaped to New York in 1939. Popper, Neurath, and Schlick belonged to the neighboring Vienna Circle of logical positivists, not the Mises Kreis. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: The Vienna room the Privatseminar met in was not the only revolutionary intellectual gathering in the city in the 1920s. In the very same decade, a Mathematical Colloquium met separately -- attended by Kurt Goedel and John von Neumann -- and hosted by a mathematician who also belonged to the Vienna Circle. He was the son of a founder of the Austrian School. Who was he?
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985), son of Carl Menger the economist, did dimension theory in mathematics, edited the proceedings of his Mathematical Colloquium (which included Goedel's incompleteness results and von Neumann's work), and sat in the Vienna Circle. The Menger name reaches into TWO of interwar Vienna's most consequential intellectual gatherings -- his father founded one tradition, and Karl the younger crossed into the other. Carnap, Hahn, and Frank were Vienna Circle members but not sons of the Austrian School's founder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: In the spring of 1934, Mises accepted a chair at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in a Swiss city, and the Vienna Privatseminar ended. The move came four years before the Nazi Anschluss -- as a Jew and a liberal, Mises's decision to leave Vienna at that moment likely saved his life. Which city did he move to?
context: The Graduate Institute of International Studies (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) is in Geneva. Mises taught there as professor of international economic relations until 1940, then emigrated to New York when the German army approached Switzerland's borders. The Anschluss came in March 1938. Basel, Zurich, and Bern all have universities but not the Graduate Institute. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Between 1931 and 1940 the whole Privatseminar emptied out -- Hayek to LSE, Machlup as a Rockefeller fellow to America, Haberler to Harvard, Morgenstern to Princeton, Mises himself to New York. What condition let a small Vienna room in the 1920s remake economics in the American universities of the 1940s and after?
answer: The seminar members were Jews or liberals who had to leave Central Europe as the Nazis rose
choices: The seminar members were Jews or liberals who had to leave Central Europe as the Nazis rose
The Rockefeller Foundation ordered all Vienna economists to come to the United States
The Austrian government paid for their emigration
They were all fired from their Vienna university positions in 1934
context: The Anschluss of March 1938 made staying impossible for the Jewish and liberal members; Mises had left in 1934 and Hayek in 1931 -- both jumps early enough that they moved as scholars, not as refugees. Machlup was on Rockefeller in America when the Anschluss happened and stayed; Morgenstern was visiting Princeton and chose to stay; Haberler was already at Harvard by 1936. The Rockefeller Foundation funded some fellowships but did not order anyone; the Austrian government did not pay; most of them never held salaried Vienna chairs to be fired from. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Fritz Machlup left Vienna for a Rockefeller Foundation fellowship in the United States in 1933 and never came back. Across the next forty years he held chairs at three American universities and pioneered the economics of KNOWLEDGE and information. Which trio of institutions did his American career pass through?
answer: Johns Hopkins, Princeton, and New York University
choices: Johns Hopkins, Princeton, and New York University
context: Machlup was Hutzler Professor at Johns Hopkins 1947-1960, Walker Professor at Princeton 1960-1971, and professor at NYU 1971-1983. His 1962 book The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States is a founding text of information economics. Haberler went to Harvard; Morgenstern to Princeton; Hayek to LSE and later Chicago and Freiburg. Machlup's specific triangle -- Hopkins, Princeton, NYU -- is his own. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup.

question: A self-identified 'democratic socialist' movement has grown in the US since roughly 2015, with a US senator making two presidential runs and a member of Congress becoming a prominent figure. Which senator ran for president in 2016 and 2020 under the democratic-socialist banner?
context: Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020, self-identifying as a democratic socialist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders.

question: The US organization associated with the modern democratic-socialist revival grew from about 6,000 members in 2014 to roughly 92,000 by 2021. What is the group's name?
context: DSA membership grew roughly 15x between 2014 and 2021. Prominent elected DSA-affiliated figures include Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib. Source: dsausa.org membership statistics.

question: Modern democratic-socialist policy proposals commonly include a $15+ federal minimum wage, national rent control, government-set drug prices, and single-payer health insurance. What is the standard shorthand for the health-insurance proposal?
context: Medicare for All (M4A) proposes a single-payer national health-insurance program with government-negotiated provider prices. Sanders's Senate version and Rep. Pramila Jayapal's House version are the reference bills. Source: sanders.senate.gov/medicare-for-all.

question: For the bank's teaching, the reasoning-move framework applies uniformly regardless of political label. Which classical reasoning move applies to a proposed $30/hr federal minimum wage set above market clearing?
answer: Seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost
choices: Seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost
The Cantillon effect -- the first recipients gain purchasing power
Moral hazard -- workers take on more risk
context: Bastiat's method: the visible beneficiary is the worker whose wage rises; the invisible cost is the worker priced out of the labor market entirely. The critic named would be Milton Friedman. The kid names the MOVE; the verdict is theirs. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The reasoning-move framework also applies to national rent control as a policy proposal. Which classical reasoning move do critics (from Friedman-Stigler 1946 to modern Austrian analysts) most sharply press?
answer: The knowledge-problem and supply-response mechanism -- fewer apartments over time
choices: The knowledge-problem and supply-response mechanism -- fewer apartments over time
The Cantillon effect on housing money
context: The critic's move: rent below cost reduces the profitability of supplying rental housing; supply falls; future tenants pay the hidden cost. This is the reasoning move -- the kid decides the verdict. Source: Friedman-Stigler, Roofs or Ceilings? (1946).

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument in 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' was not framed as a political attack on socialism. What kind of argument was it, per the bank's framing?
answer: A mechanical argument about the informational role of prices
choices: A mechanical argument about the informational role of prices
A moral argument about human freedom
context: Mises 1920's move: prices carry information (about scarcity, urgency, tastes) that no committee can substitute for. This is a mechanical claim about how information is aggregated -- it does not depend on any political verdict. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation.

question: The bank's teach-recognition-not-verdict move on this ladder means the kid learns to run one specific analytical chain. Which chain?
answer: Identify the reasoning move a specific critic would press, without demanding the kid share the critic's verdict
choices: Identify the reasoning move a specific critic would press, without demanding the kid share the critic's verdict
Reject any moral evaluation of policy
context: The Recognition-not-verdict move: the answer names the CRITIC'S move (Friedman on minimum wage, Hayek on drug pricing, Buchanan on deficit); the answer never names 'the policy is bad' or 'socialism is wrong'. Source: bank_pipeline framing rules.

question: The honest presentation distinguishes 2020s American democratic socialism from Soviet-style central planning. What is the key distinction the bank makes?
answer: No state ownership of means of production; the systematic replacement of market prices with government-set prices in specific sectors
choices: No state ownership of means of production; the systematic replacement of market prices with government-set prices in specific sectors
context: The distinction matters for accuracy: 2020s democratic socialism as advocated in America does not propose Gosplan-style planning. It DOES propose replacing market prices with government-set ones in labor, housing, healthcare, education, energy. The reasoning moves against Gosplan apply less catastrophically in scale but by the same mechanism. Source: dsausa.org platform.

question: The bank teaches the kid to run the reasoning chain but leaves the political verdict to the kid. What is the classical reasoning move that applies to government-negotiated drug pricing (as in Medicare price-setting)?
answer: The knowledge-problem applied to pharmaceutical R&D and marginal-drug innovation
choices: The knowledge-problem applied to pharmaceutical R&D and marginal-drug innovation
The Cantillon effect on medical inflation
The Phillips curve applied to drug prices
The natural rate applied to prescriptions
context: The critic's move: without price signals, planners cannot know which future drug lines to invest in; below-market negotiated prices reduce the incentive for marginal innovation. The kid names the move; the verdict is theirs. Source: mises.org/library/pharma-pricing.

question: For the ladder's core teaching, what is the general rule about political labels and the underlying reasoning-move analysis?
answer: The reasoning moves apply the same way regardless of the label the advocate uses
choices: The reasoning moves apply the same way regardless of the label the advocate uses
The reasoning moves apply only to Soviet-style planning
The reasoning moves apply only if the policy is unpopular
The reasoning moves depend on the political party proposing them
context: Mises 1920 was a mechanical argument about prices, not a political attack. The reasoning moves apply to any policy that suppresses a price signal, regardless of whether the label is 'socialism', 'progressive reform', 'social democracy', or 'consumer protection'. Source: bank framework rules.

question: In Frederic Bastiat's collection Economic Sophisms a deputy in the French Chamber rises to argue that his own port city on the Garonne would benefit if a proposed Paris-to-Madrid railway had to STOP there, so its porters and innkeepers could handle the goods. Which city does the deputy represent?
context: Bastiat's original text names Bordeaux specifically; it is the port on the Garonne midway between Paris and the Spanish border. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: The Bordeaux deputy in Bastiat's 'negative railway' passage argues that a break in the rail line at his city would generate work for exactly which three local trades?
context: Bastiat names PORTERS (to move the freight around the break), INNKEEPERS (to house travellers forced to stop), and WAREHOUSEMEN (to store the goods) as the three visible beneficiaries; every other city then has the same claim. Source: mises.org/library/economic-sophisms.

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' argument in Economic Sophisms is aimed at a proposed line between two named European capitals. Which two cities did the proposed railway connect?
context: The 1840s Paris-Madrid trunk line was a live political question in Bastiat's Chamber; Bastiat wrote the piece precisely because deputies from cities along the route were carving up the line with local-benefit arguments. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' argument, taken to its logical conclusion, requires a break at every station along the line. What does the argument, so extended, produce?
answer: A series of unconnected roads that is not a railway at all
choices: A series of unconnected roads that is not a railway at all
A perfectly efficient distribution of freight-handling employment
A modest annual improvement in national industrial output
A revenue base large enough to fund the line's construction
context: This is Bastiat's whole point: if breaking the line creates jobs, then it must create MORE jobs at every station, and the make-work argument requires the very thing that makes the work possible to be destroyed. Source: mises.org/library/economic-sophisms.

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' argument is the twin of another Bastiat sophism aimed at exactly the same make-work reasoning applied to destruction rather than friction. Which sister sophism is it paired with?
context: The broken-window says destruction is not creation; the negative-railway says friction is not creation. Together they close both flanks of the 19th-century make-work argument. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: The 'negative railway' argument was Bastiat's move against a form of reasoning that treated one specific quality of a transport network as a benefit rather than a cost. What quality?
context: The Bordeaux deputy's whole argument treats extra HANDLING (friction) as extra income; Bastiat's reductio is that if friction were income, the ideal railway would be no railway at all. Source: mises.org/library/economic-sophisms.

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' argument is now used as the standard classroom answer to any policy that says a labor-saving machine 'destroys jobs.' If breaking a rail line to give porters work were good, then to be consistent we ought also to destroy which two prehistoric labor-saving tools?
context: The spade replaced people who dug with sticks; the wheel replaced people who dragged loads on sledges. The negative-railway reductio: if every labor-saving tool destroys jobs, we should have banned all of them. Source: cato.org/commentary/luddite-arguments-then-and-now.

question: Bastiat's 'negative railway' reasoning has been reapplied in the 21st century to a specific technology-panic argument about a class of software systems that produce text and images. Which recent panic follows the same shape?
answer: That artificial-intelligence tools destroy writing jobs
choices: That artificial-intelligence tools destroy writing jobs
That electric vehicles destroy petroleum jobs
That online retail destroys shipping jobs
That smartphone cameras destroy photography jobs
context: The negative-railway shape: the visible job that the machine 'takes' is the SEEN; the UNSEEN is the new work the released labor does and the lower-cost goods everyone else now enjoys. The 2020s AI-writing panic recycles the argument almost word for word. Source: cato.org/commentary/luddite-arguments-then-and-now.

question: The 'negative railway' argument survives in modern economics as a standing warning against a family of policies that impose deliberate cost or delay to preserve visible employment. What is the modern textbook name for the general policy type Bastiat is refuting?
context: 'Make-work' is the term Sowell, Friedman, and every Austrian textbook use for policies that treat friction, breakage, or wasted effort as a job-creation benefit; Bastiat's negative-railway is the canonical refutation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make-work_job.

question: On a Sunday night in August 1971 President Richard Nixon interrupted network programming with a national broadcast announcing sweeping economic measures, including the end of dollar-gold convertibility for foreign central banks. What is the standard shorthand for that broadcast?
context: August 15, 1971. Nixon's Sunday-evening address preempted network shows to announce closing the gold window, a wage-price freeze, and an import surcharge. Journalists called it the Nixon shock immediately. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: The Nixon economic broadcast famously bumped a Sunday-night western that was the most-watched show in the country that year. Which show was preempted?
context: The Nixon speech interrupted NBC's Bonanza (running its 13th season in 1971). Journalists still cite the Bonanza-preemption as the pop-culture shorthand for the significance of the announcement. Source: whitehousehistory.org (Nixon presidential timeline).

question: The Nixon speech ended the Bretton Woods system that had governed international money since 1944 by 'closing' a specific mechanism. What is the shorthand phrase for what Nixon closed?
context: Closing the gold window meant suspending the US Treasury's commitment to convert dollars held by foreign central banks into gold at $35 an ounce. Bretton Woods had rested on that promise since 1944. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: The Nixon shock was actually a package of three simultaneous measures, not one. Along with closing the gold window, what was the second, domestic-facing measure -- the first peacetime price controls in US history?
context: The 90-day freeze was extended in successive Phases through April 1974. It bought a temporary appearance of price stability into the 1972 election year, then unravelled into the 1973-75 inflation acceleration. Source: nixonlibrary.gov/economic-policy.

question: The Nixon Treasury Secretary who quipped to European finance ministers that 'the dollar is our currency, but it's your problem' was a Texas Democrat turned Republican. Who was he?
context: Connally (Treasury 1971-72) delivered the line at a Group of Ten finance-ministers meeting in Rome, November 1971. He later switched parties to Republican and ran briefly for president in 1980. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Connally.

question: The Nixon shock's third simultaneous measure was aimed at trading partners perceived to be undervaluing their currencies against the dollar. What was that measure?
choices: A commercial tariff on farm goods
context: The 10 percent import surcharge was intended to force partners (chiefly West Germany and Japan) to revalue their currencies upward against the dollar. It was lifted that December after the Smithsonian Agreement adjusted parities. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: The Nixon shock decision was made over a weekend meeting at a specific presidential retreat, described later by aide William Safire as 'the most important act of Nixon's presidency other than opening China'. Where was the weekend meeting held?
context: The August 13-15, 1971 Camp David weekend brought Fed chair Arthur Burns, Connally, George Shultz, Paul Volcker (then Treasury undersecretary), and others together to plan the announcement. Safire's memoir 'Before the Fall' documents the weekend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: Bitcoin advocates point to August 15, 1971 as the birthday of the political-money problem their asset was designed to solve. What community website is best known for cataloging economic-trend charts that visibly bend around that year?
context: The site presents dozens of charts (wage-productivity divergence, household savings, wealth-concentration ratios) using FRED and BLS data, showing visible trend breaks near 1971. It is the standard Bitcoin-community reference for the fiat-era-began-here argument. Source: wtfhappenedin1971.com.

question: The dollar has now been fully un-anchored from any commodity for how many years as of 2026 -- a stretch longer than any earlier US monetary regime except the fiat greenback era of the Civil War?
context: From August 15, 1971 to 2026 is 54-55 years -- longer than any earlier pure-fiat regime in US peacetime history. The 1862-79 greenback interruption during and after the Civil War lasted 17 years. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: The domestic-political motivation for the Nixon shock's timing was straightforward: Nixon faced re-election the following year and wanted the pain of any dollar adjustment shifted onto foreigners rather than voters. Which year was that election?
context: Nixon won re-election in November 1972 carrying 49 states. Wage-price controls kept CPI appearances calm through the campaign; inflation exploded in 1973-74 after the controls unravelled. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_presidential_election.

question: Nixon-era fiscal recklessness that Bretton Woods could not accommodate had two main sources: costly domestic social programs and a foreign war. Which pair does the Austrian critique name as the load Bretton Woods buckled under?
answer: The Great Society and the Vietnam War
choices: The Great Society and the Vietnam War
The New Deal and the Korean War
The New Frontier and the Cold War arms race
The Fair Deal and the Marshall Plan
context: The Johnson-Nixon combination of Great Society spending and Vietnam War financing pushed the fiscal deficit into what could no longer be paid in gold at $35/oz. Nixon's 1971 announcement made the failure formal. Source: mises.org/library/nixon-shock.

question: The Bitcoin white paper (October 2008) can be read as a technical answer to the political-money problem that Bitcoin advocates trace to the Nixon shock. Roughly how long after August 15, 1971 did Satoshi Nakamoto's paper appear?
context: August 1971 to October 2008 is 37 years. The Bitcoin white paper proposed a fixed-supply digital money as an alternative to central-bank-managed fiat -- an answer, in its authors' framing, to the political-money problem that Nixon inaugurated. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: New York City has capped the number of yellow-cab licenses in the city since a 1937 statute, holding the total near 11,700 for decades. What is the name of that 1937 statute?
context: The Haas Act of 1937 created the New York City taxi-medallion system. The cap made each medallion an artificially scarce property right that would eventually trade for over a million dollars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: In 2013-14, at the peak of the New York City yellow-cab market, a single NYC taxi medallion (the government license to operate one cab) traded at auction for a price higher than most Manhattan condos. Roughly what was that peak price?
context: The NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission auction records show medallion prices rising from $2,500 in 1947 to $200,000 in 1997 to about $1.3 million in 2013-14. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: In 2011 a San Francisco company launched a smartphone-based car-service app in New York City, initially registered under the state's black-car regulatory category rather than as a taxi. Which company was it?
context: Uber's NYC launch in 2011 categorized each driver as a for-hire vehicle (FHV) rather than a taxi, bypassing the yellow-cab medallion cap entirely and letting supply expand to meet demand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Uber.

question: Between 2013 and 2019, after Uber and similar ride-hail apps had scaled up in New York City, the market price of a NYC taxi medallion suffered a roughly 92% loss. Approximately what price did the medallion fall to by 2019?
context: Medallion auction prices tracked the collapse: about $1.3M (2013) to about $700K (2016) to about $100K (2019). Many owners had borrowed against medallions as collateral. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: When a senator argues the NYC medallion cap protects taxi drivers from cutthroat competition, Bastiat's method asks: what does the cap cost that no one immediately sees? Which of these is the classic Bastiat unseen the cap imposed?
answer: The riders who could not find a cab and either walked, waited, or drove drunk
choices: The riders who could not find a cab and either walked, waited, or drove drunk
The publicly listed accounting profits of yellow-cab fleet owners
The visible fare meters ticking in every yellow cab
The published NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission auction results
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): the visible medallion owners were rich; the invisible losers were the would-be riders denied service and the would-be drivers blocked by the cap. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: Before the app-hail era, yellow cabs in New York City systematically underserved certain neighborhoods where a street hail was less economic. Which neighborhoods were the most-documented example of this undersupply?
answer: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
choices: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
The Financial District and Midtown Manhattan
context: Yellow-cab economics depended on street hails, so drivers concentrated in Manhattan; the app-hail model let for-hire vehicles serve outer-borough demand that had gone unserved for decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_and_Limousine_Commission_(New_York_City).

question: In May 2019 two New York Times reporters published a Pulitzer-finalist series documenting about 950 medallion-owner bankruptcies and 8 driver suicides after the medallion collapse. What was the series's headline focus?
answer: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
choices: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
How Uber built a monopoly in New York City
How the Haas Act created New York's first cab rules
How the NYC Taxi Commission was reformed in 2019
context: Emma Fitzsimmons and Brian Rosenthal's NYT series showed that many owner-drivers had bought medallions at peak prices using loans they could not repay after the collapse. Source: nytimes.com/2019/05/19/nyregion/nyc-taxis-medallions-suicides.html.

question: Bastiat's method reads the 2013-19 medallion collapse as more than a loss for medallion owners. On his accounting, what was the collapse actually revealing about the seven-decade run of the cap?
answer: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for 76 years
choices: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for 76 years
A one-time market crash unrelated to earlier medallion prices
Uber's illegal subsidies temporarily undercutting a fair market
A currency-inflation effect on New York asset prices
context: Bastiat's move: the medallion price had capitalized the transfer FROM riders and blocked drivers TO cap-protected owners; the collapse reversed a transfer that had run one way since 1937. Painful for owners, but a reversal. Source: bastiat.org (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, 1850).

question: From 1945 to 1969 Ludwig von Mises ran a graduate seminar in Manhattan that seeded the American Austrian revival. At which university did the seminar meet?
choices: The City University of New York
context: Mises's NYU seminar met on Thursday evenings for twenty-four years, in the Graduate School of Business Administration on Trinity Place and later on Washington Square. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Mises's NYU title was Visiting Professor of Economics, but a specific fact about his employment there was unusual for a chaired scholar of his stature. What was that fact?
answer: NYU did not pay him at all
choices: NYU did not pay him at all
NYU paid him twice the standard salary
NYU tenured him after two years
NYU required him to teach undergraduates
context: NYU paid Mises nothing; his salary was covered by outside donors. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Mises's NYU salary came from a Kansas City-based philanthropic charity that also later funded Hayek's 1950 move to the University of Chicago. What was the charity called?
context: The William Volker Fund of Kansas City funded much of the mid-century Austrian revival in America. Source: grokipedia.com/page/William_Volker_Fund.

question: A New York advertising executive personally supplemented Mises's NYU stipend for years, and was a longtime seminar attendee. Who was he?
context: Lawrence Fertig, a Madison Avenue advertising executive who admired Mises's work, personally supplemented Mises's NYU salary and endowed a lecture hall named after him. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: The most important American product of Mises's NYU seminar joined in 1949 and later wrote Man, Economy, and State (1962). Who was he?
context: Rothbard attended the NYU seminar from 1949 and remained through the 1960s. His subsequent writing carried the seminar's tradition to a wider American audience. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Mises's own NYU doctoral student later wrote a 1973 Chicago Press book that reoriented Austrian microeconomics around entrepreneurship as alertness. Who was Mises's PhD student?
context: Israel Kirzner's NYU PhD under Mises produced Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973), the foundational modern statement of Austrian entrepreneurship theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: Mises's first American doctoral student, a former Luftwaffe pilot, later held a long teaching career at a specific liberal-arts college in Pennsylvania. Where did he teach?
context: Hans Sennholz taught for decades at Grove City College, where he trained a generation of Austrian-friendly American economists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Sennholz.

question: Mises taught his last NYU seminar session in December of a specific year, when he was 88; he retired then and died four years later. In what year was the last session?
context: Mises's last seminar was December 1969; he died in October 1973 at age 92. The seminar ended without a successor; the American Austrian tradition would not have another dedicated graduate program until Auburn (1982) and George Mason. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In October 1907 a Wall Street panic spread from a failed copper-market scheme to a run on New York banks. With no central bank yet in existence, one aging private banker organized the rescue himself. Who was he?
context: J.P. Morgan (70 years old in 1907) coordinated the private rescue, summoning bank and trust presidents to his personal library and pooling their capital. It was the last major US financial rescue conducted by a private individual acting as de facto central bank. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: The 1907 New York banking panic is sometimes called the Knickerbocker Crisis after the specific institution whose collapse touched off the wider run. What kind of institution was Knickerbocker?
context: The Knickerbocker Trust Company was the third-largest trust in New York. Trust companies held bank-like deposits but faced looser reserve rules than national banks. When Knickerbocker's president was linked to the Heinze copper-corner scheme, depositors fled. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knickerbocker_Trust_Company.

question: The 1907 panic's initial trigger was a failed attempt by two brothers to corner the market in shares of a single mining company. Which brothers ran the failed corner?
context: The Heinze brothers tried to squeeze short-sellers of United Copper Company stock. When the squeeze collapsed on October 16, 1907, depositors at banks associated with the Heinzes started pulling funds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: During the crisis Morgan famously summoned rival bank and trust presidents to a specific location -- his personal book collection at his townhouse -- and reportedly locked them in until they committed rescue funds. Where were they held?
answer: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
choices: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
The floor of the New York Stock Exchange
The board room of the Bank of New York
context: The building is now the Morgan Library and Museum. The 'locked in the library' detail comes from Morgan's son-in-law Herbert Satterlee's 1939 biography and is well-attested in period accounts. Source: themorgan.org/about.

question: The 1907 crisis exposed a specific gap in the American financial system that political reformers spent the next six years arguing to fill. What crucial institution did the country lack?
context: Without a central bank, panics required ad-hoc rescues by private figures. The 1907 crisis made the political argument that the country needed a permanent institution able to supply liquidity in a run -- an argument that produced the Federal Reserve six years later. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/panic-of-1907.

question: During the rescue Morgan told the head of the New York Stock Exchange that closing the exchange 'would be too great a shock' and immediately produced a large sum from bank presidents in his library. Roughly how much did he raise -- and in how little time?
context: Morgan raised roughly $25 million from bank presidents assembled in his library in about 15 minutes to keep the NYSE open. Adjusted for the era, this was the operative moment of the private rescue. Source: Satterlee, J. Pierpont Morgan: An Intimate Portrait (1939).

question: Morgan decided to let the Knickerbocker Trust fail but organized the rescue of another major trust he judged to be solvent. Which trust did he save?
context: Trust Company of America was hit by a run in the days after Knickerbocker's failure. Morgan judged it solvent, arranged a private syndicate to backstop its deposits, and it survived. This is the earliest well-documented case of a private banker distinguishing solvent from insolvent institutions in a panic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: The Treasury Secretary who supported Morgan's rescue by depositing $35 million of federal funds in New York national banks was a former Postmaster General under Theodore Roosevelt. What was his surname?
context: George Cortelyou (Treasury 1907-09) added federal deposits to New York national banks during the crisis. This gave Morgan's private effort a substantial fiscal complement -- an early example of Treasury-Fed style coordination before the Fed existed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._Cortelyou.

question: After the 1907 panic Congress created a study body to propose reforms; it worked from 1908 to 1912 and paved the way for a permanent central bank. What was that body called?
context: Senator Nelson Aldrich chaired the Commission, which studied European central banks and produced the Aldrich Plan of 1911 -- the structural blueprint behind the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monetary_Commission.

question: Historian Charles Kindleberger described Morgan's rescue with a specific line about the impossibility of repeating it -- the argument that leaving future panics to one aging private banker was not a sustainable model. What did he say Morgan's rescue was 'the last time' any individual did?
answer: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
choices: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
Owned a majority stake in a Wall Street trust
Held gold reserves for the US Treasury
Personally set discount rates for member banks
context: Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes uses the Morgan 1907 episode as the pivot case -- the last time an individual performed the lender-of-last-resort function that permanent central banks now provide. Source: Kindleberger + Aliber, Manias, Panics, and Crashes.

question: Six years after the 1907 panic, the practical answer to its central lesson was signed into law. What was that law?
context: Signed December 23, 1913, the Federal Reserve Act created the permanent lender-of-last-resort infrastructure the 1907 crisis had shown the country lacked. Its structural design came out of the Aldrich Plan and the Jekyll Island meeting of November 1910. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/federal_reserve_act_signed.

question: Adam Smith opened Book 1, Chapter 4 of his 1776 masterpiece with a puzzle he could not solve. Nothing, he wrote, is more useful than one common substance, yet it will purchase scarce anything; a different substance has scarce any use, yet a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it. Which two substances did he compare?
context: The passage runs 'Nothing is more useful than water: but it will purchase scarce any thing; scarce any thing can be had in exchange for it. A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' It is the founding statement of the paradox of value. Source: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations Book 1 Ch 4, via geolib.com.

question: Adam Smith noticed the water-and-diamonds puzzle but did not resolve it; he drew from it a pair of contrasting senses of the word 'value' and moved on to a labour-embodied theory of exchange price. Which two senses did he distinguish?
answer: Value in use and value in exchange
choices: Value in use and value in exchange
context: Real / nominal and natural / market are also genuine Smith distinctions but they belong to different chapters; the paradox-of-value passage explicitly opens with value-in-use and value-in-exchange as the two senses of the word. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paradox of value'.

question: For a century after Smith, the classical economists tried to attach value to some objective property of the good itself -- typically the labour-time embodied in producing it. Which two nineteenth-century thinkers pushed hardest on this labour theory of value, in works of 1817 and 1867?
choices: Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill
Nassau Senior and John Elliott Cairnes
context: Ricardo's Principles of Political Economy and Taxation appeared in 1817; Marx's Capital appeared in German in 1867. Both took embodied labour to be the objective source of value -- Marx developed it into a theory of surplus value and exploitation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Labor theory of value'.

question: The 1871 Grundsaetze of Carl Menger dissolved Smith's puzzle by rejecting the whole search for an objective property of a good. Where, according to Menger, does the value of a good actually reside?
answer: In the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses
choices: In the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses
In the average number of labour-hours embodied in producing it
In the objective usefulness of the substance to human survival
In the political power of the class that produces it
context: Menger's move was that no chooser ever compares 'water as a class' with 'diamonds as a class'; a chooser always compares one more unit of a good, given current holdings, against the next-best alternative use of the same effort or money. Source: Wikipedia, 'Principles of Economics (Menger book)'.

question: Menger illustrates his valuation move with a famous example: a farmer with five sacks of grain uses the first for his own bread, the next for his livestock, the next for seed, the next for brewing, and the last for feeding parrots. If he loses one sack, which use does he give up first, and what does that determine?
answer: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
choices: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
His own bread -- and the most-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
Every use loses equally -- so the value is the average of the five uses
The bread and the seed together -- because they are the productive uses
context: Menger's insight is that a rational chooser losing one unit will drop the least-urgent use first; therefore the value of any one interchangeable unit equals the importance of the marginal use, not the peak use. This is diminishing marginal utility stated at the level of a specific person's ranking. Source: Libertarianism.org, 'Menger's Principles of Economics: The Marginal Revolution'.

question: Applied to the diamond-water puzzle by Menger's method, why does one more glass of water rank so low in a plumbed European city while one more diamond ranks so high?
answer: Water is abundant so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero so the marginal stone serves a top-ranked use
choices: Water is abundant so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero so the marginal stone serves a top-ranked use
Water is a public good and diamonds are a private good, so only diamonds carry value
Diamonds embody more labour-hours per unit than water does
The government sets the price of water below its true value
context: Once value is a ranking of the marginal unit, high total utility and high marginal utility come apart. Water's total utility is enormous but its marginal utility to a plumbed household is nearly zero; a first diamond's marginal utility to someone who has never owned one is large. Source: Study.com, 'Diamond-Water Paradox'.

question: The best test of Menger's answer is to reverse the scarcities. Put a traveller in the middle of a desert with one canteen of water and pockets full of diamonds. According to the marginal-unit move, what should happen to his ranking of the next glass versus the next stone?
answer: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
choices: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
The ranking stays the same -- diamonds always outrank water because they always cost more to make
Both goods have equal marginal value in any setting
The ranking depends on the traveller's political beliefs, not on his holdings
context: That the ranking reverses on the reverse scarcities is the diagnostic test of the marginal-unit move: value was never a property of the good, it was a ranking that depended on how much of each the chooser already held. Source: Adam Smith Works, 'Three Ways of Looking at the Water-Diamond Paradox'.

question: Once Menger's move is on the table, an entire class of nineteenth-century value theories collapses in the same stroke. Which of these theories does it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value, because it assumed value was a property of the good rather than of a chooser's ranking
choices: The labour theory of value, because it assumed value was a property of the good rather than of a chooser's ranking
The quantity theory of money, because it treated the money supply as exogenous
The theory of comparative advantage, because it depended on labour cost differences
The Malthusian theory of population, because it assumed diminishing returns in agriculture
context: Every step of the labour-theory chain -- Smith on embodied labour, Ricardo's refinement, Marx's socially necessary labour -- assumed value belonged to the good. Denying the assumption denies the whole chain. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus depend on other assumptions and are unaffected. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginalism'.

question: The distinction Menger's move drew is now standard textbook language: even though a substance may be enormously useful IN TOTAL, one more unit of it may be worth very little if a chooser already has plenty. What are the two matched terms textbooks use for these two quantities?
context: Textbooks separate total utility (the whole stack of satisfactions from all units held) from marginal utility (the added satisfaction from one more unit given current holdings). Menger's water-and-diamonds resolution is the classic teaching case for the distinction. Source: Study.com, 'Diamond-Water Paradox'.

question: The deeper lesson of the marginal-unit resolution goes beyond diamonds and water. Once you accept that value is a ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against the next-best use, you cannot go back to an older way of talking about value. Which of these older projects becomes hopeless once the marginal-unit move is made?
answer: The whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself
choices: The whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself
The project of measuring prices in a common unit of account
The project of studying international trade patterns
The project of writing economic history
context: Menger, Jevons and Walras converged on the same conclusion in the 1871-1874 marginal revolution: value is not IN the good, it is a ranking of the next unit by a chooser. Once that move is made, cost-of-production and labour-embodied theories lose their footing. Prices, trade patterns and economic history remain perfectly good subjects of study. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginalism'.

question: In 1908 Colonel Willoughby Verner wrote to The Times about the hedges along English country roads, which had been cut back so drivers could see much farther ahead. He wrote to describe what the clear sightlines had done. What did he report?
answer: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
choices: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
Drivers took to the lanes, and horse traffic vanished
Drivers kept to main roads, and village trade collapsed
Drivers slowed at bends, and crashes became rarer
context: Grokipedia's Risk compensation article records Verner's 1908 letter to The Times as the earliest documented observation of the pattern: improving the road did not buy the safety the improvement promised, because drivers spent part of it on speed. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: In November 1965 Ralph Nader published Unsafe at Any Speed, arguing that Detroit designed cars around power and styling rather than around surviving a crash. Senate hearings the next year exposed what General Motors had done about him, and the disclosure swung public opinion behind the first federal auto-safety law. What had General Motors done?
answer: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
choices: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
Quietly recalled the model Nader had singled out for attack
Bought his publisher and cancelled the second print run
Paid a rival engineer to write and publish a rebuttal book
context: President Lyndon Johnson signed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act on September 9, 1966, with Nader among roughly 200 people at the Rose Garden ceremony. The Act produced the first mandatory federal vehicle standards, effective with the 1968 model year. Sources: Wikipedia, 'National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act'; Wikipedia, 'Ralph Nader'.

question: American football teams swapped leather headgear for rigid plastic-shell helmets in the late 1940s. Skull fractures fell, as the designers expected. But cervical-spine injuries rose, and researchers traced the rise to a change in how players now hit each other. What did players start doing?
answer: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
choices: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
Gripping the facemask to swing an opponent down
Driving the helmet into the opponent's front knee
Locking both arms around the opponent's waist
context: The leather helmet made spearing too painful to attempt; the plastic shell made it survivable for the tackler, so the technique spread and the neck paid for it. The protection was real, and the behaviour moved to consume part of it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: From the 1968 model year the United States required seat belts, padded dashboards and energy-absorbing steering columns on every new car. In the Journal of Political Economy in 1975 Sam Peltzman reported that deaths per crash among people inside cars had dropped about as the crash-test engineers had promised -- yet total highway deaths had not fallen. Which finding in his data accounted for the gap?
answer: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
choices: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
Rear-seat passenger deaths rose faster than front-seat deaths
Belts were fitted in the cars but almost no driver buckled them
New highway building pushed traffic onto narrow rural roads
context: Peltzman, 'The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation', Journal of Political Economy 83(4), 677-725, August 1975. The crash-test literature implied annual highway deaths would be about 20 percent greater without the mandated devices; Peltzman argued the offsets were close to complete, with lives saved inside the car paid for by deaths outside it and by more accidents overall. Source: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/260352

question: A city council proposes to make cycle helmets compulsory, citing laboratory tests showing how much a helmet cuts head injury in an impact. An economist in the Chicago regulation tradition tells the council that the laboratory figure is the wrong number to plan on. Which objection is he making?
answer: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
choices: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
That the council cannot know which streets its cyclists actually fear most
That the helmet makers will end up writing the standard the council adopts
That the cost falls on cyclists while the credit goes to the councillors
context: The three rejected choices are real reasoning moves aimed elsewhere: Hayek's knowledge problem, George Stigler's regulatory capture (1971), and Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits with dispersed costs (1965). The move being made here is incentive recognition -- the engineering estimate describes the device, not the person using it.

question: In 1972 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ordered child-resistant caps onto aspirin and selected other drug bottles. W. Kip Viscusi checked the poisoning data afterwards and published the result in the American Economic Review in 1984: aspirin poisonings had not fallen significantly, and poisonings from other painkillers had trended upward. What did Viscusi say parents were doing?
answer: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
choices: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
Buying larger bottles because the safe caps cost more per pack
Switching to painkillers the new rule did not yet cover
Storing several drugs together in one unmarked kitchen jar
context: Viscusi named it the 'lulling effect': a cap that is hard for an adult to open gets left loose, and a cap advertised as child proof invites a parent to relax the precaution the child actually depended on. W. Kip Viscusi, 'The Lulling Effect: The Impact of Child-Resistant Packaging on Aspirin and Analgesic Ingestions', American Economic Review 74(2), 324-327, May 1984.

question: Airbags and antilock brakes reach drivers through the market rather than through a mandate, and the drivers who buy them first are the safety-conscious ones. Clifford Winston, Vikram Maheshri and Fred Mannering tested that natural experiment on individual-level crash data in the Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in 2006. What did they find the two devices had done to collisions and injuries?
answer: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
choices: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
Cut both sharply, because careful drivers used the devices carefully
Cut injuries but not collisions, matching the crash-test estimates
Raised both above the rates recorded for cars without the devices
context: Winston, Maheshri and Mannering, 'An exploration of the offset hypothesis using disaggregate data: The case of airbags and antilock brakes', Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 2006. Their disaggregate data mattered: the drivers who buy safety equipment are unusually careful to begin with, so aggregate comparisons flatter the devices. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11166-006-8288-7

question: Researchers looked for offsetting behaviour among skiers and snowboarders and did not find it: helmeted participants did not ski faster or collide harder, and head-injury reductions of 30 to 50 percent held up with no rise in risk-taking. An analyst who accepts the football and automobile findings still has to accommodate this one. What does the ski result establish?
answer: That the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law
choices: That the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law
That the offset appears under mandates but never with voluntary equipment
That the offset appears in road vehicles but never in sporting equipment
That the offset was refuted by the ski data and should now be abandoned
context: A systematic review of 23 studies of cycle-helmet use points the same way: only two found helmeted riders taking more risk, 18 found no such effect, and 10 linked helmets to more cautious riding (the categories overlap). The reasoning move tells you what to go and measure; it does not tell you the answer in advance. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: Sam Peltzman's 1975 result did not stand unchallenged. In 1977 Leslie Robertson reworked the same American automobile data and reported that belt requirements had cut deaths among car occupants with no matching rise among people outside the cars. On what ground did Robertson attack Peltzman's model?
answer: That it left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate
choices: That it left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate
That it used state records too coarse to separate rural from urban roads
That it began its series in 1947, before any of the devices had existed
That it counted serious injuries as deaths wherever hospital records failed
context: Later critics pressed the same line: Leonard Evans argued in a 1998 review that claimed evidence for full behavioural offset in transport came from aggregating dissimilar data and ignoring exposure. The dispute is about measurement, not about whether drivers respond to incentives at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: In 1982 the psychologist Gerald Wilde advanced a claim stronger than the economists had made. Where Sam Peltzman had said drivers spend part of a safety gain on speed, Wilde made a claim about how much danger someone will put up with in the first place. What did Wilde claim?
answer: That each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it
choices: That each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it
That risk tolerance climbs with age and drops away again after sixty
That drivers copy the risk level of whatever vehicles surround them
That risk tolerance is set by law and enforcement, not by the driver
context: Wilde set out risk homeostasis in 1982 and expanded it in Target Risk (1994). The theory predicts full cancellation: lower the objective risk and the person restores the felt risk by other means, so safety countermeasures are futile unless the appetite itself is addressed. That is a far stronger claim than Peltzman's, and much harder to defend -- which is why the two should not be treated as the same idea. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: The offsetting-behaviour finding is routinely reported in the press as 'safety rules do not save lives'. Writing at Econlib, David Henderson argues that this states the claim far more strongly than the economics supports. Suppose a study finds that a seat-belt law did reduce deaths, and also finds that belted drivers drove faster. What should the analyst conclude?
answer: Both results stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain
choices: Both results stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain
The two results contradict each other, so one of the datasets must be wrong
The offset shows the law failed, whatever the death figures appear to say
The death figures settle the matter, so the speed result can be set aside
context: Henderson: the effect predicts offsetting behaviour, and says nothing about whether the offset is large enough to cancel the benefit entirely. That is an empirical question, answered study by study. The reasoning move earns its keep by telling you that the engineering number is an upper bound and that you must go and measure the human response -- not by handing you a verdict on the policy. Source: David Henderson, 'What the Peltzman Effect Is and Isn't', Econlib (https://www.econlib.org/what-the-peltzman-effect-is-and-isnt/).

question: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat published, over his own name in Economic Sophisms, a mock petition addressed to the French Chamber of Deputies. Which trade did the pretend petitioners claim to represent?
context: Full title: 'Petition of the Manufacturers of Candles, Waxlights, Lamps, Candlesticks, Street Lamps, Snuffers, Extinguishers, and the Producers of Oil, Tallow, Rosin, Alcohol, and, generally, of Everything Connected with Lighting.' Bastiat published it under his own name, not anonymously. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: The petition of the candlemakers begs the French Chamber to pass a law requiring one specific piece of household infrastructure to be closed during daytime hours. Which object does it target?
context: The petition names 'all windows, dormers, skylights, inside and outside shutters, curtains, casements, bull's-eyes, deadlights, and blinds' -- every household aperture that lets in the free rival's product. Source: fee.org/resources/a-petition.

question: Bastiat's 1845 candlemakers' petition names a specific ruinous competitor whose cheap output is flooding the French market and undercutting domestic lighting-industry prices. The petitioners identify this rival in the second paragraph. Who is the rival?
context: 'This rival is none other than the sun.' Bastiat's satire lets the petitioners say the quiet part loud: their real complaint is that free sunlight is more efficient than any French candle. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: The candlemakers' petition appears as a chapter in Bastiat's larger collection of satirical economic pamphlets. What is the collection's title?
choices: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
context: First series 1845, second series 1848; the candlemakers' petition appears in the first series and remains the best-known chapter. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: The candlemakers' petition lists a chain of downstream French industries that will benefit if the sun is shut out: more tallow farms will be needed, more whaling fleets, more forests for wood, more shipping. This benefits-cascade parody is aimed at which real protectionist argument?
context: The petition ridicules the 19th-century multiplier claim ('every candlemaker's job creates jobs upstream in tallow, in oil, in wood, in shipping') by taking the exact same argument seriously and applying it to a tariff against the sun. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: The candlemakers' petition is a worked example of one specific logical move: taking an opponent's principle seriously and following it to a conclusion no one would defend. What is the standard Latin-name for that move?
context: The whole petition is a reductio: if the protectionist principle 'shelter domestic producers from cheap foreign competition' is sound, then it justifies a law against sunlight. Bastiat used the same technique in the negative-railway sophism. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: Milton Friedman's 1980 book Free to Choose refers directly to Bastiat's candlemakers' petition when arguing against 20th-century American trade policy. Friedman's move is that any argument that treats one thing as a threat and its opposite as a benefit deserves the candlemakers' test. Which pair does his move contrast?
answer: Abundance treated as a threat, scarcity treated as a benefit
choices: Abundance treated as a threat, scarcity treated as a benefit
Consumption treated as a threat, saving treated as a benefit
Imports treated as a threat, exports treated as a benefit
Immigration treated as a threat, emigration treated as a benefit
context: Friedman's Free to Choose (1980) uses Bastiat's petition to press the diagnostic question: does the policy treat MORE goods for less work as a bad thing? If so, it is the candlemakers' argument. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_to_Choose.

question: The other most-famous satirical pamphlet in economic history was published by Jonathan Swift in 1729 about Irish poverty, sharing the reductio-ad-absurdum technique with Bastiat's candlemakers. Which Swift pamphlet is the natural pair?
context: Swift's 1729 A Modest Proposal takes the exploitative-labor logic of 18th-century Irish policy seriously enough to propose eating Irish children; Bastiat's 1845 candlemakers takes protectionism seriously enough to tax the sun. Same technique, two masterpieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Modest_Proposal.

question: The candlemakers' petition is the reductio Bastiat aims at ONE of the two great political-economy arguments he classified as 'legal plunder' in his 1850 pamphlet The Law. Which of the two does the petition attack?
context: Bastiat named PROTECTIONISM and SOCIALISM as the two large categories of French legal plunder; the candlemakers' petition is his ridicule of protectionism, and the negative-railway is his ridicule of the make-work half of socialism. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: 'Petition of the Candlemakers' has become standing shorthand in economics writing for a very specific kind of argument. Which argument-shape does the phrase now flag?
answer: Any argument that treats free abundance as a threat requiring policy remedy
choices: Any argument that treats free abundance as a threat requiring policy remedy
Any argument that overstates the medium-term risks of a proposed policy
Any argument that appeals to fairness rather than efficiency
Any argument that uses foreign historical examples for a domestic case
context: Don Boudreaux's Cafe Hayek and countless econ-101 texts use 'candlemakers' petition' as the standing tag for any policy that would shut out cheaper substitutes to protect an incumbent producer. Source: cafehayek.com/tag/petition-of-the-candlemakers.

question: In 1958 a New Zealand-born economist at the London School of Economics published a paper documenting a striking historical correlation in British data between unemployment and wage inflation. The relationship was later named after him. What is it called?
context: A.W. Phillips's 1958 paper 'The Relation between Unemployment and the Rate of Change of Money Wage Rates' plotted a historical correlation. Later economists reinterpreted it as a policy trade-off. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: Through the 1960s many Keynesian economists interpreted the Phillips curve as a permanent policy menu -- lower unemployment could be bought with higher inflation, and vice versa. What did economists call this apparent choice?
context: The 1960s Keynesian view treated the Phillips curve as a menu: policymakers could pick a point along it. This became the theoretical justification for expansionary monetary and fiscal policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: In his December 1967 American Economic Association presidential address, an economist attacked the naive Phillips-curve trade-off, arguing workers eventually adjust their expectations and any long-run trade-off vanishes. Which economist gave that address?
context: Friedman's presidential address 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (published in the American Economic Review, March 1968) is the foundational statement of the natural-rate critique. Friedman won the Nobel Prize in 1976. Source: aeaweb.org (AER 1968).

question: The same year Friedman published his critique, another economist arrived at a similar 'expectations' rebuttal of the Phillips-curve trade-off independently and later won a Nobel Prize partly for the work. Who was he?
context: Phelps's 1967 papers reached the natural-rate conclusion independently of Friedman. He won the Nobel in 2006 partly for this work. The result is now called the Friedman-Phelps critique. Source: nobelprize.org (Phelps 2006).

question: Friedman and Phelps introduced a concept that recast the vertical long-run Phillips curve: a jobless rate the economy tends toward regardless of inflation. What did they call it?
context: The natural rate is set by real factors (technology, labor-market institutions, demographics) and is invariant to monetary policy in the long run. Monetary expansion can push unemployment below the natural rate only temporarily. Source: aeaweb.org (Friedman 1968).

question: The 1970s decisively falsified the simple Phillips-curve trade-off by producing an outcome the 1960s consensus said was impossible: high inflation AND high unemployment at the same time. What is this outcome usually called?
context: Stagflation was the 1970s combination of stagnant growth, high unemployment, and high inflation. The word entered mainstream use around 1970. By 1979 the US had roughly 6% unemployment and 11% inflation simultaneously. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagflation.

question: The modern version of the Phillips curve that survives in macroeconomics textbooks after the 1970s falsification adds a specific new variable to the wage equation. What is the modern textbook version called?
context: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve incorporates inflation expectations into the wage equation, matching the Friedman-Phelps critique. It is standard in modern macro textbooks and forms the basis of the Fed's inflation-targeting framework. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-inflation.

question: The 1970s stagflation followed a decade in which the Federal Reserve's chair had cooperated closely with the White House on loose monetary policy. Which Fed chair from 1970-78 is most associated with the pre-Volcker inflation drift?
context: Arthur Burns chaired the Fed 1970-78 under Nixon, Ford, and Carter. His diaries and Nixon-tape transcripts document political pressure to keep money easy through Nixon's 1972 re-election. Miller succeeded Burns briefly (1978-79); Volcker followed. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-inflation.

question: A.W. Phillips himself, before becoming an economist, had built a fascinating machine in 1949 that simulated the British economy with water flowing through transparent pipes and tanks. What was his machine called?
context: The MONIAC (Monetary National Income Analogue Computer), built by Phillips at LSE in 1949, was a hydraulic analog computer that used flowing water to model Keynesian income-expenditure identities. Working units are preserved at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and Cambridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MONIAC.

question: For an Austrian critic, Friedman's natural-rate argument was correct as far as it went but incomplete. What deeper Austrian point does Rothbard add on top of Friedman's Phillips-curve critique?
answer: Every attempt to fine-tune with monetary expansion eventually produces the same distortion-and-liquidation cycle
choices: Every attempt to fine-tune with monetary expansion eventually produces the same distortion-and-liquidation cycle
The natural rate is closer to zero than Friedman claimed
