context: The Journal des Debats was historically the paper of liberal-Orleanist bourgeois opinion under Louis-Philippe and remained an influential centrist daily under the Second Republic. Bastiat chose it deliberately -- his target reader was the propertied liberal, not the barricade fighter. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: In 1986 the Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to an American economist who, with Gordon Tullock, had built a whole formal school of thought around the point Bastiat's 1848 line stated in a sentence: that politicians and voters use state power to secure benefits from other citizens rather than serve a general interest. Who won that 1986 Nobel?
context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for his work founding public choice theory -- the formal analysis of politics using economic tools -- with his 1962 book The Calculus of Consent, co-authored with Gordon Tullock, as the flagship text. Buchanan repeatedly cited Bastiat as the classical statement of the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: Two French essays published within eleven days in September 1848 both attacked the Provisional Government's promises. One was Bastiat's 'The State,' with its 'great fiction' line. The other, published in the same paper, was an article by Alexis de Tocqueville. The two men held one seat between them on the same committee of the Constituent Assembly that autumn. Which committee was that?
context: Bastiat served on the Constituent Assembly's finance committee through 1848-1849 -- the committee handling the tax and spending questions his 'great fiction' line directly framed. Tocqueville, elected the same April, served in the Assembly as well and would soon join the government as foreign minister. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Bastiat's 'great fiction' line is quoted approvingly across the 20th-century classical-liberal tradition -- but the pedagogical payoff for a modern reader is the reasoning move it names. Which move does the line actually press?
answer: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
choices: That every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen
That any government is a criminal conspiracy against its own population
That representative democracy is preferable to monarchy on efficiency grounds
That the free market always produces the best possible distribution of wealth
context: The 'great fiction' Bastiat is naming is the illusion that the state has some independent fund of wealth of its own; the reasoning move is that every promised benefit must in fact come from someone -- the tax-payer, the money-holder, the excluded competitor. The reader can accept or reject Bastiat's evaluation; the MOVE is the transfer-recognition. James Buchanan's public choice theory, honored with the 1986 Nobel, formalized the same insight. Source: https://mises.org/mises-daily/frederic-bastiat-government.

question: For a hundred years before 1871 the classical economists -- Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Karl Marx -- had explained a good's price by the LABOR-HOURS embodied in producing it: a suit that took ten hours should be worth about twice as much as a suit that took five. Carl Menger's 1871 Principles of Economics replaced this account with a different source of value entirely. In Menger's account, where does value live?
answer: In a chooser's ranking of a specific unit at a specific moment
choices: In a chooser's ranking of a specific unit at a specific moment
In the labor-hours the producer expended
In the raw materials the good is made from
In the average price the market has historically paid
context: Menger's move was to relocate value from the OBJECT to the SUBJECT: the same loaf of bread ranks high to a hungry man and low to a full one, so value is not a property of the loaf. The labor theory (Smith 1776, Ricardo 1817, Marx 1867) had made value inhere in the good; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced it in 1871-1874 with subjective valuation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book); mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Menger's 1871 Principles of Economics illustrates the new theory with a pioneer farmer who owns five sacks of grain and no way to buy or sell more. The farmer assigns each sack to a different job -- basic food, extra food for strength, chicken feed, whisky-brewing, feed for his pet parrots. If robbers steal ONE sack, which use does the farmer abandon first, and thereby set the value of every sack he still has?
answer: The least important one -- parrot feed
choices: The least important one -- parrot feed
The most important one -- basic food
Every use loses an equal share
context: Menger's core marginal move is right here: the value of ONE sack is not the average across all uses and not the most important use, it is the LEAST important use the farmer would sacrifice on losing one. This is why the SAME grain is worth different amounts to a well-supplied farmer and a starving one -- their marginal uses differ. The example is from Book 3 of the 1871 Grundsaetze. Source: ecaef.org/carl-menger-and-the-idea-that-broke-economics-open/.

question: In The Wealth of Nations (1776) Adam Smith set down a paradox he confessed he could not solve: water is essential to human life and yet costs almost nothing, while a substance with no life-sustaining use at all sells for a fortune. The paradox stumped classical economics for the next 95 years. Which substance was Smith's high-priced puzzle?
context: Smith wrote: 'Nothing is more useful than water, but it will purchase scarce anything... A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' Smith moved on rather than solving it; the resolution waited for the 1871 Marginal Revolution. Salt was famously scarce in some ancient economies but not Smith's example; the tulip mania (1637) is a bubble story, not the paradox; silk was expensive but not paradoxically so. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: In the same year Menger published Principles in Vienna, an English economist independently published The Theory of Political Economy in London making the same core marginal-utility argument, and three years later a French-Swiss economist published Elements of Pure Economics in Lausanne doing the same again. Historians call the whole 1871-1874 cluster of THREE independent inventions of the same idea by what name?
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of the clearest cases of parallel discovery in intellectual history. The Methodenstreit was Menger's later 1883 quarrel over method with the German Historical School; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Paul Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Source: economicsandhistory.substack.com/p/the-marginal-revolution-and-neoclassical.

question: A student presses Menger on the diamond-water paradox: how can water, without which no one lives, be nearly free, while diamonds, useless for life, cost a fortune? Menger does not dispute the facts -- he says the puzzle dissolves once you stop comparing 'all water' to 'all diamonds' and look at the RIGHT unit. Which unit does he say the chooser is actually ranking?
answer: The next specific unit added to what he already has
choices: The next specific unit added to what he already has
The average per-ton price over the last decade
The total quantity produced worldwide each year
The moral desert of the person who wants it
context: A city-dweller with a full tap ranks the NEXT glass of water near-zero -- his thirst is already met; the NEXT diamond added to a collection nobody has still ranks high because it is scarce. Total utility of water is enormous and of diamonds tiny; the MARGINAL utility is the reverse, and price tracks the margin. This is Menger's founding move: value is set at the margin, not by the class. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_value.

question: Menger held that goods available in unlimited supply -- air on a mountainside, seawater at the beach -- may satisfy human wants but are NOT what he called 'economic goods'. Something must be true of a good before a chooser must rank one unit of it against another. Which condition does Menger require?
answer: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
choices: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
The good must have taken labor to produce
The good must be legally recognized as property
The good must have a market price above zero
context: For Menger, an unlimited good has utility but no VALUE, because no chooser is ever forced to give up one use to serve another -- there is no ranking at the margin. Only when the good is scarce relative to the wants it could satisfy does a chooser have to rank the marginal unit, and only then does the subjective theory generate a price. Labor-cost, legal recognition, and positive market price are consequences of scarcity, not its cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: The Austrian School's most famous German term -- Grenznutzen, 'edge-usefulness' -- appears nowhere in Menger's 1871 Principles. It was coined thirteen years later, in an 1884 book by one of Menger's two great pupils. When the term was translated back into English, it became the phrase every economics textbook now teaches. Who coined Grenznutzen?
context: Wieser (1851-1926) coined Grenznutzen in his 1884 Uber den Ursprung und die Hauptgesetze des wirtschaftlichen Werthes to name a concept his teacher had already articulated in prose. English 'marginal utility' is a direct back-translation of Wieser's coinage. Boehm-Bawerk, Menger's other great pupil, developed capital and interest theory; Menger wrote before the term existed; Walras wrote in French. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A tailor spends 10 hours making a badly-cut, badly-sewn suit that hangs poorly. A second tailor spends 5 hours making a well-cut, well-sewn suit that fits beautifully. On the labor theory of value the first suit should be worth about twice the second. On the subjective theory that Menger pressed against the classical tradition, which comparison actually holds?
answer: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
choices: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth MORE, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
The two suits are worth the same, because labor is labor
The 10-hour suit is still worth more, because it embodies more work
Neither suit has any value until a market price is quoted
context: This is the sharp edge of Menger's move against the labor theory: labor-hours cannot GENERATE value if a chooser ranks the badly-made product lower. Value flows one way only, from the ranking down to the price; labor spent producing something no one ranks highly is labor wasted, not value created. If the labor theory cannot survive this simple case, then Marx's entire theory of surplus value and exploitation -- built on the labor theory -- has no floor to stand on. Source: mises.org/articles-interest/subjective-theory-value.

question: David Ricardo laid down a labor-embodied theory of value in his 1817 Principles of Political Economy. Fifty years later a German exile in London built an entire theory of capitalist exploitation on Ricardo's foundation -- 'socially necessary labor time' as the source of every commodity's value, with the difference between that value and the worker's wage taken as surplus by the capitalist. Menger's subjective theory dissolves this whole edifice by showing that labor cannot generate value at all. Whose 1867 book carries the exploitation argument the subjective theory undercuts?
answer: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
choices: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
John Stuart Mill, in Principles of Political Economy
Thomas Malthus, in An Essay on the Principle of Population
Jean-Baptiste Say, in A Treatise on Political Economy
context: Marx's 1867 Das Kapital vol. 1 inherits Ricardo's labor theory and refines it as 'socially necessary labor time'; the entire theory of surplus value, exploitation, and the falling rate of profit depends on labor being the source of value. If Menger's subjective account is right, this foundation is gone: value comes from the chooser's ranking, not from labor-hours. Boehm-Bawerk drove the point home explicitly in Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896). Mill (1848), Malthus (1798), and Say (1803) all predate Marx and do not carry the exploitation theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_theory_of_value.

question: Under the subjective theory of value, the price a chooser will pay for the next unit lives inside his own head at the moment of choice -- it is set by his ranking of that unit against alternative uses he alone knows. A central planning board trying to set a rational price for that unit therefore faces a problem that no amount of data-gathering can solve, because the relevant fact is not in any dataset. Which later Austrian argument does this feature of the subjective theory directly feed into?
context: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth runs directly out of subjective value: if value lives in individual choosers' rankings, then a central planning board without market prices has no way to know how to allocate scarce means -- the information it would need is dispersed across millions of heads and revealed only through the choices those choosers actually make. Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' extends the same point. Ricardo, Friedman, and Coase pressed unrelated arguments. Source: mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Menger's 1871 Principles opened the German-speaking Marginal Revolution but was not translated into English for 79 years -- the tradition traveled to America through Mises's students, not through the founding book itself. When James Dingwall and Bert F. Hoselitz's English edition finally reached print through the Free Press, with an introduction by Frank Knight, which year did it appear?
context: The 1950 Free Press edition appeared 29 years after Menger's death (1921), 79 years after the German original (1871), and only after Menger's pupil Hayek had already moved from Vienna to LSE (1931) and then Chicago (1950). Frank Knight -- Milton Friedman's teacher at Chicago -- wrote the introduction. The gap is a measure of how far the Austrian tradition had traveled inside German-speaking economics before English-speaking economics noticed the founding text. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In 1912 a 31-year-old Vienna economist published his first major book, submitting the same manuscript to the University of Vienna as the thesis he needed to earn the right to lecture there. The book founded Austrian monetary economics. Who was the young author?
context: Ludwig von Mises (born Sep 29 1881) was 31 when 'Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel' appeared. He submitted it as his Habilitationsschrift to obtain the venia legendi, the license to lecture at university level. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; mises.org/library/book/theorie-des-geldes-und-der-umlaufsmittel.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1912 monetary book appeared in German first. In English, translator Harold Batson rendered its title as 'The Theory of Money and Credit'. What was Mises's original German title?
answer: Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
choices: Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
context: 'Umlaufsmittel' literally means 'means of circulation'; Batson translated it as 'fiduciary media' inside the text, but the publisher chose the cleaner 'Money and Credit' for the English title. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: Carl Menger's 1871 marginal-utility theory said all goods get their value from their subjective usefulness to individuals. That created a puzzle when applied to MONEY: money is useful because it has purchasing power, but its purchasing power comes from yesterday's prices, which came from the day before's prices, and so on. Ludwig von Mises's 1912 book gave the puzzle its standard resolution, one now known by a short name. What name?
context: Mises's move: today's demand rests on yesterday's known purchasing power, and you can trace the chain back through time until you reach a moment when the money-good had a non-monetary use (gold as jewelry, silver as ornament, cattle as food). The circularity dissolves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1912 book contained something monetary economists had never seen before: the earliest statement of what would grow into the Austrian theory of the boom-bust cycle. A younger economist worked out the full apparatus in the 1930s -- his 1931 lectures 'Prices and Production' and his 1933 book 'Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle' turned Mises's seed into what economists now call Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Who was he?
context: Hayek's LSE lectures 'Prices and Production' (1931) built the roundabout-production capital theory of Boehm-Bawerk together with Mises's monetary seed into the full ABCT: artificially low interest rates from bank credit expansion distort the structure of production, generating an unsustainable boom that must end in a bust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: In 1912 Ludwig von Mises had to explain how money escapes Carl Menger's 1871 circularity puzzle. His answer traced money-demand backward in time, one day at a time, until it landed on a specific historical moment where the chain could close. Which kind of moment did the regression have to reach?
answer: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
choices: A day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use
A day when a sovereign first stamped his image on a coin and decreed its face value
A day when a chartered private bank first issued notes payable to bearer on demand
A day when a joint-stock company first offered redeemable shares in a public market
context: Gold jewelry and dentistry, silver ornament, cattle used for food and traction, salt for preservation. Once the chain lands on a real barter-good with real demand for its own sake, the value it later carries as money is grounded in something outside the circular loop. Source: mises.org/online-book/man-economy-and-state-power-and-market/5-marginal-utility-money/b-money-regression.

question: Harold E. Batson translated Ludwig von Mises's 1912 monetary book into English in 1934, twenty-two years after the German original. But it was not until an American edition twenty years later that Mises added a whole new section, written expressly to answer the postwar mainstream that had captured monetary theory. Which press published that expanded 1953 edition?
context: The 1953 Yale edition added Part Four -- Mises's direct response to the Keynesian orthodoxy that had swept postwar Anglo-American economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1912 monetary book is a dense academic work. In 1963 a leading Austrian economist wrote a slim 134-page paperback popular restatement designed for mass distribution, titled 'What Has Government Done to Our Money?'. Who wrote it?
context: Rothbard packed the case for commodity money and against government-run currency into a booklet aimed at the general reader. Fifty years on it remains the standard introduction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Has_Government_Done_to_Our_Money%3F.

question: In January 2009 a new digital money called Bitcoin was mined into existence. It was purely digital, it had no state backing, and it had never traded as anything else. When Austrian economists took a first look, one camp declared Bitcoin ruled out on Misesian grounds -- pointing to a specific feature of the 1912 argument that Bitcoin appeared to fail. Which feature did they invoke against Bitcoin?
answer: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
choices: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
The quantity theory's requirement of stable velocity of circulation
The state theory's requirement of tax-driven acceptance
The real-bills doctrine's requirement of short-term commercial backing
context: The debate raged in Austrian circles from about 2011. Critics argued Bitcoin was born as pure money and therefore was ruled out on Misesian grounds; defenders had to find the prior demand Mises's chain required. Source: mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bitcoin-regression-theorem-and-emergence-new-medium-exchange.

question: Konrad Graf's February 27 2013 essay 'Bitcoins, the regression theorem, and that curious but unthreatening empirical world' answered the Austrian objection that Bitcoin violated Ludwig von Mises's 1912 theorem. Graf argued the objection missed a real utility the earliest Bitcoin users valued the token for. Which utility did he point to?
answer: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
choices: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
Its use as a store of value with a predictably fixed twenty-one-million supply cap
Its use as a settlement layer for high-frequency exchange trading
Its use as programmable collateral for decentralised lending contracts
context: The first buyers wanted the tokens because the underlying protocol did something no other technology could -- move digital value across a network without a trusted third party. That utility, present before any market price, was the non-monetary demand the regression theorem required. Source: www.konradsgraf.com/blog1/2013/2/27/in-depth-bitcoins-the-regression-theorem-and-that-curious-bu.html.

question: Not every Austrian accepted that the regression theorem needed defending against Bitcoin. Robert Murphy and Silas Barta broke with Konrad Graf and Peter Surda -- refusing to hunt for a prior non-monetary use at all, on the grounds that Ludwig von Mises's 1912 argument answered a different question than the one Bitcoin poses. How did they characterise the reach of the regression theorem?
answer: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
choices: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
As overturned by Milton Friedman's 1956 restatement of the quantity theory
As applying only to commodities Menger's 1892 essay classified as saleable
As already refuted by Georg Knapp's 1905 state theory of money
context: Murphy and Barta treated the theorem as a historical explanation of how commodity monies emerged, not a constraint on future ones. Konrad Graf, Peter Surda, and Jeffrey Tucker took the other route -- accept the theorem, find the prior non-monetary demand. Source: stephankinsella.com/2025/07/austrians-bitcoin-impossible/.

question: Bill Clinton's Treasury Secretary from 1995 to 1999 had previously spent 26 years at Goldman Sachs, rising to co-chairman. After leaving Treasury he joined Citigroup, where he earned about $126 million over the next decade -- through the bailout the firm received in 2008-09. Who was he?
context: Robert Rubin, Goldman Sachs 1966-1992, Treasury Secretary 1995-99 under Clinton, Citigroup executive committee 1999-2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rubin.

question: George W. Bush's Treasury Secretary from July 2006 to January 2009 -- the exact window that spanned the 2007-08 financial crisis -- had spent 32 years at Goldman Sachs and been its CEO. Who was he?
context: Henry 'Hank' Paulson joined Goldman in 1974, became CEO in 1999, and served as Treasury Secretary July 2006 to January 2009. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulson.

question: During Henry Paulson's tenure at Treasury, the September 2008 rescue of AIG has been criticized as favoring Goldman Sachs, which was AIG's largest counterparty. Roughly how much did Goldman ultimately receive as an AIG counterparty via the rescue?
context: Goldman received approximately $12.9B as an AIG counterparty via the ~$182B AIG rescue. The AIG-Goldman payments became a focal point of revolving-door criticism of the 2008 crisis response. Source: fcic.gov (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report, 2011).

question: Timothy Geithner served as President of the New York Federal Reserve from 2003 to 2009 -- the regulator most directly responsible for the systemically-important banks that failed in 2008 -- and then as Barack Obama's Treasury Secretary from 2009 to 2013. After leaving Treasury he joined which type of firm as president?
context: Geithner joined the private-equity firm Warburg Pincus as president in March 2014. His 2014 memoir Stress Test explicitly defends the 2008-09 bailouts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Geithner; warburgpincus.com.

question: Between leaving the Federal Reserve in 2018 and being appointed as Joe Biden's Treasury Secretary in January 2021, Janet Yellen earned approximately $7 million in speaking fees. From whom did that money principally come?
answer: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
choices: Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs
context: Yellen's financial disclosures documented approximately $7M in Wall Street speaking fees over the two-year interval. The pattern -- top financial-regulator role followed by high-fee industry advisory -- matches the earlier three Treasury secretaries. Source: US Office of Government Ethics disclosures 2020-21.

question: The IMF's former chief economist Simon Johnson published a widely-read 2009 essay in The Atlantic making the mainstream case that US financial-crisis policy showed the same pattern of financial-sector capture familiar from Latin American case studies. What memorable phrase did his essay title use?
context: Simon Johnson, 'The Quiet Coup' (The Atlantic, May 2009). Johnson, MIT professor and former IMF chief economist, applied his IMF-era capture-diagnosis toolkit to the US financial-crisis response. Source: theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2009/05.

question: In 2012 the Chicago economist Luigi Zingales published a book arguing that America's financial system had drifted from a free-market model toward a version he called crony-capitalism, and calling for reforms to restore genuine market discipline. What was the book's title?
context: Luigi Zingales, A Capitalism for the People: Recapturing the Lost Genius of American Prosperity (Basic Books, 2012). Zingales -- Italian-born, teaching at Chicago Booth -- became a mainstream-economics voice against financial-sector regulatory capture. Source: basicbooks.com (Zingales 2012).

question: The revolving-door pattern is not confined to Treasury and the Fed. In 2019 a former FDA Commissioner joined the board of a large pharmaceutical company shortly after leaving his agency post. Who was that commissioner?
context: Scott Gottlieb, FDA Commissioner 2017-19, joined the Pfizer board in June 2019. It is a parallel modern case of the pattern documented across finance, defense, and pharmaceutical regulation. Source: pfizer.com (board announcement June 2019).

question: The reasoning-move Simon Johnson and Luigi Zingales share is that the revolving door is best analyzed as a form of Stigler-style regulatory capture. What specific structural feature makes the capture operate?
answer: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
choices: The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it
Regulators are secretly bribed with cash payments
Federal law requires all regulators to work in industry first
The industry has hidden veto authority over hiring decisions
context: The Stigler-capture-via-revolving-door mechanism: the career incentives of every serving official partly align with the industry regardless of individual character, because the qualified pool has this shape by construction. This is institutional-incentive selection, not corruption. Source: Johnson (2009); Zingales (2012); Stigler (1971).

question: The four Treasury secretaries' Wall-Street-to-Treasury pattern illustrates a general reasoning move applied to top financial regulation. The move is NOT that these individuals were personally corrupt. What is the actual claim?
answer: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
choices: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
The pattern is criminal conspiracy prosecutable under federal statute
The pattern is entirely random and requires no explanation
The pattern is imposed by international treaty obligations
context: Each of the four served legally and by presidential appointment. The critique targets the STRUCTURAL pattern that produces the pattern: the pool of qualified candidates comes from and returns to the industry. Source: Zingales (2012); Johnson (2009); Stigler (1971).

question: The academic literature has begun to price the revolving door directly. Bertrand, Bombardini, and Trebbi's 2014 American Economic Review paper found that ex-Members of Congress and ex-senior staffers who become lobbyists command salary premiums over their government pay in a specific range. What range does the literature typically report?
answer: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
choices: 500 to 1000 percent premiums over their government pay
Essentially no premium over public pay
context: The Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi 2014 AER paper 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?' documented substantial premiums for connected lobbyists, consistent with a market pricing capture-value. Source: aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.12.3885.

question: What made Bastiat's writing distinctive against the continental mathematical style of theorists like Antoine Cournot was his commitment to a specific kind of prose. What kind of prose did he write?
answer: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
choices: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
context: Bastiat wrote so that a French farmer could follow the argument, deliberately unlike Cournot's 1838 Recherches that used calculus to model demand curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Antoine_Augustin_Cournot.

question: Bastiat's characteristic method opens each argument by giving the reader something to picture -- a shopkeeper's window, a proposed railway, a French Chamber debate -- rather than a bare thesis. What is that opening move called?
context: Part one of the Bastiat method: put a scene in front of the reader before you make the argument. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The second part of the Bastiat method requires that you first present the argument you plan to answer in a specific form before answering it. In what form must the opposing view be stated?
context: Part two: state the opposing view sympathetically and at its strongest. This is Bastiat's 'ineptly defended' discipline, later renamed 'steelmanning' in 21st-century rationalist writing. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The third and final part of the Bastiat method surfaces what the opposing view has hidden. What does the third step trace?
context: Part three: trace the unseen -- the tailor whose sale was lost when the shopkeeper repaired his broken window, the worker priced out by the minimum wage, the consumer who paid more for domestic goods. Source: bastiat.org.

question: A 1946 Harper book by an American journalist applied Bastiat's method chapter by chapter to New Deal policies, becoming the most-read popular Austrian introduction in English. What is the book's title?
context: Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) is a chapter-by-chapter application of the seen/unseen method to mid-20th-century American policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: A 1980 Basic Books treatise by Thomas Sowell applied the same seen/unseen method to modern policy questions, using ordinary decision-making to test policy claims. What is the book's title?
context: Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) is the most sustained modern application of the classical-liberal knowledge-and-decision framework to policy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Bastiat's method is powerful but limited. Which classical-liberal topic does it NOT by itself provide the technical apparatus for?
choices: Public-facing argument about the broken window
context: For monetary theory the tradition needs Menger, Mises, and Hayek; for capital theory Bohm-Bawerk; for public choice Buchanan and Tullock. Bastiat's method is the first tool, not the only one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Almost the whole of Bastiat's published output was compressed into the last few years before his 1850 death. Roughly how many years did his major writing career span?
context: Bastiat farmed at Mugron in the Landes for most of his adult life, publishing his first major essays in 1844-1845 and dying December 24, 1850. The pamphlets, sophisms, and Harmonies were all produced in that five-year window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: For decades a federal program has held the US wholesale price of one everyday grocery-store commodity at roughly twice the world price by using import quotas and price-support loans. Which commodity does that program cover?
context: The US Sugar Program, established by the Sugar Act 1934, still runs under each Farm Bill; typical US price in the 2010s was about 35 cents per pound against a world price of about 17 cents. Source: gao.gov/products/rced-00-126.

question: The US Sugar Program was created by a specific 1934 New Deal statute and is still updated in each Farm Bill. What is the 1934 statute's name?
context: The Sugar Act 1934 first structured the quota, loan, and allotment system that still supports US sugar prices today under the 2018 Farm Bill's re-authorization. Source: grokipedia.com/page/United_States_Sugar_Program.

question: In 2003 the maker of a famous ring-shaped hard candy closed its US plant in Holland, Michigan and moved production to a foreign city where sugar cost about half the American price. To which city did the plant relocate?
context: Kraft Foods moved Life Savers production from Holland, Michigan to Montreal in 2003 because Canadian sugar was about half the US price under the US Sugar Program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Life_Savers.

question: Two Chicago-area candy makers also relocated much of their production abroad in the 2000s, citing US sugar input costs. Which pair of Chicago-area candy makers made those moves?
context: Ferrara Pan Candy Company moved much of its Chicago-area production to Mexico in the 2000s; Brach's Confections closed its Chicago plant in 2003 and moved to Mexico. Both cited US sugar prices. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ferrara_Candy_Company.

question: The US Sugar Program survives every Farm Bill even though hundreds of millions of consumers pay slightly more for candy, soda, and baked goods. Which political-economy reasoning move best explains why the program keeps winning?
answer: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
choices: Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
context: Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965): about 4,000 sugar farms get large concentrated payoffs and organize politically; about 330 million consumers each pay a few dollars extra a year and do not. The smaller organized group wins. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: When a US sugar-industry lobbyist argues that a domestic industry needs government protection from cheaper foreign competition, Bastiat's most famous satire mocks exactly that argument. Which satire did Bastiat publish in 1845?
context: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat's Petition of the Candlemakers had French makers of candles and lamps demand a law blocking sunlight to protect them from unfair sun-powered competition. Source: bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: Bastiat's method points at the DOWNSTREAM industries that use sugar as an input. What outcome does his method predict for those industries when a domestic law doubles their input cost against the world price?
answer: They move production to where sugar is cheap
choices: They move production to where sugar is cheap
They automate away all remaining sugar workers
They keep US production and absorb the input cost
They petition congress to raise consumer prices further
context: The predicted move played out in 2003 when Life Savers relocated from Michigan to Montreal, in the 2000s when Ferrara Pan and Brach's moved much production to Mexico. Higher US input costs pushed candy jobs across the border. Source: trade.gov/employment-changes-us-food-manufacturing-impact-sugar-prices.

question: The politically-organized US beneficiaries of the Sugar Program are dominated by one Florida-based family that owns Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals. What is that family's name?
context: The Fanjul brothers of Florida own Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals; they are the paradigm case of a small, politically-organized beneficiary group that has kept the Sugar Program in every Farm Bill. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fanjul_brothers.

question: In September 1945 the American Economic Review published an eleven-page essay -- no equations, no data, no charts -- with the plain title 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.' Today it is the most-cited paper its author ever wrote, with over 22,000 citations on Google Scholar. Which economist wrote it?
context: F. A. Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4, September 1945, pages 519-530 -- eleven pages that became one of the most-cited economics papers of the 20th century. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society).

question: F. A. Hayek's most-cited paper, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945), appeared in the flagship journal of the American Economic Association. Which journal?
context: The essay appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London (LSE had by then returned from its Cambridge evacuation). Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945), F. A. Hayek argued that the economic problem of society is NOT primarily how to allocate given resources -- which was the problem the mathematical socialist planners of the 1930s had been solving on blackboards. What is the economic problem, according to Hayek?
answer: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
choices: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
How to equalize the marginal productivity of capital across all industries
How to compute the aggregate demand curve for a whole national economy
How to eliminate the fluctuations of the business cycle through fiscal policy
context: Hayek's reframing was the essay's central move: the socialist-calculation debate was not about better arithmetic; it was about the unavailability of the underlying data to any single mind or committee. The knowledge that a market uses to allocate resources is scattered across millions of heads and cannot be gathered up to a central board in usable time. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago hosted PDF (https://home.uchicago.edu/~vlima/courses/econ200/spring01/hayek.pdf).

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay draws a sharp line between two kinds of knowledge. On one side is the scientific knowledge in textbooks that a central board could in principle collect. On the other side is a different kind of knowledge -- inherently dispersed, held by individuals about their particular jobs, ships, warehouses, and customers. What does Hayek call this second, load-bearing kind of knowledge?
answer: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
choices: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
The general theory of aggregate demand and supply
The rational expectations of forward-looking agents
The universal grammar of market institutions
context: Hayek's phrase: the important knowledge in an economy is 'the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- that a certain ship is half-empty, that a warehouse has a surplus, that a foreman on the third shift has spotted a way to save two hours. This knowledge is inherently local and inherently dispersed. Source: Hayek 1945, Econlib version (https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html).

question: Hayek's 1945 essay contains its most-quoted concrete example on page 526: a market for one particular metal. When a new use for the metal is discovered somewhere in the world, or a mine closes, the metal's price rises; every user then economizes on it without needing to know WHY the price rose. Which metal did Hayek use as his running example?
context: The tin example on page 526 of the American Economic Review version is the paragraph everyone quotes. Hayek's point: a single number -- the tin price -- carries the whole world's changing knowledge about tin (mine closures, new uses, war coming) to every user of tin, without any user needing to know the underlying cause. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF.

question: In 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' F. A. Hayek gave a famous metaphor for the price system: it works like a piece of machinery for registering change, a system where each producer watches only the movement of a few pointers. To which modern technology did Hayek compare the price system?
context: Hayek's phrase: the price system is 'a kind of machinery for registering change, or a system of telecommunications which enables individual producers to watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials.' Prices carry knowledge no single mind holds. Source: Western Sydney Pressbooks critical-analysis version (https://westernsydney.pressbooks.pub/criticalanalysis/chapter/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/).

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay sharpened an argument Ludwig von Mises had opened in a 1920 paper. Mises had argued that without market exchange there can be no rational prices, and without prices no rational allocation. What did Hayek ADD to Mises's argument that made the case even sharper against central planning?
answer: That the planner also cannot ACQUIRE the dispersed knowledge that market prices generate in the first place
choices: That the planner also cannot ACQUIRE the dispersed knowledge that market prices generate in the first place
That workers under central planning consume less than workers in market economies
That planned economies inevitably suffer higher rates of long-run consumer price inflation
That central planning erodes property rights and thereby weakens the rule of law
context: Mises 1920 said no exchange, no prices, no rational allocation. Hayek 1945 added: even if a benevolent, honest planner had perfect intentions, the dispersed knowledge that market prices summarize is not gatherable in usable time by any central agency. The Austrian critique of planning is not about will or motive -- it is about knowability. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF; Mises Institute critical commentary.

question: Hayek's 1945 American Economic Review essay was reprinted three years later as one of the chapters of his 1948 book -- a Chicago collection of his essays on individualism, spontaneous order, and the socialist-calculation debate. What is the 1948 book?
choices: Studies in Philosophy Politics and Economics
context: Individualism and Economic Order (University of Chicago Press, 1948) collected Hayek's essays from the 1930s and 1940s including 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937), and 'The Meaning of Competition.' The Constitution of Liberty (1960), Studies (1967), and The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) are all real Hayek works of later or different focus. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In December 1974 F. A. Hayek delivered the Nobel Memorial Prize lecture in Stockholm on the failures of the mathematical macroeconomics of the day. The title of the lecture was a direct descendant of the 1945 essay's argument about what a central mind cannot hold. What was the title?
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretense of Knowledge' argued that the postwar economics profession had adopted the manner of the physical sciences while imitating something it could not actually deliver -- the pretense that macroeconomic aggregates and models could substitute for the dispersed knowledge the price system aggregates. The lecture is the direct descendant of the 1945 essay. Source: Econlib version of Hayek 1945.

question: The reasoning move at the heart of Hayek's 1945 essay is one a critic of central planning can carry into any policy debate -- rent control, minimum wages, wage-price controls, ration schemes. It is NOT a moral verdict; it is a claim about knowability. Which move does the essay actually press?
answer: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
choices: That the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board
That central planners are always corrupt and always self-interested
That a planned economy must eventually generate hyperinflation of the consumer price index
That workers in planned economies are forbidden from changing jobs by law
context: The essay's argument is a claim about the STRUCTURE of economic knowledge, not a moral or motive claim. Even a saintly, brilliant planner cannot hold the knowledge the price system aggregates because that knowledge lives in millions of individual heads about local circumstances. The student can accept or reject the move, but the essay actually presses this reasoning move, not the corruption or hyperinflation charges. Source: Hayek 1945.

question: F. A. Hayek's 1945 essay closes with a striking image of what a market economy accomplishes: without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause of a raw-material scarcity, tens of thousands of people are made to use the material more sparingly. What one word from the essay best names this achievement Hayek was praising?
context: Hayek writes: 'The marvel is that in a case like that of a scarcity of one raw material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' The word MARVEL carries the essay's astonishment -- that a system no one designed does what no committee could. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: In the late 1920s and early 1930s the private seminar of Ludwig von Mises in Vienna gathered many of the young economists who would later carry the Austrian School into the English-speaking world. One of them, Friedrich von Hayek, was the first to leave. Which British institution invited him in January 1931 to give the four lectures that led to a permanent chair?
context: Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding LSE's economics department, brought Hayek over from 27 to 30 January 1931 to give the lectures published later that year as Prices and Production. The talks landed so well that LSE offered Hayek the Tooke Chair the following year. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Friedrich von Hayek stayed at the London School of Economics for nearly two decades after Lionel Robbins's 1931 invitation. Which chair did he hold from 1932 until he left for the University of Chicago in 1950?
answer: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
choices: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
The Drummond Chair of Political Economy
The Marshall Chair of Political Economy
context: Named for the 19th-century monetary theorist Thomas Tooke, the Tooke Chair was LSE's senior economics professorship. Hayek held it from 1932, became a British subject in 1938, and finally left in 1950 for a position in Chicago's Committee on Social Thought. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Fritz Machlup had studied under Ludwig von Mises in Vienna in the 1920s. In 1933, as Central European conditions worsened, he took a Rockefeller fellowship that carried him to Columbia, Harvard, Chicago and Stanford. In 1935 he settled into an American professorship that anchored the next twelve years of his career. Where?
context: Machlup held his Buffalo chair from 1935 to 1947, later moving to Johns Hopkins and then Princeton. He was one of the first of Mises's Vienna circle to make a fully American career. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fritz Machlup'.

question: Gottfried Haberler, another Vienna student of Mises and Wieser, spent two years in the mid-1930s working as an economic expert for an international organization on the shores of Lake Geneva, an appointment out of which he wrote the trade-cycle survey Prosperity and Depression. Which body employed him from 1934 to 1936?
context: Haberler served in the economic administration of the League of Nations in Geneva from 1934 to 1936. In autumn 1936 he moved to a Harvard professorship that lasted until his 1971 retirement. Source: Britannica, 'Gottfried von Haberler'.

question: Oskar Morgenstern, a director of the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research and a member of the Mises seminar, was outside Europe when German troops crossed into Austria on 13 March 1938 and effected the Anschluss. Where was he, and what did he do?
answer: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
choices: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
In Zurich on sabbatical; he returned home the following month
In London consulting for the Bank of England; he moved on to Cambridge
In Stockholm at a conference; he stayed and took a Riksbank post
context: Morgenstern was travelling in America as a Carnegie Visiting Professor when the Anschluss occurred. From six invitations he chose a three-year appointment as Class of 1913 Lecturer in Political Economy at Princeton, and simply did not return home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar Morgenstern'.

question: Ludwig von Mises himself left Vienna in 1934 for a paid chair he had never been offered in his own city. Which foreign institution did he move to, where he taught for the next six years?
answer: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
choices: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
context: Vienna had recognised Mises with only an unpaid Privatdozent title. The Geneva institute (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) gave him his first paid professorship. He held the chair from 1934 until 1940. Source: Mises Institute, 'Ludwig von Mises: The Logician of Freedom'.

question: On 4 July 1940, with France newly under German occupation and Switzerland looking exposed, Ludwig von Mises and his wife Margit left Geneva. After being turned back three times at the Spanish frontier and finally getting a visa at Toulouse, they crossed Spain and boarded a ship for the United States. From which port did they sail?
context: Portugal's neutrality made Lisbon the great escape port for European refugees in 1940. Mises and Margit sailed from there and docked in New Jersey on 2 August 1940, where their Viennese friend Alfred Schutz met them on the pier. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Celebrating the Arrival of Ludwig von Mises in America'.

question: When Ludwig von Mises stepped off the ship in New Jersey on 2 August 1940, he was already regarded as one of the greatest economists of his generation. How old was he, and what university appointment awaited him in America?
answer: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
choices: Fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life
Forty-four, and a full Harvard professorship awaited him
Sixty-seven, and a Yale endowed chair had been arranged in advance
Fifty-two, and a Chicago professorship followed within the year
context: Mises was born on 29 September 1881. He turned 59 the month after his arrival. From 1945 to 1969 he taught at New York University as an unpaid Visiting Professor; the William Volker Fund paid his stipend until 1962, and a consortium including the businessman Lawrence Fertig, who sat on the NYU board, took over afterwards. Source: FEE, 'Ludwig von Mises: A Prophet Without Honor in His Own Land'.

question: The mathematician Karl Menger, son of the founder of the Austrian School, left Vienna a full year before the Anschluss for a visiting professorship at an American Catholic university, where he then formally resigned his Vienna chair in March 1938. Which university took him in?
context: Menger arrived in South Bend, Indiana in autumn 1937 and stayed until 1946. His father Carl Menger had founded the Austrian School with the 1871 Grundsaetze; the son carried the family name into American mathematics. Source: MacTutor, 'Karl Menger'.

question: Seven years after the Nazi collapse a small group of scholars gathered on a mountain above Lake Geneva to see whether classical liberal thought could be rebuilt after the war. Friedrich Hayek convened the meeting on 10 April 1947; 36 attended, including Ludwig von Mises, Fritz Machlup, Milton Friedman, George Stigler, Karl Popper and Lionel Robbins. What institution was founded there?
context: The Mont Pelerin Society took its name from the hotel above Lake Geneva where the founding meeting was held. Hayek served as its first President until 1961. Half a dozen of the founders were direct veterans of Mises's old Vienna Privatseminar. Source: montpelerin.org, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: By 1974 the crossing of the Austrian School to the English-speaking world was fully vindicated when the Royal Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to a former member of Mises's Vienna seminar, jointly with the Swedish social-democrat Gunnar Myrdal. Which Vienna emigre took the prize?
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel citation named his work on money, credit and interdependence between economic, social and institutional phenomena. Machlup, Haberler and Morgenstern each made major contributions in America but Hayek alone of the Vienna diaspora was Nobel-honoured. Source: Britannica, 'F. A. Hayek'.

question: In 1920s Vienna, three great intellectual seminars ran within walking distance of each other, all in the shattered capital of the former Habsburg empire. Alongside Mises's economics Privatseminar and Karl Menger the younger's Mathematical Colloquium, what was the third circle called?
context: The Vienna Circle of logical positivists, gathered around Moritz Schlick and Rudolf Carnap, was the leading interwar philosophy-of-science movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: In 1931 a young Austrian mathematician presented at Karl Menger the younger's Mathematical Colloquium a pair of theorems showing that any consistent formal system rich enough to include arithmetic contains truths that cannot be proved within it. Who presented them?
context: Kurt Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorems were presented partly through Menger's Vienna colloquium, one of the most famous mathematical results of the 20th century. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Godel%27s_incompleteness_theorems.

question: The Vienna Circle's founding leader was assassinated on the steps of the University of Vienna by a former student on June 22 of a specific year. Who was the founding leader who was killed?
context: Moritz Schlick was shot dead by Johann Nelbock on the University of Vienna's Philosophenstiege on June 22, 1936, an early hammer-blow to the interwar Vienna intellectual scene. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moritz_Schlick.

question: The Vienna Circle was ideologically opposed to Mises's classical-liberal economics group. Which political tradition was the Circle's leading socialist theorist, Otto Neurath, most identified with?
context: Otto Neurath combined logical-positivist philosophy with Austro-Marxist socialism; the Vienna Circle formally endorsed physicalism and rejected metaphysics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Rudolf Carnap left Vienna in 1935 for a chair at an American university that became a major North American home of logical positivism. Which university did Carnap join?
context: Carnap took a chair at the University of Chicago in 1935 and taught there until 1952 before moving to UCLA. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vienna_Circle.

question: Kurt Godel escaped Vienna in 1940 via an unusual route across Asia, arriving at a specific American institution where he spent the rest of his career. Where did Godel end up?
answer: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
choices: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
context: Godel fled via the Trans-Siberian Railway and Japan in 1940, arriving at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he became a colleague of Einstein and von Neumann. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kurt_Godel.

question: Vienna's whole interwar intellectual world was scattered by a specific political event in 1938. Which event effectively ended the scene?
context: The March 1938 Anschluss brought Nazi Germany into Austria and expelled Jewish intellectuals from Vienna's universities. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anschluss.

question: One Viennese philosopher developed his own philosophy of science partly in reaction to the Vienna Circle's positivism, publishing Logik der Forschung in 1934, and later became famous for the criterion of falsifiability. Who was he?
context: Karl Popper's Logik der Forschung (1934) put falsifiability at the center of scientific method, in opposition to Vienna Circle verificationism. He shared the classical-liberal politics of Mises without belonging to the Circle. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Popper.

question: On the strength of his 1871 Principles of Economics, Carl Menger was appointed to a professorship at the University of Vienna in what year?
context: Menger took the chair in 1873 in the Faculty of Law and Political Economy (economics was then taught inside the law faculty) and held it for thirty years, until 1903. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Carl_Menger.

question: On Menger's 1903 retirement his Vienna chair passed to one of his first-generation students, a nobleman who moved from Prague to succeed him. Who took the chair?
context: Wieser held the Vienna chair from 1903 to 1922. He also served as Austro-Hungarian Minister of Commerce in 1917-1918. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: The other great first-generation Menger student took a separate Vienna chair in 1904 after resigning from his post as Austro-Hungarian Finance Minister, and taught there until his 1914 death. Who was he?
context: Bohm-Bawerk held a parallel Vienna chair from 1904 until his death in 1914, giving Vienna both leading Menger students teaching side by side for a decade. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: Bohm-Bawerk's Vienna seminar in the years before World War I attracted a striking set of students who would become important figures on VERY different sides of 20th-century politics. Which trio sat in that seminar?
answer: Ludwig von Mises, Otto Bauer, and Rudolf Hilferding
choices: Ludwig von Mises, Otto Bauer, and Rudolf Hilferding
Friedrich Hayek, Fritz Machlup, and Gottfried Haberler
John Maynard Keynes, Piero Sraffa, and Joan Robinson
Milton Friedman, George Stigler, and Ronald Coase
context: The 1905-1914 Bohm-Bawerk seminar had the future greatest Austrian liberal (Mises), the future Austrian Social Democrat foreign minister (Otto Bauer), and the future Marxist finance minister of Weimar Germany (Hilferding) sitting together. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: Despite being widely acknowledged as the leading Austrian of his generation, Ludwig von Mises never received a paid Vienna chair. What was his formal Vienna affiliation from 1913?
context: Mises took his Vienna doctorate in 1906 and habilitated in 1913 as a Privatdozent -- an unpaid lecturer with the right to teach -- while working full-time for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: After Wieser's 1922 retirement the paid Vienna chair passed to a specific Austrian economist who was of the school but never of Mises's intellectual stature. Who succeeded Wieser?
context: Hans Mayer held the Vienna chair from 1922 to 1938; the paid chair thus passed out of the front-rank Austrian tradition just as the private-seminar tradition became the school's main institutional home. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Mayer_(economist).

question: One of the Bohm-Bawerk seminar's Marxist alumni wrote a 1910 classic, Finance Capital, and later served as Finance Minister of the Weimar Republic. Which alumnus was he?
context: Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910) was a leading Marxist analysis of banking; he later served twice as Finance Minister of Weimar Germany. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rudolf_Hilferding.

question: Vienna as an institutional center of Austrian economics ended for a specific political reason and year, causing the surviving school figures to emigrate. Which event ended the tradition institutionally?
context: Mises had already left Vienna for Geneva in 1934. The 1938 Anschluss ended the Vienna institutional tradition; the remaining figures (Hayek at LSE from 1931; Haberler at Harvard 1936; Morgenstern at Princeton 1938; Machlup in America 1933) had all emigrated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper, posted to the cypherpunk mailing list on October 31 2008, is short by academic standards. Roughly how long is the paper itself (not counting references)?
context: Nine pages of body text, organized into twelve numbered sections plus an abstract and references. That is the length of a typical computer-science conference paper of its era. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper opens with a specific abstract sentence about the problem the paper is trying to solve. Which of these is the actual opening line?
answer: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
choices: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
'Money is a social construct that will be replaced by decentralized applications.'
'The Federal Reserve is the enemy of every honest saver.'
'This paper introduces a new consensus mechanism called proof-of-stake.'
context: The opening sentence identifies the trusted-third-party dependency as the problem to eliminate. The rest of the paper explains the peer-to-peer solution. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper's fourth section is titled with the name of the mechanism that secures the timestamped chain against tampering. Which title does Section 4 carry?
context: Section 3 introduces the timestamped chain concept; Section 4 shows how to secure it. The section explicitly cites Adam Back's Hashcash as prior art. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The Bitcoin white paper cites specific prior work in cryptography and digital cash. Which pair of predecessors does the reference list name?
answer: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
choices: Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money
David Chaum's DigiCash and Nick Szabo's bit gold
Vitalik Buterin's Ethereum and Charlie Lee's Litecoin
Ralph Nader's Public Citizen and Milton Friedman's Free to Choose
context: Both Hashcash and b-money were cypherpunk-lineage proposals from the 1990s that Satoshi combined and extended. DigiCash and bit gold are historically related but are not cited in the paper's references. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Section 7 of the white paper introduces a specific data structure that lets old spent transaction data be pruned from the chain while still preserving cryptographic proof of the chain's history. What is the structure called?
context: Named for Ralph Merkle, who patented the structure in 1979. Each block header commits to the Merkle root of its transactions, so nodes can discard old bodies and keep only proofs. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Section 8 of the Bitcoin white paper describes a lightweight client mode that lets a wallet verify payments by holding only block headers, without downloading the entire blockchain. What is this mode called in the paper?
context: SPV enables phone-and-laptop wallets to check that a payment is in the longest chain by requesting Merkle proofs from full nodes. It is what made mobile Bitcoin wallets practical. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: The white paper's twelfth section is unusually short for a technical paper -- just a brief summary of the coin-as-chain-of-signatures and proof-of-work security argument. Which title does the twelfth section carry, and how long is it?
context: The paper is famously terse. Satoshi said what needed saying and stopped. The Conclusion recaps the peer-to-peer solution and the assumption that honest miners hold more hashing power than any attacker. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A boy born in Gastonia, North Carolina, in 1930 lost his father before he was born and his mother a few years later; a great-aunt raised him, and when he was nine the family moved to Harlem. He grew up to be one of the most widely read economists in America. Who is he?
context: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930, Gastonia, North Carolina) was adopted and raised by his great-aunt Molly and her two adult daughters after his father died shortly before his birth and his mother died a few years later; the family moved to Harlem when he was nine. Walter Williams taught at George Mason, Glenn Loury at Brown, and W. Arthur Lewis won the 1979 Nobel Prize. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell spent his first nine years in a wooden house on an unpaved street in North Carolina with no electricity and no running water. In his memoir A Personal Odyssey he measured how narrow that early world had been by one ordinary thing he had simply never learned. What was it?
answer: That blond was a hair color
choices: That blond was a hair color
That the ocean was salt water
context: Sowell wrote in A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) that his childhood encounters with white people were so limited that he did not know blond was a hair color. He recalled a small wooden house in Charlotte on an unpaved street with no electricity or running water. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell', citing A Personal Odyssey.

question: Thomas Sowell won a place at Stuyvesant High School, New York's selective academic school, and was the first in his family to study past the sixth grade. At seventeen, short of money and living in a quarrelling household, he quit and went to work. Which job did he take?
choices: Sorting mail at the main post office
Loading freight on the Brooklyn docks
Running an elevator in a midtown tower
context: Sowell dropped out of Stuyvesant at 17 because of financial difficulties and family quarreling, then worked long hours in a machine shop and as a delivery man for Western Union. He also tried out for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1948. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Drafted in 1951 during the Korean War, Thomas Sowell was assigned to the U.S. Marine Corps. After boot camp in South Carolina the Marines sent him to a specialist school in Florida, and the trade they taught him there became a hobby he kept for the rest of his life. What did they train him to do?
context: After basic training in South Carolina, Sowell was sent to a photography school in Florida and served as a Marine photographer; he was discharged in 1952 and never rose above private first class. Photography remained his lifelong hobby. Sources: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell held one political philosophy through the whole of his twenties, and he traced it to a daily bus ride home from his messenger job near Wall Street: past the Fifth Avenue stores, past Carnegie Hall, through the comfortable blocks of Riverside Drive, then over a viaduct to the tenement corner where he got off. The contrast baffled him, he said, and one thinker seemed to explain it. Which one?
context: Sowell has said he was a Marxist through his twenties. Of the bus ride he wrote: 'The contrast between that and what I'd been seeing most of the trip really baffled me. And Marx seemed to explain it.' He wrote a Harvard senior thesis on Marxian economics and a Columbia master's thesis on Marxian business cycle theory. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell picked Columbia for his master's degree in 1959 for one reason: a particular economist taught there. Arriving to find the man had just decamped for the University of Chicago, Sowell did not settle for Columbia's faculty. He packed up and followed him to Chicago that autumn. Which economist was worth the move?
context: Sowell chose Columbia in order to study under George Stigler, later a Nobel laureate; on learning Stigler had moved to Chicago he followed him there in the fall of 1959 and took his PhD at Chicago in 1968, with a dissertation on Say's Law and the general glut controversy. Friedman, Knight and Becker were all Chicago economists. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell taught at Cornell, Brandeis, Amherst and UCLA, where he won tenure. Then in 1980 he walked away from university teaching for good so that he could spend his time writing books and newspaper columns instead, moving to a policy research institute where he has stayed ever since. Which one?
context: Sowell joined the Hoover Institution at Stanford as a fellow in April 1977 and became a senior fellow in September 1980, holding the title Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow on Public Policy. He had earlier been at the Urban Institute (1972-74) and the American Enterprise Institute (1975-76), which is why those are live answers. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the summer of 1960 Thomas Sowell, whose first year of graduate school at Chicago had left his politics untouched, took a summer job at the U.S. Department of Labor studying Puerto Rico's sugar industry, where Washington set the wage floor. He saw that as that floor rose, the sugar payrolls shrank. He brought the finding to the office he had joined. What would his colleagues not do?
answer: Test whether the law was helping the workers
choices: Test whether the law was helping the workers
Release the employment figures he had assembled
Compare Puerto Rico with mainland sugar growers
Let an intern brief the division chief directly
context: Sowell has said his colleagues were surprised by his questioning and that 'they certainly weren't going to engage in any scrutiny of the law' -- their job was to enforce it, not to check it. He called this 'the beginning of the erosion of my faith in government programs.' Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Britannica 'Thomas Sowell'; New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell reached Harvard by an unlikely road -- dropout, Marine, night classes at Howard -- and graduated magna cum laude in 1958. Asked long afterwards to name the best thing about having gone there, he gave an answer that had nothing to do with the teaching. What did he say?
answer: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
choices: That you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
That nobody there ever asked where you had gone to high school
That you learn how fast a reputation starts doing your arguing for you
That it teaches you to distrust every credential, beginning with your own
context: Sowell's line: 'One of the best things about going to Harvard is that, for the rest of your life, you are neither intimidated nor impressed by people who went to Harvard.' He finished high school by equivalency after the Marines, took a civil service job in Washington and studied nights at Howard University before transferring. Source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell was asked to teach a course on the Soviet economy, and preparing it finally made sense of Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay on how the information an economy runs on is scattered across millions of separate heads. Sowell said he could suddenly see why Soviet planning failed, and he put it in one sentence about who held what. Which sentence?
answer: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
choices: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
Those who wrote the plans never had to live under the plans they wrote
Those who owned nothing were told every day that they owned everything
Those who waited longest in the queue were always served last
context: Sowell: 'There was a knowledge problem that was inherent in that system. In a nutshell, those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power.' Hayek's essay is 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Knowledge and Decisions (1980) is the book in which Thomas Sowell carried Friedrich Hayek's argument about scattered information into American courts, firms, schools and legislatures, trading graphs and equations for real institutions a reader could picture. Hayek reviewed it himself, and the title he put on his review was not modest. What did Hayek call it?
answer: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
choices: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year
A Worthy Successor to The Road to Serfdom
An American Answer to the Planners
The Case Against Expertise, Made at Last
context: Hayek titled his review of Knowledge and Decisions 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'; the book also won the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. Sowell has called it a book-length application of Hayek's 1945 essay to specific American institutions. Sources: Wikipedia 'Knowledge and Decisions'; FEE, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; New Criterion.

question: Thomas Sowell has said the summer of 1960 began the erosion of his faith in government programs -- not because the sugar numbers alone convinced him, but because of how the people around him received the numbers. He compressed that summer into one sentence he has been applying to institutions ever since. Which sentence?
answer: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
choices: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
That good intentions and good results are different things, and only results can be counted
That every program grows until it costs more than the problem it was built to solve
That the people a program is meant to help are the last whose interests anyone counts
context: Sowell's own words: 'It forced me to realize that government agencies have their own self-interest to look after, regardless of those for whom a program has been set up.' This is public-choice reasoning arrived at by observation, before Sowell had read the public-choice literature. Option two is close to Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions', a genuinely different move. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: In the late 1970s a young physicist at Intel helped solve one critical semiconductor problem -- alpha-particle contamination in memory chips -- and cashed enough stock options to retire in his thirties. Which cypherpunk thinker took that early retirement?
context: Timothy C. May was the retired Intel physicist. Gilmore was Sun's fifth employee; Hughes was a Berkeley mathematician; Chaum was an American cryptographer at a different company. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: In November 1988, Timothy May handed out copies of a short essay he had written at the CRYPTO academic conference in Santa Barbara and read it aloud to the assembled cryptographers. What did he call the essay?
context: May's 1988 essay is 'The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto'. 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' was Eric Hughes's separate March 1993 essay; 'The Cyphernomicon' was May's later 1994 book-length FAQ; 'The Sovereign Individual' is a 1997 book by Davidson and Rees-Mogg. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto opens with a deliberate echo of a famous 19th-century political document. Which specific opening did May borrow to announce that a new political force was arriving?
answer: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
choices: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.'
'Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent...'
'When in the course of human events, it becomes necessary for one people...'
context: May's opening deliberately echoes the 1848 Communist Manifesto's 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' The other openings are Declaration of Independence (1776) and Gettysburg Address (1863). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: The 'specter' that Timothy May's 1988 essay warned would soon haunt the modern political world was a specific set of technical capabilities. Which set of capabilities did he predict strong cryptography would deliver?
answer: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
choices: communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government
cheap global manufacturing and rapid international logistics for goods moving across every continent
solar power and unlimited clean energy sufficient to end civilization's fossil-fuel dependence permanently
artificial intelligence sophisticated enough to replace most human labor across every category of employment
