context: May's specter was strong cryptography enabling anonymous communication, contracting, and trade beyond state surveillance. The other categories are separate technological forecasts May did not centrally address in the manifesto. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's specific prediction inside the 1988 manifesto includes one sentence about what individuals and groups would soon be able to do. Which forecast does he make about anonymous interaction?
answer: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
choices: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
'The internet will soon make all of human knowledge free of charge and instantly available to every person on the planet regardless of their nation.'
'Computers will one day think and feel as humans do, and will eventually claim rights of their own from the human governments that built them.'
'Every citizen of every industrial nation will one day own a personal computer more powerful than anything a national laboratory possesses today.'
context: The exact quote from May's manifesto. The other statements are broadly attributed to different figures (Stallman on knowledge freedom, Minsky/Kurzweil on AI, various early PC forecasts). Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May's 1988 essay explicitly listed several specific technologies he expected the mathematics would enable, including some the cypherpunk movement would go on to build over the next thirty years. Which of these specific technologies did May sketch in the 1988 manifesto?
answer: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
choices: anonymous remailers, digital pseudonyms, cryptographic contracts, and untraceable payments
smartphones, social media, video streaming, and cloud storage
gene therapy, artificial hearts, brain implants, and space elevators
hydrogen fuel cells, fusion power, and orbital solar arrays
context: May specifically anticipated remailers, pseudonyms, smart contracts, and untraceable payments -- all built between 1990 and 2010. The other technology lists are unrelated. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May did not predict Bitcoin by name, but his 1988 essay predicted the specific shape of something that would arrive twenty years later. Which specific 2008 event most directly realized the untraceable-payments capability May sketched?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008
the Federal Reserve's 2008 quantitative easing program
the introduction of chip-and-PIN credit cards
context: Bitcoin's 2008 white paper realized in engineering form the untraceable-payments capability May had forecast in 1988. QE, Facebook, and chip-and-PIN cards are unrelated technologies. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: In 1994 Timothy May followed his manifesto with a much longer document -- a book-length FAQ on cypherpunk topics that circulated widely inside the community. What did he call the 1994 work?
context: 'The Cyphernomicon' (1994) by Timothy May is a book-length FAQ. 'The Crypto Handbook' is a fabrication; 'The Anarchist Cookbook' (William Powell, 1971) is a separate unrelated pamphlet; 'A Cypherpunk's Grimoire' does not exist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A modern cypherpunk historian argues that Timothy May's 1988 essay is best read not as a description of what already existed in 1988 -- there was no code, no infrastructure -- but as a specific type of intellectual contribution. Which characterization does the argument give the essay?
answer: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
choices: a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software
a summary of already-shipping cryptographic tools that had reached ordinary consumers by the late 1980s
a proposal for a specific new company that May intended to found using his Intel stock-option wealth
a legal brief prepared for a specific US court case involving the export of cryptographic software
context: The essay was pure forecast in 1988 -- no working code, no infrastructure. Every specific technology May named would be built over the next thirty years by the movement he named. It was not a shipping summary, corporate proposal, or legal brief. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: When Timothy May died in 2018, his memorial obituary in the cryptocurrency press credited him with a specific role in the intellectual lineage that led to Bitcoin. Which role did the community assign to him at his death?
answer: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
choices: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
the actual person behind the Satoshi pseudonym
the founder of the Bitcoin Foundation
the CEO of the first Bitcoin exchange
context: May's 2018 obituaries credited him as a co-founder of the cypherpunk movement from which Satoshi wrote. He never claimed the Satoshi identity, did not found the Bitcoin Foundation, and did not run an exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A child is offered a cookie today or two cookies tomorrow, and grabs the one cookie today. A lender is offered $100 back today or $100 back next year, and demands $105 for the wait. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk formalised the plain psychological fact behind both scenes in his 1889 Positive Theory of Capital. What did he call it?
context: Boehm-Bawerk's time preference is the ranking every chooser puts on a present good above the SAME good in the future -- two apples today over two apples next year, dinner tonight over dinner tomorrow. Marginal utility (Menger 1871, Wieser 1884) is a different concept about the LAST unit; opportunity cost (Wieser again) is about the next-best forgone use; the endowment effect (Thaler 1980) is a modern behavioural finding about ownership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914), the Austrian economist who formalised time preference in 1889 and later served three terms as Austrian finance minister, was Carl Menger's student and later the teacher of another Austrian who would carry the school forward. Which second-generation Austrian did Boehm-Bawerk personally teach?
context: Mises attended Boehm-Bawerk's celebrated Vienna seminar 1905-1913 and inherited both the time-preference framework and the general Austrian method. Hayek was Mises's own student at Vienna in the 1920s (Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914 when Hayek was 15); Rothbard was Mises's American student in the 1950s at NYU; Kirzner was another Mises student at NYU. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: A hedge-fund analyst asks a plain question: WHY should anyone pay interest? If I lend you $100 for a year and you give me back exactly $100, I'm no worse off -- I got my money back. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference account says the lender IS worse off, because being made whole after a wait is not being made whole at all. What has the lender given up that must be compensated?
answer: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
choices: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
The labor-hours he spent earning the money
The physical wear on the coins from being handled
The cost of writing up the loan contract
context: This is the pure time-preference theory of interest in its cleanest form: interest is the price of WAITING, not a payment for risk or wear or paperwork. The lender defers a year of spending; only a promise of MORE than the original sum next year compensates him for that deferral. Mises would call the pure-time-preference component 'originary interest' in Human Action (1949); Rothbard would build his entire interest theory on this alone in Man, Economy, and State (1962). Source: econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html.

question: Time preference varies wildly between choosers. A child grabs the cookie NOW. A monk under vows may live indifferent to whether the meal comes today or next week. A grandmother forgoes a cruise to leave money for a grandchild who will spend it decades from now. What does the Austrian tradition say every chooser -- however patient -- still has some of?
answer: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
choices: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
A precise numerical discount rate they can state on request
A moral obligation to prefer later over sooner
A market-determined interest rate identical to everyone else's
context: Even the patient monk still prefers a good NOW to the same good in the infinite future -- a promise of an apple in a thousand years is worth zero today to anyone who will not be alive to eat it. Time preference is positive for every actor with a finite horizon; only the SIZE varies. The child has a very high time preference (cookie now); the grandmother has a very low one; both have some. Source: mises.org/library/brief-defense-misess-conception-time-preference-and-his-pure-time-preference-theory-interest.

question: In Human Action (1949), Ludwig von Mises argues that time preference is not a psychological quirk that some people happen to have and others do not -- it is a category built into every purposeful human action, because every choice ranks something sooner against something later. The interest component that flows from this pure time-preference source Mises gave a distinctive name. Which name?
context: Mises separated three components in market interest: (1) originary interest, the pure time-preference core; (2) an entrepreneurial component covering business risk; (3) a price premium covering expected inflation. Only the originary interest is praxeological -- built into human action itself -- and would remain in Mises's evenly rotating economy where risk and inflation are removed by assumption. Nominal, compound, and marginal are unrelated finance terms. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: Murray Rothbard's 1962 Man, Economy, and State stripped the interest-rate analysis down to its bones: business risk and expected inflation can be modelled as separate premiums layered on top, but the ROOT rate is set by one thing alone. What did Rothbard treat as the sole determinant of the pure interest rate?
answer: The aggregate time preferences of borrowers and lenders
choices: The aggregate time preferences of borrowers and lenders
The scarcity of gold in circulation
The wage bargains of organised labour
context: Rothbard's is a Pure Time-Preference Theory of interest (PTPT) -- the productivity-of-capital account (going back to Boehm-Bawerk's own THIRD reason for interest, and to Fisher) is rejected as confused; risk and inflation get modelled as separate premiums added on top. The market rate you actually see is time preferences plus those premiums. Frank Fetter's 1904 Principles gave the pure account first; Mises and Rothbard both credit him. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf.

question: Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 Positive Theory of Capital pressed a further consequence: a society whose people defer more consumption -- lower time preference on average -- can build things individuals with high time preference cannot. It can support long production chains, tools that make tools, decade-long infrastructure projects. A society that consumes everything as fast as it can produce cannot. What did Boehm-Bawerk call these long chains where present resources are patiently rearranged to produce more later?
context: Roundabout production is Boehm-Bawerk's central capital-theory concept: instead of catching fish with bare hands, first make a net; instead of walking, first build a car factory; instead of a car factory, first build a machine-tool industry to build the factory. Each step adds waiting time and requires deferred consumption. Comparative advantage is Ricardo 1817 on trade; aggregate demand and full employment are Keynesian macroeconomic constructs from the 1930s. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: Two societies of equal population and equal starting resources go different ways. Society A saves aggressively and defers consumption for a generation. Society B spends every dollar the moment it lands and borrows against next year to spend today. Boehm-Bawerk's time-preference framework predicts which society will end the generation with the more capital-intensive economy?
answer: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
choices: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
Society B -- higher spending drives more investment
Both equally -- time preferences do not affect capital structure
Society B -- consumption is what stimulates growth
context: Deferred consumption is what FREES real resources for long-term projects: workers and materials not consumed today can be used to build tools, factories, and infrastructure whose payoff comes years out. Society B's aggressive present consumption leaves nothing for the long projects. This is why Austrians (Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek) argue that SAVING -- not spending -- is the engine of a capital-intensive economy, directly against the Keynesian priority given to aggregate demand. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: A central bank pushes short-term interest rates well below the rate that would balance actual saving against actual borrowing. Entrepreneurs looking at the low rate start long-term projects -- factories, subdivisions, mining operations -- on the reading that lots of long-term saving is available. But consumers have not in fact deferred any consumption; the low rate was a policy choice, not a signal from real saving. Which Austrian move names what the low rate has done?
answer: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
choices: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
It efficiently reallocates resources to their highest-value use
It cures the shortage of aggregate demand
It permanently raises the economy's growth rate
context: This is the time-preference core of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929-1931): when the central-bank rate is held below the market-clearing rate, entrepreneurs get a false signal that consumers have saved more than they have. Long projects get started that cannot in fact be finished with the real resources available. The bust is the market discovering the truth -- capital gets written down, malinvested projects are liquidated, workers laid off, and the economy returns to a structure the real time preferences will support. The other three options describe Keynesian, Chicago-neoclassical, and stimulus-permanence claims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: In Democracy: The God That Failed (2001), Hans-Hermann Hoppe argues that democratic government does not merely reflect the time preferences of its citizens but systematically PUSHES them upward -- politicians face short electoral cycles, campaign on borrow-now-pay-later promises, and treat state assets as temporary caretakers rather than long-term owners. What phenomenon does Hoppe say the rising time preference produces over generations?
answer: Decivilization -- rising crime, moral decay, and swelling debt
choices: Decivilization -- rising crime, moral decay, and swelling debt
A permanent rise in the standard of living
A stable long-run equilibrium of the political system
context: Hoppe's central thesis links rising time preference to decivilization: short-horizon political incentives crowd out long-horizon private planning, borrowing-against-the-future replaces saving, and the visible symptoms are rising crime, degenerating standards, and swelling public debt. The book is controversial and Brandon's bank presents it as one named critic's argument. Time preference is Hoppe's master variable; the argument runs straight out of Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Boehm-Bawerk laid three separate reasons for positive interest in the 1889 Positive Theory of Capital: (1) future goods will generally be more plentiful; (2) people underestimate future needs from carelessness and shortsightedness; (3) present goods are technically superior for starting production. Frank Fetter, Mises, and Rothbard would later strip the theory down and argue that only ONE of these truly belongs to the pure interest rate -- the other two are separate effects. Which reason survives as the pure-time-preference core?
answer: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
choices: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
The greater physical productivity of tools made today
The larger future supply of goods
context: The Fetter-Mises-Rothbard purification argues that Boehm-Bawerk's first reason (larger future supply) collapses back into the second (it works only via preferences), and the third (productivity of present goods) is a productivity effect, not a time-preference effect. What is left as the ROOT of interest is the pure ranking of present over future -- reason two, in Boehm-Bawerk's numbering. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: Through the first half of 2021, as US consumer price inflation began climbing above the Fed's 2% target and hit 5.4% by June, the Fed chair and Treasury Secretary repeatedly used one word to describe the rise. Which word did they use?
context: Jerome Powell, Janet Yellen, and most Federal Open Market Committee members publicly called the 2021 inflation 'transitory' at press conferences and hearings from April through November. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: The chair of the Federal Reserve who kept insisting through most of 2021 that rising inflation would prove temporary took office in February 2018 and remains chair today. Who is he?
context: Powell was appointed by President Trump and reappointed by President Biden. He led the FOMC through the pandemic response, the transitory-inflation call, and the 2022-23 tightening cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2021 argument that inflation would prove short-lived rested on three specific supports: pandemic-era base effects, supply-chain disruptions, and one further claim about the state of the American labor market. What was the third support?
answer: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
choices: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
Higher productivity would offset any wage pressure
Immigration would keep wage growth low
Automation would eventually replace scarce workers
context: The 'transitory' case argued that with unemployment still elevated, workers lacked bargaining power for the wage gains that would sustain price inflation. Critics pointed out that a 25%+ expansion in the M2 money supply is not absorbed by labor-market slack. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: A prominent Democratic-aligned mainstream economist -- Treasury Secretary under Clinton, Obama-era NEC director -- published a February 2021 op-ed warning that the pending American Rescue Plan risked overheating prices. Who was he?
context: Summers's February 4 2021 Washington Post op-ed argued that the size of the Biden fiscal package created substantial inflation risk. Fed officials publicly dismissed the warning. He was largely proven right within twelve months. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2021).

question: The Fed chair repeated the transitory framing at the June 2021 press conference, at Jackson Hole in August, and at September's FOMC meeting. He finally retired the word publicly in a Senate Banking Committee hearing. On what date did he abandon it?
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30 2021: 'I think it's probably a good time to retire that word.' CPI was already at 6.8% year-over-year that month. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: Six months after the Fed chair retired the transitory framing, US year-over-year consumer price inflation reached its cycle peak in a specific month. What did that peak reading come in at?
context: The June 2022 CPI print of 9.1% was the highest US year-over-year inflation since November 1981. It came six months after the transitory framing was abandoned and marked the peak that Powell then aggressively tightened to reverse. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian and monetarist critique of the transitory framing rested on a specific point about the money supply that the Fed's supply-chain explanation could not answer. Which point?
answer: A 25%+ expansion in M2 cannot be absorbed without eventual price adjustment; supply-chain effects are transient but the monetary cause is not
choices: A 25%+ expansion in M2 cannot be absorbed without eventual price adjustment; supply-chain effects are transient but the monetary cause is not
Supply chains only affect goods, so inflation would have shown up only in services
Base effects would guarantee lower inflation prints within three months
The Fed's dot plot showed rate hikes had already been priced in
context: The monetarist point: transitory factors resolve, but a large one-time expansion in the money supply flows through prices over a lag of 12-24 months. The Fed was staring at the monetary cause and offering a supply-side explanation. Source: Steve Hanke, Johns Hopkins Money and Growth papers (2021).

question: As late as the November 3 2021 FOMC meeting, when consumer price inflation was already running at 6.2% year-over-year, the Fed continued asset purchases and held rates at zero. This monetary posture is what critics called by what specific label?
answer: Monetary-easy in the face of the very inflation the Fed was dismissing
choices: Monetary-easy in the face of the very inflation the Fed was dismissing
Tight money that would guarantee a hard landing
context: The Fed maintained QE and zero rates through November 2021 despite inflation already at 6.2%. The critique: the Fed was pouring gasoline on the very fire it was calling a mirage. Source: federalreserve.gov (FOMC statements November 3 2021).

question: The transitory episode is now cited as the modern Fed's most consequential forecasting error. What specific reasoning move does the Austrian tradition draw from it about central-bank inflation forecasting?
answer: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
choices: Central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them
Central banks always over-tighten in response to inflation forecasts
Central bank models correctly predict inflation trajectories within two years
Central bank forecasts are unbiased on average and only occasionally wrong
context: The transitory episode is a case study in institutional motivated reasoning: the Fed had run enormous QE and preferred an explanation that did not implicate its own actions. A recognition move about how central banks talk about inflation. Source: George Selgin, Cato Institute commentary (2022-23).

question: The transitory miscall is also linked to the earlier Senate rejection of a specific Trump-era Fed nominee whose written record had warned about exactly this inflation setup. Which nominee?
context: Shelton's 1994 book Money Meltdown and later writings argued that unrestrained Fed discretion produced asset inflation and currency debasement. Her November 2020 Senate cloture defeat is often cited by Austrian analysts as a lost hard-money oversight opportunity. Source: Grokipedia 'Judy Shelton' (2026-09-05).

question: In 1938 a Norwegian economist and businessman published a doctoral dissertation on the socialist calculation debate that became the most comprehensive book-length restatement of Mises's position between Mises's 1922 Socialism and Hayek's 1945 knowledge essay. Who was he?
context: Hoff (1895-1982) took his doctorate at the University of Oslo. Ohlin, Frisch, and Myrdal were other Nordic economists of the same generation but on different sides of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff's 1938 Norwegian doctoral dissertation on the calculation debate was translated to English 11 years later in 1949 by M. A. Michael and published by William Hodge of London. What was the English title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
context: The Norwegian original was 'Okonomisk kalkulasjon i socialistiske samfund.' The 1949 English edition brought Hoff's argument to a wider audience just as Human Action was appearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff's 1938 book surveyed the state of the calculation debate as of the late 1930s. Which literatures did it draw on?
answer: The German-language literature (Mises 1920, Weber, German critics), the Anglo-American literature (Hayek 1935, Lange 1936-37), and Soviet planning experience
choices: The German-language literature (Mises 1920, Weber, German critics), the Anglo-American literature (Hayek 1935, Lange 1936-37), and Soviet planning experience
context: Hoff defended Mises against Oskar Lange in careful detail, marshalling the German, English, and Soviet evidence. The book was in a real sense the definitive 1938 statement of the Austrian side of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff was not primarily an academic; he was a businessman and magazine editor. During World War II he suffered a specific consequence of his other career. What was it?
answer: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
choices: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
He fled to neutral Sweden and taught at Stockholm University for the duration
He served as economic advisor to the Norwegian government-in-exile in London
He worked as a translator for the Allied forces in Iceland
context: Hoff edited the anti-Nazi magazine Farmand. Nazi occupation authorities arrested him for the editorship. He survived; after the war Farmand became a leading Nordic classical-liberal publication and Hoff a major figure in the small postwar European liberal revival. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In April 1947 Friedrich Hayek convened a gathering of 39 economists, philosophers, and historians at a specific Swiss mountain resort to found a scholarly society dedicated to the defense of classical liberalism. Trygve Hoff was one of the founders. What was the society called?
context: Named for Mont Pelerin above Vevey, Switzerland, where the founding meeting was held April 1-10, 1947. Hoff joined Mises, Hayek, Friedman, Ropke, Rustow, Robbins, Popper, Polanyi, Stigler, Machlup, and Knight in the founding cohort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mont_Pelerin_Society.

question: In 1981 an American institution reprinted Trygve Hoff's 1938 book with a foreword by another economist, bringing it back into circulation for a new generation. Which institution reprinted it?
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
context: The foreword was written by Karl Brunner, the Swiss-born monetarist. The reprint made Hoff's careful pre-Hayek-1945 defense of Mises available to modern Austrian scholars for the first time in decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: In 1967 a nine-page paper in the Western Economic Journal by Gordon Tullock argued that the standard textbook deadweight loss from monopoly massively understated the real social cost. What title did Tullock give that paper?
answer: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
choices: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
context: Gordon Tullock, 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' (Western Economic Journal, June 1967, later renamed Economic Inquiry). It was initially rejected by more prestigious journals before finding a home. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Tullock 1967).

question: A firm sees a $100-million-per-year tariff protection sitting in front of Congress. How much will it be willing to spend on lobbying, campaign contributions, and law-firm hours to obtain that tariff, according to Tullock's 1967 analysis?
context: Tullock's insight: firms will burn real resources on the competition for privilege up to the full value of the privilege sought. If competing firms fight the tariff, they will burn resources on the other side. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: Textbook monopoly analysis had focused on a triangular deadweight loss -- the value of trades that would happen at competitive prices but do not happen at monopoly prices. Tullock argued the true social cost is much larger. What SHAPE, in the standard diagram, does his additional loss occupy?
answer: The whole rectangle of monopoly profits
choices: The whole rectangle of monopoly profits
A thin outer band around the triangle
A separate triangle above the demand curve
A crescent below the marginal-cost curve
context: The 'Tullock rectangle': resources spent competing for the monopoly rent equal in expectation to the full monopoly-profit rectangle. Later scholars named it after him. Source: Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975) formalized the Tullock rectangle.

question: Tullock illustrated his rectangle argument with a homespun example. What did he argue was the TRUE social cost of theft in a society?
answer: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
choices: The resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools
The dollar value of stolen goods
The lost tax revenue from unreported income
The cost of judicial trials for accused thieves
context: Tullock's illustration: theft merely TRANSFERS wealth from victim to thief -- the total is unchanged. The real deadweight loss is the whole edifice of prevention and preparation on both sides. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967), section on theft.

question: Tullock's 1967 paper introduced a concept that Anne Krueger's 1974 paper on Indian import licenses would formalize and give a memorable modern name. What is the concept now standardly called?
context: Tullock originated the concept in 1967; Krueger's 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' (American Economic Review, June 1974) coined the phrase 'rent-seeking' and cemented the term. Source: jstor.org (Krueger 1974).

question: Anne Krueger's 1974 paper applied Tullock's insight to a specific developing-country regulatory system whose licenses were worth enormous sums and attracted correspondingly huge lobbying investments. Which country's system did she study?
context: Krueger studied India's License Raj -- the elaborate system of import and industrial licenses that allocated the right to operate certain businesses. Her estimates suggested rent-seeking losses of a large percentage of Indian GNP. Source: Krueger, American Economic Review (1974).

question: Tullock's paper reframed monopoly, tariffs, and theft under a common structural analysis. What common feature makes all three of them generate his enlarged deadweight loss?
answer: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
choices: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
Each involves foreign parties competing with domestic firms
Each requires central-bank money-printing to sustain
Each is prohibited by the US Constitution
context: Whenever there is a REDISTRIBUTIVE prize on offer -- a rent -- real economic inputs get burned competing for the prize rather than producing value. The productive economy loses those inputs. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: Tullock's 1967 paper described a specific category of workers as unproductive from society's point of view -- talented, hard-working, but engaged in an activity that transfers wealth rather than creating it. Which workers did he single out as the archetypal example in his critique of the rent-seeking economy?
context: Tullock argued that talented lawyers and lobbyists whose entire work was securing regulatory privilege were engaged in a socially wasteful zero-sum contest. The productive economy loses their talent. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Baumol, Journal of Political Economy (1990) on productive vs unproductive entrepreneurship.

question: Tullock's argument turns on a strong assumption about the outcome of competition among firms seeking a government-granted rent. What does he assume the competition dissipates in expectation?
answer: The full value of the rent being sought
choices: The full value of the rent being sought
Half the value of the rent being sought
Only a small fraction of the rent
None of the rent, since competition is impossible
context: Under free entry into the competition for rents and constant returns to lobbying, expected dissipation equals the full rent. Later scholarship (Posner 1975, Rogerson 1982) explored conditions under which dissipation is less than full. Source: Tullock 1967; Posner, Journal of Political Economy (1975).

question: Tullock's 1967 paper is now widely regarded as the founding text of a whole subfield of political economy. What single sentence best captures its enduring reasoning move?
answer: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
choices: Every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it
Monopoly profits are always immediately competed away
Foreign tariffs impose no domestic welfare cost
Theft has no social cost because it merely transfers wealth
context: The rent-seeking move: whenever a redistributive prize is on offer, real economic resources will be burned competing for it, and society loses the value of those resources. This is a general result, not a partisan claim. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Buchanan + Tollison + Tullock, Toward a Theory of the Rent-Seeking Society (Texas A&M 1980).

question: The rent-seeking framework identifies a specific reason to prefer STABLE, GENERAL rules over targeted political redistribution. Which policy design tends to MINIMIZE rent-seeking loss according to the framework?
answer: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
choices: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
Elaborate industry-specific carve-outs and case-by-case licenses
Discretionary agency waivers granted by senior political appointees
Rotating tax preferences renegotiated each Congress
context: Broad rules leave nothing worth lobbying over; carve-outs and discretion create rents. This is why constitutional political economy favors general rules and why Buchanan named 'generality' as a core principle. Source: Buchanan + Congleton, Politics by Principle, Not Interest (Cambridge 1998).

question: In Chapter 12 of his 1962 book 'Capitalism and Freedom,' Milton Friedman proposed a specific cash-transfer design intended to replace the multi-program US welfare stack with a single unified mechanism. What did he call it?
context: Friedman's motivation was administrative simplification and preservation of work incentives via a gradual known phase-out. It differed structurally from the modern UBI concept, which typically adds a universal payment on top of the existing safety net. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: Milton Friedman's Negative Income Tax proposal was actually tested in large-scale randomized-controlled experiments in the US and Canada in the 1968-1979 period. What was the main finding on work hours?
answer: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
choices: Modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted
A total 80 percent reduction in work hours across all recipients
No measurable change in work hours in any subgroup
A doubling of work hours as recipients gained financial security to seek new jobs
context: The New Jersey/Pennsylvania (1968-72) and Seattle/Denver (1970-77) US experiments and the Manitoba MINCOME (1974-79) Canadian experiment all found modest work-hour declines with substantial administrative-cost savings over the multi-program comparison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: In the 2020 US Democratic presidential primary, one candidate centered his campaign on a universal $1,000-per-month payment he called the 'Freedom Dividend,' partly funded by a value-added tax. Who was the candidate?
context: Yang, a tech entrepreneur, made UBI the signature of his campaign. His proposal was a universal flat payment with no income phase-out, structurally different from Friedman's NIT. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Andrew_Yang.

question: The largest recent US randomized study of unconditional cash transfers, funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch, gave $1,000/month to 1,000 recipients in Illinois and Texas for three years. When it published in August 2024, what did the study find about work hours?
answer: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
choices: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
Recipients doubled their work hours on average
Recipients quit the labor force entirely at a rate of 80 percent
Recipients showed no change in work hours whatsoever
context: The study also found modest health improvements and no clear positive employment outcomes despite proponent hopes. The findings largely echoed the 1970s NIT experiments' pattern of moderate labor-supply reductions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Milton Friedman's NIT and Andrew Yang's UBI differ on one key structural point that has opposite implications for total government footprint and marginal work incentives. What is the difference?
answer: The NIT REPLACES the existing safety-net stack; the modern UBI typically ADDS a universal floor on top of the existing system
choices: The NIT REPLACES the existing safety-net stack; the modern UBI typically ADDS a universal floor on top of the existing system
The NIT applies only to citizens; the UBI applies to all residents including tourists
The NIT is paid weekly; the UBI is paid yearly
The NIT is funded by tariffs; the UBI is funded by property taxes
context: Friedman would have supported replacing programs with an NIT and opposed adding a UBI on top of them. The two proposals share a label but have opposite structural implications for the state's role and for the effective marginal tax rate facing the recipient as income rises. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: The libertarian scholar Charles Murray proposed a $10,000-per-adult basic income in his 2006 AEI book 'In Our Hands: A Plan to Replace the Welfare State.' What structural feature made his proposal Friedman-style rather than Yang-style?
answer: It would REPLACE nearly all existing US welfare and social-insurance programs
choices: It would REPLACE nearly all existing US welfare and social-insurance programs
It would supplement existing programs with additional monthly payments
It would apply only to residents over 65 years of age
It would be paid only in food stamps rather than cash
context: The Murray design is a UBI in label but an NIT in structure -- a flat universal payment that eliminates the existing multi-program stack. Same-label proposals with different phase-out and replacement structures produce very different outcomes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: The longest-running actual universal cash-transfer program in the United States has paid every state resident an annual per-capita share of state oil-royalty revenue since 1982 -- typically $1,000-$2,000 a year. Which state runs it?
context: The Alaska Permanent Fund was created in 1976 and the Dividend program began payouts in 1982. Every Alaskan resident (regardless of income) receives the annual share. It is the closest real-world US analogue of a UBI. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Alaska_Permanent_Fund.

question: A high-school student asks a Sowell-influenced economist whether UBI is 'obviously a good idea.' The economist declines to pick a side and instead points to a reasoning move. Which move is he pressing?
answer: Read the statutory design, not the label -- same-label proposals with different phase-out structures produce different outcomes
choices: Read the statutory design, not the label -- same-label proposals with different phase-out structures produce different outcomes
Any cash transfer to households below the median income is always beneficial
Any cash transfer to households above the median income is always harmful
The specific policy design has no effect on outcomes because behavior is invariant
context: This is Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only tradeoffs' at the policy-design level. A UBI on top of existing programs has different effects from an NIT that replaces them. The kid learns to look under the label at the actual mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Since the Agricultural Act of 1949, the US government has run a price-support program for one specific agricultural commodity, guaranteeing to purchase surplus at above-market prices and store or dispose of it. Which commodity?
context: The federal purchases were made largely as butter and processed cheese, which stored better than fluid milk. The program has been renamed and modified many times but the above-market-support core has persisted for 75+ years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: By 1981, after decades of the federal milk price-support program buying up surplus dairy, the US government owned an eye-opening stockpile of one specific processed dairy item sitting in caves and warehouses across the country. Which item, and roughly how much?
answer: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
choices: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
About 5 million pounds of ice cream
About 100 million pounds of powdered milk only
context: The stockpile became a national embarrassment. Congressional hearings and press coverage forced action; the Reagan administration began a distribution program the same year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: In 1981 the Reagan administration launched a distribution program handing out the government's surplus dairy stockpile to food banks and welfare programs. The specific processed cheese loaves gave a phrase to American vocabulary. What did the phrase become?
context: The loaves were shelf-stable pasteurized processed cheese food. The distribution continued through the 1990s and became a cultural touchstone in low-income neighborhoods (referenced in hip-hop and stand-up comedy). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: Milton and Rose Friedman analyzed the US dairy price-support in 'Free to Choose' (1980) as a case of a specific incentive asymmetry: roughly 100,000 dairy farm households benefit while over 300 million Americans pay a little more each. Which analytical framework does this asymmetry fit?
context: The concentrated beneficiaries organize (dairy lobby, state-level dairy compacts) because the per-household benefit is large. The dispersed victims do not organize because the per-household cost is small enough not to warrant political effort. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: Milton Friedman's dispersed-costs analysis of the dairy program relied on a classical theoretical account of why small concentrated groups win political battles against much larger dispersed groups. Which 1965 book laid out that theory?

'The Calculus of Consent' by Buchanan and Tullock
'The Road to Serfdom' by Friedrich Hayek
context: Mancur Olson (1932-1998) was an American economist at Maryland. His 1965 book (Harvard University Press) argued that concentrated beneficiaries face lower coordination costs than dispersed victims, explaining why regulated industries can capture their regulators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: The 2014 Farm Bill modified the older milk-purchase program with a new mechanism, though the above-market-support structure persisted. What did the 2014 bill replace the older program with?
choices: A federal ban on all dairy subsidies
context: DMC pays farmers when the margin between milk price and feed cost falls below a chosen threshold. The mechanism is different from bulk purchase but the underlying above-market income guarantee for dairy producers persists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: From 1999 the government of Venezuela began systematic price controls on food, fuel, and consumer goods, alongside heavy nationalization of private industry. The president who launched this economic program held office until his death in 2013. Who was he?
context: Chavez ruled Venezuela from 1999 to 2013 and built the model his successor Maduro inherited. Source: Grokipedia 'Hugo Chavez' (2026-09-05).

question: After Chavez's 2013 death, his vice-president took over and inherited the price-control apparatus and the accelerating monetary expansion. Who is that successor?
context: Maduro won a disputed April 2013 election and remains in power. His tenure saw hyperinflation, mass emigration, and near-total dollarization of the informal economy. Source: Grokipedia 'Nicolas Maduro' (2026-09-05).

question: Venezuelan price controls set below market-clearing levels produced a predictable outcome inside the country's supermarkets and pharmacies. What was that outcome?
answer: Widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine

A rapid rise in real wages
Falling emigration as living standards improved

question: By 2018 the International Monetary Fund estimated Venezuela's annual inflation rate at a striking figure that put it in the same historical league as Weimar Germany. What did the 2018 rate reach?
context: The IMF's 2018 estimate of Venezuelan annual inflation was roughly 130,000%. By 2019 a wheelbarrow of banknotes was needed for basic groceries -- the Weimar image replayed a century later, in Latin America. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Venezuela' (2026-09-05).

question: As the Venezuelan economy collapsed, millions of citizens fled. By 2024 the UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimated the total displacement at roughly what fraction of the pre-crisis population?

About one tenth, about 3 million people
About one twentieth, about 1.5 million people

Neighbors like Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, and Chile have absorbed the majority. Source: Grokipedia 'Venezuelan refugee crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: By the early 2020s the formal Venezuelan economy had partially recovered through a spontaneous adaptation that the government did not decree. What did Venezuelans start doing informally with prices and wages?

Bartering exclusively for gold coins minted before 1999
Reintroducing a fixed exchange rate to the Argentine peso
Adopting the Ecuadorian sucre as everyday money

question: The Austrian economist who first named the deep reasoning problem the Venezuelan case illustrates -- that central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices signal, so their allocations must be blind -- did so in a specific 1920 paper. Which Austrian was that?
context: Mises's 1920 paper 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' argued that without market prices for capital goods, socialist planners have no way to know whether a proposed use of resources creates or destroys value. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: The Austrian argument Mises made in 1920, updated to a 21st-century case, is called by economists today the 'socialist calculation problem'. Which specific defect in central planning does it name?
answer: Central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices would signal about scarcity and value
choices: Central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices would signal about scarcity and value
Central planners always cheat and skim revenues for personal gain
Central planners cannot enforce laws without the consent of unions
Central planners fail because workers refuse to work for low wages
context: The calculation problem is epistemic, not moral. Even honest, well-intentioned planners cannot substitute for a working price system because prices aggregate dispersed knowledge that no central authority possesses. Source: Mises, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920).

question: The 2013-present Venezuelan collapse is important pedagogically because it is the only modern case with a specific accessibility feature that older Soviet or Maoist examples lack. What does Venezuela have that older cases do not?
answer: It is happening now, on smartphone video, in a Western Hemisphere country a plane ride from Miami

It happened in a country with no oil resources or export commodities
It happened without a preceding period of price controls
It happened under a government that publicly renounced socialism

question: The Venezuelan case teaches a specific recognition move that Mises's 1920 argument tried to make abstractly, and that the modern student can now verify empirically. Which move?
answer: The socialist calculation problem is not an abstract academic dispute; it is an observable, current phenomenon
choices: The socialist calculation problem is not an abstract academic dispute; it is an observable, current phenomenon
Price controls always eventually work if enforced hard enough
Central planning is a good idea in principle but hard to execute in practice
Modern digital tools solve the calculation problem central planners once faced
context: The Mises argument that seemed like a theoretical dispute in 1920 is now a public fact playing out on smartphone video. The empirical case makes the theory unavoidable for any honest student. Source: Mises, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920).

question: During Venezuela's hyperinflation from about 2015 onward, ordinary Venezuelans discovered they could use one specific national resource -- capped far below its production cost -- to mine Bitcoin and hold sound money instead of the collapsing bolivar. Which resource?
answer: Electricity, whose domestic price was set far below production cost

Coffee, whose export price was set by state marketing boards
Petroleum, whose retail gasoline price was heavily subsidized
Cocoa, whose government purchase price was above world levels

Cheap electricity plus hyperinflation made mining locally-generated sound money one of the most rational responses available to a Venezuelan saver. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: The Nicolas Maduro government responded to Venezuelans' Bitcoin mining not with market reform but with a specific enforcement approach beginning around 2018 and culminating in an outright ban in 2023. What did it do?

Signed a free-trade agreement with the United States
Legalized Bitcoin as a second national currency alongside the bolivar
Distributed government-owned mining equipment to every household

question: On the other side of Venezuela's collapsed economy, state-distributed food parcels became the sole reliable food source for millions of families. The parcels were named for the neighborhood collectives that distributed them. What is the acronym?
answer: CLAP (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion)
choices: CLAP (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion)
context: 'Local Committees for Supply and Production.' The boxes typically contained rice, cornmeal, oil, sugar, and canned goods. Distribution was tightly controlled by neighborhood collectives loyal to the ruling PSUV party. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comit%C3%A9_Local_de_Abastecimiento_y_Producci%C3%B3n.

question: Journalists including Anatoly Kurmanaev at the New York Times documented that access to Venezuela's CLAP food boxes was conditioned on a specific non-food criterion. Which criterion?

Educational attainment -- a completed high-school diploma
Residency length -- five years in the same neighborhood

question: A high-school student asks what specific 1920 prediction Venezuela's dual economy (Bitcoin mining plus CLAP-box political allocation) illustrates. A Mises-influenced economist points to a specific essay. Which essay?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
choices: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth'
John Maynard Keynes's 'The General Theory of Employment'
Karl Marx's 'Critique of the Gotha Program'
Milton Friedman's 'A Program for Monetary Stability'

Venezuela's fall-back to Bitcoin (for those with technical skill) and to political loyalty (for everyone else) is what that groping looks like at national scale. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: A Human Rights Foundation report in 2019 documented Bitcoin's role in Venezuela as more than a speculative asset -- for many Venezuelans it was a bypass around a captured national currency. Who authored the report?
context: The report catalogued how Bitcoin (and Ethereum) let Venezuelans preserve savings, receive remittances, and transact outside the bolivar. It became one of the standard cited sources on the Venezuelan case in Bitcoin policy debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: When market prices are abolished by government fiat, allocation MUST fall back on some other mechanism. Venezuela's dual economy under Maduro made this pattern unusually visible. Which two mechanisms specifically filled the vacuum?

The World Bank's grants program, and remittances from Venezuelans abroad
A restored gold standard, and barter networks in coffee
Chinese state loans, and Colombian food aid

The Austrian-tradition prediction was that suppressed prices would reappear as SOMETHING; Venezuela made the something visible. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: In April 2013, after the death of Hugo Chavez, a specific successor won a narrow election and extended and expanded Venezuela's Chavez-era price controls on food, medicine, and consumer basics. Who was that successor?
context: Nicolas Maduro won the April 14, 2013 special election following Chavez's death on March 5, 2013. He extended and later expanded price controls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Maduro.

question: In January 2014 Maduro passed a landmark price-control law setting maximum retail prices on hundreds of items and jailing merchants who charged more. What was its Spanish name (Fair Price Law)?
context: The Fair Price Law (Ley Organica de Precios Justos, January 2014) created a new agency (SUNDDE) to enforce maximum retail prices. Overcharging carried criminal penalties. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela.

question: Within weeks of the Fair Price Law, a specific consumer product became the emblem of Venezuela's empty shelves and generated international news coverage in 2013-14. What was the shortage item everyone was queuing for?
context: The 2013 Venezuelan toilet-paper shortage became a symbol of the price-control-induced supply collapse. Flour, cooking oil, milk, rice, and soap also disappeared -- but toilet paper became the political news story. Source: reuters.com Venezuela shortage coverage 2013.

question: The Bastiat seen-versus-unseen reading of the 2014 Fair Price Law: SEEN was the low mandated price on the shelves of state supermarkets. What was UNSEEN?
answer: The shelves themselves -- basic goods disappeared and Venezuelans queued for hours
choices: The shelves themselves -- basic goods disappeared and Venezuelans queued for hours
The tax revenue lost on capped items
context: The visible low price hid the invisible cost: flour, cooking oil, milk, rice, toilet paper, and soap disappeared as suppliers withdrew rather than sell at a loss. Queuing filled the gap. Source: bastiat.org, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela.

question: As the black market ('bachaqueo') took over most consumer commerce, the Venezuelan government responded with a specific biometric system to ration state-store purchases. What did it install?
choices: A national ID card with QR codes
context: The Sistema Biometrico used fingerprint scanners at state supermarket checkouts to limit each household to weekly quotas of basic goods. It was the government's response to the bachaqueo secondary market. Source: bbc.com Venezuela biometric rationing.

question: The Venezuelan government eventually distributed government food boxes through neighborhood collectives, allocated by political loyalty. What are these boxes called?
context: CLAP boxes (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion) were distributed via neighborhood committees with proven allegiance to the ruling party. When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something became political loyalty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CLAP_(Venezuela).

question: By 2018 Venezuelan CPI inflation had reached staggering levels driven by monetary emissions and the collapsing bolivar. What is the standard IMF estimate for peak annual inflation in 2018?
context: The IMF estimated Venezuelan annual inflation peaked around 130,000% in 2018. The bolivar was redenominated several times. Salaries paid in bolivars became nearly worthless within days. Source: imf.org WEO Venezuela.

question: By 2024 the number of Venezuelans who had left the country in the crisis reached the largest displacement figure in modern Western Hemisphere history. What is the standard UNHCR figure?
context: About 7.7 million Venezuelans had emigrated by 2024 -- roughly a quarter of the pre-crisis population. Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, and the US absorbed the largest flows. Source: unhcr.org Venezuela emergency data.

question: The reasoning-move chain the Venezuelan case illustrates most sharply -- from price controls through queues to biometric rationing to political-loyalty allocation -- teaches one core Mises 1920 point. What is that point?
answer: When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something becomes political power
choices: When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something becomes political power
When market prices are abolished, government revenue rises steadily
When market prices are abolished, consumers benefit uniformly
When market prices are abolished, producers self-organize efficiently
context: The chain: price controls -> supply withdrawal -> queues -> rationing -> political-loyalty allocation. When the price mechanism is suppressed, allocation becomes political -- and the CLAP boxes made this literal. Mises's 1920 prediction reappeared inside three years in a previously middle-income country. Source: mises.org/library/venezuela.

question: For accuracy the bank stipulates that Venezuela's collapse had multiple causes, not price controls alone. Which other factors are the standard honest accounting?
answer: Oil-price collapse 2014, sanctions from 2017, monetary chaos
choices: Oil-price collapse 2014, sanctions from 2017, monetary chaos
context: The full picture includes the 2014 oil price collapse, US sanctions escalating from 2017, and monetary emission chaos. The Fair Price Law's supply-collapse effect began before major sanctions and tracked enforcement of the law itself. Source: piie.com Venezuela analysis.

question: On April 30, 1975 North Vietnam's forces captured the South Vietnamese capital, ending the war. What was that capital city, later renamed for Ho Chi Minh?
context: The Fall of Saigon on April 30, 1975 ended the Vietnam War. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976 after reunification. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Saigon.

question: After Vietnam's 1975 reunification, the government sent former South Vietnamese officials, soldiers, teachers, journalists, and Catholic clergy to a network of camps for terms ranging from weeks to more than 15 years. What were these camps called?
context: Vietnamese hoc tap cai tao (re-education camps) held an estimated 1-2.5 million people between 1975 and the mid-1980s. Vietnam's own government has admitted over 165,000 deaths in the system. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-education_camp_(Vietnam).

question: The collectivization of southern agriculture and the state seizure of southern private commerce in 1977-78 (targeting ethnic-Chinese business families particularly) triggered a mass emigration by sea. What are these emigrants collectively called?
context: About 800,000 Vietnamese fled by sea in unseaworthy craft between 1975 and 1990. The exodus was concentrated in 1978-79 following the state seizure of Chinese-Vietnamese commerce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_boat_people.

question: The UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimates a large death toll among the Vietnamese Boat People from storms, thirst, pirate attacks in the Gulf of Thailand, and refoulement by neighboring countries. What is the standard UNHCR range?
context: The UNHCR's range for at-sea deaths is 200,000-400,000. The crisis prompted the 1979 Geneva conference and the international resettlement of about 1.5 million Indochinese refugees over the following two decades. Source: unhcr.org.

question: By the early 1980s Vietnam's Soviet-model central planning had produced rice shortages in the rice-exporting Mekong Delta, chronic urban shortages, and hyperinflation. In December 1986 the Sixth Party Congress adopted a reform program modeled on China's 1978 turn. What is the reform called?
context: Doi Moi (renovation) restored household farming, legalized private enterprise, permitted foreign investment, and deregulated prices. Vietnam became a rice exporter within three years and joined the WTO in 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doi_Moi.

question: Within a few years of Doi Moi's introduction, Vietnam achieved a specific dramatic reversal in its rice trade. What happened by around 1989-90?
context: Vietnam went from chronic rice shortage in the mid-1980s to net rice exporter within three years of the 1986 reforms. By the 2000s it was among the world's top three rice exporters. Same land, same farmers, market prices restored. Source: worldbank.org Vietnam data.

question: The Vietnamese collectivization drive of the late 1970s particularly targeted the ethnic-Chinese business community of what southern Vietnamese city?
context: The 1977-78 nationalization of southern private commerce hit ethnic-Chinese (Hoa) business families in Cholon district of Ho Chi Minh City hardest. Many became Boat People. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholon.

question: One outflow-normalization program negotiated between the US and Hanoi from 1979 allowed some Vietnamese to leave legally rather than by sea. What was the program called?
context: The Orderly Departure Program, negotiated 1979 under UNHCR auspices, allowed Vietnamese with US ties to emigrate legally. Over 500,000 Vietnamese eventually left through the program by the 1990s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orderly_Departure_Program.

question: Vietnam's 1985 hyperinflation rate -- one of the numbers that made the 1986 reforms politically possible -- reached roughly what annual rate?
context: Vietnam's inflation rate reached roughly 500% per year in 1985, driven by monetary emissions to finance state-owned enterprises. The 1986 reforms brought inflation under 40% within three years. Source: World Bank Vietnam data.

question: For the calculation debate, the Vietnamese experience since 1975 tells a specific story about market pricing. What is the ladder's teaching?
answer: The same farmers can go from famine to export within a few years once prices return
choices: The same farmers can go from famine to export within a few years once prices return
Only foreign aid can lift a country out of shortage
Central planning succeeds if run long enough
Market prices work only in industrial economies
context: Same land, same farmers, chronic shortage before 1986; rice-exporter within three years after. The Vietnamese case is the smaller-scale confirmation of the Chinese Reform-and-Opening pattern. Source: mises.org/library/vietnam-reforms.

question: In 1973 two Indiana University professors -- a husband-and-wife team -- co-founded the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, the institutional home of what became known as the Bloomington School. Who were they?
context: Vincent Ostrom (1919-2012) was a political scientist; Elinor Ostrom (1933-2012) was an economist who won the Nobel Prize in 2009 for her commons research. Both died in June 2012 within weeks of each other. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom's foundational contribution to political science was a concept describing systems in which multiple overlapping decision-making centers each have some autonomous authority, rather than a single centralized hierarchy. What did he call these systems?
context: The term captures Ostrom's core intuition: federalism, overlapping jurisdictions, and multiple service providers each performing part of a governance function. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: In 1961 Vincent Ostrom co-authored one of the most-cited public-administration papers ever, published in the American Political Science Review. Who were his two co-authors?
context: The paper, 'The Organization of Government in Metropolitan Areas: A Theoretical Inquiry,' attacked the 1950s metropolitan-consolidation movement by showing that fragmented local governments often performed better than consolidated ones. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: The 1961 Tiebout-Warren-Ostrom paper challenged a specific mid-century movement in American public administration. What movement did it push back against?
answer: The metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged
choices: The metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged
The federal-revenue-sharing movement, which held that Washington should send block grants to states
The zoning-relaxation movement, which held that local land-use rules should be repealed
The public-broadcasting movement, which held that municipal radio should replace commercial media
context: The consolidation view had held that thousands of cities, school districts, and water districts in American metropolitan areas were inefficient and should be merged. Ostrom's team showed empirically that fragmented systems often had more responsive service delivery, more experimentation, and more citizen exit-and-voice options. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: Vincent Ostrom's 1971 book 'The Political Theory of a Compound Republic' applied his polycentric analysis to a specific historical case in political design. Which case?
answer: The American founders' choice of federalism as a deliberate polycentric institutional design
choices: The American founders' choice of federalism as a deliberate polycentric institutional design
The 1789 French Revolution's abolition of provincial parlements
The 1919 Weimar Constitution's centralization of Prussian ministries
The 1917 Bolshevik consolidation of soviet councils under one party
context: The Federalist Papers (Publius) were Ostrom's core primary sources. He argued the founders had deliberately chosen multiple layers of government with separately-derived authorities over the alternative of unified national government. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom's later books -- including 'The Meaning of Democracy and the Vulnerability of Democracies' (1997) -- carried a specific warning about the direction of twentieth-century American governance. What did he warn about?
answer: Centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders designed
choices: Centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders designed
Federalism made America ungovernable in the modern administrative state
Local government should be abolished in favor of national administration
Direct democracy should replace representative federalism at every level
context: Ostrom saw the New Deal, Great Society, and post-9/11 security-state expansions as a long-run drift away from the American founders' polycentric design. The 1997 book carried a Tocquevillean warning: democracies whose polycentric structure is dismantled become vulnerable to collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom's wife Elinor was awarded a specific 2009 prize for her research on how communities govern shared resources. What did she win?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences
The National Book Award for Nonfiction
The Templeton Prize for Progress in Religion
context: The Nobel Prize in Economics. Elinor Ostrom was the first woman to win it. Her work on the commons demonstrated that community self-governance often solves resource-management problems that neither pure state ownership nor pure private ownership handles well. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Elinor_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom died on June 29, 2012 -- an unusually specific timing that made his death coincide with a family loss. What had happened seventeen days earlier?
answer: His wife Elinor Ostrom had died on June 12, 2012
choices: His wife Elinor Ostrom had died on June 12, 2012
The Ostrom Workshop at Indiana University had been formally shut down
James Buchanan had died and Ostrom had traveled for the funeral
The Nobel Prize committee had rescinded Elinor's 2009 award
context: The two co-founders of the Bloomington School died within weeks of each other -- unusual for a scholarly couple who had shared a research program for 40 years. The Ostrom Workshop at Indiana continues today under that name. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: From 1922 to 1936 the New York Times had a Moscow correspondent whose famine-denial coverage of the Soviet Union won him a Pulitzer Prize. What was his surname?
context: Walter Duranty (1884-1957) was the New York Times Moscow correspondent 1922-36. His friendly coverage of Stalin's Five-Year Plan won the 1932 Pulitzer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty.

question: Walter Duranty won a specific major American journalism prize in 1932 for a series on the Soviet Five-Year Plan. Which prize?
context: The 1932 Pulitzer for Correspondence praised Duranty for 'scholarship, profundity, impartiality, sound judgment and exceptional clarity'. Formal requests to rescind the prize have been repeatedly denied. Source: pulitzer.org/winners/walter-duranty.

question: In March 1933, as the Holodomor peaked, Duranty wrote in the New York Times that reports of famine in Russia were exaggeration or malignant propaganda. What euphemism did he use for the mass starvation?
answer: Widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition
choices: Widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition
context: Duranty's March 1933 New York Times phrasing -- 'there is no actual starvation or deaths from starvation, but there is widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition' -- became the emblematic euphemism-sentence of press cover-up. Source: New York Times, March 31, 1933.

question: The truth of the Ukrainian famine was broken in Berlin in March 1933 by a young Welsh journalist who had walked through Soviet Ukraine without a state minder. What was his surname?
context: Gareth Jones (1905-35), former private secretary to David Lloyd George, walked through Ukraine in March 1933 and published his account at a Berlin press conference on March 29, 1933. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist).

question: The day before his thirtieth birthday, in August 1935, Gareth Jones was murdered while reporting in a remote location -- shot by bandits under circumstances some historians have argued may have been arranged by Soviet intelligence. Where was he killed?
context: Jones was shot in Inner Mongolia on August 12, 1935, one day before his 30th birthday. His great-nephew Nigel Linsan Colley and others have argued the murder may have been NKVD-arranged, given the timing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist).

question: Duranty answered Jones's Berlin press-conference account in the New York Times three days later, dismissing what he had seen. What did Duranty call Jones's report?
context: Duranty's April 1, 1933 New York Times column dismissed Jones's account as 'a big scare story'. Jones responded in a letter to the editor pointing out he had walked the ground, unaccompanied. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty.

question: A Manchester Guardian Moscow correspondent filed truth-telling dispatches about the Ukrainian famine in March 1933 and was blacklisted from Soviet coverage as a result. Who was he?
context: Malcolm Muggeridge's March 1933 Manchester Guardian series described what he had seen in Ukraine. He was denied further Soviet access. He later became one of the most prominent Western Cold War-era commentators. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Muggeridge.

question: The Pulitzer Board conducted a formal review of Duranty's 1932 prize in 2003. What was the outcome?
answer: It acknowledged 'serious defects' but declined to withdraw the prize
choices: It acknowledged 'serious defects' but declined to withdraw the prize
It transferred the prize to Gareth Jones posthumously
context: The Pulitzer Board's 2003 review concluded there was 'no clear-and-convincing evidence of deliberate deception' and declined to withdraw the prize -- despite the New York Times itself calling Duranty's work in 1990 'some of the worst reporting to appear in this newspaper'. Source: pulitzer.org/duranty-statement.

question: A 2019 feature film directed by Agnieszka Holland dramatized the story of Gareth Jones's Ukraine journey and Duranty's cover-up. What was the film called?
context: Mr. Jones (2019), directed by Agnieszka Holland, starred James Norton as Gareth Jones and Peter Sarsgaard as Walter Duranty. The film brought the story to a mass audience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Jones_(2019_film).

question: President Ronald Reagan mentioned Duranty by name in a specific 1983 speech at the Cathedral of the Holy Trinity in Washington, invoking him as a warning about Western press coverage of the Soviet Union. This became a milestone in the historical reevaluation. In what decade did serious pressure to rescind the prize gather momentum?
context: Reagan's 1983 speech was among many voices raising the issue publicly. Ukrainian-American groups intensified the campaign in the 1990s and 2000s. The Times finally added a note in 1990 disavowing Duranty's work. Source: reaganlibrary.gov speeches.

question: A Chinese-American cryptographer active on the cypherpunk mailing list in the 1990s wrote a widely-used open-source cryptography library that is still in production software today. Who is he?
context: Wei Dai wrote the Crypto++ library and posted b-money in November 1998. Back wrote Hashcash; Szabo drafted bit gold; Finney wrote RPOW. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei_Dai.

question: The open-source cryptography library that Wei Dai wrote and still maintains has a distinctive name. What is the library called?
context: Wei Dai's library is Crypto++. OpenSSL, BouncyCastle, and libsodium are separate popular crypto libraries with different authors. Source: https://www.cryptopp.com/.

question: In November 1998 -- one month before Nick Szabo posted bit gold -- Wei Dai published a short proposal on his personal website (weidai.com/bmoney.txt) describing a decentralized digital cash where every user maintained their own copy of the ledger. What did he name the proposal?
context: Wei Dai's b-money was posted in November 1998; the text is only about two pages long. Bit gold is Szabo's separate proposal; Hashcash is Back's 1997 anti-spam scheme; DigiCash is Chaum's 1989 company. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: The b-money design Wei Dai sketched in November 1998 assigned a specific ledger-management responsibility to each participant in the network. What did each user have to do in b-money's model?
answer: maintain their own separate copy of every user's balances
choices: maintain their own separate copy of every user's balances
delegate all record-keeping to a trusted central server
wait for a monthly ledger snapshot from a coordinator
run a physical vault storing paper receipts
context: b-money's model: every user keeps a copy of the ledger and updates it on receipt of signed broadcast transactions. A central server, snapshot coordinator, or paper-vault model is the opposite of the design. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: In Wei Dai's b-money, new money was created by users solving small computational tasks whose difficulty was tuned so the money supply grew at a predictable rate. Which cryptographic primitive did b-money adopt from Adam Back's earlier anti-spam work?
context: b-money adopted Hashcash-style proof-of-work for money creation. Zero-knowledge proofs, elliptic-curve pairings, and public-key encryption are separate primitives that b-money did not use for issuance. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Wei Dai explicitly acknowledged in the b-money paper that two specific technical problems were still open in his design -- problems he sketched but did not fully solve. Which pair of problems did he leave open?
answer: how to reach consensus on transaction ordering, and how to keep ledger-keepers honest
choices: how to reach consensus on transaction ordering, and how to keep ledger-keepers honest
how to sign transactions, and how to encrypt payloads
how to convert existing dollars, and how to advertise the currency
how to prevent counterfeiting, and how to route the network traffic
context: b-money's two acknowledged open problems were distributed consensus and honesty enforcement -- exactly the two problems Satoshi's 2008 longest-chain-plus-PoW design solved. Signing, encryption, dollar conversion, advertising, counterfeiting, and traffic routing were not the specific gaps. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Wei Dai noted in the b-money paper that the proposal was not intended to be a finished blueprint. Which specific self-description did Dai give the two-page essay?
