answer: that 'this proposal is intended to be provocative rather than practical'
choices: that 'this proposal is intended to be provocative rather than practical'
that this is 'the definitive design for digital cash'
that this proposal 'should be adopted by every central bank'
that this proposal 'must be patented before release'
context: Wei Dai wrote that b-money 'is intended to be provocative rather than practical' -- an invitation for further work. The other statements are the opposite of his stated intent. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Ten years later, on October 31, 2008, when Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper, the paper's very first citation credited one specific earlier proposal. Which cypherpunk proposal is Reference 1 of the Bitcoin white paper?
context: Reference 1 of the Bitcoin white paper is Wei Dai's b-money. Hashcash is Reference 6; bit gold and DigiCash are not cited. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: One well-documented email exchange in the pre-publication history of Bitcoin shows Satoshi Nakamoto reaching out to Wei Dai personally in the summer of 2008. Which action did Satoshi take with Dai before publishing the white paper?
answer: he emailed Dai in August 2008 asking for comments on the draft
choices: he emailed Dai in August 2008 asking for comments on the draft
he asked Dai to co-author the paper
he asked Dai to fund Bitcoin's launch
he asked Dai for permission to fork Crypto++
context: Satoshi emailed Wei Dai in August 2008 asking for comments on the draft; the correspondence has been made public. Co-authorship, funding, and library-forking requests are not part of what Satoshi actually asked. Source: https://www.gwern.net/docs/bitcoin/2008-nakamoto.

question: A tribute to Wei Dai's role in the Bitcoin lineage lives inside the smallest denomination of a specific competing cryptocurrency that was launched in 2015 to run programmable smart contracts. Which cryptocurrency named its smallest denomination in Wei Dai's honor?
context: Ethereum names its smallest denomination the 'wei' in Wei Dai's honor (1 ETH = 10^18 wei). Litecoin's smallest unit is the litoshi; Monero's is the piconero; Dogecoin uses simple doge subdivisions. Source: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/intro-to-ether/#denominations.

question: After the First World War, Germany's central bank -- freed from gold discipline since August 1914 and burdened with Versailles reparations -- kept printing paper notes on an accelerating scale. What is that central bank called?
context: The Reichsbank was Germany's central bank from 1876 to 1948. Under Weimar-era pressure it printed paper marks -- Papiermark -- until the 1923 collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Reichsbank' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 1922 one US dollar bought about 190 German marks. By October 1923 -- 21 months later -- what had that same dollar come to buy?
context: The dollar-mark exchange rate blew from about 190 in January 1922 to about 25 billion by October 1923. Peak monthly inflation reached roughly 29,500% in October 1923 -- prices doubling every two days. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: At the peak of the German hyperinflation in October 1923, workers were paid twice a day and ran to shops before afternoon prices arrived. What visual scene from that era became the world's mental image for currency collapse?
answer: A wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread
choices: A wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread
An empty shipping container tipped over in the harbor
A locomotive stranded on rusting rails
A crowd shouting at a bank teller
context: Photographers documented Berliners pushing wheelbarrows of paper marks to bakeries. Children built block towers out of bundled 100,000-mark notes because paper had less use-value than firewood. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: One famous Weimar anecdote records a woman leaving a shopping basket unguarded for a moment. When she returned, one thing had been stolen and one thing had been left behind in disgust. What was the specific detail?
answer: The basket was stolen; the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk
choices: The basket was stolen; the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk
The money was stolen; the basket was left where it stood
The vegetables were stolen; the money was left in the basket
The basket was refilled; the money was replaced with newer notes
context: By late 1923 a woven basket was worth more than the paper banknotes it carried. The anecdote circulates in memoirs and later histories as a compressed image of what hyperinflation does to the use-value of a currency. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: In November 1923 the German finance minister introduced a new currency nominally backed by a mortgage on German industrial and agricultural land. Confidence returned within weeks. Who introduced it?
context: Schacht became commissioner for national currency in November 1923 and later Reichsbank president. His introduction of the Rentenmark ended the hyperinflation within weeks. Source: Grokipedia 'Hjalmar Schacht' (2026-09-05).

question: The new German currency Schacht introduced in November 1923 was called the Rentenmark. What was its conversion rate to the collapsing paper mark it replaced?
answer: One Rentenmark equaled one trillion Papiermark
choices: One Rentenmark equaled one trillion Papiermark
One Rentenmark equaled one thousand Papiermark
One Rentenmark equaled one million Papiermark
One Rentenmark equaled one hundred thousand Papiermark
context: The conversion rate was 1 : 1,000,000,000,000 (one trillion). Confidence returned within weeks because the new note was scarce, believed to be backed, and the old note was withdrawn. Source: Grokipedia 'Rentenmark' (2026-09-05).

question: The Weimar hyperinflation lasted only about 27 months total, but the destruction was concentrated on a specific German social group. Whose lifetime savings were wiped out?
answer: The middle class -- professionals and small savers who held bonds and cash
choices: The middle class -- professionals and small savers who held bonds and cash
The urban working class living hand to mouth
The rural peasantry with tangible farm assets
The industrial magnates with foreign-currency holdings
context: A retired doctor with a lifetime of savings in mark-denominated bonds was destroyed. A day laborer paid weekly was less devastated because he could spend before prices rose again. Rural farmers with real assets did comparatively well. The destruction was asymmetric. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: The asymmetric destruction of the German middle class in 1923 helped destroy the political center of the Weimar Republic and prepared the ground for what happened ten years later. Which specific reasoning move do Austrian economists press about this pattern?
answer: It is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction, playing out in real time
choices: It is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction, playing out in real time
It is Say's law working through wage stickiness
It is Ricardian equivalence collapsing under debt
context: The Cantillon effect: newly created money reaches some holders before others; the last to receive lose the most. Weimar concentrated that loss on savers and rentiers -- exactly the middle-class base of any liberal political order. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Bastiat would describe the Weimar experience as a contrast between what was visible in the moment and what was systematically hidden from the citizens experiencing it. Which pairing best captures that seen-and-unseen structure?
answer: Seen: money still being paid; Unseen: a generation's savings evaporating in 27 months
choices: Seen: money still being paid; Unseen: a generation's savings evaporating in 27 months
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: full employment; Unseen: rising real wages
Seen: political stability; Unseen: high tax rates
context: The wages kept arriving in nominal terms -- workers still got paid on Friday. What was invisible: every existing mark of savings was being systematically destroyed at the same time. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: The Weimar hyperinflation ended not because the government suddenly discovered discipline but because a specific structural change made further printing impossible. What made the printing stop?
answer: The introduction of a scarce new currency the old one was replaced with, ending demand for the old paper
choices: The introduction of a scarce new currency the old one was replaced with, ending demand for the old paper
The refusal of German workers to accept any paper money at all
A foreign occupation that seized the printing presses
A referendum in which citizens voted to reject fiat money
context: Schacht's Rentenmark was scarce, believed to be backed, and legally replaced the collapsing Papiermark. Confidence recovered within weeks. The technical fix was simple; the political fix (a plausibly credible new currency) was the hard part. Source: Grokipedia 'Rentenmark' (2026-09-05).

question: A 'welfare cliff' is the point on the income distribution where an additional dollar of earned wages triggers the LOSS of one or more means-tested government benefits, sometimes worth more than the extra wages. Because the lost benefits can exceed the added earnings, the effective marginal rate on that dollar can APPROACH OR EXCEED what percentage?
context: Because lost benefits can exceed added wages, a raise that increases earned income can decrease total household resources. The effective marginal rate on the raise dollar can exceed 100%. Source: Atlanta Fed CLIFF documentation (2018-).

question: In 2018 the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta launched an interactive online tool that lets a household map its specific welfare-cliff exposure across the stack of federal, state, and local means-tested benefits. What is the tool's memorable name?
context: The Career Ladder Identifier and Financial Forecaster (CLIFF) tool was developed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta starting in 2018 to map household-specific benefit phase-outs. Source: atlantafed.org (CLIFF tool).

question: In 1995 Thomas Sowell published a book cataloging cases where policies aimed at helping a group produced outcomes opposite their stated intentions. What was the book's memorable title?
context: Thomas Sowell, The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic Books, 1995). Sowell's move: judge policies by results, not by intentions. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 1995).

question: Sowell's Vision of the Anointed documents that in the early 1960s, before the Great Society welfare expansion, one measured US family-structure statistic was actually higher for African Americans than for whites. Which statistic was it?
choices: The average number of children per household
The average family income relative to whites
context: Census / Moynihan Report data showed the pre-1965 African-American two-parent family rate was HIGHER than the white rate. Post-Great-Society welfare expansion's marriage-penalty phase-outs and household-aggregation rules reversed the pattern within a generation. Source: Sowell, Vision of the Anointed (Basic 1995).

question: In 2012 the Chicago economist Casey Mulligan published a book that quantified how the safety-net expansion during the Great Recession raised effective marginal tax rates on low-income workers. What was the book's title?
context: Casey Mulligan, The Redistribution Recession: How Labor Market Distortions Contracted the Economy (Oxford University Press, 2012). Mulligan estimated that safety-net expansions during 2008-11 raised effective marginal tax rates on low-wage labor to levels comparable to a 60-90% top-bracket income tax. Source: global.oup.com (Mulligan 2012).

question: Milton Friedman's 1962 Capitalism and Freedom proposed a unified alternative to the stack of separate means-tested programs -- one benefit with a single, gradual, known phase-out rate. What did Friedman call this proposal?
context: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 12. The negative income tax would replace the multi-program stack with one benefit and one gradual phase-out, avoiding the multi-program cliff by design. Source: Friedman (1962), Chapter 12.

question: The closest existing US approximation of Milton Friedman's negative-tax proposal was established in 1975 as a targeted wage subsidy for low-earning working families and has grown steadily since. What is this program?
context: The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) was established in 1975 as a targeted refundable tax credit for low-income working families. It carries the Friedman NIT idea partially into US law, though its own phase-out kinks contribute to some cliffs. Source: irs.gov (EITC history).

question: One of the largest and most-discussed individual welfare cliffs in modern US policy sat at 400% of the Federal Poverty Level for premium subsidies under a specific 2010 statute. Which statute created that cliff?
context: The ACA (2010) originally cut off premium subsidies at 400% FPL, creating a large cliff. The American Rescue Plan (2021) and Inflation Reduction Act (2022) temporarily removed the cliff through 2025. Source: healthcare.gov (ACA subsidy schedules).

question: The Congressional Research Service counts approximately how many separate federal means-tested benefit programs in operation, whose interaction produces the welfare-cliff pattern in different combinations for different households?
context: The CRS count is approximately 82 separate federal means-tested benefit programs. Any specific household's cliff depends on which subset it participates in and how those programs' phase-outs interact. Source: crsreports.congress.gov (federal welfare programs counting).

question: The welfare-cliff analysis illustrates a general reasoning-move Sowell and Milton Friedman both press against poorly-designed antipoverty programs. What is the two-part move?
answer: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
choices: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
Judge policies by their moral intentions alone
Judge policies by the wealth of their sponsors
Judge policies by their length in pages
context: The Sowell / Friedman move recurs across Sowell's books and Friedman's Free to Choose television series. Programs designed to help can, through their phase-out incentive structures, produce the opposite outcome. The move is diagnostic, not moral. Source: Sowell (1995); Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (Harcourt 1980).

question: The welfare-cliff pattern is not a moral failing of program designers. What is the correct STRUCTURAL characterization of why it happens?
answer: It is a mechanical consequence of stacking multiple means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-outs
choices: It is a mechanical consequence of stacking multiple means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-outs
It is a deliberate design choice by federal agencies
It is required by international treaty obligations
It is a rare bureaucratic error affecting few households
context: Each program is often reasonable in isolation. The cliff emerges when several programs phase out in the same income range without coordinated schedules. Friedman's NIT proposal addresses this by design; the current stack does not. Source: Friedman (1962); Mulligan (2012); Atlanta Fed CLIFF documentation.

question: In 1919 an American Progressive-era muckraking journalist (author of 'The Shame of the Cities,' 1904) visited Soviet Russia with the diplomat William Bullitt and returned with a famous line that he later put into his 1931 autobiography verbatim: 'I have seen the future, and it works.' Who was he?
context: Steffens said the line to the US financier Bernard Baruch in Paris on the return trip. It became the model epigraph for a whole century of Western-intellectual reporting on planned economies. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lincoln_Steffens.

question: Sidney and Beatrice Webb, founders of the Fabian Society and of a prestigious British university, visited the USSR in 1932 and published a large book praising Stalin's five-year plans in 1935. Which university had the Webbs founded?
context: The LSE was founded in 1895 by the Webbs and other Fabians. Their 1935 book 'Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation?' was published by Longmans in London and New York. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sidney_and_Beatrice_Webb.

question: Sidney and Beatrice Webb's 1935 book 'Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation?' was reissued in 1937 with one specific change to its title. What did the second edition do?
choices: Added a subtitle referring to Trotsky
Removed all references to Stalin by name
context: The dropping happened at the peak of Stalin's Great Terror (1937-38). The Webbs are now interred in Westminster Abbey; Prime Minister Clement Attlee arranged their reinterment there in 1947. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sidney_and_Beatrice_Webb.

question: Walter Duranty, the New York Times's Moscow correspondent, won the Pulitzer Prize in 1932 and in 1933 wrote columns denying the Ukrainian famine while a Welsh journalist named Gareth Jones was publishing accurate reports. What line by Duranty about the famine became the most-cited example of the pattern?
answer: 'You can't make an omelette without breaking a few eggs'
choices: 'You can't make an omelette without breaking a few eggs'
'I have seen the future, and it works'
context: Duranty applied the line to the ongoing famine in his New York Times columns. Gareth Jones's accurate reports were dismissed in the same paper as a 'big scare story.' Duranty's Pulitzer has never been rescinded. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Walter_Duranty.

question: Friedrich Hayek's 1944 book 'The Road to Serfdom' diagnosed a specific professional attraction he thought explained why Western intellectuals kept excusing planning regimes. What did Hayek say attracted them?
answer: The appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project
choices: The appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project
The generous salaries paid by Moscow and Beijing to Western correspondents
The personal connections to Soviet cultural figures made through official tours
The tax deductions available to authors of pro-USSR books
context: Hayek's point was that intellectuals professionally trained in orderly rational administration mistook the visible order of a planning bureaucracy for actual competence, while dismissing the invisible market coordination they could not see. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: Chapter 10 of Friedrich Hayek's 'The Road to Serfdom' carries a title that has become one of the most-quoted phrases in political theory. What is the chapter's title?
context: The chapter argues that totalitarian regimes reward specifically the personality traits Western intellectuals were slowest to recognize, because those traits are the opposite of the professional-administrative virtues the intellectuals themselves prized. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: A high-school student in 2025 asks why the Webbs' 'Soviet Communism' book, Duranty's Pulitzer, and Steffens's autobiography remain uncensored, unrescinded, and un-removed from Westminster Abbey a generation after the archives opened. A Hayekian historian points to a specific institutional pattern. Which is it?
answer: The Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its 20th-century apologetics record
choices: The Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its 20th-century apologetics record
The Soviet archives never actually confirmed the underlying famines and purges
The Pulitzer committee rescinded the Duranty prize in 2003
The Fabian Society formally repudiated the Webbs' book in 1990
context: This is the pattern Hayek diagnosed in 'The Road to Serfdom' chapter 10. Individual figures have been criticized; the institutional prestige structures (Pulitzer, Westminster Abbey, LSE, Nobel-adjacent recognition) have largely remained intact. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: In ancient Egypt, in Rome, in Han China, in the Andes under the Inca, and in Mansa Musa's West African empire, the same metal was independently adopted as high-value money -- with no contact between these civilizations at the time of adoption. Which metal did every literate civilization converge on?
context: Convergent independent adoption is strong evidence that gold's monetary role reflects its physical properties rather than any single cultural tradition. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold as an investment' (2026-09-05).

question: The classical list of physical properties a good must have to serve well as money includes durability, portability, divisibility, fungibility, scarcity, and one last property that describes how easily traders can verify the good on sight. What is the sixth property?
context: Recognizability -- verifiability by inspection, weight, and simple test -- is why traders learned the bite test for gold and the density check that distinguishes gold from pyrite. The six properties are a diagnostic checklist for any candidate money. Source: Grokipedia 'Money' (2026-09-05).

question: Diamonds fail one specific monetary property that gold passes cleanly. Which property do diamonds fail?
answer: Divisibility -- diamonds cannot be split without loss of value
choices: Divisibility -- diamonds cannot be split without loss of value
Portability -- diamonds are too heavy to carry
Durability -- diamonds decay in ordinary conditions
Recognizability -- diamonds cannot be visually identified
context: A one-carat diamond is worth more than two half-carat diamonds. Splitting a diamond destroys value. Gold splits without loss because a gold coin has the same value per gram whether whole or halved. Source: Grokipedia 'Divisibility' (2026-09-05).

question: Seashells, cowries, and clay tokens have all been used as money in various cultures. Each of them fails one specific monetary property in a way gold does not. Which property do they fail?
answer: Scarcity -- they can be gathered or fired at will
choices: Scarcity -- they can be gathered or fired at will
Durability -- they rot or rust rapidly
Divisibility -- they cannot be split cleanly
Recognizability -- traders cannot identify them on sight
context: The cowrie shell was money in West Africa for centuries; European traders eventually undermined the system by shipping cheap shells from the Indian Ocean. Any money that can be produced cheaply loses its ability to store value. Source: Grokipedia 'Cowrie shell money' (2026-09-05).

question: A common way to game gold visually is to pass off a similar-looking metal that has about half the density. What is this counterfeit metal, and what test would catch it?
answer: Iron pyrite -- caught by the weight test, because pyrite is much less dense than gold
choices: Iron pyrite -- caught by the weight test, because pyrite is much less dense than gold
Silver -- caught by the color test, because silver is white not yellow
Copper -- caught by the acid test, because copper reacts to nitric acid
Bronze -- caught by the sound test, because bronze rings differently
context: Pyrite (fool's gold) has a density of about 5 grams per cubic centimeter; gold is about 19.3. Traders historically used weight tests and the archimedes displacement test to catch the substitution. Source: Grokipedia 'Pyrite' (2026-09-05).

question: The most rigorous modern measure of monetary scarcity is the stock-to-flow ratio, popularized by an economist in a 2018 book on Bitcoin. What is that measure?
answer: The ratio of existing above-ground stock to annual new production
choices: The ratio of existing above-ground stock to annual new production
The ratio of central-bank reserves to total public money supply
The ratio of jewelry demand to industrial demand
The ratio of mined ounces to remaining reserves in the ground
context: Stock-to-flow measures how hard the supply is to inflate. Gold's ratio is roughly 60 (60 years of current production to equal the above-ground stock); silver's is about 22; copper's is under 1. Source: Saifedean Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: The economist who wrote The Bitcoin Standard (2018) and used the stock-to-flow ratio to compare gold, silver, and Bitcoin is a Lebanese-American academic. What is his name?
context: Ammous's The Bitcoin Standard is the most widely cited Austrian-tradition argument for Bitcoin as gold's successor. His stock-to-flow framing became the standard analytic move in Bitcoin economics. Source: Grokipedia 'Saifedean Ammous' (2026-09-05).

question: The reason gold's stock-to-flow is so high is a physical fact about the metal that no other commodity shares. What is it?
answer: Essentially all the gold ever mined is still around, so annual production adds only about 1.5% to the total stock
choices: Essentially all the gold ever mined is still around, so annual production adds only about 1.5% to the total stock
Gold decays radioactively over long periods, keeping the stock roughly constant
Gold is largely locked in central-bank vaults and is legally prohibited from resale
Gold is inedible, so annual consumption is essentially zero
context: Gold does not corrode or oxidize. A gold coin buried in 500 BC comes out shiny. The world's above-ground stock is roughly 200,000 tonnes; annual mining adds about 3,000 tonnes -- 1.5% of the total. Source: World Gold Council (goldhub.com).

question: The convergent-selection argument for gold as money teaches a specific recognition move about how monetary goods are chosen. Which move?
answer: Gold's monetary role reflects its physical properties, not cultural accident -- so any successor must beat gold on at least one property without losing others
choices: Gold's monetary role reflects its physical properties, not cultural accident -- so any successor must beat gold on at least one property without losing others
Gold's monetary role reflects only the accident of ancient trade routes
Gold was chosen by governments for legal reasons, not by markets
Gold's success is due entirely to its aesthetic appeal in jewelry
context: The convergent-selection argument sets an engineering test for any candidate money: you must beat gold on at least one property (portability, divisibility, verifiability) without giving up any of the six. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Bitcoin was engineered to pass the six-properties test that gold passes, but with specific improvements in three of the six. Which improvements does it offer?
answer: Unlimited divisibility, effortless portability by wire, and cryptographic verifiability capped at 21 million units
choices: Unlimited divisibility, effortless portability by wire, and cryptographic verifiability capped at 21 million units
Physical backing, government issuance, and legal-tender protection
Higher industrial demand, larger physical bulk, and slower supply growth
Continuous supply expansion, community memory, and central-bank governance
context: Bitcoin's architecture matches gold's durability and fungibility, and beats it on three specific properties: it splits to eight decimals, travels at the speed of a wire transfer, and is cryptographically verifiable with a fixed 21-million cap. Source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008).

question: On the evening of November 9 1989 an East German government spokesman, Guenter Schabowski, held a press conference in East Berlin. Reading from a note he had not fully prepared, he mistakenly announced that new travel rules took effect 'immediately, without delay'. Within hours crowds were climbing over a concrete barrier that had divided the city since 1961. What barrier did they climb?
context: Schabowski's slip triggered the physical opening of the wall that same night. The wall's fall became the visible signal that the Soviet-bloc planned economies had lost the argument. Source: www.archives.gov/news/topics/berlin-wall-anniversary.

question: Two years and six weeks after the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet Union itself formally dissolved. On the evening of December 25 1991 its president resigned on live television, the hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered from the Kremlin for the last time, and fifteen successor states took its place. Which Soviet president resigned that night?
context: Gorbachev's resignation ended the Soviet state that had run the world's largest planned economy for 69 years -- exactly the span from Ludwig von Mises's 1920 essay warning that such an economy could not calculate. Source: history.state.gov/departmenthistory/short-history/berlinwall.

question: The Soviet collapse of 1989-1991 came 69 years after a specific 1920 Vienna essay by Ludwig von Mises had predicted that a fully socialist economy would suffer chronic shortages, gluts, and misallocations because it lacked the market prices needed to compare costs. What is the standard name of the essay?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
context: The German original 'Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen' appeared in Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik volume 47 (1920), pages 86-121. Its predictions were tested at scale on hundreds of millions of people for seven decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: After 1989 an American historian and researcher, Stephane Courtois, gathered work by six European scholars into a single documentary reckoning of the twentieth-century Communist regimes. First published in France in 1997 and by Harvard University Press in 1999, it counted deaths at roughly 100 million across the USSR, China, Cambodia, North Korea, Eastern Europe, and elsewhere. What is the book called?
choices: The Rise and Fall of Communism
context: 'Le Livre noir du communisme' (Robert Laffont, Paris, Nov 6 1997); English translation by Jonathan Murphy and Mark Kramer as 'The Black Book of Communism: Crimes, Terror, Repression' (Harvard University Press, 1999). Its introduction placed the total at around 100 million, compared with an estimated 25 million for the Nazi regimes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: In its September 10 1990 issue The New Yorker ran a Reflections essay by Robert Heilbroner containing his admission that Ludwig von Mises had been right about socialism. Alongside that concession Heilbroner named the specific pathology the Soviet-bloc pricing methods had produced -- the pattern Mises had predicted in 1920. Which phrase did Heilbroner apply to the Soviet pricing outcome?
choices: Unresolved contradictions between owner and worker
context: Heilbroner conceded that the Soviet pricing methods had produced 'grotesque misallocations of effort' -- steel factories with no buyers, warehouses of unsalable shoes, chronic shortages of what people actually wanted -- exactly the pathology Mises had predicted seventy years earlier. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument focused on the impossibility of comparing costs without market prices. Friedrich Hayek reframed the problem in a September 1945 American Economic Review essay, arguing that the deeper obstacle to central planning was not the arithmetic but a specific kind of information markets generate and planners cannot obtain. Which kind of information did Hayek say the planner could never assemble?
answer: The dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
choices: The dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
The stable long-run demand elasticities for each consumer good
The public opinion polling on preferred production targets
The confidential cost accounts held by state enterprise managers
context: 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (AER 35:4, September 1945) argued the planner is missing the knowledge that only exists at the point of production and consumption. That knowledge is what prices summarise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: On December 18 1978, at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, a paramount leader unveiled a set of pilot reforms opening rural markets, allowing private plots, and starting to dismantle central price controls. His policies eventually pulled China out of Maoist planning and became the reference model for other transitioning Communist states. Who was he?
context: The December 1978 Third Plenum is treated as the birth of the reform-and-opening-up era. From 1978 to 2019 China's per-capita GDP rose more than fifty-fold -- but only where and when the market replaced planning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up.

question: In 1986 the Vietnamese Communist Party's Sixth National Congress adopted a package of market-oriented reforms modelled explicitly on Deng Xiaoping's 1978 Chinese opening -- deregulating agriculture, ending most price controls, and opening to foreign investment. Vietnamese per-capita GDP has since risen roughly eightfold. What Vietnamese-language name is given to this reform program?
context: 'Doi Moi' means 'renovation'. Vietnam went from about $422 per-capita GDP in 1986 to nearly $3,700 in the following decades. Central planning was quietly abandoned; the Party stayed in charge but stopped setting most prices. Source: thediplomat.com/2023/01/the-myth-of-doi-moi-in-vietnam/.

question: In 1985 the American economist Don Lavoie published 'Rivalry and Central Planning' arguing that the mainstream profession had answered Ludwig von Mises's narrower point about prices but had never engaged Friedrich Hayek's deeper point about dispersed knowledge. Modern Austrians including Joseph Salerno, Peter Boettke, and Juergen Guido Huelsmann drew a specific inference about how the profession handled the 1989 collapse of the planned economies. Which pattern did they identify?
answer: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
choices: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
The profession quietly withdrew all remaining market-socialist proposals by 1995
The profession credited the Austrians in its textbooks by the mid-1990s
The profession dropped comparative-systems economics from graduate curricula
context: Lavoie, Salerno, Boettke, and Huelsmann observed the same pattern Thomas Kuhn described in 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' -- a discipline can accept the outside facts while continuing to teach the old textbook framing. That, they argued, is why market-socialist proposals keep reappearing in every generation. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: Robert Heilbroner's 1990 New Yorker admission that Ludwig von Mises had been right was, in his own account, an acknowledgment of a test that had been running for 69 years on the largest scale in the history of the social sciences. What was the deep lesson Heilbroner conceded -- the general question the twentieth-century planned economies had been made to answer with hundreds of millions of lives?
answer: Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
choices: Whether Marx's labour theory of value could be salvaged with better mathematics
Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
Whether socialist countries could avoid dependence on world trade
Whether workers' councils could substitute for private firms as legal owners
context: The 1920 essay had said no -- not because central planners lacked good intentions, but because the information needed to compare production plans exists only in the dispersed heads of the people doing the producing and consuming. The 20th-century death toll of Communism, put by the Black Book of Communism at roughly 100 million, was the price of running the experiment. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 essay was published in an obscure German-language academic journal. In 1935 it appeared in English for the first time, inside an edited volume that put the whole calculation problem before Oskar Lange, Abba Lerner, and the English-speaking economics profession -- and thereby set the terms for the debate whose empirical verdict came in 1989. Who edited that 1935 volume?
context: 'Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism', edited by F.A. Hayek (Routledge, London, 1935). Hayek's own introductory essay 'The Nature and History of the Problem' framed the debate for a whole generation. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: In 1971 the publisher Aldine-Atherton released a slim volume that applied economic reasoning to the incentives facing federal bureaucrats. Its author later chaired Ronald Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers and, for decades, the Cato Institute. Who wrote the book?
context: William Niskanen (1933-2011) was a Chicago-trained economist who served in Nixon's OMB, chaired Reagan's CEA (1981-85), and chaired the Cato Institute from 1985 until his death. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Niskanen.

question: William Niskanen's 1971 book applied economics to bureau behavior. What title did he give this founding text of bureaucratic economics?
context: Bureaucracy and Representative Government (Aldine-Atherton, 1971). It built directly on Gordon Tullock's earlier Politics of Bureaucracy (1965). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Niskanen.

question: Niskanen's central move: instead of assuming bureaucrats maximize 'public welfare' or 'agency mission,' ask what actually accrues personally to a bureaucrat over his or her career. What single variable did Niskanen argue bureaucrats effectively maximize, since salary, prestige, staff, and promotion prospects all correlate with it?
answer: The size of their agency's budget
choices: The size of their agency's budget
The public opinion of their agency
The number of press releases per year
The judicial rulings favoring their agency
context: Niskanen's model: salary, staff, prestige, perquisites, agency power, and promotion prospects are all positively correlated with agency budget. A bureaucrat rationally advancing his or her career therefore fights for a bigger budget. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 4.

question: Niskanen's argument does NOT accuse bureaucrats of any personal wickedness. What is the actual logical structure of his claim?
answer: The career incentive structure REWARDS budget-expanding behavior
choices: The career incentive structure REWARDS budget-expanding behavior
Bureaucrats are corrupted by contact with lobbyists
Bureaucrats consciously conspire to defraud the public
Bureaucrats are less ethical than private-sector employees
context: Niskanen models an INCENTIVE STRUCTURE, not a moral failing. Whatever an agency's official mission, the structure that rewards its staff systematically favors expansion. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface.

question: Niskanen's model predicts that a federal agency will almost NEVER announce that its founding mission is complete. Why not, given his mechanism?
answer: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
choices: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
Federal law prohibits announcing mission completion
The agency cannot legally hire external consultants to certify completion
Congress passes laws to keep agencies alive regardless of mission
context: A completed-mission announcement is against every staff member's career interest. The predictable behavior is instead mission creep -- redefining the mission as new problems the agency must address. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 5.

question: President Reagan's administration made an ambitious rhetorical case for shrinking federal agencies. Niskanen's model would predict a specific empirical pattern for total federal civilian employment during his two terms. What actually happened?
answer: It barely moved despite the political pressure
choices: It barely moved despite the political pressure
It fell by roughly forty percent
It rose by roughly a hundred percent
context: Federal civilian employment stayed essentially flat under Reagan (1981-89) despite aggressive rhetoric. Individual agency budgets fluctuated modestly; the total was very sticky. Niskanen predicts exactly this stickiness. Source: OPM historical federal civilian employment data (bea.gov, opm.gov).

question: Anthony Downs preceded Niskanen by four years with a 1967 book that offered a typology of bureaucratic personality types -- climbers, conservers, zealots, advocates, statesmen. The two works are usually treated as complementary rather than rival. What was Downs's book called?
context: Anthony Downs, Inside Bureaucracy (Little Brown, 1967). Downs classifies bureaucrats by mix of self-interest and mission-interest; Niskanen models the aggregate effect. The two frameworks fit together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: Niskanen resigned from Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers in 1985 over a specific policy disagreement with the administration. Which fiscal issue was the immediate cause?
answer: The administration's abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda
choices: The administration's abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda
The administration's tariff on Japanese steel
The administration's monetary policy under Volcker
context: Niskanen resigned in protest of the administration's growing deficits and its failure to pair tax cuts with a serious spending-cut program. He then moved to chair the Cato Institute for the rest of his career. Source: Niskanen, Reaganomics (Oxford 1988).

question: Niskanen's 1971 model predicts several observable patterns about federal agencies that would be surprising if the naive 'agencies maximize public welfare' assumption held. Which of the following is NOT one of the patterns his budget-maximization model predicts?
answer: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
choices: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
Agencies rarely announce that their mission is complete
Agencies with unclear performance metrics tend to grow fastest
Agencies grow during friendly administrations and shrink little under opposition
context: Niskanen predicts the OPPOSITE: agencies with UNCLEAR performance metrics grow fastest, because failure cannot be measured. Where failure IS measurable, budget increases become harder to justify. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 6.

question: William Niskanen's whole 1971 argument can be summed up in one sentence about what economics adds when applied to public employees. Which sentence best captures the payoff?
answer: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions about agency behavior
choices: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions about agency behavior
Bureaucrats are morally worse than other workers
All federal agencies should be abolished
context: Niskanen's contribution: give up the benevolent-planner assumption and predictions about bureau behavior become far more accurate. This is the symmetric application of standard economic reasoning to political actors. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface and Chapter 12.

question: In the first week of August 1914, as the great powers mobilized for war, each major belligerent immediately did something to its money that ended the century-long classical gold standard. What did every belligerent do?
answer: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
choices: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
context: Germany suspended convertibility on August 4 1914; Britain effectively followed within days; France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary all did the same within the week. The gold standard died in one week. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: The reason every belligerent suspended gold convertibility in August 1914 was that a full gold standard would have limited how a government could raise money for war. Under gold, what were the only two funding options?
answer: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
choices: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
Selling colonies or licensing trade monopolies
Devaluing the currency or issuing new coins
context: Under gold, states could raise money only by taxing (unpopular, slow) or borrowing (limited by lender willingness). Once off gold, they could print paper and defer the reckoning until after victory. Source: Grokipedia 'World War I reparations' (2026-09-05).

question: Over the four years of the First World War, Germany's outstanding paper notes expanded by roughly what multiple?
context: Germany's monetary base grew roughly 12-fold between 1914 and 1918, seeding the postwar hyperinflation. Britain's price level roughly doubled; France's roughly tripled; Russia's ruble collapsed entirely in the 1917 revolution. Source: Grokipedia 'Papiermark' (2026-09-05).

question: Only one major belligerent kept relative monetary discipline through the war because it entered late and committed less domestic spending. Which country?
context: The US entered the war in April 1917, roughly two and a half years after the European powers. Its shorter war and smaller relative commitment kept dollar inflation modest compared to the belligerents already fighting since 1914. Source: Grokipedia 'United States home front during World War I' (2026-09-05).

question: The Austrian economist who made the specific counterfactual argument that the First World War could not have been fought for four years under a full classical gold standard published that argument in an early 1919 book. Which economist made the case?
context: Mises's 1919 book Nation, State, and Economy argued that gold discipline would have forced belligerents to a negotiated settlement within months. The four-year industrial slaughter (~17 million dead) was economically possible only because paper-money printing had been unleashed. Source: mises.org/library/nation-state-and-economy.

question: In 1925 Britain formally returned to the gold standard at a specific historical rate that made the pound sterling significantly overvalued and forced painful deflation on British workers. At what rate did Chancellor Churchill fix the pound?
context: On advice from Bank of England officials, Churchill returned sterling at the 1914 rate of $4.86, even though the pound's real value had fallen. British exports became uncompetitive; unemployment stayed high through the late 1920s. Source: Grokipedia 'Return to gold' (2026-09-05).

question: John Maynard Keynes attacked Churchill's 1925 return to gold in a famous pamphlet whose title named Churchill directly. What did Keynes call it?
answer: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
choices: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
The Return to Gold: A Warning
context: Keynes's 1925 pamphlet echoed the title of his 1919 attack on the Versailles Treaty, 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'. Keynes and the Austrians agreed about the 1925 decision (both thought it wrong) though for different theoretical reasons. Source: Grokipedia 'John Maynard Keynes' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1922 Genoa Conference tried to reduce the pressure on world gold reserves by proposing a weaker version of the classical system in which only central banks would hold physical gold, and commercial reserves would be foreign currencies redeemable for gold. What is this weaker system called?
context: The gold-exchange standard emerged from the 1922 Genoa Conference and became the interwar norm. It was already collapsing by 1931 when Britain permanently abandoned gold; it died fully with WW2. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold exchange standard' (2026-09-05).

question: The MOVE the ladder teaches about the relationship between sound money and state power is a specific historical thesis Austrians press hard. Which thesis?
answer: Sound money is a constraint on government power; states that want to fight big wars always want to be freed from that constraint
choices: Sound money is a constraint on government power; states that want to fight big wars always want to be freed from that constraint
Sound money is a technical arrangement with no political significance
Sound money encourages military spending by making it cheaper
Sound money is preferred by governments and opposed only by bankers
context: Every 20th-century abandonment of gold discipline was driven by governments that wanted to expand spending -- usually war spending -- beyond what taxpayers would voluntarily fund. The pattern is not incidental; it is structural. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: The Austrian reading of the 20th century holds that political catastrophe and monetary catastrophe are causally linked, not two separate stories. Which pairing best captures that linkage?
answer: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
choices: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
The wars caused monetary collapse and the collapse then caused more wars
Monetary experiments and wars were independent 20th-century phenomena
The wars were entirely funded by taxes on wealthy citizens
context: The Austrian counterfactual: no four-year Great War without paper-money printing; no paper-money printing without abandoning gold discipline. The 20th century's political catastrophes and its monetary catastrophes have a shared root cause. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: In 2008 a 68-year-old retired Chinese journalist -- who had spent 35 years inside the official state news agency Xinhua -- published a two-volume book in Hong Kong giving a bottom-up provincial death toll for the 1958-62 Great Leap Forward famine. Who was he?
context: Yang was born 1940 in Hubei province. Dikotter, Banister, and Ashton are Western scholars of the same famine; Yang was the insider-journalist who counted from within. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: Yang Jisheng's 2008 two-volume book on the 1958-62 Chinese famine carried a Chinese title that has become the shorthand for the whole work. In its English rendering, what was the title?
context: Tombstone (Mu Bei in Chinese) referred to the author's father, to whom the book was dedicated, and to the millions unnamed in Chinese public memory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: Yang Jisheng's life project was triggered by a specific personal event during the 1958-62 Great Leap Forward famine. What was it?
answer: His own father, a rural schoolteacher, died of starvation in April 1959
choices: His own father, a rural schoolteacher, died of starvation in April 1959
His own village was destroyed by a Red Guard raid
His own mother was denounced as a class enemy
His own house was seized by the local commune
context: The party had denied there was a famine; the young Yang, then a high-schooler and Communist Youth League member, believed them. Discovering later that his father had been one of tens of millions became his life's work. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: Yang Jisheng's 2008 book gave a bottom-up count of excess deaths in the 1958-62 Great Leap Forward famine, based on seven years of provincial archive research. Roughly what figure did he arrive at?
context: Prior Western estimates (Judith Banister 1987, Basil Ashton 1984, both around 30 million) had been top-down demographic estimates from national census gaps. Yang's was the first bottom-up count from actual provincial records. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Great_Chinese_Famine.

question: Yang Jisheng's methodological breakthrough was different from previous Great Leap Forward death-toll estimates. What did he do that Judith Banister and Basil Ashton had not been able to do in the 1980s?
answer: He counted from actual provincial party records rather than inferring from national census gaps
choices: He counted from actual provincial party records rather than inferring from national census gaps
He interviewed exactly 100,000 survivors in a randomized survey
He used a computer model of Chinese demography from 1949 to 2000
He worked entirely from published Chinese government White Papers
context: Yang's Xinhua credentials and personal connections gave him access to provincial archives that had never been available to Western scholars. The bottom-up method vindicated the older top-down estimates and added specificity province by province. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: Tombstone was translated to English in 2012 and published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux. Who did the translation, and what was the abridged English title?
answer: Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian; 'Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962'
choices: Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian; 'Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine 1958-1962'
Perry Link and Andrew Nathan; 'The Tiananmen Papers'
Wu Ningkun and Li Yikai; 'A Single Tear'
Ha Jin and Yan Lianke; 'The Four Books'
context: The two-volume Chinese original was abridged to one English volume. Wu Ningkun and Li Yikai wrote a different memoir (A Single Tear); Ha Jin and Yan Lianke are novelists of adjacent Chinese trauma but not Yang's translators. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: In 2013 the Manhattan Institute awarded Yang Jisheng the Hayek Prize for the English edition of Tombstone. In 2016 the Chinese government did what regarding Yang and the prize?
answer: Denied him permission to leave China to accept the prize in person
choices: Denied him permission to leave China to accept the prize in person
Allowed him to travel and receive the prize in New York
Awarded him a competing state honor to counterbalance the Hayek Prize
Rescinded the Hayek Prize under diplomatic pressure
context: Tombstone remains banned for mainland Chinese publication. The prize is named for Friedrich Hayek and is the Manhattan Institute's annual award for a book that best reflects Hayek's principles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: On November 8 2002, a Fed governor spoke at a University of Chicago conference honoring the 90th birthday of a Nobel-laureate economist and closed his remarks with a public apology on behalf of the Federal Reserve. Whose birthday was the conference honoring?
context: The University of Chicago hosted a two-day conference in November 2002 to mark Milton Friedman's 90th birthday. Friedman (born July 31 1912) sat in the audience for Bernanke's remarks. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 Fed governor who made the public apology to Friedman was a Princeton economist who specialized academically in the Great Depression. Later he became Fed chair from 2006 to 2014. Who was he?
context: Bernanke had joined the Fed Board in 2002 after two decades as an academic at Princeton. His scholarly work focused on the monetary history of the 1929-33 downturn -- exactly the topic of his apology. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: The 1963 Friedman-Schwartz book that made the case Bernanke's speech was accepting -- that the Federal Reserve caused the Great Depression by letting the money supply contract about 33% between 1929 and 1933 -- carried a specific title. What is that book called?
answer: A Monetary History of the United States
choices: A Monetary History of the United States
context: The full title is A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960, coauthored with Anna Schwartz and published by Princeton University Press in 1963. Chapter 7, 'The Great Contraction,' contained the specific argument. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: The specific claim in the Friedman-Schwartz book that Bernanke's 2002 speech accepted on behalf of the Federal Reserve was about what the Fed had done -- or failed to do -- between 1929 and 1933. What did the Fed do?
answer: Allowed the money supply to contract about 33% by failing to act as lender of last resort during bank failures
choices: Allowed the money supply to contract about 33% by failing to act as lender of last resort during bank failures
Deliberately raised interest rates to attack speculators
Devalued the dollar against gold in coordination with Britain
Printed money to bail out farmers hit by drought
context: Bank failures cascaded 1930-33, wiping out deposits and shrinking the money supply. Friedman and Schwartz argued a competent central bank should have flooded the system with liquidity -- exactly what Bernanke did in 2008. Source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History (1963).

question: Bernanke closed his November 2002 birthday speech with a direct address to Friedman and Anna Schwartz in the audience. Which specific concession did his closing sentences make?
answer: You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
choices: You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
You were wrong, but we forgive the theoretical mistake
We agree partially, but the fiscal side matters equally
You may be right but the evidence is not yet decisive
context: Bernanke abused (his word) his official status as a Fed representative to deliver the extraordinary concession directly to the 90-year-old Friedman. The full text is on federalreserve.gov. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2002 birthday-party admission stands as one of the most remarkable concessions a central bank has ever made in public. What did Bernanke's speech acknowledge that his institution had caused?
answer: The worst economic catastrophe in modern American history
choices: The worst economic catastrophe in modern American history
The dot-com stock-market bubble of the 1990s
The 1970s inflation of the Great Inflation era
The 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital Management
context: The Great Depression (1929-33) was the deepest and longest downturn in US history. An official Fed representative publicly conceding institutional responsibility for it was unprecedented. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: Six years after the birthday-party apology, the same Fed chair who had made it was in charge during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. What did he do that contradicted the humility of the 2002 speech, in the view of his Austrian critics?
answer: Launched massive quantitative easing and zero interest rates that his critics argue mispriced capital and seeded a later inflation wave
choices: Launched massive quantitative easing and zero interest rates that his critics argue mispriced capital and seeded a later inflation wave
Allowed bank failures to cascade unchecked through the whole system
Raised interest rates aggressively into the recession to protect the dollar
Publicly refused to serve as lender of last resort in September 2008
context: The Austrian critique: in avoiding the 1930s error, Bernanke committed an opposite error -- keeping rates artificially low for years, mispricing capital across the economy, and setting up the 2020-24 inflation wave. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012, updated 2014).

question: Milton Friedman died in November 2006, before he could see the full Fed response to the 2008 crisis. His coauthor Anna Schwartz lived until 2012 and gave a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview about the same Fed chair Bernanke. What did she say?
answer: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
choices: That he has no true understanding of what is going on
That he was implementing exactly the policy she and Friedman had recommended
That his intervention would restore price stability within a year
That she supported his aggressive rate cuts unreservedly
context: Schwartz's October 2008 Wall Street Journal interview sharply criticized Bernanke's crisis response, effectively reversing the endorsement Bernanke had claimed six years earlier. Source: Wall Street Journal, 'The Fed and the Financial Crisis' interview (October 18 2008).

question: The 2002 birthday-party admission and the 2008 Schwartz critique together form a specific recognition move about central-bank institutional learning. Which move does the ladder press on the reader?
answer: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next crisis
choices: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next crisis
Central banks steadily improve their forecasting record over decades
Public apologies from central bankers reliably predict better future policy
Academic historians consistently produce better central-bank chairs than practitioners
context: Bernanke avoided the 1930s mistake and possibly caused a 2020s one. The pattern is not incidental. Every crisis-forged lesson becomes doctrine that the next crisis violates. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: The 2002 speech is important as evidence that even the Federal Reserve now formally accepts a specific monetarist thesis about a landmark 20th-century episode. Which thesis?
answer: The Fed itself caused the Great Depression through failure to act as lender of last resort
choices: The Fed itself caused the Great Depression through failure to act as lender of last resort
The Great Depression was primarily caused by the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff
The Great Depression was primarily caused by rigid wage-price rules under Hoover
The Great Depression was primarily caused by foreign currency depreciations
context: The Friedman-Schwartz thesis is now standard even inside the Fed. The remaining dispute is not whether the Fed failed but what the correct alternative response would have been -- which is where Austrian critics part ways with the monetarist prescription. Source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History (1963); Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: From about 2000 Zimbabwe's president ordered the seizure of white-owned commercial farms as part of a land-reform program. The farms had produced most of the country's grain and export earnings; production collapsed and tax revenue collapsed with it. Who was the president behind these seizures?
context: Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017. The fast-track land-reform program of 2000 onward is the direct fiscal cause of the later hyperinflation. Source: Grokipedia 'Land reform in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: To pay the army and civil service as tax revenue collapsed, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe began printing money on an accelerating scale. By November 2008 the country's monthly inflation reached an official peak that put it in the top two hyperinflations of all recorded history. What was the November 2008 monthly rate?
context: November 2008 Zimbabwean monthly inflation is officially estimated at 79,600,000,000% -- prices doubling roughly every 24 hours. Only Hungary's July 1946 pengo (41.9 quadrillion percent) was worse in recorded history. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: In January 2009 the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued a banknote whose face-value denomination broke the world record. What was the denomination?
context: The 100,000,000,000,000-Zimbabwe-dollar note is the highest-denomination banknote ever issued by any government in monetary history. When issued in January 2009 it bought roughly three eggs. Source: Grokipedia 'Zimbabwean dollar' (2026-09-05).

question: By late 2008 and 2009 the formal Zimbabwean economy collapsed. Citizens spontaneously abandoned the domestic currency and began using foreign money for everyday transactions. Which foreign currencies did they adopt?
answer: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
choices: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
The British pound and the euro only
The Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan
The Kenyan shilling and the Egyptian pound
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans used whichever foreign currency they could get. The government formally accepted the dollarization; the Zimbabwe dollar was demonetized in June 2015. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: When the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe formally demonetized the Zimbabwe dollar in June 2015, it converted remaining bank balances at a specific exchange rate to the US dollar. What was the rate?
answer: 175 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
choices: 175 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
1 billion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
10 trillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
1 million Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar
context: The demonetization rate was Z$175,000,000,000,000,000 for USD 1 -- the government's formal admission of the currency's collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Zimbabwean dollar' (2026-09-05).

question: Zimbabwe's 100-trillion-dollar notes did not simply disappear after demonetization. They are now sold worldwide as inexpensive keepsakes. What is their new market role?
answer: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
choices: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
Legal tender in Zimbabwe's tourist areas
Reserve assets held by African central banks
Backing for a new Zimbabwean cryptocurrency
context: A Zimbabwean 100-trillion-dollar note now sells for roughly $2 to $15 USD on collector sites -- a physical, cheap, permanent reminder of what fiat-currency collapse looks like. Source: collector-market listings on eBay and specialist numismatic sites (2020-2025).

question: The mechanism that produced the Zimbabwean hyperinflation was textbook Austrian. Which two ingredients combined to produce the collapse?
answer: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
choices: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
A trade deficit from failed exports plus a currency peg to gold
A shortage of labor plus a rise in wages
A political crisis plus a foreign embargo
context: The land-seizure program destroyed the productive tax base. The Reserve Bank was ordered to fund the state anyway. Money-printing without a growing real economy produces the Cantillon-effect destruction of savers, then hyperinflation, then abandonment. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: The 2007-2009 Zimbabwe episode teaches a specific recognition move that undermines a common assumption Western students bring to older hyperinflation stories. Which assumption does it correct?
answer: That modern hyperinflations are relics of the 1920s and no longer happen
choices: That modern hyperinflations are relics of the 1920s and no longer happen
That all hyperinflations end quickly through spontaneous market recovery
That hyperinflations are always the result of foreign invasion
That hyperinflations always require the presence of gold reserves
context: Zimbabwe is not history; it is a live monetary experiment students can watch on YouTube today. The same mechanism runs identically in Africa, Latin America, and the modern world whenever it is unleashed. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation' (2026-09-05).

question: The Zimbabwe hyperinflation, like every other in recorded history, ended in a specific way that reveals what money actually is. What did the country's monetary system do at the end?
answer: Ordinary people spontaneously adopted foreign currencies from below, before the government formally allowed it
choices: Ordinary people spontaneously adopted foreign currencies from below, before the government formally allowed it
The government successfully re-anchored the Zimbabwe dollar to gold
The IMF imposed a new central-bank currency by treaty
A regional currency union in Southern Africa absorbed the Zimbabwe dollar
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans were already pricing goods in USD, rand, and pula in the informal economy. The government then formalized what citizens had already done. Money is what people accept; the government simply catches up. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: Bastiat would describe the Zimbabwean episode as a contrast between what appeared to be a government policy and what actually happened to real people. Which pairing best captures the seen-and-unseen structure?
answer: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
choices: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
Seen: land redistributed to landless workers; Unseen: rising urban employment
Seen: rising exports; Unseen: falling imports
Seen: an independent central bank; Unseen: rising foreign reserves
context: The visible policy achievement (paying the army and civil service) hid the invisible destruction (every existing bank balance and cash holding in the country evaporating). The Cantillon effect on a national scale. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: On June 26, 2007, facing hyperinflation driven by his own government's money-printing, an African president ordered all retail prices in his country cut roughly in half, with imprisonment as the penalty for non-compliance. Who signed the order?
context: Zimbabwe's president since 1980. Police and army units enforced the order in Harare and Bulawayo supermarkets, arresting shopkeepers who did not comply. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: Within a very specific short window after Robert Mugabe's June 26, 2007 price-halving order, Zimbabwean retail shelves were completely empty. Roughly how long did it take?
context: Consumers rushed to buy at below-cost prices; merchandise vanished into private hoarding or black markets. The collapse happened at time-lapse speed compared to normal economic-policy failures. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: Within days of Mugabe's June 2007 price-halving order, a specific downstream effect began cascading through Zimbabwe's economy beyond the immediate empty shelves. What was it?
answer: Factories (meat processors, dairies, bakeries) began shutting down because they could not produce at below-cost mandated prices
choices: Factories (meat processors, dairies, bakeries) began shutting down because they could not produce at below-cost mandated prices
The Zimbabwean central bank raised interest rates to defend the currency
The IMF signed an emergency lending program with Harare
Neighboring Botswana closed its border to prevent smuggling
context: The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries reported that hundreds of manufacturers closed operations or laid off staff within the first two weeks of the order. The reasoning: no firm can produce a loaf of bread at a mandated price below the cost of the flour and fuel to bake it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: Roughly how long did Robert Mugabe's June 2007 price-halving order remain formally in force before being quietly abandoned as unenforceable?
context: The order was not formally rescinded; enforcement simply lapsed as the visible collapse of shelves and factories made it politically impossible to sustain. The underlying hyperinflation continued. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: Robert Mugabe's June 2007 price-halving order was aimed at the symptom (rising prices) while ignoring the underlying cause. What was the underlying cause of Zimbabwe's inflation?
answer: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget
choices: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget
Global commodity prices had risen because of Chinese demand
Zimbabwean workers had gone on strike for higher wages
The US Federal Reserve had raised interest rates
context: The classic Friedman monetary diagnosis: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. The price ceiling attacked the symptom (visible prices) while the disease (money creation) continued and accelerated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: In January 2009 the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued a physical banknote that became the world's most famous illustration of hyperinflation. What was the note's face value?
context: The country formally adopted the US dollar as its functional currency the same year 2009, abandoning the Zimbabwean dollar entirely. Cato senior fellow Steve Hanke had tracked the Zimbabwean hyperinflation in real time and published widely-cited estimates through the collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: A high-school student in 2025 asks what makes the June 2007 Zimbabwe episode uniquely useful for teaching price controls. A Hayekian economist points to a specific property. Which one?
answer: The whole seen-versus-unseen chain from order to visible collapse ran in about 48 hours
choices: The whole seen-versus-unseen chain from order to visible collapse ran in about 48 hours
The order was rescinded by international treaty within one day
The Zimbabwean parliament unanimously vetoed the president's order
The affected supermarkets sued the government and won
context: Most price-control failures unfold over years and can be argued about. Zimbabwe compressed the entire chain -- decree, seen legal price on labels, unseen goods disappearing, shortages, factory closures -- into a single school-week. It became the fastest, cleanest demonstration in modern economic history. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: In 1926 the US Supreme Court upheld a suburban Ohio village's power to restrict how privately owned land could be built on, giving American cities the legal authority they still use today to write land-use codes. What is the case's name?
answer: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty
choices: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty
Kelo v. City of New London
Penn Central v. New York City
context: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926) upheld comprehensive municipal zoning against a Fourteenth Amendment challenge and became the constitutional backstop for every US zoning code since. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Village_of_Euclid_v._Ambler_Realty_Co..

question: One large US city is famously unique among all major American cities for never having adopted a conventional zoning code; it uses private deed restrictions instead. Which city is it?
context: Houston, Texas is the largest US city without a conventional zoning code. Land-use control there is done through private deed restrictions, not city ordinance. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zoning_in_Houston.

question: In 2002 a Harvard economist and a Wharton economist quantified how much land-use restrictions cost city dwellers by comparing the construction cost of an apartment to its market price. Which pair of economists published that paper?
context: Glaeser (Harvard) and Gyourko (Wharton) published 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' as NBER working paper 8835 in 2002 and in the FRBNY Economic Policy Review in 2003. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: Glaeser and Gyourko called the price gap between the construction cost of an apartment and its market price the 'zoning tax'. Roughly how large was the zoning tax per Manhattan apartment in the early 2000s?
context: Their 2002 paper found a zoning tax of roughly $500,000 per apartment in Manhattan; by the 2010s the Manhattan figure was well over a million. Loose-zoning cities such as Houston and Atlanta showed essentially zero zoning tax. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: When a homeowner argues zoning protects neighborhood character, Bastiat's method asks what the zoning cost that no one immediately sees. Which unseen does his method surface?
answer: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
choices: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
The construction jobs on the buildings that were built
The listed prices of the homes that already exist
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): existing homes and their prices are visible; the never-built housing, the families priced out of the metro area, and the 2-hour commuters are the invisible casualties. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The victims of restrictive zoning are typically people who WOULD live in the city if housing were built. Which political-economy pattern best explains why local zoning codes stay tight for decades?
answer: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
choices: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
Cities lack the legal authority to change zoning codes at all
Construction companies uniformly oppose new residential building
Federal law preempts almost all local land-use decisions
context: Concentrated benefit + dispersed cost with a franchise twist: existing owners benefit from constrained supply and vote for it; the priced-out do not live in the city yet, so their preferences carry no votes. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: In December 2018 one large US city became the first in the country to abolish single-family-only zoning across every neighborhood, effective January 2020. Which city took that step?
context: The Minneapolis City Council adopted the Minneapolis 2040 plan in December 2018, ending citywide single-family-only zoning. Every residential lot became eligible for up to a triplex. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Minneapolis_2040.

question: In 2021 the California legislature signed a state law that allowed the by-right splitting of single-family lots into up to four units in most residential zones, overriding local single-family-only rules statewide. What was the bill's designation?
context: California SB 9 (signed September 2021, effective January 2022) plus SB 10 gave the YIMBY movement its first big statewide preemption win. Source: grokipedia.com/page/California_Senate_Bill_9.
